sources.title: How to diagnose and fix stalled growth: Jason Cohen's five-question checklist
sources.originalTitle: The surprising advice from a founder who built 2 unicorns | Jason Cohen (WP Engine)
sources.summary: Jason Cohen walks through an ordered diagnostic for stalled SaaS growth: logo churn, pricing and positioning, net revenue retention, channel saturation, and whether you need to grow at all. Includes the churn-cap formula, the Double Down 8x pricing story, and why A/B testing mostly yields false positives.

principles.text: Churn caps your size: max customers = new customers per month divided by monthly cancellation rate.
principles.quote: it's simply the amount of new customers you add divided by that cancellation rate. That is the amount that that is the limit.

principles.text: Cancellations grow automatically with your base while marketing output stays flat, so churn always overtakes acquisition.
principles.quote: cancellations grow faster than marketing and so cancellations overpower the growth of the company and slow it to a halt

principles.text: Ask 'what made you cancel?' not 'why', and never accept 'too expensive' as the real reason.
principles.quote: The wrong way is to ask why did you cancel?

principles.text: Early-stage prices are usually too low; raising them often leaves signups flat because pricing selects the market.
principles.quote: What often happens is you raise prices and signups don't change.

principles.text: Position around what the buyer values (growth) rather than savings to unlock a far higher price ceiling.
principles.quote: sell more of what the company values like growth.

principles.text: Channels saturate and then sag, so don't just push marketing harder or add a feature.
principles.quote: Do you know right now which channels are saturated and which aren't?

sources.title: Jason Cohen at MicroConf 2015: validating ideas, pricing up, product-market fit and staying fulfilled
sources.originalTitle: Question + Answer: Jason Cohen, Founder of Smart Bear and WPEngine – MicroConf 2015
sources.summary: Jason Cohen answers bootstrapper questions on validating ideas by trying to invalidate them, getting paid upfront, raising prices aggressively, recognizing product-market fit, and why reseller distribution faded. He also live-coaches three founders on cash runway, finding new channels and marketplaces, and talks about motivation and stress.

principles.text: Validate by trying to invalidate: if feedback diverges after 'that's perfect,' the idea is weak.
principles.quote: the next person says that's perfect you know what you should do is take that and make it just for ad Tech and do that and someone else would say that's great you don't you should do is make that a freemium model

principles.text: Talk price in validation and take real payment up front; interest without a price is not validation.
principles.quote: it's important to talk about price because price does determine the product

principles.text: Raise prices far more than feels safe; test and keep doubling until signups drop.
principles.quote: what you gonna do next is double it again and feel that stops happening right

principles.text: Price to how customers buy: keep totals under the approval threshold so buyers need no permission.
principles.quote: if I spend less than five hundred dollars on my credit card I don't have to ask permission

principles.text: When small, raise existing customers' prices with an honest, personal note inviting them along on the journey.
principles.quote: honesty wins most of the time with most things of life including business

principles.text: Product-market fit shows up as sudden growth you can't fully explain, after a random walk of trying things.
principles.quote: you start growing faster all of a sudden and you look around say why and there's not really a great reason

sources.title: Jason Cohen on WP Engine: customer interviews, pricing, key metrics, and stepping down as CEO
sources.originalTitle: Building a Billion-Dollar SaaS Business with Jason Cohen 📈📈
sources.summary: Jason Cohen explains how WP Engine started from 50 customer interviews and hit product-market fit via pricing changes and a 60-day money-back guarantee. He covers picking a leading "moment of value" metric over laggy MRR, when to raise VC, and his joy/skill/need framework for handing the CEO role to Heather.

principles.text: Validate a business with dozens of customer interviews about a real pain before building; the core promise can stay valid for over a decade.
principles.quote: I did 50 5-0 customer interviews

principles.text: Interviews must be directed; asking "do you like this feature" teaches you nothing because people just say yes.
principles.quote: if you're just asking like do you like this feature they're gonna say yeah sure that's you know that seems pretty good and you haven't learned a damn thing

principles.text: Pricing hinges on customers' mental price steps, not just willingness to pay. A tier jump they can't stomach in one shot blocks sales.
principles.quote: it probably is worth 50 but they can't do that in one shot like mentally that's not how they think about it

principles.text: When a free trial converts at 90%, you're losing revenue; charge up front with a longer money-back guarantee, which can raise sales.
principles.quote: we had a 90 percent 90 success rate after the two weeks so I was looking at going like well number one that's product Market fit when your trial is a 90 conversion rate

principles.text: Pick a leading metric at the moment customers get value; MRR is too laggy and multi-input to operate on (e.g. Netflix's 3+ DVDs queued).
principles.quote: if you imagine the customer moving through their Journey from like oh I found out about you in the website

principles.text: Use the joy, skill, need framework to decide your role; any two without the third is a trap (burnout, mediocrity, or building the wrong thing).
principles.quote: the joy skill trap is you love it and you're good at it so you do it and it feels good

sources.title: Jason Cohen on strategy, bootstrapping and customer development: lessons from WP Engine and Smart Bear
sources.originalTitle: He Scaled Two $1B+ Companies (WP Engine & A Smart Bear) | Jason Cohen
sources.summary: Jason Cohen explains why you shouldn't set out to bootstrap a billion-dollar company, and how to design a bootstrapped business with recurring value and annual prepay. He also covers strategy as a self-reinforcing set of decisions, running hypothesis-driven customer interviews, and managing executives.

principles.text: Strategy is how you win: a set of decisions that fit together, so copying one piece doesn't copy the system.
principles.quote: strategy is overall how you're going to win.

principles.text: Conflicting advice (niche vs broad) isn't right or wrong. Ask when it applies, then make surrounding decisions that fit.
principles.quote: A better question is when is this advice applicable?

principles.text: Annual prepay lets a bootstrapper fund acquisition with customer cash, removing the marketing budget cap while the channel is profitable.
principles.quote: you went from a marketing budget that was limited to $100 a month or less to unlimited marketing budget

principles.text: Recurring revenue only works if the value is also delivered on a recurring basis, not just billed monthly.
principles.quote: I think one thing people do wrong a lot is they don't deliver value in a recurring pattern as well.

principles.text: Run customer interviews as experiments with hypotheses and open questions. Stop when you stop being surprised.
principles.quote: you do enough of these to where you're not learning anything anymore. You can tell because you're just never surprised.

principles.text: Find the trigger event that makes customers switch, or your marketing is just shouting ads at people.
principles.quote: Whatever that is, you've got to find out what that is. Cuz otherwise, you're just yelling ads at people

sources.title: Designing a self-funded "cash machine": 150 customers, high prices, annual prepay
sources.originalTitle: Designing the Ideal Bootstrapped Business with Jason Cohen
sources.summary: Jason Cohen lays out his model for a bootstrapped business: aim for predictable recurring revenue of $10k/month per founder from about 150 customers at roughly $70 each. He covers raising prices, annual prepay for cash flow, B2B markets with naturally recurring pain, and paid acquisition over social media.

principles.text: Design for a cash machine: predictable recurring revenue of $10k/month per founder, built on about 150 customers at ~$70/month rather than 1,000 fans.
principles.quote: something that predictably and repeatedly always gives you $10,000 a month per founder in revenue and hopefully more like 20 30 40

principles.text: Raise prices far more aggressively than feels comfortable. Doubling price often leaves signups unchanged, and low prices force you to find thousands of customers.
principles.quote: they doubled it to 49 or whatever it was and signups didn't change at all

principles.text: Push annual prepay so each customer's cash arrives upfront. This lets you out-spend acquisition cost and run marketing with no money constraint.
principles.quote: we literally operate with an infinite marketing budget the marketing budget at W engine is not limited by money because we'll make it back

principles.text: Replace free trials with a long money-back guarantee. You collect cash up front, customers get more time, and signups and customer counts went up.
principles.quote: we switched to a 60-day money-back guarantee instead of a 15-day free trial

principles.text: Sell B2B, not to consumers, because consumers won't pay meaningful monthly prices. Favor markets where the pain or cost is naturally recurring, not temporary.
principles.quote: I want to make a very strong argument that you should absolutely never not not not sell to consumers people don't spend money on stuff

principles.text: Prefer paid acquisition you can model over social media. Use a rule of thumb for what you can pay per click: average revenue per customer divided by 25.
principles.quote: you take how much average revenue you get per customer divided by 25 and that's what you can pay per click

sources.title: Jason Cohen: Why founders burn out, and how to build a company that doesn't need you
sources.originalTitle: From Burn-Out to $100M in ARR with Jason Cohen, Founder of WP Engine
sources.summary: Jason Cohen uses an anonymous burned-out founder's post to argue that founders must make emotionally difficult choices early. Fire fast, hire people better than you and manage them by results, and place yourself where what you like, what you're good at and what the company needs overlap. He draws on selling SmartBear and handing the CEO role at WP Engine to Heather Bruner.

principles.text: If you can't stop thinking about a decision at 2am, you're avoiding the hard choice. Take action.
principles.quote: when you wake up at 2:00 in the morning you're like oh no ha like that that simple thing not a deep analysis just that simple thing if I can't stop thinking about how this person's here and they shouldn't be that indicates you do need to take action

principles.text: Make hard calls like firing quickly, because delay hurts everyone. Be decisive, then kind.
principles.quote: General Patton on the decision mother Teresa on the exit be decisive and then be kind that's the right way to do it

principles.text: You can't become an expert in an entire career's worth of work in a few months. Hire A players for functions you don't know.
principles.quote: the idea that you can become an expert in something important something that's an entire career for someone else in a few months and then hiring a player that's of course not true so you're actually a C player at best

principles.text: Hire results-oriented people and manage them on outcomes, since you can't tell them how to do a job you don't know.
principles.quote: you have to manage the results of it and hold them to that bar so by hiring for people who are already think that way already like to be measured by the results that they make instead of what they do then that's how you're gonna manage them

principles.text: Aim for a strong, resilient organization in which people are better than you and the company doesn't depend on the founder.
principles.quote: if you can agree that the best thing is to have everyone in the organization be better than you then you can create a resilient organization

principles.text: Choose your role at the overlap of what you like, what you're good at and what the company needs. Don't do needed work you dislike, find someone who loves it.
principles.quote: what the company needed and what I liked not to mention what I was good at did not mix I like product and engineering so I went and became the CTO

sources.title: How Jason Cohen scaled WP Engine past product-market fit: focus, org design, and hiring execs
sources.originalTitle: We just hit $400m in revenues. 9 org chart moves I had to make to scale (Jason Cohen WPEngine)
sources.summary: Jason Cohen explains how the playbook changes after product-market fit: stop experimenting broadly, concentrate scaled headcount on a few strategic initiatives, set a quarterly one-page plan, and shape the org chart around that focus. He also covers hiring managers and executives better than you, and why he became CTO and hired a CEO.

principles.text: After product-market fit, 'keep experimenting' stops working; scaling a working business needs different behaviors and a different identity.
principles.quote: just saying things like, "We'll keep experimenting." is not how you scale something that's already working.

principles.text: Don't dilute scale across many initiatives; put many people on a few things so you can dominate them.
principles.quote: you want to not dilute your scale across a bunch of projects, but still have just a few things. That way you're using your leverage to win.

principles.text: Each quarter, define the ideal strategy, name what blocks it, then attack or work around the obstacles; keep it to one page.
principles.quote: if you do this every quarter, and it takes no longer than a page to say it, everyone knows at a high level exactly what to do.

principles.text: Reflect the few focus areas in the org chart, either matrixed or by dedicated initiative teams; neither is free.
principles.quote: the bottom line is the org chart somehow needs to reflect this focus so that you don't get bogged down again in crap.

principles.text: Great managers are team builders, not the best individual contributors; interview for that skill.
principles.quote: Their job is to build the team and to work on conflicts and to figure out these priorities and to work with other teams and so on.

principles.text: Hire executives better than you by asking references to describe the scenarios where the person thrives and where they'd be destroyed, then check fit with your company.
principles.quote: What is the perfect scenario where this person is an absolute superstar?

sources.title: Hidden Multipliers: reposition for value, pick frameworks that fit, and what AI can't replace
sources.originalTitle: RS362: Hidden Multipliers with Jason Cohen
sources.summary: Jason Cohen explains how repositioning a product around more of a positive outcome (not less of a negative) can multiply price up to 10x. He covers deciding under uncertainty, why frameworks rarely transplant into a company's culture, and which jobs and products AI will and won't automate.

principles.text: Reposition from saving a cost to creating more of something customers already value; you can often charge 10x.
principles.quote: almost all products like that can be repositioned so that you're selling more value, more transformation, more of something positive that they value rather than less of a negative thing they'd like to go away.

principles.text: Pitch 'double the leads at the same cost per lead' instead of 'half the cost'; same product, far bigger price ceiling.
principles.quote: by p pitching it as double the number of leads at the same price per lead I can 10x or okay 8x in this case whatever the the price of the product same product

principles.text: Under uncertainty, anchor on what will still be true in 10 years and treat AI as part of the solution, not the problem.
principles.quote: AI is part of the solution space like how will I execute this product not problem part of the problem space which is what is it the customer is trying to do.

principles.text: Where a 'best version' exists, the job gets automated; where none exists (design, strategy, entertainment), AI augments but doesn't replace.
principles.quote: Any job where there is such a thing as a best version of that job will get automated. But there are many jobs where there's no such thing as a best.

principles.text: Frameworks rarely transplant; adopt one as 'better but wrong' and review what to change every two weeks.
principles.quote: this is probably better than what we're doing now, but it's also probably just 70% of what it needs to be.

principles.text: Aim for 'special' fit between your strengths and a slice of the market, not a unique selling proposition.
principles.quote: Special side of the market. Special. You're special in some way.

sources.title: Why SaaS growth stalls: cancellation beats paid marketing, and how to raise the ceiling
sources.originalTitle: Why Your SaaS Has a Growth Ceiling (And How to Break It)
sources.summary: Jason Cohen explains why every SaaS hits a growth ceiling: paid acquisition flattens (the "elephant curve") while cancellations scale with customer count. He shows how to compute the ceiling, diagnose churn, raise prices to move into a better market, and build strategy around an ideal customer who loves your weaknesses.

principles.text: Compute your growth ceiling: new MRR per month divided by monthly cancellation rate. That is the max you reach if nothing changes.
principles.quote: It's just the new dollars per month divided by the monthly cancellation rate. That is the max you will grow if you don't change something.

principles.text: Paid channels don't scale with your size but churn does, so cancellation eventually beats paid marketing.
principles.quote: Marketing doesn't care. Like AdWords doesn't care how many customers you have. It still just works the same way. It doesn't scale with you, but cancellation does.

principles.text: 'Too expensive' is rarely the real cancellation reason. Find the root cause (missing feature, wrong expectation) and fix that, not the price.
principles.quote: The thing they wanted is the thing to fix. Not lowering the price.

principles.text: Catch at-risk customers before they leave by finding behaviors that differ between cancellers and stayers, then reach out early.
principles.quote: how what characteristics are different on the people that cancel than the people that stay? These are your early signals.

principles.text: When unsure where to cut churn, start with onboarding: most cancellations happen early, so improving the start has the biggest financial effect.
principles.quote: Almost always onboarding has the most impact with cancellation.

principles.text: Your price is probably too low. Raising it can move you from hobbyists to serious business customers who stick, and sign-ups may even rise.
principles.quote: there's no way your prices are optimal. Full stop.

sources.title: Naked Business: Why radical honesty in marketing and sales makes bootstrappers more money
sources.originalTitle: Naked Business: How Honesty Makes You More Money – Jason Cohen – MicroConf 2012
sources.summary: Jason Cohen argues that proactive honesty (admitting weaknesses, being small, showing negatives) is a competitive differentiator that raises sales, cuts returns and churn, and builds believability. He backs it with Canon review data, his hosting outage cancellation data, Balsamiq's one-person About page, and enterprise sales stories.

principles.text: Showing negatives alongside positives lifts sales and profit, because buyers who know the trade-offs decide sooner.
principles.quote: it is a universal rule that if you say the good and the bad you sell more and you make more profit

principles.text: Honest expectations cut returns, and returns are very expensive relative to thin margins.
principles.quote: returns of the products went down 20% and the returns went down for the same reason because I know the door opens then I don't return it

principles.text: Be proactively honest, not just honest when asked. Admitting flaws earns the credibility to make positive claims believed.
principles.quote: when you admit the problems or admit things that could be a negative you you earn the ability to then say happy things and people believe you

principles.text: During outages, communicate immediately and openly; proactive updates can fully offset the churn silence would cause.
principles.quote: because we proactively talked about every problem as it came out it mitigated a hundred percent of people's negative opinion about what was going on

principles.text: Don't hide being small. A customer who rejects you for it would have been unhappy anyway, and pretending sours the relationship.
principles.quote: they don't want to work with you because you're too small and if you try to pretend like you're not too small Lockheed Martin's going to find out

principles.text: Lean into the advantages only a small company has: take on risk, move faster, be all-in on the customer, and say so plainly.
principles.quote: these are your competitive advantages you don't have many these are what they are so you must bang them on the head and use them

sources.title: Jason Cohen: Bootstrapping SmartBear vs raising $250M for WP Engine, and founder decision-making
sources.originalTitle: $0 to 2 Unicorns: Bootstrap vs $250M VC -  Jason Cohen [WP Engine]
sources.summary: Jason Cohen explains why there is no single blueprint after building SmartBear (bootstrapped) and WP Engine (VC-backed). He covers raising only what ARR justifies, how to think about AI as a founder, why customer outcomes should drive strategy, and how to make big life decisions by widening options.

principles.text: Raise no more than your ARR, at a valuation you can grow into, so the next round stays possible.
principles.quote: I never wanted to raise more money than the amount of ARR we had. Get that way we're not We're have enough money to do something that's appropriate to our size, but not so much that you know, sometimes you drown in that.

principles.text: Most businesses aren't venture-sized, and that is fine; VC funds very few successful companies.
principles.quote: Most things aren't, and that's not saying anything bad. Most of my companies weren't, and that's not saying anything bad about them. Just most products aren't going to make billions in revenue or be worth tens billions.

principles.text: AI predictions without a timeline are useless; instead build around customers' unchanged problems solved in new ways.
principles.quote: the customer have the same problems they always had

principles.text: Aim your vision at the customer's ultimate success metric (revenue, clean audit), even if you can't measure it directly; ask customers whether you are delivering it.
principles.quote: the best way for any company to think about it is how do you make your customers successful in the way that they measure it? Best is revenue.

principles.text: Expand new bets from adjacent strengths: existing distribution and data make new products a better bet. In AI, distribution is easier than building something that works.
principles.quote: it still needs to be adjacent, which means leveraging some of the things I just said, where it's like, "Well, if we built this at our current customers would want it." So the distribution channel would be in.

principles.text: Pick strategies that use your strengths, with weaknesses either irrelevant or seen as strengths by your target market.
principles.quote: understand your strengths, your weaknesses, the capabilities and assets that you have and then ask, "Can I do a project or startup where the the startup strategy is that it will succeed if the things that you're strong in are used?

sources.title: Jason Cohen on hidden multipliers, niching down, and building an AI company in 2026
sources.originalTitle: Episode 817 | Bootstrapping in the Age of AI with Jason Cohen
sources.outlet: Startups for the Rest of Us
sources.summary: Jason Cohen explains why small systematic changes beat big investments, how to de-risk the weakest link first, why niching down sells to more than just your niche, and how WP Engine won a commodity market. He closes with how he would pick an AI product today: solve an existing problem, serve experts, and aim for 3x+ value.

principles.text: Many things must go right; tackle the weakest link first instead of building the product you already know you can build.
principles.quote: the limiting factor here is can you find customers? And if you build the product, you will have made no progress whatsoever on the question, can you go find customers?

principles.text: Niche to a narrow ideal customer; clarity about tradeoffs also wins non-ideal buyers who accept your set of weaknesses.
principles.quote: if I'm very specific about what I am then my ideal customer will definitely buy which is already a reason to do it but like 100 times larger market than that will see that specificity as a reason to buy your set of tradeoffs

principles.text: Culture and incentives of competitors can be a moat: they could copy you but won't, e.g. funded firms avoid expensive human support.
principles.quote: it's not that they couldn't have copied us, it's that they they wouldn't have because it wasn't in their nature, their culture, etc.

principles.text: Great execution wins in fields where most competitors execute poorly, even without a technical moat.
principles.quote: if you have great execution and most don't in your in your field, that's a reason to win.

principles.text: Brand is a real edge only when customers buy you despite losing on other dimensions; it follows execution, and consistency matters more than the specific logo.
principles.quote: how do you tell when brand is really starting to matter either competitively at all or maybe a moat as opposed to just the identity of the thing like a handle of the thing is when customers are making buying decisions because of it.

principles.text: Commodity products escape commodity status by being many multiples better (4x faster, not 30%), which you can feel immediately.
principles.quote: when it's not just quote unquote better or faster, more efficient, cheaper, but five times better, three times cheaper D, right? Where you could measure it, but like you don't even need to to see like, holy crap

sources.title: Jason Cohen on unfair advantages: adjacency matrix, premium value, and founder role fit
sources.originalTitle: RS313: Unfair Advantages with Jason Cohen
sources.summary: Jason Cohen explains how WP Engine justifies premium pricing through perceived value and authentic culture, and how to evaluate new products with a simple three-level adjacency analysis. He also covers the joy/skill/need test for founder roles, why big decisions get harder at scale, and treating AI as a solution to existing customer problems.

principles.text: Premium pricing works when the customer's perceived value is far above the cost, so make that value specific.
principles.quote: the value they perceive they're getting is 10 times more than that cost even though it's premium that's the question to answer

principles.text: Authentic mission and community can't be bolted on later; they start at day zero and come from who the founder is.
principles.quote: you don't bolt on something that requires being authentic and genuine like that

principles.text: Obsess over brand polish after product-market fit; early on, work out who the customer is and what the product should be.
principles.quote: after product Market fit when things start working it starts to become easy to get customers they're flooding in

principles.text: Good strategy leverages your existing assets and strengths; avoid areas where you're weak unless there's an overwhelming reason.
principles.quote: good strategy leverages those things because that's what you're good at

principles.text: Judge a new product by rating each functional area as trivial, adjustment, or overhaul. No scores, just see the risk and cost.
principles.quote: either you can say it's trivial there's almost no changes required

principles.text: Treat AI as a possible solution to problems customers already have, not as the problem to sell.
principles.quote: it's in the solution space and not the problem space

sources.title: Jason Cohen on selling SmartBear, the freedom line, and the Joy/Skill/Need framework
sources.originalTitle: Ep 415 Jason Cohen on Starting Two Unicorns Worth More Than $1 Billion: SmartBear & WP Engine
sources.summary: Jason Cohen reflects on selling SmartBear and co-founding WP Engine. He covers the Rich vs King choice, the freedom line, options short of selling, sharing equity with employees, and a Joy/Skill/Need framework for deciding which role a founder should hold.

principles.text: Don't treat selling as binary; list every option first: partial financing, handing the company to your team, recurring revenue, coaching.
principles.quote: I thought it was binary black or white I sell or I you know I'm miserable

principles.text: Judge a decision by the options considered, not by the outcome, because luck plays a part.
principles.quote: you can't judge the decision based on the outcome um you can't judge whether your poker decision was good based on the outcome because there's luck also

principles.text: Founders often hold their company back; stepping aside and vesting hungry operators in can grow it far more.
principles.quote: the company doubled the next year and it had been growing at like 5% per year

principles.text: Wealth isn't linear: past a freedom line, more money changes little. Gross up taxes and inflation honestly when finding your number.
principles.quote: there's some line Beyond which even adding another zero doesn't really change whether you're happy

principles.text: Expected value is useless for one-shot decisions like selling a company; use a sure-thing versus gamble thought experiment to find your own risk appetite.
principles.quote: the concept of the weighted average or the concept of expected value is useless

principles.text: Use Joy, Skill and Need to check your role. Any two without the third is a trap; the goal is work that is all three.
principles.quote: if you have two of the three it's a trap because you feel good you feel like it's good and it's bad

sources.title: Jason Cohen on the growth ceiling, weaknesses as strategy, and adopting AI with urgency not chaos
sources.originalTitle: SaaSpocalypse 2: Jason Cohen of WP Engine on Why Your Weaknesses Are Your Strategy
sources.summary: Jason Cohen explains the growth-ceiling math (new customers per month divided by churn rate), argues a defensible strategy is a unique set of strengths and weaknesses that reinforce each other (WP Engine), and says to adopt AI with urgency but not chaos. He also covers ICP focus, craft lost to AI coding, and being your own advocate.

principles.text: Your growth ceiling is new customers per month divided by monthly cancellation rate; marketing doesn't scale with your size but churn does.
principles.quote: it's just this new customers per month divided by the cancellation rate.

principles.text: Show founders the hard cap on customers to reframe churn; it sidesteps arguing about whether a given rate is acceptable.
principles.quote: instead of arguing about that, which is so abstract, it's much better to say you're never going to have more than 2,000 customers. You good with that?

principles.text: Strategy is a unique set of strengths and weaknesses where the weaknesses enable the strengths; competitors can copy strengths but not your trade-offs.
principles.quote: the important thing is that those weaknesses are feeding enabling the strengths not just weak right and then you have a special set to me that's a strategy

principles.text: Nothing was ever uncopyable on code; competitors could copy you but it doesn't fit their business model, so they won't.
principles.quote: it's not that nobody could copy it. They could, but it doesn't make sense for them in their set of trade-offs to do so.

principles.text: Adopt AI with urgency but not chaos: learn the mindset (skills, agents) rather than chasing one tool, or you fall behind.
principles.quote: you should be getting into AI not because this is how it's going to be from now on. It's not but because if you don't start now then when and how far behind will you be?

principles.text: Build everything for one specific ideal customer; a wider swath will still buy, but the bullseye gives focus and clear decisions.
principles.quote: Nevertheless, that's your north star. That's your vision. That's your strategy. That's what you're working for. It's focus.

sources.title: Jason Cohen on bootstrapping vs. raising money, competitor incentives, and hiring people better than you
sources.originalTitle: Jason Cohen — Two Exits & Two Unicorns
sources.summary: Jason Cohen explains why he raised money for WP Engine after two years of bootstrapping, and why dogma on funding is unhelpful. He covers studying competitors' incentives to build a distinct strategy, hiring people better than you, and making consistent decisions, including how building in public forces a stronger strategy.

principles.text: Raise money when market size makes it a logical option, not out of ideology; WP Engine's market proved bigger than expected.
principles.quote: about two years in it became clear that the market was way bigger than I thought it really was an opportunity size that you could raise money for

principles.text: Treat every new company with beginner's mind; past experience only makes a few things easier.
principles.quote: you really have to have beginners mind with each company

principles.text: Study competitors' different constraints and goals; that gap is where a distinct strategy comes from.
principles.quote: they have a different set of things they're solving for different set of constraints different different goals than you that's that's the Genesis of a good strategy

principles.text: Calling competitors dumb or evil blinds you to their real strengths and weakens your strategy.
principles.quote: if your attitude is there dumb or bad then then you are not thinking about where they're strong and good and that's what you need to do

principles.text: A founder's job is to hire people better than themselves in each function, or the company never exceeds your own skill.
principles.quote: you're hiring people that specifically are better than you at that function so that that function becomes better than it currently is

principles.text: Make strategic choices that are consistent with each other (e.g., solo means no 24/7 support burden), or you will burn out.
principles.quote: any decision you make is to me is like that's fine but inconsistent decisions they're not fine you need to pick

sources.title: Jason Cohen on bootstrapping's hard truths: judging advice, filtering tradeoffs, and finding your role
sources.originalTitle: Jason Cohen: "The hard truth about bootstrapping startups." (Part 2)
sources.summary: Jason Cohen talks with Justin Jackson about why most startup advice is survivorship-biased and tied to the giver's goals. He covers how to decide among incomparable options with filters, the real time cost of bootstrapping, why "struggle porn" is a symptom, and a like/good-at/company-needs framework for deciding your role.

principles.text: Most advice is the giver advising themselves. Weigh whether their goals and context match yours before acting on it.
principles.quote: when people give advice what they really are doing is giving themselves advice

principles.text: Beware survivor bias: a practice shared by winners proves little unless failures didn't do the same thing.
principles.quote: the problem is that five years later forty percent of those companies were bankrupt

principles.text: When equally plausible strategies conflict, pick the one that excites you; your extra energy and time tips the odds.
principles.quote: why not pick the one that you're personally really jazzed about because whatever you're jazzed about you're going automatically to put in that extra energy in that time

principles.text: Trade-offs across incomparable dimensions can't be stack-ranked. Set hard limits as filters, then optimize one or two dimensions.
principles.quote: you can decide there are certain limits or certain thresholds I will not cross

principles.text: Bootstrapping takes far more than a few hours a week. Admit the real time cost; struggle means the business isn't working yet.
principles.quote: you take something like 40 hours a week of work for something like two years to get the damn thing off the ground

principles.text: Choose your role by what you like, what you're good at, and what the company needs. Founders miss the 'company needs' leg because nobody tells them.
principles.quote: what do I like what am I good at what does the company need yeah those are the three things

sources.title: Jason Cohen on expanding a plateaued $1M ARR SaaS into a new market segment
sources.originalTitle: E02 w/ Rob Walling: $1M ARR, how to expand into a new market
sources.summary: Jason Cohen and Rob Walling coach the founder of Drop In Blog, a bootstrapped $1M ARR product that has plateaued, on moving upmarket. Jason covers delight versus table stakes, positioning around the buyer's personal stake, using ads to learn messaging, focusing on agencies and BigCommerce, and organizing the team around a new initiative.

principles.text: Utility and table stakes are not delight. Aim for something that makes buyers excited and talk about you to peers.
principles.quote: I'm hearing useful stuff, and that's great, but like, where's the part where they're excited?

principles.text: Position on the buyer's personal stake, like keeping their job, not only on features or utility.
principles.quote: If I'm a marketer at a big company and I want my job to not go away because big companies are in fact letting people go, aren't they? Like, you just save my job

principles.text: Don't let enterprise requirements erode the simple UX that made customers love you; add only the checkboxes you must.
principles.quote: If this is a strength of yours that it's simple and approachable and easy, you wouldn't want like, enterprise has lots of needs and demands of various sorts.

principles.text: Ads can be a temporary learning tool to find positioning fast, with a known budget, not only an ROI channel.
principles.quote: You can also think of ads instead of ROI to sale, you can think of it as, I'm gonna use this as a temporary tool.

principles.text: Focus on channels that compound, like agencies that bring multiple clients over time, plus the niche where you already win (BigCommerce).
principles.quote: Agencies is how you get multiple clients per year and therefore internal growth. And big commerce is is is your best single way of getting the big growth.

principles.text: Give each new strategic initiative a dedicated owner and separate revenue tracking, or the existing business will always trump it.
principles.quote: When you do a big initiative, someone has to be the owner and they're getting up and going to sleep thinking about only that.

sources.title: Intentional Weakness: How Craigslist and Southwest built uncopyable strategies
sources.originalTitle: Intentional Weakness: Create an uncopyable strategy like these companies
sources.summary: Jason Cohen argues that durable strategies come from interlocking decisions that include deliberate weaknesses, which create unique strengths competitors won't copy because nobody copies weaknesses. He uses Craigslist and Southwest Airlines as examples, then shows how to focus on the ICP and ignore out-of-scope customers.

principles.text: Pick weaknesses on purpose; they enable special strengths that would otherwise be impossible.
principles.quote: This is that weaknesses enable special strengths that otherwise wouldn't be possible, and this is what gives them a unique and very durable strategy.

principles.text: Competitors copy strengths, never weaknesses, so a strategy built on weaknesses is uncopyable.
principles.quote: You're not going to copy weaknesses only strengths. But as I've said multiple times now, the weaknesses created unique strengths. So if you're not willing to copy that too, you are not going to win on those strengths.

principles.text: A good strategy is a network of reinforcing decisions, which creates coherence inside the company.
principles.quote: his point is that a good strategy is a network of decisions that reinforce each other

principles.text: Craigslist's minimal, stagnant site is a strength: anyone can use it, it's fast, selection is big and cost is tiny.
principles.quote: So what we see here is that these weaknesses enable special strengths that other sites don't have.

principles.text: Focus everything (marketing, sales, site, product) on the ICP, who sees no weaknesses in you.
principles.quote: you have to focus on them. And by focus I mean everything, marketing, sales, the website, product development features, everything for the ideal customer and not for the whole addressable market.

principles.text: Make strengths and trade-offs clear and the addressable market will sign up too; ignore out-of-scope feature requests.
principles.quote: You have to know who is my out of scope customer who's addressable. So that you don't listen to the out of scope feature requests and bug reports and confusions, they will drag you to a place that's not your strategy.

sources.title: "You didn't do it right": Why frameworks like OKRs fail and how to try them on like clothes
sources.originalTitle: "You didn't do it right"
sources.summary: Jason Cohen describes four sincere failed OKR attempts at WP Engine and names the "Precision Fallacy": the unfalsifiable claim that any framework failure is the implementer's fault. His fix is to treat frameworks like off-the-rack shirts, tailoring them through small experiments, and he shares how a self-chosen, controllable metrics framework worked instead.

principles.text: "You didn't do it right" is an unfalsifiable excuse (the Precision Fallacy); every framework works only inside some context.
principles.quote: There is context inside which the framework works, and outside which it doesn't work. And I believe that not-working is the most common case.

principles.text: Treat a framework like an off-the-rack shirt: expect it to fit wrong in a few places, then tailor it from what you liked and didn't.
principles.quote: The rest of the time the shirt fits OK, but it's wrong in three places. That's the normal case, and why wouldn't it be? So the answer is to tailor it

principles.text: Roll out a new process as a one-team experiment, not a company-wide announcement that creates instant detractors.
principles.quote: If you stand in front of the whole company and announce: "We're switching to OKRs," you create instant detractors, and the rollout will probably just fail.

principles.text: A framework must match your culture, people and other processes; even its creators rarely know when it will succeed.
principles.quote: Frameworks, like people and products, must match the culture, the people, the other processes, and the collective desires of the organization.

principles.text: Team metrics only stick if the team believes in them; don't hold people accountable for outcomes they influence but don't control.
principles.quote: Whenever management requires a KPI that the team doesn't believe in, doesn't respect, doesn't care about, the team always wins.

principles.text: Start metrics with one the team personally wants, tied to pride in their craft, then grow outward one or two at a time.
principles.quote: The only real requirement was that *you personally wanted* it: not because a manager asked for it, not even because it's "good for the company"

sources.title: Lost confidence: replacing RICE-style confidence scores with decisions that work under uncertainty
sources.originalTitle: Lost confidence
sources.summary: Jason Cohen argues that confidence scores in frameworks like RICE are noise: undefined, untrustworthy, and they bias prioritization toward small safe projects. He proposes uncertainty-proof techniques instead: bet on what is always true, validate with behavior, measure impact, invest in leverage, maximize optionality, and choose between portfolios and asymmetric bets.

principles.text: Confidence scores in prioritization frameworks systematically favor small safe projects over large high-value ones.
principles.quote: we're typically confident in small projects and unconfident in larger projects, as well we should be. But that systematically skews the prioritization away from delivering as much value as possible

principles.text: Even experienced PMs are regularly certain about features that flop, so stated confidence is not reliable evidence.
principles.quote: Can you recall a feature you were *certain* would be well-received, but wasn't?

principles.text: Invest in things that are true under any circumstance, like speed, rather than estimating user interest percentages.
principles.quote: identify the features where essentially all customers will either value them, or at least enjoy them.

principles.text: Test demand with behavior, such as dummy-feature buttons, not hypothetical survey answers.
principles.quote: Observed behavior beats stated intentions.

principles.text: Define high impact concretely: used by a majority, or cited as a top-three reason by a passionate minority.
principles.quote: A high-impact feature is either (1) regularly used by at least 51% of customers, or (2) cited by at least 15% of customers in their top three reasons for choosing or retaining your product.

principles.text: Use portfolios for reliable incremental results; use asymmetric bets with time-boxed, bounded downside to hunt outliers.
principles.quote: If the worst case is "we lose two months" and the best case is "we're completely differentiated," the probability barely matters.

sources.title: How to hire people better than you when you can't judge their domain
sources.originalTitle: How to hire people who are better than you
sources.summary: Jason Cohen argues you must hire people better than you at every role, or the company just gets bigger, not better. Since you can't assess domain expertise, he offers proxies: ideas you want to implement, learning from them, leadership breadth, a real problem test, and reference checks aimed at culture fit.

principles.text: Hire people better than you at every role, or the organization just gets larger instead of better.
principles.quote: you _must_ hire people who are better than you at every position--that's the only way the organization grows stronger and smarter and better rather than just growing larger.

principles.text: Leaving the interview wanting to implement their ideas is a meaningful hiring signal, even without domain knowledge.
principles.quote: If they change how you think about your own company in an hour, imagine what they could do in a year.

principles.text: Real expertise is specific to your context; generic frameworks not tied to your problems signal parroting.
principles.quote: Genuine expertise produces specific, actionable ideas that feel tailor-made to your context.

principles.text: Test whether you and others would learn from them, and whether the department would be measurably better after a six-month sabbatical.
principles.quote: if you took a six-month sabbatical and never checked in, when you returned would the department be *measurably better* under their leadership?

principles.text: Give candidates a real company problem and judge how they think and their direct experience, not the answer's details.
principles.quote: You're not evaluating the details of the answer--you don't know how--you're watching how they think, and what direct experience they have.

principles.text: Use reference checks to find the ideal and worst-case scenarios for the person; hire for superpowers your company needs now, not absence of weakness.
principles.quote: you're not looking for someone without weaknesses. Rather, you need someone who has a few special strengths _that your company needs right now_.

sources.title: Strategic choices: Pick between two good options and accept the painful consequences
sources.originalTitle: Strategic choices: When both options are good
sources.summary: Real strategy is a small set of macro-level choices between two genuinely good options, with all consequences accepted. Platitudes like "great design" are non-decisions. Good choices have real alternatives, explicit downsides, and reinforce each other so decentralized teams compound instead of dilute.

principles.text: Autonomous teams still need alignment on a few macro-level strategic choices, not tactics or platitudes.
principles.quote: Not alignment on tactics (those change weekly), nor on platitudes (those change nothing), but alignment on a small set of macro-level decisions. These are the **strategic choices**.

principles.text: A strategy that never says no is not a strategy; saying no even to universally desirable things is the hallmark.
principles.quote: A strategy that never says "no" is not a strategy. It should say "no" most of the time; that's a signal that you are actually [focusing]

principles.text: A real choice has a smart opposite: many successful companies have chosen each side. If the opposite is nonsense, it's a platitude.
principles.quote: "Good design" isn't a real choice because "bad design" was never a smart alternative.

principles.text: Every strategic choice is a package deal. Write the unfortunate consequences into the strategy so the whole company can apply it.
principles.quote: A strategic choice is a package deal: you don't get advantages without weaknesses.

principles.text: Aim for mutually reinforcing choices, not merely consistent ones. Check second-order effects for hidden conflicts, then interlock them.
principles.quote: Even better than "not conflicting" is "reinforcing." "Extensible" helps the product be "feature-rich." A small team forces the core to stay small, maintaining space for the ecosystem to thrive.

principles.text: When the choice conflicts, follow it; when it doesn't, take the best of both. Never settle for a balance that satisfies no one.
principles.quote: When in conflict, adhere to the strategic choice. When not in conflict, do whatever is best.

sources.title: Creating space: why focus means stopping most things so the important ones can win
sources.originalTitle: Creating space
sources.summary: Jason Cohen argues that "focus" only works if you actually stop doing most things. Each thing you drop (bad-fit customers, generic marketing, minor metrics, parallel opportunities) frees time and energy to execute the few things that decide whether a company thrives or perishes.

principles.text: Only by stopping most things do you get the time and energy to execute the important ones deeply; those decide thriving versus perishing.
principles.quote: Only when we stop doing most things, do we have the time and energy to fully, deeply execute the most important things. And the important things are the difference between thriving and perishing.

principles.text: Stop selling to poor-fit prospects: you gain 3x the pitches, each closing at 3x the rate.
principles.quote: When you stop trying to sell people who aren't a good fit, you create space for 3x more sales pitches, each with 3x the close-rate.

principles.text: Help draining customers leave so you can spend time on easy, happy ones who spend more every year.
principles.quote: When you help draining customers exit the business, you create space to spend time with easy, happy ones, who want to spend more every year while giving you positive energy.

principles.text: Skip the 1% improvements everywhere and put effort into the one biggest thing for a 30% gain.
principles.quote: When you stop trying to improve everything by 1%, you create space to improve the biggest thing by 30%.

principles.text: Stop pleasing ill-fitting customers so satisfied ones become fanatics who drive word of mouth, reviews and retention.
principles.quote: When you stop trying to please every ill-fitting customer, you create space to convert "satisfied" customers into "fanatics" who increase word-of-mouth growth, leave positive reviews, and never cancel even if something bad happens.

principles.text: Don't be novel in everything (UX, code, pricing, org); choose a few truly impactful ways to differentiate.
principles.quote: When you stop trying to do everything in a novel way (UX, coding, pricing, org structure), you create space for a few truly impactful modes of differentiation.

sources.title: Purpose, N-Year Vision, Next Milestone: a practical replacement for mission and vision statements
sources.originalTitle: Mission, Vision, poTAYto, poTAHto
sources.summary: Jason Cohen argues "mission" and "vision" are fuzzy terms and replaces them with three concrete tools: a Purpose bigger than the company, an N-year Vision (what you build, for whom, the insight), and a measurable Next Milestone. He also separates purpose-driven from purpose-derived companies, citing Smart Bear and WP Engine.

principles.text: Define Purpose as a transformation bigger than your company, about others, never fully achieved, and not a goal in your operating plan.
principles.quote: The transformation in the world that is bigger than ourselves, that we hope everyone involved is excited to help bring about.

principles.text: Welcome others who adopt your Purpose: they are allies, not competitors.
principles.quote: If others adopt the same purpose, we are happy. That isn't competition, that's an ally.

principles.text: Write the N-year Vision as what you built, for whom, and the special insight. Set N by company age divided by three, rounded up.
principles.quote: Rule of thumb: Divide the age of the company by 3, and round up.

principles.text: Keep the Vision to one or two sentences and bold but plausible; detail belongs in the strategy document.
principles.quote: The Vision should be clear, concise, declarative, and describe a specific future. Be bold, but plausible.

principles.text: Pick the Next Milestone by working backwards from the Vision, and make it specific with an objectively observable finish line.
principles.quote: The most important thing to achieve next, and how we'll know when we've arrived.

principles.text: You don't need to start purpose-driven. You can be purpose-derived: find the positive difference you make, state it, and build it into strategy and positioning.
principles.quote: What does create a Purpose, is figuring out the positive difference you can make in the world, then writing that succinctly, then incorporating it into your strategy and positioning and goals

sources.title: Your target market isn't demographic: define it by shared needs and use-cases, not size or geography
sources.originalTitle: Your target market isn't demographic
sources.summary: Jason argues that demographics and firmographics (company size, geography, age) usually misdescribe a market. Using WP Engine, where Google and big banks bought "SMB" hosting, he shows the real target is people who share needs and reasons for buying. He gives the testimonial test and a long list of better segmentation dimensions.

principles.text: Define your target market by what customers value and the use-case they have, not demographics or firmographics.
principles.quote: Rather, the target market depends on the use-cases and characteristics of the users.

principles.text: Large companies buying your small-business product is not a signal to go up-market; individual teams buy too, for the same reasons.
principles.quote: The reason is that _individual teams_ at large companies also buy things.

principles.text: WP Engine's target was people who valued enterprise-grade quality, open-source flexibility, and mid-priced hosting, not 'small businesses with WordPress'.
principles.quote: This happened because our target market wasn't "small businesses and individuals with WordPress."

principles.text: Keep asking 'why do they value that?' to find the common threads, then write specific positioning like 'Enterprise-Grade WordPress'.
principles.quote: You can find more pieces of that definition by continuing to ask "why do they value those things?"

principles.text: Testimonial test: profile B is in your market if they'd be swayed by an effusive testimonial from existing customer A.
principles.quote: Would customer [B] be swayed by a genuine, effusive testimonial given by [A]?

principles.text: Derive the target market from your best customers (high retention, upgrades, 10 NPS, advocates) and their shared characteristics.
principles.quote: Your target market is the set of potential customers that your best customers self-identify with, in the sense that they would view each other's testimonials as compelling.

sources.title: Max MRR: Why churn sets your growth ceiling and how to track it
sources.originalTitle: Max MRR: Your growth ceiling
sources.summary: Jason Cohen introduces Max MRR (monthly new MRR divided by monthly cancellation rate), a leading indicator of where revenue will plateau. Using toy models and Buffer's public data, he shows why modest churn caps growth, why accelerating new MRR still yields linear growth, and why NRR at or above 100% is the next lever after retention.

principles.text: Max MRR = new MRR per month divided by monthly cancellation rate. Growth stops when churned dollars equal new dollars.
principles.quote: Eventually cancellation-dollars are just as large as new-dollars, and the company stops growing, reaching a steady-state.

principles.text: Early growth tapers because churn, not the market, slows you. Fixed new MRR plus churn proportional to size means a plateau long before the market is saturated.
principles.quote: As customers accumulate, churn grows, and then it's the churn that's slowing growth, not the market.

principles.text: Track Max MRR as a leading indicator. It jumps as soon as churn or new MRR changes, while actual MRR lags.
principles.quote: "Max MRR" is therefore a leading indicator of long-term growth, because it shoots up quickly when conditions change, whereas "Current MRR" is a lagging indicator.

principles.text: Accelerating new MRR doesn't make revenue accelerate, because cancellations accelerate too. Most companies still grow revenue roughly linearly.
principles.quote: The acceleration from cancellation cancels out the acceleration from New MRR.

principles.text: Cutting churn is the biggest lever on the ceiling. Halve the cancellation rate and Max MRR doubles; 6% monthly churn is precarious.
principles.quote: If you halve the cancellation rate, you double Max MRR.

principles.text: After retention, push NRR to 100% or more. Then revenue grows without new customers, for solopreneurs as much as VC-backed firms.
principles.quote: After high retention, the most powerful growth lever is to have NRR ≥ 100%.

sources.title: Ruthless prioritization: 10x / 0.1x tasks and explaining why the dog pees on the floor
sources.originalTitle: Ruthless prioritization while the dog pees on the floor
sources.summary: Time is zero-sum and you can do maybe 1-10% of what you "need" to, so Jason Cohen proposes a binary 10x / 0.1x framework: hunt for the few transformative tasks, and delegate, batch, automate or archive the rest. Then keep explaining the "not doing" list so the team doesn't lose faith while some fires burn on purpose.

principles.text: Time lets you do only 1-10% of what you need to, so prioritization is mandatory.
principles.quote: So, time is a fixed constraint that limits us to 1%-10% of what we "need" to execute. Unintuitively, the fraction diminishes with scale; we will never defeat it.

principles.text: If you can't name your one or two 10x tasks, finding them is your top priority.
principles.quote: If you don't know what one or two 10x tasks you should be working on, then *identifying that is your highest priority*.

principles.text: A true 10x bet must survive running 2x longer and delivering half the impact.
principles.quote: Their upside must be so massive, that even when it inevitably takes 2x longer to implement and is $\frac{1}{2}$ as impactful as you thought, it was still worth it.

principles.text: Minimize 0.1x work: eliminate it by design, delegate even if worse, batch or automate, and archive old tickets.
principles.quote: Archive loose tickets that are older than 100 days. Because of the rule that more than 90% of our ideas will never be done, realize that these are already among that 90%

principles.text: Easy is not the same as low impact; don't conflate effort with impact when sorting tasks.
principles.quote: It's tempting to assume that small, easy tasks are automatically 0.1x tasks, but that is a fallacy of conflating "impact" with "effort".

principles.text: Ruthless prioritization leaves real fires burning; keep telling the full story and the "not doing" list or the team loses trust.
principles.quote: You have to acknowledge the twenty things other that also deserve attention, explaining why we're intentionally letting those fires burn, those dogs pee, because the top priorities are even more important.

sources.title: More or less: pick one of three pricing strategies and commit to its consequences
sources.originalTitle: More or less
sources.summary: Jason Cohen argues there are three viable pricing strategies: more for more, more for less, and less for less. Each carries consequences for product, marketing, hiring and funding that must be accepted together. The only wrong move is not choosing, which leaves a confusing message and a product that's right for no one.

principles.text: Pick one of three pricing strategies and accept its full batch of consequences, or you get a Frankenstein product.
principles.quote: You must pick one approach, and accept its batch of consequences. If you don't incorporate those consequences into the rest of your strategy, you'll have a confusing market message, a Frankenstein product, and the wrong pricing model.

principles.text: Being 'the best' means being best at something specific, and customers must agree it's worth the higher price.
principles.quote: So, the first question is: The best at what? It could be anything, but it has to be specific, and customers have to agree it's worth the higher price tag.

principles.text: Founders wrongly assume 'I built it for myself' means others will pay; use your spark as a starting point, then interview customers.
principles.quote: They think that just because *they* love it, and they "built it for myself" and therefore "I am the customer," and therefore other people will also to pay to solve that problem, in that way. They rarely do.

principles.text: More for less wins most customers, revenue and profit; treat it as its own strategy, not a compromise between best and cheapest.
principles.quote: it is in fact the "More for less" category that wins most of the customers and most of the revenue and most of the profits.

principles.text: Target an ideal customer for whom you're the best; leniency elsewhere means you still win many more customers than you expect.
principles.quote: For your ideal customer, you are in fact "the best," and they cannot believe they're getting the "More for more" product for the "More for less" price.

principles.text: On a more-for-less price, only build features used by at least half of customers or that 15% buy you for.
principles.quote: build only those features used by at least 50% of customers, or where at least 15% of customers buy you specifically for that reason.

sources.title: How a $700 tool sold into hospitals that already owned a million-dollar competitor
sources.originalTitle: When customers buy your competitor's product… and then buy yours
sources.summary: Jason tells how, while selling environmental-monitoring hardware at ITWatchDogs, he found a hospital using a tiny bootstrapped product alongside HP OpenView. The lessons: price so procurement is a non-event, define the market by an individual's need rather than company size, ask customers about adjacent products to learn their life and channels, and land small then expand.

principles.text: When selling to businesses, price for procurement pain, not buyer psychology; stay under the no-approval threshold.
principles.quote: when you're selling to businesses--especially mid-sized to large businesses--it's less about the psychology of the buyer but rather how much of a pain in the ass it is for the buyer.

principles.text: A price under the credit-card limit is effectively free, so customers buy even if you add only a little incremental value.
principles.quote: you understand that $500 is not the same as $499.99; it's the same as $0.

principles.text: Customers will buy a second product for a problem already "solved"; you needn't beat the incumbent head-on.
principles.quote: What's Up Gold would never win against that line-up. But it doesn't matter--they sold their product to the same customer anyway.

principles.text: Define your target market by an individual's need, not "SMB" versus "Enterprise."
principles.quote: A target market defined by the needs of an individual IT person, not "SMB" vs "Enterprise."

principles.text: Ask customers about adjacent products and their daily life; they are more honest and reveal distribution channels you'd never guess.
principles.quote: we learned a lot about the customer even though it wasn't questions about our product.

principles.text: Enterprise sales can start small and affordable, then expand once you're a proven quantity.
principles.quote: It's not always a large top-down deal; it can start small, start accessible, start simple, start affordable, and then expand outward once you're a proven quantity.

sources.title: Product Purgatory: why customers love it but don't buy, and how to find urgency
sources.originalTitle: Product Purgatory: When they love it but still don't buy
sources.summary: Jason Cohen explains why a product can pass the polite-interest test and still not sell. First, apply the Magic Wand Test: would they take it free, fully implemented? Then find the missing ingredient, urgency, by narrowing your target to customers who need it right now.

principles.text: Run the Magic Wand Test: if it were free and fully implemented, would they say yes? Many say no.
principles.quote: So! Do you want me to wave this magic wand? Shockingly, the answer is often: "No."

principles.text: Customers see the friction, risk, time and cost of adopting; value must far exceed that activation energy.
principles.quote: Furthermore, it's not good enough for value to merely exceed penalty; the value must be far larger than the penalty.

principles.text: New companies carry extra risk with no brand or track record, so even free can be refused.
principles.quote: This challenge looms even larger for new companies, because you have neither brand nor track record.

principles.text: If the product passes the wand test but isn't bought, the missing ingredient is urgency: you aren't a top-three priority.
principles.quote: the problem exists, the customer knows it, the customer has budget, the customer has the desire... but there's no urgency, no reason it has to be done now.

principles.text: Escape Purgatory by narrowing your ICP to 'and needs it right now', then aim marketing, sales and features at that segment.
principles.quote: In general, you solve Purgatory by further narrowing your target market with a condition of "...and needs it right now."

principles.text: No product is always a top priority; there are segments where it is and segments where it isn't, so find the former.
principles.quote: There's no such thing as a product that is always valuable or always risky or always a top priority.

sources.title: SSEBITDA: measuring steady-state profitability of a SaaS company that is spending to grow
sources.originalTitle: SSEBITDA⁠--A steady-state profit metric for SaaS companies
sources.summary: Jason Cohen argues EBITDASM (EBITDA plus S&M) is flawed because stopping S&M doesn't freeze revenue and it assumes efficient acquisition. He proposes SSEBITDA = EBITDA + S&M − COC, counting only the S&M needed to replace cancellations. A Profitable Growth Rate falls out of it, letting you justify "spend to grow" precisely.

principles.text: To test whether a growth-spending SaaS is truly profitable, measure profit as if you spent only enough to stay flat.
principles.quote: How profitable would we be, if we were spending only enough to maintain the current state of the company, neither growing nor shrinking?

principles.text: SSEBITDA adds back all S&M but subtracts the Cost of Cancellation, so it works regardless of sales efficiency.
principles.quote: SSEBITDA = EBITDA + SM − COC

principles.text: Stopping S&M spend doesn't mean flat revenue; cancellations shrink it, and a shrinking company that looks profitable is dying.
principles.quote: Halting Sales & Marketing does not mean revenue remains flat.

principles.text: Divide SSEBITDA by the cost of a dollar of new revenue to get the growth you can self-fund; faster growth means a known, quantifiable loss.
principles.quote: Profitable Growth Rate = SSEBITDA / p

principles.text: Don't strip feature-development costs to get a purer steady state; a product that stops evolving isn't steady because the market keeps moving.
principles.quote: A product that never adds a new feature is _not_ in a "steady-state," because the market is changing around it

principles.text: Watch the metric's direction and its component inputs more than its absolute value; the insights and actions come from the inputs.
principles.quote: The overall number is useful as a sort of combined north-star metric, but all the insights and actions come from backing out of the inputs to the number

sources.title: Never compete on price alone: how low prices work as the outcome of a strategy
sources.originalTitle: Sometimes never compete on price
sources.summary: Jason Cohen explains why "never compete on price" is right for commoditized markets but wrong when low price is the outcome of interlocking trade-offs, as at Costco, Southwest, Vanguard and IKEA. He covers the price-cut math, why weaknesses deter copycats, and seven shared traits that let bootstrappers pull this off.

principles.text: Price cuts hurt more than they look: a 20% cut needs 25% more customers just to hold revenue.
principles.quote: A 20% price cut needs a 25% increase in number-of-customers to maintain the same amount revenue.

principles.text: Even a small price cut can gut profit, since it comes straight out of margin.
principles.quote: even a seemingly-minor 10% price reduction can easily mean a 50% profit reduction

principles.text: Low price works only as one outcome of a comprehensive strategy, not as a last-ditch tactic against competitors.
principles.quote: successful low-price strategies treat price as just one component of a comprehensive strategy to win.

principles.text: Build strategy on deliberate trade-offs. Weaknesses that some customers hate are what stop copycats.
principles.quote: Others want to copy strengths, but won't copy weaknesses. Because the weaknesses were mandatory to produce their strengths, they were never replicated.

principles.text: Bootstrappers underprice from fear and ignorance, attracting the worst customers and leaving no money to reinvest.
principles.quote: Low prices leave room for neither reinvestment nor profit.

principles.text: A sustainable low-price model needs healthy unit economics from early on, not only at scale. Reinvest profits and expand gradually.
principles.quote: Profitable unit economics, with GPM above 70%, with a CAC payback period of less than a year.

sources.title: Judging frameworks: why ugly, asymmetric models beat pretty ones
sources.originalTitle: All pretty models are wrong, but some ugly models are useful
sources.summary: Jason Cohen argues that business models and frameworks, like physics theories, can be useful without being correct, but the useful ones try to capture the messy real world. Symmetric, tidy diagrams and round-number lists are red flags that a framework was built for slides and consulting pitches rather than reality.

principles.text: A model can be useful (predictive) without being correct, so judge models by whether they help you decide, not by how true they sound.
principles.quote: Their model was _wrong_ in describing the universe, but _useful_ in predicting eclipses.

principles.text: Test a framework by asking if it models the messy real world or just looks nice in presentations and consultants' materials.
principles.quote: Does the framework attempt to model the messy real world, or does it seem like a pretty fantasy that looks nice in presentations, HBR articles, and consultants' sales materials?

principles.text: Distrust frameworks about people packaged in symmetric diagrams with identical counts of bullets and subcategories.
principles.quote: I immediately disbelieve any framework about human beings that comes packaged in a nice, symmetric diagram, with identical quantities of bullets and sub-categories

principles.text: A list with exactly ten items is a red flag; a list should contain however many items actually make sense.
principles.quote: Another red flag is any list with exactly 10 items. That's how many fingers we have, not how many things should probably be on that list.

principles.text: Models of organizations must reflect real human incentives, emotions and personalities, not treat people as fungible, predictable worker-units.
principles.quote: is it modeled as if people are fungible worker-units with predictable responses to stimuli, built by a professor who has never managed a team beyond six sycophantic grad students?

principles.text: Good strategy models grapple with interacting, dynamic systems rather than one rubric of 2x2s applied identically to every company.
principles.quote: I trust more in diagrams that are imbalanced, asymmetrical, or even ugly, because perhaps they're primarily interested in modeling the messy truth of the world

sources.title: Why "I scratched my own itch" isn't enough: seven implied claims founders must test
sources.originalTitle: "I scratched my own itch" isn't good enough
sources.summary: Jason Cohen argues that the common "I had the problem myself" origin story hides seven assumptions, several false, which explains why most such startups fail. Treat your own problem as a spark and a starting theory, then interview real customers, validate the market, and build the non-code skills a company needs.

principles.text: "I had the problem myself" implies seven claims; some are true, which blinds you to the false ones.
principles.quote: Because some are true, you can't see why some are false.

principles.text: You are not your customer; you built your own solution out of frustration, so you resemble none of the buyers.
principles.quote: You are absolutely not like your customers.

principles.text: Treat your own experience as a theory to test through customer interviews, not as proof you understand the market.
principles.quote: Treat this initial understanding as a starting point rather than the end-point, and interview customers purposefully to get the full answer.

principles.text: The biggest failure is assuming others share the problem and will pay; many conditions must hold for a market to exist.
principles.quote: There have to be enough people who have the problem, and know they have the problem so that they're out searching for a solution, and have a budget for solving it, and would rather buy from you than a competitor, and will stick around for longer than a couple of months.

principles.text: A real problem does not imply a market; legitimate problems vastly outnumber markets willing to buy solutions.
principles.quote: There are a hundred times more legitimate problems in the world than there are markets to buy solutions to those problems.

principles.text: Executing the company means marketing, hooks, leads and interviews, not writing code. Don't retreat into coding.
principles.quote: But "it" isn't the code. "It" is everything else a company must do to succeed.

sources.title: How to select your first marketing channel: where customers are plus what comes naturally
sources.originalTitle: How to select your first marketing channel
sources.summary: Jason Cohen argues your first marketing channel should sit at the intersection of where your customers already are and what you are naturally good at or genuinely want to master. Go deep on one channel, even a small one, and expand later from strength. If the overlap is empty, change the business or partner with someone for whom that channel is a superpower.

principles.text: Pick your first channel at the intersection of where customers already are and what comes naturally to you.
principles.quote: you should operate at the intersection of where the customers already are, and what comes to you naturally and joyfully.

principles.text: You can't control where customers hang out. Fish where the fish are.
principles.quote: You don't control where your customers already go for industry news or to discover new software. You have to fish where the fish are.

principles.text: Forcing an unnatural channel fails: audiences spot impostors, algorithms bury them, and your disdain leaks into the work.
principles.quote: Doing something unnatural, that you despise, will fail.

principles.text: A small channel where you can be a top creator beats being a tiny fish on a huge one, since algorithms promote the biggest voices.
principles.quote: It is better to be one of the top three creators on this topic on Threads than to be the 200th biggest creator on LinkedIn, even though LinkedIn has many more people.

principles.text: Win one channel first, then expand to adjacent ones from a position of strength, repurposing content and funding help with revenue.
principles.quote: Now you're expanding into a second marketing channel from a position of strength.

principles.text: If no channel fits both constraints, rethink the business or partner with someone who is a wizard at that channel.
principles.quote: Another possibility is you need to partner with someone for whom this particular marketing channel is their superpower.

sources.title: The Startup Drake Equation: why startups fail by default and how to stack the odds
sources.originalTitle: The Startup Drake Equation
sources.summary: Jason Cohen models startup success as a chain of "ands" where any single failing factor is fatal, so failure is the default outcome. He lays out moves to improve the odds: crush a few areas, pick the easiest market for you, build a complementary founding team, design out your weaknesses, play asymmetric games and attack the highest risks first.
