principles.text: Startups fail by default because many things must all go right; one failed factor is fatal, so spend time on the biggest risks.
principles.quote: The failure of just one element is fatal, so we should spend more time identifying and then addressing the biggest areas of risk.

principles.text: Be overwhelming in one or two areas (distribution, expertise, community) so it compensates for weaknesses elsewhere.
principles.quote: You gain both focus and a higher probability of success when you have a singular winning attribute, even when you're terrible at everything else.

principles.text: Pick the market that is easiest for you to serve and profitable, not just the one that would be delighted. Big growing markets are easier.
principles.quote: What would be the *easiest* customer segment for us to target?

principles.text: Choose co-founders who zero out different risks, such as one builder and one growth marketer, rather than two of the same.
principles.quote: Two technical co-founders is far less interesting.

principles.text: Design your strategy to route around your weaknesses instead of trying to fix them; a constraint can become an advantage.
principles.quote: you can make choices that slalom around most of your weaknesses, making them irrelevant, rather than forcing you to do the impossible

principles.text: Play asymmetric games with capped downside and large upside; a few big wins can outweigh many failures.
principles.quote: Pick games where the downside is 1x but the upside potential is 10x or 100x.

sources.title: Stealth mode and other "brilliant" strategies: Jason Cohen's satire of common startup mistakes
sources.originalTitle: "Stealth mode" and other f'ing brilliant strategies
sources.summary: A sarcastic essay where Jason Cohen lists the worst startup habits as if they were winning tactics. Read in reverse, it argues for talking to customers early, shipping imperfect v1s, validating willingness to pay, treating marketing and sales as the hard part, raising money after traction, and focusing on a differentiated niche.

principles.text: Satire, read in reverse: don't hide in stealth. Talk to potential customers and experienced founders and advisors early.
principles.quote: That means you can't talk to potential customers either, because the word might get out!

principles.text: Ship an imperfect v1 and gather feedback instead of waiting years for perfection. Software is never bug-free or complete at launch.
principles.quote: With all those fully-completed products, it's a mystery why "feedback gathering" tools or bug trackers even exist.

principles.text: Always ask if customers will pay. Buying isn't a cold ROI calculation, so a time-savings argument doesn't prove demand.
principles.quote: That's how buying decisions are made--cold, rational, and based on micro-economics 101--so why waste your time and theirs, just to verify the obvious?

principles.text: Getting attention and making sales is the hard part, not the code. Don't hide in the work you're comfortable with.
principles.quote: The easy part of this startup will be getting attention and making sales.

principles.text: Get customers and revenue before raising money. Raising pre-traction means giving up control and dodging real validation.
principles.quote: They won't ask questions about those meddlesome customers or revenue.

principles.text: Differentiate and target a specific segment. Copying competitors' features and pricing, or selling to everyone, is a trap.
principles.quote: And forget about differentiation. Just match their features but 20% better and 20% cheaper.

sources.title: Explore vs Execute: why the post-PMF company needs a different culture, team and mindset
sources.originalTitle: Explore vs Execute
sources.summary: Jason Cohen argues that hitting product/market fit demands a radical shift from "Explore" (figure out what works) to "Execute" (become excellent at what works, at scale). The founder belief that "what got us here will get us there" is the trap. Roles, quality bar, risk, predictability and even which people fit all change, including the founder.

principles.text: After PMF, what got you here won't get you there; the company, and the founder, must change.
principles.quote: What Arrogant Founder doesn't realize is that the needs of the company dramatically change after Product/Market Fit. Everyone and everything at the company will change. Including the founder.

principles.text: Explore means finding what works fast; Execute means getting excellent at it while scaling. Applying the wrong one fails.
principles.quote: Prior to Product/Market Fit, you don't yet know what ought to be repeated, what should be excellent, and you have to discover and jettison whatever is wrong as quickly as possible.

principles.text: Executives must shift from building things themselves to building teams that build them.
principles.quote: Executive roles transition from building things themselves to building teams that build those things.

principles.text: Post-PMF, operations rather than business model is what kills you, so de-risking becomes the priority.
principles.quote: Before, the company was likely to fail because it hadn't figured out a business model that works, but now the thing that will cause failure is operations.

principles.text: At scale, rare problems become daily problems, so quality, requirements and process start to matter.
principles.quote: Before, a bug that affected 1% of customers didn't matter. Now it causes 5 support tickets every day, and mad customers who complain on Twitter.

principles.text: Hiring lag of six months or more forces predictability, playbooks and forecasting of future needs.
principles.quote: The time between deciding to open a position, and having a trained, productive person in that position, is at least six months.

sources.title: How to find customers to interview before you have a product: Jason Cohen's tactics
sources.originalTitle: When you have nothing: How to find potential customers to interview
sources.summary: A practical menu of ways to get customer-development interviews when you have no brand, product or audience. Jason Cohen covers ground rules (talk only to your ICP, frame it as asking for advice, make scheduling trivial) and tactics from referrals and LinkedIn to forums, ads, influencers and events, drawing on how he got interviews for WP Engine.

principles.text: Interview only your ideal customer profile. Friends and family give polite praise, not buying signal.
principles.quote: Family and friends will tell you "that sounds cool" and cannot tell you whether actual potential customers agree, and want to pay.

principles.text: Frame outreach as asking for advice, not surveying, and flatter their expertise.
principles.quote: People hate being surveyed but they love getting asked for their opinion.

principles.text: End every interview by asking for more introductions; one referral per interview creates an endless supply.
principles.quote: at the end of every interview, ask who else you should talk to.

principles.text: Respectful, personalized LinkedIn outreach with an offer to pay produced a very high hit rate for WP Engine's early interviews.
principles.quote: Out of 50 requests, 40 agreed, and 30 eventually became customers.

principles.text: Prioritize people who have taken action (switched, built workarounds) over those who merely complain; action signals real pain.
principles.quote: It's free to complain, but expensive to act, so they must really mean it.

principles.text: Treat investors' input as ideas, not validation, but use them for introductions to real ICPs.
principles.quote: take everything they say as "ideation" and not "validation" nor "insights," because ultimately they don't know any more than you do.

sources.title: Brittle Points: how to make companies robust against single points of failure
sources.originalTitle: Brittle Points: How to make companies robust
sources.summary: Jason Cohen defines "brittle points" as single dependencies (a platform, marketing channel, big customer, key employee, or the founder's whole identity) whose failure kills an otherwise healthy company. He borrows redundancy from server engineering and argues you fix them serially, one at a time, with each fix costing money and sometimes creating new brittle points.

principles.text: Brittle points are single dependencies where one sudden change can kill the company, however well everything else is going.
principles.quote: I call these "brittle points"--places where sudden changes mean the company catastrophically fails, regardless how wonderful everything else is.

principles.text: The core fix is redundancy: two things doing the same job. It costs about double, and it buys robustness.
principles.quote: In short: redundancy--having two things that do the same job. It's twice as expensive, but it buys robustness.

principles.text: Add marketing channels: it creates growth and mitigates risk at once, so it's a double win worth investing in.
principles.quote: "One marketing channel" is brittle, because if anything happens to the channel, that could be the end of an otherwise-healthy company.

principles.text: With one big customer, use its cash to win other customers rather than pouring more development into keeping it.
principles.quote: The typical attitude is, "We now have a large customer, so pour extra money into development to make sure we don't lose it," but the right attitude is to use that money to win other customers.

principles.text: Keep a list of brittle points and periodically pick the single cheapest, highest-leverage one to attack now.
principles.quote: Therefore, the right attitude is to maintain a list of these risks and then periodically ask: Which single one is best to attack right now?

principles.text: Manage risk rather than eliminate it all at once; tackle one or two brittle things at a time.
principles.quote: Then tackle one or two of those things at a time--you have to manage risk, not try to eliminate all of it at once.

sources.title: Why half your "winning" A/B tests are false positives, and how to test with theories instead
sources.originalTitle: p-Hacking your A/B tests
sources.summary: Jason Cohen explains how stopping A/B tests when they look conclusive (p-hacking) and running many tests at 80-90% confidence produces a flood of false positives, which is why stacked "wins" never add up. His fix: rerun tests, don't stop early, chase large effects, and design each test to validate a theory of the customer.

principles.text: A 'successful' A/B test at 90% confidence is wrong about one time in ten, so a string of tests will produce false wins by chance.
principles.quote: All experiments sometimes give false-positives. An experiment that gives the correct result 95% of the time, still gives the wrong answer 5% of the time.

principles.text: Never stop a test just because it looks conclusive; early random fluctuations often mimic significance and then revert.
principles.quote: when N is small, random fluctuations will often cause a result that looks like "90% confidence of a positive result," whereas if you continue the experiment, the data shifts back into the territory of "negative result."

principles.text: Roughly half of declared A/B wins are false, which is why individual improvements rarely compound into the expected total lift.
principles.quote: Why didn't all those improvements add up? Because they were false-positives.

principles.text: Check wins over the long run: even Shopify finds about a third of short-term significant results vanish within a year.
principles.quote: Of the tests which show statistically-significant improvement in the short-term, 35% of the time the effect disappears over the long run.

principles.text: Protect yourself by rerunning the test, not stopping early, and seeking large effects, which means testing drastic changes over incremental ones.
principles.quote: Large effects are unlikely to be caused by randomness; small fluctuations are far more likely to be false-positives.

principles.text: Make every test validate a theory of the customer; throwing variants at the wall teaches you nothing whatever the result.
principles.quote: Not only is this thoughtless and lazy, it also means **you haven't learned anything, regardless of the result of the test.**

sources.title: No single SaaS metric rules: pick the few that matter for your stage right now
sources.originalTitle: No wait, of course THAT is the single most important SaaS metric
sources.summary: Jason Cohen argues the case for retention, growth, profit, sales efficiency, LTV, Rule of 40 and NPS in turn, then shows the real lesson is that no one metric is always the most important. Metrics are tools for your stage and goals, so narrow to a few that the whole company aligns on.

principles.text: Retention matters at every stage because cancellations signal missing Product/Market Fit, whatever the cause.
principles.quote: cancellations](https://blog.asmartbear.com/cancellation-rate-in-saas-business-models.html) indicate [lack of Product/Market Fit](https://longform.asmartbear.com/product-market-fit/), no matter the cause (price, features, severity of need, duration of need).

principles.text: At scale, cancellations grow with total customers while new growth scales only linearly with spend, so churn eventually caps growth.
principles.quote: cancellation scales exponentially with total customers--whereas new-customer growth scales linearly with sales and marketing costs--which means cancellation necessarily and always outgrows inbound activity, thus growth ceases.

principles.text: High acquisition cost means you are pushing the product into the market rather than the market pulling it, which caps size and profit.
principles.quote: if it's expensive to acquire new revenue, it means the product is being stuffed into the market rather than [embraced by it]

principles.text: Component metrics mislead alone; combine them (as LTV does), since improving one often worsens another.
principles.quote: When you optimize one number in LTV, often the others change in contrary directions. For example, you can increase price which increases MRR but also increases cancellations as people can't afford it.

principles.text: A metric is a tool in service of your goals, timeline, size and circumstance, not a master to obey blindly.
principles.quote: The purpose of a metric is to be a tool in service of](https://longform.asmartbear.com/product-metrics/) your goals, timeline, size, circumstance, even philosophy, not a master you that you thoughtlessly obey.

principles.text: Find what is most important right now, lean into what's working, then simplify to a few goals and metrics the whole company aligns on.
principles.quote: Your job is to figure out what's most important *right now*, what's on fire, what's most important for getting the company to its next milestone, lean into what's working well, and then *simplify* and *clarify* the few goals and metrics that your entire company should align on.

sources.title: Fallacies that aren't fallacies: why heuristics like loss aversion and overconfidence are rational for founders
sources.originalTitle: The Serengeti Plain: Fallacies that aren't fallacies
sources.summary: Jason Cohen pushes back on the habit of calling common biases "fallacies," arguing that maximizing expected value is itself the fallacy for one-shot, high-stakes decisions. He walks through ten biases and shows why each can be the right call for founders and startups.

principles.text: Expected value only applies to repeated plays; for a one-shot, catastrophic bet it's the wrong frame.
principles.quote: you are using statistics that apply only if you were to play the game a million of times, and where you're allowed to keep the average result, and yet applying that to one instance of playing the game, which is just wrong.

principles.text: Loss aversion is rational when the loss is catastrophic; people happily take small bets where losses are immaterial.
principles.quote: It is not irrational to be much more protective of losing it than you are greedy about getting more. Especially if the loss is catastrophic

principles.text: Perseverance through long projects can beat 'fail fast'; invoking sunk cost is often just an excuse to bail when it gets hard.
principles.quote: Sometimes we pretend we're so smart in avoiding so-called "sunk cost fallacy," when really we're justifying bailing out when times got tough.

principles.text: Startups lack complete data, so act on what's in front of you instead of falling into analysis paralysis.
principles.quote: Instead of getting mired in analysis paralysis, scared to act on the data we have at hand, we must act with what's in front of us, and under conditions of uncertainty.

principles.text: Founders must be overconfident in the vision yet skeptical about every detail, because failure is the likeliest outcome and early signals look identical.
principles.quote: Being confident in the vision, but skeptical about every detail, is how you find the truth.

principles.text: Be different only where it matters to your target customer; everywhere else follow norms, because surprises are bad.
principles.quote: But in every _other_ way, surprises are bad.

sources.title: Pivot Points: finding the fixed facts of you and your company, then building strategy around them
sources.originalTitle: Pivot Points
sources.summary: Jason Cohen replaces "strengths/weaknesses" and SWOT thinking with "Pivot Points": non-judgmental facts about a person or company that you build around. He gives prompts to find personal ones, a reverse-engineering workshop for a company's, and nine ways to apply them to strategy, positioning and ICP, plus a rule for when changing one is worth it.

principles.text: Treat traits as non-judgmental Pivot Points, not strengths or weaknesses, because their value depends on context.
principles.quote: Pivot Points are strengths in some situations, hindrances in others, and irrelevant in still others.

principles.text: Build strategy around fixed Pivot Points in the short term; only invest to change one when the upside is enormous.
principles.quote: Change Pivot Points only when the upside is so enormous, that even if you achieve only 30% of the transformation you were hoping for, it was still worthwhile.

principles.text: Ask references for the ideal and the worst-case scenario for a person to surface their real Pivot Points past sanitized praise.
principles.quote: What is the ideal scenario, under which this person thrives?

principles.text: Your biggest edge is what comes so naturally you can't see it; ask others to name it.
principles.quote: Definitionally you can't see them yourself, because you don't realize how special they are. Ask others.

principles.text: Find company Pivot Points by observing behavior and results like an outside consultant, not by asking people why they did things.
principles.quote: You're allowed to observe behaviors and results, but not allowed to interrogate people to understand *why* they took those actions.

principles.text: Pick a strategy that matches the founder's Pivot Points and the market, e.g. a competitive founder attacks a stagnant market with a 10x product.
principles.quote: All of these are wonderful strategies, so long as they match the founder's Pivot Points, and the needs of the chosen market.

sources.title: Legacy: Why ideas that outlive your name matter more than fame
sources.originalTitle: Legacy
sources.summary: Jason Cohen argues that the best legacy is the ongoing impact of ideas, not name attribution. Using his own SLC concept being repeated and even plagiarized, he reframes ripples of repetition as the goal, and urges creators to focus on ideas worth repeating over personal attention.

principles.text: Aim for ideas worth repeating, not content that merely drives eyeballs to you.
principles.quote: It means we should worry less about "content" for the sake of "eyeballs" and more about creating ideas that are worth repeating

principles.text: Ideas spread like water waves, independent of their originator; growth comes from repetition and from inspiring remixes.
principles.quote: Waves fizzle out without support, but they grow if whipped up by winds of repetition, and they grow when they inspire other creators, remixing additional ideas into new stones.

principles.text: Treat others repeating or even copying your idea as proof of impact, and meet it with gratitude rather than bitterness.
principles.quote: If the ripples are the legacy, then they can be met instead with gratitude and pride.

principles.text: Make ideas important, true and compelling enough that people want to repeat them even without your name attached.
principles.quote: ideas that are so important and true and compelling and repeatable that people *wish* to repeat them, even if our names aren't attached to the broadcast

principles.text: Focus on positively influencing others and helping them become better versions of themselves rather than on attention to yourself.
principles.quote: We should worry less about the attention we bring to ourselves, and more about how we can positively influence others

principles.text: Attribution and money still matter: artists should be paid, and plagiarism is theft. Ask 'and what else?' beyond fame and money.
principles.quote: Of course attribution is not without value. Artists should be paid for their work.

sources.title: Profitable on day one? Jason Cohen on what "profitable" really means for bootstrapped founders
sources.originalTitle: Profitable on day one!
sources.summary: Jason Cohen argues that bootstrapped founders who claim day-one profitability are ignoring the cost of their own labor. He offers stricter tests (could you pay someone else to do your job, would a new owner be profitable) and reminds founders that almost every great company, including his own, took years to get there.

principles.text: You're not profitable if you couldn't afford to pay someone else to do your job.
principles.quote: If you couldn't afford to pay someone else to do the job that you are doing, you're not profitable yet.

principles.text: The strongest test: would the business stay profitable if sold to an operator who hires people to do all the work?
principles.quote: The company is profitable when it would also be profitable in that scenario.

principles.text: A practical bar: the business replaces what the job you quit paid, since the market already priced your time.
principles.quote: The market has already decided your time and skills are worth at least that; if the startup replaces it, it's fair (in my book) to call it profitable.

principles.text: Claiming 'profitable from day one' on a tiny revenue base costs credibility with experienced people.
principles.quote: when you say "I'm profitable" it's a turnoff, because it's actually bullshit, and anyone with a modicum of experience knows it.

principles.text: Lower your required income through lifestyle and location to reach ramen-profitability sooner; it's easier when young and unattached.
principles.quote: You can dramatically change that income requirement through lifestyle and location; this is why it can be easier to start a company when you're young and unattached and childless

principles.text: Businesses are not profitable on day one; slow starts are normal, even for companies that later make millions in profit.
principles.quote: It's just that businesses aren't profitable on day one. They're profitable later (if ever).

sources.title: Individual efficiency vs administrative efficiency: when to standardize and when to leave people alone
sources.originalTitle: Individual efficiency vs administrative efficiency
sources.summary: Jason Cohen argues that individual autonomy should be the default, since it yields both happiness and efficiency, but local optimization often fails to produce global optimization. He gives concrete rules for when to standardize (outcomes not implementations, minimal scope, explicit individual benefits) and shows how self-organized trading, like a motorcycle courier token system, beats top-down control.

principles.text: Default to individual autonomy; override it with administrative needs only when local optimization clearly hurts the whole.
principles.quote: Individual autonomy should be our paramount goal, and thus our default. But often local optimization does not lead to global optimization, and the latter is what we should all want for our organization.

principles.text: Keep the scope of standardization as narrow as possible: mandate the rules or outcomes, not the tool or method.
principles.quote: But that's over-scoping the solution, because many IDEs are capable of enforcing the same formatting rules.

principles.text: Every policy should spell out how it benefits the people it burdens, not just administrators.
principles.quote: Require policies to have sections that detail how this is beneficial for various parties; if any piece of that section is found wanting, that means our policy isn't good enough yet.

principles.text: Watch for local optimizations that quietly damage the overall system, such as low-quality traffic wrecking downstream conversion.
principles.quote: Sometimes, optimizing of one component of a system harms overall system performance.

principles.text: Accept sub-optimal efficiency in non-bottleneck teams if it raises throughput at the true constraint.
principles.quote: This is definitionally sub-optimal from the point of view of all teams who aren't the bottleneck, but the result is higher throughput for the entire organization, and therefore it is the right choice.

principles.text: Let people self-organize and trade within policy constraints; this creates win-win gains without management involvement.
principles.quote: The bikers self-organized far more efficient routes, all made more money per day than they were previously, and the company could handle more clients without hiring more bikers.

sources.title: Retire dead marketing words: be specific, show, name the cliché, or own it
sources.originalTitle: "Authentic" is dead. And so is "is dead."
sources.summary: Jason Cohen argues that overused marketing phrases like "authentic," "powerful," "secure," and "the leading provider" have lost meaning through repetition and misuse. He offers four fixes for website and sales copy: use specific numbers, show proof instead of claiming, name the cliché out loud to earn credibility, or back a claim so completely that you own it.

principles.text: Repetition kills even powerful words. Once everyone uses a phrase, it stops persuading.
principles.quote: repetition of even powerful, wonderful phrases will kill them.

principles.text: If you have to say it, it's probably not true. Claims like "innovative" or "secure" get disproved by behavior.
principles.quote: if you have to say it, it's probably not true

principles.text: Replace vague adjectives with concrete numbers and facts, like requests processed daily or attacks blocked.
principles.quote: Instead of "powerful" say "processes 6,253,427 requests daily."

principles.text: Show the product in action instead of describing it: speed tests, 60-second demos, changelogs, real unsolicited testimonials.
principles.quote: Instead of saying it's easy, have a video demonstrating your tool solving someone's problem in 60 seconds flat.

principles.text: Open a pitch by mocking typical pitches and saying the quiet part out loud. Candor earns credibility.
principles.quote: Because you're willing to say the quiet bit out loud, to say what others hide, especially when we all know the truth, you earn credibility.

principles.text: You can use a worn-out claim only if you own it completely with proof, and communicate that proof rather than leading with the phrase.
principles.quote: if you *lead* with the dead phrase I'll leave before you get the chance to prove it.

sources.title: How annual pre-pay creates an infinite marketing budget: payback math and cash-flow
sources.originalTitle: How annual pre-pay creates an infinite marketing budget
sources.summary: Jason Cohen shows how to compute the real payback period of a SaaS customer (CAC / (MRR × GPM)) and why fast growth eats cash. Annual prepay plans collect a year of revenue up front, so ad spend on a credit card is repaid before the bill is due, transforming bootstrapped cash-flow. He also ranks levers: raise prices first, cut costs last.

principles.text: Compute the cost to create $1 of MRR (CAC / ARPC); the number is usually eye-opening.
principles.quote: The cost to create one more dollar of `MRR` = `CAC / ARPC`

principles.text: Real payback must be measured on gross-margin dollars, not revenue: p = CAC / (MRR × GPM).
principles.quote: `p` = "payback period" = `CAC / (MRR ✕ GPM)`

principles.text: Faster growth consumes more cash because every dollar spent takes the full payback period to return.
principles.quote: And **the faster you grow the more cash it takes**, because no matter how much you spend, it still takes a year to get it back.

principles.text: Pricing and marketing are uncapped strategic levers; cost-cutting is capped, so don't let engineers default to it.
principles.quote: Remember, you can only cut costs so much, but the potential upside of better marketing or pricing is uncapped.

principles.text: Launch an annual plan at 12x the current monthly price, then raise monthly about 20%; it's a natural excuse to lift prices.
principles.quote: Offer the annual plan at 12 times the _current_ monthly price, then increase the month-to-month price by something like 20%

principles.text: Annual prepay lets you collect the customer's year of cash before the ad bill comes due, removing the cash drag of acquisition.
principles.quote: We received the $80 from the customer _before_ we sent away the $80 for the ad, even after setting aside `GPM` costs.

sources.title: Conflicting choices: when to balance, choose, limit, or invent "both"
sources.originalTitle: "It's a Balance" isn't always the answer
sources.summary: Jason Cohen gives a framework for resolving two conflicting options. Balance only when both extremes are bad, choose when both are rational, choose-to-a-limit when one goal needs a constraint, and invent "both" only with a web of reinforcing decisions that becomes a moat.

principles.text: Seek a balance only when both extremes are bad; it rarely means equal parts.
principles.quote: This is the correct approach when both extremes are bad.

principles.text: When both extremes are rational but contradictory, make a clear choice. A middle path fails to decide.
principles.quote: When the extremes are bad you seek a balance, but when the extremes are both rational choices, it is not a *balance* but rather a _choice_, and choose you must.

principles.text: Pick one customer segment and focus everything on it; don't default to the mid-market as a compromise.
principles.quote: A new startup must [find its Carol--it's ICP--then focus] positioning, marketing, brand, and most of all, product, on that one segment.

principles.text: Claiming 'it's a balance' is often a way to avoid a hard decision.
principles.quote: Often people claim "it's a balance" to justify their refusal to make a decision.

principles.text: Maximize the goal metric while satisficing a constraint, using an objective measure to know when to switch attention.
principles.quote: In this mode, the answer is "Maximize A, while satisficing B." One is the goal, the other is the governor.

principles.text: A 'why not both' strategy needs invention, risk, and a web of other decisions that makes you uncopyable.
principles.quote: Because it requires a network of other self-reinforcing decisions, it creates a unique offering, which remains unique even if competitors copy a subset of your strategy.

sources.title: Three Languages: translating between Customer, Product, and Business to stop cross-purpose conflicts
sources.originalTitle: Disentangling the three languages: Customers, Product, Business
sources.summary: Most internal conflicts between CEOs, product managers, customers, marketing and finance come from people speaking three different "languages": customer desires, product work, and business financials. The fix is to recognize each is valid, then build translations: JTBDs and user stories from Customer to Product, and clear contribution metrics from Product to Business.

principles.text: Apparent conflicts between teams usually come from three languages (Customer, Product, Business), not real disagreement.
principles.quote: The key to resolving these (apparent, not real) conflicts is to recognize that there are three distinct "languages" being spoken simultaneously.

principles.text: Conflict arises when one party applies their language to someone speaking another; you must build systems that translate.
principles.quote: Conflicts happen when one party applies their language to a party that is using a different language. It doesn't translate automatically.

principles.text: Everyone is right within their own corner; recognize that first, then translate.
principles.quote: The first step in resolving these apparent conflicts is to recognize that everyone is doing what they think is best, operating from their own area of excellence. The second step is to translate.

principles.text: Translate customer language into product work using JTBD (context, inciting event, job) and then user stories.
principles.quote: The bridge between customer language and product language, in modern terms, is the JTBD (Job To Be Done), further broken down into the "story."

principles.text: Customers describe pain well but lack context to design solutions; product must integrate their desires with constraints and other customers.
principles.quote: Customers can completely describe their own pain or requests. They often have ideas for features but lack the context and expertise to integrate their desires with the constraints of development

principles.text: Product should articulate its contribution to business goals without owning total business outcomes like marketing, sales, or support effectiveness.
principles.quote: Therefore, it's Product's job to clearly articulate how they are contributing, without having full responsibility for the total impact on the business's goals.

sources.title: Adjacency Matrix: how to decide where to expand after PMF
sources.originalTitle: Adjacency Matrix: How to expand after PMF
sources.summary: Jason Cohen gives a framework for choosing expansion moves after product/market fit. Score each idea by how much marketing, sales, service, product, engineering and business model must change (trivial, adjustment, overhaul). Multiple overhauls make an idea a bad bet unless the upside is enormous. He illustrates it with WP Engine's enterprise options.

principles.text: Expand only when growth is bottlenecked, your market is saturating, you want diversification, or you can afford to lose the bet.
principles.quote: If existing marketing and sales channels are at their limit--when spending more time or money doesn't yield more output, or at least, not cost-efficiently. In that case, an expansion to a new channel, or new geography, or new market segment, accelerates growth.

principles.text: A great strategy that doesn't leverage your existing strengths is a bad strategy for you. Judge expansion ideas by adjacency.
principles.quote: A great strategy--that doesn't align with your strengths--is a bad strategy _for you_.

principles.text: Rate each functional area as Trivial, Adjustment, or Overhaul for a new idea. Forcing three buckets avoids false precision.
principles.quote: Now evaluate the "adjacency" of your proposal by determining **how much each of these activities must change** to support the new initiative.

principles.text: More than one area needing a full overhaul is a deal-breaker for incremental innovation, unless you accept big investment, big risk, and enormous upside.
principles.quote: In particular, when more than one area requires a "full overhaul," that's a deal-breaker if this is supposed to be an incremental, sustaining innovation.

principles.text: Early startups claiming an enterprise growth path at ~$500k ARR are usually wrong. Start with simple use-cases at larger companies instead.
principles.quote: Often startups claim this as their growth path, even when they're at only $500k in ARR. This is definitely the wrong strategy at that moment

principles.text: Expanding into a different segment diversifies positioning and makes growth robust to downturns. At WP Engine, small firms saw it as expensive and large firms as low cost.
principles.quote: When one segment has difficulty, the other grows; the net effect is stability.

sources.title: Why early startup growth looks like failure: HubSpot, Balsamiq, ConvertKit and the chaos before traction
sources.originalTitle: It's a torturous chaos until it isn't
sources.summary: Jason Cohen argues the first years of even hugely successful startups are chaotic, slow and indistinguishable from failure. HubSpot ended 2006 with 3 customers and 2007 with 48. Nothing objective reliably separates the winners from the failures, so struggle and doubt prove neither success nor failure.

principles.text: Runaway successes spent their first years in slow, near-invisible growth that looked like failure.
principles.quote: after ending 2006 with just 3 (three!) customers, they ended the next year with only 48. That's less than one per week. For a year.

principles.text: The early days of winners and losers feel identical: the same struggle, uncertainty and mess.
principles.quote: The same struggle, same uncertainty, same near-impossibility, same mess.

principles.text: You can't reliably tell productive chaos from chaos that leads nowhere, and standard analyses don't explain the difference.
principles.quote: what *doesn't* explain it is a "feature comparison chart." Or a SWOT. Or financial metrics. Or social media. Or whether they raised money.

principles.text: Every startup rule has exceptions, even founder-market fit, so treat frameworks as guides, not guarantees.
principles.quote: there are exceptions to everything. I say in that article that there needs to be founder-fit, but the founders of AirBnB weren't experienced in hotels or hospitality

principles.text: Most attempts fail, so persistence guarantees nothing. Still, feeling lost and exhausted doesn't mean you're failing.
principles.quote: These things mean you haven't yet succeeded, but neither do they prove that you're failing.

sources.title: Avoid blundering: why not blundering is 80% of a winning startup strategy
sources.originalTitle: Avoid blundering: 80% of a winning strategy
sources.summary: Jason uses his own chess game data and Simon Ramo's amateur tennis finding to argue that amateur outcomes are mostly decided by errors, not brilliance. He applies this to startups, listing preventable blunders (skipping customer contact, no target audience, premature scaling, coding instead of selling) and separating them from bad luck and non-causes.

principles.text: Amateurs mostly lose by erring, not win by brilliance, so avoiding avoidable mistakes is a large share of winning.
principles.quote: There is a way to build startups with lower risk, in large part by avoiding those blunders

principles.text: Look for the underlying cause of failure, not the proximate one like 'ran out of cash' or 'founder stopped'.
principles.quote: We need to identify the cancer, not just say "the founder stopped."

principles.text: Pick a specific target audience and speak to them; trying to address everyone is a blunder.
principles.quote: Speaking to everyone means speaking to no one.

principles.text: Before product/market fit, discover what works; scaling comes only after, and scaling early wastes time and money.
principles.quote: scaling is about doubling-down on what works--doing it more, faster, better, higher quality, more efficiently.

principles.text: Builders retreat into code because marketing and sales are hard; getting customers requires putting down the compiler.
principles.quote: Coders like to code; everything else is hard, and not fun, and unclear how to execute, and costs money

principles.text: Win your target market before expanding to a second segment or product; premature expansion dilutes focus.
principles.quote: This blunder dilutes your attention, marketing dollars, positioning, messaging, and product sharpness, and is easy to avoid.

sources.title: Stubborn Visionaries & Pigheaded Fools: how to decide when to persist or quit
sources.originalTitle: Stubborn Visionaries & Pigheaded Fools
sources.summary: Jason Cohen argues that success-through-perseverance and failure-through-obstinance look identical at the moment of decision, so nobody can know in advance which one they're in. The job is to decide decisively, measure honestly, and use practical questions (timeboxes, existence proofs, sounding boards) to find out fast.

principles.text: At the decision point, persevering and obstinate paths are indistinguishable; you can't know which one you're on.
principles.quote: Consider S1 and S2 at time (B). Up to this point they are identical.

principles.text: Even experts and professional investors can't tell which path you're on, so don't expect certainty before deciding.
principles.quote: Not even the experts know which path you're on.

principles.text: Stopping guarantees failure while persisting at least leaves success possible, so quitting early has a real cost.
principles.quote: Stopping means you'll never create something great.

principles.text: Hindsight stories about perseverance or obstinacy are rationalizations; judging decisions by outcomes teaches less than we think.
principles.quote: The typical, backward-looking interpretation of these two scenarios is not the best way for us to understand the choices in front of us today

principles.text: Accepting uncertainty frees you to decide quickly, with less second-guessing and less guilt or cockiness afterward.
principles.quote: it liberates you to make decisions more easily--with less second-guessing in the moment, and less guilt afterwards.

principles.text: Use a hard timebox, and an existence proof from others who succeeded, as practical tests for whether to keep going.
principles.quote: Set a hard deadline for how much longer you'll work on it without seeing improvement.

sources.title: AI startups need new strategies: why the usual startup-vs-incumbent advantages don't apply
sources.originalTitle: AI startups require new strategies: This time it's actually different
sources.summary: Jason Cohen argues AI breaks the normal David-vs-Goliath playbook. Incumbents are embracing AI, already have the tech, data and talent, and "the AI market" is really existing markets with tougher competition. Startups need a strategy built on rapid differentiation and distribution, not the old assumptions.

principles.text: Startup strategy must start from real advantages over incumbents; in AI many of the usual ones are missing or reversed.
principles.quote: The typical startup strategies are wrong because typical strategies rely on the typical advantages of David against Goliath, which are largely untrue in AI.

principles.text: Disruption Theory fails when incumbents eagerly adopt the new tech instead of dismissing it as cheaper but worse.
principles.quote: They say "this technology is groundbreaking and if we don't embrace it, we will become irrelevant" and "our shareholders are demanding that we invest huge percentages of our annual revenue to do it."

principles.text: When everyone rents the same foundation models, matching incumbents' capabilities is not a winning strategy; you must differentiate and get distribution faster than usual.
principles.quote: In a market where everyone has access to the same core technologies, simply matching the capabilities of established players is not a winning strategy.

principles.text: The classic race is distribution vs innovation, but in AI incumbents already have innovation, so startups still face the hard distribution problem, now in saturated markets.
principles.quote: in AI, the incumbents already have the innovation (whether through closed APIs or open source), while startups struggle as mightily as ever to find distribution.

principles.text: Data is a moat: incumbents own it through their customers and can afford to buy more, while model tech gets cheaper but training data does not.
principles.quote: Incumbents have the data because they have the customers. They can immediately leverage customers' data to train models and tune algorithms, so long as they maintain secrecy and privacy.

principles.text: 'The AI market' isn't a market. AI is a solution-space tool inside existing markets; analyze how AI transforms a specific market and where you fit.
principles.quote: AI is in the solution-space, not the problem-space, as we say in product management. The customer problem you're solving is still the same as ever.

sources.title: How startups beat incumbents: attack where big companies cannot or will not defend
sources.originalTitle: How startups beat incumbents
sources.summary: Jason Cohen argues that every big-company advantage (scale, brand, process, profit centers) creates a weakness a startup can exploit. He lists ten attack vectors: unquantifiable risks, niches below the materiality threshold, non-scalable work, founder-led support, new tech, drastic change, personality, non-zero-sum channels, being worse-but-acceptable, and low-cost against a profit center.

principles.text: A startup wins by doing what incumbents cannot or will not do; never fight them head-on where they are strong.
principles.quote: The way a startup wins, is to do things that incumbents cannot or will not do.

principles.text: Pick big bets by potential outcome, not ROI; incumbents avoid risks they can't quantify, so projects that look low-ROI face no competition.
principles.quote: A startup who selects "apparently" low-ROI projects, will probably have no competition from incumbents.

principles.text: Target niches too small for an incumbent's materiality threshold; the bigger the incumbent, the less competition you face.
principles.quote: The startup can focus on a niche and ICP that a big company cannot afford to target, either because that niche wouldn't hit the overall revenue materiality threshold, or wouldn't hit the one-team P&L threshold.

principles.text: Founders handling support personally gives an advantage incumbents can't match: product insight, retention, loyalty, forgiveness and word of mouth.
principles.quote: Some startups aren't interested in providing great support, but those that do are naturally and even effortlessly orders of magnitude better than a large incumbent.

principles.text: Do things that are hard to scale from day one; incumbents won't wait years to reach material revenue, but a slow ramp suits a startup.
principles.quote: if the product is naturally difficult to scale from day one, that's ideal for a startup.

principles.text: Most customers don't care about most dimensions; choose one or two to excel at, be worse-but-acceptable elsewhere, and win on price while incumbents chase complexity.
principles.quote: Most customers don't care about most things. This is great news for startups, who can select one or two dimensions to care about

sources.title: How to decide if a big long-term investment is worthwhile (without expected value)
sources.originalTitle: Deciding whether an investment is worthwhile
sources.summary: Jason Cohen argues expected value misleads for one-shot, all-in investments like a career path or startup, since a guaranteed $1M and a 10% shot at $10M are not equivalent. He offers a framework: outsized payoff, accumulating value, stable conditions over ten years, alignment with global trends, a personal edge, and fit with your long-term vision.

principles.text: Expected value is the wrong tool for big, singular investments; it only works across many uncorrelated bets.
principles.quote: There is one case where expected value is the right tool: A portfolio of bets.

principles.text: Require an outsized payoff, and estimate it to the nearest power of ten, rounding down rather than up.
principles.quote: When it can pay off 10x or 100x, or when it can be life-altering, then even if you fall short of the goal--only 3x or only life-improving--then it was still worthwhile.

principles.text: Pick investments where value accumulates and doesn't erode, ideally with a positive feedback loop. Consulting doesn't compound like SaaS.
principles.quote: At a minimum, value must accrete, but ideally you construct a positive feedback loop, where growth or size itself begets more growth.

principles.text: Invest in what won't change over ten years, since the world must still value it when your payoff arrives.
principles.quote: If you spend 3-5 years investing, expecting a payoff in the subsequent 5 years, the world had better still value that thing during years 5-10.

principles.text: Pick a large, growing market so you answer 'why buy from me' instead of 'why buy at all'.
principles.quote: It means people are already spending money, so you're answering "why buy from me" rather than "why should I allocate budget for this at all"

principles.text: Build an edge by being top 25% at a few uncorrelated things; passion alone doesn't lower risk or raise payoff.
principles.quote: The other way, and the way available to all of us, is to be in the top 25% at a few uncorrelated things, which together creates a special edge.

sources.title: Good problems to have: "errors" that signal you're making great decisions
sources.originalTitle: The "errors" that mean you're doing it right
sources.summary: Jason Cohen lists apparent mistakes that are actually expected side-effects of good decisions, such as pivoting a fresh strategy, removing then re-adding features, or shipping buggy early. Each is a signal you're culling, learning fast and holding to strategy and values rather than over-engineering or waiting for perfect.

principles.text: A new strategy is most likely wrong right after you write it, so pivot quickly and say so out loud.
principles.quote: A strategy that never changes is wrong, and the most likely time to discover that it's wrong is just after you wrote it down, because you have the least practical experience with how it intersects with real life.

principles.text: If you never refactor after 10x growth, you over-engineered; you can't know what breaks at scale until you're scaling.
principles.quote: If you're not refactoring your infrastructure after a tenfold increase in growth, you over-engineered your original infrastructure.

principles.text: Marketing is far more likely too wordy and vague than too terse; keep messages punchy and specific.
principles.quote: It's 100x more likely that your messages aren't punchy enough, aren't specific enough, than that they're so brief as to be unintelligible.

principles.text: Release early and fix bugs afterwards; customer contact shows which bugs matter and reveals ones you'd never find alone.
principles.quote: If you're not fixing bugs due to releasing quickly, you released too late.

principles.text: Keep support and sales in your own hands until it breaks from lack of scale, because middlemen kill your learning pace.
principles.quote: The second you put someone else between you and a customer, your pace of learning and understanding falls off a cliff. Wait until it's breaking for lack of scale, then scale.

principles.text: Ignore most competitor moves and react only when customers signal it by asking for features or churning to a rival; turn down lucrative deals that don't fit your strategy.
principles.quote: If you're not ignoring most of your competitor's moves, then you're playing their game, not yours.

sources.title: Selling to Carol: why targeting a narrow ICP wins 10x-100x more customers than expected
sources.originalTitle: Selling to Carol: Why targeting an ICP brings 10x more customers than you expected
sources.summary: Jason Cohen argues you cannot speak to everyone, so write for one perfect customer (Carol) with vivid, specific messaging. Because buyers decide by trade-offs, a Carol-focused message also pulls in 10x-100x more people with similar preferences. He shows how to separate ICP data from noise and why turning down non-ICP revenue marks a seasoned founder.

principles.text: Speaking to everyone means saying nothing to everyone; pick one specific customer type and be evocative.
principles.quote: by *not* speaking to a specific customer, you're saying _nothing_ to _everyone_ and thus _everyone_ will bounce off the home page, and never think of you again.

principles.text: Define a concrete perfect customer (Carol) with professional attributes only: her problems, budget, and why she's buying now.
principles.quote: Whatever problems your product solves, Carol has *all* those problems. She has all the problems, she knows she has the problems, she already has the budget to spend on those problems

principles.text: Test messaging against Carol: if the ad can't grab your perfect customer in seconds, it won't grab anyone else.
principles.quote: If your ad can't grab Carol's attention--your perfect customer--why do you think it will grab anyone else's attention?

principles.text: Targeting Carol doesn't shrink your market: people with similar trade-off preferences buy too, making the effective market 10x-100x larger.
principles.quote: your effective target is actually at least 10x larger (because of Diana) and more like 20x-100x larger (because of Eddie).

principles.text: Segment ICP customers in all your data (cancellations, activation, usage, support) and ignore non-ICP noise, or you build for nobody.
principles.quote: If we treat all customers as if they are Carol, and therefore all cancellation data as a vital signal, we lose track of building for Carol and we end up building for nobody.

principles.text: Turn down or let go of big non-ICP customers; chasing their revenue wastes time better spent finding more Carols.
principles.quote: You'll know that you're doing this right when you turn down a sale, even though it would have been your largest customer, simply because they're not your ICP

sources.title: Jason Cohen's 8-step roadmap to Product/Market Fit, from WP Engine
sources.originalTitle: The roadmap to Product/Market Fit (PMF)… maybe
sources.summary: Jason lays out the eight-step process that took WP Engine from idea to unicorn: personal fit, market fit, customer interviews, shipping an SLC, marketing before code, retention-driven product work, ruthless prioritization, and managing founder psychology. He admits Smart Bear only half followed it, and warns that most founders retreat to coding instead of doing the uncomfortable work.

principles.text: Passion is required but not enough; you need a unique personal edge from your mix of talents and experiences.
principles.quote: Passion _is_ required; it's just not enough. Passion is the motivator, especially in the dark times

principles.text: Most good ideas aren't good businesses; build a plausible theory of why customers will buy before building.
principles.quote: That's why most "indie hacker" startups and "AI is cool" startups fail--the genesis was "fun project," not "plausible business."

principles.text: Talk to customers before building; their "no" is a real no and saves months of wasted work.
principles.quote: When they say "yes," it's a "maybe," but when they say "no," it's a "no," and you just saved yourself months or years of wasted time.

principles.text: Aim everything at an over-specified ICP; it expands rather than limits your market.
principles.quote: for every ICP there are 10x more people who make similar buying decisions, and 100x more who take more convincing but ultimately also agree

principles.text: Ship a Simple, Lovable, Complete product fast; real learning begins only when customers use it.
principles.quote: If you're building for six months and a customer hasn't used it, you're not on the road to Product/Market Fit

principles.text: Do so much marketing and sales it feels like too much; retention is where you learn if you kept your promise.
principles.quote: Marketing is where you discover the promise the customer wants you to make, and retention is where you discover whether you're fulfilling that promise.

sources.title: How many things should there be on a list? Why the answer is almost never 10
sources.originalTitle: How many things should there be? (Hint: Not 10)
sources.summary: Jason Cohen argues that "Top 10" is an arbitrary number, and that the right count of items on a list depends on its purpose. He walks through cases (1, 3, 5-7, one per team, a full audit checklist, bankruptcy) and concludes that fewer is usually better.

principles.text: Before making a list, ask what its purpose is and whether the count has a good reason; the answer is almost never 10.
principles.quote: Always Ask: **What is the purpose of this list?**

principles.text: Usually fewer items is better; 10 is arbitrary, a product of having ten fingers.
principles.quote: Usually, fewer is better, and the right answer is almost never "10."

principles.text: One priority ensures it gets done as quickly as possible.
principles.quote: It's reductive to say [only one thing is important](https://longform.asmartbear.com/maximized-decision/), but it also ensures that it gets done, as quickly as possible.

principles.text: If you can't hold the list in your head even when trying hard, it has too many items; around seven is the cap.
principles.quote: If you can't keep it in your head, even when you're trying very hard, it's too many items.

principles.text: A fixed set like an audit's flags can be a good list: finishing 100% gives a checklist, felt progress and a clear state-change.
principles.quote: Getting through 100% of a specific set of things is a powerful statement.

principles.text: When a backlog or inbox is hopelessly large, declare bankruptcy: archive it all and let the important things come back.
principles.quote: Declare "bankruptcy"--whether it's the email inbox or the Jira backlog. Archive it all. The important things will come back.

sources.title: Jason Cohen's Fairytale Plan: quarterly strategic planning in five parts
sources.originalTitle: Quarterly strategic planning using the fairytale structure
sources.summary: Jason Cohen shows how to build a quarterly strategic plan using the fairytale story structure: Objectives, Obstacles, Actions, Measures, and Not Doing. He argues most planning time belongs on defining obstacles, picking a few big "rocks," and stating out loud what you are choosing not to do.

principles.text: Structure a strategic plan as a story: objectives, obstacles, actions, measures, and what you're not doing.
principles.quote: Our brains are pre-wired for fairy-tales, so we naturally follow the presentation as it flows into those primordial ruts in our gray matter.

principles.text: Spend most planning time on obstacles; don't jump to solutions before fully exploring the problem.
principles.quote: Without fully exploring the problem-space, you're not in a position to even know the goal of the solution-space.

principles.text: Narrow obstacles to the 1-3 that, if solved, would unlock the objectives even if everything else festered.
principles.quote: Narrow these down to 1-3 most critical issues.

principles.text: When obstacles are serious, prioritize in order: retention, people, throughput, growth, competition, code health, execution risk.
principles.quote: 1. Retention (if customers are leaving, the business model and product isn't working)

principles.text: Pick a few big, impactful 'rocks' rather than incremental work; judge by impact on critical things, not ROI.
principles.quote: For your most critical pieces of work, the goal is not to optimize your time, but rather to maximize your impact on the most critical things.

principles.text: Publish a 'Not Doing' list: most deferred items are really 'not ever', and saying so keeps the team focused.
principles.quote: When you don't articulate what we're not doing, it can appear that you don't even know those things exist.

sources.title: Product/Market Fit: what it feels like and the numbers that define it
sources.originalTitle: Product/Market Fit (PMF): Experience & Data
sources.summary: Jason Cohen defines PMF as a felt shift from push to pull, backed by three tests: sudden sustained growth, low churn, and critical mass. He shows the same linear-then-steeper-linear curve across bootstrapped, VC-funded, viral and media businesses, and argues high churn means no fit.

principles.text: PMF is unmistakable: it's a shift from pushing for each customer to being pulled by demand. If you're unsure, you don't have it.
principles.quote: there is no doubt when you have it**. (If you're not sure whether you have Product/Market Fit, you don't.)

principles.text: Define PMF as three things together: easy growth, high retention, and critical mass.
principles.quote: **I define Product/Market Fit as _all_ of the following:**

principles.text: Churn must be under 3%/mo for B2B or 5%/mo for B2C. Customers leaving in droves means no fit, however fast you grow.
principles.quote: cancellation higher than 3% for B2B or 5% for B2C indicates a lack of Product/Market Fit

principles.text: PMF growth is linear, then a sudden bend to a steeper linear slope, not exponential. This holds for bootstrapped, VC-funded, viral and media businesses.
principles.quote: Revenue growing linearly, slowly, often for about two years, then in a moment--Product/Market Fit--when it suddenly turns upward, and continues growing at that new trajectory.

principles.text: High churn caps growth: churn scales with your base while acquisition doesn't, so cancellations eventually win the race.
principles.quote: 5%/mo" definitionally grows in lock-step with your total size, but marketing and sales does not continue to automatically grow just because your company is bigger.

principles.text: Judge fit by customer behavior, not dollars. PMF also brings a crushing workload, so hire ahead of need.
principles.quote: Don't get distracted by dollars. Pay attention to customer behavior.

sources.title: Unmeasurable metrics: what you can't measure even in retrospect, so don't set goals on it
sources.originalTitle: Metrics that cannot even be measured in retrospect
sources.summary: Jason Cohen argues that some enticing metrics can't be measured even after the fact, so you shouldn't predict them or turn them into goals. Examples: single-feature revenue impact, incremental churn initiatives, risk probabilities, brand value, culture ROI. Use KPIs that measure specific aspects of your systems instead.

principles.text: If a metric can't be measured in retrospect, it can't be measured now, predicted, or used as a goal.
principles.quote: If they cannot be measured in retrospect, they cannot be measured now, and you certainly cannot predict them or make a goal from them.

principles.text: You can't attribute revenue to individual features; usage is a valid KPI but not the same as revenue.
principles.quote: Even after the fact, with 100s of 1000s of customers (in our case at WP Engine), it's still not possible to attribute revenue to individual features.

principles.text: Rare events like small churn changes drown in noise: a 10% churn cut from 3% to 2.7% is below normal monthly variance.
principles.quote: If churn is 3%/mo, an initiative that reduces churn by 10%--a big impact!--will result in 2.7%/mo. How hard is it to measure a difference of 0.3%, month over month?

principles.text: Churn lags action: customers leaving today decided weeks or months ago, so new initiatives can't change them.
principles.quote: An activity you start today is unlikely to change the trajectory of customers who have already decided to leave, and only today happened to push the red button.

principles.text: Still work on churn even though single initiatives can't be measured, because retention compounds and SaaS profit comes in later years.
principles.quote: retention compounds, and all the profit generated by a customer of a SaaS business happens in the later years

principles.text: Don't put probabilities on a risk slide; one-off independent risks can never be validated. List only risks worth action or awareness.
principles.quote: So don't put probabilities on the slide at all. Only list the risks that you feel are so important that they either merit action or awareness.

sources.title: Why scaling is hard: the fundamental forces that make big companies slower but stronger
sources.originalTitle: The fundamental forces of scale
sources.summary: Jason Cohen explains why founders can't run a 500-person company like a 50-person one. Two forces drive it: rare things become common, and complexity exceeds human comprehension. He walks through consequences for team robustness, predictability, materiality thresholds, recruiting, communication, infrastructure and risk.

principles.text: At scale, rare events become daily events, so manual handling must be replaced by new processes.
principles.quote: Rare things are difficult to predict, and typically difficult to prevent. Before scale, they are, well, rare, so this doesn't matter; they can be handled manually. But when they start happening daily, new processes become necessary.

principles.text: A team of one is fast but brittle; at scale you trade per-person productivity for continuity.
principles.quote: So a team of one is fast, but brittle. When you're small, this is a good trade-off, because speed is critical for combating the things that are constantly about to kill the company

principles.text: Robustness always costs more than expected, in people and in infrastructure.
principles.quote: Robustness always carries a cost. Whether it's running four servers instead of one, or a team of four instead of one, you trade local inefficiency for whole-company continuity.

principles.text: Large companies need predictability because hiring and launches have long lead times; it is an advantage of scale, not a bureaucratic excuse.
principles.quote: Therefore, we have to predict the demand for technical support four to six months in advance, because we need to be hiring for that right now.

principles.text: The bigger the company, the higher the materiality threshold: projects must be big enough to move the business, or they are failures.
principles.quote: This principle is called the "Materiality Threshold," i.e. the minimum contribution a project must deliver, for the project to materially affect the business.

principles.text: Communicating to hundreds requires simple messages repeated in many formats, times and voices; complex messages can't reach everyone.
principles.quote: The answer is: Repeating simple messages.

sources.title: Stop saying "fail": use words that describe what's happening and what to do next
sources.originalTitle: Stop saying "fail"
sources.summary: Jason Cohen argues "fail" is almost always the wrong word for setbacks because it is final and suggests no next step. He maps different situations (experiments, innovation, learning, optimizing, problem-solving, major errors) to more precise vocabulary that points toward action, reserving "failed" for true shutdowns.

principles.text: Words should explain what's going on and suggest the next step; "fail" does neither.
principles.quote: Words have meaning. They can explain what's really going on, and suggest what should be done next. The word "fail" accomplishes neither.

principles.text: Treat unsuccessful paths in building a business as backtracking in a maze, not failure.
principles.quote: If you're solving a maze, and a path doesn't work out, you haven't "failed," you've only backtracked.

principles.text: Frame attempts as experiments: either result is evidence, so neither is a failure, even when most A/B tests find no win.
principles.quote: The result of an experiment is evidence supporting or rejecting the hypothesis. Neither result is a "failure." A/B testing is a good practice, even though most of the time you will not have stumbled upon an improvement.

principles.text: Innovation requires many trials; an attempt that doesn't revolutionize things yet just hasn't found the breakthrough.
principles.quote: Often innovations require many trials before the right solution is uncovered. If the right answer were obvious, it wouldn't be an innovation.

principles.text: Fast-moving problem-solving in complex organizations inevitably includes setbacks; adapt rather than label them failure.
principles.quote: Problem-solving in a complex space--whether a one-person startup or a thousand-person organization--cannot possibly proceed with innovation and speed and yet also no setbacks, no complications, no false-starts.

principles.text: Even for a major misjudgment, name its nature (pivot, overhaul, redesign) so the label points to the fix; reserve "we failed" for real shutdowns.
principles.quote: Still, that doesn't explain its nature, and doesn't point towards a solution, which would be the constructive thing to do.

sources.title: Worse, but unique: why a "refuted" strategy beats the popular one for startups
sources.originalTitle: Worse, but unique
sources.summary: Using chess openings as an analogy, Jason argues that an objectively worse but unusual strategy beats a popular, objectively better one, because opponents are prepared for the popular one and not for yours. Startups should fight on their own terms, pick an extreme difference, and accept that many customers won't want their game.

principles.text: Don't attack where the incumbent is strong; fight the competitive battle on your own terms.
principles.quote: A startup needs to fight the competitive battle on its own terms, not attack where the opponent is already strong.

principles.text: Popular strategies are the ones competitors have prepared against; a niche, 'refuted' one catches them unprepared.
principles.quote: exactly because the Queen's Gambit is popular, it's likely that your opponent has also studied it.

principles.text: Playing a different game on your own terms can make a 'worse' strategy better, even if your team, product and company are weaker.
principles.quote: Playing on your own terms changes the game. "Worse, but unique," is in fact "better."

principles.text: Be extreme in your difference, not merely different; one extreme trait is already powerful.
principles.quote: Even better than "different," is to be extreme in that difference.

principles.text: Competitors can't match an extreme choice, so they are definitionally not the best at your game.
principles.quote: All those competitors *cannot* play the game as well as you, because you picked something that was not only different, but extreme.

principles.text: Accept losing customers who don't want your game; the ones who do will see you as the best, and you can still win big in a large market.
principles.quote: The customers who *do* want to play your game, will see that you're the best in that game.

sources.title: What makes a strategy great: six traits of a "how we will win" document
sources.originalTitle: What makes a strategy great
sources.summary: Jason Cohen argues that strategy is simply "how we will win," and that most documents titled strategy are vague wishful thinking. He lays out six traits of great strategy (simple, candid, decisive, leveraged, asymmetric, futuristic), with examples like Craigslist, Zappos and Amazon, plus tell-tale signs of bad strategy.

principles.text: Strategy must be simple, even simplistic, because no one reads or remembers long documents; it exists so everyone can make aligned daily decisions.
principles.quote: No one reads anything. You're in the Top 1% just for reading this sentence. No one remembers anything. Certainly not an 86-slide PowerPoint.

principles.text: Real threats are specific, present-tense and data-backed, not generic 'could happen' worries; a strategy that skips the scary facts is wrong.
principles.quote: Real threats are either happening now or are at least 70% likely to happen.

principles.text: Decide who you target and who you ignore, and accept the negative consequences up front so complaints from non-target customers don't derail you.
principles.quote: When those consequences inevitably arise, the team must be able to say "we expected that" rather than "we have to address that" or even "this is a signal that the strategy is wrong."

principles.text: Use the Opposite Test: a real strategic decision has a rational opposite that other successful companies have chosen; 'customer-first' fails it.
principles.quote: deciding to be open source is strategic, because plenty of companies are successful with a closed-source strategy. However, deciding to be "customer-first" is not a serious decision

principles.text: Leverage existing strengths and avoid weaknesses rather than trying to fix them; better still if the strength is differentiated and durable.
principles.quote: Great strategy leverages the strengths and assets of the organization; a bad strategy asks the organization to win even while acting unnaturally, often under the cover of "overcoming weaknesses."

principles.text: Build asymmetric bets where upside far exceeds downside, so the plan wins even with bad luck; a plan where everything must go right will fail.
principles.quote: If everything has to go right for the plan to succeed, it won't succeed.

sources.title: In command: what it means to lead a business without being "in control"
sources.originalTitle: In command
sources.summary: Jason Cohen argues that control is impossible but command is achievable. A leader who is in command still has bugs, missed metrics, mistakes and threats. What sets her apart is that she has expectations, watches the right metrics, writes down her thinking, and reacts honestly when reality diverges. The essay lists what command looks like across metrics, hiring, strategy, sales, backlog and decisions.

principles.text: Being in command means having expectations and reacting when you miss them, not always meeting them.
principles.quote: It means you *have* expectations of yourself and your team, and when you don't meet them, it bothers you, and you react.

principles.text: Decide which few metrics matter up front, so you spot problems first and respond in proportion to their importance.
principles.quote: When metrics go awry, you're the first one to identify that, and are already taking action in proportion to their importance and how far off the mark they are.

principles.text: A long backlog is fine if you pick a few strategic bets and have a system for prioritizing, which means doing almost none of the rest.
principles.quote: It means you've identified the few Rocks that are your bets on how to win strategically, and you have a system for prioritizing the rest, which also means doing almost none of the rest.

principles.text: If you constantly do others' work, it's your fault: you hired wrong or won't let good hires do their job. Edit rather than write.
principles.quote: If you're constantly having to do someone else's work, that's your fault. Either you've hired incorrectly, which is your fault, or you have hired correctly and you're not allowing them to do their job, which is your fault.

principles.text: Write down what you believe so you can tell when your mind needs to change, then communicate what changed and why.
principles.quote: It means you wrote down what you think, so that it's more obvious when your mind needs to change, and then you communicate that change--both what and why.

principles.text: Seek out surprises and hard truths. Surprises should come from new facts, never from negligence.
principles.quote: It means when they do occur, it's not due to negligence. It means something actually changed, or an important new fact was uncovered.

sources.title: Selecting product metrics: a value-chain KPI system for teams, execs and stakeholders
sources.originalTitle: Selecting the right product metrics (KPIs)
sources.summary: Jason Cohen proposes mapping product metrics as a value chain across time (leading to lagging) and across hidden, internal, external and strategic domains, so every department sees itself in the result. He pairs this with a checklist for good metrics, including plain-language definitions, causing action, and signal at least 2x stronger than noise.

principles.text: Map metrics as a value chain by time, actor and type of value; each box then yields its own metrics.
principles.quote: A product sits in the middle of a chain of events, executed by the team, customers, and peers across all departments.

principles.text: Separate maximizers from satisficers; act on satisficing KPIs only when they hit a pre-agreed violation threshold.
principles.quote: "satisficing" KPIs are tracked continuously, but the team acts only when a KPI slips into "violation" territory, as opposed to fielding requests to invest in improving those KPIs.

principles.text: Hold teams accountable for immediate, controllable work. Treat revenue as a lagging, multi-input outcome.
principles.quote: Work can--and should--be measured sprint-by-sprint, whereas revenue is a multi-input, lagging indicator of success.

principles.text: Measure both direct results and lagging outcomes; missing an outcome is a learning, not a failure.
principles.quote: But "not yet achieving the outcome" is not a complete failure, but rather a learning that will shape the work that will be executed in the next two weeks.

principles.text: A metric belongs on the main board only if a change would make you act; otherwise keep it operational.
principles.quote: If the answer is "no," it doesn't belong on our main metrics board.

principles.text: A KPI the team doesn't believe in will be ignored; the team must want to depend on it.
principles.quote: Whenever management requires a KPI that the team doesn't believe in, doesn't respect, doesn't care about, the team always wins.

sources.title: Why probability words fail, and how to use Fermi-style numbers instead
sources.originalTitle: For probabilities, use Fermi numbers, not words
sources.summary: Jason Cohen argues that words like "unlikely" or "probable" mean wildly different things to different people, even after training, so they should not be used for risk or strategy. He recommends a few crisp numeric probabilities (Fermi-style), rounded by context, with teammates estimating independently.

principles.text: Probability words are unreliable because individual interpretations differ more than the words themselves.
principles.quote: Words don't work, because *the differences between individual interpretations are larger than the differences between the words themselves*!

principles.text: Training people on an official word-to-number scale still fails; CIA officers missed their own ranges about half the time.
principles.quote: when officers were assessed against the scale, fully half the time they failed to stay in-range

principles.text: Use numbers, chosen from a small set of options, rather than vague words or falsely precise values.
principles.quote: Use numbers, not words. Select from a small set of options.

principles.text: Don't haggle over 20% vs 30%; nobody knows the true number, you just need crisp signals to decide.
principles.quote: it's unproductive to haggle over details like "is it a 20% or 30% probability." None of us likely knows the true number, and anyway we need crisp signals to make smart decisions.
