principles.text: Round off in the direction of known bias, e.g. projects run late more often than early, so round on-time odds down.
principles.quote: in general things are more likely to be late than early, therefore we should "round off" towards the lower probability.

principles.text: Have each teammate give independent numeric estimates; discuss disagreements and skip the agreements.
principles.quote: Ask everyone in the team to supply their own numbers independently; where there's disagreement, that's worth a discussion; where there's agreement, you can save time by just moving along.

sources.title: Leverage: why winning strategy comes from strengths, differentiation and durability, not fixing weaknesses
sources.originalTitle: The three kinds of leverage that anchor effective strategies
sources.summary: Jason Cohen argues effective strategy rests on three nested layers of leverage: strengths, differentiated strengths, and durable differentiated strengths (moats). He says to sidestep weaknesses rather than fix them, and shows how interlocking choices (Southwest) and competitor lock-in create lasting advantage.

principles.text: Win by leveraging strengths, not by shoring up weaknesses.
principles.quote: Leveraging strengths is the only way to do great work. (Not "fixing weaknesses.")

principles.text: Fixing a weakness is hard and usually yields only neutral, so lean on innate greatness instead.
principles.quote: Reversing weakness is hard, painful, likely to result in something merely neutral, not great, and is at high risk of failing completely.

principles.text: Avoid weaknesses through target market, persona and product choices rather than fixing them.
principles.quote: Better is to avoid weaknesses through decisions on target market, target personas, and product

principles.text: Use the tool or language you already know, since it leverages your scarcest resource: time.
principles.quote: the best answer to "what tool/language/framework/process should I use to do ______?" is "the one you already know."

principles.text: For weaknesses that only matter past a threshold (like uptime), set an agreed threshold and invest only when it is breached.
principles.quote: while the metric exceeds the threshold, we do not attempt to improve it--that's like over-investing in a weakness that will never become a strength.

principles.text: Exploit competitors' ossified structure (cost base, values, platform trade-offs) to create differentiation they cannot match.
principles.quote: A competitor with a high cost structure *must* charge high prices, therefore a strategy of have "40% of the features at 10% of the price" leverages a point of differentiation that the competitor cannot match.

sources.title: The Needs Stack: positioning against competitors by climbing your customer's chain of goals
sources.originalTitle: Using the Needs Stack for competitive strategy
sources.summary: Jason Cohen explains the Needs Stack: every customer need is a means to a higher need, and a product serving a higher level makes lower-level products obsolete. He shows how to use it for positioning (features at the customer's current level, benefits one level up), for competitive attack, for choosing metrics, and for finding higher purpose.

principles.text: Map your customer's Needs Stack: each need is a means to a higher need. Customers rarely want what you literally sell.
principles.quote: You need to understand the Needs Stack of your target customers. Not just your "market" or your "product" or "solving the problem" or even the immediate Jobs-To-Be-Done of your customer--those are all means to ends.

principles.text: Your real competitors include anyone serving a higher level of the stack, because they make your level obsolete.
principles.quote: a company who provides the higher-level need of "WordPress site" makes the lower-level need of "infrastructure" *obsolete*.

principles.text: Higher-level products trade flexibility for speed to the goal. Lower-level products keep customization. Both survive for different customers.
principles.quote: Up the stack, customers achieve their end-goal faster; down the stack, customers have more flexibility and customization.

principles.text: Resolve 'sell benefits vs features': talk features at the level the customer is thinking, and sell the benefit one level higher.
principles.quote: If someone has in their head "get a WordPress site," you want to meet them where they are, and talk about how your product is the best way to "get a WordPress site." That's the part where you talk about features.

principles.text: Position lower levels as irrelevant by focusing on the next level up, so the customer sees your product as the end, not a means.
principles.quote: In short, make "infrastructure" irrelevant by focusing on the next level up. The customer never wanted to think about infrastructure in the first place.

principles.text: Measure one level above your product to predict long-run retention, even if you can't control it. Shopify reports GMV for this reason.
principles.quote: It's strategic to measure further up the stack. Not too far, otherwise it's not only difficult to measure, but too many external factors drive the number. But the very next level up could be a critical way to measure value

sources.title: Willingness-to-pay: why Love beats Utility and Coercion as a durable growth and pricing strategy
sources.originalTitle: Willingness-to-pay: Creating permanent competitive advantage for the right reasons
sources.summary: Jason Cohen splits willingness-to-pay into three sources: Love, Utility and Coercion. Each one changes growth, retention and exposure to competitors in a different way. His conclusion is that even a cold-blooded investor should build WTP through Love and Utility, and treat Coercion as the weakest base.

principles.text: Create value for the customer first, then decide how to split it: leave surplus for advocacy and retention, or raise prices.
principles.quote: Creating value for the customer comes first. Then--and only then--you can decide how to "split it with the customer," either leveraging Consumer Surplus for advocacy, high-retention, and growth, or indeed by raising prices.

principles.text: Love-based WTP produces cheap, non-linear growth, because happy customers repeat-buy and advocate with no extra sales cost.
principles.quote: **Love** creates *inexpensive, non-linear growth*, because your customers are your allies.

principles.text: Customers who love you stay when a better or cheaper competitor shows up, so Love works as retention and defense against rivals.
principles.quote: When a new competitor arrives, *even when it is superior* in features or price, your customers will stay, because they're here for more than just the features and the price.

principles.text: Utility WTP grows revenue inside existing accounts but does not create advocates and does not stop customers evaluating new competitors.
principles.quote: But, a customer's willingness to buy another ten seats of JIRA doesn't imply the customer is going on forums, spending personal credibility to advocate on your behalf.

principles.text: Coercion (lock-in, monopoly, policy mandates) turns customers into allies of your competitors and leaves you open to disruption by mediocre rivals.
principles.quote: You are constantly vulnerable to disruption, even by mediocre competition. This is the weakest position you could be in, because you're coercing customers instead of delighting them.

principles.text: With identical revenue and profit, the Love-based company is the better bet. Love can add Utility later, but Coercion rarely converts into Love.
principles.quote: It is also possible for (1) to add Utility or even Coercive WTP to their strategy, further strengthening their position, whereas it is much more difficult for (2) to generate Love starting from their current position.

sources.title: Why solving a real problem isn't enough: a viability model from problem to business model
sources.originalTitle: Excuse me, is there a problem?
sources.summary: Jason Cohen explains why many startups fail despite a real problem and a working product. He lays out a chain of filters (Plausible, Self-Aware, Lucrative, Liquid, Eager, Enduring) and a multiplicative Fermi-estimate score to test viability, plus exceptions and how niching can fix a bad score.

principles.text: Solving a real problem is not enough to build a company; many failures had a real problem and a product that worked.
principles.quote: These companies fail because solving a problem is--perhaps surprisingly--not nearly enough to build a successful company.

principles.text: Funnel math sets minimum market size: ~1% click and ~1% pay means ~10M impressions for 1,000 customers, so you need ~10M consumers or ~100k businesses.
principles.quote: 10,000 × (1% click-through) × (1% convert-to-pay) = 1.

principles.text: Customers who don't know or care they have the problem won't search for or buy a solution; you can't force a market.
principles.quote: If a person does not already believe they have a problem, they will not be surfing the internet looking for a solution, and even if they happen upon your website somehow, you cannot get them to spend money to solve a problem they don't think they have.

principles.text: Consumers rarely pay; self-funded companies should target businesses, who spend to solve problems and to make money.
principles.quote: In general, consumers don't like paying for stuff, hence the multi-trillion-dollar success of having people "pay" with attention (advertisement) and data (privacy).

principles.text: Lock-in, contracts and bundling can block a sale regardless of product quality or price; build lock-in that protects you from competitors.
principles.quote: Notice that **all these forces have nothing to do with your product or its price**.

principles.text: Targeting a niche often yields a better business model, since it can raise willingness, budget and urgency even as it shrinks the customer count.
principles.quote: **targeting a niche often results in a better business model**, because although it reduces the number of target customers, it can increase several other numbers.

sources.title: Navigating the unpredictability of everything: strategy when you can't predict the future
sources.originalTitle: Navigating the unpredictability of everything
sources.summary: Jason Cohen shows that even elite experts fail at forecasting markets, sales, winners and products, then lays out how to build strategy anyway. Have a strategy, follow customer behavior (especially product "abuse"), and use moats, optionality, hedges and bets on what won't change.

principles.text: A strategy is required even when it's wrong; it gives direction and produces something interesting that early fans can reveal the real answer through.
principles.quote: A strategy gives you a direction. A direction creates something interesting. Something interesting might be used by zealous early fans, even if it ends up uncovering the answer rather than being the answer.

principles.text: Decide and move forward rather than deliberating, because deliberation assumes we can reason about the future, and gain experience instead.
principles.quote: Making a decision and moving forward is often more effective than extended deliberation about the decision.

principles.text: Follow customer behavior to upgrade your strategy; treat requests as signals of intent, not as the new strategy itself.
principles.quote: Customers are where you discover how to upgrade your strategy. Since you know your initial strategy is wrong, following customers' lead is how you correct it.

principles.text: When customers abuse your product to do something else, that's a strong signal to change strategy. Code Historian's peer-review abuse became Code Collaborator, 97% of company revenue.
principles.quote: "Abuse" is a strong, positive signal for customer demand, and worthy of a change in strategy.

principles.text: Build a plan out of "or" not "and": create optionality with many ways to succeed, since a plan needing everything to go right rarely works.
principles.quote: A resilient plan is built of "or" not "and."

principles.text: Bet on what will not change (e.g. fast, cheap, secure) rather than predicting what will, and leverage your own existing strengths.
principles.quote: it is difficult to predict how the future will change, but it can be easy to predict the ways the future will *not* change.

sources.title: Finding Fulfillment: Joy, Skill, Need and the three traps that cause burnout
sources.originalTitle: Finding Fulfillment
sources.summary: Jason Cohen presents a framework for fulfillment at work: you need Joy, Skill, and Need together, and any two without the third create a predictable trap (useless flow, indulgent failure, or burn-out). He used it to step aside as CEO of WP Engine and become CTO, and pairs it with Pink's motivation model and Sinek's "Start with Why."

principles.text: Fulfillment requires Joy, Skill and Need together; any two without the third creates a specific trap.
principles.quote: Not only do you need *all three* of the following components, but any two alone create a specific trap

principles.text: Joy plus Skill without Need is pleasant but unproductive flow, and founders often have nobody to tell them so.
principles.quote: there's no one willing or able to tell you to your face that you're not contributing to what the company needs, so you stay in your happy place.

principles.text: Joy plus Need without Skill leads founders to indulge in jobs they're bad at, wasting months and drawing wrong conclusions.
principles.quote: You might even erroneously conclude "AdWords doesn't work" because that's an easier conclusion than "I don't know what I'm doing."

principles.text: Skill plus Need without Joy is burn-out, hidden because great results make it look like no problem.
principles.quote: Because you create great results that the company needs, it doesn't look like a problem--not to you, nor your team.

principles.text: Don't hoard work you hate; someone else may enjoy it, and you're blocking them and yourself from being happier.
principles.quote: Some people actually *like* the thing you hate, and you're preventing them--and you--from being happier.

principles.text: Ego can keep founders in the CEO role even when it makes them unhappy; moving to the center of the Venn diagram served both the person and the company.
principles.quote: So it's hard to convince the ego to let go of being the CEO, as I did at WP Engine, even if being the CEO creates unhappiness.

sources.title: Iterative-Hypothesis customer development: how Jason Cohen interviewed customers before WP Engine
sources.originalTitle: The Iterative-Hypothesis customer development method
sources.summary: Jason Cohen lays out a five-step interview method (goals, written hypotheses, open-ended questions, iterating, stopping when it's boring) used to vet WP Engine and reject other startup ideas. The aim is to disconfirm assumptions and learn how customers live, not to pitch or ask what to build. He adds tips on discussing price, segmentation, and using customers' exact words.

principles.text: Interviews exist to uncover truth, not to sell; if you learn nothing new and actionable, the hour was wasted.
principles.quote: If you don't come away knowing something new and actionable at the end of the interview, you've wasted your time and theirs.

principles.text: Don't ask customers what to build or if they'd buy a feature; learn what their current life, pain, and coping look like.
principles.quote: I asked a customer "Would you buy if we build ______?" and they say "Yes", and then we build it, and then they don't buy.

principles.text: Write down hypotheses before interviewing, even obvious ones, to fight confirmation bias and generate questions; about half of his were wrong.
principles.quote: After dozens of hours of interviews, I found that half of these hypotheses were wrong.

principles.text: Ask open-ended questions that don't hint at an answer and invite more information; leading questions just get polite yeses.
principles.quote: Of course everyone will say "yes." They would sound dumb if they didn't agree. That's why it's a useless question.

principles.text: Treat surprise as the signal to dig deeper, and stop interviewing only when surprises stop, not after three calls.
principles.quote: When the surprises stop, that means learning has stopped, and that means you should stop the process.

principles.text: Discuss price in early interviews; a specific price triggers a visceral reaction that reveals segments and what the product means to them.
principles.quote: The responses were immediate, emotional, and vehement.

sources.title: JIT selection from independent streams: replace the big backlog with separate prioritized lists
sources.originalTitle: JIT selection from independent streams: An alternative to the "big backlog" of work
sources.summary: Jason Cohen argues that one big ordered backlog conflates prioritization (what is most important) with work-planning (what we do next), and forces comparison of incomparable things. His fix: keep separate prioritized lists per stakeholder group, customer journey stage or other category, then pick from the top of each list just in time when planning work.

principles.text: Prioritization (what is most important) is not work-planning (what we work on next); don't use one backlog for both.
principles.quote: Prioritization means: What is most important? Critically, it does not mean: What will we work on next?

principles.text: A single sorted list mixes incomparable kinds of importance (customer retention, competition, security, tech debt), so no one metric can order it.
principles.quote: The first problem is that you're sorting things that are incomparable.

principles.text: Have each stakeholder group (Sales, Support, Engineering) prioritize its own list, answering one question for just that group.
principles.quote: The solution is to prioritize items in separate, actually-comparable streams, and to keep that prioritization effort cleanly separate from work-planning.

principles.text: Forcing a group to rank its own ideas builds empathy for PM tradeoffs and prevents everything being Priority #1.
principles.quote: By forcing that group to prioritize their ideas, they'll argue amongst themselves over which are most impactful.

principles.text: Wait until the last moment to cross streams: pick the next work from the top of each list, then order it in a backlog.
principles.quote: By waiting until the last second to compare incomparable things, prioritization remains organized and clear.

principles.text: Selecting from the top items of each stream is easier, easier to explain to stakeholders, and lets you audit starvation and spot cross-stream wins.
principles.quote: It's a lot easier to pick the best from 12 instead of from 1000, and in some sense you can't go wrong

sources.title: Rocks, Pebbles, Sand: prioritizing work by size with a different goal and process for each
sources.originalTitle: Rocks, Pebbles, Sand: How to implement in practice
sources.summary: Jason Cohen extends Covey's jar analogy into a practical system. Rocks (3+ months) maximize strategic impact and need deliberate decisions. Pebbles (1-4 sprints) maximize ROI and are decided by the PM. Sand (up to 1 sprint) maximizes throughput with minimal process. He also gives a sprint-planning order and fixes for common failure modes.

principles.text: Prioritization is about impact, not task size; easy or urgent work must not crowd out strategic work.
principles.quote: It's about maximizing *impact* by not allowing the easy or urgent things to crowd out the strategic things that take years to unfold but are more important than everything else combined.

principles.text: For Rocks, maximize strategic impact rather than ROI, because a quick, less impactful idea becomes trivial when things go worse than planned.
principles.quote: Do _not_ maximize ROI. Your primary job is to execute your strategy to the fullest, spending the most-possible time on the most-impactful thing.

principles.text: Impact estimates are as unreliable as time estimates, so set the impact bar higher than feels necessary.
principles.quote: Over-shooting is the antidote to Hofstadter's Law.

principles.text: Choose the mountain deliberately; agility only helps once you are climbing the right one.
principles.quote: But if you're climbing up the wrong mountain in the first place, being "agile" doesn't help; the result is a team self-managing themselves into a mediocre, unfulfilling result.

principles.text: Sand creates quality only in bulk, so maximize throughput and strip out administrative overhead rather than measuring impact.
principles.quote: Administration is the biggest impediment to throughput, therefore PM's must ruthlessly fight against the natural urge to debate and arrange and carefully assess and estimate the work, instead of just going about the business of completing the work.

principles.text: Estimation errors on impact and effort compound in ROI math, so naive ROI rubrics can be mostly noise.
principles.quote: This item has *half* the ROI than we originally thought. This is an immense magnitude of error, swamping the signal you thought you computed.

sources.title: Binstack: Choosing the single most impactful option with binary materiality and stack-ranked attributes
sources.originalTitle: Binstack: Making a maximal multi-dimensional decision
sources.summary: Jason Cohen argues that weighted rubrics fail for multi-dimensional decisions because scores are imprecise, incomparable and tie easily. His Binstack method replaces scores with binary "material or not" judgments against a stack-ranked list of attributes, producing a clear winner and an easy-to-explain decision.

principles.text: Weighted-score rubrics produce ties and noise; differences in totals are more error than signal.
principles.quote: Even with weights, a clear winner often does not emerge, and again we're back to a weak, indefensible decision.

principles.text: Summing incomparable attributes implicitly claims they are interchangeable, which sounds absurd when said aloud.
principles.quote: By adding them together, we're implicitly saying "these are comparable," but they are not.

principles.text: Score each option as binary materiality: it either moves an attribute by a measurable amount or it doesn't. Write the concrete expected change down.
principles.quote: Either an item *materially* contributes to that attribute, or it doesn't. "Materially" means the effect is so large you can measure it easily

principles.text: Hard decisions are hard because smaller decisions were avoided. Decide what matters by ordering attributes in a single ranked list.
principles.quote: A general rule of complex decisions, is that often they're difficult because we've avoided making other, smaller decisions.

principles.text: Filter candidates attribute by attribute from the top rank down; the first option left alone on an attribute wins.
principles.quote: Cross out items that don't materially address the top-ranked attribute.

principles.text: A good decision must be explainable, including why rejected options lost; involving the proposer makes rejection easier to accept.
principles.quote: Not only do you need the best decision, you also need to be able to **explain your decision to others**, especially to those who wish the decision had gone a different way.

sources.title: Fermi ROI: Replace precise ROI spreadsheets with power-of-ten estimates for prioritization
sources.originalTitle: Fermi ROI: Fixing the ROI rubric
sources.summary: Traditional ROI rubrics produce false precision because impact and effort estimates are mostly noise. Jason proposes Fermi estimation: score impact and effort using only a few widely-spaced values (powers of ten, or 2d/2w/2m) so errors don't flip rankings and decisions are easy to explain. It also covers qualitative scoring, multi-factor combination, and tie-breaking.

principles.text: ROI scores computed from estimates are mostly noise; a 20% impact miss plus 50% effort miss halves the ROI.
principles.quote: In this reasonable scenario, it ended up producing *half* the ROI than originally calculated. Therefore, in retrospect, the initial ROI estimate was largely noise.

principles.text: Estimate with powers of ten only, so wrong adjacent choices are obviously absurd and scores are either identical or very different.
principles.quote: The trick--useful everywhere in life--is to estimate values using only orders-of-magnitude, a.k.a. powers-of-ten. No "low/high ranges," no precision, not even any digits other than a 1 followed by a quantity of 0s.

principles.text: Debates over Fermi-scale estimates are the valuable ones, because they expose different assumptions about customers, market, or idea.
principles.quote: But this debate is a wonderful use of our time, because it means people have wildly different assumptions, or different levels of optimism, or a different understanding of the customer, the market, or the idea.

principles.text: Estimate effort with only three choices (2 days, 2 weeks, 2 months), rounding up; it saves debate and keeps plans accurate.
principles.quote: We placed time estimates in the bottom-right corner, but the only three choices were: `2d`, `2w`, `2m`--two days, two weeks, or two months. Whatever you think the real estimate is, round up.

principles.text: For qualitative goals, break them into sub-goals, turn each into a specific question, and define exactly what each Fermi value means; multiply scores when all are required.
principles.quote: The key is to *be specific* as to what each number *means*, otherwise two people will have different interpretations for a phrase like "Insight is a 2 out of 5."

principles.text: Don't combine unlike attributes like revenue and delight; pick the most important one for ROI and use the other only to break ties.
principles.quote: There is no way to compare "revenue" with "delight." These are different units of measurement, so any combination is nonsensical.

sources.title: Talk vs Walk: plotting claims against delivery to sharpen marketing and product strategy
sources.originalTitle: The "Talk vs Walk" workshop
sources.summary: Jason Cohen describes a workshop from WP Engine that plots each company claim by how loudly you say it versus how well you deliver it. Each quadrant (exaggeration, trusted brand, unspoken weakness, silent strength) points to specific marketing or product actions, and the same chart can be run against a competitor.

principles.text: Chart each claim by how loudly you say it versus how well you deliver it, to find actions for both Marketing and Product.
principles.quote: Plotting items on a "talk" vs "walk" chart is not only useful in analyzing current-state, but also in uncovering ways that both the Marketing and Product groups can sell better and create better products.

principles.text: Collect ideas independently (write-storm) instead of live brainstorming, which follows the fastest and loudest voices.
principles.quote: Do not brain-storm items one-by-one. In live brain-storming the conversations follows the fastest and loudest people, rather than leveraging everyone's brains to invent different ideas.

principles.text: Overclaiming attracts the wrong customers; if you can't deliver on a claim, either build it or stop saying it.
principles.quote: We're attracting the wrong sort of customers--people who expect something we don't deliver.

principles.text: Where you already talk and deliver, don't over-invest; hold a minimum bar and put effort into new strengths or fixing weaknesses.
principles.quote: We're doing well here, but doing incrementally better will not win us more customers

principles.text: Don't announce a fix for a weakness before you've actually delivered it; it tips off competitors and trains customers to disbelieve you.
principles.quote: Should you shift it up (start talking publicly) before you've shifted it right (pay off the claims)? Probably not: You tip your hand to competitors, allowing them to react before you can defend.

principles.text: Avoid racing a competitor on their strength; invest in differentiating advantages where you lead, and claim credit for strengths you already have.
principles.quote: Before you decide to knuckle down and match the competitor strength-for-strength, critically consider whether you want to run a race where you're starting out behind.

sources.title: Productive meeting activities: leverage the team, empower the individual
sources.originalTitle: Productive meeting activities: Leverage the team, empower the individual
sources.summary: Jason Cohen lays out four meeting formats (ranting, ideation, decision-support, sparring practice), each defined by what one person needs from the room. He argues for declaring the type of conversation up front and keeping ownership with one individual, even when the boss is present.

principles.text: Meetings are best used to create something no one could make alone, while the decision stays with one person.
principles.quote: Meetings are most productive when we create something that none of us could have created alone.

principles.text: In ideation sessions, ask the group only to widen your options, not to pick one or decide your strategy.
principles.quote: I don't want you to solve the puzzle or decide which option is best, I just want you to help me see options that I'm not currently seeing.

principles.text: In decision-support, send your analysis ahead and ask for input. A vote is one input, not a verdict.
principles.quote: I might even ask the room to vote; not to dictate my future, but because I trust the room's opinion and I want it as another input in my decision process.

principles.text: Use sparring practice: invite Devil's Advocates to attack your work so it becomes bullet-proof, even from misinformed angles.
principles.quote: Whenever you see a brief, tight, bullet-proof document, it took a lot of work to get there.

principles.text: Declare the type of conversation you want so everyone participates correctly and facilitators can reroute it.
principles.quote: It's counterproductive when someone wants a Ranting, but receives a Sparring Practice. Declare what kind of conversation you want

principles.text: Name one owner for each decision. A decision owned by "us" is owned by no one; leaders should assist without usurping.
principles.quote: a decision made by "us" is owned by "no one," when in actual fact it *is* owned by X.

sources.title: Moats: Why durable differentiation, not just advantage, beats commoditization (AWS case)
sources.originalTitle: Moats: Durable competitive advantage
sources.summary: Industries commoditize toward zero profit unless a company builds moats: advantages competitors cannot easily copy. Using AWS as the example, the essay shows how to turn a generic moat from a taxonomy into an explicit multi-year strategy with named costs and accepted downsides.

principles.text: Industries commoditize: competitors copy features and costs, converge, and compete on price until profits hit zero.
principles.quote: Companies copy the best ideas from each other, whether in features to attract customers or cost-savings to build profits, so they converge to similar products with similar cost structures.

principles.text: A competitive advantage is not enough; it must be durable, meaning hard for rivals to copy.
principles.quote: It's not enough to have a "competitive advantage;" the advantage must also be *durable*.

principles.text: Prefer differentiation customers value (higher prices and share); cost-structure differentiation is second best.
principles.quote: Best is product differentiation that customers value, because that should lead not only to higher prices (because customers cannot get the same value elsewhere) but also greater market share.

principles.text: Even in a commoditizing market, stacking several moats (scale, ecosystem, learning curve, brand, switching costs) avoids commoditization.
principles.quote: AWS has largely avoided commoditization. The proof is in the market-share and in the profit.

principles.text: Moats take years of consistent investment, so they must be the core of strategy, not left to reactive agility.
principles.quote: Moats don't appear quickly or by accident; they require consistent investment and prioritization over a course of years.

principles.text: Naming a moat is not a strategy; specify how you'll build it and the second-order costs and failures you'll accept.
principles.quote: A strategy that states "We will create switching costs" is not a strategy; it is a statement of what you hope will become true, rather than an explanation of how you will cause that to become true.

sources.title: The Impossible Product Manager: why a great PM team beats a mythical great PM
sources.originalTitle: The "Great" Product Manager, a.k.a. the Impossible Product Manager
sources.summary: Jason Cohen argues that "Great PM" checklists describe an impossible superhuman. He splits product management into four roles (Strategist, Customer Whisperer, Scrum Product Owner, Orchestrator) and says one person can be excellent at one, good at a second, and no more. The leader's job is designing a team that covers all four.

principles.text: A great PM is excellent at one area, good at another, and has no time for a third.
principles.quote: A "Great PM" is excellent in one area, good in at least one other, and doesn't have time for more than two.

principles.text: Don't hunt unicorns. Assemble excellence across the whole product team in all four areas.
principles.quote: While one person cannot be all things to all people, across the entire product team, you do need excellence in all four areas.

principles.text: Product management centers on deciding what to build, fed by strategy and customer research, then execution and coordination.
principles.quote: The role and scope of "Product Manager" varies between companies, but the role centers on deciding what to build

principles.text: Strategy means saying no to most ideas so you can say yes to exactly the right ones.
principles.quote: Having the fortitude to make decisions that will affect us for years, and cause us to say "no" to 90% of our ideas, so we say "yes" to exactly the right ideas.

principles.text: Revenue and retention are outputs of strategy plus execution, not a strategy or operational goal themselves.
principles.quote: revenue and retention are outputs of great strategy plus great execution, not themselves a strategy or even an operational goal.

principles.text: Even small improvements in team design matter, because most organizations have excellence nowhere in these roles.
principles.quote: Even incremental improvements here can be impactful, because so often organizations have excellence nowhere.

sources.title: Failure to face the truth: why avoiding hard facts blocks strategy, teams and companies
sources.originalTitle: Failure to face the truth
sources.summary: Jason Cohen argues that a primary blocker of progress is refusing to face the truth, in feedback, meetings and strategy. He draws the pattern across Radical Candor, Five Dysfunctions, Good Strategy Bad Strategy and Good to Great (Kroger vs. A&P), and shows how fluffy language hides it.

principles.text: Failure to face the truth is a primary, invisible blocker of progress, because denial and rationalization are our default mode.
principles.quote: A primary blocker of progress, from our personal lives to our corporate strategies, is a Failure to face the truth.

principles.text: Strategy must name the monster in the room: write down the scary challenge crisply, then build a plan that attacks it head-on.
principles.quote: In every strategy discussion, there's a monster in the room no one will name, even though the point of strategy is to identify and then construct a battle plan against the monsters.

principles.text: Use meetings to surface insights; in most meetings someone is thinking something and not saying it.
principles.quote: In almost every meeting, someone is thinking something and not saying it, even though one of the best uses of a meeting is to unveil and discuss insights.

principles.text: Telling someone the truth is a courtesy, and withholding it is impolite at best and ruinous at worst, but it needs a foundation of trust.
principles.quote: The truth is a courtesy; conversely, failure to face the truth is at least impolite, and at worst "ruinous" in Scott's terminology

principles.text: Great teams build trust first so that it is safe to have constructive conflict and discuss the real issues together.
principles.quote: We must have enough trust in each other to face the truth, together.

principles.text: Seeing the truth isn't enough. Companies that win act on it; A&P saw the superstore data and shut the test down, while Kroger pivoted.
principles.quote: A&P saw the truth, but failed to face the truth.

sources.title: Extreme brainstorming questions: stretch one dimension of your business to nonsense to find 10x ideas
sources.originalTitle: Extreme brainstorming questions to trigger new, better ideas
sources.summary: Jason Cohen offers a set of "extreme" hypotheticals (10x prices, no customers, no website, no tech support, one thing this year) that jolt you out of incremental thinking. Each forces a rethink of pricing, positioning, onboarding, growth, and strategy, and sometimes one extreme becomes a company's whole moat.

principles.text: Stretch one dimension to an absurd extreme; a 60% solution there can be a 10x idea in reality.
principles.quote: An idea that would be a 60% solution in an extreme hypothetical case, could be a 2x or even a 10x idea in reality.

principles.text: Unique business models come from being extreme on a dimension competitors and critics consider impossible.
principles.quote: Unique business models emerge when at least one dimension is so extreme that it defies critics and competitors to even conceive of its possibility.

principles.text: Startups undercharge and incumbents fear raising prices; ask what would justify 10x and you can likely justify 2x.
principles.quote: Often early startups charge too little, and established companies struggle to charge more to existing customers.

principles.text: Don't win on features alone; copycats will match them, so differentiate emotionally through brand, trust, and mission.
principles.quote: All your good ideas will be copied; it's just a question of when. Competing only on features results in bullet-point battles; this is the weakest way to win sales.

principles.text: Make the product itself a growth channel; advocates already use it, so build marketing into the product.
principles.quote: Your advocates are already using your product, yet so often we leave "getting more customers" to the marketing department, rather than realizing the product is already a platform for growth.

principles.text: Ask what single initiative you'd ship if you could only ship one thing this year; a business trajectory is usually 1-2 big decisions per year.
principles.quote: When you look back over years of a business, often the whole trajectory comes down to 1-2 big decisions per year.

sources.title: Why hypergrowth is quadratic, not exponential: the Elephant Curve model of growth
sources.originalTitle: The Elephant in the room: The myth of exponential hypergrowth
sources.summary: Jason Cohen shows with data from Facebook, Slack, Dropbox, HubSpot and others that "hypergrowth" companies grow quadratically, not exponentially. Each marketing campaign, product or geography follows an "Elephant Curve" (ramp, plateau, decline), and stacking many of them produces a wavy quadratic. He turns this into a way to model growth by component and to manage marketing and product portfolios.

principles.text: High-growth companies grow quadratically, not exponentially, even "viral" ones like Facebook and Slack.
principles.quote: My thesis is that **High-growth companies grow quadratically, not exponentially.**

principles.text: Measure growth in absolute numbers, not percentages. CAGR language implicitly assumes an exponential process.
principles.quote: In general when you use "CAGR" or "percentage growth" as a metric, you are implicitly saying "This is an exponential process."

principles.text: Every marketing campaign has a life cycle: unproductive start, rapid ramp to a natural level, optimization, then decline from saturation, channel decay or uneconomical auctions.
principles.quote: At the foot of the curve, we've launched a new campaign, but it's ineffective; we haven't figured out the best design and messaging and calls-to-action for this new medium and audience.

principles.text: Overall growth is a layer-cake of campaigns, products and geographies, each roughly linear once going. Adding linear things over time yields a quadratic.
principles.quote: "Adding more linear things over time" is the definition of a quadratic.

principles.text: Viral and word-of-mouth products are exponential only early, then follow a logistic curve as the market saturates, flattening into linear growth.
principles.quote: The logistic curve *is* exponential in the early days when it is far away from its natural limit.

principles.text: Forecast growth by modeling components separately (market size, market share, revenue per customer), then multiply them.
principles.quote: You get better models by predicting each of these components separately, then multiplying for a final growth prediction.

sources.title: Who's lying?: use redundant, differently-built data sources to catch bad metrics
sources.originalTitle: Who's lying?
sources.summary: Using a pilot's lesson (stuck fuel gauges, checked with a wooden stick), Jason argues that important business metrics must be derived two different ways, because some data is always lying. Redundancy catches errors and also gives a fuller picture of what is driving the numbers.

principles.text: Redundancy must be differently implemented, not just duplicated; two things sharing a failure mode fail together.
principles.quote: It's not even good enough to just have "two of everything." If two things both rely on electricity, and the electricity goes out, you lose both.

principles.text: Always ask 'Who's lying?' about your metrics: usually they're right, but sometimes one is wrong and you won't know.
principles.quote: Usually your instruments are correct, but sometimes one is lying.

principles.text: Cross-check key numbers across independent systems, such as billing vs bank, Stripe vs your user portal, analytics vs raw logs.
principles.quote: Revenue from your billing system compared to cash flows from your bank statements.

principles.text: Data errors come from mundane causes: formula bugs, missing tracking code, unsent surveys, bad query filters, dead update scripts.
principles.quote: The spreadsheet had a subtle bug in a formula, the analytics JavaScript code was accidentally left off one page, the survey email didn't get sent to all the customers in the cohort

principles.text: Computing the same data multiple ways also improves understanding of the forces behind it; biased sources partly cancel when combined.
principles.quote: None has the full picture; all are biased. But taken together, your picture of the world is more complete, and biases might be cancelled through averaging

principles.text: Any metric watched daily and acted on deserves a second, independent check for accuracy and comprehension.
principles.quote: If a metric is important enough to watch it every day, and to act if its behavior deviates from expectation, then it's important enough to be double-checked.

sources.title: The Important Thing: one thing done so well it overrides all of a startup's deficiencies
sources.originalTitle: The Important Thing⁠--powerful enough to override all your deficiencies
sources.summary: Jason Cohen argues that breakout startups don't fix their many weaknesses. They deliver one thing so compelling that customers tolerate everything else. Using the iPhone, Heroku and Basecamp as examples, he says founders should pick the one thing they can obsess over for years and let other fires burn.

principles.text: Startups win by getting one thing so right that it overrides the torrent of things going wrong.
principles.quote: they need one thing to go really _really_ right, to overcome the torrent of things that are going wrong.

principles.text: A single compelling benefit can make customers tolerate a product's flaws; the first iPhone launched with a mountain of issues yet won.
principles.quote: But, the iPhone did something so well, that people wanted so badly, they would put up with all the other crap: You could use the internet.

principles.text: When the Important Thing is strong, customers adapt to you. Heroku's users changed their workflows and code around it.
principles.quote: Developers changed their workflows and their code around Heroku and "12-Factor" apps; Heroku did not change to suit developers.

principles.text: A great Important Thing cancels weaknesses: referrals offset no marketing, tolerance offsets weak support, and excitement offsets no brand.
principles.quote: So great that people tell their friends or force their colleagues to use it too (defeating the lack of marketing). So great that they'll use it even if support is slow and releases have bugs (defeating the lack of operational excellence).

principles.text: The Important Thing need not be a feature. It can be a lifestyle, reputation, overlooked market, culture, or a cause people want to support.
principles.quote: It could be a feature (e.g. disappearing messages with Snapchat), but you can look beyond features. It could be enabling a lifestyle (such as remote-work or with-kids-work).

principles.text: Don't attack every weakness at once. Pick one thing you can obsess over for 5-10 years that excites customers and is executable, and let the other fires burn.
principles.quote: You should select something that you *want* to obsess over for the next five to ten years, that gets your customers excited, and which you at least have a possibility of executing.

sources.title: Capturing luck: use "or" paths instead of stacking "and" requirements
sources.originalTitle: Capturing luck with "or" instead of "and"
sources.summary: Startups need many things to go right at once, and multiplying those probabilities makes success unlikely. Jason Cohen argues you can improve your odds by reducing the number of "and" dependencies and building in many parallel "or" paths, because optionality is strength.

principles.text: Startup success is a chain of "and" requirements, so total odds are the product of each probability.
principles.quote: Each one has a probability of success, and you compute the total probability of success by multiplying them.

principles.text: Even optimistic odds collapse when many things must all go right.
principles.quote: 70% multiplied by itself six times is only 12%; most of these things we're listing have a probability less than 70%, and there are more than six things that have to go right.

principles.text: Remove "and" risks up front by choosing a big, healthy market and a niche where incumbents don't care.
principles.quote: You can pick a large, growing, and healthy market so that the risk that "no one wants to solve this problem" goes to zero.

principles.text: Reduce people risk by hiring someone you've worked with before, or avoiding the hire entirely.
principles.quote: You can hire someone you've worked with before, or build something sustainable without hiring.

principles.text: Stack "or" options: you only need one acquisition channel to work, so try several.
principles.quote: Only one of these needs to work! So although the probability of success for each one of these is low, the probability that *something* will work is higher.

principles.text: Optionality is strength: many ways to win is a strong position even before any of them has worked.
principles.quote: The general rule is **optionality is strength.** When there are lots of ways for things to go right, that is a strong position even if you haven't actualized one of those ways.

sources.title: Distributed Logical Time: a simple, constant-memory clock for decentralized replicas
sources.originalTitle: Distributed Logical Time
sources.summary: A technical essay on a hybrid logical clock with skew correction that orders events across independent replicas without central coordination or vector clocks. The takeaways for builders are about design constraints: bound the error, keep memory constant, avoid central points, and favor simplicity.

principles.text: Simplicity is a core requirement for scalability and truly bug-free code.
principles.quote: Simplicity is a core requirement for scalability and truly bug-free code.

principles.text: Design so error is a small bounded constant, not proportional to system state or configuration.
principles.quote: `e` must be small (e.g. 1-2 seconds), and be a constant, not proportional to some state or configuration.

principles.text: Avoid central coordination: no leaders, no join/leave announcements, no peer list, so participants can come and go freely.
principles.quote: No leaders, no special designations, no central API. Peers can communicate in arbitrary patterns. Peers never need to announce their joining or leaving the collective.

principles.text: Use constant memory per item regardless of scale, rather than structures that grow with the number of participants.
principles.quote: Use a fixed number of bits to represent LT, regardless of factors like the number of replicas.

principles.text: Don't depend on infrastructure you can't control; make the system tolerate unreliable inputs like bad clocks.
principles.quote: However, our implementation does not assume control over PT. A replica might be a browser or laptop that we don't control, or a virtual machine that isn't running NTP.

principles.text: Be precisely correct on what must never break (happened-before) and accept best-effort on what is merely nice, and state non-goals explicitly.
principles.quote: If A happens, then the two replicas communicate, then B happens, then it is *always* true that `LT{ B>A }`, even if `RT{ B-A } < e`.

sources.title: Jason Cohen: When to make decisions fast vs. slow
sources.originalTitle: When should a decision be fast, or slow?
sources.summary: Jason argues decisions should default to fast, because speed accelerates action and learning. He lists the conditions that justify slowing down: irreversibility, huge effort, unfamiliar decision types, unmeasurable progress and imperfect information. He frames these as honest questions, not a scorecard.

principles.text: Default to fast decisions; speed drives action and the feedback loop that out-learns competitors.
principles.quote: Fast decisions leads to rapid action, which accelerates the loop of production and feedback, which is how you outpace and out-learn a competitor, even one that already has a lead.

principles.text: Don't decide now what you'll decide much better later, once you have real customer experience.
principles.quote: If we haven't launched a product yet, we're in no position to decide what the next few features should be; we should launch and earn experience through customer interactions.

principles.text: If a decision costs less to implement than to debate, just do it.
principles.quote: If the effort to implement the decision is smaller than the effort to make a decision, just knock it out.

principles.text: Slow down for irreversible decisions; invest in analyzing upsides and risks.
principles.quote: If you can't easily undo the decision, it's worth investing more effort into analyzing the likelihood of the upsides and risks.

principles.text: Under time pressure, dragging out a decision adds risk by eating implementation time.
principles.quote: time-pressure means the more time you spend deciding, the less time you have for implementation and unanticipated problems, so you're actually adding risk by dragging out the decision.

principles.text: Be more deliberate on decision types your organization has never made before, like pricing or acquisitions.
principles.quote: When the organization has never made this type of decision before, the decision is at great risk, and being more deliberate with research, data, debate, or even outside advice, is wise.

sources.title: How repositioning from "save money" to "create growth" lets you charge 8x for the same product
sources.originalTitle: How repositioning a product allows you to 8x its price
sources.summary: Jason Cohen argues that pricing is driven by positioning and perceived value, not cost analysis. Using a hypothetical AdWords tool, he shows that a "generate growth" pitch is worth a multiple of a "save money" pitch, both in value created and in the share of it customers will pay. Frame your product in the way your customer already measures value.

principles.text: Pricing depends on positioning and perceived value, not cost analysis or ROI calculators.
principles.quote: Pricing is much more about positioning and perceived value than it is about cost-analysis and unconvincing ROI calculators.

principles.text: A business values growing faster about 10x more than saving money, so sell growth.
principles.quote: It's always 10x more valuable for a business to grow faster than it is for the business to save money.

principles.text: Under a savings pitch you can only charge a fraction of the savings, because the customer must keep most of the value.
principles.quote: In the "saves money" pitch, the value was $20,000, and the customer needed to keep 75% of that value-creation.

principles.text: Under a growth pitch the customer will pay all of the value created, since the extra spend buys more growth at a similar unit cost.
principles.quote: in the "generate growth" pitch, the value is $40,000, and the customer is happy to pay 100% of that value-creation to a vendor.

principles.text: Repositioning raises both the value created and the share the customer will pay, so price rises by a multiple.
principles.quote: Both the amount of value created, and the percentage of value the customer is willing to pay, is a multiple higher for the "growth" pitch versus the "save money" pitch.

principles.text: Don't pitch saving time, money or efficiency; tie the product to how the customer already measures value.
principles.quote: figure out how your product creates value in the way your customer already measures value, and position your product as a way to accomplish that.

sources.title: Build a SLC, not an MVP: Simple, Lovable, Complete first versions
sources.originalTitle: Your customers hate MVPs. Make a SLC instead.
sources.summary: Jason Cohen argues the MVP is a selfish process that hands customers unfinished, embarrassing products. He proposes SLC (Simple, Lovable, Complete) as the first version: small enough to ship fast, loved enough to win customers, and complete enough to stand alone. Delight can be prioritized over utility from day one.

principles.text: Customers hate MVPs: they are too minimal and rarely viable, which serves the team's learning at the customer's expense.
principles.quote: The problem is: Customers hate MVPs.

principles.text: Ship a version 1.0 of something simple, not a version 0.1 of something complex. Simple is fine; incomplete is not.
principles.quote: Not because it's version 0.1 of something complex, but because it's version 1.0 of something simple.

principles.text: Love beats features. A loved product with few features outperforms a feature-rich product people dislike, and growth loops depend on love.
principles.quote: Products that do less but are loved, are more successful than products which have more features and are disliked.

principles.text: Love can come from many sources beyond UI design: company culture and transparency, genuinely helpful content, or a deep connection to the customer's psyche.
principles.quote: There are many ways to generate love. "Minimum" and "viable" are definitely *not* among those ways.

principles.text: A SLC product holds value even with no further investment, whereas an MVP that stops getting investment is just a bad product. Starting simple doesn't prevent growing complex later.
principles.quote: An MVP that never gets additional investment is just a bad product. A SLC that never gets additional investment is a good, if modest product.

principles.text: Product development needn't climb from utility up to delight. Prioritizing delight early, within a narrow but complete scope, wins hearts and can even deliver meaning and identity.
principles.quote: The "pyramid" is useful for mapping out where you're going to spend your time, but we need not traverse it from bottom to top. Products that prioritize delight win over products that don't.

sources.title: Change: Why the right choice is almost always to change, and how to manage it kindly
sources.originalTitle: Change: Damned if you do, damned more if you don't
sources.summary: Jason Cohen argues that everyone wants change but nobody wants to change, yet the right choice is almost always to change because it reflects new facts or a shifting environment. Leaders must recognize that change is exhausting, watch for burnout, and manage it with kindness while still holding organizations accountable for striving to improve.

principles.text: The right choice is almost always to change, since change responds to new facts, learning, or environment shifts.
principles.quote: **The right choice is almost always "change."** This is because change is a reaction to uncovering facts, getting smarter, or a shift in the external environment.

principles.text: Organizations that prefer the comfort of the familiar over the discomfort of change die.
principles.quote: Death awaits any organization that chooses the comfort of the familiar over the discomfort of change.

principles.text: Strategy that never changes despite new information is wrong, but constant flux makes strategy ineffective too.
principles.quote: [Strategy](https://longform.asmartbear.com/great-strategy/) is ineffective if it's constantly in flux, but a strategy that remains unchanged in the presence of new information is incorrect.

principles.text: Even change-loving people need breaks; leaders should watch for burnout and decision-fatigue and address it proactively.
principles.quote: Even your most stoic, change-loving mortals sometimes need a break from change.

principles.text: Distinguish a rudderless company from a culture of self-reflection, since constant change can feel like no plan.
principles.quote: Constant change can feel like management has no plan and no strategy. It takes careful consideration to distinguish between being rudderless and a culture of self-reflection and improvement.

principles.text: What got you here won't necessarily get you there; success can stall from losing core insights or from dogmatism when the world or scale changes.
principles.quote: It is not generally true that "what got us here will get us there," and that means deep change is required.

sources.title: Satisficing vs Maximizing: when to decide fast and when to obsess
sources.originalTitle: Satisficing vs Maximizing
sources.summary: Jason Cohen separates maximizing (finding the best option) from satisficing (taking the first acceptable one) and argues you must pick deliberately for each decision. Speed is a startup's edge, so satisfice almost everything, and save maximizing for slow, foundational calls like product and business strategy.

principles.text: Decide on purpose whether each decision calls for maximizing or satisficing.
principles.quote: You must choose when to Maximize, and when to Satisfice.

principles.text: Speed is a major competitive advantage, and it requires satisficing rather than maximizing.
principles.quote: Speed is one of the greatest competitive advantages, partially explaining why small up-starts are able to beat large incumbents. Speed requires satisficing, not maximizing.

principles.text: Ship and let customer reaction and real data pick your next move instead of planning many moves ahead.
principles.quote: using customer reaction and real data to decide your next move, rather than planning many moves ahead

principles.text: Maximize product and business strategy, since teams and careers are built on it and it shouldn't change often.
principles.quote: Strategy isn't something you want to change often, with entire teams and careers being built on top of it, so maximization is best.

principles.text: Perfectionists tend to over-maximize, so default to satisficing for anything that isn't a major decision.
principles.quote: Be careful; the same perfectionism that makes you a force to be reckoned with (and that drives your impostor syndrome) will lead you to maximize too often.

principles.text: For areas you satisfice, set an objective bar for 'good enough' and stop investing once you clear it.
principles.quote: For satisfying activities, define an objective threshold for "what is satisfactory."

sources.title: Look what we did: why a founder says "we" and sees a company as a tree, not a seed
sources.originalTitle: Look what we did
sources.summary: Jason Cohen reflects on being credited with creating WP Engine and reframes the founder as only the seed of a tree that hundreds of people sustain. He argues a company's purpose lies in the journey and in what each person gains from their time there, not in the founder's glory.

principles.text: The founder is the seed, not the tree. Credit the hundreds of people who build the company every day.
principles.quote: "WP Engine is an oak tree," I explain. "I was the seed. The tree wouldn't exist without the seed, so the seed *was* important, and holds a special and permanent place in the history of the tree. But nothing you see today is the seed.

principles.text: Most of what keeps a company alive is invisible: security upgrades, finance, quality practice. All of it is vital.
principles.quote: things you cannot are the 3am security upgrade and the start of a long-term new product category and brand strategy and collecting accounts receivable and quarterly financial reporting

principles.text: Employees will eventually leave, so make the company a place they look back on as time well spent.
principles.quote: It's up to all of us to make sure each person will look back on their time at WP Engine as well-spent.

principles.text: Judge a company by what it does for people's lives: growth, careers, firsts, and impact on customers and the next generation.
principles.quote: Did they grow as a person, as well as professionally? Did they have an impact on others' lives, where they helped the next generation thrive as they have?

principles.text: A company, like a life, finds its purpose in the journey, not the end.
principles.quote: The purpose of a company--or a life--resides in

sources.title: Building in public: why it forces durable competitive advantage, quality code, and great culture
sources.originalTitle: Building in public forces true competitive advantage
sources.summary: Jason Cohen argues that building in public isn't a risk to your moat but a forcing function. Public code gets judged so quality rises, and if copying is easy you must build non-technical, permanent advantages. Open pay and transparency push you toward a culture of autonomy, growth and purpose.

principles.text: Public scrutiny forces higher quality because ego, the desire to impress peers, is a universal motivator.
principles.quote: In this sense, **building in public would force you to create quality, artful code.**

principles.text: If your product can be copied, you must build a non-technical moat like a marketplace or network, whose value money can't replicate.
principles.quote: You are therefore forced to build some other, non-technical [competitive advantage](https://longform.asmartbear.com/moats/) into your business.

principles.text: Technical advantages are usually fleeting and copiers often do it faster and cheaper, so first to market rarely means winning.
principles.quote: But this is rare; typically a technical advantage is a fleeting advantage, because most technical things can be replicated.

principles.text: The most valuable company assets, like buyers and sellers on a marketplace, can't be replicated by copying software.
principles.quote: The value in these companies  [cannot be replicated with money](https://longform.asmartbear.com/startup-money/), which is exactly why those companies are valuable.

principles.text: Transparent pay removes the extra-cash lever, forcing you to attract talent through culture and mission, not mercenary compensation.
principles.quote: This forces you to build a company where great talent *wants* to work, where people are there for the culture and mission rather than as mercenaries.

principles.text: Great talent environments rest on autonomy, growth, and purpose.
principles.quote: in general they include **Autonomy** (i.e. freedom to explore, the control and empowerment to invent solutions to problems

sources.title: Why 10x patterns show up everywhere in startups: pricing, people, channels, products
sources.originalTitle: Laws of 10x found everywhere
sources.summary: Jason Cohen argues that a "10x rule" is a useful default assumption across startups. Best products, channels, people, products-in-a-portfolio and decisions tend to outperform the rest by roughly 10x, so you should hunt for the one 10x truth instead of fiddling with a hundred variables.

principles.text: Assume a 10x truth exists in your business and spend your time finding it, rather than tuning many minor variables.
principles.quote: it's useful to assume there is a 10x truth, and spend your time seeking that truth, rather than worrying about and fiddling with one hundred variables, almost none of which will turn out to be important.

principles.text: Winning products need at least one attribute that is 10x better than all competitors.
principles.quote: Winning products have at least one attribute that's 10x better than all competitors (and it's not necessarily design, though it can be).

principles.text: Your best marketing channel is often about 10x as productive as the next best, so concentrate on one.
principles.quote: Your best marketing channel is often 10x the productivity of the next-best. True of content-marketing also.

principles.text: SaaS markets follow a power law: the winner can take 10x the profits of the runner-up.
principles.quote: SaaS returns in a market are a power law; winner can take 10x the profits of the next.

principles.text: Companies don't naturally grow 10x in size or quality; it takes intentional focus and investment.
principles.quote: Companies do not naturally 10x their size or quality; that achievement requires intentional focus and investment.

principles.text: In a multi-product company, one product often outearns all the others combined; one or two decisions matter more than the rest together.
principles.quote: For multi-product companies, often one product generates more revenue than all the rest combined.

sources.title: Worrying is self-fulfilling: replace it with preparation
sources.originalTitle: Worrying is self-fulfilling; what to do instead
sources.summary: Jason argues that worry actively causes the bad outcomes it fears, because it injects second-guessing and fear into the moment of execution. The antidote isn't apathy but preparation: long-term deliberate practice and short-term visualization, then clearing your mind and executing. He applies this to the many worries founders carry.

principles.text: Worry is a self-fulfilling prophecy; it breaks things that aren't broken instead of leading to solutions.
principles.quote: "Worry" causes the thing you're worried about, to actually happen.

principles.text: The opposite of worry is preparation, not apathy.
principles.quote: The opposite of "Worry" isn't "Apathy". The opposite is "Preparation".

principles.text: Prepare long-term: purposeful repetition of specific skills and planning effort across a season so you peak when it matters.
principles.quote: They plan energy output and practice-schedules across an entire season, such that they peak during the most important meets.

principles.text: Visualize the action ahead of time, then clear your mind and execute on muscle memory rather than thinking mid-action.
principles.quote: you should visualize the shot ahead of time, then clear your mind and execute using muscle-memory.

principles.text: Once you've done the practice, stop second-guessing; mistakes matter less than you think since nobody is counting but you.
principles.quote: you should realize you've already done all the practice required, and mistakes don't actually matter anyway. No one is counting except you.

principles.text: Founder worries (payroll, competitors, closing a customer, metrics) are destructive; tackle the root constructively, prepare, then proceed.
principles.quote: Instead, tackle the root of the worry constructively, prepare yourself as best you can, and then just proceed.

sources.title: Jason Cohen on simplifying complex decisions by separating upside from downside
sources.originalTitle: How to simplify complex decisions by cleaving the facts
sources.summary: Circular debates happen because pros and cons are mixed together. Jason Cohen says to split upside from downside, decide and invest based on upside, use downside only as a veto, reduce the choice to at most three dimensions, then pick a process and move on.

principles.text: Separate upside from downside to escape circular arguments; each side can be true and the debate still never converges.
principles.quote: The symptom of not following this advice is arguing in logical circles.

principles.text: Decide primarily on upside, and use downside only as a veto when it is unworkable and can't be mitigated.
principles.quote: By basing the primary decision on the upside, and using the downside only as a "veto" when it is unworkable, you have further clarified how to make the decision.

principles.text: Hire leaders for exceptional strengths and fill their weaknesses through the rest of the team.
principles.quote: you should hire based on their exceptional strengths, and then fill in weaknesses using the composition of the rest of the team.

principles.text: Over-invest in a 10x strength rather than lifting weaknesses to neutral; weaknesses are tolerated if the strength is big enough.
principles.quote: developing a 10x strength is far more valuable than shifting a weakness to neutral.

principles.text: Deliberately over-simplify to at most three key dimensions; otherwise you never reach a firm decision.
principles.quote: if you don't intentionally over-simplify, you will never reach a firm and clear decision.

principles.text: Decide quickly with a chosen process; defining the conditions of the decision is most of the work.
principles.quote: Remember that defining the conditions of the decision is 80% of the decision, so invest your time in that.

sources.title: What if there isn't another 10x? Why growth isn't the only path for a mature company
sources.originalTitle: What if there isn't another 10x?
sources.summary: Jason Cohen argues that no company 10x's forever, and that tech's obsession with growth multiples eventually stops being the right question. Once a business has likely peaked, he says its true impact comes from applying its success to betterment (jobs, working conditions, community) rather than only biggerment.

principles.text: Asking "how do we 10x?" suits a young startup but cannot remain the right question forever.
principles.quote: "How do we 10x" is a great question when a startup is young. Does it always remain the right question?

principles.text: No company grows 10x forever; even Google responds by becoming a conglomerate of separate companies that could each 10x.
principles.quote: At some point it cannot be the right question. No company 10x's forever. Not even Google.

principles.text: The tech industry overweights growth in valuation, even when a slower-growing company produces far more cash profit.
principles.quote: Nevermind that Microsoft created more cash profit in 2015 than Facebook made in revenue.

principles.text: If another 10x isn't plausible, redirect attention to employees, communities, and using your infrastructure for something important.
principles.quote: how could you be redirecting your attention to other important things, like creating more jobs and better working conditions, to be a catalyst for employee's personal growth, to give back to relevant communities

principles.text: Ploughing everything back into 10x growth isn't optimal for making your dent in the universe; true impact is set when you turn to betterment.
principles.quote: it is at that moment, when a company is applied to betterment instead of (only) biggerment, that the nature of a company's true dent in the universe is determined.

principles.text: Expanding beyond a core product is hard: Dropbox, OpenTable and Yelp may simply be excellent at one thing, not platforms for everything.
principles.quote: What if Dropbox is just an awesome file-sharing and backup service but not a universal key/value storage API and native document format?

sources.title: How to measure forecast accuracy: Brier score, discernment, and the climatic baseline
sources.originalTitle: How to measure the accuracy of forecasts
sources.summary: Jason Cohen explains how to grade probabilistic forecasts like lead scoring or churn prediction. Accuracy alone is gameable, so you also need discernment, and you judge both against the baseline of just guessing the average. He shows the math with a weather example.

principles.text: Judge a probability forecast by bucketing predictions and checking actual outcomes per bucket, never by a single data point.
principles.quote: Gather all the days in which the meteorologist predicted 30%. If the meteorologist is accurate, it will have rained 30% of those times.

principles.text: Accuracy alone is a trap: a forecaster who always predicts the average scores perfectly while being useless.
principles.quote: If all we compute is Accuracy Error, we fall for a trap in which we easily forecast with perfect accuracy, while also being utterly useless.

principles.text: A good forecast must be discerning: it segments the population and takes a stand instead of echoing the overall average.
principles.quote: Staking a claim that isn't just copying the overall average.

principles.text: Discernment is core to forecast quality. A bold forecaster who is usually right beats a safe one with less error.
principles.quote: So the idea of "discernment" isn't just a curiosity, it's a fundamental component of how "good" a forecaster is.

principles.text: Judge discernment against what the data allows. Where outcomes barely vary, there is little room to be discerning.
principles.quote: It's not fair to ask the forecaster to be more discerning than the variation that is actually available to discern.

principles.text: Use churn, upgrade, and lead-conversion predictions as testable models, and score each iteration to see if it truly improves.
principles.quote: If you could predict the chance that a given customer will churn in the next thirty days, you could be proactive and perhaps avert the loss

sources.title: Invention is Drudgery: why great things take unglamorous, relentless trial and error
sources.originalTitle: Invention is Drudgery
sources.summary: Jason Cohen argues that every creation, from Edison's light bulb to a band's gig, rests on enormous hidden drudgery. We see only the finished result, so we feel bad about being mid-journey, and quit. Those who succeed are the ones who plodded through the failures.

principles.text: Success is built on hidden drudgery; we only see the visible glory, so we underestimate the work required.
principles.quote: In the audience, we enjoy the show, blind to the hundred hours of toil behind each visible hour of glory.

principles.text: Don't compare your Chapter Four to someone else's last page; everyone has to take the whole journey.
principles.quote: Having skipped to the last page of other peoples' book, we forget that they took the journey of the whole book.

principles.text: Creating something great demands trial and error through thousands of failures, not a single flash of invention.
principles.quote: But the ones who eventually succeed are the ones who plodded through the 5,999 filaments that didn't work, put in the 10,000 hours master a craft, and fought through the overwhelming pile of challenges and drudgery that is always required to create something great.

principles.text: Products have no clear finish line like a book, which makes it hard to know whether to persist or quit.
principles.quote: A book has a clear end; products don't. It's often unclear whether it's smarter to continue or to quit.

principles.text: Quitting is tempting because the grind is real; the next job or startup won't be free of drudgery either.
principles.quote: We quit the job thinking wrongly that the next company will be so much better.

principles.text: Outsiders will dismiss hard-won success as luck, and they are not entirely wrong; do it for the meaning of accomplishment.
principles.quote: And that's the cue for others to dismiss it as mostly luck. The most annoying part is: They're not altogether wrong.

sources.title: Darwin doesn't pick the best companies: why growth at all costs fails and values can drive growth
sources.originalTitle: Darwin doesn't automatically select the best companies
sources.summary: "Survival of the fittest" means most prolific, not best. When growth rate is the only measure of fitness, profitability and betterment of humanity go unsolved. Cohen argues founders should let their values drive growth, citing Buffer, TOMS and USAA as examples.

principles.text: Growth is the right goal in winner-take-all markets, but growth at all costs is the problem.
principles.quote: There's nothing inherently wrong with obsessing over growth. In winner-take-all markets, growth is objectively the correct goal.

principles.text: If growth rate is your only fitness metric, other metrics like profitability stay unsolved.
principles.quote: When "growth rate" becomes the only important metric for company "fitness," other metrics are left unsolved.

principles.text: Winning the growth race is not a business model; many winners never convert from virus to business.
principles.quote: Many companies who won the growth battle never figure out how to convert themselves from a virus to a business.

principles.text: Don't trade growth off against values; use your values to drive growth.
principles.quote: The real question is not how to retard growth in submission to other values, but rather how to use our insistence values to drive growth.

principles.text: Transparency and positivity attract talent even at lower pay and with an undifferentiated product (Buffer).
principles.quote: talent nevertheless beats their door down to work there even in cases where they know ahead of time they'll take a pay-cut

principles.text: A mission people want to retell is a viral story that can beat a superior product (TOMS).
principles.quote: TOMS shoes is a massive success, not because of a superior product, but because of a viral story that people want to support and retell, exactly because its mission is so commendable and pure.
