sources.title: Why 90% utilization breaks teams: the non-linear cost of running without slack
sources.originalTitle: Your non-linear problem of 90% utilization
sources.summary: Using a web-server analogy, Jason Cohen argues that running people and teams near full capacity makes them brittle. Variation and interruption are inevitable, so teams need slack and should reserve high-gear surges for short, justified periods.

principles.text: Running at 90% utilization makes a system brittle: normal variation alone pushes it past capacity.
principles.quote: Even normal variations in traffic will drive the server past its capacity. The average time to respond to a request will skyrocket, and often requests will be dropped altogether.

principles.text: Pooling at 70% across a team still fails when one member drops out; redundancy needs real spare capacity.
principles.quote: The 2 remaining servers now have to deal with 2.1 servers' worth of traffic. Both are at 105% capacity, and we're back to broken and brittle.

principles.text: Overloaded people don't absorb shocks; they pass them on, causing cascading failure across the org.
principles.quote: Since they are over capacity, rather than absorb the spike, they too will ripple the problem to others--a cascade like the run-away chain reaction of an atom bomb.

principles.text: High utilization costs output, not just wellbeing, because of constant context-switching and interruption.
principles.quote: This condition is a combination of frequent context-switching and interruption--the Twin Enemies of productivity.

principles.text: Variation is inevitable, so design work-styles to be resilient to it rather than trying to plan it away.
principles.quote: you need to build a system that assumes variation and interruption, and design your personal and team's work-style to be resilient to that variation.

principles.text: Stay in a safe zone most of the time; allow surges only briefly and for good cause, such as launches or time-bounded rallies.
principles.quote: The ideal is probably a situation where most of the time you're in the safe zone, with occasional surges into high gear for a short period of time and for good cause.

sources.title: Why acquisitions aren't always failures: independent companies change and fail too
sources.originalTitle: Refutation: An acquisition is always a failure
sources.summary: Jason Cohen refutes the claim that every acquisition is a failure. Companies change constantly whether independent or acquired, most startups fail either way, and a well-chosen sale can create liquidity, jobs, and opportunity for founders, employees, and products. He argues the useful question is when acquisition is wise.

principles.text: Companies change constantly; expecting a startup to keep its early 'youthful energy' by staying independent is naive.
principles.quote: A company won't be a band of six people doing whatever they want forever, whether you sell or stay independent.

principles.text: Don't judge an acquisition by the founder's feelings; post-exit sadness is typical even after great exits.
principles.quote: More likely, the typical postpartum depression that naturally follows even the most successful of exits.

principles.text: Judge a deal by what it does for employees too: most people prefer stability, better pay, and new opportunities over founder-style risk.
principles.quote: Most people don't have a founder's temperament for independence and risk. What if those people *wanted* those jobs?

principles.text: Bad outcomes happen at independent companies too; compare acquisition failure rates against the failure rate of staying independent.
principles.quote: People love quoting statistics about how most acquisitions are failures, but they forget to mention that most independent startups also fail

principles.text: A sale can be the right call even if founders later leave; leaving doesn't prove the choice was wrong for them, employees, or the product.
principles.quote: In many of those cases the founders left ahead of others, and yes they went back to founder-y types of activity. That doesn't prove it wasn't the right choice at the time

principles.text: Replace superlatives with the real question: under what conditions is acquisition good for all parties?
principles.quote: we ask "When is acquisition wise?" and "What are the conditions under which acquisitions are likely to be good for all parties?"

sources.title: Why it's nice to compete against a large, profitable company: their profit stream is a prison
sources.originalTitle: Why it's nice to compete against a large, profitable company
sources.summary: Jason Cohen argues that a big, profitable incumbent is a better target than it looks, because defending its revenue stream stops it from matching a cheaper, just-good-enough upstart. The exception is attacking a loss-leader, where the incumbent can outspend you and has nothing to lose.

principles.text: An incumbent's large, profitable revenue stream proves a big market, willingness to pay well above cost, and a slow decline you can exploit.
principles.quote: The profitable revenue stream is a prison. It's the Achilles heel that allows the little guy to win.

principles.text: Undercut a profitable incumbent on price with a new cost structure; a just-good-enough product at a fraction of the price can win.
principles.quote: A startup with new cost structures, new technology, and new ideas can be competitive at 1/2 or possibly even 1/10 the price, even if the product is merely just-good-enough.

principles.text: Big companies protect profit at all costs, so they won't cut prices to chase you, even if it means giving up on innovation or speed.
principles.quote: The goal of a large company is to protect the profit stream at all costs, even if that means giving up on innovation or speed.

principles.text: Price cuts hit incumbents' profits disproportionately, so they cannot follow a startup's deep discount.
principles.quote: If you lower top-line prices by 20%, your costs don't magically decrease 20%, so now your profits are 0%.

principles.text: Large companies are valued on future earnings, not growth for its own sake, so they will not sacrifice earnings for growth to fight you.
principles.quote: In the big-boy and big-girl world of real, at-scale companies, valuation is about total future earnings.

principles.text: Never attack an incumbent's loss-leader; with deep pockets and no profit motive in that line, they are the scariest competitor.
principles.quote: Attacking a profitable business on its loss-leaders is a terrible strategy, because it can use all its powers against you, plus orders of magnitude more dollars

sources.title: Zero-sum marketing channels: why startups should invest in non-zero-sum channels instead
sources.originalTitle: Zero-sum marketing channels: Good or bad for a startup to pursue?
sources.summary: Jason Cohen argues that channels like AdWords and top-ranking SEO are zero-sum: winners lock out others, cost top dollar, and are capped in volume. Startups are better off investing in non-zero-sum channels like social, content, long-tail SEO and resellers, where success depends on yourself and the ceiling is the market itself.

principles.text: Zero-sum channels (AdWords, top SEO slots) mean winning costs top dollar for capped inventory.
principles.quote: So, even if you win a zero-sum channel, your growth in that channel is capped, and expensive.

principles.text: Invest in non-zero-sum channels, where the limit is the market itself, not one ad platform's slice of it.
principles.quote: Whereas if you invest in non-zero-sum channels like social media, long-tail SEO, brand-building, content, value-added resellers, or even cold-calling, the limit of the channel is closer to the limit of the market itself

principles.text: Prefer channels where success depends on you, not on a platform's rules or a competitor's willingness to burn money.
principles.quote: your success is dependent almost exclusively on yourself, not dependent on how some advertising platform works, or how much money some competitor is willing lose.

principles.text: Small companies can't outspend big or funded ones in zero-sum fights, but big players can't stop you winning elsewhere.
principles.quote: there's nothing the big guys can do to prevent you from shining in the other games.

principles.text: Focus on the few things a startup controls: product, culture and your voice online.
principles.quote: There are few things in startups that you control. The product, your culture, and your voice online are among the few

sources.title: Why delegation doesn't scale: hire people better than you and build teams
sources.originalTitle: Scaling by "delegation" isn't good enough
sources.summary: Jason Cohen argues that founder-style "delegation" (do it, understand it, then hire someone to do it your way) yields a team no better than the founder. Real scale comes from hiring people better than you at every role, trusting teams to own outcomes, and building teams that themselves attract greatness, even replacing yourself as CEO.

principles.text: Delegation doesn't scale a business; building a team better than the current team, including you, does.
principles.quote: Delegation doesn't scale your business.  What does: Creating a team that is better than the current team.  Including you.

principles.text: Hiring someone who works like you only yields a substitute for your own non-world-class performance, not greatness.
principles.quote: When you're looking for someone who knows what you know, and works like you work, you're not finding greatness, you're finding a substitute for your already-not-world-class performance.

principles.text: A founder's or manager's job is to hire people who are better than them at every position.
principles.quote: To hire people who are better than you at every position**, because only then is your organization increasing its strength and abilities.

principles.text: Micromanaging or constantly fixing hires is bad management: either you hired wrong or you're blocking a capable person.
principles.quote: If the person isn't better than you at the position, you're not making the organization better. If the person is better than you, then your micromanagement is destroying that improvement while also destroying their morale and your schedule.

principles.text: Team-building means the team owns the outcome and its obligations; delegation leaves you owning it and as the bottleneck.
principles.quote: "Delegation" means you still own it but someone else does the work. "Team-building" means the team is trusted to own it, own its obligations, can figure out and execute the details

principles.text: No one is exempt, including the founder where they're excellent; aim to never be the most knowledgeable person in the room.
principles.quote: your goal is for you to never be the most knowledgeable and experienced person in the room, because you've surrounded yourself with greatness, who each do the same.

sources.title: New Year's Questions: stage-by-stage questions for founders instead of resolutions
sources.originalTitle: New Year's Questions (neé Resolutions)
sources.summary: Jason argues resolutions fail and suggests asking yourself sharp, stage-specific questions instead. For bootstrappers, consultants, new startups, post-PMF and scale-phase companies, he lists the levers that matter: price, retention, marketing, focus, ICP alignment, hiring and unit economics.

principles.text: To double bootstrapped profits, raise price before cutting costs, improve retention before new markets, and invest in marketing before features.
principles.quote: it's usually increasing price, not cutting costs, and usually increasing retention, not expanding to new markets, and usually better marketing, not more features

principles.text: Ask what single spend could be game-changing, and consider paid marketing may deserve more money than you think.
principles.quote: what's the *single* most impactful thing you could spend non-trivial money on? For example, could you be spending more than you think on something like paid-marketing?

principles.text: Test your consulting rates by imagining you had to double them: what would you change in positioning, website and service to justify it?
principles.quote: If I *forced* you to double your rates, what would you have to do to justify it?

principles.text: New companies should immediately try to get 20 people to pay $50, and be completely honest about what the market says, price included.
principles.quote: How can you get 20 people to give you $50?

principles.text: After product/market fit, align the whole company on one most-important thing and one clarified target customer, saying no to distractions.
principles.quote: if I asked any employee what's the one thing the company has to do to be successful, they'd all have the same reply?

principles.text: In scale-phase, focus on what will be critical in three months: today's minor irritants become massive, and spend disproportionate time hiring 10xers.
principles.quote: what is only of minor importance today will be trivial in three months, whereas what is important but a minor irritant today will become critical and massive in three months

sources.title: Don't benchmark against outliers: judge your startup on your own trade-offs
sources.originalTitle: The wrongness of relativism
sources.summary: Jason Cohen argues that comparing your startup to Instagram, WhatsApp or Slack, or even to averages, breeds needless depression and bad decisions. The better question is what the best move is for your own company given your specific challenges, and whether a metric change is the right trade for you, your customers and your employees.

principles.text: Don't measure yourself against rarefied outlier companies; the yardstick of extremes is meaningless for your situation.
principles.quote: You mustn't judge yourself with the yardstick of other companies, particularly not against the rarefied few who dwell in the extremities of reality.

principles.text: Average or median benchmarks are no better: another company can be worse on a metric yet very successful for other reasons.
principles.quote: For every such condition, I can show you another company in an even worse condition with regard to that metric, but which is extremely successful because of other reasons.

principles.text: Ask what's best for your company given the specific challenges and benefits in front of you, not how you rank.
principles.quote: The right thing to ask is: "What is the best thing I can do for my company, with the specific challenges and benefits that I have in front of me?"

principles.text: For any metric, ask whether you're happy with it and whether changing it is the right trade against other metrics, innovation, lifestyle, and the people involved.
principles.quote: "Am I happy with this metric, and if I change it at the expense of other metrics, or of innovation, or of my lifestyle, or of my happiness, is that the right trade for me, for the company, for my customers, and for my employees?"

principles.text: If you can't reason about your own situation confidently, you'll compare your worst fears to others' public façades, which leads to bad answers.
principles.quote: If you're not confident in reasoning about yourself, you have no choice but to compare your worst fears (exaggerated negative) with the public façade of other people (exaggerated positive)

sources.title: Marketing at early startups: go deep on one channel you already understand
sources.originalTitle: Marketing at early startups: Deep, not wide
sources.summary: Jason argues early startups should not spread thin across many marketing channels. Successful companies find one channel that works and exhaust it before adding others. Pick that channel from the few you personally use and understand, because social channel success depends on natural resonance with its culture.

principles.text: Early startups rarely win by spreading small efforts across many channels; trickles from each don't add up to a river.
principles.quote: Spreading your precious money and even more precious time over many channels doesn't get a company off the ground.

principles.text: Find one channel that really works and exhaust its maximum inventory before layering on more channels.
principles.quote: Typically, successful companies find **one channel that really works**, and then plumb it to its [maximum inventory](https://longform.asmartbear.com/low-budget-marketing/) before layering on additional channels.

principles.text: Choose your first channel from the handful you personally use and understand, not by spray and pray.
principles.quote: Start with the handful of channels that you *personally use and understand*.

principles.text: Social channel success comes from resonance between your personality and the channel's norms and language.
principles.quote: success in social marketing channels arises from a resonance between your personality and the norms and language of that channel.

principles.text: Authentic resonance arises naturally; you can't A/B test your way into a persona on a channel you don't get.
principles.quote: The best chance you have for developing that resonance is when it arises naturally, not because you A/B test your Twitter persona

principles.text: Stay in your comfort zone and focus on doubling the business on that one channel; spreading thin is worse than leaving it.
principles.quote: So, stay with what you know, where you're comfortable, and focus on doubling your business on that channel.

sources.title: The Lindy Effect on startup potential: 2x is assumed, 10x must be proven
sources.originalTitle: The Lindy Effect on startup potential
sources.summary: Jason Cohen applies the Lindy Effect to startup growth: however big you are, you can probably double by doing what you already do, but 10x needs new channels, innovation, or hyper-growth. He explains why early tactics don't scale and why investors fixate on fast growth.

principles.text: You can probably double by repeating what works, but 10x requires innovation.
principles.quote: You can probably double your size by doing what you're already doing, but 10x will require innovation.

principles.text: Early-customer tactics rarely scale: what got you 10 customers won't get you 100.
principles.quote: the actions that got you your first 10 customers are probably not sufficient for generating 100, even though they're probably sufficient for getting another 10.

principles.text: A single marketing channel has limited inventory, so 10x needs multiple new channels.
principles.quote: it's unlikely that there is 10x the inventory inside that one channel to get you to 10,000 customers. Thus you'll need to make other channels work

principles.text: Very fast growth at meaningful size is the proof that 10x is within reach.
principles.quote: One answer is having very fast growth. If you're doubling every six months, you clearly have line-of-sight for more growth than just 2x.

principles.text: Investors and founders chasing huge outcomes obsess over hyper-growth because it's the only route to something enormous.
principles.quote: This is why investors (and founders) wishing to build enormous companies are so fixated on hyper-growth. It's the only way to have even the potential of building something enormous.

principles.text: Break the Lindy Effect by expanding into an adjacency: keep one foot in your strength, step into something riskier with bigger upside.
principles.quote: Another way to break the Lindy Effect is to change something substantial. I think of this as expanding into an adjacency.

sources.title: Pricing determines your business model: what each price order-of-magnitude implies
sources.originalTitle: Pricing determines your business model
sources.summary: Jason Cohen argues price isn't an afterthought but core business design, tied to brand, product, buyer, and go-to-market. He walks through each order of magnitude ($0 to $100,000/mo) and what it forces on support, sales, funding, and product, and says to discuss price in customer interviews.

principles.text: Price is business design, not a late-stage optimization; it shapes product, brand, buyer, and company structure.
principles.quote: Price is not an exercise in maximizing some micro-economic supply/demand curve, slapped post facto onto the product. Rather, it fundamentally determines the nature of the product and the structure of the business that produces it.

principles.text: Talk about price in customer development interviews; price is as much a fit factor as any feature.
principles.quote: Price is as important as any other feature to determine product/market "fit."

principles.text: In interviews, probe cost expectations, who writes the check, who approves, and whether an ROI pitch would be welcomed.
principles.quote: Talk about their expectations of cost, and why, who would write the check, who would need to approve it, whether an ROI argument would be welcomed or scoffed at

principles.text: $100/mo is the sweet spot for bootstrappers: broad B2B market, profitable with 200-300 customers, and you can afford to acquire them.
principles.quote: I love this price zone for bootstrapped companies, because it's low enough that you can address a broad business market, but high enough that you can get nicely profitable with a reasonable, achievable number of customers (e.g. 200-300)

principles.text: At $10/mo you can't afford marketing or sales; reaching $1M/yr takes 8000+ customers and growth is slow, so scaling fast usually needs venture funding.
principles.quote: it takes over 8000 customers to make only $1m/yr in revenue

principles.text: At $1,000/mo you face real buying processes and discount requests, with sales costs like much bigger deals but without the revenue, so profit is hard.
principles.quote: This can be a surprisingly difficult zone to become profitable in, because the sales and marketing motions and engineering costs are the same as for much larger sales, but without the attendant revenue.

sources.title: Find what stays constant: why a startup's values are its essence and how WP Engine used them
sources.originalTitle: In its emptiness, there is the function of a startup
sources.summary: Jason Cohen uses the Ship of Theseus and Lao Tzu to argue that everything in a startup changes except its values, so values define its purpose. Written values, lived and signed by everyone, let any employee act like an owner without approval chains. Financial success is the means, not the end.

principles.text: Everything in a startup changes over time. The few things that don't change are its essence, and you must decide what they are.
principles.quote: Everything about a startup changes over time. The few things that don't, are its essence. The voyage is meaningless, unless you decide what those things are.

principles.text: Features, marketing copy, people, metrics, logo and office all change. What stays constant defines the startup and why anyone should join it.
principles.quote: Whatever it is, **that is what defines the startup and its purpose**, and is the answer to the all-important question: Why should anyone--employees and customers alike--join the founder on this journey

principles.text: Values are an inviolable constitution that decides tough calls: customer over money, and fire the skilled but dishonest or self-serving person.
principles.quote: if in some choice we must either lose money or do what's right for the customer, we will do what's right for the customer.

principles.text: Clear shared values empower everyone to act like an owner, so decisions happen without approval chains, which helps scale.
principles.quote: a clear agreement of core values **is how you empower everyone in the company to act like an owner.**

principles.text: Write your values down and have everyone sign them. Hire people who already embody them, not people who just agree to them.
principles.quote: You have to ensure everyone not only agrees to them as a condition of employment, committing them to memory due to external requirement, but because in their bones they already embody those values

principles.text: Financial success is necessary for sustainability but is the means, not the end. Without a higher purpose, success may not matter.
principles.quote: **Financial success is the means, not the ends.** Without financial success the company isn't sustainable, so that component of success is absolutely necessary.

sources.title: Why startup success is the journey, not the exit
sources.originalTitle: The only way to guarantee startup success
sources.summary: Using Depeche Mode's Rose Bowl peak as a cautionary tale, Cohen argues that tying success to a single outcome (an exit, a metric, a funding round) almost guarantees failure and unhappiness. Keep score with metrics and money, but make the years of building the point. It also helps recruit people who want to join the journey.

principles.text: Don't define success as one peak moment; the peak means your next steps are downhill, so value the building itself.
principles.quote: The way you let this happen is to believe that the goal is to achieve a single moment of success--a big sale, going public, or passing it on to your daughter.

principles.text: You spend nearly all your time on the journey, so the journey is where happiness has to come from.
principles.quote: You spend 99.99% of your time on the journey of building a startup, and 0.01% basking in the temporary euphoria of "success," such as selling it to someone else or ringing the bell on the morning of your IPO.

principles.text: Outcome-based definitions of success (metrics, money, exits, funding) almost guarantee failure by your own definition.
principles.quote: But if your measure of "success" is based on a specific outcome--based on metrics, or money, or growth-rate, or number of employees, or whether you had an exit, or how much money you raised

principles.text: Keep score with metrics and money, but don't confuse the game with life.
principles.quote: Keep score, so long as you can distinguish between the game and life.

principles.text: Valuing the journey helps hiring: later employees join to be part of the journey, not just for early-stage upside.
principles.quote: the first employee joins because it's the ground floor of an exciting startup, but why will the 20th person join? Or the 200th?

sources.title: Why startup biz dev deals fail: pitch big companies growth in the way they already make money
sources.originalTitle: Why startup biz dev deals almost never get done
sources.summary: Jason Cohen explains why startups' "win-win" distribution proposals get ignored by larger companies: a one-time revenue sliver is immaterial and costs the big company its reputation. Good biz dev brings the big company new customers in its existing business model, or generates material, repeating revenue (2%+ of top line).

principles.text: Startups lack distribution; big companies have it but struggle to innovate. That mismatch feels like a deal, but it isn't enough.
principles.quote: Distribution is the hardest thing for a young startup, defined as "getting in front of potential customers." Large companies, on the other hand, have solved the distribution problem

principles.text: A one-time revenue share from emailing a big company's customers is immaterial to them, so it never gets approved.
principles.quote: By definition a company earns 1% of their monthly revenue in about 8 hours. Increasing revenue, once, by 8 hours, isn't interesting.

principles.text: Pitching a partner's customer base costs them reputation that your equation ignores; asking them to market to customers is asking them to spam.
principles.quote: The amount of revenue in question is not interesting for the big company, yet it requires the big company to spend something not accounted for in the above equation: Reputation.

principles.text: Design the deal by asking how you can make the bigger company money in the way it already makes money.
principles.quote: How can the smaller company make money for the larger company *in the manner that the larger company already makes money?*

principles.text: Bring customers to the big company instead of milking its customers. Even a few recurring customers move the needle.
principles.quote: If you can bring customers to a big company--even a few--rather than milking their existing customers for a sliver of revenue, you're much more likely to execute a deal that genuinely makes both of you significant money.

principles.text: Alternatively, find a mechanism that repeatedly generates material revenue, which means 2% or more of the partner's top line.
principles.quote: "Material" is 2% or more of their top-line revenue, repeatedly.

sources.title: Scale: why rare events become daily problems and automation isn't enough
sources.originalTitle: Rare things become common at scale
sources.summary: Jason Cohen uses WP Engine's 1,000+ servers to show that scale turns rare failures into daily events and strains how you handle them with customers. Automation helps but cannot replace human support or forensic engineering, so founders projecting growth must budget well beyond linear costs.

principles.text: At scale, rare events become common: a once-in-three-years failure across 1,000 servers happens daily.
principles.quote: Three years is about 1,000 days. So that means, on average, every single day we have a fatal server error.

principles.text: Scale changes your ability to handle problems, not just the problems: each incident cascades into notifications, support load, social media and reviews.
principles.quote: It's not only problems that morph with scale, but your ability to handle problems.

principles.text: Fast customer growth means incidents hit new customers, creating bad first impressions that are harder to repair than for long-tenured customers.
principles.quote: it's likely that any given server issue will affect a customer who has only been with us for a month or two. Thus the issue causes a "bad first impression," which is harder to address than a customer who has been with us for three years and has built up a bank account of patience.

principles.text: "Automate everything" is only part of the answer; rare problems and caring human teams can't be automated away.
principles.quote: And you can't "automate" away the rare things, even the technical ones. By their nature they're difficult to define, hence difficult to monitor, and difficult to repair without the forensic skills of a human engineer.

principles.text: Individual customers can have fewer problems while the company-wide worst case gets harder; managing the tail takes non-linear effort.
principles.quote: "rare things" means you probably never experienced it, but at scale, someone is experiencing it each day.

principles.text: When projecting growth, budget for specialist hires and battle-hardened leaders, or you'll get an ugly surprise.
principles.quote: When you show 5x growth in projections but don't budget for new hires in areas like security, technical automation, specialized customer service areas, and managers and executives who have trod this path before and come battle-hardened with play-books on how to tackle all this, you're heading for an ugly surprise.

sources.title: You can have two Big Things, but not three: time-boxing a life and a startup
sources.originalTitle: You can have two Big Things, but not three
sources.summary: Jason argues that a normal 24-hour day leaves room for roughly two time-consuming "Big Things" (job, kids, spouse, social life, major hobby, startup). Trying to hold three means one or more suffers, and you can't escape the limit by cutting sleep or by believing you're an exception.

principles.text: You get two Big Things in life, not three; pick which two.
principles.quote: The rule of life is: **You can have two "Big Things" in your life, but not three**.

principles.text: Big Things (job, kids, spouse, social life, hobby, startup) each need 40+ hours a week of concentrated time.
principles.quote: This is the amount of time it takes to tackle something huge. A career. A parent. A startup.

principles.text: Weekends and vacations don't add up to enough concentrated time to run a startup alongside a job and family.
principles.quote: There are weekends and vacations and sick days and such, but those don't add up to enough *concentrated* time to carry off something like a startup without causing work or home to suffer.

principles.text: A side-project startup on top of a day job costs you your family time, and sometimes the family itself.
principles.quote: You can do a startup on the side while you have a day job, but your family will never see you. You might even lose your family.

principles.text: Starting a company is easier before you have a family or even a spouse.
principles.quote: This is partly why it's easier to start a company before you have a family or even a spouse.

principles.text: Don't cut sleep to fit a third Big Thing; it degrades performance at everything.
principles.quote: cutting out sleep doesn't work--then you can't function at a high level at *anything*.

sources.title: Why a startup always needs more money than planned, even if you plan for it
sources.originalTitle: More money if you do, more money if you don't
sources.summary: Jason Cohen argues that investors are right to say "raise more than you think you need." Any deviation from plan, whether revenue grows slower or faster, requires more cash than the base plan. Since you can't predict finances 18 months out, raising only the planned amount creates a cash crunch 9-12 months in.

principles.text: You only need the planned amount of money if everything goes exactly to plan; any deviation, up or down, costs more.
principles.quote: The only way you need the actual amount of money you thought you needed, is if everything in the next 18 months goes exactly according to plan--a deviation *in either direction* means you need more money.

principles.text: If growth lags plan, you've already committed to costs and should keep going, which burns more cash than planned.
principles.quote: You're burning more money than you expected, but the correct course of action is to forge ahead and let revenue catch up, not fire half your team and retreat.

principles.text: Faster-than-planned growth also drains cash, because new customers cost more upfront than their early revenue and you must hire ahead.
principles.quote: You incur customer on-boarding costs faster than planned, so although in the long-run your revenue will more than make up for it, right now these unexpected new customers cost much more than their revenue contributions, and cash reserves plummet.

principles.text: Customer acquisition costs rise faster than revenue, so growth itself needs a cash investment.
principles.quote: It costs money to acquire a customer, but takes time for the monthly revenue to cover those costs, therefore costs rise faster than revenue, so you need a cash investment to fund that growth.

principles.text: Precisely predicting startup finances 18 months out is delusional; raising only the planned amount denies that and creates a cash crunch.
principles.quote: You're delusional if you think you can predict your startup's finances 18 months out with precision!

principles.text: Treat money needs like Hofstadter's Law: a business takes more money than expected even after accounting for that.
principles.quote: A business always takes more money than you expect, even when you take this fact into account.

sources.title: The Code is your Enemy: why technical founders should stop coding and talk to customers
sources.originalTitle: The Code is your Enemy
sources.summary: Jason Cohen argues that builders default to coding because they love it, yet startups fail on attention, marketing, positioning and selling, not code quality. He says to attack the high-risk, poorly understood business problems first: interview 50 customers and get daily website traffic.

principles.text: Your strength as a builder is also your weakness: you code because you love it, not because it's what the startup needs most.
principles.quote: The weakness is the same as your strength as they often are: Your love of creation.

principles.text: Startups rarely fail on code or design; they fail on traffic, trial, payment, acquisition cost, word of mouth, or an unsolved pain.
principles.quote: Most startups fail because not enough people show up on the home page, or people show up but they don't try the product, or they don't pay for the product, or it's too expensive to get them to show up

principles.text: Customers don't pay for test coverage or typography; ugly sites and buggy code can still make millions.
principles.quote: Customers don't open their wallets based on your unit test coverage or whether you used Bodoni instead of Times New Roman on the home page.

principles.text: Interview fifty potential customers, not a dozen, and vet price at the same time; small samples carry hidden bias and false positives.
principles.quote: Have you talked to 50 potential customers? By that I mean fifty, not a dozen.

principles.text: Daily traffic is harder and less controllable than software, so prioritize getting attention; a buggy product with traffic beats a clean one with none.
principles.quote: Would you rather get hired as the CTO of a company with 1,000 daily new, unique, qualified visitors with a buggy product, or the CTO of a company with a clean, stable product and 10 uniques visits to the home page?

principles.text: Treat the business like a dev project and tackle the riskiest, least-understood parts first: attention, marketing, positioning, selling.
principles.quote: in a business it's the attention, marketing, positioning, selling, defining part that's high-risk and inadequately-understood, and all of the coding and design is low-risk and well-understood in comparison.

sources.title: Imbalanced People: why a great hire is infinitely better than average ones
sources.originalTitle: Imbalanced People
sources.summary: Jason Cohen argues the "10x developer" idea understates reality: a great person in any role (developer, designer, writer, manager, support, product, sales) produces ideas and results that 100 average people never will. Because of this, he says you can't afford to hire anyone less than great.

principles.text: A great performer is not 10x an average one; they are better than any number of average people, because they create ideas others wouldn't.
principles.quote: A great developer, or a great designer, is more than 10x an average one--they're better than an infinite number.  Because they'll come up with ideas and implementations that 100 others wouldn't.

principles.text: The greatness rule holds in every role, including sales, support, management and product.
principles.quote: In fact, if you think there's any position at your company where this rule of "better than 10x" doesn't hold, you've never worked with greatness at that position.

principles.text: A great salesperson creates thrilled, referenceable customers and rallies the whole company around growth, rather than just closing leads.
principles.quote: A great salesperson is a factory producing cheerleader customers who are actually thrilled and referenceable after the sale

principles.text: Great managers develop their people's careers; average managers are just glorified project managers.
principles.quote: A great manager who develops the careers of their folks versus several average ones who are glorified project managers.

principles.text: Since greatness is a universal rule, you can't afford to hire less; if rivals can hire the best and you don't, you need a special plan to still win.
principles.quote: Now, if you understand this universal, timeless, human rule, you then realize you cannot afford to hire anyone less.

principles.text: Work with the best: you do amazing things together and learn daily, and life is too short for mediocrity.
principles.quote: Life's too short, and high tech moves too fast, to mess about with mediocrity.

sources.title: Why LTV misleads: use payback period, MRR, churn, GPM and CAC instead
sources.originalTitle: Why I don't like the LTV metric (LifeTime Value)
sources.summary: Jason Cohen argues the LTV metric blends three unstable variables (MRR, gross margin, cancellation) into one falsely precise number that drives confident but bad decisions. He recommends payback period and tracking MRR, cancellations, GPM and CAC individually, since those are short-horizon and actionable.

principles.text: LTV multiplies three unpredictable, changing variables, so its apparent precision is false and invites confident bad decisions.
principles.quote: Three variables, all changing, unpredictably, which you multiply together and.... you expect the result to *mean* something?

principles.text: Metrics that bundle many processes give an illusion of understanding; the danger is thinking you understand something you don't.
principles.quote: And then you *think* you understand something that you don't. That's how bad decisions are made with confidence.

principles.text: Replace LTV:CAC with payback period (CAC divided by monthly gross profit per customer) to judge a reasonable CAC.
principles.quote: This payback period is also useful to see

principles.text: Rule of thumb for payback: 6 months is fine, 3 is fantastic, 12+ is poor unless strategic benefit, improving efficiency, or mature/enterprise customers justify it.
principles.quote: A good rule of thumb with pay-back period is that 6 months is fine, 3 months is fantastic, and 12+ months is poor

principles.text: A steady LTV can hide trouble; always track MRR, cancellations, GPM and CAC individually rather than one combined number.
principles.quote: Thus, measuring MRR, cancellations, GPM, and CAC individually are always necessary.

principles.text: Metrics with short time horizons point to actions, unlike LTV's long horizon.
principles.quote: Every "insight" that LTV is supposed to give you, you can get from different metrics that work better, because they don't involve long time horizons. And they point to actions you can take.

sources.title: Sandy Visions: look beyond optimizing metrics, obsess over customer happiness, and explore the bigger opportunity
sources.originalTitle: Sandy Visions
sources.summary: A reflective essay on the magic of landing the first customer and how founders become hooked on growth metrics. Cohen argues that obsessing over customer and employee happiness is the right path to financial results, but metric optimization can blind founders to bigger, truly innovative opportunities beyond the incremental.

principles.text: Obsess over customer and employee happiness at least as much as financial ratios; they are the most efficient path to the financials.
principles.quote: We're not wrong to obsess, so long as we obsess over customer happiness and employee happiness at least as much as self-serving financial ratios, trusting--as I do--that the formers are the most efficient and personally fulfilling path to the latter.

principles.text: Founders are hooked on the thrill of the sale, and that drive escalates into chasing ever larger metrics like MoM growth and scale.
principles.quote: Then single hits aren't enough and you need "biggest ever" to feel the rush, and we become slaves to the mantra of %MoM growth

principles.text: Metrics optimization is necessary but incomplete; the biggest opportunity lies beyond incremental improvement.
principles.quote: our visions must lift beyond the incremental metric and the hourly order rate. Those are necessary and just, but incomplete.

principles.text: A purely metrics-driven compass can't point toward true innovation; you can't see a new dimension if you only measure two.
principles.quote: Where is the space for true innovation and exploration in a land of metrics optimization?  How do you realize you can move vertically when your compass measures only two dimensions?

principles.text: Don't get stuck fighting competitors over a scrap when a vast unexplored ocean lies beyond; step back and explore.
principles.quote: Tomorrow I'll return to the office, fighting the other crabs for seaweed, the wider beach forgotten, oblivious to the vast ocean beyond the surf

principles.text: Each customer acquisition is the product of countless improbable events, so treat every sale as something remarkable.
principles.quote: Each event improbable, yet collectively inevitable.

sources.title: COC: the metric that prices cancellations in the currency of customer acquisition
sources.originalTitle: COC: A new metric for measuring cancellations in SaaS business models
sources.summary: Jason Cohen introduces COC (Cost of Cancellations) = payback period × monthly revenue churn, the share of revenue a SaaS company must spend each month just to avoid shrinking. It shows churn alone is a third of the story and that CAC, ARPC and net negative churn matter just as much.

principles.text: Measure the cost of churn as COC = payback period (p) × monthly revenue cancellation rate (c): the share of revenue spent just to stay level.
principles.quote:
**The *percentage* of our revenue we'll have to spend this month, just to keep from shrinking**:

`COC = p ✕ c`

principles.text: Payback period equals CAC divided by ARPC, which is also the cost to acquire one more dollar of MRR.
principles.quote: `p` = "the cost to acquire one more dollar of MRR" = `CAC / ARPC`

principles.text: Cancellations eat a startling share of revenue: a healthy SMB SaaS (3% churn, 7-month payback) spends 21% of revenue a month just to stay flat.
principles.quote: In this case, `COC = 0.21`, which means a whopping 21% of its revenue *every month* will be spent *just keeping revenues level.*

principles.text: A short payback period can overwhelm a bad cancellation rate; a long payback with the same churn is deadly.
principles.quote: a very good pay-back period can overwhelm a crappy cancellation rate.

principles.text: Metrics literature fixates on churn, but COC shows there are three levers: cancellations, CAC and ARPC. When churn has a floor, shift CAC or ARPC instead.
principles.quote: **typical metrics literature focuses only on reducing cancellation rate, which is only a third of the story.**

principles.text: Treat c as net churn (cancellations plus downgrades minus upgrades). Reaching zero net churn makes COC zero, so build upsell paths.
principles.quote: **getting to zero net churn is the strongest thing you can do** in terms of COC.

sources.title: Low-budget online marketing: use inventory limits, quit bad channels fast, fix the website first
sources.originalTitle: Solving the Low-Budget Online Marketing Dilemma
sources.summary: Jason Cohen explains how cash-strapped startups should choose among marketing channels. Decide whether to optimize a channel by how much untapped inventory remains, abandon channels that fail out of the gate, optimize the website before any single campaign, and chase only large effects because small-sample data is mostly noise.

principles.text: Decide whether to optimize a channel by remaining inventory; if you can get 2x or more, go get it.
principles.quote: If you think there's 2x or more inventory you could go get, I say go get it.

principles.text: When a channel nears its inventory limit, stop optimizing it and find new campaigns that can double the business.
principles.quote: Once you approach inventory limits, you need to find other campaigns which can [double your business]

principles.text: Don't give a failing new channel the benefit of the doubt; campaigns that start bad tend to stay bad, so cut out early.
principles.quote: the ones that were bad out of the gate tended to stay bad.

principles.text: Optimize the website before individual campaigns, since every campaign flows through it and gains compound.
principles.quote: Optimizations you do on your website are more valuable than those you do on individual marketing campaigns. The reason is obvious in retrospect: all marketing campaigns lead there!

principles.text: When small, only pursue large effects: little data is statistically significant, so small gains are indistinguishable from noise.
principles.quote: When you're small, almost no data you have is statistically significant.  Therefore, most variation you see is due to random fluctuations, not real results

principles.text: With big budgets, try many channels fast and burn cash for learning; with low budgets, don't copy that approach.
principles.quote: Accelerated (cash) burning for accelerated learning.

sources.title: Bootstrapped CPC rule of thumb: max click bid = ARPU/25
sources.originalTitle: Bootstrapped CPC rule of thumb: ARPU/25
sources.summary: Jason gives a pre-data formula for bootstrapped SaaS founders deciding how much to pay per click. Assume 20-month customer life, CAC at one fifth of LTV (four months of revenue), and 1% visitor-to-paid conversion. That gives max CPC = ARPU/25, which also argues for charging more.

principles.text: With no data, bootstrapped founders should assume a 20-month customer life; a low LTV guess is safer than an inflated one.
principles.quote: a good **pre-data rule of thumb is 20 months**.

principles.text: Keep CAC at LTV/5, stricter than the funded-company LTV/3, because early cheap channels exist but saturate.
principles.quote: I urge profit-seekers to instead adopt an even more strict model of CAC = LTV / 5.

principles.text: CAC should be no more than four months of revenue, so payback is about four months (three if you collect month one upfront).
principles.quote: the cost to acquire a customer should be no more than four months of revenue.

principles.text: Profit-seeking bootstrappers can't afford CAC > LTV or 'land-grab' justifications; funded firms can pay to find out, you can't.
principles.quote: Profit-seeking bootstrapped companies cannot afford those delusions.

principles.text: Assume 1% visitor-to-paying conversion pre-data, so max CPC = ARPU/25 (e.g. $50/mo ARPU allows $2/click).
principles.quote: So for example if your average customer generates $50/mo, you can spend $2/click.

principles.text: Charge more than you think: higher ARPU lets you pay more per click, opens more channels and outbids low-LTV competitors.
principles.quote: **you should charge a lot more than you think**, in part because it enables you to pay quite a lot per click

sources.title: Freemium as a marketing expense: charge the marketing department and measure the ROI
sources.originalTitle: Reframing "Freemium" by charging the marketing department
sources.summary: Jason Cohen argues freemium is a marketing cost, not a product strategy. Free users cost more than expected, convert poorly, and skew your feedback away from paying customers. Charge the marketing department the true per-user cost and compare the ROI against AdWords, SEO and other channels.

principles.text: Free users are not your target customer, so they don't represent what paying customers want.
principles.quote: Trouble is, those freemium users are not like those who will actually give you money.

principles.text: Free users vastly outnumber payers and drown out the feedback that matters.
principles.quote: Your problem is that freemium users outnumber your paying customers 20:1 or even 100:1, so in feedback forums they drown out the voices of those who actually matter.

principles.text: Freemium's two-step conversion makes paid acquisition uneconomic unless you can absorb big losses.
principles.quote: This essentially takes paid-advertising and almost all other forms of marketing off the table for driving growth in a freemium business, unless you're willing to take big losses to get things rolling.

principles.text: Ignoring free-tier support undermines the word-of-mouth and conversion freemium is meant to create.
principles.quote: if you really do ignore them they'll be less successful with your tool, which means far less chance of them converting, and less chance they'll evangelize to friends and coworkers.

principles.text: Treat freemium as a marketing cost and judge it like any other acquisition channel.
principles.quote: Retool your expectations of Freemium: It's a marketing cost. It's more expensive than you give it credit for, but it could very well be the best marketing strategy.

principles.text: Measure the net cost per free user and compare it to other marketing channels.
principles.quote: You have no excuse to not be measuring this net cost-per-user so that you're running this Freemium program with full knowledge of the costs, and comparing it to other forms of marketing.

sources.title: Startup identity and the sadness of a successful exit: why founders feel loss after selling
sources.originalTitle: Startup identity & the sadness of a successful exit
sources.summary: Jason Cohen explains why nearly every founder feels deep sadness after selling, even after a big win: the startup is the founder's identity, not a job. He argues selling can still be right, and that founders should decide based on the CEO role they want as the company matures, not on money.

principles.text: A startup is the founder's identity, not a job, which is why selling it feels like losing yourself.
principles.quote: A startup is an obsession. You do it because you couldn't stop yourself. Because when you were doing anything else, you were thinking about it.

principles.text: Painful does not mean wrong: sell when it's the right call, even if you love the company.
principles.quote: Just because it's painful doesn't mean you don't need to do it.

principles.text: Don't expect a big payout to make you fulfilled or happy; build fulfillment independent of the exit.
principles.quote: You must resist the urge to believe that getting millions of dollars will make you fulfilled, or happy.

principles.text: The CEO job changes as the company grows, whether or not you sell, so check you want the later-stage role.
principles.quote: The CEO's job description changes over time, and so does the company, whether you sell it or not. Are you emotionally prepared for this as well?

principles.text: Successful startups mature into process-heavy businesses; founders must be ready to give up hands-on control.
principles.quote: The fact is, successful startups grow up. They grow into businesses and mature into sustainability, risk-avoidance, HR law, strategic planning, executive meetings, and all that.

principles.text: Time the exit to the role you want: Cohen sold before needing to manage managers, once the payout crossed the Freedom Line.
principles.quote: So for me I sold at a good point: before I needed a C_O, but after the company was big enough to garner enough money to cross the Freedom Line.

sources.title: Why Jason Cohen ignored "that's how it's done" and sold to the Enterprise at Smart Bear
sources.originalTitle: "Because that's the way it's done" -- should a founder listen?
sources.summary: Jason Cohen recounts how Smart Bear broke every conventional rule for selling to enterprises (silly name, no traditional sales force, slide-free demos, amateur design, human voice) and still reached millions in revenue. His point: conventional wisdom describes what works for most, but you can choose your own way if you go in eyes open and accept the harder road.

principles.text: Conventional wisdom describes how most successful companies do it; it isn't wrong, but it isn't the only way.
principles.quote: "They" are in fact describing the way most *successful* companies sell to The Enterprise. Nothing wrong with "tried and true."

principles.text: Smart Bear sold to the Enterprise while breaking the usual rules: odd name, no sales force, slide-free demos, human voice.
principles.quote: Oops. I accidentally went and did *all* that at Smart Bear, and only had millions of dollars of revenue to show for it. Largely from The Enterprise.

principles.text: If the tried-and-true path doesn't fit who you are, don't force it; compete with big companies instead of imitating them.
principles.quote: Unless tried and true doesn't happen to jibe with you.

principles.text: Going unconventional is often not strategy but inability to do it the standard way; follow your own constraints.
principles.quote: I wasn't trying to be "disruptive" or "innovative" or a "maverick." I just *couldn't do it*.

principles.text: Ignoring convention makes the road harder and removes your safety net, so go in eyes open; being different can be enough if for a good reason.
principles.quote: Once you buck "Their" wisdom, you can't rely on "Them" when you get yourself into an unusual pickle. You've exited the safe and well-travelled road.

principles.text: Don't let "it's not done that way" alone decide; maybe it should be done your way.
principles.quote: Don't let the "it's not done that way" people win on that basis alone.

sources.title: Better for whom?: why "we'll build it better" is never a valid business idea
sources.originalTitle: Better for whom?
sources.summary: Jason argues that "better" has no meaning without a specific market segment, so "we can do it better" is not a real idea for a business. Defining who your product is better for turns a vague claim into an actual proposal. It also tells you how to advertise, what to build, and who to interview.

principles.text: "We can do it better" is never a valid business idea; "better" only exists for a specific market segment.
principles.quote: You quickly realize there's no such thing as "better."  There's only such thing as "better for a specific market segment."

principles.text: Always ask "better for whom?" when a founder claims their product is better than the incumbents.
principles.quote: So when someone says their product is "better," my next question is always: "Better for whom?"

principles.text: A real pitch defines "better" by naming the audience and the use-case the incumbents serve poorly.
principles.quote: at least they are *actual ideas,* actual proposals, in that they *define* "better:"

principles.text: Naming your audience tells you how to advertise, where to go, what words to use, and what features to build.
principles.quote: If you know your audience, you can create targeted advertisements, go to specific conferences, and even cold-call them on LinkedIn.

principles.text: Knowing who it's better for gives you the basis for customer development: who to call and what to verify.
principles.quote: Or if you're still in the ideation stage, it gives you the basis for [customer development](https://longform.asmartbear.com/customer-development/), both in finding potential customers to call, and what you're verifying when you get them on the phone.

principles.text: Differentiate against crowded markets by picking an underserved segment, such as beginners, complex projects, or mobile-first users.
principles.quote: My PM tool is best for large, complex projects with modern technology requirements.

sources.title: A compass is not a map: why startup rules and frameworks can't predict success
sources.originalTitle: A compass is not a map
sources.summary: Jason Cohen argues there is no map to startup success. Every piece of advice has successes and failures on both sides, and successful startups are by definition outliers that statistics can't predict. Treat frameworks and famous origin stories as a candy store for inspiration, not laws, and find your own way.

principles.text: Startup advice is a compass, not a map: it shows a direction, not whether you should go that way.
principles.quote: A compass tells you **which way is north, not whether you should be heading north**.

principles.text: For any piece of startup advice, both followers and opposites have succeeded and failed, so the advice alone proves little.
principles.quote: for every piece of advice `P`, there are many successes and failures of startups who did `P`, and also many successes and failures of startups that did the opposite of `P`.

principles.text: Successful startups are anomalies, and trends can't predict outliers.
principles.quote: by definition the successful ones are anomalies**. Statistics show trends, but **trends don't predict outliers**.

principles.text: A successful startup looks like an unsuccessful one at the start, so nothing reliably predicts the outlier.
principles.quote: What *does* predict an outlier? Nothing.

principles.text: Don't treat frameworks, dogma or favorite-startup origin stories as laws; mine them for sparks and pick what fits you.
principles.quote: Don't confuse startup frameworks or dogma or the origin story of your favorite startup with laws.

principles.text: Use advice like a candy store: choose what suits who you already are, then keep moving.
principles.quote: There's no map. That's OK. Keep moving.

sources.title: Why second-guessing competitors is a losing game: build the best company for yourself
sources.originalTitle: But I know that he knows that I know
sources.summary: Using Rock, Paper, Scissors as an analogy, Jason Cohen shows how trying to outguess what competitors know and think leads to endless recursive fakes. His startup takeaway is to stop reacting to rivals and instead focus inward on building something you're proud of for your customers.

principles.text: Don't try to outwit competitors; do your best work directly for your customers.
principles.quote: Even better than trying to outwit the competition, is to not react to them at all, and just do your best, directly for your customers.

principles.text: Second-guessing competitors' knowledge and reactions is an endless recursion with no stable answer.
principles.quote: This is like trying to second-guess what your competitors think, what they know, what they think they know, whether they'll react to your knowledge of that guess, etc..

principles.text: Build the best company you can for yourself, and focus inward rather than on rivals.
principles.quote: In the end, screw it, just build the best company you can, for you.

principles.text: Your beliefs about competitors, good and bad, are mostly wrong, so build something you're proud of.
principles.quote: You're wrong about most of what you think about those competitors anyway--both the good and bad--so focus inward, and build something you're proud of.

principles.text: In an adversarial game, whoever has more information wins more often, though every edge gets countered once known.
principles.quote: That, at least in regard to this study, people with more information win more often.

sources.title: Sustainable growth: why "successful" companies like Color, Groupon and Zynga fail
sources.originalTitle: The rise of the "successful" unsustainable company
sources.summary: Jason Cohen argues that investors and press reward growth and "shareholder value" while ignoring sustainability, producing companies that look successful and then collapse. He contrasts Groupon, Zynga and serial-exit founders with HubSpot, Rackspace, Freshbooks and SEOMoz, and says growth is necessary but not sufficient.

principles.text: Growth is necessary but not sufficient; if you want a lasting company, be honest about what "lasting" means.
principles.quote: But if your goal is to build a lasting company, be honest about what "lasting" means. **Growth is necessary, but not sufficient.**

principles.text: Growth bought with capital is not the same as building a product; force-fed revenue growth without long-term payback is not a business.
principles.quote: executives and investors are over-eager to value growth over sustainability (i.e. Groupon's engine that turned capital into revenue growth was a form of force-feeding rather than building a product)

principles.text: Validate the real value of your product to customers early; simple customer development reveals when claimed value is overstated.
principles.quote: the actual value of the product to small businesses wasn't as high as claimed, even though the simplest of customer development reveals this fact (ask any restaurateur)

principles.text: Real revenue and a big market are not enough if individual product wins are fleeting and you can't keep innovating enough to justify your size.
principles.quote: whose individual product successes are fleeting, who were financially successful at a certain scale, but it's doubtful they can continue innovating enough games to justify their current size

principles.text: Sustainable high growth comes from obsessing over customer service, retention and measurement, which also earns premium prices.
principles.quote: Rackspace whose maniacal obsession with excellence in customer service allows them to charge premium prices and sustain an amazing 30% annual growth even at the massive scale of $1b in revenue

principles.text: Sustainability isn't determined by how you finance the company; it's determined by what you decide to build.
principles.quote: Note that some of those companies were bootstrapped, some bootstrapped and took money later, and some had huge funding from the start. It's not about the financing path, it's about what you've decided to build.

sources.title: Why ROI spreadsheets don't sell software: create obvious value and price to budgets
sources.originalTitle: "ROI" is the wrong way to sell your product
sources.summary: Jason Cohen explains why ROI and cost-savings arguments never closed a sale at Smart Bear, even when the math was sound and customers asked for it. Savings are unmeasurable and budgets are siloed, so he advises building value so obvious it needs no calculation and pricing by willingness to pay and budget structure.

principles.text: ROI and cost-savings arguments don't close sales, even when the math is sound and the customer asks for it.
principles.quote: But this argument never worked, not once, even though the reasoning is sound and customers requested it. The reason is that these "savings" aren't how budgets actually work.

principles.text: Productivity gains are real but unmeasured in practice, so the savings you promise are invisible to the buyer.
principles.quote: But it's also essentially impossible to measure, and is in fact not measured. So the "savings" are invisible, even if real.

principles.text: Budgets are siloed: savings in one budget (salaries) never fund spend in another (tools), so "it pays for itself" fails.
principles.quote: Never once in my seven years selling software at Smart Bear, whether 10 seats or 2500 seats, did a company make a decision in which savings in the "Salaries" budget resulted in an increase to the "Tools" budget.

principles.text: Customers buy on belief that the product helps, not on a spreadsheet; they either believe or they don't.
principles.quote: Spreadsheets are worthless--they either believe, or they don't.

principles.text: Create so much value that no computation is needed: change workflows so drastically that customers can't live without it.
principles.quote: create so much value that there's no need to "compute" it.

principles.text: Price by ability and willingness to pay and by business model structure, matching the buyer's budget constraints, not as a direct function of "value".
principles.quote: price according to ability and willingness to pay and the structure of your business model, rather than as a direct function of so-called "value."

sources.title: Pascal's Wager for life: why humility cannot fail and arrogance can
sources.originalTitle: A life-changing challenge guided by Pascal's Wager
sources.summary: Jason Cohen borrows Pascal's Wager as a decision rule: when you act on scant knowledge, pick the stance that holds up in every outcome. Using WP Engine tech support as the example, he argues that assuming you are ignorant and asking for help beats accusation, and he challenges readers to try humility for a week.

principles.text: Pick the assumption that fares well in every eventuality, not just some of them.
principles.quote: You have to make assumptions of course, but Pascal points out that some assumptions fare better in all eventualities, whereas other assumptions result in positive outcomes only sometimes.

principles.text: Running a startup means deciding on scant knowledge, so most decisions are educated guesses and humility is the sane default.
principles.quote: We react to most things from a position of scant knowledge, especially when we're running a startup where essentially every decision is a guess. An educated guess, but not terribly educated.

principles.text: Being humble cannot fail; being arrogant can. Assume you are missing information and ready to learn.
principles.quote: You can't fail if you assume you're ignorant, that you're missing information, that you're ready to learn, that you need help to understand.

principles.text: Approach support from helplessness or curiosity, not accusation. People who chose to help will go further for you.
principles.quote: So if you open up the conversation from a posture of helplessness or curiosity, they're inclined to help, even if it's your own fault.

principles.text: If it really is the company's fault, a humble customer gets the most sympathy and the most personal advocacy.
principles.quote: And if turns out not to be your fault, imagine how sympathetic they'll be to your cause--here's the nicest person on Earth, blaming themselves from the get-go, and yet it's our fault!

principles.text: Be extra humble in text, where emotion is hard to convey and messages get misread; try it for a week.
principles.quote: It's everyone, any time, especially if you're communicating over email where emotions are hard to convey and text is misread.

sources.title: What a startup does to you: the founder crucible, and why it's worth it
sources.originalTitle: What a startup does to you. Or: A celebration of new life
sources.summary: Jason Cohen reflects on his daughter's birth and colic to argue that a startup, like a child, is a crucible that pushes you past your limits. Reading about the founder roller coaster doesn't prepare you; living it changes you permanently, even if the company fails. A personal essay with little tactical content.

principles.text: A startup is a crucible that doesn't probe your limits, it repeatedly blows past them. Expect that, and it's still worth doing.
principles.quote: A startup is a crucible -- a fiery place that tests your limits, not by probing them but by violently exceeding them, all of the time. It's worth it.

principles.text: You can't learn the founder experience from tweets and books; you only understand it by living it.
principles.quote: You've read the words, now you see that they're only words. Words that don't help much, not really.

principles.text: Even a failed startup leaves you stronger, wiser, and unable to go back to being a cog.
principles.quote: if you do it, even if you "fail," you will come out stronger than you could have ever been without it.

principles.text: Founders who tried and failed rarely regret it; they'd do it again.
principles.quote: I've never met a person who tried a startup, failed, and said they wouldn't have done it all over again.

principles.text: Unlike a child, a startup rarely survives on its own; founders' actions often cause its death.
principles.quote: a startup usually dies regardless of and often due to the actions of the founders

sources.title: Convergent validation: how Jason Cohen tells a real startup idea from polite "sounds good"
sources.originalTitle: The "Convergent" theory of finding truth in darkness
sources.summary: Using Feynman's physics lectures as an analogy, Jason Cohen argues a real startup idea converges: the deeper you dig in customer interviews, the more people agree on the pain, the solution and the price. A false idea diverges into contradictory advice. He contrasts a divergent first idea with WP Engine, where 30 of 40 interviewees agreed to sign up.

principles.text: A real idea converges as you dig: more interviews bring more agreement on pain, solution and price.
principles.quote: my experience vetting WP Engine was convergent. The more people I spoke with, the more agreement there was over the pain they had, whether my solution was an acceptable, and the amount they were willing to spend.

principles.text: Everyone saying "great idea" means little; truth diverges when each person's details contradict the others.
principles.quote: Everyone said "That's a great idea, you should do it!" Except, as I dug in with each person, the "truth" started diverging.

principles.text: A true law holds up in novel situations; a shallow one crumbles outside its safe space. Test ideas the same way.
principles.quote: with Conservation of Energy, the closer we look the more powerful the law becomes, the more applications we have for it, the more accurate predictions it makes, and that is the characteristic of a bona fide Fundamental Law of the Universe.

principles.text: Strong validation is people agreeing to buy during the interview, at a clear price and feature set.
principles.quote: $50/mo to make a WordPress site fast, scalable, secure, and when tech support answers the phone, they should be knowledgeable about WordPress. Kick in a staging area and backups and it's a done deal. Thirty of forty people agreed to sign up during their interview.

principles.text: There is no rubric, but convergence or divergence feels strong if you are honest with yourself.
principles.quote: Of course there'll be no rubric to determine whether an idea is tenable or whether the situation is so bleak that you should give up. But in my experience this feeling of convergence or divergence is very strong

principles.text: Your hardest battle is biasing evidence toward validation; staying ignorant only makes the failure costlier.
principles.quote: Just remember how expensive it is to remain ignorant. You will meet the same, bitter end, only after a significantly larger investment in time, money, heart, and reputation.

sources.title: How to pick where to advertise: measurable, quick, cheap, comfortable
sources.originalTitle: How do I know where to advertise?
sources.summary: After running a hundred ad campaigns at Smart Bear across paid search, trade shows, mailers, newsletters and print, Jason Cohen concluded he could not predict which would work. His fix is to rank options by measurability, speed of learning, low cost and personal comfort, then start and test rather than agonize over the "right" channel.

principles.text: You can't predict which ad channel will work; only accurate measurement plus a real trial tells you.
principles.quote: I learned I have zero ability at predicting which campaigns would produce. The only way to tell was to ensure accurate measurement was in place and try it.

principles.text: Negotiate a lower first-time rate for the trial of any new ad channel.
principles.quote: And negotiate a lower "first time" rate for the trial.

principles.text: Channel quality decays over time, so keep re-measuring and push prices down as results fall, whatever the seller's audience stats say.
principles.quote: But as the years wore on it became less and less effective, like clockwork, and I kept demanding a lower and lower price.

principles.text: First priority when choosing a channel: measurable. You must know objectively whether the value gained exceeds the money spent.
principles.quote: you have to know objectively if the value to your company is greater than the amount of money spent.

principles.text: Early on, optimize for fast, cheap learning about what advertising works, not total revenue; scale spend once you know how money turns into more money.
principles.quote: At this stage the valuable thing is seeking/learning what advertising works, not trying to maximize total revenue right out of the gate.

principles.text: Since your gut can't predict winners, pick channels you know and like, where you understand the culture and can craft a fitting ad.
principles.quote: Since your gut isn't too useful, you might as well pick something you like, especially if you already understand the culture of the site

sources.title: Why selling to the mid-market is the worst of both worlds (and what WP Engine learned)
sources.originalTitle: The mid-market briar patch
sources.summary: Jason Cohen argues that mid-sized companies combine large-company bureaucracy and slow sales cycles with small-company budgets, so the reward rarely justifies the effort. He also says "mid-sized" isn't a real market segment, and uses his early WP Engine thinking to show why focusing on one end of a market lets you optimize the whole business.

principles.text: Mid-market is the worst of both worlds: big-company sales friction, small-company budgets.
principles.quote: But the reality is **it's the worst of both worlds.**

principles.text: Mid-sized firms resist change; fear of change outweighs the upside of improvement.
principles.quote: Shackled by budgets and internal politics, technology changes require expensive coordination and retraining, and **fear of change trumps potential rewards from improvement.**

principles.text: Sales effort is roughly the same for 75 seats or 750, so small deals mean much more work per revenue dollar.
principles.quote: And since the sales effort isn't much different between selling 75 seats or 750, this is a lot more work for the revenue.

principles.text: Company size isn't a market segment; industry and the problem being solved define who you sell to.
principles.quote: "Mid-sized companies" have less in common than you'd think; it's much more important to know what industry they're in, or what problems they're trying to solve, and in what manner.

principles.text: Don't assume a gap between small and large is an opportunity; incumbents may have skipped it because it isn't cost-effective.
principles.quote: But there isn't *necessarily* an opportunity. Maybe those competitors have figured out that it's not cost-effective to sell to the middle.

principles.text: Pick one end of the market so hiring, automation, marketing and sales can be optimized around it.
principles.quote: If we chose just one or the other, we could optimize the rest of the business around it--hiring, automation, marketing, sales--and maybe we should

sources.title: How to pick between two good business options: choose the one that sounds most fun to build
sources.originalTitle: How do I stop "analyzing" and pick between two good choices?
sources.summary: Jason Cohen answers a founder torn between raising money and staying bootstrapped. When both options are valid, outside advice can't settle it and delay is costly, so use your own fulfillment as the tiebreaker. Ask which kind of company sounds most fun to build.

principles.text: When both options are rational, there is no wrong answer; never feel guilty for not choosing the other.
principles.quote: This is one of those few dilemmas where there's no wrong answer. So, whichever you choose, never let anyone else make you feel guilty about not choosing the other.

principles.text: Outside opinions can't settle it: critics exist on both sides, so the answer has to come from you.
principles.quote: Who's right? Both. Neither. This is why you cannot look externally for the answer.

principles.text: Dithering is costly: it drains time and energy and blocks other decisions like hiring, spending and features.
principles.quote: Dithering doesn't move you closer to either goal--it's draining time and energy, and it's blocking other decisions about spending money, hiring, your lifestyle, stories for the press, features, everything.
