principles.text: Use fun and fulfillment as the tiebreaker: ask what kind of company sounds most fun to build.
principles.quote: What kind of company sounds like the most fun to build?

principles.text: Founders undervalue joy and fulfillment in the calculus, which is a mistake.
principles.quote: I think fulfillment and joy barely enter into the calculus for most founders, and that's a mistake. Why build a company--or anything else for that matter--if it's not fulfilling?

principles.text: Hindsight won't tell you which path was right, so don't expect certainty later; others can help you ask better questions but not decide.
principles.quote: five years from now when you look back on this with hindsight, you still won't know which one would have been "right."

sources.title: Many low-priced customers vs few high-priced ones: why investors prefer volume but small teams should pick price
sources.originalTitle: Which is better: Many customers at low price-point or few at high price?
sources.summary: Jason Cohen compares two companies with equal revenue: 1,000 customers at $10/mo versus 10 at $1,000/mo. For raising money and maximizing growth, the many-customer company wins on market proof, market risk, time-based improvement and pivot data. A small, happy company is better served by the few-high-price model.

principles.text: Winning 1,000 paying customers at any price proves a large market exists; 10 big customers prove little.
principles.quote: If you've already found 1,000 customers, there's 10,000, and likely 100,000. If you've only found 10, there *might* be 10,000 out there, but if so, you don't have supporting evidence. Riskier.

principles.text: Market risk (finding people who will pay) kills more startups than weak product, so de-risk it first.
principles.quote: Many companies die because they can't find enough people to pay. Many more die that way than die because the product sucks or doesn't have enough features or because they don't have a staff designer.

principles.text: Landing a handful of large customers via your network is easy, so it doesn't prove a repeatable acquisition method.
principles.quote: Getting 10 people to pay you--even a large amount--is actually not that hard. If a co-founder has a Rolodex in the industry--extremely common--then it would be surprising *not* to find 10 people.

principles.text: Acquisition cost tends to fall and revenue per customer tends to rise over time, but unlocking a growth driver is not guaranteed.
principles.quote: **What's *not*true is that you always unlock big growth drivers.**

principles.text: More customers means more data and faster experiments, which makes finding the right pivot easier.
principles.quote: Lean Startup tells us that the speed at which theories can be tested is directly proportional to learning; the company who can do that faster and more accurately has a significant advantage.

principles.text: If you want a small, happy company, build for few high-paying customers; if you want growth and financial value, build for many.
principles.quote: If you want happiness and fulfillment from a small company, strive for B; if you want to maximize growth, influence, and financial value, strive for A.

sources.title: Intense Asymmetry and Self-Flagellation: why comparing your business to others is irrational
sources.originalTitle: Intense Asymmetry and Self-Flagellation
sources.summary: Jason Cohen uses Erica Douglass's self-doubt after selling her company for $1M to show why driven founders torment themselves with comparisons. Businesses are asymmetrical in time, market, team, location and everything else, so comparing yours to another is comparing the incomparable.

principles.text: No two businesses are symmetrical, so comparing your results to another company's is irrational.
principles.quote: Well it's obvious where two businesses are symmetrical: Nowhere!

principles.text: Businesses differ in time, location, market, team, features, investors and followers; you can't predict success from apparent similarity.
principles.quote: In fact they're asymmetrical in everything--location, the market they serve, the features they have, the founding team, their natural talents and gaps, the investors (if any), the amount of money raised (if any), the number of social media followers and everything else.

principles.text: Use apparent similarity to a competitor only as a spark for ideas (like a marketing tactic), not as a yardstick for yourself.
principles.quote: It's healthy to use (apparent) symmetry to spark an idea, e.g. "That's a creative marketing campaign, maybe we could try something similar."

principles.text: Analogy pitches like "Netflix for X" imply a symmetry that doesn't hold; each company has new variables and is unpredictable.
principles.quote: each company is a new challenge, with new variables, and unpredictable.

principles.text: Driven people self-select the metrics that make them feel inadequate; the stated reason is a rationalization, not the cause.
principles.quote: In fact, you could credibly argue that she's intentionally selecting only those elements which will cause her to feel inadequate, ignoring those to the contrary.

principles.text: Stop comparing yourself to something that is objectively incomparable.
principles.quote: Stop comparing yourself to something that is objectively incomparable.

sources.title: Learn by Copy: how Jason Cohen learned to write by copying others' style, not their words
sources.originalTitle: Learn by Copy
sources.summary: Jason Cohen argues that copying style (not plagiarizing) is one of the best ways to learn a craft and discover your own voice. He shows how copying Seth Godin and James Altucher taught him what he likes and can do, and applies the same idea to racquetball, chefs and Picasso.

principles.text: Copy style, not words: imitating how others do things is a legitimate way to learn, as long as it's a means to an end.
principles.quote: Rather, copying is one of the best ways of learning, growing, evaluating, and exploring. It's a valid tool so long as we regard it as a means to an end.

principles.text: Imitation reveals what you like and what you're actually able to do, which is how you find your own voice.
principles.quote: By copying I learned what I liked, what I had some ability to do.

principles.text: Try on other people's approaches like clothes; keep the bits that fit you and discard the rest.
principles.quote: The way to discovering who you are, what you value, what you're good at, what you believe, is to try things on, like clothes, to see what fits.

principles.text: Keep experimenting with other styles even after you've found your voice; the goal is growth, not matching the master.
principles.quote: "being as good as James at James' style" is not the goal. The goal is to learn and grow as a writer, and this was fun to do.

principles.text: Copying works in any pursuit: watch the best performers and mimic their specifics until you absorb what works.
principles.quote: I learned by watching the good players and trying to copy their movements--their swing, where they'd run, where they'd place the ball.

principles.text: Copying a style teaches concrete lessons about your own preferences, such as wanting a framework rather than only inspiration.
principles.quote: I like evocative examples, but I don't like leaving the reader without a framework for finding a solution.

sources.title: Scars: how your baggage shapes decisions and how to guard against its blind spots
sources.originalTitle: Scars
sources.summary: Jason Cohen argues that our emotional baggage defines who we are but also creates blind spots. Using a hosting-cost example from WP Engine, he shows how bootstrapper habits can misallocate time once a company is funded. His fix: define core values, build a company that fits them, and seek compatible outside counsel.

principles.text: Bootstrapped habits (grab cash now) become wrong once you have money in the bank; invest time in growth instead.
principles.quote: If you're bootstrapping, getting that $1000/mo *right now* is the better choice. Money is scarce, time is precious, and $1000 today is better than $5000 next year (which you might not survive to see).

principles.text: A good hourly-rate argument can still hide a worse use of time; compare against growth investments.
principles.quote: I could have used those 10 hours to make it easier to share a website speed report, and that might have resulted in 1000 people trying it over the next year

principles.text: With money in the bank, the point of investment is to turn money today into a growing, predictable revenue machine.
principles.quote: The whole point of an investment is to turn "money today" into long-term value, meaning a growing, profitable, predictable revenue machine.

principles.text: Define core values you'd hold even at the cost of money, fame or relationships; they also form company culture.
principles.quote: First, you have to decide what your core beliefs are: The inalienable tenets by which you want to live your life, no matter what--even if it means making less money, or increasing risk

principles.text: Build a company where the natural, consistent decisions match your temperament and values.
principles.quote: Decide to build a company in which the correct, consistent decisions are the ones you'll naturally take.

principles.text: You can't see your own blind spots; surround yourself with honest trusted advisors and actually listen.
principles.quote: Escape the echo chamber of your own head. Because, as in the example above, you **cannot know you're wrong**.

sources.title: Why a startup founder's time is worth $1000/hour, and how it should change your decisions
sources.originalTitle: What is the value of one hour of a startup founder's time?
sources.summary: Jason Cohen argues founders should value their time at roughly $1000/hr, not their consultant rate. Working for a startup is like a client paying in four years with a high chance of never paying. That price forces focus, delegation, and spending money to save time.

principles.text: A founder's time is worth about $1000/hour, far above any consultant hourly rate.
principles.quote: Your time is worth $1000/hour, and you need to act accordingly.

principles.text: Founding a startup means accepting deferred, high-risk payment, so the hourly value must be priced up for that risk.
principles.quote: this isn't hypothetical, this is *exactly* the terms you're accepting for yourself when you create a startup.

principles.text: Dividing your rate by the survival odds only breaks even; you need a much larger premium to justify the risk.
principles.quote: But in fact, you need to charge far more! This formula merely brings you back to break-even!

principles.text: Skip projects that can only deliver small incremental results; focus on a few things that really matter.
principles.quote: It means you don't have time for projects that have the potential only for small, incremental results.

principles.text: Delegate far more than feels natural and spend money to buy back time (assistants, bookkeepers, CPAs, help at home).
principles.quote: It means you should delegate far more than you think.

principles.text: Stay where your maximum excellence overlaps with what is most important.
principles.quote: you need to stay in the intersection of [your zone of maximum excellence] and [the zone of importance].

sources.title: When being "first" is not a competitive advantage (WP Engine's lesson)
sources.originalTitle: When being "first" is not a competitive advantage
sources.summary: Jason Cohen argues that being "first" is rarely a real advantage: it implies a buggy v1 and legacy baggage, and lets later entrants copy your public mistakes. First only wins when paired with relentless innovation and fast expansion that builds a moat, as with Amazon, McDonald's and Ford.

principles.text: "First" is not a benefit customers experience; compete on tangible advantages like uptime, speed, security and support.
principles.quote: Being "first" isn't an end in itself--it's not an advantage, not a feature, not a benefit the customer can experience.

principles.text: Most market leaders weren't first; they won by out-innovating what came before.
principles.quote: Google wasn't the first search engine, the iPod wasn't the first MP3 player, DropBox wasn't the first cloud filesystem, Excel wasn't the first spreadsheet, Dell wasn't the first PC manufacturer, Facebook wasn't the first social network

principles.text: Being first can be a shackle: legacy features, unprofitable grandfathered customers, old architecture and a sticky reputation.
principles.quote: being first can be a shackle because you're stuck with supporting the legacy of that first version

principles.text: First movers make their mistakes in public, and later competitors copy the learnings in pricing, positioning and design.
principles.quote: Worse, being first means you made all the mistakes in public. New competitors get to swoop in afterwards with the hindsight that you created

principles.text: First-mover advantage only works if you expand fast, keep innovating, and growth builds a moat that stops latecomers catching up.
principles.quote: This arises when you're not only first, but also able to expand fast and continue to innovate, and when fast expansion creates a moat which prevents late-joining competitors from catching up.

principles.text: Use a lead to fund stronger growth by constantly cutting costs and adding desirable features, as McDonald's, Ford and Amazon did.
principles.quote: But McDonalds and Ford were first and kept their leads, because they never stopped innovating in process and product, constantly driving down costs while adding new desirable features, using their lead to fund even stronger growth.

sources.title: Hiring Employee #1: screen for startup fit, writing, and gut-level partnership
sources.originalTitle: Hiring Employee #1
sources.summary: Jason Cohen explains how to make the first startup hire: write a personality-filled job post, filter hundreds of resumes with a free-form writing test, avoid bounty recruiters, and hire constantly by building a company good people seek out. He treats the first hire like a marriage, not an HR exercise.

principles.text: Hire people comfortable with startup chaos, not those who want defined processes and written expectations.
principles.quote: Startups are chaotic, rules change, and there is no "job description." It's better to make a strong decision that turns out wrong, and admit it, than to plan ahead or wait for instructions.

principles.text: Put your personality and culture in the job description so cover letters reveal who fits.
principles.quote: Be funny, reflect your personality, reflect the uniqueness of your company.

principles.text: Bounty recruiters have opposite incentives; they get paid the same however long it takes and push you to settle.
principles.quote: They make *the same amount of money* whether it takes you four days or four months to find that someone.

principles.text: Resumes are only conversation starters; dig deep on an odd detail to test real experience.
principles.quote: Resumes are conversation-starters, but they imply *nothing* about whether the person is right for you.

principles.text: Everyone, even a heads-down programmer, must communicate clearly, so screen with a free-form writing test.
principles.quote: Therefore, some part of the interview process has to include free-form writing.

principles.text: Good hires take 3-6 months, so hire constantly and make your company a place good people seek out.
principles.quote: Your company has to be a place good people will seek, not where you have to go fishing.

sources.title: Easy to criticize, hard to create: build with humility instead of trying to be right
sources.originalTitle: Easy to criticize, hard to create
sources.summary: Jason Cohen argues that tearing apart any business idea is trivial and useless, since the entrepreneur's job is to build, learn and stay humble rather than be right. He also warns against dismissing criticism wholesale, and suggests asking whether a sting hides a truth you don't want to face.

principles.text: Criticizing a business is easy and useless; betting against every startup makes you right often but ensures nothing new is created.
principles.quote: I suppose if your goal in life is to be *right*, you should bet against every startup, certainly against any novel ideas. You'll be right much more often than wrong.

principles.text: The entrepreneur's goal is not to be right but to build with humility, hold strong opinions while seeking better ones, and admit mistakes before they're fatal.
principles.quote: It's to construct with humility. To have strong opinions but seek better ones. To infect customers and employees with your peculiar disease. To live to fight another day. To acknowledge being wrong before the fault turns fatal.

principles.text: Treat startups like science: generate many ideas, expect most to be wrong, and don't get attached to a single one.
principles.quote: Real science is mostly being wrong, but staying vigilant and honest enough to continue being wrong until you're not wrong. So it is with dating. Or startups.

principles.text: A "failed" venture is never really a failure; founders come out with new skills, clarity on what motivates them, and more confidence.
principles.quote: I've never met a "failed" entrepreneur who doesn't proudly declare they're better off now: developed skills they never thought possible, learned what makes them excited to get up in the morning

principles.text: Builders must temper wanting to be right with shipping: ship before it's ready, even with bugs, and build what customers want.
principles.quote: Programmers want to be "right," but have to temper that with getting things built and shipped, even before it's ready, even with bugs

principles.text: Listen to critics with half an ear, but don't dismiss criticism without consideration; ask whether the sting reveals a truth you're avoiding.
principles.quote: Ignore the messenger, ignore the emotion, and see whether it's a gift of truth, poorly wrapped.

sources.title: Focus on one metric: why startups should chase 2x-3x moves, not small tweaks
sources.originalTitle: The full story of "the one important thing" for startups
sources.summary: Jason Cohen relays Noah Kagan's advice that a startup can focus on only one metric and should ignore the rest. Using WP Engine, he shows why shaving cancellation rate from 3% to 2.5% pales next to doubling or tripling sign-ups, even if cancellations rise. Small optimizations can wait.

principles.text: A startup can focus on only one metric. Pick it and ignore everything else.
principles.quote: A startup can focus on only one metric. So you have to decide what that is and ignore everything else.

principles.text: A small company has no time for small changes; 10x traffic beats a tiny conversion bump.
principles.quote: At a little company there's no time for small changes achieving small goals. Increasing conversion rates from 0.9% to 1.1% doesn't matter if only 100 people come to the website every day. Much more important is getting 1,000 people to come to the website every day.

principles.text: Optimize the small stuff later. It is mechanical, doable and in your control.
principles.quote: you can always optimize that little stuff later. You can always eke out 0.1% more conversion rate. Or even 1%. Of course you can.

principles.text: Pursue needle-moving levers: doubling revenue, the funding story, viral coefficient above 1, or an active user base.
principles.quote: Focus on the big thing where, if you moved the lever, it would significantly change the business. It doubles revenue or solidifies the funding story or pegs the viral coefficient above 1 or builds the asset of having an active user base.

principles.text: Don't let a secondary metric block growth: tripling sign-ups while cancellations double still nearly triples growth speed.
principles.quote: What if you got sign-ups to triple? And cancellation rate doubled, from 3% to 6%. You'd still be growing almost three times faster.

principles.text: Choosing one metric tells you which actions count as big stuff versus secondary, and breaks you out of incremental changes.
principles.quote: part of this "only do big stuff" means knowing what "big stuff" is, versus the secondary stuff. And to do that, you have to focus on only one metric.

sources.title: When being an "expert" is harmful: why assuming you know your market blocks learning
sources.originalTitle: When being an "expert" is harmful
sources.summary: Jason Cohen argues that expertise makes founders skip customer conversations and miss what has changed. A founder certain about pricing learned more in one week of quick vendor calls than in a year. Use experience for hypotheses, not decisions, and test every assumption with real customers.

principles.text: Learning happens when an assumption gets kicked out from under you, so go test the ones you're surest about.
principles.quote: whenever an assumption is kicked out from under you, that's when you learn the most.

sources.title: Being who you are, while becoming better: feed the motor, manage its side effects
sources.originalTitle: Being who you are, while becoming better
sources.summary: Jason Cohen argues that "be yourself" must include being a person who strives and keeps improving. He uses his own fight with procrastination to show why you shouldn't just accept faults. He also lists the common entrepreneur side effects of that internal "motor" and how to manage them.

principles.text: Being yourself includes being someone who strives. Don't accept faults as fixed; keep improving who you are.
principles.quote: I've decided to continue to the fight, because I know something else about "who I am"--I'm a person who strives.

principles.text: Successful entrepreneurs have an internal 'motor' that compels them to keep building, which is why serial entrepreneurs repeat.
principles.quote: You do the third one for the same reason you did the first one--because you are *compelled* to.

principles.text: Procrastination excuses sound logical but are bullshit. Time exists; you're choosing to spend it elsewhere, so delegate or delete instead.
principles.quote: Time always exists, you're deciding to do something else with that time.

principles.text: Be the best at one thing and keep improving at the rest, rather than needing to beat everyone at everything.
principles.quote: the new challenge was to (1) be the best at *one thing* (telling a computer what to do), and (2) be constantly improving in other things.

principles.text: Manage the motor's side effects (spread too thin, shiny-new-thing, overwork, perfectionism) by acknowledging them and saying no to new projects.
principles.quote: Learn to say "no" to new projects (allowing you to continue a healthy obsession over a few).

principles.text: Decide what you believe and run your company accordingly and publicly, rather than writing empty marketing prose; never compromise ethics or taste.
principles.quote: decide what you believe, then run your company accordingly and publicly and you *will* be more proud, more fulfilled, and likely more successful.

sources.title: Startup Weekend pep talk: build a company, not a website
sources.originalTitle: Startup Weekend pep talk: It ain't the code
sources.summary: Jason Cohen tells Startup Weekend builders that code and design won't win; judges and customers reward a clear pitch, validated pain, a plausible business model and evidence of demand. He urges working outside your comfort zone on those things instead of defaulting to building.

principles.text: Code and design quality rarely decide success; customers don't buy on technical difficulty or aesthetics.
principles.quote: Customers don't patronize companies on the basis of the difficulty of the code or the unit test coverage percentage or whether you used Bodoni instead of Times New Roman on the home page.

principles.text: Sharpen your pitch to extreme brevity; the real value is the strong choices it forces on you.
principles.quote: Your verbal pitch should be under 60 seconds; your home page should entice in three words and explain in under fifty.

principles.text: Get feedback from five strangers early; a validated concept beats an unreviewed working app.
principles.quote: A concept validated by five people is far more valuable than a working application that no one has critiqued.

principles.text: Build a simple unit-economics spreadsheet to prove revenue can outweigh acquisition, salary and operating costs.
principles.quote: It's surprisingly difficult to build a company where revenues outweigh costs of marketing, salaries, and operations, even at scale.

principles.text: Find evidence people are already looking for a solution; it proves need and hints at how to reach them.
principles.quote: Evidence of searching and asking demonstrates not only need but suggests a way to reach those people.

principles.text: Demand beats product: a landing page with 50 signups is more of a company than a built product nobody asked for.
principles.quote: Because if you can identify a *need*, all of you have the skills to meet that need. The opposite is not true--a website cannot generate people who are interested in it.

sources.title: Does design matter? Jason Cohen on WP Engine's redesign, ITWatchDogs and deciding where design fits your strategy
sources.originalTitle: On the (un?)importance of design
sources.summary: Jason Cohen shows that a full WP Engine redesign didn't move bounce rate, time-on-site or conversion. Smart Bear and ITWatchDogs grew fast with ugly sites, while Hipmunk won on design alone. His conclusion is to decide whether design is core to your identity and act consistently. If it isn't, nail something else harder.

principles.text: A full redesign can delight customers and staff yet leave bounce rate, time-on-site and conversion unchanged. Measure before assuming design drives growth.
principles.quote: Hmm. Looks like the data are objectively saying "design doesn't matter."

principles.text: Subjective signals count even when metrics don't move: embarrassed staff, customers who wince referring you, and a bigger customer judging you mature.
principles.quote: But as much as I respect Lean Startup theory, objective measurements aren't the only things that matter.

principles.text: Ugly sites can still grow fast. Smart Bear doubled revenue and profit yearly for five years, and ITWatchDogs grew every month to a successful exit.
principles.quote: This doesn't prove design *doesn't* matter, but it does suggest design may not be the deciding factor.

principles.text: When design is your core strategy, how you win and acquire customers, it can be the most important thing. Hipmunk's only edge was a quantum leap in design.
principles.quote: When design is fundamental to the strategy--how you _win_, how you acquire and retain customers, garner attention and referrals, and be distinguished in the market--then design can be the most important thing.

principles.text: Message and brand fit can beat polish. ITWatchDogs' messy site matched its low-cost, relatable culture and customers' cluttered offices, and the message was clear.
principles.quote: The site might have *looked bad*, but our message couldn't have been clearer.

principles.text: Decide whether design is core to your startup's identity, then act consistently. If it's not, nail your real strengths harder, since design-led rivals will mask their weak spots.
principles.quote: if design is not important to you, you'd better decide what *is* important and **nail those things all the harder**

sources.title: Why Jason Cohen finally called bullshit on a spammy guest-post offer
sources.originalTitle: Do I dare call bullshit aloud? Do you?
sources.summary: Jason Cohen reflects on why he answers spam and pandering offers politely: fear of offending famous or soon-to-be-famous people. He asks when a blogger earns the right to say what they think and argues that social-media "honesty" is mostly performance. Reflective and personal, light on tactics.

principles.text: Politeness toward bad offers is often fear of offending influential people, not real courtesy.
principles.quote: I'm afraid I might piss off someone famous or potentially famous who then might not want to work with me in future or even say something bad about me in public.

principles.text: Don't hand your audience's channel to anonymous affiliate marketers pushing products under the guise of content.
principles.quote: these people are affiliate marketers, and what they neglected to mention in the introductory email is that these auto-published articles would furthermore push products for them to monetize.

principles.text: Saying what you honestly feel, even if it annoys someone, is a milestone worth reaching.
principles.quote: I finally grew the stones to say what I feel even if it pisses someone off.

principles.text: Most social media 'authenticity' is performance: bloggers project more confidence and certainty than they have.
principles.quote: Bloggers fluff their feathers, coming off more confident, smarter, and more sure than they are

principles.text: Pandering to minor celebrities for reciprocity undermines honest engagement.
principles.quote: Twitterers RT and "follow" and pander to the most minor of celebs

principles.text: You don't need to earn the right to disagree with respected people; waiting for an audience size threshold is a trap.
principles.quote: When do I earn the right to say what I think? Why do I think I need to "earn" that right?

sources.title: Never say "no," but rarely say "yes": qualify your yes so it funds what you want
sources.originalTitle: Never say "no," but rarely say "yes."
sources.summary: Jason Cohen resolves the tension between startup focus and experimentation by never refusing outright, but attaching terms to "yes" so strong that acceptance funds your real goals and rejection costs nothing. He illustrates with $100/hr consulting, WP Engine's large-blogger deals, and $2,500/day code-review trips at Smart Bear.

principles.text: Don't say "no" to off-strategy opportunities; say a heavily qualified "yes" so you can still explore and learn if you were wrong.
principles.quote: Here's what I do: I never say "no." But I carefully qualify "yes."

principles.text: Set the terms so both outcomes win: if they accept, it more than compensates for the distraction; if they decline, it wasn't a fit anyway.
principles.quote: If they say "yes," you're happy because the terms or money are *so good*, it more than compensates for the distraction, perhaps funding the thing you really want to do.

principles.text: Price unwanted work far above your normal rate; people may well accept. Quoting 4x his rate got a yes instead of a laugh.
principles.quote: The difference between saying "no" and getting $150 for about two hours of my life was all in how I phrased "yes."

principles.text: Quote a distracting big customer high enough to cover a whole person's salary, since the deal will eat much of that person's time.
principles.quote: This deal needs to be big enough to not only make a reasonable profit on the operating expenses, but pay for an entire developer's salary

principles.text: Anchor your qualified yes to funding something you already want to do, such as a hire, runway, or marketing efforts.
principles.quote: "Yes" if it pays for an entire additional person.

principles.text: Treat distracting revenue like funding: it must be transformative to be worth the interruption, otherwise let the price filter it out.
principles.quote: Funding is always a distraction from actually running your business, so the amount of money you get must be transformative to the business.

sources.title: Why copying #1 is a trap: luck, survivorship and tournament effects in business
sources.originalTitle: Our unhealthy fixation with emulating #1
sources.summary: Jason Cohen argues that markets work like single-elimination tournaments, so the "undefeated" winner proves less about repeatable skill than we assume. He urges skepticism toward "be more like Google/Apple/37signals" advice, learning from companies at every rank, and striving to become a better version of yourself rather than a clone of #1.

principles.text: The market is a tournament that always yields one winner, so #1's success may not come from a repeatable, codifiable law.
principles.quote: I'm not sure we can assume the contest (marketing, sales, product) and tournament (the marketplace) picks #1 based on a repeatable, codify-able law.

principles.text: Don't assume the top company is the rightful leader; skill and luck are mixed in unknown proportions.
principles.quote: We tend to fixate on whoever is #1, in business as with sports, tacitly assuming that the contest is mostly skill and therefore the tournament has selected the rightful leader.

principles.text: Lessons exist well below the top ranks; smaller successes can teach as much as the giants.
principles.quote: Isn't the #4253 largest company in the world still a success story, perhaps with new lessons and perspectives?

principles.text: When told to 'be more like Google', question whether the advisor simply has no other reference point.
principles.quote: When someone insists you need to be "more like Google," consider that perhaps it's the only thing they know to compare to.

principles.text: Celebrity-company playbooks rarely fit a young startup; most successful companies don't resemble them.
principles.quote: When someone insists you need to be "more like 37signals," consider that almost no successful companies are like 37signals.

principles.text: Aim to become a better version of what you already are, not a copy of the market leader.
principles.quote: It's fine to muse about being #1, but let's not all strive to become just like #1.

sources.title: Specificity: swap generic words for concrete ones to write clearer, funnier copy
sources.originalTitle: Specificity: A weapon of mass effectiveness
sources.summary: Jason Cohen argues the single best writing advice for marketing copy, pitches and humor is to be specific. He walks through a workshop that replaces generic words, tightens accuracy, adds named examples, and shows how specificity is the easiest route to funny.

principles.text: The best advice for any writing (marketing, blog, sales pitch, investor pitch, humor) is to be specific.
principles.quote: My single best advice about writing--whether for marketing copy, blogging, a sales pitch, an investor pitch, or even humor, is: BE SPECIFIC

principles.text: Generic words signal lazy writing and get interpreted differently by each reader, so the message received is unclear.
principles.quote: Generic words are a sure sign of lazy writing.

principles.text: Move from merely true to accurate: pick the precise word (e.g. "evangelist" not "expert") that says what you actually mean.
principles.quote: After disposing with the obviously-useless generic words we're still left with words which, while technically correct, are still not contributing enough to the meaning and persuasiveness of your writing.

principles.text: Concrete examples make persuasive arguments clearer, more believable, harder to counter, and easier to apply and research.
principles.quote: Examples make arguments more believable.

principles.text: Naming real people and industries makes a claim tangible, even if the reader has never heard of them.
principles.quote: See how much more evocative it is to put a name to the evangelists; even if you've never heard of those guys, knowing their names makes it tangible.

principles.text: Specific nouns, verbs and adjectives are the easiest way to be funny; exaggerate, invent an example, or highlight the absurd.
principles.quote: It's odd but true that almost any statement can be made funny merely by being specific, and there are many ways to do it.

sources.title: Startup Exercise: what money can't solve (team, authority, learning) is what's most valuable
sources.originalTitle: Startup Exercise: What can't be solved with money?
sources.summary: Jason Cohen separates what money can fix (execution, ads, code, QA, runway) from what it can't (finding great people, authority, knowing what to build, learning). He argues exploration can't be bought while execution can, and shows how to use this when pitching investors or competing against better-funded rivals.

principles.text: Execution can be bought with money; exploration cannot. Money only accelerates once you know what to do.
principles.quote: Execution can be solved with money; exploration cannot.

principles.text: Great people are scarce and always have options, so money alone won't find them. Money helps only after you find the person.
principles.quote: If someone handed me a million dollars it wouldn't help me find an awesome person; they're just scarce.

principles.text: Most marketing can be bought (ads, campaigns, landing page tests, freemium), but authority-driven attention from blogging and social media cannot.
principles.quote: You can't buy authority.

principles.text: Concepts, behaviors, knowledge and process can't be bought. Money becomes an accelerant once you know how to learn quickly.
principles.quote: Concepts, behaviors, knowledge, and process cannot be fabricated with money, and possibly cannot even be accelerated.

principles.text: When raising money, name the unsolved problems before investors do and bring a clear plan. Without one, wait.
principles.quote: If you don't have a clear, plausible plan, don't raise money yet.

principles.text: Don't raise money before the core team is assembled, since cash can't fix a missing team.
principles.quote: Specifically, don't raise money if you haven't assembled the core team.

sources.title: Startups are emotionally draining: how to get through the urge to quit
sources.originalTitle: When you want to quit because it's just not worth it
sources.summary: Jason Cohen argues most small startups fail because founders stop, often from emotional exhaustion. He tells how a bullying enterprise procurement manager made him want to quit, even though the man had no real power. His point: you don't need to be stoic or confident, just keep going.

principles.text: Most small startups fail because the founders stop working on them, often from emotional drain.
principles.quote: Most startups fail "only" because the founders stop working on them, and often it's because it's emotionally draining.

principles.text: Emotional lows are not just an early-stage problem; they persist years later despite revenue, profit and a great team.
principles.quote: The pain is not limited to the beginning of the venture. It's still there years later, despite real revenue, profitability, customers arriving every day, and a great team.

principles.text: Surviving a startup doesn't require constant confidence, stoicism or wisdom; it requires sticking through the tough parts despite your weaknesses.
principles.quote: Getting through this slog of a thing that's a startup--or anything difficult and worthwhile--doesn't require that you're always confident or stoic or smart or right or wise.

principles.text: Aim to live through hard emotional moments rather than beat them; reasoning often never erases the feeling.
principles.quote: Living through it, not beating it.

principles.text: Publish prices on your website and don't discount, even in enterprise deals; bulk pricing is already built in.
principles.quote: We don't discount; instead we put our pricing on our website so there's no misunderstanding.

principles.text: Stopping is the real way little startups fail, so tenacity matters even if it isn't all it takes.
principles.quote: I'm not saying tenacity is all it takes. Just that without it, you'll stop.

sources.title: The unfortunate math behind consulting companies: why hiring is less profitable than it looks
sources.originalTitle: The unfortunate math behind consulting companies
sources.summary: Jason Cohen shows that an employee's true cost per billable hour is about double their nominal rate once holidays, taxes, non-billable time, downtime and training are counted. He then covers the levers for consulting profit (charging more, billing more hours, subcontractors, treating a product like a client) and why scaling or launching a side product rarely works.

principles.text: An employee's true cost per billable hour is about double the nominal rate, so a 2x markup only breaks even.
principles.quote: The true cost of an employee is double the nominal cost. If you bill out a so-called "$30/hour" employee at $60/hour, you'll only break even.

principles.text: Clients price an employee on nominal rate plus a little profit, not your true cost, which caps what you can re-bill.
principles.quote: they'll base it on the person's nominal rate plus a little profit for you. This caps the amount you can actually re-bill before client feels ripped off.

principles.text: If an employee can be billed at a rate, bill yourself higher and work fewer hours, skipping the hiring and management hassle.
principles.quote: If your underling can be billed at $100/hour, can't you bill at $150/hour at least? And if you worked just 20 hours/week (on average) at that rate you'd clear $150,000 annually without the hassle of hiring and managing an employee.

principles.text: Price increases go straight to profit and small discounts crater it; raise price by P% before offering a P% pre-pay discount.
principles.quote: A better idea is to raise your prices by P%, then offer a P% discount for pre-pay. Then your cash-rich customers are paying the same, but others are creating more profit in exchange for delayed payment

principles.text: Scaling a consulting firm adds pipeline, hiring and management drudgery that eats the apparent profit.
principles.quote: With these new expenses it's not unusual to see that so-called $300k in profits came back to $150k. And now you're doing things you hate doing.

principles.text: Side-product attempts by consultancies fail from no owner, no marketing skill and no focus; treat the product as a client with budget and scheduled hours.
principles.quote: Most of the problems above can be fixed by treating the product as a client

sources.title: Marketing Platform Independence: avoid betting your whole startup on a volatile platform
sources.originalTitle: Marketing Platform Independence
sources.summary: Jason Cohen argues that building a business on a platform you don't control (Twitter, the App Store, SEO) is risky, using TweetUp and Ad.ly as cautionary tales. Choose stable platforms or ecosystems, or diversify across many acquisition channels so no single rug-pull kills you.

principles.text: Bootstrapped companies can't afford the platform risk that funded startups can absorb by pivoting.
principles.quote: Both of these companies have millions in funding, so they can afford to try new things or just flounder around. Bootstrapped companies have no such luxury.

principles.text: Using a platform as one tactic is fine; making it the whole business is the danger. The test: would it kill you if it vanished tomorrow?
principles.quote: If an iPhone app is a fun, useful addition to your offering but it wouldn't kill you if it vanished tomorrow, that's great. If your entire company is based on an iPhone app, this is critical.

principles.text: Treat SEO as one lead-gen tactic among many, never the only bet, because the rules keep shifting and a competitor or Google can oust you.
principles.quote: If you're doing SEO as one of ten tactics to get people to show up to your site, that's great. If you're betting the entire business on getting traffic through search results, at any moment a competitor or the platform itself could oust you.

principles.text: A dependency is safe if you can leave it and survive: exploit the tool rather than depend on it for the business's success.
principles.quote: you're exploiting Heroku as a tool; your business's success does not depend on them.

principles.text: Stable ecosystems with mutually dependent participants (like WordPress) are safer than single-owner platforms; good platform owners protect their ecosystem.
principles.quote: Salesforce knows they're the shark, and ensuring the survival of the remora fish is vital for their own health and continuation.

principles.text: Diversify your customer acquisition channels so losing one doesn't sink you.
principles.quote: The other way is to diversify. Like with SEO for lead-gen, you still do it, but it's not your only means of lead-gen.

sources.title: Why a big blog audience didn't launch WP Engine: reputation's real payoff was recruiting
sources.originalTitle: Reputation isn't as powerful as you imagine
sources.summary: Jason Cohen launched WP Engine to 18,000 blog subscribers and got just two signups, far below his 10-50 estimate. The audience's real value was recruiting a cofounder-caliber team member, and the first 50 paying customers came from other work. Fame helps, but startups stay hard.

principles.text: A large audience converts far worse than you expect; don't count on it to launch a product.
principles.quote: WPEngine got two new signups. Only two. That with 18,000 wonderful, loyal, friendly, supportive RSS subscribers and as many page-hits from Twitter and HackerNews.

principles.text: Forecasts of audience conversion can be off by an order of magnitude, so don't plan around them.
principles.quote: I figured on 10-20 new customers at minimum and dreamed of 50. I was wrong by an order of magnitude.

principles.text: Early customers come mostly from direct customer-getting work, not from the audience's halo.
principles.quote: So whatever we did without the advantage of this blog was far more important, at least for getting initial customers.

principles.text: An audience's best use may be attracting talent: your writing shows people your attitude and credentials.
principles.quote: Well we got Aaron, and it's because of this blog.

principles.text: In a commodity market you need severe differentiation or moats; a standout team can be one.
principles.quote: In a mature market you need severe points of differentiation or moats, and one of those (I felt) had to be the team itself.

principles.text: Fame is a real unfair advantage, but it doesn't make a startup easy or likely to succeed.
principles.quote: So fame does help in important ways--enough even to deserve the title of "unfair advantage"--but startups are still hard and unlikely to succeed no matter who's at the helm.

sources.title: Why "if you build it they won't come": five ways startups break through marketing noise
sources.originalTitle: If you build it, they won't come, unless…
sources.summary: Jason Cohen argues that generic tactics like A/B-tested AdWords, SEO and Twitter followers are not a marketing strategy, since every startup lists the same ones. He offers ways to stand out: radical transparency, virality built into the product, a real story, a paid-acquisition machine where cost to acquire is below lifetime revenue, and borrowed credibility from relationships.

principles.text: Tactics every startup lists (A/B tests, SEO, Twitter, blog reviews) are not a strategy; you stay invisible.
principles.quote: every new startup on Earth says exactly these things.

principles.text: Radical transparency only works if you go all the way: publish revenue, make public promises, reveal your playbook.
principles.quote: you have to *truly* bare your soul if you want to compete on the transparency front. It's not for everyone, and I'm not suggesting it ought to be, but if you're going to employ it, don't half-ass it.

principles.text: If a product is meant to be viral, build it into the core usage loop; share buttons don't make a product viral.
principles.quote: if it *is* supposed to be viral it better be encoded in the DNA of the application, not bolted on as an afterthought.

principles.text: Press and word of mouth come from a story about why anyone should care, not a description of what the product does.
principles.quote: The number one mistake founders make when trying to generate press is talking about what the company *does* rather than telling a compelling *story*.

principles.text: One well-tuned story beats piles of ad tests, though finding it can take years.
principles.quote: It took me *five years* to figure out (a) I needed a story and (b) what the story was. It's hard. But one story beats a pile of AdWords A/B tests.

principles.text: Paid acquisition works if you find a repeatable model where cost to acquire a customer is below lifetime revenue, and count all true costs.
principles.quote: The average cost of acquiring a customer is `$C` (advertising, sales, support, doing demos) and the lifetime revenue you get from that customer is `$R`, so if `C < R` you have a business.

sources.title: Customer validation: find ten people who say they'll buy before you build
sources.originalTitle: Yes, but who said they'd actually BUY the damn thing?
sources.summary: Jason argues that the minimum proof for a startup idea is ten real people saying they'll pay. He dismantles the common excuses (scratching your own itch, mock-ups don't work, a great product sells itself, friends like it) and says to attack the riskiest non-code parts of the business first.

principles.text: Before building, find ten people who say they'll buy it; otherwise the company isn't real.
principles.quote: If you can't find ten people who say they'll buy it, your company is bullshit.

principles.text: Being your own customer is only the spark of an idea, not market validation.
principles.quote: "Scratching your own itch" is how all three of my companies started, but it's only that--the start.

principles.text: If the market is millions strong, finding ten buyers is trivial; failing means the market isn't there or isn't interested.
principles.quote: If there are millions, it's trivial to find ten. If you can't find even ten, then either there's not millions or those millions aren't interested in you.

principles.text: You should be able to validate with a short pitch or mock-up; a 30-second pitch is the test of a clear concept.
principles.quote: If your concept is so esoteric that you can't describe it in 30 seconds at a cocktail party, it's either too complex or you don't understand it yourself.

principles.text: Good software alone doesn't make a business, so tackle the riskiest non-code unknowns (finding and convincing customers) first.
principles.quote: If your goal is a business (not a hobby), building charming, novel software isn't enough.

principles.text: Only willingness to pay counts as validation, not opinions from friends, family or even experts.
principles.quote: The only thing that matters is that people are willing to give you money!

sources.title: Real Unfair Advantages: only what can't be copied or bought is a moat
sources.originalTitle: Real Unfair Advantages
sources.summary: Anything that can be copied will be copied, including features, copy and pricing. Jason Cohen argues the only real competitive advantages are those that can't be copied or bought: insider knowledge, an obsessive hard One Thing, personal authority, a dream team, the right celebrity endorsement, and existing customers. Build toward them on purpose.

principles.text: Assume anything copyable will be copied; passion, hard work and being lean are not an edge.
principles.quote: Anything that *can* be copied *will* be copied, including features, marketing copy, and pricing.

principles.text: The only durable advantage is something competitors can neither copy nor buy.
principles.quote: The only real competitive advantage is that which cannot be copied and cannot be bought.

principles.text: Deep industry knowledge and pain-point insight is a legal unfair advantage that is hard for rivals to assemble.
principles.quote: using intimate knowledge of an industry and the specific pain points within an industry is a perfectly legal unfair advantage for a startup.

principles.text: Pick One Thing that is hard and refuse to lose on it; a merely unique feature is easily duplicated.
principles.quote: To remain un-copyable, your One Thing needs to be not just central to your existence, but also difficult to achieve.

principles.text: Authority can't be purchased; it takes years of effort, which is exactly why it is an untouchable edge.
principles.quote: **Authority cannot be purchased.** You can't raise VC money and then "have authority" in a year.

principles.text: A dream team (varied skills, common vision, insider knowledge) cuts startup risk and is hard to duplicate.
principles.quote: Of course a Dream Team doesn't guarantee success but it **significantly reduces the risk** of the startup, and furthermore is difficult for the competition to duplicate.

sources.title: Be human and fallible: why sincere, specific personality beats sterile corporate polish
sources.originalTitle: Human + Fallible = Love; Corporate + Sterile = Refund
sources.summary: Jason Cohen argues customers now expect providers to try hard, care, and treat them well when things inevitably break, and they forgive sincere human error but turn adversarial toward sterile corporate behavior. He offers practical ways to find your voice and warns that a strong persona will alienate some people while making the rest love you.

principles.text: Customers forgive sincere human error but grow adversarial and distrustful toward sterile corporate relationships.
principles.quote: People readily forgive sincere human error, but become adversarial and distrustful with the typical, sterile customer/provider relationship.

principles.text: The modern expectation isn't zero mistakes; it's that you care and respond well when you inevitably screw up.
principles.quote: The new attitude is not "Those assholes better not *ever* screw up," but rather "I expect them to try hard, to care, and to treat me well *when* they inevitably screw up."

principles.text: Earn forgiveness through ongoing effort, learning from mistakes, and a culture of excellence, not a faux-heartfelt crisis apology.
principles.quote: You're learning from your mistakes, evidenced by problems tending towards the esoteric, and by explaining in your apology what steps you've taken to avoid this and similar classes of error.

principles.text: Find your voice by criticizing others, deciding what you are not, and copying something you love as a rough draft.
principles.quote: It's easy to identify corporate stuff that pisses you off; use that to decide both what not to do and what to do instead.

principles.text: Every strong decision alienates some people while thrilling others; be strong, specific, and honest anyway.
principles.quote: every strong decision you make will necessarily alienate many people even while it's thrilling others.

principles.text: Having no persona gives nobody a reason to get excited, tolerate faults, or tell friends, so be soulful.
principles.quote: Then why would anyone get excited about you? Why would they put up with your faults? Why would they tell their friends about you?

sources.title: Local minima in A/B testing: run a radically different variant alongside incremental tweaks
sources.originalTitle: Out of the cesspool and into the sewer: A/B testing trap
sources.summary: Incremental A/B testing tends to get stuck in a local optimum, like water pooling in a backyard instead of reaching the sewer. Jason argues you should always test a radically different version next to the small tweaks, because a discontinuous change in message, value proposition or audience can pay off far more than polishing the current page.

principles.text: Incremental A/B tests eventually plateau when you only tweak small things.
principles.quote: Often what happens is you get to a point where small changes aren't doing anything.

principles.text: Use statistics, not gut feel, to tell whether small changes are actually moving results.
principles.quote: It can be hard to recognize this effect which is why you need to (horrors!) use math to decide empirically whether anything's actually happening.

principles.text: When tweaks plateau, don't give up; change message, layout, value proposition or target audience wholesale.
principles.quote: Completely changing your perspective, your message, your layout, your value proposition, your colors, or your target audience might reveal an entirely new, discontinuous, non-incremental change.

principles.text: Hunt for discontinuous wins from the start, since new territory beats incremental polish.
principles.quote: because looking in completely new places has the potential to yield far more results than incremental improvement, you need to be looking for discontinuous results from the start.

principles.text: Run both: the incremental variant against baseline and a radically different variant.
principles.quote: Instead of just running A versus incremental-change A2, also run a B version that's radically different from A.

principles.text: If a radically different message wins big, let it reshape your messaging and possibly the business.
principles.quote: Better still, if a radically different message gets you massively better results, perhaps all your messaging should change accordingly.

sources.title: The Pattern-Seeking Fallacy: why mining marketing data for "insights" finds noise
sources.originalTitle: The Pattern-Seeking Fallacy
sources.summary: Humans see patterns in randomness, and slicing analytics or A/B test data many ways guarantees some "significant" result appears by chance. Jason Cohen argues you should form a theory first, then test that specific theory, rather than hunting through combinations after the fact.

principles.text: Humans are bad at telling real patterns from randomness, even when trying to be analytical.
principles.quote: We humans are terrible at discerning patterns from randomness, and in marketing data we unwittingly find "insights" that are actually noise.

principles.text: Combing a mountain of data for a pattern guarantees you will find one, and it means nothing.
principles.quote: This is the epitome of Pattern-Seeking--combing through a mountain of data until you find a pattern.

principles.text: Rare events become inevitable when you run enough trials, so a striking result from many comparisons isn't evidence.
principles.quote: Those events are rare, but I'm flipping so much that rare events will naturally occur.

principles.text: Slicing analytics many ways is like running 1000 coin-flip trials and reporting only the all-heads one.
principles.quote: Except you're running 1000 coin-flip trials, looking only at the trial where it came up all heads and declaring the coin "biased."

principles.text: Use apparent patterns to form a theory, then test it deliberately; don't treat the pattern as the insight.
principles.quote: You can use apparent patterns to form a theory; that's good. [...] But then you have to test it, so that it's science, not baseball announcing.

principles.text: Decide beforehand which metrics and cohorts matter, and test a specific hypothesis instead of generating many ad variants.
principles.quote: Instead of rooting around Google Analytics hoping to find a combination of factors with a good conversion rate, decide beforehand which conversion rates are important for which cohorts, then measure and track those only.

sources.title: Competing with big companies: go where gorillas can't follow and do what they can't
sources.originalTitle: Telling the 800-lb Gorilla to Shove it up his Ass
sources.summary: Jason Cohen argues founders overfear the 800-lb gorilla. Big companies are slow, only play in big markets, and are boxed in by their brand and existing revenue, so a small company can use their entry to validate its market, pick niches they ignore, and win by doing what they structurally cannot. The more dangerous rival is another scrappy startup.

principles.text: Fear the nimble small startup copying you more than the slow incumbent, who will likely be doing the same thing in two to four years.
principles.quote: What *is* scary is another scrappy, smart startup like yours--another tree-shrew. The one who silently observes you from afar, then drives down the road you paved, skipping the mistakes you made and copying the good parts.

principles.text: Your goal is to earn more customers on your own terms, not to beat or destroy another company.
principles.quote: **It's not your purpose to "beat" another company.** It's your purpose to define yourself on your own terms, not in terms of how you're like or unlike someone else.

principles.text: A big player entering your market validates it and can raise your company's value, since their rivals then need an answer.
principles.quote: In short, Microsoft copying the idea would only validate the market, causing the value of Smart Bear to increase.

principles.text: Big companies only play in big markets, so pick a market worth about $100M that they can't justify entering, but not a micro-niche.
principles.quote: Big companies play only in big markets.

principles.text: A big company's strengths (brand, customer base, revenue stream) also restrict it: it can't take risks, ship quickly, or change its image.
principles.quote: They can't take a risk because protecting the existing revenue stream is more important than *anything* else, even if it means their ultimate demise.

principles.text: Do what incumbents can't: change the product, fill the image gap, and act on customer feedback within a week.
principles.quote: They can't change their product, so you can innovate without competition. They can't change their image, so you can fill the gap. They can't listen to a customer and make an impact one week later; you can.

sources.title: Tech Support Is Sales: Turning support into your brand, sales channel and product research
sources.originalTitle: Tech Support is sales
sources.summary: Jason Cohen argues tech support is the face of your company and often the only human contact customers have with you. At Smart Bear, great support closed individual and six-figure enterprise deals without a traditional sales team, and doubled as the closest thing to customer development for a bootstrapper.

principles.text: For most customers, tech support is the only human interaction they have with your company, so staffing it with your worst-treated, least-qualified people is a mistake.
principles.quote: For most of your customers, **tech support is the only human interaction they'll have with you.** Are you really going to leave that up to your worst-treated, least-paid, least-qualified employees?

principles.text: You can win large deals without a classic sales team if your support genuinely makes customers successful.
principles.quote: At Smart Bear we made millions of dollars in both individual and enterprise sales without "sales."

principles.text: The purpose of support is to make customers fantastic at their jobs, not just to answer their literal question. Find out what they are trying to accomplish and help with that.
principles.quote: I say **the purpose of tech support is to make your customers fantastic at their jobs**, which happen to involve your product.

principles.text: Make the customer awesome and she will pay you so she can keep being awesome. Enablement is a whole-company job, not only a product feature.
principles.quote: Make your customer awesome and she'll give you money so she can keep being awesome.

principles.text: Because customers expect bad support, simply acting human (a non-automated email reply) earns outsized goodwill and word of mouth.
principles.quote: When your customers expect a turd sandwich and you deliver a turkey club with chipotle aioli, you earn major bonus points

principles.text: Mine support conversations for the meta-questions behind each problem: confusion, terminology, mismatched worldview, and unmet needs that point to new products or pivots. This is how Smart Bear found code review.
principles.quote: This last line of questioning is exactly [how Smart Bear came to be](https://longform.asmartbear.com/product-market-fit-formula/) a company about peer code review and not "version control data mining."

sources.title: Not disruptive, and proud of it: why modest, incremental products beat chasing disruption
sources.originalTitle: Not disruptive, and proud of it
sources.summary: Jason argues founders should build something people want to buy rather than aim to be "disruptive." Disruption is hard to pitch, unwanted by most people, often unprofitable for the disruptor, and usually a hindsight label. He cites Smart Bear, ITWatchDogs and WP Engine as modest, well-executed wins.

principles.text: Aim to make something useful and delightful, not to be disruptive. Disruption is a side effect of success, not a goal.
principles.quote: You should be worrying about making something useful and delightful, not about how "disruptive" you can be.

principles.text: Incremental improvement on a known problem in a known market is a legitimate way to build a great business.
principles.quote: What's wrong with taking a known problem in a known market and just doing it better or with a fresh, unique perspective?

principles.text: If a product's benefits are hard to explain, it makes a terrible sales pitch.
principles.quote: "It's hard to explain" means it's a terrible sales pitch.

principles.text: Most people resist change and only switch when in real pain, so sell a point-solution to a specific pain point rather than a better world.
principles.quote: Selling a point-solution for a point-problem is easier than getting people to change how they live their lives.

principles.text: Products later called disruptive often began as simply "better" than predecessors (Google was ~11th search engine; iPod won on design alone).
principles.quote: Disruptive in hindsight, sure, but the genesis was just "better" than the 10 search engines that came before.

principles.text: Disruptors often don't capture the profit. Later entrants skip the cost of version 1 and jump to version 3.
principles.quote: They were the disruptors, but they didn't profit from the disruption.

sources.title: Why creative "taste" beats pure optimization: the Code Historian mini-viewer
sources.originalTitle: Maybe not so much with the "optimization"
sources.summary: Jason Cohen argues that Lean, A/B testing and metrics-only thinking can crowd out creative product decisions that earn customer love. Using the costly, "non-optimal" mini-viewer in his first product, Code Historian, he shows that extra-effort delight can win customers in ways metrics don't capture.

principles.text: Sometimes build something just because it's cool; product taste matters and can't be reduced to data.
principles.quote: Sometimes you should do something just because it's cool. There's such a thing as product "taste."

principles.text: Aim for customer love, not just utility; love comes from emotional, gut-feel, less incremental work rather than feature checklists or A/B tests.
principles.quote: This is beyond utility--this is love.

principles.text: A feature can be a terrible business decision on paper (costlier, riskier, no measurable usability gain) and still be what customers love most.
principles.quote: And yet, everyone loved the mini-viewer.

principles.text: Extra-effort, endearing touches create real value that metrics and spreadsheets don't capture.
principles.quote: It took extra effort but it was endearing--an important attribute not easily captured with metrics and spreadsheets.

principles.text: Doing only the minimum makes you efficient but not thrilling; Lean can't stir hearts on its own.
principles.quote: When we do the minimum necessary to get the job done, we're efficient but not thrilling.

principles.text: Still cut corners in most areas (80% of benefit for 20% of effort), and save the extra effort for moments that delight.
principles.quote: Often we can and should accept 80% of the benefit if it means 20% of the effort. Customers generally prefer the right features over more features.

sources.title: Why subtle tweaks get drowned out: focus on the big, in-your-face effects
sources.originalTitle: A butterfly flaps its wings and you make a sale
sources.summary: Jason Cohen argues the "butterfly effect" idea in marketing, where tiny design or psychological nudges drive big results, is mostly noise. In a world of competing stimuli, subtle influences cancel out, so effort should go to large, obvious levers like a popular blogger's mention, a spreadable story, or thrilling one customer.

principles.text: Subtle influences cancel out amid constant ambient stimuli, so don't build strategy on them.
principles.quote: If I'm constantly influenced in all directions, the forces cancel each other out, and none of them matter.

principles.text: Spend time on big, obvious, non-subliminal effects instead of chasing tiny psychological tricks.
principles.quote: instead of chasing subtle subliminal effects, most of which will be wiped away by the ambient noise of life, we could spend our time on the big-ass, in-yo-face, non-subliminal effects.

principles.text: A mention from a popular blogger beats cosmetic tweaks like logo color.
principles.quote: if you get a popular blogger to mention you, that's more influential than the color of your logo.

principles.text: A story people want to spread outweighs polish like a snappy home-page animation.
principles.quote: if you have a compelling story that people intrinsically want to spread, that's more influential than building a snappy animation for your home page.

principles.text: Thrilling one real prospect in a demo is worth more than thousands of branded website hits.
principles.quote: if you thoroughly thrill one person in a product demo, that's more money in the bank than 1,000 people hitting your website and getting "branded" that you're "trustworthy" because of your steel-blue color palette and stoic font.

principles.text: Most of our small-detail efforts are drowned out by the distraction of the internet and life; take care of the big stuff.
principles.quote: I just think most of our efforts are drowned out by the seething distraction that is the internet and life in general.

sources.title: Employed with a side of startup: how to run a startup on the side of a day job
sources.originalTitle: Employed with a side of startup
sources.summary: Jason Cohen explains how to start a company while employed without legal trouble. He covers choosing a business that fits your constraints, embracing slow growth, being open with your employer, and managing scarce time. Goal: build something solid enough to quit your day job.

principles.text: Turn side-gig constraints into competitive advantages instead of fighting them.
principles.quote: The right attitude is not only to work inside your constraints, but to turn them into competitive advantages!

principles.text: Pick a product where simplicity and few features is the selling point, since you lack time to build a bloated one.
principles.quote: "We do only one thing and we do it better than anyone" is a great marketing slogan. You don't have the time to make a Microsoft Excel knock-off, so don't!

principles.text: A bootstrapped side business should aim for slow, consistent growth; it maximizes odds of success and lets you change course early.
principles.quote: Slow growth maximizes your chance for success. Slow means your success is not dependent on some unlikely, massive event that's totally outside your control.

principles.text: The immediate goal is a business just solid enough to quit your day job, not millions.
principles.quote: your immediate goal isn't to make millions of dollars, it's to build a business just solid enough to quit your day job.

principles.text: Tell your employer about the side project, in writing, signed by someone with authority, to avoid lawsuits.
principles.quote: The best way to avoid a lawsuit is to prove that your employer knows you have a side project.

principles.text: Never use company laptops, software, or internet for the side business; assume everything is monitored and discoverable.
principles.quote: If your project is really on the side, you have no business doing business at work.

sources.title: Pick one and own it: win positioning by owning a single advantage
sources.originalTitle: Pick one and own it
sources.summary: Jason Cohen proposes an exercise: imagine your company may have only one advantage over competitors, and build the whole sales talk-track around it. Focusing on one owned benefit sharpens the pitch, homepage, ads, demos and product, and he shows how a single advantage can answer a range of skeptical objections.

principles.text: Hang your hat on one advantage you can own completely; it beats diluting your message with many assertions.
principles.quote: Hanging your hat on just one advantage *that you can own completely* is stronger than diluting your message by making many assertions.

principles.text: Run the one-advantage exercise; it is a skill that pays off in every sales call, including defending against competitors or missing features.
principles.quote: You should go through this exercise because this skill is valuable in every sales call.

principles.text: A single focused advantage sharpens everything: homepage, ads, 30-second pitch, blog topics, demo, and your ideal customer.
principles.quote: Your homepage becomes laser-focused. Your advertisements become pointed, powerful, pithy, and other words starting with "p." Your 30-second pitch becomes compelling.

principles.text: Reframe objections through your one advantage. 'Most expensive' becomes the cost of failing, plus real support and expert help.
principles.quote: When you factor in the cost of the tool, also factor in the cost of *failing* to be successful with the tool.

principles.text: Counter the 'more features' objection: more bullet points often means worse features, and the real goal is solving the customer's specific needs.
principles.quote: Usually the more features a product has, the worse each feature is.

principles.text: Focus everything on one or two points: message, behavior, UX, product, target customer, and pitch. Don't try to defend ten.
principles.quote: Why try to defend ten points when you only need one or two to make your case?

sources.title: Why you don't need to be an "expert" first: expertise and success grow together
sources.originalTitle: Enough with the "expert" guilt
sources.summary: Jason Cohen pushes back on the "10,000 hours to expertise before success" idea. He argues successful entrepreneurs don't start as experts; career and expertise develop together, helped by luck, and genuinely new things have no prior experts. The takeaway: stop chasing arbitrary credentials and get back to work.

principles.text: Expertise is not a prerequisite for success; build the career and the expertise at the same time.
principles.quote: Not one of the successful entrepreneurs I know *started* as an expert. Rather, **career and expertise were developed simultaneously**

principles.text: Success comes from expertise plus a few key events, and those events owe as much to luck as to effort.
principles.quote: eventually resulting in success when coupled with a few key events

principles.text: Innovation defies prior expertise: when you invent something new, no one can be an expert in it yet.
principles.quote: Innovation defies prior expertise.

principles.text: Effort alone doesn't explain skill; talent matters, and hours practiced don't map cleanly to results.
principles.quote: supposing it does take that much sheer effort, clearly it also takes talent

principles.text: Feeling like a non-expert is often impostor syndrome, not a real gap in people who are already succeeding.
principles.quote: her problem isn't a lack of expertise but rather that she shares

principles.text: Drop arbitrary definitions and unnecessary prerequisites to success, and get back to work.
principles.quote: So let's stop being distracted with these arbitrary definitions, artificial goals, and unnecessary prerequisites to "success."

sources.title: Sunk Costs: why you must ignore past spend and kill what isn't working
sources.originalTitle: Sunk Costs: An invisible, pervasive peril
sources.summary: Jason Cohen explains that sunk costs (money, time and effort already spent and unrecoverable) should be ignored when deciding what to do next, yet human loss aversion makes us cling to them. He applies it to startup situations: pet features, marketing slogans, bad hires, endless A/B iteration, and long-shot enterprise deals.

principles.text: Ignore sunk costs: spent money and effort is gone whatever you do next, so decide only on future costs and benefits.
principles.quote: "Sunk Cost" is money you've already spent and cannot get back.

principles.text: Sunk-cost bias is human nature, not just big-company politics. Startups fall for it too, so be vigilant.
principles.quote: It's not just politics, it's human nature.

principles.text: Kill a feature customers don't care about, even if it was hard to build and you're proud of it.
principles.quote: But that effort is sunk whether or not it's the right fit for your product; kill the feature.

principles.text: Don't force a clever idea, like a slogan, into the business just to avoid wasting it. Learn to throw things out.
principles.quote: You don't want to "waste" this great concept; surely you can use it somehow, somewhere? No. As with all writing, you have to learn how to throw things out.

principles.text: Don't keep a bad hire because of the effort spent finding and training them. Prolonging it is worse, for you and for them.
principles.quote: You can't get that time back, and yes this is one of the most expensive mistakes you can make, but even worse is prolonging the inevitable.

principles.text: Drop a long-running big-name sale that keeps finding reasons not to buy. It signals poor fit; you need profitable customers and advocates.
principles.quote: All this is just an indicator that you don't have a good fit; this time-suck isn't going to vanish once they buy. Let it go.

sources.title: Rude Q&A: Stress-testing your startup with a brutal devil's advocate
sources.originalTitle: Rude Q&A: The constructive devil's advocate
sources.summary: Jason Cohen borrows Scott Berkun's "Rude Q&A": write down the nastiest, smartest, even unfair questions about your company, then answer them. The exercise tests your ideas and forces sharper messaging, target customer and features. He gives a starter list of startup questions and a worked answer about why his own blog should exist.

principles.text: Write a Rude Q&A: the questions you least want to hear about your work, then answer them as practice for pitching and raising money.
principles.quote: What would the meanest, nastiest, but smartest people in the world grill you on when you show your work?

principles.text: Grilling yourself does more than test the idea: it forces specific messaging, customer profile, differentiation and feature set.
principles.quote: It's not just about testing the mettle of your ideas, it also forces you to refine and clarify your marketing messages, your target customer profile, and your feature set.

principles.text: Include unfair questions and ones built on wrong assumptions, since reporters, clients and the public will ask them.
principles.quote: Make sure to include questions that are unfair or based on erroneous information.
