principles.text: Answer unfair questions politely and maturely, refuting the false assumptions without being dismissive.
principles.quote: They also need to carefully refute assumptions in the questions without being dismissive.

principles.text: Make generic tough questions specific to your own business, with the real comparisons and competitors that make it hurt.
principles.quote: These are generic; you'll need to come up with more specific attacks.

principles.text: Being dissatisfied with some of your answers is a good sign; keep looking for answers and discuss the hard ones with others.
principles.quote: Don't get discouraged if you're not happy with all your answers. That's a good sign--it means you're being honest about the exercise and you're not yet satisfied.

sources.title: Tradeshow playbook: how Jason Cohen ran booths at dozens of shows
sources.originalTitle: A Tradeshow Checklist, born of experience
sources.summary: A practical checklist from running dozens of tradeshow booths at Smart Bear. Covers setting a goal, presenting, booking meetings with press and customers, using the booth as live market research and pitch testing, and following up afterward.

principles.text: Set one primary goal for each tradeshow so you can decide and judge success.
principles.quote: A goal helps you make the decisions below and provides a yardstick for whether the tradeshow was "successful," and therefore whether you should do more.

principles.text: Always give a vendor presentation; depth with 20 people beats seconds with hundreds at the booth.
principles.quote: Even if just 20 people come to your talk, that's 20 people you get to talk to in depth for 45 minutes--far more valuable than talking to 100 of people at your booth for 5-60 seconds.

principles.text: Book meetings before the show, especially with editors, bloggers, customers and partners.
principles.quote: I've been published in every major programming magazine; almost all of that I can directly attribute to talking with editors at tradeshows!

principles.text: Treat the booth as an A/B test of your pitch, then move the winner to your home page.
principles.quote: A tradeshow is a wonderful place to test attention-grabbers. What gets people to stop? To laugh? To say "OK, fair enough, tell me more?"

principles.text: Ask questions instead of pitching; curiosity earns you permission to sell and doubles as market research.
principles.quote: If you start chatting they will actually ask you for a pitch as a form of reciprocation. Then you've got permission to "sell," and they're truly listening.

principles.text: Follow up after the show; people forget you within days, so quality beats swag volume.
principles.quote: Attendees are saturated with presentations and vendor pitches, so there's a 99% chance they've forgotten about you.

sources.title: Impostor Syndrome: why founders feel like frauds and how Jason Cohen turned it into fuel
sources.originalTitle: Impostor Syndrome: Why I felt like a fraud, and how I overcame it
sources.summary: Jason Cohen explains that feeling like a fraud is near-universal among high performers and founders, and that it comes from perfectionism rather than confidence. He separates constructive self-doubt, which drives learning and effort, from harmful doubt, which drives hiding and avoidance. He also gives concrete reframes for answering the inner voice.

principles.text: Founder drive comes from perfectionism and a need to do it your way, not from confidence that your way is right.
principles.quote: Our entrepreneurial motivation is not confidence, it's an insatiable desire to do it our way. Doing it our own way is not the same as being confident that it is the correct way.

principles.text: Self-doubt is useful when it pushes you to learn, fix and earn your reputation; harmful when it pushes you to hide or avoid.
principles.quote: I doubt my title as "expert," so every day I read, write, and immerse myself in my field.

principles.text: Emotions don't follow logic, so the fraud feeling persists even when the facts contradict it. Recognize it and deal with it logically.
principles.quote: Still, emotions don't respond to logic.

principles.text: When you doubt your skills, append "yet": you are a student on the way, not an impostor.
principles.quote: Whatever it is you think you're not good enough for, append the word "yet." I can't do this job... yet.

principles.text: Feeling stretched and unsure is the normal condition of anyone who strives, not proof you shouldn't be doing it.
principles.quote: That is the human condition... for humans who strive.

principles.text: Broad hands-on exposure can make you the real expert in a new field, even while you feel like a fraud.
principles.quote: I had developed more experience with more teams in more situations than any one person could

sources.title: Rich vs. King: Why Jason Cohen sold Smart Bear for life-changing certainty
sources.originalTitle: Rich vs. King in the Real World: Why I sold my company
sources.summary: Jason Cohen explains why he sold Smart Bear in 2007 despite 100% annual growth. He argues you can chase "Rich" while behaving like "King" by running a profitable, durable business, and that crossing the "Freedom Line" matters more than squeezing out a bigger exit.

principles.text: Profit is the best route to being acquired: it proves the market, sets a floor on valuation, and gives you walk-away power.
principles.quote: my attitude was (and still is) that the best way to get yourself acquired is to be profitable.

principles.text: You can only negotiate well if you don't need the deal and can happily walk away.
principles.quote: Most of all, profits mean you don't *need* to sell, which gives you the ability to walk away from a deal. You have little negotiating power in any deal unless you can happily walk away.

principles.text: Aiming for "Rich" and acting like "King" is not contradictory: sustainable, long-term businesses are exactly what get acquired.
principles.quote: although the goal was "Rich," I achieved it by behaving like the goal was "King." I don't know why people find this contradictory

principles.text: Be explicit about the exit with your team up front: hires should know the company is there to make money and may be sold.
principles.quote: even before hiring someone, I would tell them that we're here to make money, and if someone offers to buy the company someday, I'm going to sell it, and all of us will make money.

principles.text: Financial freedom is non-linear: crossing the line where savings fund your lifestyle matters far more than how far past it you go.
principles.quote: If you're crossing from left to right, it doesn't matter how far to the right you go.

principles.text: Don't gamble certain life-changing money for a chance at more (the Box Game); the 2008 crash and a stalled rival deal proved the risk real.
principles.quote: a "chance of moving even further" isn't worth giving up the certainty of that life-altering event.

sources.title: How to find out why trials don't buy: 11 cheap ways to collect lost-sales feedback in a day
sources.originalTitle: Discover what's blocking sales with less than a day of work
sources.summary: Jason Cohen argues the top way to raise revenue is learning why the 99.9% of prospects who look but don't buy walk away, not talking only to existing customers. He lists eleven low-effort tactics, such as optional download forms, paying for lost-sale interviews, uninstaller surveys, and free licenses in exchange for feedback sessions.

principles.text: Existing customers can't explain lost sales; you need feedback from the far larger group of prospects who didn't buy.
principles.quote: talking to existing customers isn't good enough! They bought in spite of your faults; you need to talk to the other 99.9% of your potential customers who aren't so forgiving and understanding.

principles.text: A short optional form before a download need not cut downloads, and without contact info you can't fix the funnel.
principles.quote: if a hundred people download in silence and don't buy, it doesn't matter that they downloaded.

principles.text: Collect opt-in emails from interested non-buyers even before you have a newsletter; they give you reasons to follow up later.
principles.quote: There's no reason not to build an honest, opt-in, no-spam list of people who are interested in your product.

principles.text: Pay lost-sale prospects (charity gift, coupon, swag, ~$25-50) for 15 minutes on why they didn't buy; run it until answers repeat or the budget runs out.
principles.quote: You don't have to offer it forever, just until you start hearing the same things over and over again. Or budget $1000 and run the offer until the budget is gone.

principles.text: Ask in-product at the moment of rejection (uninstaller, 'Complain' link, quit prompt) using a plain email or web form; most responses are noise but some are gold.
principles.quote: Sure, most of the time you'll get nothing and sometimes you'll get useless crap like "You suck," but sometimes you'll get gold.

principles.text: Give free licenses to non-buyers only in exchange for a feedback call; they weren't going to pay anyway, so you lose little.
principles.quote: You're not losing money on the sale because they weren't going to buy anyway.

sources.title: Put down the compiler: learn why non-buyers walk away before building more features
sources.originalTitle: Put down the compiler until you learn why they're not buying
sources.summary: Early-stage companies with a shaky v1.0 and downloads but few sales should stop coding and interview the people who left without buying. Cohen dismantles the common excuses (new feature, polish, I'm a user myself, it's marketing's job) and argues feedback from lost sales is the only real fix.

principles.text: When downloads or signups don't convert, the fix is feedback from lost sales, not your own theories about why people aren't buying.
principles.quote: This problem is solved only one way: **You need feedback from lost sales.**

principles.text: Prioritize talking to people who found you, read your copy, downloaded, then left silently; they are the low-hanging fruit who should be buying today.
principles.quote: You need to talk with the people who were interested enough to find your website, read your marketing copy, download your product, and then *give up without even an email*.

principles.text: Existing customers can't reveal sales barriers because they bought despite them; learn about conversion from the 98% who didn't buy.
principles.quote: Existing customers bought *in spite of* barriers to sale, so they're no help in identifying the barriers.

principles.text: 'One more feature' is almost never what blocks sales; the real blocker is often mundane, like a blank first screen or a broken installer.
principles.quote: Often the real impediment to sales is as mundane as "New users are presented with a blank screen, so they don't know what to do next, so they abandon the trial,"

principles.text: Being a user of your own product makes you the worst judge of the new-user experience; you are not your typical user.
principles.quote: Most of your users are dumb; almost all are dumber than you are. You are not your typical user.

principles.text: In a startup, getting revenue is everyone's job. If you don't know why people aren't buying, that is the #1 bug and #1 feature to work on.
principles.quote: In a startup, it's *everyone's* job to get revenue.

sources.title: If Kindergarten were like Social Media Marketing: satire of social media tactics
sources.originalTitle: If Kindergarten were like Social Media Marketing
sources.summary: A satirical essay that applies social media marketing rules to kindergarten to expose their absurdity. It implicitly critiques forced authenticity, content-formula thinking, daily posting for top-of-mind, how-to eBooks from the already-popular, transactional compliments, and monetizing attention too early. Mostly humor with little direct actionable advice.

principles.text: Forced 'authenticity' backfires: radical honesty isn't rewarded the way marketers promise.
principles.quote: After a stern lecture on the value of being authentic, little Richard Neuman courageously admits that during recess he pooed his pants and buried the evidence in the gravel under the blue slide. His bravery is not met with the loving acceptance the teacher had promised.

principles.text: Advice from the already-popular doesn't transfer; knowing the tactics doesn't give you their audience.
principles.quote: It's well received from pre-K through third grade, but although it contains clear examples and actionable advice, somehow the unpopular kids still never get invited to the cool kids' slumber parties.

principles.text: Transactional flattery to build relationships reads as insincere and damages reputation.
principles.quote: Learning that making nice comments about people helps forge relationships, little Bobby Gray compliments the entire kickball team. He is denied the coveted spot and earns the nickname "Bobby Bootlicker."

principles.text: Mechanically posting daily to 'stay top-of-mind' is a questionable tactic that devalues the work itself.
principles.quote: Children are encouraged to make at least one drawing or painting every day. Refrigerator art goes stale quickly and you want to stay top-of-mind with your parents.

sources.title: Early-stage startups: act like a little company to win Early Adopters
sources.originalTitle: You're a little company, now act like one
sources.summary: Jason argues that early-stage founders hurt themselves by posing as big, "professional" companies. Your next sale is an Early Adopter, not Lockheed Martin, so your public persona should be human, specific, and small-team, which attracts the customers who will actually help you build the right product.

principles.text: Your next sale won't be a big enterprise deal; early on you're mismatched with large companies.
principles.quote: My next sale won't be a 1000-seat order from Lockheed Martin.

principles.text: Early Adopters are the perfect match for a young product: they tolerate bugs and want a personal relationship with founders.
principles.quote: They don't mind putting up with a hundred bugs so long as they get fixed fast. They want to be involved in the process.

principles.text: Early Adopters take risks because new technology can give them a competitive advantage; most companies won't.
principles.quote: Most companies aren't willing to take risks for any reason, so this is a winning strategy for those willing to take risks.

principles.text: Early on you need engaged customers who help shape the product, not silent downloaders.
principles.quote: You don't need people who download, get discouraged, and then never call you back. You need a chatty Cathy who wants to dive in and help out.

principles.text: Write your site for the Early Adopter: expose your phone and Twitter, promote community over unbuilt features.
principles.quote: Should you hide behind "Contact Us" forms or display your phone number and Twitter account on your home page?

principles.text: Replace corporate marketing-speak with specific, human language.
principles.quote: Say something specific and meaningful. Be human. Be yourself.

sources.title: Survivor bias: why most business advice from successful founders is unreliable
sources.originalTitle: Business Advice Plagued by Survivor Bias
sources.summary: Jason Cohen argues that learning only from successes is a deep statistical trap. Using WWII bomber armor, the file-drawer effect, ESP experiments, and Good to Great, he shows how business advice may be luck dressed up as insight, and says to prefer advice that makes you think.

principles.text: Studying only successes systematically biases conclusions; the real data is in the failures you never see.
principles.quote: Planes with bullets in the cockpit or fuel tanks didn't make it home; the bullet holes in returning planes were "found" in places that were by definition relatively benign. The real data is in the planes that were shot down, not the ones that survived.

principles.text: Ask how many others did the same things and failed before crediting a famous winner's playbook.
principles.quote: what if twenty other coffee shops had the same ideas, same product, and same dedication as Starbucks, but failed? How does that affect what we can learn from Starbucks's success?

principles.text: With enough people trying, someone will hit improbable streaks by chance; picking the winner afterward proves nothing about skill.
principles.quote: The chance that somebody in a crowd of a thousand would flip heads ten times is a whopping 62%! Because so many people are attempting the feat, some normally-unlikely events will happen.

principles.text: A founder's own track record, including Cohen's, may just be the lucky one in the crowd, so past success doesn't guarantee the advice generalizes.
principles.quote: I've started three consecutive successful companies, so that's proof that I know what I'm doing and that you should do everything I say, right? Except maybe I'm just the one in the crowd who guessed right on the Zener cards three times

principles.text: Backward-looking business books that pick winners from a large pool may not predict future performance and ignore whether non-winners shared the same traits.
principles.quote: Jim started by combing through 1435 companies looking for good candidates for the book, and picked eleven. It's the ESP experiment all over again!

principles.text: You can't fully remove survivor bias from advice, but awareness helps; prefer advice that provokes thinking and builds on your own strengths over prescriptive answers.
principles.quote: prefer advice that makes you think rather than giving you answers, forces you to answer tough questions, and causes you to extend your existing strengths

sources.title: Going viral: why the message itself must invite retransmission
sources.originalTitle: Darwinian advice for "Going Viral"
sources.summary: Jason Cohen uses a Darwinian analogy (the sterile mule) to argue that virality needs "grandchildren": content your followers want to repeat, not just consume. He recommends making retransmission frictionless by writing the share text for people, but admits the real driver is genuinely remarkable content.

principles.text: Virality needs second-generation spread: content must be worth repeating, not just interesting to direct followers.
principles.quote: It's not enough for the message to be interesting to your *direct* followers (children), it needs to be something your followers would be interested in *repeating* (grandchildren).

principles.text: Build the ask for retransmission into the message itself.
principles.quote: The message itself needs to suggest retransmission.

principles.text: Vague requests to 'tell everyone' give people work; remove that friction.
principles.quote: The problem is that you've just given Francis work to do.

principles.text: Do the thinking for your promoters: supply ready-made tweet and email copy tailored to each channel.
principles.quote: Instead, help Francis. Tear down every barrier they have for retransmission. Do the thinking for them.

principles.text: Real virality came from genuinely useful, entertaining or inspiring content, not from sharing tactics.
principles.quote: when my posts have gone viral it wasn't because of these techniques!

principles.text: The number one rule is overwhelmingly good content that people intrinsically want to spread; then also help them share.
principles.quote: So the #1 best rule is: Have overwhelmingly awesome content. So good that people intrinsically want to spread the word.

sources.title: Why bootstrapped startups demand obsession and sacrifice, not balance
sources.originalTitle: Sacrifice your health for your startup
sources.summary: Jason Cohen argues that a bootstrapped company consumes all available time, and that maximizing the chance of success means putting work before health and family for a period. He frames it as a deliberate, time-boxed tradeoff best made when you have few dependents and enough savings, not a lifelong lifestyle.

principles.text: A bootstrapped company will absorb all your time, because there's always more to do than the few people running it.
principles.quote: How much time does a bootstrapped company take? All of it.

principles.text: Small-company success takes obsession, not just passion: you can't stop working, and your whole self is at stake.
principles.quote: It takes obsession to make a little company go. Forget "passion"--everyone's favorite word--it's "obsession." It's not just that you love working, it's that you can't stop working.

principles.text: Maximizing your odds as a small-business founder means sacrificing health and family, at least for a while.
principles.quote: Maximizing your chance for success means sacrificing health and family.

principles.text: Time-box the sacrifice and choose the right life stage: do it when you have no kids, enough savings to risk, and an understanding partner.
principles.quote: I did all this in my 20's when I had no kids, I had enough savings to risk everything for a while, and I had a wife who had her own business and who therefore understood how much work it took

principles.text: Work-life balance advice is right in general but doesn't describe the early startup phase; decide consciously whether to pay the penalty now.
principles.quote: You need to accept that this is going to happen and ask whether it's OK to incur this penalty right now.

principles.text: More hours alone don't produce more output, but optimizing how you spend time can multiply productivity.
principles.quote: Indeed, study after study has shown that "working more hours" doesn't translate into "accomplishing more shit."

sources.title: Too small to fail: Why small, focused niche businesses survive and grow in recessions
sources.originalTitle: Too small to fail: How startups can grow in recessions
sources.summary: Jason argues that "small is risky" is backwards. Using Bingo Card Creator and Balsamiq as examples, he shows a tiny, focused niche with a strong customer need keeps growing in a recession, while a venture-funded company chasing a hot market is more fragile. A goal of $200k-$1M/year removes most failure risks.

principles.text: If the niche is small, the need strong and the product good, customers buy regardless of the economy.
principles.quote: If your niche is small enough, the customer need strong enough, your marketing targeted enough, your product good enough, your customers happy enough, they are going to buy, recession or not.

principles.text: Aim for a small, profitable business rather than a giant one; a modest revenue goal removes most ways to fail.
principles.quote: But if your goal is to run a smaller successful business and be independently wealthy, it's different. If you'd be happy making $1,000,000/year or even $200,000/year, many potential problems fall away.

principles.text: In a focused market you know where customers gather, so marketing costs time rather than a big budget.
principles.quote: In a small, focused market, you don't need a big marketing budget to get noticed. You know where your customers hang out--the forums, blogs, community sites, influencers, local groups.

principles.text: A tiny market lets you become the recognized expert and own the niche's content, community and product.
principles.quote: In a small, focused market, you can become the world expert of your niche.

principles.text: Niches too small for big players mean the 800-lb gorilla may never show up, and later entrants fall behind if you keep moving.
principles.quote: It's possible that you'll never see an 800-lb gorilla because the addressable market is too small for them to ever be profitable (Microsoft isn't going to make a Bingo-card creator).

principles.text: Small is less risky: needs are strong, customer relationships are personal, and most customers are still in your future.
principles.quote: Prevailing wisdom is that "small is risky." It's just the opposite. When you just need to be Ramen-profitable, you can do so even in a recession.

sources.title: Show, don't tell: communicate company values through actions, not marketing adjectives
sources.originalTitle: Communicating Values: Show, don't Tell
sources.summary: Jason Cohen argues that listing brand adjectives like "fast, easy, scalable, robust" destroys believability. Authentic values are demonstrated through concrete actions (return policies, answering the phone, real testimonials), and only after you walk the walk have you earned the right to call it out.

principles.text: If you have to tell people something is true, they automatically don't believe you; actions speak louder than words.
principles.quote: The cardinal rule of authenticity and believability is that actions speak louder than words. A corollary is that if you have to tell me something's true, I automatically don't believe you.

principles.text: Piling on adjectives (easy, fast, scalable, robust) makes every claim suspect, since no real product has zero trade-offs.
principles.quote: Since I don't know which of these claims are true, now I distrust them all. And you haven't communicated anything tangible. Fail.

principles.text: Values are the reason behind your actions and the consistency in how you do business, not taglines or mission statements.
principles.quote: Values are the reason for your actions, the theme behind your words, and the underlying consistency in how you do business.

principles.text: Prove quality with policy, not a promise: a no-questions-asked return policy beats saying 'your satisfaction is important to us'.
principles.quote: If you have a high-quality product, you don't say "Your satisfaction is important to us," you have a 90-day no-questions-asked return policy.

principles.text: Prove you care about customers by answering the phone and showing 100 real testimonials, not claiming '100 companies use us'.
principles.quote: If you care about talking to customers, you don't play a recorded message saying their call is important to you, you simply answer the phone.

principles.text: Once you're walking the walk, you've earned the right to call it out, as tangible demonstrations rather than trite phrases.
principles.quote: Once you're walking the walk, then you've earned the right to call it out

sources.title: How Jason Cohen won loyal customers by being honest about being a one-man company
sources.originalTitle: How to get customers who love you even when you screw up
sources.summary: Jason Cohen tells how an early customer, Tom, put up with a buggy first product and drove a big enterprise order because Jason was honest about being a one-person shop. Early adopters want to take part in building the product, and pretending to be bigger than you are loses the people who would have loved you as you are.

principles.text: Customers forgive honest mistakes from earnest people, not from cold corporations.
principles.quote: Customers love you when you're honest, even about your foibles. We forgive honest mistakes from earnest people, not stolid, cold, inhuman corporations.

principles.text: When a customer sees through your facade and accepts you anyway, match their honesty instead of going defensive.
principles.quote: Tom was saying: "I know who you really are, and I accept it. I still want to do this. How about a few features since we put up with those bugs?" I *had* to match that honesty.

principles.text: A customer who champions you inside their company stakes their own reputation on you, so keep your word and make them look good.
principles.quote: So he pinned his own reputation on it and won. As a bonus, he lived vicariously through Smart Bear as a product designer.

principles.text: Your first hundred customers are early adopters who want to shape the product and say they were there at the start.
principles.quote: they'll be early-adopters--folks who like trying new stuff and like working with new companies who still have spark and something to prove. Folks who want to be part of the creative process

principles.text: Pretending to be something you're not betrays the people who would have loved the real you.
principles.quote: If you pretend to be something you're not, they'll see right through it. Then what have you done? You've lied to those who would have loved you for who you are

principles.text: Honesty is a real advantage small companies have over big ones, so use it.
principles.quote: And it's one of the few advantages small companies have over big ones. Use it.

sources.title: Easy A/B test significance: the D² > N rule and why you should test big differences
sources.originalTitle: Easy statistics for A/B testing and hamsters
sources.summary: Jason Cohen gives a simple, statistically sound formula for judging A/B tests: take half the gap between winner and loser (D) and the total trials (N), and the result is significant only if D² > N. Small samples can't detect modest differences, so test radically different variants rather than tweaks.

principles.text: An A/B test is significant only if D² > N, where D is half the winner-loser gap and N is total trials.
principles.quote: The test result is statistically significant only if D^2 > N.

principles.text: With few data points you know nothing yet, even if one variant leads six-to-one. Trust the math over gut feel.
principles.quote: So the test is still inconclusive, even though A is beating B six-to-one. Trust the math here--with only a few data points, you really don't know anything yet.

principles.text: Seek big differences: test wildly different designs, because tweaks only become testable at enormous sample sizes.
principles.quote: It means **you need to be seeking big differences**, not subtle ones.  Test wildly different designs, rather than tweaks.  Tweaks can only be tested when N is enormous.

principles.text: Detecting a winner only 10% better takes around 1800 trials; at N=100 the winner must beat the loser by 50%.
principles.quote: It takes N = 1800 to detect the case where the winner is only 10% larger than the loser.

principles.text: If a test never reaches significance, the variants aren't meaningfully different; stop tweaking and create a completely new test.
principles.quote: That's when you realize you're not learning anything new; the variants you picked are not meaningfully different for your readers. That means it's time to come up with something new.

principles.text: Don't trust gut feel or A/B tool significance claims; compute significance yourself.
principles.quote: Human intuition sucks when it comes to these things, and A/B testing tools often use misleading or incorrect math, so let this formula help you draw the right conclusions.

sources.title: How much of success is luck? Using luck by treating every decision as an empirical test
sources.originalTitle: How much of success is luck?
sources.summary: Jason Cohen argues that success is neither pure luck nor pure merit: good and bad luck swirl constantly, and what is not luck is how you use it. His practical answer is to treat every decision as an empirical test, measuring everything so you can keep what works and eject what doesn't.

principles.text: Both can be true: success rests on intentional choices and on luck. Don't deny either one.
principles.quote: In fact, I can pick any decision in the history of Smart Bear and the same rhetorical pattern appears: Success tied to something intentional, but also leveraging something lucky.

principles.text: Luck is constant, but how you use it is not luck.
principles.quote: Good luck and bad luck are constantly swirling around you. How you use it, is not luck.

principles.text: Success means using luck: exploiting the good and identifying and ejecting the bad.
principles.quote: Overall success in business doesn't only mean you "got lucky," it means you used luck, taking advantage of the good, identifying and ejecting the bad.

principles.text: Build measurement in so you can tell success from failure; otherwise luck alone controls your fate.
principles.quote: In fact, ensuring that we could measure the efficacy of individual print ads was also a choice. Had we not done this, we wouldn't have been able to distinguish success from failure, and then indeed our destiny would be controlled by luck alone.

principles.text: Treat every decision as an empirical test: try anything, measure everything, follow what works.
principles.quote: Your best bet for success is to treat all your decisions as empirical tests. Confidence and experimentation are not contradictory. Try anything, measure everything, and follow what works, even if that means changing everything.

principles.text: Ask how you knew an idea was right, not what inspired it. Learn how to think, not how to copy.
principles.quote: The wrong question is: "What inspired that idea?" The right question is: "How did you know when an idea was right?" Or even more specific: "How does one know whether a print ad is working?"

sources.title: Double your productivity: eliminate low-velocity time instead of chasing 1% daily gains
sources.originalTitle: Double your productivity without more work or stress
sources.summary: Jason Cohen debunks the "1% better per day = 37x" idea and shows why a one-time 2-3x productivity gain is still achievable. Using an average-speed puzzle, he argues low-velocity activity (email, idle meetings, calendar management) drags down your average, so the lever is eliminating it, measured with a tool like RescueTime, not working harder.

principles.text: Compounding 1% daily improvement in productivity is unrealistic; other factors overwhelm the simplistic math.
principles.quote: Things rarely compound like that, even at slow rates. Or at least, there are other factors that overwhelm that simplistic idea.

principles.text: Low-velocity periods wash away high-velocity gains, so your average is dominated by your slow time.
principles.quote: It's amazing how periods of low velocity wash away gains of high velocity.

principles.text: You can't make up for lost time with bursts of speed; when half your day is slow, the other half can't compensate.
principles.quote: When half your day moves at 30 mph, it's impossible to make up the time during the other half.

principles.text: The biggest productivity lever is eliminating low-velocity work (useless email, idle meetings, calendar management), not speeding up what you already do well.
principles.quote: Once you realize that the low-velocity stuff is responsible for most of the drag on your productivity, you realize that the thing to do is eliminate the low-velocity stuff.

principles.text: Measure where your time actually goes with a tool like RescueTime; seeing the numbers makes correction easy.
principles.quote: Once you see the numbers it's easy to correct.

principles.text: Roughly doubling productivity is achievable without longer hours or more stress: stop averaging down, and make sure your big-rock tasks are the right ones.
principles.quote: The best part is, none of this means working late or working harder. Just stop averaging down!

sources.title: Why high-concept pitches ("iPhone for projectors") backfire and a clear positioning statement wins
sources.originalTitle: High-concept pitches are not your friend
sources.summary: Jason Cohen argues against the "X is Y for Z" high-concept pitch because it is too brief, ambiguous, and defines you as a copy of something else. He prefers a clear positioning statement and a full product pitch, illustrated with a compact-projector example.

principles.text: Brevity has a limit: a three-word analogy to something famous leaves it unclear what message the listener receives.
principles.quote: When you use only three words and when you invoke something well-known and complicated, it's not clear what message will be received. I'm brevity's biggest fan, but there's such a thing as "too brief."

principles.text: Analogy pitches import every attribute of the referenced product, including its negatives, not just the ones you want.
principles.quote: But these aren't the only attributes of the iPhone. iPhones have a reputation of not working well with Microsoft Office, something particularly troubling for the traveling salesperson.

principles.text: Analogy pitches define you as a copy of something else; define yourself on your own terms.
principles.quote: And it defines you as a copy of something else.

principles.text: Use a one-line positioning statement that keeps the primary features and benefits as the guide for all marketing.
principles.quote: A compact, portable, rugged projector that eliminates surprises on the road.

principles.text: Think about your audience's existing associations: a traveling salesperson on PowerPoint and Outlook reads "iPhone" very differently than a Gmail user does.
principles.quote: Readers of this blog are likely to use GMail and Open Office, but your typical salesperson is on a strict diet of PowerPoint and Outlook.

principles.text: Investors need to understand product; strategy with zero product understanding isn't strategy, so steer clear of investors who think product is nothing.
principles.quote: Strategy with zero product understanding isn't strategy.

sources.title: Ignoring the Wisdom of Crowds: why votes work for facts but veto innovation
sources.originalTitle: Ignoring the Wisdom of Crowds
sources.summary: Jason Cohen explains why crowds are brilliant at estimating facts (jelly beans, Millionaire audience polls) because random errors cancel out. The same mechanism ruins creative work, where votes act as vetoes that leave bland, lowest-common-denominator output. Startups need a niche they can own, not a safe middle.

principles.text: Crowds are wise only when there is an objectively correct answer and individual errors cancel out.
principles.quote: There is "wisdom in the crowd" when there is an objectively-correct answer, and when the errors cancel out

principles.text: A small group that knows the answer can dominate a poll because ignorant voters cancel each other out.
principles.quote: The ignorant people vote randomly and *their votes cancel out*, leaving the few in control of the result.

principles.text: In creative work, votes are vetoes: consensus settles on what everyone hated least, not on something wonderful.
principles.quote: Votes don't converge on something wonderful. Rather, votes are *vetoes*.

principles.text: Design by committee strips out the interesting edges and leaves a boring residue, so great products aren't made that way.
principles.quote: In creative work, votes eliminate the interesting edges**, because votes result in subtracting rather than adding

principles.text: Startups should own a niche completely rather than occupy a gray middle that offends no one and excites no one.
principles.quote: Little companies need a niche--a market space they can completely, unquestionably own, not some gray middle-ground where your attempt to offend no one also means exciting no one.

principles.text: Building average products for the average consumer is the opposite of innovation and likely a bad product strategy.
principles.quote: design-by-committee is the antithesis of innovation.

sources.title: How to tell constructive criticism from bad business advice: Franks vs. Gerrys
sources.originalTitle: Distinguishing constructive criticism from bad business advice
sources.summary: Jason Cohen recounts nearly giving a "sales veteran" partner 50% of Smart Bear and renaming it, and uses dieting as an analogy: no advice is objectively right, only right for you and sustainable. He lists practical filters for judging advice (context match, questions over commands, measurable ideas, gut feel).

principles.text: Startup advice is contradictory; ask what works for this company and founder, not what is objectively best.
principles.quote: For every example that incontrovertibly proves "X is right," there's another equally compelling story of success where the mantra was "X is wrong."

principles.text: Advice must be sustainable for you; don't force yourself into channels you dislike and won't keep up.
principles.quote: if you think Twitter is insipid and Facebook is unserious and Instagram is fake, will you really be successful if you force yourself to post there?

principles.text: Advisors mostly give advice to themselves; trust it only if their goals, market, customers and competitors match yours.
principles.quote: The rule of thumb is: Advisors give advice to themselves.

principles.text: Good advisors ask pointed questions rather than issuing commands; be wary of axioms handed down as gospel.
principles.quote: Frank presented his view as a series of statements; axioms, even. Gerry couched his perspective as pointed questions that required either rebuttal or agreement.

principles.text: "This is how it's done" is neither a reason to follow nor to reject; investigate tradition like any other idea.
principles.quote: So, traditional answers carry neither positive nor negative baggage; they should be investigated like all other ideas.

principles.text: Prefer advice that comes with a way to measure success, so you can drop it if it doesn't work for you.
principles.quote: Does the advisor volunteer a clear way to measure the success of her new idea? If so, the idea is self-evaluating, and you can change if it happens to not work for you.

sources.title: Your idea sucks, now go do it anyway: the first idea rarely survives, so start and iterate
sources.originalTitle: Your idea sucks, now go do it anyway
sources.summary: Jason Cohen argues that a founder's first idea is probably wrong and rarely matters, because the real business emerges from building and watching what happens. He cites PayPal, Flickr and his own Smart Bear as companies that pivoted away from weak initial ideas. Waiting for a perfect idea is the mistake; a small market is enough to start.

principles.text: Your first idea probably sucks, and it doesn't matter, because the business will likely turn into something different.
principles.quote: Your idea probably sucks, and it doesn't matter because your business will probably turn out to be something completely different.

principles.text: Don't wait for a fully fleshed-out idea before starting; the right idea only appears by trying the wrong one.
principles.quote: the only way to find the right one is to try the wrong one and see what happens. You won't find it by fiddling around with PowerPoint slides and Photoshop mock-ups.

principles.text: Follow what users actually value in the product; Flickr emerged because testers cared about sharing more than real-time chat.
principles.quote: people were interested in the *sharing* part more than the *real-time* part.

principles.text: Expect to cut most of your product lineup; of six tools Smart Bear sold, only one mattered in the end.
principles.quote: At one point we were selling six different tools; the only one that mattered in the end was Code Reviewer.

principles.text: A tiny market is enough to bootstrap; you'll figure out the rest once you've started (Cohen quotes Neil Davidson).
principles.quote: A $50,000 market opportunity is enough to get you off the ground--once you get started you'll figure out the rest.

sources.title: Breaking the Rules: Master the rules first, then break them with purpose
sources.originalTitle: Breaking the Rules
sources.summary: Using Picasso's classical mastery and Volkswagen's "Lemon" ad, Jason Cohen argues that rules are reasonable defaults, not straightjackets. Breaking them works only when you understand them and do it deliberately. Innovation often comes from breaking a rule no one else will.

principles.text: Learn the rules first; mastery turns rule-breaking into a credible choice rather than incompetence.
principles.quote: Had Picasso never proven he could paint classically, he could be dismissed as a hack. When you know the rules, you're allowed to break the rules.

principles.text: No rule is unbreakable, provided you break it with purpose.
principles.quote: There's no rule that can't be broken, so long as it's broken with purpose.

principles.text: Treat rules as reasonable defaults when you have no better idea, not as a straightjacket.
principles.quote: Rules exist to guide us--a reasonable default when we don't have a better idea--but they're not a straightjacket.

principles.text: Inspired ideas often come from breaking a rule nobody else is willing to break.
principles.quote: In fact, the truly innovative, inspired ideas are frequently the result of breaking a rule that no one else is willing to break.

principles.text: Breaking a rule well requires calibration: grab attention without being so subtle the point is lost. Understanding the rule gets the balance right.
principles.quote: They played with words exactly enough to get your attention but not so subtly that you missed the point. Without appreciating the rule, the balance might not have been achieved.

principles.text: Break a rule without knowing it and you're probably just mistaken, not innovative.
principles.quote: But if you never bothered to learn the rules, you're probably just mistaken.

sources.title: Standing out from the noise: make your pitch work even when attention is scarce
sources.originalTitle: Standing out from the noise
sources.summary: Jason Cohen argues that a pitch must survive real-world distraction, not just ideal full-attention conditions. Like Snoop Dogg testing tracks on a crackly cassette player, test your messaging in noisy conditions, check that fragments still intrigue, and repeat your message so some of it breaks through.

principles.text: Test your pitch under bad conditions: if it works through noise and distraction, it works anywhere.
principles.quote: If it sounds good on crap, it will sound good anywhere.

principles.text: Your real competition is for attention, not just rival products, features or benefits.
principles.quote: These aren't even "competitors" in the "products, features, services, benefits" sense. It's competition for *attention*.

principles.text: Record your spoken pitch in a noisy place and check it still makes sense with only part of it audible.
principles.quote: Record your pitch in a noisy environment (a bar, a playground). Play it back; does it still make sense when you can only make out sixty percent of the syllables?

principles.text: Printed material should be eye-catching in fragments, so partial glimpses still spark interest.
principles.quote: Your entire message doesn't need to shine through, but is it eye-catching enough for someone to notice the fragments, to become interested?

principles.text: Repeat your message across channels, since distractions will block most single exposures.
principles.quote: Repeating often enough (using newsletters, blog, Twitter, Facebook) can push *some* of your communications through the chaos.

principles.text: Don't rely on a captive audience; a pitch that only works with full attention will fail in practice.
principles.quote: It's not enough to be compelling when you have 60 uninterrupted, full-attention seconds.

sources.title: Why "and more" is lazy marketing: just say what you are and own it
sources.originalTitle: Bed, Bath, Linens, Things, Beyond, and More!
sources.summary: Jason Cohen argues that "and more" in business names and signage is usually untrue, dilutes passion, and signals an incomplete message. Instead, state specifically what you are, be passionate about it, and make sure your ideal customer understands.

principles.text: "And more" is a weak declaration that your message is incomplete; say what you are instead.
principles.quote: In the end, "and more" is a weak declaration that your message is incomplete.

principles.text: Specific, singular passion beats vague breadth; "and more" dilutes an otherwise compelling message.
principles.quote: Look how the phrase "and more" dilutes this otherwise incredible message.

principles.text: Replace filler with enthusiasm: show you are fully committed to your niche.
principles.quote: Instead of wasting time with a useless, incorrect phrase, why not punch up the enthusiasm?

principles.text: Non-committal phrases fail to interest, excite, or get people through the door.
principles.quote: non-committal phrases don't get me interested, don't get me excited, and don't get me in the door.

principles.text: Listing extra categories rarely wins over people uninterested in your core offer.
principles.quote: The person who is completely uninterested in bed and bath products is unlikely to be interested in air fresheners and cutlery.

principles.text: Own your identity and make sure your ideal customer persona gets it; the rest follows.
principles.quote: So forget about "more."  Just say what you are.  Own it.  Make sure Carol gets it and the rest will follow.

sources.title: Strong opinions, weakly held: how to decide when to change a proven marketing message
sources.originalTitle: Strong opinions, somewhat weakly held
sources.summary: Jason Cohen reconciles two conflicting rules: always search for disproof of your beliefs, yet never change a proven strategy flippantly. His answer is that how weakly you hold an opinion should depend on how much work went into forming it. Illustrated with an AdWords specialist asking to change battle-tested landing page copy.

principles.text: Conviction is needed to act, but must be tempered by a constant search for disproof.
principles.quote: conviction, while necessary for action, must be tempered with a constant search for disproof.

principles.text: Being wishy-washy kills execution, but ignoring contrary evidence is irresponsible and dishonest.
principles.quote: Being wishy-washy is an impediment to inspiring people, working towards a goal, and getting things done, but turning a blind eye to contrary evidence is irresponsible and even dishonest.

principles.text: A strategy needs to be stable enough to execute but open enough to be corrected.
principles.quote: A strategy that changes all the time cannot be executed, but a strategy that never changes is definitely incorrect.

principles.text: Hold opinions more loosely when they were formed casually; change them readily if someone has a rationale.
principles.quote: some opinions were made without consideration. Why do we have a "Resources" web page separate from an "External Articles" page? No reason, it just ended up like that. So if someone else has a different idea and some rationale behind it, make the change.

principles.text: Opinions forged through testing, customer listening and debate deserve the same rigor to change as to create, and shouldn't be changed flippantly.
principles.quote: If it deserved this much consideration before, it deserves the same consideration now. Perhaps more.

principles.text: Don't use 'branding' as a shield against good ideas, but challenge new ideas against proven ones with proportionally high standards.
principles.quote: But when the existing ideas are proven, when great works have molded them, new ideas should be challenged with proportionally high standards.

sources.title: Why "a leading provider of solutions" is meaningless marketing, and how to write specific messaging instead
sources.originalTitle: The leading provider of meaningless marketing solutions
sources.summary: Jason Cohen attacks generic marketing language ("a leading provider of...", "solutions") using real company descriptions as examples. He argues the causes are fear, laziness, and incompetence, and that if you can't say what you do in a few specific words, customers won't get it either.

principles.text: Say plainly what you do, then spend your words on how you differ from competitors.
principles.quote: Turns out they do web analytics.  Oh.  They could have just said so and spent the rest of their words telling you how they're different from other web analytics companies.

principles.text: Filler phrases like "a leading provider of" carry no meaning; at best readers gloss over them, at worst they leave.
principles.quote: At best you gloss over it--an overused phrase, devoid of meaning.  At worst you lose interest and click the "Back" button.

principles.text: Startups can't afford bland, wishy-washy copy; generic phrasing is a big-company luxury born of fear.
principles.quote: This excuse might work at Big Company Inc, but in a startup you can't afford to be bland and wishy-washy.

principles.text: Nailing your message is hard work: know your customer, boil the company to its essentials, be succinct and specific.
principles.quote: You have to know your customer, boil your company down to its essentials, and be succinct and evocative and specific.  It's easier not to.

principles.text: Vague messaging often signals you don't know your differentiator, your niche, or your ideal customer.
principles.quote: What if you don't actually know what sets your product apart?  What if you can't articulate the niche your company owns?

principles.text: If you can't state your product in a few specific words, customers won't understand it either; cut every word that doesn't count.
principles.quote: If you can't articulate your product in a few, choice, specific, words, your potential customers won't get it either.

sources.title: Love the messenger: genuine passion from the person sells better than a polished message
sources.originalTitle: Love the messenger
sources.summary: Jason Cohen uses a Korean restaurant waiter's broken-English answer ("Dolsot bibimbap better!") to argue that the messenger matters more than the message once a human relationship begins. Websites need specificity, but in sales, support and tradeshow conversations, genuine passion, knowledge and a desire to make the customer successful is what sells.

principles.text: Obsessive, genuine excitement is contagious and is itself good sales, in any industry and for any product.
principles.quote: Being obsessively and genuinely excited about something is contagious. And good sales. In any industry, with any product.

principles.text: In a live human interaction, who delivers the message matters more than the polish of the message.
principles.quote: It's the messenger, not the message, that made the experience wonderful.

principles.text: Be specific on websites, because websites are attention-getters and information-distributors, not relationships.
principles.quote: So yes, on websites you do need to be specific because websites aren't relationships; they're attention-getters and information-distributers.

principles.text: Once the human relationship starts (sales pitch, tech support, tradeshow booth), lead with genuine passion, knowledge and a desire to make customers successful.
principles.quote: But as soon as the human relationship begins--whether by sales pitch or tech support or tradeshow booth--the most important thing is to be genuine in your passion, knowledge, and desire to make your customers successful.

principles.text: A sincere recommendation from someone who cares beats a mechanically recited pitch, and can steer a customer to the higher-value choice.
principles.quote: It was perfect because it wasn't in an ad, wasn't in a datasheet, wasn't part of a 30-second elevator pitch mechanically regurgitated on a tradeshow floor.

sources.title: Procrastinate for Success: why an overwhelmed founder should deliberately ignore most tasks
sources.originalTitle: Procrastinate for Success!
sources.summary: Jason argues that in an overwhelmed small company, gut-feel procrastination can beat formal prioritization. Many problems resolve themselves, many tasks matter less than they seem, and batching low-value chores frees time for the one or two things that win. He also says to allow some fun to avoid burnout.

principles.text: You can't do everything, so deliberately put things off and don't feel guilty about it.
principles.quote: Yeah I know I'm rationalizing. But you can't do everything, so don't.

principles.text: Many urgent-seeming items resolve themselves if you just ignore them: features, customer demands, bugs, meetings, emails.
principles.quote: Many things blow over if you just ignore them. The big feature you got worked up about yesterday seems unimportant in the cold light of today.

principles.text: Even critical-sounding admin like accounting can wait; the cost is smaller than the revenue from one more customer.
principles.quote: Late fees, lost receipts, penalties from the IRS: financial burdens more than compensated by additional revenue gained by signing up one more customer.

principles.text: Batch repetitive chores into one sweep to avoid context-switch overhead and get faster.
principles.quote: It's faster to enter 100 receipts into Quickbooks once a month than to enter three a day.

principles.text: Companies win by getting a few things really right, not by having no flaws, so skip details to focus on the 1-2 most important things.
principles.quote: Companies succeed because they got just a few things really right, not because they had no problems, no bugs, no design flaws, and perfect books.

principles.text: Let yourself do some fun work; burnout costs more than the duties you put off.
principles.quote: Whatever the cost of putting off duties, burn-out is even more costly.

sources.title: Software Quality Mortgage: treating tech debt like a home loan you must repay
sources.originalTitle: Software Quality Mortgage
sources.summary: Jason Cohen argues that shipping fast with messy code is the right early choice, but it creates tech debt that behaves like a mortgage: you pay interest in bugs and only slowly reduce principal. He explains when to shift from time-to-market to quality and how to win the argument for refactoring with non-technical stakeholders.

principles.text: Early on, ship fast even with bugs; it's the right call while you're still seeking your niche.
principles.quote: When companies are new and unknown, still seeking their niche, the most important thing is to get the software out the door fast, bugs and all.

principles.text: Tech debt works like a mortgage: you borrow to ship v1.0 sooner, then pay interest in bugs without reducing principal.
principles.quote: But eventually you have to pay back the debt. With interest. You pay interest in the form of bugs.

principles.text: Opportunistic cleanup alone never pays it off; growing software is an interest-only mortgage, so allocate real time for major rework.
principles.quote: At some point you can't tolerate this anymore. It's time to pay down the principal in earnest. But this requires allocating time for major rework.

principles.text: Counter 'cleanup is invisible to users': messy code's bugs are visible and slow every new feature.
principles.quote: The bugs constantly produced by messy code are visible to users too. Time spent fixing those bugs could have been spent adding features. The longer we stay in quality debt, the more time it takes to add each new feature.

principles.text: Fix root causes, not symptoms, like pulling weeds up by the roots instead of whacking them weekly.
principles.quote: You'd rather spend your time fixing bugs generated by the problem rather than fixing the problem? That's like whacking weeds every weekend instead of pulling them up by the roots.

principles.text: Don't blame developers for the mess; challenge them to reduce measurable bug reports, and take it seriously when they beg for time to fix bugs.
principles.quote: Finger-pointing impedes resolution. Instead, challenge your developers to reduce bug reports. This is easily measured, so you can track time versus results.

sources.title: Limiting Options: Beat competitors by shrinking their choices, not growing yours
sources.originalTitle: Limiting Options
sources.summary: Jason Cohen takes the winning Othello AI strategy (minimize the opponent's legal moves) and applies it to competitive strategy. Rather than only maximizing your own position, force competitors into low-percentage, expensive paths via exclusive deals, overpaying for top ad slots, and owning the "expert" position in your market.

principles.text: Limiting a competitor's choices matters more than which choices they have.
principles.quote: Limiting choice is more important than what the choices are.

principles.text: Ask how to push competitors into low-percentage or expensive options, costing them money, luck or creativity.
principles.quote: How can you limit their choices to things that are low-percentage or expensive?** Make them have to spend more money, get more lucky, or be more creative.

principles.text: Honoring competitors' coupons removes coupons as a way for them to beat you.
principles.quote: This eliminates the coupon as a way for your competitor to "beat" you; coupons are no longer a "choice" to develop a competitive edge.

principles.text: Overpay for the best ad slots: the value includes forcing rivals into low-converting positions, not just direct ROI.
principles.quote: You are paying too much if you measure the direct ROI only, but there's also the value of forcing competitors into a low-converting ad position, leading to many fewer customers at any price.

principles.text: Lock up exclusive deals with the largest affiliates so competitors are left with affiliates generating far fewer leads.
principles.quote: You are (again) paying too much if you measure the direct ROI only, but you force competitors to work with affiliates who can generate only 1/10th the leads.

principles.text: Become 'the expert' in your category so claiming that position is too expensive for rivals, especially when selling to Enterprise.
principles.quote: we're so strongly established as "the experts in code review," it would take an expensive, time-consuming effort for someone else to claim par, much less surpass what we've done.

sources.title: The "Opposite Test": How to Kill Generic Product Positioning
sources.originalTitle: The "Opposite Test"
sources.summary: Jason Cohen explains the Opposite Test for product marketing: negate each feature or benefit bullet, and if the negative is ridiculous, the original is meaningless and undifferentiating. Real positioning comes from claims whose opposite is a valid strategy, ideally with acknowledged trade-offs. The one exception is a generic claim you can truly own, like "fastest."

principles.text: Negate every feature bullet; if the opposite is ridiculous, the original claim is trivial and undifferentiating.
principles.quote: For each feature/benefit bullet point, construct its negative and see if that statement is ridiculous. Would anyone be able to construct a rational strategy with that negative?

principles.text: Generic claims like "easy to use" or "innovative" waste space that should hold differentiating strategy.
principles.quote: If you want to *not* stand out from the crowd, use statements that everyone uses. Would anyone claim to be non-innovative? Anyone claim that they put customers third?

principles.text: A good claim names a real trade-off: choosing it has a negative consequence you acknowledge.
principles.quote: Another good way of understanding whether you're passing the Opposite Test is **whether there are negative consequences** from your statement, which you acknowledge.

principles.text: A claim passes when its opposite is a valid, actually-practiced strategy, such as depth on one integration vs. breadth across many.
principles.quote: it can be a good strategy to be deep and feature-rich against a single API, rather than support a wide number of APIs, limited to features that are common to all.

principles.text: Replacing generic bullets forces you to work out what is strongest about your product and how it beats the alternatives.
principles.quote: You have to really think about what's strongest about your product, about how specifically it beats the alternatives, and how make it pithy.

principles.text: A generic claim like "fastest" is acceptable only if you are truly 10x better and own it as your identity, proven with benchmarks.
principles.quote: You can use a generic if it's your single biggest differentiator, where you're truly 10x better than the competition along that dimension, and therefore you really "own" this concept as your identity and value.

sources.title: Discount gambit: why refusing to discount (and locking in rates instead) builds a better business
sources.originalTitle: Discount gambit
sources.summary: Jason Cohen argues that "act now" discounts breed mistrust, invite endless haggling, attract the worst customers and signal a weak brand. Instead, announce a coming price increase and offer to lock in the current rate, which protects customers, implies growth and builds loyalty.

principles.text: Offer price-lock protection against a future increase instead of a discount for acting now.
principles.quote: The price is going up, but if you buy now I will lock in your rate.

principles.text: A discount reveals the original price included padding, which breeds customer mistrust.
principles.quote: Thus #1 breeds mistrust--the opposite of what you're trying to establish with me, your customer.

principles.text: Discounting teaches buyers there's no price floor, turning the relationship into an adversarial haggle.
principles.quote: Meanwhile your "customer relationship" is now more of a "hostage situation."

principles.text: Inconsistent pricing is unfair once word gets around, and can cost you the large follow-on order.
principles.quote: Yet another problem with discounting--word gets around, meaningless differences in pricing is unfair, and now I, the customer, see you as plain old dishonest.

principles.text: Not discounting signals market leadership; discounting signals desperation to hit numbers.
principles.quote: The leader doesn't have to compromise. The leader isn't desperate for orders.

principles.text: Discount-driven offers attract the least valuable customers and repel the best, while weakening the brand.
principles.quote: Strategy #1 attracts the least-valuable customers and repels the best ones, while establishing a weak brand.

sources.title: Tell me a story: why great storytelling beats being right, and what it means for marketing
sources.originalTitle: Tell me a story
sources.summary: Jason Cohen uses Malcolm Gladwell's success despite debunked theories to argue that stories persuade more than correct logic does. His takeaway is Seth Godin's: marketing is telling a good story, and most other factors are second-order effects.

principles.text: Marketing is telling a good story; most other factors are second-order effects.
principles.quote: So it's just another way to reinforce Seth's admonishment that marketing should be defined as telling a good story. Sometimes everything else is a second-order effect.

principles.text: Great stories carry audiences past weak or wrong conclusions; people accept the argument after being captivated.
principles.quote: After being beguiled with interesting, provocative stories, the reader is happy to receive Gladwell's unproven, non-sequitur conclusions.

principles.text: Story quality can make content worth consuming even when its logic is flawed.
principles.quote: The stories are so good, they're worth reading anyway.

principles.text: Correlation is not causation; check whether a result happened everywhere regardless of your intervention before crediting your tactic.
principles.quote: correlations don't imply causal relationships. Just because you did X and Y happened afterward doesn't mean X necessarily caused Y.

principles.text: Defending a flawed theory with 'we only see a piece of the picture' is a cop-out; admit error instead.
principles.quote: To me this is a cop-out, too embarrassing to just say, "Yeah, it's wrong, but at least it had a lot of great stories."

sources.title: Outside-In: Sell great support by demonstrating it, not announcing it
sources.originalTitle: Outside-In
sources.summary: Jason argues that claims like "unmatched customer service" are meaningless noise ("if it's on the outside, it's not on the inside"). Instead, invite prospects to test your support during the trial and let them draw their own conclusions. This builds trust during the initial demo.

principles.text: If something is true you don't need to announce it; loudly claiming a virtue signals it may be missing.
principles.quote: When something is true, you don't need to announce it. You don't need to convince people of it. You don't have to draw attention to it.

principles.text: You can't convince people you have good support by telling them; claiming it can even turn them off.
principles.quote: But you can't convince people you have good support by telling them so. In fact, telling them so might turn them off.

principles.text: In demos, invite prospects to trial your tech support alongside your software.
principles.quote: While you're trialing our software, also trial our tech support. Give 'em a call and test it out. Make sure we're responsive and helpful.

principles.text: Customers are numb to stock service slogans, so words alone are meaningless even when true.
principles.quote: People are so used to hearing things like "We have unbeatable customer service" and "Customer service is priority number one," the words are water off a duck's back. Even if true, they're meaningless.

principles.text: Great support drives relationships, word-of-mouth and can win a sale despite a weak first impression.
principles.quote: having good service is not only a competitive advantage, it's also the primary way to develop solid relationships, promote word-of-mouth advertising (the best kind), and can even make a sale even when the first impression was unfavorable.

principles.text: Don't say it, do it: encourage prospects to notice and let them reach their own conclusions.
principles.quote: So don't say it, do it. Encourage potential customers to notice, but let them come to their own conclusions.

sources.title: You're a real company when…: Jason Cohen on the milestones that make a startup feel real
sources.originalTitle: You're a real company when…
sources.summary: Jason Cohen lists the small, tangible milestones that made Smart Bear feel like a real company, from POs and a first employee to a sign on the building. He adds that the pitch even a receptionist can give matters more than polish, and closes with a 2023 story of seeing the WP Engine sign go up.

principles.text: Milestones that make a company feel real are concrete and personal, like a sign on the building, not abstract metrics.
principles.quote: I made one of those bold because that's the one that's always stuck with me. We got the sign about a year ago, and it really was a proud moment.

principles.text: Everyone in the company, even the receptionist, should be able to say what you do and why people buy in about 15 seconds.
principles.quote: The receptionist, by the way, knew exactly what their branch of Adobe (Ottawa) did and could articulate why people bought their products in about 15 seconds.

principles.text: Maturing means accepting enterprise buying norms: take POs, and ship before you get paid.
principles.quote: You take PO's in addition to credit cards, and you've gotten over the fact that, yes, you have to actually ship the product before they give you money.

principles.text: Outsource admin chores like payroll once they're a distraction; it's a sign of growing up.
principles.quote: You pay someone else to print pay stubs and pay your monthly employment taxes because you're just tired of doing it yourself.

principles.text: Growing user counts are a real validation milestone for a small software company.
principles.quote: The 8000'th user of our various software products just came on-line. That makes me feel like a real company.

principles.text: A book can serve as a credibility asset and marketing channel for a software company.
principles.quote: we do have a book with a glossy cover with over 7000 copies in circulation

sources.title: How a guy in a bear suit made a tradeshow booth impossible to ignore
sources.originalTitle: Guy in a bear suit
sources.summary: Jason Cohen describes using a developer in a panda suit as the Smart Bear tradeshow mascot. The bear drew crowds, created a physical traffic funnel past the booth, and started real conversations because people assumed it was a hired student. A lesson in unconventional, memorable booth tactics, with the bear's calm presence at an awards show getting repeated mentions.

principles.text: Give your tradeshow booth something unmistakable that makes everyone notice and gravitate toward you.
principles.quote: Tradeshow booths need something to help them stand out.  A guy in a bear suit is one way to do it.

principles.text: Position the attention-getter so that even people avoiding it must pass your booth and see your pitch.
principles.quote: if you want to get past the bear you must swing all the way to one side of the aisle (where our booth was) or the other, so (d) you end up getting our pitch and seeing our stuff even if you avoid the bear

principles.text: Put a real expert inside the gimmick; people assume a hired hand, so real product conversations surprise and engage them.
principles.quote: People assume you've hired some poor high school student to stand around in the suit. So when the bear engages you in a discussion of peer code review you might be surprised enough to actually talk about it.

principles.text: Commit fully to the stunt and practice it; the person who wanted to be the bear was great at it.
principles.quote: Roy really wanted to be the bear, and he was really good at it. He spent a lot of time in the bear head back at the office to get used to where the ears and head and eyes and chin were.

principles.text: A crowd around the mascot grows the draw and slows traffic in front of your booth, giving you time to show your stuff and give away a free book.
principles.quote: there was always a crowd around the bear, checking it out, seeing if it could talk, which increases the no-fly zone

principles.text: Calm, deadpan presence beats flailing for attention; acting like it's normal made the bear memorable at an awards show.
principles.quote: He was just calmly sitting there, as if it's normal that a bear would be attending the Jolt Award.

sources.title: Selling to the Bottom: sell to the top with the same pitch as the developer
sources.originalTitle: Selling to the Bottom
sources.summary: Jason Cohen explains how Code Collaborator was sold bottom-up by genuinely removing pain for developers, long before "product-led growth" had a name. When pitching a CTO top-down, he refuses ROI-chart selling and gives the same honest pitch: this saves developers time and increases happiness.

principles.text: Sell by genuinely removing pain for the people doing the work; they then beg their bosses to buy.
principles.quote: Genuinely solve a genuine problem for the folks in the trenches, then they beg their bosses to buy the tool to alleviate pain.

principles.text: A tool that only serves managers' reports gets circumvented by users, which makes the reports meaningless anyway.
principles.quote: If it only generated metrics and reports, the managers would like it but developers would (rightly!) revolt and circumvent the system. And then the reports wouldn't mean anything anyway.

principles.text: Don't rely on imagined ROI formulas; if the buyer already believes in the value, the tool's cost is trivial next to the problem it prevents.
principles.quote: If you don't believe that proof-reading code will uncover defects, an ROI formula isn't going to convince you otherwise! If you do believe review will uncover defects, the cost of our little tool is clearly trivial

principles.text: Give executives the same truthful pitch you give end users, rather than a different top-down script.
principles.quote: So I sell to the top exactly as I sell to the developer: "This will save your developers time and increase happiness."

principles.text: Be skeptical of top-down mandates; stick to the truth and stand by the people in the trenches.
principles.quote: The sales books say otherwise, but I think you have to stick to the truth and stick by your mates in the trenches.

principles.text: Executives are more receptive to honest value than conventional sales wisdom assumes.
principles.quote: The brass aren't as insensitive as the sales books would have you believe.

sources.title: Buy your company's domain on day one: Jason Cohen's $2000 SmartBear.com lesson
sources.originalTitle: Idiot! Buying SmartBear.com
sources.summary: Jason Cohen explains how he skipped registering smartbear.com when it cost almost nothing, a squatter grabbed it, and he ended up paying $2000 after failed offers and a legal letter. The lesson: cheap protective purchases like a domain should be made immediately, because squatters watch business records and excuses don't help.

principles.text: Delay on cheap protective purchases like your company-name domain can cost thousands; act fast.
principles.quote: Being slow cost me $2000. **IDIOT!**

principles.text: Don't assume nobody is watching you; squatters monitor business registrations and grab any domain they find.
principles.quote: I didn't think anyone was paying attention to little ol' me, which was true, but that's not an excuse, the domain trollers watch the chamber of commerce records and grab anything they can find.

principles.text: Being broke or unsure of success is no excuse for skipping cheap insurance.
principles.quote: I didn't think things would go so well, which was true, but that's not an excuse, it would have been cheap insurance.

principles.text: A squatter's price is effectively set by your legal costs, so fighting them rarely beats paying.
principles.quote: I asked the lawyer how much it would cost to actually pursue this. Minimum $2500. (Oh. That's how the price is set.)

principles.text: An unregistered trademark gives little leverage against a squatter, and registration is slow, so start early.
principles.quote: He responded by saying it wasn't a registered trademark. I started the process of registering all our trademarks, but years later we're in the last stage of the process but still waiting.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jason Cohen walks through an ordered diagnostic for stalled SaaS growth: logo churn, pricing and positioning, net revenue retention, channel saturation, and whether you need to grow at all. Includes the churn-cap formula, the Double Down 8x pricing story, and why A/B testing mostly yields false positives.

chunks.heading: Diagnosing stalled growth: work through the questions in order
chunks.text:
Jason has built four companies (two unicorns, WP Engine being one; the earlier ones included a bootstrapped company, and one was VC-funded) and invested in about 60 startups. He says growth usually doesn't stop suddenly. It "slowly gets slower," like running through mud: lots of work, less impact.

He diagnoses it with a series of questions, asked in a fixed order. If an earlier one is broken, fixing a later one won't help enough. The order:

1. Are customers leaving (logo churn)?
2. Is pricing and positioning right?
3. Are existing customers growing (NRR)?
4. Are marketing channels saturated?
5. Do you actually need to grow?

He notes the same list also works as a "how do I grow more" checklist, not only a stall diagnosis. The rules hold across B2B and consumer because they come from the mechanics of finance, though the levers differ by segment.

chunks.heading: Churn: why cancellations cap your size, and how to find the real reason
chunks.text:
