**Why it comes first**
- Once a customer leaves, nothing can save them or grow their revenue.
- Churn often travels with negative reviews that hurt growth further.
- Emotionally: the customer found you, didn't bounce off the homepage, survived the pricing page, had the budget, bought and onboarded, then left. "Wait a minute, that's terrible."

**The ceiling math**
- Cancellations grow automatically with your customer count; marketing does not. Triple your customers overnight and ads/SEO still deliver the same new leads, but cancellations triple.
- Maximum size = new customers per month ÷ monthly cancellation rate. Example: 100 new customers a month at 5% churn is 100 ÷ 0.05 = 2,000. The company never exceeds 2,000, and growth slows sharply as it approaches that number.
- The same math works with dollars instead of customers. He uses customer counts because "we will never have more than 2,000 customers" feels visceral.
- Vague rules like "anything above 3% a month is terrible" get argued about; the ceiling number is concrete.
- For SMB, 2% monthly cancellation is good, so he'd check whether there's still much to gain.

**Getting the real reason**
- Dropdown reasons are mostly noise. At Smart Bear, one option got picked a lot; he realized it was the first on the list. After randomizing the order, all options were picked equally.
- Ask open-ended questions, and ask "What made you cancel?" rather than "Why did you cancel?" He took this from a Groove case study: the same email went from 10% to 20% usable responses.
- "Too expensive" is never the real reason. The customer already saw the pricing page and chose to buy. Something else failed: an unmet promise, a missing integration (for example, it only works with Jira and they use Linear).
- "Project ended" isn't a dead end either. A more successful product might have kept the project alive, or you may have picked a target segment whose projects end (small businesses, consumers).
- He dislikes the idea of a single root cause. Complex systems have several interlocking causes. His analogy is cause of death: stopped breathing, car crash, passed out, undiagnosed diabetes.
- Talk to customers who are in trouble but haven't canceled yet. Signals include never uploading data, calling support too much or too little, or not logging in. Guessing at signals is fine without much data.
- Good customers share traits with bad ones. Look for what good customers have that bad customers don't.
- If unsure where to start, work on onboarding. Most cancellation happens early, and small onboarding changes have big effects. In his YouTube retention analogy, about 50% drop in the first 30 seconds; moving that to 55% could lift the final 20% retained to roughly 25%.
- AI (LLMs) is good at themes in cancellation feedback but weak at actionable details, because it averages. He asks it to pull every specific detail under each theme with the customer who said it, then reads them himself.

chunks.heading: Pricing and positioning
chunks.text:
- Quoting Patrick Campbell's data on 4,200 startups: "Your prices are way too low because you just guessed and you haven't changed them." Often prices were copied from competitors or tweaked arbitrarily.
- The textbook demand curve (raise price, demand falls) often fails in practice. Often you raise prices and signups don't change, or go up, because pricing selects the market.
- Larger companies (his example: 1,000 employees, $400M revenue) see a $2 or $100 a month product and assume it isn't good enough, with weak support and governance. A higher price puts you in their consideration set. The real curve is more like a mesa than a line.
- Example: a founder selling to enterprise and government charged $300 per year and got 1-2 signups a week. Jason had him switch to $300 per month (12x). Still 1-2 signups a week. His advice: raise prices again.
- Price is also structure and positioning (per site, per usage, per seat), not just the number.

**The "Double Down" positioning story**
- Pitch 1: "cut your AdWords cost in half." For a customer spending $40K a month, they save $20K and would pay maybe $5K.
- Pitch 2: "double your leads for the same money." The customer already accepts spending $40K for that volume of leads at the same cost per lead, so doubling the leads is worth up to $40K.
- Same product, 8x the price ($40K vs $5K). The CMO can also tell the CEO "I increased the growth rate" rather than "I saved money."
- Lesson: sell more of what the company values (growth, retention, competitiveness) rather than saving time or money, which caps the price.
- Caveats: moving up-market brings new demands (SOC 2, governance, integrations, professional services), and may not fit your culture (his example: Buffer is for "the little people"). Pricing is a strategy decision, not a knob.

chunks.heading: Net revenue retention and expansion
chunks.text:
- Cancellations always overtake direct marketing, so a way to offset them is existing customers paying more through upgrades, usage or seats. NRR is the revenue from today's customers one year later, and can end above 100% if upgrades exceed cancellations and downgrades.
- NRR can mislead. If logo churn is high, too few customers remain to upgrade. Also percentages are asymmetric: a 20% loss needs a 25% gain to recover (100 to 80 needs 25% to return to 100; a 20% gain only reaches 96).
- Public SaaS evidence: of over 100 public SaaS companies, about two have NRR below 100%, and those have poor financials. Median NRR at IPO is 119%.
- To raise NRR, the customer should feel they get more value as the price rises ("the price doubles, but I'm getting five times the value"). Measure the value the customer gets, not only usage. Use proxy or qualitative measures if no number exists. His framing: "create more value for the customer and then split that with them."
- Ask whether a change is good for the customer, not only for you. Don't let investors push policies that aren't.
- If a segment doesn't expand (consumer, SMB), other levers exist: a second product sold to the same customers (his comparison: AG1's added supplements), or existing customers referring new ones. Referrals also offset exponentially growing cancellations.

chunks.heading: Channel saturation and the "elephant curve"
chunks.text:
- Marketing channels saturate and then decline. He calls the pattern the "elephant curve": an S-curve with a sagging "butt" rather than a flat top. Audiences have seen your message, and channels themselves shrink (magazines, conferences). It affects Adwords, Facebook ads, SEO and affiliates. AI's effect on channels is unknown.
- Key question: "Do you know right now which channels are saturated and which aren't?" If not, "flogging" the ads or SEO team harder or adding one feature won't fix it.
- Adding adjacent channels (SEO and ads) can work, but in his experience a product that sells well direct often does poorly in SEO or social, and vice versa.
- More creative options:
  - Constant Contact held in-person workshops in cities teaching small businesses email marketing, using power users who were also agencies. It restarted growth despite the $20-a-month price.
  - HubSpot tested selling through agencies; about 50% of revenue after four or five years.
  - WP Engine sells many sites through agencies that build WordPress sites.
  - A new product or new market that plants one foot in an existing strength or asset and the other in a risky new area (he has a written framework for this).
- When channels are full, he says it forces more drastic bets, since the marketing department can no longer be the answer.

chunks.heading: Do you need to grow? Plus other views
chunks.text:
**Whether to grow**
- "If you're not growing, you're dying" may be investor rhetoric. Bootstrapped companies (his example: 37signals) can choose profit over revenue growth, and growth might mean a bigger organization or a market segment you don't want.
- He still thinks the idea applies to people. Ask whether you and your team are fulfilled doing the same thing every day, and if you're stuck, something dramatic (leaving, selling, changing the company) may be needed.
- He rejects growth at all costs: grow as much as possible within things you're proud of. Early on you can be looser, then tighten standards as you can afford to.
- On decisions under uncertainty (quit, sell, move), he says probability and expected value don't help, because the probabilities are unknowable and it's one life. This is the topic of a book he'd like to write next.

**Common thread**
- Customers must actually get value: the product promises the right thing, delivers it, customers onboard, they realize they're getting it, and you measure it. Many failures are targeting the wrong customer or segment, or poor positioning, rather than lack of value.

**A/B testing**
- His contrarian view: A/B testing "doesn't work very well and it doesn't work on most things." It can't test strategy or vision. On details, most "wins" are false positives, because the true effect is rare, so even a 95%-accurate tool produces more false positives than real wins. Teams stack winners for a year and see no change in conversion rates.
- He cites the Shopify CTO's account of holdout groups: roughly a third of effects disappear. Unless you're very sophisticated, "you're the sucker at the table."

**Book and writing**
- His book *Hidden Multipliers* (hiddenmultipliers.com) is about small decisions with outsized impact, such as moving cancellation from 5% to 4%.
- He has written at asmartbear.com for almost 20 years (roughly 150-200 posts he's proud of out of about 300-350), free with no ads or courses. Rule: publish only what's his best, so quality over consistency.
- He recommends *Crossing the Chasm* (a market is defined partly by its members respecting each other's opinions) and *On Writing Well*.
- He uses Gemini to turn chart images into tables that paste into Google Sheets.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jason Cohen answers bootstrapper questions on validating ideas by trying to invalidate them, getting paid upfront, raising prices aggressively, recognizing product-market fit, and why reseller distribution faded. He also live-coaches three founders on cash runway, finding new channels and marketplaces, and talks about motivation and stress.

chunks.heading: Validating by trying to invalidate, and testing price early
chunks.text:
- Jason's rule for validation: go in trying to invalidate the idea, not confirm it. Most ideas are "pretty okay", and a few friendly conversations will always feel like validation.
- His example: before WP Engine he tested a different product. Everyone said "that's perfect", but then their suggestions diverged. One said price it at $5,000/month and sell through agencies, another said make it ad-tech only, another said make it freemium for millions. Divergence is the signal that the idea is not good, even though the first reaction was positive.
- Always ask about price, because "price does determine the product". Someone with 120 interested emails had never asked whether they would pay, or whether it would be $1 or $1,000 a month.
- For both WP Engine and the earlier idea he floated $50/month as a starting number. No flinch is a good sign; "I thought it would be free" tells you something else.
- He validated WP Engine by getting about 30-40 people to commit to $99/month.
- Take money up front if you can. Cash the checks ("you can always give it back later") or use Square for card numbers.
- Crowdfunding is weaker validation than it looks. Kickstarter backers are very early adopters and not a repeatable distribution system, so they may not represent a market. Still worth doing: "it's getting the engine turned over".
- If you can't describe the product in a short phrase, you haven't found the root of what it is. You need that phrase anyway for headlines, buttons, AdWords and a t-shirt.
- The phrase's job is only to make the right person say "tell me more", not to state price, market and plan. Google's "organize the world's information" is a mission (know everything about us, which powers ads, maps and self-driving cars), not a business-model description.

chunks.heading: Deciding whether to quit a slow-growing business
chunks.text:
- Jason says there is no formula; he calls Seth Godin's book *The Dip* useless for this question.
- His best test is whether you are fulfilled and glad to do it, separate from the stress and slow revenue. "Revenue not growing fast enough and I love it, so who cares" versus "not growing fast enough and I hate it".
- Entrepreneurship is almost always a bad financial choice. Everything will be slower and harder than you want; that's life, like remodeling a kitchen.
- He cites Steve Jobs' morning question (if this were my last day, would I want to do what I'm about to do?). The point is not loving every moment but being proud and fulfilled.
- Most of what a founder needs to do is uncomfortable. Engineers want to open the IDE and build features, but the right work is usually distribution, the website, new customers, support or hiring.
- Bootstrapped founders have more freedom to shut something down, since they have no investors to see it through for.

chunks.heading: What product-market fit felt like across his four companies
chunks.text:
- Consulting version: you are telling people no instead of scrambling for work, and can raise rates and be choosy.
- Product version: growth speeds up and you can't explain why. No new ads, social campaign or release. At WP Engine this happened in January 2012 as a literal hockey stick, and it never dropped back after the holidays.
- He says "that's actually signal". The same unexplained shift happened at Smart Bear and IT Watchdogs.
- His path at every company was a "random walk" seeking something:
  - Smart Bear started as a .NET tool integrating with version control. It sold poorly until he noticed people abusing it for code review, then rebuilt around that and rewrote everything in Java (a full rewrite he says is usually wise to avoid, but it worked there). Code review was the real market, and it did not exist as a category yet.
  - Smart Bear's customers moved to mostly large enterprise (Lockheed Martin, Adobe, Microsoft, Qualcomm, Cisco) with zero salespeople. It started around three years in.
  - IT Watchdogs made server-room climate monitors. Sales rose a lot when the product went from a USB-style dongle to a rack-mounted unit.
- Once at scale you need predictability to hire, but early on you can't predict it.
- Experience is not a durable asset. Smart Bear got going because AdWords was new, he was the only ad on the page, and clicks were five cents. That world no longer exists, so keep a "beginner's mind".

chunks.heading: Pricing around how the customer buys
chunks.text:
- At IT Watchdogs a buyer said he'd take a base unit and two sensors for about $490-ish because "if I spend less than $500 on my credit card I don't have to ask permission." They rejiggered the bundles so typical purchases totaled roughly $450-$490, and sold a lot as long as totals stayed under about $600.
- Lesson: ask what the buyer can approve without permission. Austin Independent School District's limit was $20, which Jason uses as a reason not to sell to schools or government.
- Hardware channel margins stack. A web-enabled power strip with a $15 board in it sold for $3,500 because every reseller/distributor step took roughly 30%. Software and the internet remove those middlemen.

chunks.heading: Raising prices and moving upmarket
chunks.text:
- Jason says to always push prices up, and going upmarket (e.g. $99 minimum) is smart if you want a couple hundred customers paying more instead of many paying little. It must fit your company style (one or two founders can't service IBM).
- Example 1: a company at Capital Factory sold at $300/year. He told them to change it to $300 per month ("just to see what happens"). Sales were exactly the same, a 12x price increase. Their customers included the USGA.
- Example 2: a Facebook-ads optimization tool at $15/month. He had them test $30 for a week; signups did not change. His advice was to double again until signups drop.
- Fear of "what if my customers say this" is solved by "do the right thing": you can keep old customers on the old price.
- Raising prices on existing customers when small: he helped craft an email that was honest and personal. It said they are two founders with a few hundred customers at $20/month who can't feed their families, hope the customer likes the product, and are raising prices (to roughly $79-89 at the low end). It acknowledged "you did not sign up for this", said they'd understand if people leave, and explained the money would hire an engineer and keep phone support. Signed with names and photos. Only about two of hundreds of customers quit.
- His principle: "honesty wins most of the time", and customers want small companies to succeed. Bring them along on the journey; they already know a two-person product has rough edges.
- Enterprise buying (POs): quote high so you can give procurement a 20% discount and land where you wanted. Get into their vendor system and get the PO issued early, even if payment is triggered on delivery, so you don't wait an extra six months after shipping.

chunks.heading: Resellers, old-school channels and enterprise selling
chunks.text:
- Reseller and distributor models (Graybar, VARs) fit physical goods in warehouses with setup and shipping; each layer takes about 30%, and the vendor carries inventory and buy-back risk. IT Watchdogs used some resellers abroad (e.g. the UK).
- For software he thinks the model mostly fails because the internet disintermediates it: no inventory, and you can sell directly. He sold to Cisco and made seven-figure-scale sales to Adobe himself, and says enterprise buying is complicated but "not that hard", just under-written-about.
- When everyone ignores something there may be an opportunity, so a Graybar-style channel could still be an overlooked edge for someone.
- Going against the grain worked for Smart Bear: he sent out over 100,000 copies of a physical book (while people said ebooks and PDFs). A physical book arrives in the office, nobody throws away a book, "basically a brochure that never gets thrown away". He made it bright red so it stands out.

chunks.heading: Finding channels, ignored buyers and unseen personas (live Q&A coaching)
chunks.text:
- For a purchase-order software company (30 customers, about 5 new a month, all from paid comparison sites like Capterra/GetApp) wanting 20 a month, he advised:
  - Don't just broaden, go specific but different. Instead of CFOs (hard and expensive to reach at 50-100 employees), target the controller, VP of Finance, junior accountants entering receipts, or executive assistants.
  - "I love it when there's people who are underserved and ignored." They are harder to find (not at conferences) but love a tool that gives them a win; a junior accountant can replace part of their job and move up.
  - Pitch the real value: PO control is control over spend and approvals, auditability and Sarbanes-Oxley; the controller's job is to control.
  - Find out where the buyers already go. If comparison sites aren't the only way people find tools, work out where competitors get traffic (AdWords, etc.) and what buyers use instead (even an Excel template as a foot in the door).
- For a founder with a time-management app (25 companies pitched, 7 using the method in Excel, $49/user/month, 10-25 users per company) and 2-3 months of cash: get cash sooner. Start PO and vendor-onboarding paperwork now. Don't worry if they stay on Excel as long as they pay $50/month. Pitch 25-75 more companies at the same rate, since about a quarter said yes.
- For a two-sided hiring marketplace: charge from day one, because free or cheap implies low quality and sets precedent. Small scale is still compelling (placing one person with one company is real value and that company will want a second). The hard part of hiring is scaling, not starting. Matching on fit matters; he cites letting go of strong engineers who were a culture fit for Facebook but not WP Engine.

chunks.heading: Why keep going, and stress
chunks.text:
- Jason says starting companies is irrational and "on chromosome 13 or something", which is why he's doing a fourth for the same reason as the first. The higher reasons: giving jobs to people without college degrees (fewer than half of WP Engine's roughly 300 staff have degrees), hiring on attitude, aptitude, empathy, curiosity and accountability; benefits including same-sex marriage coverage even when small; and helping non-technical customers who would be victims of technology.
- WP Engine put some of its stock into a nonprofit and gives back to Austin and WordPress.
- He says entrepreneurs have "almost an obligation" to create important things; making money is fine, but ask what you do with it.
- Stress doesn't go away with experience. Personnel decisions (letting people go) stay emotionally hard. Letting someone leave a bad fit is doing them a favor, since they often won't leave on their own.
- What helps him: meditation, distancing himself from angry internet comments ("it's probably about them"), accepting that all companies end, and focusing on the journey over the exit.
- "No one in this room is their own boss": customers, the market, family and employees (whom you pay first) are all bosses.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jason Cohen explains how WP Engine started from 50 customer interviews and hit product-market fit via pricing changes and a 60-day money-back guarantee. He covers picking a leading "moment of value" metric over laggy MRR, when to raise VC, and his joy/skill/need framework for handing the CEO role to Heather.

chunks.heading: Starting WP Engine from customer interviews
chunks.text:
- In the late 2000s Jason's blog kept crashing when it hit Hacker News each Monday. He asked other bloggers how they kept WordPress running under that load. The answer was always "I don't know, but if you find it tell me."
- That gap became the seed for WP Engine. He ran about 50 customer interviews, and the same exercise showed him his other idea was "a fine idea" but "wasn't a good business."
- The interviews led to the pitch: if hosting were fast, scalable, secure and came with good service, people would pay about 10x what they paid GoDaddy or Bluehost for WordPress hosting.
- Those four points were literally bullet points on the first website, and they are still what people sign up for 13 years later.
- His takeaway is that "customer development and figure out the pain" is still the core work.
- He doubts the Lean Startup book works as a manual. It got founders to "get outside the building," but he sees no evidence that people who follow it fail less.
- Asking "do you like this feature?" teaches nothing because people say yes. The questions have to be directed.
- He recommends Teresa Torres's "Continuous Discovery Habits." Nearly every chapter is usable, including what to do with interview data afterward.
- From that book he also likes "right-storming." Everyone first understands the problem together. Then each person brainstorms alone, in whatever rhythm suits them. Then the group meets to discuss ideas already written down in a Miro board or Google Doc. He says this works on Zoom, where live brainstorming does not.

chunks.heading: How Jason knew WP Engine had product-market fit
chunks.text:
- He dates it to January 2012, about two years in, when the team was 4-5 people.
- The signal was that all he could do was keep up with demand. Orders and support tickets flew in, and he couldn't think about new features.
- Hiring was hard because the team was too busy and had no hiring practice.
- Revenue went from roughly $1M to $5M that year, a hockey stick.
- He credits a pricing change as the cause, though he admits it is hard to rerun the experiment. He also notes a first-quarter seasonality effect, since people build websites then, but says growth "never ended" so it wasn't only that.
- The trial had about a 90% conversion rate, which he reads as product-market fit in itself.

chunks.heading: The pricing changes that unlocked growth at WP Engine
chunks.text:
All of these came from customer conversations.

- **More sites on higher plans.** Customers said they would happily pay $100/month for one big site, but would not keep a second account elsewhere for a tiny site, such as one for their mom's art studio getting two hits a month. Higher plans should allow more sites. Freelancers also need a place to host a site before launch.
- **Lowest tier from $50 to $29.** Customers on GoDaddy at $5/month could be moved to $20-30, but "mentally" not to $50, even if it was worth $50. His point is that this isn't generic willingness to pay or anchoring. People can't make the jump in one shot.
- **Plug-in products anchor on the host product.** Products that sit inside another ecosystem (WordPress, Salesforce) have a price ceiling set by the main product. People ask how they could pay something similar to a component.
- **A top tier called "Business."** He added the most expensive tier. He says he has "no clue" if that helped.
- **Money-back guarantee instead of free trial.** Hosting costs money immediately, so the two-week free trial lost two weeks of revenue on customers who stayed anyway (90% converted).
  - He switched to charging up front with a 60-day money-back guarantee.
  - He expected it to hurt, but sales went up.
  - Customers said two weeks wasn't enough to check the product out, but two months was.
- A cheap way to test this is to apply it to new customers only, since you can undo it at will.
- He points to his 2012-13 talk "building the ideal bootstrap business" for more on the money-back guarantee and charging up front.

chunks.heading: Picking the key metric: a moment of customer value, not MRR
chunks.text:
- Early on, before hypergrowth, his only metric beyond MRR was keeping customers happy. Churn looks good early because there hasn't been time for people to decide they don't like the product. After product-market fit, "who can even think about the metrics," because you have to operate.
- Any number you wouldn't react to if it changed a lot (like raw traffic) is a vanity metric, not a key metric.
- MRR and retention are the most important numbers, because without them you starve. But they are poor to operate on: they lag, and they have many inputs (sales, marketing, upgrades, downgrades, product, service).
- His preferred key metric is the moment in the customer journey where they get value and are likely to succeed and stay. You'll know revenue follows if it happens, and it happens daily, so you can act on it and see results within a week.
- Netflix example: the number of people who put 3 or more DVDs in their queue on day one. This correlated, not necessarily causally, with being about 7x more likely to become a customer and stay at least 6 months. Obvious tactics follow: ask their favorite genre and fill the queue, or suggest the 10 most popular titles.
- Instacart example: total cart value as the Northstar. Its inputs are the number of customers, average cart size and items per cart. The inputs overlap, and "this is not an equation."
- The key metric can and should change over time, especially early.
- Treat the supporting metrics like a car dashboard, not goals: "it's just what's going on." At any moment you can decide to focus on one for a few months.
- A single central metric also helps at scale. Engineers don't own revenue, and sales has quotas. MRR is the output of everyone doing well, so it isn't any one team's primary metric. This avoids "who owns what" fights.
- A central metric lets you ask a directed question like "how do we raise average cart size?" instead of the undirected "how do we make MRR go up?"

chunks.heading: Using excitement as a tiebreaker for prioritization
chunks.text:
- Excitement alone is a bad reason to do something. But when several projects all sound good and nobody can tell which will work, he says the tie should go to the one people are excited about.
- His reason is that people "work on it harder and care more and just want to do it more," which is a huge advantage. It also gives that project the best chance of success.
- He says WP Engine does this at scale.
- If one option is clearly better, do that one.

chunks.heading: Whether to raise venture money
chunks.text:
- His default answer for traditional venture is "you shouldn't accept it," unless a set of conditions hold. Like any tool, it has a time and place.
- At WP Engine he didn't expect VC to be the right tool at first. Then it became clear, two years in, that the market was huge and growing, with tailwinds, and that this could be a billion-dollar-plus company.
- Personally, he was a bootstrapper by default. He wanted a different journey this time: the constraint shifts from profit to growth, the mandate becomes growth, and money is less of a constraint. He frames it as different, not better.
- He calls it "simply a fact" that if you haven't quit your day job, the company has a lower chance of success. Taking a little money to work on it full time clearly reduces risk.
- Other reasonable uses of money:
  - Hiring one person (the gap between one and two people is big, even if the second isn't a cofounder).
  - Paying for design if design matters and you aren't a designer.
  - Funding marketing experiments.
- You should know exactly what the money is for. "So I can quit my job and buy ads" isn't a plan.
- A good plan looks like this: the next phase (a version, a partnership, a customer count) is blocked only by money. You have a theory backed by customer conversations, competitor observation and people asking you to go in that direction.

chunks.heading: Stepping aside as CEO: the joy, skill, need framework
chunks.text:
- Jason gave up the CEO role at WP Engine himself, a few years after the VC round. No investor forced it. He became CTO and brought in Heather Brunner as CEO. Heather is still CEO nine years later, and he calls her the "late joining co-founder," a phrase he borrowed from Reid Hoffman about Jeff Weiner at LinkedIn.
- The framework is three circles: **joy** (what you love), **skill** (what you're good at), and **need** (what the company needs done). It was synthesized from other sources and tweaked by him.
- Each two-circle overlap is a trap, and founders are especially exposed because nobody can tell them otherwise:
  - **Joy + skill, not need.** You love it and you're good at it, so you stay in flow. Classic case: the engineer-founder building the next feature that two people asked for, when they should be doing sales and marketing.
  - **Skill + need, not joy.** This is burnout land. His own example was accounting: Smart Bear's acquirers called its books "the cleanest" they had seen. Bootstrappers do this work because they can't afford to hire. They think they're protecting their team, but the team wouldn't want them burned out, and he says you should ask them.
  - **Joy + need, not skill.** The engineer doing AdWords badly for three months, becoming a self-declared expert, and still not knowing how to manage a hire. He asks who tells the founder they're bad at marketing, and says the answer is a cofounder.
- The goal is not mediocrity but excellence everywhere.
- He applied it to the CEO role at about 70-80 people. Managing people and the board, and building a global sales team, were things he didn't enjoy and wasn't best at. Engineering and product were joy, skill and need.
- It took about four months of struggle. His board member, a repeat founder, told him: "You're thinking one day maybe you'll ring the bell on the NASDAQ and you want the credit." The clincher was "you're the founder, you'll always get the credit."
- That freed him to keep the credit and the ego forever, so he had no reason to run the board meetings. He says the move has been "fantastic."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jason Cohen explains why you shouldn't set out to bootstrap a billion-dollar company, and how to design a bootstrapped business with recurring value and annual prepay. He also covers strategy as a self-reinforcing set of decisions, running hypothesis-driven customer interviews, and managing executives.

chunks.heading: Why Jason says not to aim at a bootstrapped billion-dollar company
chunks.text:
- Jason argues you "shouldn't" go in trying to bootstrap a billion-dollar business. Reaching that scale on a reasonably short timeline requires fast growth, and fast growth almost always requires raising money.
- Growing slowly (about 20% per year for 20 years) doesn't work, because a 30-year-old technology is probably no longer relevant by then. Even at venture-style growth rates, he says it takes 7 to 10 years just to reach about $100M.
- Spending only money you already have almost never produces that growth speed.
- He started WP Engine bootstrapped, expecting it to be a company making roughly $30K-$50K in profit per month. After about two years (4 or 5 people, strong unit economics) he raised a first round of $1M.
- Why he changed his mind and raised:
  - The market was far bigger than he expected. WordPress was already about 10% of the internet (W3Techs numbers) and winning in corporate homepages and media, not only blogs. It is now about 43%.
  - Demand was higher than he expected.
  - He wanted a different kind of challenge: a bigger team, with the load not all on him.
- Jason says optionality is a strength. If you only have one definition of success or one way to go to market, the company is brittle. Being in a large, growing market is good even for a small company: the market proves demand exists, and it has many niches too small for the big players.
- He raised every round at a fair valuation: not so low that it over-dilutes operators, and not so high that you can't grow into it. Even the hundreds-of-millions rounds came when ARR was also nine figures.

chunks.heading: Strategy as a set of mutually reinforcing decisions (Southwest Airlines)
chunks.text:
- Jason says conflicting advice such as "riches are in the niches" versus the opposite is useless as stated. The better question is "when is this advice applicable?"
- A niche suits a solo founder who wants high profit, has no hires and no real competition, because they can be "the best" for a narrowly defined customer. That lets them charge more and avoid fighting on marketing spend and features.
- A general product could also work for a solo founder, but only with other decisions that fit together. His made-up example: no tech support, a very visual product with almost no text so it supports 50 languages, and a price of $1 to $5 per month.
- Strategy is "overall how you're going to win." It is a set of decisions that is unique in aggregate, not any single decision. He cites Thomas Sowell: "there are no solutions, only trade-offs." He adds that decisions also come with downstream consequences (second-order effects).
- A competitor can copy one decision but not the whole system. His example is Southwest Airlines (a Michael Porter diagram, published in HBR in 1995):
  - Southwest is the only US airline to never go bankrupt and to be profitable every year.
  - Its edge is the lowest fares, strong on-time performance and friendly staff.
  - Those follow from other decisions: one type of plane (mechanics learn one thing, one set of tools, deep expertise, cheaper training) and short-haul routes only.
  - The costs to customers are no overseas routes, no long routes, no transfers to other airlines and no food.
  - The question is whether enough customers want the benefits and tolerate the negatives. For Southwest the answer is yes.
  - Decades later nobody has copied it, partly because the strategy shapes culture and people, so copying may be effectively impossible.
- Play to your strengths and avoid your weaknesses. Jason says if you can't write code and don't want a technical partner, don't build a technical product. A non-technical solo founder can't hire a good developer, so the product should be easy to build.

chunks.heading: Designing a bootstrapped business: recurring revenue and annual prepay
chunks.text:
- **Recurring revenue.** Jason calls one-time revenue a "terrible idea" (support is one reason). Knowing next month's revenue can be the difference between quitting your job or not, so it matters beyond the math.
- **Value must also recur.** Many founders bill monthly for something customers use once a year (event software is his example). A telltale sign is someone saying "2K MRR but churn is 20% per month." Half the customers are gone in about 4 months, so it is not recurring revenue.
- Recurring examples he gives: accounting tasks that happen monthly, and daily workflows like marketing analytics. He asks founders to explain how a customer gets value in month 6 and month 30.
- **Annual prepay.** Example with a $100/month plan:
  - Offer a year up front for two months free, so $1,000 now.
  - You get the cash immediately, while AdWords is billed to your credit card and paid one to two months later.
  - If you spend the $1,000 on ads and even one person signs up within 30 to 60 days, the ad spend is paid for.
  - As long as the channel is profitable, your marketing budget goes from limited by monthly income to effectively unlimited.
- Accountability without control: he thinks "building in public" on Twitter is weak. A group of about five like-minded peers who know each other's businesses works better, and nobody in it has control.

chunks.heading: Governance, control and operating like a public company
chunks.text:
- Jason says even selling 5% with preferred stock gives up some control, such as deciding to sell the company alone. Typical board-level items are governance, big investments or acquisitions, big expenditures, and leases longer than 1 year.
- He says super-voting-rights situations like Zuckerberg's are rare and overrepresented in the press.
- As a company grows (WP Engine has about 1,200 employees), it needs more controls and the available exit paths shrink to a short list: stay independent, private equity, IPO, or being acquired.
- WP Engine has operated like a public company for at least 5 years, maybe 7: public-company-standard audits and books. The reasoning:
  - If it goes public, nothing changes.
  - If it is acquired, probably by a public company, due diligence is easiest after years of clean audited books.
  - He says it is "the right move regardless of which thing happens."
- If you don't want to give up freedom, "then don't make a big company" and don't claim to want a billion-dollar company at the same time.

chunks.heading: Customer development before launch
chunks.text:
Jason did this at WP Engine in 2009, before the Lean Startup book came out in 2011. He kept using the same approach for 14 years and has written it up on smartbear.com under "customer development."

1. Decide what you want to learn. This is not a sales pitch, which teaches you nothing. His list of questions to settle:
   - What is the customer's life like, and what are their problems in their own words?
   - What tools do they use now, or do they do it manually?
   - Is there a budget already allocated, and what is it named?
   - Are there different kinds of customers?
   - Where do they go to buy tools, and what do they read?
2. Find the trigger event (idea borrowed from Bob Moesta): "Who wakes up in the morning and says, 'today's the day I'm going to buy new WordPress hosting?'" What happened that day? For WP Engine one answer was getting hacked, after which paying $50/month instead of $5 feels worth it.
3. In a spreadsheet, write your hypothesis for each question.
4. Write non-leading questions. Bad: "The internet is scary, hackers are everywhere, what do you do to keep your site safe, and how much do you spend?" Good: "What do you think about internet security? How much do you spend on it? What do you buy?"
5. Run the calls and adjust your hypotheses. Some will be right, some wrong, and a third category will be things you hadn't thought of. Look for customer types (for example "two kinds of people").
6. Stop when you are never surprised anymore. That means the method has run out of value, not that you know everything.
- Numbers: he tried 50, talked to about 40, and 30 became paying customers before launch. He launched officially with 30 paying customers at $50/month, then later lowered the price.
- He criticizes taking too long to ship. If it takes longer than about 4 months to get a first paying customer, "you're doing a project, not a company," because the difference is customers. He says a long build can be justified only if it is de-risked some other way, such as an existing big audience.
- He built the first version of WP Engine in 36 hours, and notes he is technical.

chunks.heading: Knowing your strengths, avoiding burnout, and changing roles
chunks.text:
- Jason says it took decades to know his strengths and weaknesses, and they change over time.
- A 360 review by a third party, interviewing people around you, surfaces strengths you didn't know you had. Often your personal bar is so high you underrate yourself on exactly the things you are best at.
- He also suggests probing questions (on his Smart Bear site under "fulfillment"): what you do when you've been off work for 3 weeks, what you did as a kid. A fun exercise is to have a spouse, friend or colleague answer them about you and compare.
- Link to strategy: knowing your strengths makes for a better strategy and prevents burnout. Many founders end up building a company they hate. He did this at Smart Bear (2002 to 2007, sold for single-digit millions), burned out and sold. He says nearly every study he knows of finds founders are unhappy after selling.
- At WP Engine, about 4 years in (50 to 70 people), he realized he wouldn't enjoy being CEO as it scaled (a global sales team, global offices, a big support operation) and that he'd be learning on the job in every area at once. It took about 4 months of struggle to reach that conclusion, and he stepped aside.
- His roles at WP Engine over 14 years: CTO running all product and engineering, then product, then special projects, then corporate strategy, and now the corporate data team (a personal strength). He talked it through with the CEO and adjusted his role every 6 to 12 months.
- He is proud that the culture allows others to try management, change their minds and go back, and he sees that as a good culture.

chunks.heading: Managing executives, and hiring above yourself
chunks.text:
- Jason rejects both "hire and get out of their way" ("what people who don't know how to manage say") and micromanaging. Your job is to hire people better than you, even in areas you are good at, and hold them accountable for results.
- Accountability includes numbers, culture fit of their team, strategic contributions, and whether they make other people better. Executives should also look across the company, not just their own department.
- If you are getting into the details of their work, either they aren't capable (your hiring mistake) or you're interfering unnecessarily (also your fault): "it's always your fault."
- Founders carry "an invisible hammer." A casual "how's that project going?" was taken by a support person as an order to resume work his manager had paused.
- When the CEO and CFO came in, the three of them met about 3 times a week for 3 hours at first, for knowledge transfer. Now the exec team has a weekly 2.5-hour meeting plus another meeting of about an hour.

chunks.heading: Strategy vs. planning, and AI startups
chunks.text:
- **Strategy** is the broad, market-level decisions: target customer, channel, price, product shape, and why. It contains no deadlines or dates. It can be a page or half a page.
- **Planning** (his simple method):
  1. Pick the 1 to 3 strategic objectives that most advance the strategy, assuming no problems.
  2. List the 1 to 3 biggest obstacles.
  3. Decide the 1 to 3 things to do next (about the next month or two) that attack or sidestep those obstacles. If money is the obstacle, tackle it by raising money or switching to annual billing, or sidestep it by getting creative on a low budget.
  4. Tell the whole company. Everything after that is just work.
- He ran this once a quarter on a team of about 50 people, changing something each quarter, and says it got better over roughly two years.
- A strategy that never changes is wrong, but a constantly changing one can't be followed. The bigger the company, the simpler and slower-changing the strategy should be, with more fanfare when it does change.
- Frameworks like OKRs fit some cultures and not others. He suggests trying a framework with a team and deciding together whether to keep or tune it, instead of announcing it top-down.
- Before product-market fit, experiment constantly. After it, you test how to talk to the customer, not who the customer is.
- **AI startups:**
  - The usual startup edge versus incumbents is that incumbents avoid risky, uncertain new markets. With AI that doesn't hold, because public-company incumbents must have an AI story or their stock drops.
  - Using the same models (e.g. GPT-4) gives no differentiation, and your own prompts are easily copied by Adobe and others. Training your own model costs too much for a bootstrapper.
  - Niches (for example, the existing model but local, such as for Norway and in Norwegian) can still work.
  - He likes a "human API" approach: expose the interface, have a human do the work behind it at first (e.g. a Jira ticket), then automate what scales. AI fits well by shortening human steps.
  - Today, he says, AI often gets things about 70% right, which is impressive but not dependable enough to fully replace humans.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jason Cohen lays out his model for a bootstrapped business: aim for predictable recurring revenue of $10k/month per founder from about 150 customers at roughly $70 each. He covers raising prices, annual prepay for cash flow, B2B markets with naturally recurring pain, and paid acquisition over social media.

chunks.heading: The ideal bootstrapped business is a "cash machine"
chunks.text:
- Jason prefers "self-funded" to "bootstrapped" or "lifestyle business" (a term he got from Heaton). Small friends-and-family money or modest debt is fine if it doesn't cost meaningful equity.
- He frames the target as a "cash machine": a predictable way to make profit every month. His test is whether you could do nothing next month and still be certain of $10,000 in revenue. Under 20% of a room of founders could say yes.
- The goal is $10K a month per founder in revenue, ideally $20-40K.
- He says most startups fail by building something nobody wants, and also by building something wanted but structured badly for low money, low time and small-team constraints.
- He bootstrapped four companies, each past $1M a year and profitable, two of them sold. WP Engine was bootstrapped to $1M+ before he raised money to swing for the fences.
- He passed on a company idea he couldn't fit to these constraints.

chunks.heading: Recurring revenue and the "150 customers" model
chunks.text:
- His third company, Smart Bear, sold one-off downloaded software. Even with millions in revenue he woke up at night panicked about covering payroll, with 1 person or 12. "It never got better ever."
- He rejects Kevin Kelly's "1,000 true fans". Kelly retracted it after artists said they couldn't get 1,000 fans or $100-200 a year from them, and $200K wouldn't cover costs anyway. Seth Godin's popularization stuck.
- Jason proposes 150 customers instead, paying about $70 a month on average, which gets you to $10K a month.
- You can scratch together the first 50 through outreach and conversations. Then add some guest posts and social, then paid marketing such as AdWords or ads on relevant sites.
- If you can't scrape together 150 over months, he doubts it can become a company.
- Customer-development outreach that worked for WP Engine: he found WordPress consultants on LinkedIn and emailed them. He said he was founding WordPress hosting designed for them, wanted to learn their pain, and would pay whatever they thought fair for an hour, even above their hourly rate.
  - He sent 42 emails and got a 100% response rate.
  - He talked to 38, and none asked for money.
- Before WP Engine had a name, deck, employees or servers, he got 30-40 people to commit $50 a month. A previous idea failed because he couldn't find enough payers.
- At Capital Factory (the Austin incubator he helped start) he tells every company to try this. About half do, and many get 20-30 people to give a check for something that doesn't exist yet.

chunks.heading: Charge more: price, tiers and the "boutique" frame
chunks.text:
- Many self-funded founders charge $9-19 a month because the product feels rough, then need thousands of customers. He says that's the harder path.
- WP Engine's tier prices produce an average revenue per customer above $100 a month.
- Tactics:
  - Highlight the middle tier. Add a big tier on the end for people who always want the most.
  - Add a "business" plan; Erica Douglas's lesson is that businesses sign up for it automatically.
  - List $99 and run coupons all the time. Hand bloggers a 30% off for a year coupon. Everyone feels they got value, but you average about $70.
  - Cross out a $79 list price and show $49. Sales went up.
  - Double the price and watch for a week. A Capital Factory company at $19 a month doubled to about $49 and signups didn't change. He told them to double again or go up at least 50% until something bad happens.
- He treats revenue per customer as the most important early metric, more than cancellation rate.
- "Boutique" is the mental model: one or two people, expensive, sometimes slow to reply, but with attention, unique work and the good feeling of backing a founder making a go of it. Customers will pay about 3x for a dress or a consultant like Patrick McKenzie.

chunks.heading: Annual prepay and cash flow
chunks.text:
- He says annual prepay is mandatory for self-funded companies. His example:
  - Spend $300 to acquire a customer paying $50 a month; one blog post or a few AdWords clicks might do it.
  - $60K of spend gets you to a $10K a month run rate.
  - With annual prepay at 2 months free, those signups produce about $100K in cash up front, versus $120K collected over a year. That is $40K in the bank now to spend on ads, development or a designer.
- WP Engine numbers: about a quarter of website signups choose annual prepay by revenue. They pay 10 months' worth instead of 12. That gives over 3x the cash flow per signup cohort.
  - Because of this, cash collected each month exceeds acquisition cost. Card revenue lands today while ad bills hit next month, so cash flow is negative one month on ads. Marketing was never limited by money; it stopped when support got overwhelmed.
- Ways to push annual:
  - Give affiliates and bloggers a coupon for 3 months free that works only on annual plans.
  - Raise the monthly price and make the annual discount large, like 6 months free. A Capital Factory company moved from $99 a year to $49 a month plus a big annual discount, and signups didn't change.
  - Another Capital Factory company charged $50 a year. He told them to charge monthly instead; signups didn't change, then add annual.
- On free trials: he dislikes them for self-funded companies. Most people who enter a card stay, so a 15-30 day free trial gives away money you never recover. WP Engine switched from a 15-day free trial to a 60-day money-back guarantee, charging the card immediately.
  - Signups went up. People emailed to say 15 days wasn't enough time.
  - He showed a chart of customer count with a visible change point around January of the previous year, when they also reworked tiers and added the business plan.
- He avoids "picking up pennies" models such as Kickstarter. Kickstarter moved over $100M of funding but earned about $6M and lost money.

chunks.heading: Which markets suit a cash machine
chunks.text:
- B2B only: "you should absolutely never not not sell to consumers."
  - Consumers won't pay $70 a month; Gmail charging $5 a month looked crazy, and a $1.99 app was called overpriced.
  - Backblaze-type consumer backup was only $40 a year, so they moved to business.
  - Every self-funded speaker at the event, including Patrick, Rob and Heaton, sells B2B.
- Avoid temporary pain or one-time moments.
  - A wedding-photo video tool had happy customers but you only marry two or three times, and you must catch brides during planning among many sellers.
  - Event tools sell once a year.
  - A code profiler he acquired: users fixed the slowness during the free trial, so no reason to pay.
- Favor value that is naturally recurring:
  - Ongoing costs, like hosting with servers and bandwidth.
  - Financial cycles: invoicing, reconciliation, taxes, reporting, compliance, HR admin. A mobile-app study showed finance apps averaged $6,000 a month and IT apps $1,500 a month.
  - Fields that keep changing: SEO, AdWords, email marketing, content, social measurement and A/B testing.
  - Support tiers. A premium support package is $500 a month at WP Engine. A simple version is $100 a month where a paid queue gets worked first; it's nearly free money since you answer all tickets anyway.
- Avoid viral-dependent products: they rarely work, and with 100 users and 1% inviting a friend you get rounding error.
- Avoid real-time products. Hosting woke him up at night for outages. Prefer decision support, analytics, monitoring, finance, project management and content, which can tolerate delay.
- Avoid marketplaces: you have two chicken-and-egg businesses (buyers and sellers). They are defensible once working (the asset is people typing etsy.com, not the code), but too risky self-funded.
- Prefer products that can be "done," so you aren't in a feature war with better-resourced rivals. Example: Nico Mak made about $1M a year in the 90s with WinZip shareware.
- Prefer aftermarkets that attach to an incumbent product with a following:
  - Smart Bear added code review to Perforce, Subversion and CVS.
  - Balsamiq started as a Basecamp add-on.
  - Woo Themes, WP Engine (WordPress), Alien Skin (Photoshop plugins) and QODBC (an ODBC interface for QuickBooks, around since 1984, bootstrapped).
  - Benefits: obvious pain points, obvious keywords, and vendors may help. He gave talks at Perforce's user conference while promoting Perforce, with no money changing hands.
  - Ecosystems like Salesforce and Heroku (plugins, AppExchange) are even better because the platform intentionally avoids competing with you; the App Store is riskier.
- Pick a big market, even though you start in a niche. Reasons:
  - Optionality if a niche fails or succeeds.
  - You needn't be the best; there are hundreds of CRMs, project tools and invoicing tools, and many earn well.
  - The pain and spend are already validated.
  - It keeps the option to raise money and swing for the fences, as he did with WP Engine.

chunks.heading: Acquiring customers: paid, measurable, not social
chunks.text:
- He doesn't like social media as the main channel: it's time-heavy, ever-changing, and not a repeatable "put in $1, get $4" machine.
- His blog had 40,000 readers; when he launched WP Engine he expected 30-50 signups from it and got 2.
- Heaton, internet-famous, told him it's always like that. He allows that Buffer succeeded through great social execution, but says it's the exception.
- Rule of thumb for what to pay per click: average revenue per customer divided by 25. At $50 a month, pay about $2 a click. He admits it rests on assumptions and wrote a blog post deriving it.
- Rule of thumb is for when you have no data. Below roughly 1,000 signups a month you can't get statistical significance.
- WP Engine actually spends more:
  - It measures cost per acquisition by channel (affiliate, sales-assisted, coupon), retention, server cost and support cost per customer, and payback period.
  - Most signups come from word of mouth, social and the consultant channel without advertising, so paid can be priced aggressively; a customer has extra value via referrals and upgrades.
  - At the time they got four-figure new customers per month.
- Affiliates:
  - Work well for hosting and WordPress; not for enterprise.
  - You have to pay a lot to get big affiliates' attention (hundreds of dollars per sale, versus a typical $30). That works only with high price points and annual prepay, since affiliates are paid in about 45 days.
  - Pair with annual-only coupons.
  - Affiliates are predictable because it's their job to send new customers every month; you pay only on a sale.
  - Vet them. WP Engine avoids shady affiliates and gray-hat SEO to protect its reputation for service.

chunks.heading: Enterprise sales on a bootstrap
chunks.text:
- Enterprise SaaS is still recurring: annual contracts, one PO and invoice a year, auto-renewal. Budgets are annual anyway.
- At Smart Bear almost all sales were enterprise with no salespeople. Jason did the demos and sales calls, and staff were smart generalists who could code, talk to customers and do support. Revenue was about $1M per head.
- Harder to bootstrap because of long sales cycles, legal, slow payment (a PO with net 130), and cold outreach.
- Tactics:
  - Charge a lot to make it work.
  - Use commission-heavy pay for salespeople since you can't float a $100-150K package.
  - Run pilots (like 30 seats) and land and expand. Smart Bear's first deals averaged $12K and lifetime deals about $60K, sometimes six or seven figures over 18 months or so.

chunks.heading: Growth dilemma and regrets
chunks.text:
- Success causes problems: if it keeps growing you either give bad support or hire and become a manager, which may not be what you wanted.
- Options he lists, none perfect:
  - Sell it: hard, usually modest money. A sale to a partner or employee can use an earn-out (a few grand a month or a percent of revenue over 3 years).
  - Raise prices: changes the clientele.
  - Raise money, which is what WP Engine did, but if you knew that was the goal you should have optimized for it from the start.
- He says there's no great answer. His example: IT Watchdogs built a device for a client that earned them millions; the client asked why not sell it to other power-strip makers, and the client bought the company four months later.
- His advice: "know thyself" (Thales). Work out what you want from the company and revisit it as it changes; talk it through with people who've done it.
- His regrets, which he says he keeps repeating:
  - Not removing someone fast enough. It's almost always cultural, not skills. "No one ever says we fired that person too quickly."
  - Not standing up for what he believes is right about how people are treated and the standards inside the company. Because the company's identity is so tied to the founder in a self-funded business, he always regrets staying quiet.
- His summary formula: predictable customer acquisition, recurring revenue, annual prepay to solve cash flow, a market that fits your constraints and advantages, and being a boutique rather than working a million hours a week.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jason Cohen uses an anonymous burned-out founder's post to argue that founders must make emotionally difficult choices early. Fire fast, hire people better than you and manage them by results, and place yourself where what you like, what you're good at and what the company needs overlap. He draws on selling SmartBear and handing the CEO role at WP Engine to Heather Bruner.

chunks.heading: Founder burnout is predictable, and the cause is avoiding emotionally hard choices
chunks.text:
- Jason cites a Columbia Business School study of 22 entrepreneurs who exited and made $10M+ personally. 21 of the 22 were depressed afterward. He says this is what "always happens," not a rare case. His example is Markus Persson, who sold Minecraft to Microsoft for hundreds of millions and spoke publicly about being near suicide.
- He compares it to frog boiling: nobody intends it, it unfolds slowly, and the "balloon payment of emotional toil" arrives at the end.
- His thesis is that you must make emotionally difficult choices early to build a healthier company and avoid that payoff.
- He has built companies both ways. He sold earlier startups for millions. At WP Engine (CTO and co-founder, about eight years in at the time of the talk) the company passed $100M ARR, and he is still there and not burned out.
- He read an anonymous Hacker News post from a founder who was about to be acquired and cried in the bathroom each morning. Jason says the stated reasons ("the product is too complex for anyone else," "it's boring so I can't retain developers") are good-sounding excuses, not the real reasons. The "only I can understand it" framing is itself the self-importance problem.

chunks.heading: Why founders fire too late, and how to act
chunks.text:
- Jason asks a room who has fired someone too late (most hands) versus too soon (about 1 in 100). He calls this a predictable, universal failure of judgment.
- The excuses founders give:
  - "The team can't cope until I have a replacement."
  - "I'm a bad manager and haven't set expectations, so it's my fault."
  - He counters that if you are a bad manager, the other seven people on the team are thriving anyway, and the company has to operate now. Someone not fitting here does not make them a bad person.
- The real reason is simple: it is scary. He lists real risks (they cry, you cry, other employees react, someone turns violent, a former employee becomes depressed afterward). He says some of these have happened to him, including needing a restraining order and a death after a firing. He still says to do it.
- How to do it: act quickly, because delay hurts the team, the person and you. His CEO Heather Bruner's phrase: "General Patton on the decision, Mother Teresa on the exit." Be decisive, then be kind.

chunks.heading: A 2x2 for spotting avoided work: the 2am test
chunks.text:
- Two axes: things you want vs. don't want to do, and things the business needs vs. doesn't need done. Founders drift into doing what they want that the business doesn't need, because no boss stops them.
- The task you should be doing but are avoiding is in the "needs doing, don't want to do" quadrant (for example sales work or dealing with a difficult person).
- His diagnostic: if you can't stop thinking about it when you wake at 2am, you are probably delaying something that needs to happen.
- His logic: when one choice is easy and one is hard, you only get stuck if the hard one is the better one. If the easy one were clearly right, there would be no dilemma.

chunks.heading: Build an organization that doesn't depend on you
chunks.text:
- If "quitting would kill the company," Jason says the founder has built a brittle organization, either by not hiring people who can run functions or by not letting them.
- He rejects the "hire A players" slogan as incomplete. A founder who is an A player in one area (say, engineering) hires A players there. For everything else (AdWords, sales, marketing), founders try to learn it themselves over a few months so they can hire and manage well. Jason says that makes you a C player at best, and you end up with an organization where most functions are weak.
- His alternative is the editor model. He points to Steve Jobs as someone who hired the best designers and operations leader (Tim Cook) and held them to a very high standard, acting as editor rather than maker.
- The goal is that everyone in the organization is better than you in their area, so the company feels like it is boosting you rather than leaning entirely on you.

chunks.heading: How to hire and manage people who know more than you
chunks.text:
- In interviews, look for someone who enlightens you: you learn a lot just by talking to them and think "even if we don't hire this person, we should do half of what they said." He also repeats Zuckerberg's idea: hire someone you'd work for if circumstances were a little different.
- Hire for results orientation, not action orientation. His event planner example:
  - Action-oriented answer: curtains, up-lights, a deal on the shrimp, "people seemed to really like it."
  - Results-oriented answer: the goal was 150 attendees; 200 registered and 168 came; leads came out of it, two have already closed; they plan three more events in other countries.
- Why it matters: by definition you can't tell them how to do their job, so you manage the results and hold them to the bar. People who like being measured by results are comfortable with that.
- He says this is the right way to manage everyone, including people in your own specialty. If the architect does all the inventing and everyone else does scut work, you have taken away the only fun part of the job.

chunks.heading: Selling, staying and stepping aside as CEO
chunks.text:
- Jason argues "never sell" is not a rule. He founded SmartBear and sold it to Insight Partners in 2007. It was later sold again for $450 million (the talk says "Frisco Partners," likely a transcription error). He jokes that his regret about selling is real, but says the company was not on that trajectory under him and he was burnt out.
- When Insight made an offer, his wife told him he had to sell because he was unhappy, which he hadn't recognized. He then spent a year as a stay-at-home dad (2009), "wouldn't give that back for anything," and founded WP Engine in 2010.
- Counterexample for staying: other bootstrapped, profitable companies in his space did worse over a 15-year span, so neither "always sell" nor "never sell" holds in hindsight.
- WP Engine now has over $100M annual revenue, a $250M investment from Silver Lake, and by his account is worth more than SmartBear.
- Startups always change. The CEO's job is different at 100 and at 500 people (WP Engine was around 500 at the time). You may be unhappy, give up the CEO seat, or get bored after ten years, so you have to build change in.
- Heather Bruner joined WP Engine four years after founding and became CEO. Jason says much of today's success is due to her building the executive team and strategy, and that would not have happened with him as CEO. They won EY Entrepreneur of the Year together. Both she and he got credit; the executive team is majority female and half of engineering management is women.
- The emotional unlock, from a board member in an Austin bar: "You want the credit... you'll always get the credit." Jason says founders don't have to hold the CEO title for ego reasons.
- He knew at about 80 employees that he was not a good CEO, moved to CTO (product and engineering), stopped managing once engineering hit about 100 people, then ran product with zero direct reports.

chunks.heading: A career-fit framework: like, good at, and what the company needs
chunks.text:
- Start with the Venn diagram of what you like and what you're good at. The overlap is where you are happy and effective. Liking but not good at it is learning; good at it but not liking it is toil.
- Then add a third circle: what the company needs. Jason says each mismatch is a failure mode.
  - Flow trap: you like it and are good at it, but the company doesn't need it (for example, an engineer shipping a feature three customers want when the company needs to double sales).
  - Wrong focus: you like it, the company needs it, but you aren't good at it. Startups are constrained by time more than money, so it has to be done well.
  - Burnout: you're good at it and the company needs it, but you don't like it. Jason criticizes "servant leadership" as a way founders take on scut work and burn out. Find someone who is good at it and likes it.
- The target is the center of all three circles. He admits it's an idealization and you can't live there always, but the more you do, the better.
- He encourages everyone at WP Engine to use this framework in career talks, and says if someone's overlap no longer exists at the company, that is an acceptable conversation to have. He frames fulfilled employees as more important than ARR.
- His closing quote is from the Tao Te Ching (the best leaders are barely known; "we did it ourselves"). His summary advice: hire the right people and let them do it themselves, be a shepherd not an emperor, be an editor not a tyrant, do the hard things, and set your ego aside.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jason Cohen explains how the playbook changes after product-market fit: stop experimenting broadly, concentrate scaled headcount on a few strategic initiatives, set a quarterly one-page plan, and shape the org chart around that focus. He also covers hiring managers and executives better than you, and why he became CTO and hired a CEO.

chunks.heading: Why post-product-market-fit is a different game
chunks.text:
- Jason (WP Engine founder, "the Smart Bear") says WP Engine hit $1M ARR in its first 18 months, then went from $1M to $5M in one year in 2012. It reached $100M in a little less than 7 years.
- He argues the company changes more than founders expect. Before product-market fit you explore: who is the customer, what is the unique thing, which channel. Experimentation and pivoting fast are right then.
- After fit, "just keep experimenting" is not how you scale something that works. The work becomes hiring and managing humans, defending customers and growth you can lose, and fixing the "kind of crappy product" you rightly built first.
- Rare problems become common. A bug hitting 1% of customers is zero or one people early on. At scale it means 30 support tickets and 30 negative tweets in a day, so you need processes to detect and handle rare things.
- Predictability becomes required. If hiring and ramping support takes 6-9 months, you must know how many people you need 6-9 months out.
- "What got you here won't get you there." He stresses the emotional cost: founders were proud of being scrappy experimenters who beat stupid big companies, and now have to change that identity. He thinks this is underestimated.

chunks.heading: Don't dilute scale across many initiatives
chunks.text:
- Having 30 people versus a competitor's 3 does not make you 10x faster. Extra people mostly add extra things to do: a YouTube channel, micro projects, moving up-market to enterprise.
- Jason argues against that. Splitting everyone across initiatives means each one lacks the people and money to be good, so you waste the scale advantage.
- His example: two people on YouTube against a startup's two people on YouTube means you are no better. Put 10 people and heavy investment on it and you might dominate YouTube in your area.
- His rule: keep only a few things and point all of the company's scale at them.

chunks.heading: Quarterly process for picking the few priorities
chunks.text:
Jason runs this at WP Engine with teams and groups of teams, once a quarter:

1. **Ideal moves.** "If we weren't encumbered by problems, challenges, constraints, how would we advance our strategy right now?" Examples: a feature customers keep asking for that competitors lack, opening a new sales channel. Brainstorm broadly and bring as many people into the room as possible, so they buy into the answer.
2. **Obstacles.** Ask what stops you. It could be churn of 5% per month (customers fleeing, which matters more than a new geography), or losing a key person. Pick the top couple of obstacles.
3. **Plan.** Either attack each obstacle or work around it. Example: not enough money can be attacked with debt or customer financing (annual prepay), or worked around by treating it as an "enabling constraint" and making progress without money.

- The output is a Google Doc of bullets, about one page. Linking to Jira epics is optional.
- The first run is messy (some use Miro to brainstorm and cluster). His corporate data team's first pass took about 3 weeks. A later one took 2 days because most of it matched the prior quarter.
- Why quarterly: about every 100 days this falls out of people's heads, like the social fabric of a distributed team weakening. More often than that is too much overhead.
- It also gives a ready answer when someone claims a top-priority request: "Here's our priorities. Is it really?"

chunks.heading: Reflect the focus in the org chart
chunks.text:
- If the whole company works on a few things, projects cross teams, which causes meetings, turf fights (marketing wants the product redesigned to match the site, engineers want to refactor) and escalation to the CEO. He says this is inefficient and bad for morale.
- Two options:
  - **Matrixed.** One person runs the project across teams and sets priorities and metrics, while direct managers (and the CEO) don't direct that work. Better for careers, since a designer sits with designers and has a manager who makes them a better designer. The cost is org chart complexity.
  - **Initiative-based.** A place in the org chart is the initiative, and everyone under it is who you need to get it done. Simpler, but worse for the designer case.
- "There's no free lunch." Pick the one that fits your culture and whose downsides you can live with, but the org chart has to reflect the focus.

chunks.heading: Hiring managers is not hiring your best individual contributor
chunks.text:
- Early on you have a "hero developer" doing 100 tickets a day. If they leave or have a baby, that work grinds to a halt. At scale anything important must be a team, so you need managers.
- Engineers (and founders new to this) assume a good engineering manager is the best coder. Jason says that's wrong. A manager must speak the language but their job is to build the team, handle conflicts, set priorities and work with other teams. Engineers rarely interview their manager on any of this.
- He calls building people a different skill from building products.

chunks.heading: How to hire executives who are better than you
chunks.text:
- Jason's premise: at C-level every hire must be better than you or the company doesn't progress, and fast scaling outpaces anyone's growth. The puzzle is "how do I hire a pancreatic surgeon" when you aren't one.
- **Giddy test.** After the call you should be excited, with notes on things to go do whether or not you hire them. Their ideas may not be perfect, but your excitement signals culture, skill and process fit.
- **Up-level test.** Ask whether they will up-level peers, not just their own team. He says that is part of an executive's job description, not a manager's. Example: someone in support who is strong on metrics could help everyone.
- **Reference calls, reframed.** Asking "how are they?" gets "great" and tells you nothing. Instead ask: "What is the perfect scenario where this person is an absolute superstar?" Then ask the negative: construct a scenario where you'd crush their spirit. Some people say "tell me exactly what to do and I will crush it", others will leave if told what to do. Neither is wrong, they are different modes. The references don't know your company, so the answers are unbiased. Then map those modes to your culture and the specific slot.
- **Someone who has done it before.** He says there's a big difference between zero people who have done it and one. At WP Engine it was the CEO. He became CTO and hired Heather Brunner as CEO, "the second best decision I've ever made" (after marrying his wife, married 20+ years). He has seen it be a COO or CFO elsewhere, often forming a trinity with the founder CEO and the product or engineering co-founder.

chunks.heading: Deciding to hire a CEO as a founder
chunks.text:
- Jason framed it with an ikigai- and Dan Pink-style test (mastery, autonomy, purpose): you are in a good place when you do work you love, are good at, and the company needs.
- At about 70-80 people and growing fast, the company needed a global sales team, more fundraising, a more serious board, and a plan to keep culture at scale. These were things he was either unskilled at, didn't like, or both. Lacking skill but liking it is a growth path, but not liking it means doing a poor job.
- That intellectual conclusion took about 3 months. What got him over the line emotionally was a founder-investor at a wine bar who said he was thinking he'd one day ring the NASDAQ bell and want the credit. Jason agreed it was ego. The reply: "You're the founder. You'll always get the credit."
- His title today is Chief Innovation Officer. He says he has an article on hiring a CEO at smartbear.com.

chunks.heading: Measuring your own growth as a leader
chunks.text:
- Jason recommends a 360 review: anonymous feedback from reports and peers, processed by someone who knows what they're doing so you can't tell who said what.
- He is unsure about AI summarizing it. Summaries drop the detail, and "you need to listen more" only lands when you hear the specifics of what you did to someone.
- It also surfaced strengths. People consistently said he gets them excited about the company's vision, which he hadn't considered. So a 360 shows what to lean into as well as what to fix.
- He also notes he knows some of his weaknesses and tries to stay out of those positions or not stay in them long.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jason Cohen explains how repositioning a product around more of a positive outcome (not less of a negative) can multiply price up to 10x. He covers deciding under uncertainty, why frameworks rarely transplant into a company's culture, and which jobs and products AI will and won't automate.

chunks.heading: Reposition from "less of a negative" to "more of a positive" to charge up to 10x
chunks.text:
- Jason argues almost every product sold to a pain point can be repositioned so it sells more value or transformation (something positive the customer already values) instead of removing a negative like time or cost.
- Most tools pitch "saves time, saves money, saves cost". He says that is easy to fall into, and repositioning often lets you "charge 10 times as much".
- Worked example (from his book Hidden Multipliers): a tool cuts AdWords cost per lead in half.
  - Pitched as savings: a marketer spending $40K a month saves $20K, so they might pay around $5K a month and keep most of the savings.
  - Pitched as growth: at the same cost per lead, the same $40K now buys double the leads, or they spend $80K for double the leads and double the revenue. The CEO hears "doubled leads", not "saved $15K".
  - The same product could then be priced around $40K a month instead of $5K.
- Principle: customers already spend heavily on what they value (more leads, more revenue), and they will spend even more if they get more of it. Pitch the product as creating more of that.
- The book gives about 15 other quick examples in different shapes and sizes, including consulting companies.

chunks.heading: Handling AI uncertainty: anchor on what stays true and the customer's core value
chunks.text:
- Jason says the future is especially uncertain, and past experience, pro/con lists, rubrics, and statistics and probability are not useful tools for it. You need different tools for making decisions under uncertainty.
- Two failure modes: doing nothing, or spreading thin across many things when you can't tell which one matters most.
- Tactic: use Bezos's question of "what will still be true in 10 years". People will always want to save money and time, get more leads, close more revenue, be entertained, get things faster, get good service, and (for a billion people) get the cheapest option.
