- Treat AI as part of the solution space (how you execute the product), not the problem space (what the customer is trying to do).
- Ask "how do I use AI to get more leads?" not "how do I put AI on the page?". Putting "powered by AI" on the homepage is just a box to check so you get seen.
- If you double a marketer's hot leads and revenue rises, they will pay a lot "no matter how you achieve that. Could be gremlins in a box."
- If you can't articulate the core transformation you deliver, adding AI won't fix it. Don't be surprised when nobody cares, because you're either not delivering value or you're identical to everyone else.

chunks.heading: Where AI replaces work and where it doesn't
chunks.text:
- Jason's rule of thumb: "Any job where there is such a thing as a best version of that job will get automated." Where there's no such thing as a best, AI changes how the work is done but doesn't replace it.
- Example of a "best": a Honda plant machine that bolts wheels on and records the exact torque on each bolt. The best is perfect, measured tension, and a robot beats a human on speed, accuracy and repeatability. Once you reach the best, only cost is left.
- No "best" exists for design, software, writing, ideas, entertainment, strategy, or deciding to make Linear instead of Jira. He says he doesn't know if this is a law, but it's a guide for what to invest in and how to avoid having your legs cut out from under you.
- Chess analogy: computers have been better than humans for 25 years, yet chess is more popular than ever. Nobody watches computers play, and people watch human creators. Computers did change how humans play (for example, how pawns and pieces are valued).
- He expects human personalities to keep winning for ads, videos and podcasts. In his view, companies that don't fire all their marketers will have better marketing and content, and the best company videos and ads he sees are always people.
- Systems of record and precision tools (finance and tax systems, customer service desks, sales, GitHub, CI/CD, deploy) are not being replaced by LLMs, which are "amazing and not precise". He says AI needs GitHub and CI/CD more than ever.
- AI supercharges senior developers but not juniors, who produce demo-ware that can't become a real product. Vibe-coded output is impressive when there's nothing there yet, but AI gets worse as a codebase grows. He sees "not hiring because of AI" as largely an excuse.
- He says model leadership is unpredictable (for example, OpenAI is no longer the leader, which nobody predicted), so he declines to forecast 18 months out.

chunks.heading: Why he writes and how he works: quality over schedule
chunks.text:
- Jason has written for about 20 years, and his only motivation is doing work he's proud of. He doesn't sell courses or consulting, has no sponsors and no ads, so he can wait until something is good enough. He says he has hundreds of drafts he never published.
- He writes strategic concepts and patterns, evergreen, not news, tips, tactics, workshops or checklists. Goal: understand patterns deeply enough that readers can make good decisions themselves.
- His frameworks come from iterating them inside his company WP Engine. If an idea didn't work, he didn't write it up. If it half-worked, the teams morphed it and retried, and he re-explained it many times. He compares this to the reps that give you a tight pitch after a conference.
- He wrote Hidden Multipliers so it can't be summarized as one idea repeated ten times, and he edited it for reading aloud. He recorded the audiobook himself.
- He built free, open AI skills to go with the book (at hidden multipliers.com). They never tell you what to do. They facilitate and grill you using his ideas and don't let you off the hook for wishy-washy answers. Examples: building customer interview questions, finding your ICP, and finding a strategy that leans into your strengths and sidesteps your weaknesses.
- Distribution of the book: sold on his own site as a bundle (book, audiobook, e-pub, with a higher-quality print), and also on Amazon, Audible and Kindle.

chunks.heading: Adopting a framework in a team: why it usually fails and how to make it stick
chunks.text:
- Jason says most frameworks fail when one excited person tries to bring them into a company, because the culture and mechanisms reject them "like the body rejects the organ". He doesn't know how to predict fit. His own blog frameworks work for him but probably not for most people, and there may be 20 good frameworks for something like feature prioritization, of which a couple fit you.
- If other people aren't already interested in the specific thing, it almost never works: "It's a self-fulfilling prophecy if you didn't want it to work."
- Tactics:
  - Share the article or video with the team and ask whether it might work before starting.
  - Try a subset of it.
  - Frame it as "better than what we do now, but probably only 70% right". Agree to review every two weeks what's still wrong and change it.
- His experience: he tried OKRs about four times at WP Engine and they never worked. The version that eventually stuck doesn't resemble OKRs but keeps the spirit and ownership.
- Use the Crucial Conversations idea of finding "common truth" first. If you don't agree on the facts, goals and assumptions, nothing else works, and getting there is often 70% of the conversation. For example, a team resisting OKRs may really not want accountability at all, so the framework isn't the issue.
- Getting a metrics-averse team comfortable with metrics (from his KPI framework):
  - Admit that many important things aren't numbers, but some are, so why be blind to those?
  - Have each person pick one metric they actually believe in and would want to know for themselves.
  - Keep it private (for example, a Google spreadsheet visible only to them) so nobody can be held accountable to it. Do it for one quarter.
  - Later, show a few metrics alongside an equally prominent column of important non-metric items on the same slide.
- On metrics generally: everyone wants to know how they're doing, but metrics can be gamed and can mislead. Example: a support rep closing 27 tickets a day with great ratings versus one closing 2 a day with mixed ratings who gets the hardest problems and may be the best on the team. Metrics are an ingredient and don't replace good management.

chunks.heading: Strategy: aim for "special" fit, not "unique"
chunks.text:
- Jason thinks "unique advantage" and USPs are overplayed. Gmail isn't unique, and Yahoo Mail has plenty of customers. Many successful companies have no USP, and someone can often copy a unique thing anyway.
- He prefers being "special": your strengths, capabilities and assets built up over time make a strategy, product or market natural and easier for you, so you do it better than others or they'd have to spend 10x as much.
- Pair that with a subset of the market whose wants, dislikes and indifferences match what you offer. That is not most of the market, but "that puzzle piece, that's where you win."
- You'll still do things outside your wheelhouse and get non-ideal customers, but be clear on the fit. He says this is very hard and that the book and the skills show how.

chunks.heading: Giving blunt help to founders
chunks.text:
- Jason's style is direct and honest, aiming to get to the crux fast while having the founder's best interest at heart. Most of the time goes to solving the problem.
- Founders may feel bad in the moment but often email a week or two later to say "you're the only one who told me the truth".
- He has done this since around 2009 as a founding mentor and investor in the Capital Factory incubator in Austin. He later turned it into the show Smart Bear Live, which he describes as half startup advice, half therapy.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jason Cohen explains why every SaaS hits a growth ceiling: paid acquisition flattens (the "elephant curve") while cancellations scale with customer count. He shows how to compute the ceiling, diagnose churn, raise prices to move into a better market, and build strategy around an ideal customer who loves your weaknesses.

chunks.heading: Why every SaaS hits a growth ceiling: cancellation always beats paid marketing
chunks.text:
- Jason argues that cancellation beats marketing because the two scale differently. Paid marketing (AdWords, Facebook ads) adds a fixed number of customers per month regardless of how many customers you have. Cancellation is a percentage of the base, so it grows as you grow.
- Worked example: 1,000 customers, marketing adds 100 a month, 5% monthly cancellation. At 1,000 customers, 50 leave. At 3,000 customers, 150 leave, so the company shrinks even though nothing else changed.
- Many founders think 5% monthly cancellation is good. Jason says "You're wrong." At that rate, growth stalls once cancellations equal new customers.
- He uses real Kit (formerly ConvertKit) data: new customer adds were holding up, but at a 5% cancel rate the math shows top-line growth plateauing around $3 million MRR at roughly $150K of new MRR per month.
- Buffer shows the same plateau. Its cancellation rate was about 5% and essentially never changed, and its growth flattened. Kit kept growing because it continually pushed its cancellation rate down.

chunks.heading: The "elephant curve" and the growth ceiling formula
chunks.text:
- Jason calls the typical shape of a marketing channel the "elephant curve". It rises quickly once you figure the channel out, then flattens and often sags.
- Reasons channels sag:
  - The people who will see the ad have already seen it.
  - Competitors bid up ad costs until it is no longer cost-effective.
  - The audience moves to other platforms.
- Stacking several channels does not escape the curve, because each channel follows the same shape and channels run out. He cites a content affiliate campaign at WP Engine from 10 years earlier and his own content marketing as real examples.
- He says to search "elephant curve" for about 20 real-world examples and a longer analysis.
- Growth ceiling (maximum MRR) formula: new MRR per month divided by monthly cancellation rate. That is the most you will reach if you change nothing.
- Examples: $150K of new MRR a month at 5% cancellation gives $3 million.
- He recommends computing this number and tracking it every month. "We'll never get more than 2,500 customers unless we do something differently" is more motivating than a vague goal like moving from 5% to 4.5% cancellation. It "lights a fire under your ass".
- Cancellation is also personal to him. A customer has gone through a gauntlet to sign up: roughly 1% get through the website and about another 1% pay, so around 1 in 10,000. If they still cancel, "I failed them."

chunks.heading: How to find out why customers cancel
chunks.text:
- Cancellation surveys with a "Why did you cancel?" form fill in randomly. Jason says he has tested this, because leavers are not spending time on you. "Too expensive" is a common answer and is picked at random.
- "Too expensive" is never the real reason, because the customer saw the price and bought anyway. The real reason is something specific: a feature that did not do what they thought, a missing integration.
- Do not lower prices because "too expensive" shows up in 30% of responses. Lowering the price would not have saved that customer. Fix the thing they actually wanted.
- Groove's email example, A/B tested until it worked:
  - Informal, not capitalized, short, from a named person (Adam), no images and no template.
  - Usable response rate of 10%, meaning feedback they could use to improve the product.
  - Changing "Why did you cancel?" to "What made you cancel?" doubled the usable response rate.
  - Jason's theory: "Why did you cancel?" puts the problem on the customer, while "What made you cancel?" admits you failed them, which makes it easier to answer. He says to test it yourself.
- Catch people before they leave, because once they cancel they do not want to talk to you.
  - Compare behavior a week, a month and 3 months before cancellation against customers who stayed.
  - What matters is behavior that differs between cancelers and stayers. Many customers contact support whether or not they are in trouble, so support contact alone may not be an early signal.
  - Reach out to at-risk customers while they are stuck. You may save some, and even if not, you learn why.

chunks.heading: Fix onboarding first
chunks.text:
- If you do not know where to focus on cancellation, Jason says onboarding almost always has the most impact.
- He shows a retention curve from his own video (the "profit whale curve") where about half the viewers leave in the first 30 seconds. Cohorts in a SaaS company often look the same, with many customers leaving in the first 3 months, week or day.
- Improving the early drop-off can double the number who stay to the end. Customers who survive the start and stay long create a long lifetime value, so a few more long-term customers has a large financial effect.
- Trying to save customers late in the curve makes little difference.

chunks.heading: Ways to keep up with cancellations: proportional growth and upgrades
chunks.text:
- Jason separates two kinds of marketing:
  - Paid channels: fixed output regardless of customer count, so cancellation overruns them.
  - Marketing proportional to your size: reviews, referrals, referral programs. With 10 times the customers you can get about 10 times the reviews or referrals, so this can keep pace with cancellations.
- Early on, with few customers, proportional channels do nothing because no one is there to promote you. Start with the paid or direct channels, then add proportional channels once you have customers and product-market fit.
- Upgrades (expansion revenue) can also offset cancellations, but with caveats:
  - They work when the cohort is still large and the cancel rate is low.
  - If the cancel rate is high, too few customers remain to upgrade enough.
  - "Flogging the people that remain" is not the solution when people are leaving in droves. Fix why they leave first.

chunks.heading: Pricing: you guessed low, so raise prices
chunks.text:
- Jason borrows the phrase from Pat Walls that you guessed too low. His line: "There's no way your prices are optimal. Full stop," and they are probably too low.
- Standard economics (the law of demand) says higher prices mean fewer sign-ups. Too cheap means lots of customers but little money, with costs per customer (marketing, support) still there. Too expensive means barely any customers. You want the middle where revenue (the rectangle) is largest. Founders fear they are in the middle and will fall off to the right, but they are probably on the left.
- In practice, sign-ups often increase when bootstrapped companies raise prices. His explanation, using Tibo Maker's account of Tweet Hunter (launched at $9 a month, bootstrapped, sold for $8 million):
  - Tweet Hunter raised prices repeatedly and expected people to leave, but "revenue exploded each time."
  - $9 a month attracts casual users and hobbyists who quit and optimize for cost. $50 a month attracts business owners who need results and do not quibble over $20 to $50.
  - Businesses may also assume a $9 product "can't be good" and will not consider it.
- Jason's view: raising prices does not just move you along one demand curve. It changes the market you are in, to a healthier one. Hobbyists really will leave, but they are poor customers with no money and little commitment.
- He cautions that you do not want to price into the enterprise zone by accident. Pricing selects the market.

chunks.heading: Strategy and the ideal customer profile: Craigslist and Buffer
chunks.text:
- Craigslist is, in his words, "hideously minimal" and has barely changed in 25 years. Niche competitors (he shows several, each worth billions) beat it in categories. Yet in 2024 Craigslist made about half a billion dollars in revenue with 50 people, roughly five times more profitable per person than Google or Facebook. He says only OnlyFans is more profitable per employee that he knows of.
- His explanation: its weaknesses enable strengths that competitors will not copy.
  - Looks like newspaper classifieds, so non-technical users can use it.
  - Never changing is a plus for people who hate tech and change.
  - Huge selection, and very low cost: simple CRUD, cheap servers, few engineers.
  - Works on old phones and slow connections.
- He calls these strategic choices: a choice that closes a door but enables something others cannot compete on, because competitors will copy your strengths but not your weaknesses. For the right person, your weaknesses are not even weaknesses.
- Definition of the ideal customer profile (ICP): "the person that loves you for you, loves all of you." They see your weaknesses as irrelevant or as strengths. Build everything for them: product features, copy, positioning, advertising, community, events. Most customers will be in the wider target market who accept the trade-offs, and you win them by being opinionated and special for the ICP.
- Strategy, as he puts it: self-reinforcing choices that include weaknesses, producing something special (not necessarily unique) that an ICP loves.
- Buffer example, which contradicts his own pricing advice:
  - CEO Joel Gascoigne wrote an open strategy letter saying they had forgotten who their best customer was and tried to be everything to everybody.
  - The best customer is the prosumer, the roughly 100 million people not very good at social media who want to get on board.
  - Buffer refocused on them and lowered prices, with lower introductory prices and a free trial, because that is what that customer needs.
  - Jason's takeaway: knowing and staying true to your ICP wins over the generic "raise prices" advice. Raising prices is more likely right if you know nothing else about the business, but ICP knowledge overrides it.
- Niching down is one way to focus on the ICP, but not the only way and not the primary idea. Craigslist did not niche down and Buffer did not either.

chunks.heading: What "grow or die" means
chunks.text:
- Jason agrees "if you're not growing, you're dying" is true in a broader sense. People at shrinking companies report poor morale, trouble keeping talent and unhappy founders.
- He suggests defining growth as "constructive evolution" rather than only number go up. Example: Sarah Savage plans never to exceed 1,000 customers to keep a special relationship with each, but is constantly innovating on infrastructure and automation to stay lean.
- Plain growth can mean profit, not only revenue. If you the human are not growing or evolving, feeling stuck or burnt out, marketing tactics will not fix that.
- He mentions his book "Hidden Multipliers" (pre-order at hiddenmultipliers.com), about ways to jump-start growth with an existing budget and team.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jason Cohen argues that proactive honesty (admitting weaknesses, being small, showing negatives) is a competitive differentiator that raises sales, cuts returns and churn, and builds believability. He backs it with Canon review data, his hosting outage cancellation data, Balsamiq's one-person About page, and enterprise sales stories.

chunks.heading: Honesty as a competitive differentiator
chunks.text:
Jason argues that lying in marketing, sales and social media is so common that being brutally honest makes a business stand out. He treats this purely as a way to make more money, not as ethics.

- Most websites sound like "the People's Republic of North Korea": claims that fool no one, so visitors stop believing anything. Examples he gives are "the leading provider" language and Smuckers' "100% fruit spread" jar that is only 30% strawberries.
- People say they want honesty (the standard "be authentic" social media advice) but rarely do it. A sentiment check on Gary Vaynerchuk's and his own Twitter followers found almost no real negativity.
- Jason says James Altucher told him that after he decided in November 2010 to tell only the truth on his blog, readership went from about 10,000 to 100,000 people a day within a couple of months. Jason notes that honesty alone does not make you a celebrity.
- The key is being proactively honest, not just answering truthfully when asked. Volunteering the bad news earns believability for everything else you say.

chunks.heading: Showing the bad with the good: the Canon reviews experiment
chunks.text:
Jason cites a field experiment by Bazaarvoice, a company in Austin. Canon added customer reviews to its camera pages, and Bazaarvoice says it saw the same pattern across about 500 companies over roughly seven years.

- Highly rated cameras roughly doubled their sales.
- Low-rated cameras gained almost as much, which surprised Canon.
- Profit rose more for the low-rated products than for the high-rated ones, because returns fell about 20%.
- Why it works: buyers of cheaper products expect flaws, and knowing exactly what the flaw is lets them decide to buy without shopping around. Jason's example is his daughter's toy spaceship. A relative bought it after reading reviews that said the door pops open but everything else is good, and it was the best option under $40.
- Returns are very costly. On a $100 camera, Canon's profit is about $10, so one return wipes out the profit on roughly ten more sales. Software returns also cost support time, bad Twitter comments and a wasted bad-fit customer.
- Jason's summary: if you say both the good and the bad, you sell more and profit more.

chunks.heading: Rethinking the competitor comparison chart
chunks.text:
Jason calls the usual feature-comparison chart (your column all green checkmarks, competitors' columns mostly crosses) a lie by omission. Buyers know the competitor has features you left off.

- Skip the chart. Instead state the two or three things you uniquely do better and say "we're the best at the following three things". This promotes you without attacking anyone or naming competitors.
- Also say who you are bad for. For his WordPress hosting company, he tells small-traffic bloggers to use wordpress.com or shared hosting because they would overspend with him, and tells huge sites like CNN to use a different, larger provider. Telling people "we're no good for you, go over there" makes the people who do fit trust you more.
- Rewrite the About page the same way. Contrast Web Methods' buzzword-filled blurb with Balsamiq's early page, where Peldi wrote that he was one dude and that supporting a whole software company alone "sounds iffy" and "remains to be seen". Jason says Balsamiq's first-year revenue was about a million dollars. He is clear that honesty does not guarantee that, only that it does not stop sales.

chunks.heading: Cancellation data: owning outages
chunks.text:
Jason shares a trailing 30-day chart of his hosting company's cancellations within the first 30 days of signup. The normal rate was about 6-8%.

- After a one-hour full outage that the company did not announce, the early cancellation rate jumped to around 20%.
- After a 12-hour outage handled differently, there was no visible increase at all. The team tweeted and posted on its status blog immediately and kept updating as the problem developed.
- Both outages were data-center-wide and not the company's fault. Jason says that does not matter, because customers' sites were still down.
- His conclusion: proactively talking about every problem neutralized essentially all of the damage.

chunks.heading: Don't copy the page, copy the principle: TOMS vs. Skechers Bobs
chunks.text:
Jason warns that copying a tactic that worked for an honest company does not work if you are not the same kind of company.

- TOMS gives a pair of shoes to a child for every pair bought. Skechers launched "Bobs" with the identical one-for-one model in 2010 and pulled it within 24 hours after a backlash. The campaigns were identical except that TOMS was honest and Skechers copied it as a marketing trick.
- Copy the idea behind Balsamiq's page: be forthright about who you are and what you value.
- Jason's hosting site lists the whole team and says "when you host with us, you're betting on us personally". He argues that in a commoditized market, where servers and RAM look the same, the people are the differentiator.
- He also publishes his company's values on the careers page: how far the company goes for customers and where it stops, including when it decides a customer is abusive. He says a company will have a culture either way, so you should decide it, hire to it and act on it. Customers have told him they are impressed that he said it.
- Presentation is still fine. His analogy is picking your best true profile photo. OkCupid data suggested that angled, from-above "MySpace" style photos got the most messages for women, while for men an animal or muscles beat travel photos. Selecting the best true thing is not lying.

chunks.heading: Turning small-company weaknesses into advantages (sales scripts)
chunks.text:
Jason's approach is to admit the limitation first, which earns credibility, and then pivot to the specific advantage only a small company can offer. The examples below come from his own sales conversations.

- **No 24/7 support:** "You can go to a competitor and get 24/7 support." Rackspace will answer at 2am Sunday, but that person is not a WordPress expert. Jason says his team are true experts who can solve deep problems and are unlikely to be awake at 2am. He says he never lost a customer on the 24/7 point using this argument.
- **"You'd be our biggest customer":** agree and say it could cause problems because the company has not done this before. Then add that the customer will be so important that everyone will work on it day and night, because the company cannot grow unless customers like them succeed, and a company where they are the hundredth-biggest customer won't care the same way. Offer to connect them with the current biggest customer to ask how it has gone. Jason says he never lost a biggest-customer deal with this approach, and that he has told prospects they should go with someone else, which makes them keep talking.
- **Enterprise sales without suits:** at SmartBear he sold five-figure deals when it was just him and six-figure deals with a handful of employees and no salespeople. He opened demos by saying he didn't have the expected 44 PowerPoint slides about the mission statement, only a demo. He told prospects to include his tech support in their trial, and one buyer pulled out his wallet and bought on the spot because that honesty implied the support would be good.
- **Lean on small-company advantages:**
  - Take on risk that incumbents can't, such as doing a special project that you might not get paid for if it fails.
  - Move faster and structure unusual deals, like lower rates in exchange for paying upfront or later payment.
  - Have no legacy customers or code to protect.
  - Be fully committed. Jason's line to customers was that if it didn't work "we all have to go back to working at Sonic", and people laughed and wanted him to succeed.

chunks.heading: Why people lie about size, and why it doesn't pay
chunks.text:
Jason says that when he said "three" employees when it was just him, there were two motives: continuing a lie already implied on the website, and fear of losing the deal.

- The upside is tiny. A Lockheed Martin team of a dozen people won't treat three employees differently from one, so you can't stretch the lie far enough to matter. The downside is huge, because you lose all your credibility if it is discovered.
- He cites a book by two New York women who interviewed hundreds of women entrepreneurs. They said small white lies about the business consistently backfired and left them feeling bad about the work that was supposed to be fulfilling.
- He sold SmartBear to AutomatedQA in about four months. The buyer asked how much he wanted in the bank, and they simply worked backwards from that number instead of the usual haggling. He says 17 advisers reviewed it and all but one called the deal generous. He gives this as another case where honesty worked, not as a template.
- He points to Howard Stern, who says his secret is simply being honest. Jason's view is that shock jocks who copied only the shock never matched his popularity.
- His closing view: honesty is hard to do in every sales call, page and phone answer, so almost nobody goes all the way. That is why doing it is a large competitive advantage.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jason Cohen explains why there is no single blueprint after building SmartBear (bootstrapped) and WP Engine (VC-backed). He covers raising only what ARR justifies, how to think about AI as a founder, why customer outcomes should drive strategy, and how to make big life decisions by widening options.

chunks.heading: Choosing between bootstrapping and venture funding at WP Engine
chunks.text:
- Jason bootstrapped SmartBear, sold it in 2007, and by his account it only became a unicorn about 10 years later. He says the two companies were built very differently, so "there is not a blueprint."
- WP Engine was his fourth company. About 2 years in he saw it "could actually be really big": a big and growing market, easy to sell, lots of people wanted it, and a great niche. He calls this "venture sized" and says most products, and most of his own companies, are not.
- Most companies are not venture backed. He notes VCs fund a few thousand companies a year, a few hundred of which survive, against a million small businesses in America alone. "Very few successful companies are funded by VCs, so let's not get carried away."
- Personal reasons mattered too. It was his fourth bootstrapped run, he was a father and older, and he wanted a different journey.
- Having already had a nice exit at SmartBear meant he wasn't forced into any particular timeline.

chunks.heading: How he raised money at WP Engine
chunks.text:
- Rounds started small. The first was $1.2M from angels and the second was $2M. The $250M from Silver Lake came later.
- He never raised more money than the company's ARR. That gave enough to act appropriately for its size, "but not so much that you sometimes drown in that."
- He never raised at a crazy valuation. A low valuation dilutes you for nothing. A valuation too high means you have to grow into it, and the next round might be hard.
- Fast growth helped, but he says that if they had raised at too high a valuation it might still have been hard to raise again.
- He sees healthy companies with decent growth struggling to raise now because "you don't have AI." Keeping your metrics together is what prevents that.

chunks.heading: Why SaaS is not dying, and why timelines matter
chunks.text:
- He has "yet to find someone" paying for a substantial SaaS product who then vibe coded a replacement and stopped using SaaS.
- His HubSpot example: over $2B in revenue, growing 30% year over year, profitable, and the stock still fell. He reads that as temporary or previously overvalued, not as HubSpot going away.
- Predictions without a timeline are meaningless. His examples: people predicting a stock market crash in 2010 (it came in 2020-21, which is "terrible investment advice"), and Elon's self-driving cars "in about 2 years" for 15 years. A prediction that doesn't help you make decisions now isn't useful.
- Customers have the same problems they always had. AI offers new and possibly better solutions to the same problems.
- Legacy non-AI products face a shrinking market. The only way to get a new customer is to steal one from another legacy product, and a switching customer is unlikely to pick another legacy one.
- Building a big company takes many years, even in AI. "Almost all of them don't" get big in a month, so "settle down."

chunks.heading: Applying AI to the same customer problems at WP Engine
chunks.text:
- Customers want to build WordPress sites, add content, get found on SEO, track visitors, be found globally, and convert visitors. Media sites want clicks for ad revenue and e-commerce sites want purchases.
- Example: shoppers who use site search on an e-commerce site are 3x more likely to buy, because they show intent. WP Engine has tens of thousands of e-commerce stores with significant revenue, so it has the data.
- They built an AI-based e-commerce search bar that is semantic and understands the product catalog. A shopper can type "I pronate my foot and I like a wide toe box" and get a relevant shoe. It makes sense for WP Engine to build it because it has access to the customer's product database and is physically there running the website.
- The best question for any company: how do you make your customers successful in the way they measure it? For e-commerce that is revenue. For a finance tool it might be "zero discoveries in the next audit."
- Even if you can't measure that outcome, state it as a vision statement. It aligns everything you control (features, sales pitch, homepage promises, weekly reports). You can also simply ask customers whether the product is helping.
- Time-in-product is a weak metric. Long time can mean the product is confusing, and short time can mean it just works.

chunks.heading: Capital allocation and three kinds of AI products
chunks.text:
- At scale (WP Engine has 1,000+ people) the CEO becomes a capital allocator. Some budget goes to big new bets, but they still need to be adjacent: "It doesn't make sense for us to try self-driving cars." The usual bet is a new product for existing customers, because distribution is harder than building.
- In AI that flips: distribution is easier than building because "AI products almost never work." Everyone tries a new AI product, then "they all cancel in 4 months."
- He splits AI products into three categories:
  - **Incumbents adding AI** (Notion, Google Sheets, SharePoint): it doesn't work very well yet, but they should keep doing it.
  - **AI for experts** (developers, designers, marketing writers): often works, because the expert knows what to do when the AI is wrong and can fix or discard its output. A startup in this zone can tolerate AI not working every time.
  - **AI for "muggles"** (non-coders building apps, non-designers making sites, non-writers writing books): not good enough. It is fun for demos, but people can't get the last bit to make it good or maintainable. "I've never heard of someone getting to that point who's not a coder. Not once ever."
- If you do bet on the muggle category, put a timeline on it. The odds of success are lower than people give it credit for.
- He doesn't write about AI because it changes every 6 to 12 months. He aims to write things that are true 50 years from now, and some of his articles are almost 20 years old.

chunks.heading: Founder psychology, customer discovery, and the evergreen topics
chunks.text:
- He considers these topics unchanged by AI:
  - Founder psychology: believing your ideas are better than everyone's while also having imposter syndrome, and deciding whether to persevere or give up after 6 months.
  - What kind of company to build, how to make a good strategy, and which markets are good.
  - Poking at your own ideas with intellectual honesty.
  - Interviewing customers before you have a product.
- "With AI you can build something no one wants, I don't care how efficient it is that you built it."
- The discovery question is what people would actually want to buy, "where the word want and buy are both doing a lot of work."
- Before WP Engine he did 40 customer interviews (he asked 50). He found many people wanted a fast, scalable, secure website and that he knew how to reach them. He wrote out his full interviewing system online and says it still works and he used it throughout WP Engine.
- He started WP Engine partly because of his love for optimization and fast, scalable engineering.

chunks.heading: Finding your CEO role and handing it off
chunks.text:
- He says he was a great CEO up to roughly 50 people. He was WP Engine's CEO for 4 years, then hired Heather Brunner, who has been CEO for 11 or 12 years. He calls it "such a good decision" and moved to CTO.
- His test for any role is the intersection of three things: what you like, what you're actually good at, and what the company needs done. He compares it to ikigai and Daniel Pink's work. He kept shifting roles over the years as that intersection changed.
- You can't know ahead of time what running a company is like (he compares it to having kids). Pro/con lists don't help because you don't know what to put on them or how to weigh it. So don't second-guess daily, but don't cling to your original plan. Check in once a year or when something happens: "Is this right? Am I up for this for another 3 months, 12 months? Does something need to change?"
- Burnout and "two options" thinking: "If you're picking between only two options in that sort of huge life-changing situation, then you haven't explored the options enough." Burned-out founders often think they must leave or sell cheaply. Other options he lists:
  - Promote someone internal to CEO and keep some of the profits.
  - Get a partner.
  - Change your own role.
  - Step out of the CEO role but stay, as he did for 12 more years.
  - Change from growth to profit.
  - Choose a smaller, lower-risk company or a larger, higher-risk one.
- Basecamp, in his example, chooses profit over headcount because the founders would hate having lots of people.
- Get someone who has seen these options to act as a mirror and expand the menu, not someone who tells you what to do.
- He burned out at SmartBear, didn't realize it, didn't consider options, and sold. He says that was the wrong decision even though WP Engine worked out after: "If you make the wrong decision and get lucky, that's still wrong. If you make the right decision and get unlucky, you still made the right decision" (the Annie Duke poker idea).
- How he stepped out of the CEO role without confusion: he was openly vulnerable about SmartBear burnout so people understood why. Then, whenever someone came to him, he asked "What did Heather say when you asked her?" and sent them back to her, every single time. Boundaries and redirects, "a 301 redirect, not a 302." CTO matters still came to him.

chunks.heading: After the exit: identity, optionality, and the book
chunks.text:
- He cites a Credit Suisse paper on about two dozen entrepreneurs who sold and no longer needed to work. All but one had symptoms like postpartum depression. He also describes MRI studies in which an entrepreneur's company logo lit up the same brain areas as a picture of their kids.
- There is no blueprint for what to do next, so you have to redefine who you are. He notes you have money and experience but less energy, so he wouldn't start a company and wrestle with AI now.
- His strategy rule: understand your strengths, weaknesses, capabilities and assets, then do a project where the strengths are used and the weaknesses either don't matter or are even strengths to your target market. His example: long-form writing is a weakness if people don't read, but a strength for readers who want depth.
- His book is *Hidden Multipliers*, on pre-order at hiddenmultipliers.com, about jump-starting growth with your current budget and team. Each of the 10 or 11 chapters covers a systematic, fairly repeatable mechanism he has experienced himself or seen others use. He doesn't claim every chapter will double revenue, but expects some to apply.
- His goals for the book: make the best book he can, and maximize the number of readers who actually get benefit. He would rather sell a couple thousand books to people who read and use it than a million where 1% read it. "One of those emails is worth like selling 10,000 books."
- His articles are free online (no ads, courses or paywall) at his site "a smart bear" .com, with an RSS feed containing every article in simplified markdown so people can load them into an AI.
- Optionality is both a blessing and a curse: it's better to have it, but you may need to impose your own limits, goals and deadlines for motivation. He frames a game as self-imposed rules and restrictions, and says with money you get to pick your games. He also suggests asking what purpose bigger than yourself you could pursue, such as philanthropy.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jason Cohen explains why small systematic changes beat big investments, how to de-risk the weakest link first, why niching down sells to more than just your niche, and how WP Engine won a commodity market. He closes with how he would pick an AI product today: solve an existing problem, serve experts, and aim for 3x+ value.

chunks.heading: Marketing and finding customers: de-risk the weakest link first
chunks.text:
Jason's core claim is that a company only works if many independent things go right at once: a real problem, reachable customers, winning against alternatives, and the founder's own stamina. Probabilities multiply, so even ten "reasonable" 70% odds give a low overall chance, and many are closer to 10%.

- Identify the weakest link and decide whether strengths elsewhere can overwhelm it or whether it is a deal breaker. The test question: "what else is true that makes this okay?" "We'll have good features" is not an answer, because everyone says it.
- Tackle the weakest link first. An engineer who is unsure they can get customers should not build the product, because that does nothing to answer whether customers can be found. He says go find customers instead, interview them, and learn what to build.
- Narrowing the niche improves several odds at once. You can be the best product as defined by a specific customer, even if the market gets smaller.
- A small market can be okay if offset by something overwhelming, for example a co-founder who already knows 70 of the 100 potential buyers and customers who pay very high prices.

chunks.heading: Niche down without refusing other customers
chunks.text:
Jason argues you should always focus on the narrowest ideal customer profile you can, but he says people misread this as "I can only sell to them."

- Being specific lets your homepage message, advertising, pricing and feature choices be compelling to the ideal customer, who sees your strengths as strengths and your supposed weaknesses as irrelevant or even good (a high price can signal quality).
- A much larger group outside the niche (he says possibly 100 times larger) still buys, because the clear trade-offs make it easy to judge. "When the trade-offs are clear people are more willing to accept the weaknesses."
- Evidence he cites: products whose negative reviews are specific about what is wrong have higher sales and fewer returns than products with the same star rating (for example 4.1 stars). Buyers already accepted the flaw.
- Expand later. WP Engine began with small and mid-size businesses, often via freelancers. Around four or five years in it saw appetite from larger companies for campaign use cases, then spent tens of millions of dollars over a couple of years on sales and marketing with a separate message for that segment.

chunks.heading: Why WP Engine won in a commodity market
chunks.text:
WordPress is open source and there were around 20 easy competitors. Jason is careful to say he can't be certain of the causes, but his best reasons:

- **Pay more, get more:** managed hosting cost about 10 times as much as shared hosting and was multiples faster. The first swag shirt read "My blog is four times faster than your shirt." Security and service were also much better.
- **A "moat" of things competitors won't do:** great human support hurts gross margin (VCs don't want it, since under 70% margin means "not a software company"). Funded competitors skipped it for cultural and incentive reasons, not because they couldn't copy it. Companies rarely change their culture, and when they try they often fail.
- **Execution in a field where few execute well:** it was his fourth bootstrap-style company, he hired strong people, and the first raise was only $1 million (two years in), followed by a $2 million round. Execution is a poor moat in AI, where everyone is strong, but is a real edge in sleepy fields like hosting or grocery.
- **Pricing reset in 2012:** after customer conversations and stories, WP Engine adjusted its prices (not dramatically). He says that is when the growth curve "bends and starts shooting up and never stops," while noting he cannot isolate variables. Attending WordCamps and talking to people probably helped too.

chunks.heading: Brand follows execution
chunks.text:
Jason's view is that brand usually comes from being obsessed with a topic or product and delivering well, not from designing a brand up front.

- Every company has a brand, but not every company has a moat. Brand matters competitively when customers choose you because of it, as a top-three reason, even while you lose on features or price. His example is "no one ever got fired buying IBM"; Apple is another.
- WP Engine's brand grew out of execution, customer love and word of mouth. He thinks a different logo would not have changed its trajectory.
- What you need is consistency, so there is a memorable handle. He compares it to code brace style: studies suggest the specific style doesn't matter, but everyone using the same one does.
- Linear is his example of a product winning on design decisions and sharp focus on the user (not the buyer), not on its name.

chunks.heading: Thinking about AI: it's the solution space, not the problem
chunks.text:
If starting a company today, Jason separates AI used internally (coding, marketing) from AI in the product, and says the second needs care.

- Corporate budgets are heavily biased toward AI, so a product probably needs some AI component to avoid a budget and attention fight. But "I need an AI product" is the wrong frame.
- People have the same problems as always: more leads, better conversion, good customer service, fewer bugs. Nobody says "I need AI in sales"; they say "I want 10x outbound volume at the same conversion rate." AI is part of the solution space.
- His example of a good framing: a restaurant phone line handled on the first ring in 40 languages (menu, ordering, hours), where voice AI is just the mechanism.
- Pitch decks that list AI as the problem space are a red flag to him.

chunks.heading: Which AI products to build: experts over beginners
chunks.text:
Jason notes that AI "doesn't really work" reliably yet. When researching his book, he found its deep research simply wrong about half the time when he checked primary sources. His three categories:

1. **Incumbents adding AI to existing products** (talking to Notion or Sheets): not very useful so far, but they have to do it.
2. **AI for experts** (developers, writers, designers): his preference. You sell to a narrower audience and face incumbents, but errors are fine because the expert fixes them.
3. **AI for beginners ("muggles"):** the market is 100 to 1,000 times larger, but users get to 70-80% and then get stuck and can't fix it. A vibe-coded app is not a SaaS company. He doesn't judge it, but it is not what he would build.

He personally takes a B2B problem-solution approach: solve a real existing problem, with budget, using AI to do something previously impossible, aimed at experts.

chunks.heading: Look for 3x to 10x, not 20%, and ignore competition
chunks.text:
- Marginal gains don't motivate buyers. "30% faster" hosting was weak, which is why WP Engine said four times faster and had customer data to back it. At that multiple, he says, a commodity stops being a commodity.
- Apply the same to AI: going from one article a week to two good ones a day is a product; a 20% boost isn't worth the hassle. Prefer 3x more value for the customer, not just cost savings, which is a weaker pitch.
- Be specific about context. Studies in real engineering departments don't show 10x from AI coding, and individual claims often come from people selling AI. But in some contexts, like using an unfamiliar library, it saves days in minutes, while in a 100-developer code base it can be slower. Find the narrow domain where it is truly a big multiplier.
- He assumes every reasonably sized market will be flooded with AI products using the same models and prompts, so there is no tech moat. His answer is a vision for one narrow ideal customer, built so well that others also want it, then following his nose once real customers are using it.

chunks.heading: Hidden multipliers: his framework for small, systematic improvements
chunks.text:
His book *Hidden Multipliers* (pre-order at hiddenmultipliers.com) collects ten ideas, one per chapter, with new material rather than blog rehashes. He defines a hidden multiplier by three tests:

- **Small change, outsized effect.**
- **Systematic:** it relies on how companies, buyers, teams or math (such as A/B testing) reliably work, so it is not luck.
- **Doable with your current team and budget,** without a big investment. Usually the fix to slow growth is not raising money.

"Hidden" means you didn't know it, or it sat on a to-do list without being seen as important, or you knew it but didn't know what to do or feared acting. He notes that when people say "I already knew that," their actions often show they didn't. He also says strategies often fail not from missing information but from not realizing how important one thing was. He will speak at MicroConf US in Portland in April on what to do when growth slows.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jason Cohen explains how WP Engine justifies premium pricing through perceived value and authentic culture, and how to evaluate new products with a simple three-level adjacency analysis. He also covers the joy/skill/need test for founder roles, why big decisions get harder at scale, and treating AI as a solution to existing customer problems.

chunks.heading: How Jason decides whether a new product or market is worth pursuing: the adjacency matrix
chunks.text:
- Jason says good strategy leverages the assets you already have: strengths, existing customers, brand, culture, a unique advantage. Doing something you are weak at is usually a bad idea unless there is an overwhelming reason, because it takes heavy investment and carries high risk of failure.
- His first question is whether to expand at all. If the current market has real headroom, stay put. Going elsewhere too quickly is a common mistake.
- If the current business is at about 0.1% of its market, the issue is that it is not working yet, or there is plenty of growth right in front of you.
- If the current business is at about 2% penetration, that is actually a lot for a small company. Getting to 3 or 4% is plausible over years; getting to 20% is "nuts". That is a reason to look at adjacent products.
- Diversification is another valid reason, but not for a young product. Early on, when the first product is "still getting legs", it is not the time to diversify.
- He calls his tool the "adjacency matrix" and says the name sounds more complicated than it is.
  1. List the functional buckets of the company, such as marketing, sales, support, product, and design if relevant.
  2. For each candidate idea, rate how adjacent it is in each bucket using only three options. **Trivial**: almost no change, such as one email or one slide. **Adjustment**: manageable with current people and processes, about the size of a large feature release. **Overhaul**: you lack the people or expertise, need to hire for specialty or capacity, or face big retraining or a completely new market.
  3. There are no scores. He dislikes rubrics and numeric scoring ("this is not a Cosmo quiz").
- The output is an understanding of the impact and risk: which parts of the business get shaken up and which stay easy. It also narrows the field, because some ideas are clearly too far afield.
- Easiest is not necessarily best. An easy idea may also be low-value or uninteresting.
- Which buckets are overhauls matters. An engineering-led company may accept a product overhaul but treat a big sales overhaul as a deal breaker because sales is a weakness.
- A key hire can change what you can say yes to. His example: poaching a VP of Sales who has spent seven years selling podcast ads could make an ad business feasible in a way competitors can't follow.
- Applied to Craig's podcast-hosting company: going horizontal (CMS, blogging, email) or vertical (recording, editing, promotion) would each be analyzed bucket by bucket. A CMS would change every competitor, all marketing and all sales, which makes it an overhaul.

chunks.heading: Real WP Engine example: Enterprise was an overhaul in sales but trivial in engineering
chunks.text:
- WP Engine deliberately expanded into new market segments. It invested "tens of millions of dollars" in sales, marketing, customer service and account management to create "hundreds of millions of dollars of revenue" in a new segment.
- Jason describes WP Engine's pricing position as depending on the segment. It is expensive relative to GoDaddy for low-end customers, but cheap relative to Adobe for Enterprise customers. He calls it "the cheap but Enterprise grade alternative for McDonald's" and "the expensive but worth it" option for a dentist's office.
- Enterprise scored as an overhaul in sales and marketing but trivial in engineering and product. Existing customers already had sites bigger than McDonald's' site, since a five-person media site can get far more traffic than IBM.
- Diversification paid off during COVID. Small-business customers canceled or got invoice suspensions, while Enterprise customers flocked to WP Engine because Adobe became too expensive.
- Enterprise means millions of dollars a year, so $100 a month is nowhere near Enterprise.

chunks.heading: Justifying premium pricing: the value the customer perceives
chunks.text:
- Jason says to be premium you must be better at something customers will pay more for, and be specific about what. The test is whether the value the customer perceives is about 10 times the cost, even at the premium price.
- WP Engine examples he gives:
  - Better, more knowledgeable, friendlier tech support that spends more time.
  - A visibly faster WordPress site. You can see it when you log in, and Core Web Vitals scores rise.
  - Security with a bullet-point list that other security people agree is good.
- For a non-technical customer, doubling site speed means a lower bounce rate and better Google SEO. For media or e-commerce sites that earn per page view or traffic, that is worth a lot, so paying $100 instead of $50, or $30 instead of $5, is an easy decision if it changes the revenue curve.
- Value is not only features. Community can be the differentiator: Genesis developers have hundreds of thousands of peers on Facebook groups and Slack, which is not a line in the Genesis roadmap. Mission can too: Patagonia, or customers who pay ten times more for sustainable coffee beans.

chunks.heading: Brand versus the real thing behind it, and when to invest in each
chunks.text:
- Jason says Patagonia's brand is not a logo, colors or name. It is the actual mission and how the company is run; for example, the company bails employees out of jail if they are arrested protesting. "That's not brand, that's company culture and policy and genuinely believing in the mission." The brand is just the handle for it.
- Traditional brand work (logo placement, typography consistency) comes later. Before product-market fit you don't know your target customer or right products, and nobody knows you yet, so obsessing over brand is a mistake. The exception is that founders often pour their identity into the name and font, which he understands.
- After product-market fit, customers flood in and you are fighting bugs, scalability, tech debt and support load. Once you are on top of that, brand consistency starts to matter because many people now know you and you are placing a specific feeling in their minds.
- Authentic elements like community and mission can't be bolted on later. The Genesis community started on day zero. A jacket company that later declares it cares about the environment would be inauthentic to customers and employees, and he says he can't name a company that built a genuine community only after years of operating.
- It should come from who the founder is. If you are an introvert who hates community, don't do it; there are dozens of other marketing tools. He notes that podcasting is a big, fast-growing market, and "there isn't just one way to grow."

chunks.heading: Joy, skill and need: choosing your role as a founder
chunks.text:
- Jason uses a three-part test for whether he is in the right role: does he love the work (joy), is he good at it (skill), and does the company need it (need). He says he made the decision to stop being CEO about ten years ago using this, and has kept using it as he moved to CTO and then to Chief Innovation Officer. He notes it is one of several possible frameworks, mentioning Ikigai.
- Each missing piece has a specific trap:
  - **Missing joy**: you do work you are good at and the company needs, but come to resent it. He burned out at SmartBear this way without realizing it.
  - **Missing skill**: founders like the work and the company needs it, but they are bad at it, and as founder nobody tells them no. His example is messing with AdWords for three months with no experience, concluding AdWords sucks when the real conclusion is "you suck", and thinking you're an expert after wasting the time. Even once at some scale, "we don't have time for people to just be messing about."
  - **Missing need**: common with indie hackers. You love making things and are good at it, but the company needs customers who actually want the product, and only people on Twitter tell you otherwise.
- It is an ideal state, and nobody is in the middle of all three every day. The point is to notice when you are drifting too long or too often.
- His roles: CEO for four years, CTO for roughly the next eight, and recently Chief Innovation Officer. He has worked on corporate strategy, helped teams with their strategy, and in the last year worked on corporate data, including data teams and machine learning models. He says the CIO title is a bit silly but common among founders.

chunks.heading: Hiring someone better than you, and diagnosing flat growth
chunks.text:
- When a founder says they can't afford someone better than themselves, Jason pushes back: if that person did the job well you could afford them, so the math doesn't add up.
- He suggests hiring someone who is ahead of you but earlier in their career, so they are cheaper. They have a higher slope and the company becomes a place for them to crush it. Look for someone better in both "point and slope."
- If a hire doesn't change the growth trajectory, they can't stay. If they do, you can afford them. This is true of every position.
- If several hires have not changed a flat growth curve, the hires may not have been effective.
- When interviewing a growth hire, ask why predecessors didn't change the growth rate, what it is about this market or the work, and how specifically they know it will be different this time. If they can't answer, that is bad; if they can, you still evaluate the answer.
- Look at competitors: if they all grow at the same rate, maybe there is nothing to figure out. If they grew a lot, check what they are doing (partners versus advertising) without assuming that copying works.
- If getting new customers is just too hard, a valid strategy is to grow from existing customers: raise ARPU through segmentation, different kinds of value, underpricing, new products, or acquiring something and feeding it into the customer base. He calls that "a great strategic statement" and says to ask where growth can come from if not acquisition.

chunks.heading: Making big, scary decisions and the limits of "two-way doors"
chunks.text:
- Jason says big decisions are hard because they cost time, attention, energy, money and expectations from employees and customers, and fear of them is reasonable.
- "Two-way door" thinking is overused. A Google ad you took down is a two-way door, but many big bets technically reversible are painful to reverse, and the team wonders whether leadership knows what it is doing.
- Experimenting at scale is different in kind from small tests. Running a pricing test for a month differs from a bet that could lead to laying off 30 people. "This is people's lives and we all know it."
- He recommends setting culture expectations ahead of time: a company that never tries big bold things is going to die; some attempts will fail; we will call it out after three or six months instead of three years; people should support each other when it fails and celebrate when it works. If you want a company that never admits mistakes, work elsewhere.
- Frameworks like the adjacency matrix don't give the answer but give confidence that you have thought it through, with five decent options and the risks of each known. You will never know what would have happened with another choice.

chunks.heading: Thinking about AI at WP Engine: solution space, not problem space
chunks.text:
- WP Engine uses AI in three places: internally in operations such as support and sales, with an internal tool not yet shown to customers; in developer tooling such as Copilot; and in products.
- He argues that building a standalone AI product doesn't make sense, because there will be a billion AI products and a team or two can't overtake 100 other startups building the same thing.
- The first product step is to add AI to products WP Engine already has, which fits the adjacency idea. Example: AI-powered e-commerce search where a shopper can type "a shoe that's good for people with plantar fasciitis" and get the right results. He says people who use the search bar are three times more likely to convert, so improving that experience is where to invest.
- On uncertainty: "there's zero people who know what AI looks like in five years." In that situation you don't make five-year plans; you play, explore, act and see what happens. He cites the Cynefin chaos domain, where the correct response is to act first. Play now so you are present as the future unfolds.
- Customers don't wake up wanting more AI. They want what they always wanted, such as media companies wanting more visitors, longer visits, more newsletter sign-ups and more ad revenue. AI "should always be thought of as the potential solution or potential execution" that delivers the thing the customer always wanted in a new way. "It's in the solution space and not the problem space."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jason Cohen reflects on selling SmartBear and co-founding WP Engine. He covers the Rich vs King choice, the freedom line, options short of selling, sharing equity with employees, and a Joy/Skill/Need framework for deciding which role a founder should hold.

chunks.heading: How Jason decides whether to sell, and why he sold SmartBear
chunks.text:
- Jason told every employee who joined SmartBear that the goal was to sell someday. He likes starting things and making things, and he wanted to make money. He calls this "just as mercenary as that" while stressing it was never at the expense of customers.
- He says most people start companies for two reasons: they hate having a boss, and they want money. He argues it's fine to admit the second one.
- An earlier offer for SmartBear was not good, so he didn't consider it. The Insight Partners offer was a strong revenue multiple, all cash, with no performance-based second bite, and it moved fast: first email to close in four months, closing December 20th. He notes that WP Engine's $250 million round also closed at the end of December, so "no deals are done in December" is false.
- The deciding moment was at home. After the first in-person meeting with Insight in Austin, his wife told him "you have to sell" because she could see how unhappy he was: always in a bad mood, even when things went well. He calls it classic burnout.
- He thinks selling was a good decision but says you can't judge a decision by its outcome (the poker point). He had treated it as binary, sell or stay miserable, when there were many other options.
- Burnout and feeling stuck are, in his experience, the most common reason founders of 5-10 year-old companies want out. He says there are few people to complain to about it, so peers and podcasts are where it gets talked about.

chunks.heading: Options Jason missed besides a full sale
chunks.text:
- **Take some money without selling the whole company.** Financing or a secondary can create breathing room.
- **Step back and let the team run it.** Become part-time or take a smaller role, vest more equity into the people who step up as CEO or CTO, and accept dilution. A smaller percentage of a much bigger company is worth more in dollars. "The percentage of the company is not important, the dollars are important."
- **Example (Bluefish Group, an Austin consulting firm):** the founder handed it to the CTO after 12 years and took a small stipend while keeping ownership. The company had been growing about 5% a year and doubled the next year. The founder's reaction: "I should have left sooner, I was holding it back."
- Jason says founders can't believe they're holding the company back because they think they're the smartest. Often they're mostly right, but hungry superstars with no room to move can unlock growth.
- **Change the business model.** SmartBear sold one-time licenses and tried to get roughly 20% a year in support contracts. Revenue reset toward zero each month, which was stressful. Recurring revenue would have lowered the stress and made the business more predictable.
- **Find a real coach or therapist.** Founders dismiss them, but Jason says good ones exist (he cites Jerry Colonna) and finding one is worth the time. His analogy: Federer's tennis coach isn't as good at tennis as Federer, because a coach "holds up a mirror" and offers insight, not skill.

chunks.heading: The freedom line and how much money is enough
chunks.text:
- Wealth isn't linear. Jason points to the St. Petersburg paradox, where people value money roughly logarithmically: you need to add a zero before it changes your life. Beyond some personal line, even another zero doesn't change whether you're happy.
- Below the line you have money worries and conflict. Above it, many problems disappear (no debt, a car that works, a comfortable house). Offers that push you over the line are the interesting ones.
- After SmartBear sold, he didn't buy a new house or car. At WP Engine, secondary sales have paid him orders of magnitude more than the SmartBear sale, and his car is nine years old.
- If a company already throws off $1M a year in profit, you're probably past the line, so selling isn't how you get there. That opens options like letting employees run it.
- He warns founders to be realistic. $5M in the bank in America does not mean you never work again: taxes, inflation and low real returns mean you need far more.
- His back-of-envelope math: if you could earn $200K a year in a job, and you expect a 2-3% real return, you divide $200K by 0.02 to get about $10M. Adding inflation and conservatism, he guesses "20 is right." Don't sell for less than the income a job would give you.
- Secondaries (selling some of your own shares, which doesn't make the pie bigger) can go either way. Founders may disengage, or they may take bigger risks because the downside no longer feels like zero.

chunks.heading: The box game for thinking about risk
chunks.text:
- Box A has $5M. Box B is 50/50 between $0 and $10M. You pick once.
- Economists say expected value is identical ($5M), but Jason says no one treats them as identical and expected value is useless here. The problem is non-ergodic: you run it once, not a million times. His example: Russian roulette played repeatedly ends in death, not "one in six."
- Founders sell once, so the group average doesn't matter. The point of the game is to find your own risk and reward preference.
- Change the numbers (box B is $0 or $50M, or $0 to a billion) to find whether any upside would make you give up a sure amount near your freedom line. He says there may be no number you'd take.
- Real decisions like "will the company grow over three years" have invented probabilities, and only one outcome will happen, and it could be bad.

chunks.heading: Advice, blowback and employees in a sale
chunks.text:
- Jason made index cards after calling everyone he could find for advice, about 17 in total. Opinions split evenly between "never sell" and "take it, deals often fall through." He recommends getting people who help intensely during the sale, not just one-off conversations.
- He got blowback from people who think you should never raise money or sell (he alludes to the 37signals camp). He notes people who have actually gone through it tend to be supportive: "God bless, I hope it worked out well for you."
- One critic outweighs 19 kind comments emotionally. His only tip is to name the feeling, which sometimes diffuses it.
- Employees didn't want to sell even though selling was the stated goal. Some resented it, some understood. They were generous in the payout, so there was no resentment about wealth.
- He believes founders should share proceeds with people who contributed, even if nothing was promised. He doesn't call it immoral to pay only salaries. He says employee one can deserve something close to a third or fourth of what the founder has, and a late joiner can also be valuable. Zero "seems like a small number" to him.
- Do it with a system, not ad hoc. A lawyer will warn that after-the-fact gifts invite lawsuits. His example: a consultant who got a $20,000 thank-you check after a sale and sued for more.
- SmartBear used a non-option system where people got paid at sale, modeled on vesting. He describes other ideas:
  - Set aside a pool and issue everyone a unit each quarter, so long-tenured people hold more.
  - Hiring more people dilutes everyone's units, which discourages unnecessary hiring.
  - Optionally let each person give one unit per quarter to someone else, though it could become cliquey.
- Cash-bonus-style payments are taxed as regular income, not capital gains, and rules differ by country. WP Engine operates where employees can't hold stock.
- This kind of spreadsheet system works for small companies (up to about 30 people, a 50-60 person consultancy in Austin tried it), not WP Engine's 1,200.

chunks.heading: Two unicorns and why the company is not your child
chunks.text:
- Jason is a founder of two unicorns (SmartBear, still a 21-year-old brand under a different owner, and WP Engine, with over 1,200 employees and a round of roughly $300M). He thinks it says he has good product taste and intuition about business models and customers, not design.
- About 3.5 to 4 years into WP Engine, he hired Heather Brunner as CEO and became CTO. He says the company is a unicorn because Heather is the CEO and that he wouldn't have been nearly as good.
- He takes full credit for the early work: the idea, the market choice, the product, all the customer interviews, and no first hire for over a year.
- He cites an MRI study: a person's brain responds to pictures of their startup's logo the way it does to pictures of their kids. That is why identity gets tangled with the company.
- But he says the child analogy is wrong. You never sell a child, yet sometimes selling or shutting down a company is right (e.g., indie hackers boasting about $1,600 MRR after three years). Likewise "team is a family" is wrong because you fire people who aren't right and you don't fire family. A healthy team is more like a sports team.
- Knowing your brain is doing this to you lets you be more intellectual about the decision.
- Unlike a parent, a founder keeps credit forever and can use it on a Twitter bio, so he feels no resentment when the company succeeds without him.

chunks.heading: The fulfillment framework: joy, skill and need
chunks.text:
- Jason built a three-circle Venn diagram to decide whether to hire a CEO and to stay at WP Engine. He wrote it up as "Fulfillment" on his blog (asmartbear.com). The circles:
  - **Joy:** what you love doing.
  - **Skill:** what you're good at.
  - **Need:** what the company needs done right now.
- You want the center. Two out of three is a trap:
  - **Joy + skill but the company doesn't need it:** the developer happily coding features while the company needs sales. "You're running very fast but in the wrong direction," and as a founder nobody tells you.
  - **Skill + need but no joy:** he did sales at SmartBear, closing 50% of demos, and burned out. Fine short term, bad long term.
  - **Joy + need but not skill:** founders think they're best at everything, which proves they don't know what good looks like. Example: trying affiliates, failing, and concluding "affiliates don't work." Jason says competitors said that publicly while affiliates work well for WP Engine.
- Applied at 60-70 people: the company needed a CEO to scale from 60 to 500, run the board, hire an executive team, and build a global sales org, real marketing, scaled support, finance and HR. Jason didn't love or excel at much of it, so he stepped aside.
- He showed the framework to the whole company to explain the change (so nobody thought he was on his way out) and suggested people use it for their own careers.
- He keeps re-asking the question periodically, and moved from CTO to smaller product roles. He briefly took all of R&D (250 people) temporarily, knowing it wasn't forever.
- Founders have an extra role that doesn't fit the framework. A VP of sales who came from Rackspace (employee 16) told him the thing people missed most when founders left was them walking around and talking to people with no agenda. Jason says that's real and special, but floating around with no real responsibility isn't healthy enough.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jason Cohen explains the growth-ceiling math (new customers per month divided by churn rate), argues a defensible strategy is a unique set of strengths and weaknesses that reinforce each other (WP Engine), and says to adopt AI with urgency but not chaos. He also covers ICP focus, craft lost to AI coding, and being your own advocate.

chunks.heading: The ceiling comes from math: new customers divided by churn rate
chunks.text:
Jason's "max MRR" or growth-ceiling idea: marketing channels add a roughly fixed number of customers per month, but cancellations are a percentage of the whole base, so they grow with you.

- Formula: new customers per month ÷ monthly cancellation rate = the most customers you can ever have if nothing changes.
- Example: AdWords adds 100 customers a month and 5% cancel monthly, so growth stops at 2,000 customers (100 ÷ 0.05). At 2,000, 5% churn is 100 leaving, matching the 100 arriving.
- Marketing "doesn't care how big your company is." Each channel tops out fast (only so many searches, words and profitable ROIs), and most companies get only a few channels that really work.
- If nothing changes, you "will never ever" exceed that number. Without action you grow slower and slower until cancellations win.
- He says everyone should compute this for their own company, charted over time and ideally by cohort or segment.
- It is visceral ("Oh crap, this is it") and it skips the abstract argument over whether 5% churn is okay. He asks instead: "You're never going to have more than 2,000 customers. You good with that?"
- If a competitor selling to similar consumers has 2% churn, your high churn is a choice of market segment, and you control it.
- Cancellation also matters emotionally and financially. People saw everything you offer, believed the promise, and left anyway, so find out why.
- When growth slows for everyone at once, that is a secular shift (AI), not coincidence. The ceiling math is true regardless.

chunks.heading: A strategy is a unique set of strengths and weaknesses, not one unique thing
chunks.text:
Jason says seeking one thing nobody else does is a platitude "said by people who aren't operators." Occasionally it exists, but typically the whole set is unique.

- No one copies your weaknesses. What matters is that the weaknesses are trade-offs that enable the strengths, not just weak spots.
- WP Engine example:
  - It over-invested in the fastest CPUs, the fastest memory and attention across the whole stack, so customers think "what the heck is going on?" about the speed.
  - It charged more than everyone else and staffed capable support people, which is expensive.
  - It disallowed slow WordPress plugins. "That's a massive weakness. If you have a website, you depend on this plugin, it won't work here... You don't want my business. I want it, but no."
- Competitors could copy all of it, but low-priced shared hosts at $2 a month can't afford it, it doesn't match their model, and their customers don't need it.
- His summary: "You can copy our strengths but are you going to copy our weaknesses?" That special shape is the strategy, and some customers will prefer it and some won't.
- He has been building for 25 years and says he can't remember anything he did that was uncopyable from a code perspective.

chunks.heading: Copyability and competition in the AI era
chunks.text:
- Everything has always been copyable (successful software had clones before AI). AI makes copying faster and cheaper, but you and the copier both speed up, so the strategic rules hold on a multi-year timeframe.
- He concedes absolute time does change: 6 months vs 3 months differs from 3 months vs 2 weeks.
- Markets with lots of money are busy and noisy, and AI floods them with mediocre marketing that makes it harder to be seen, but it also lets you build faster. The need to be special in a way customers pay for remains.
- Big companies are not asleep this time, unlike mobile or the internet. HubSpot, Salesforce, Google and Microsoft are all investing in AI. You can't discount them, and a startup chat product must fight Intercom, HubSpot and Salesforce.
- Incumbents aren't necessarily succeeding, and startup AI products often don't work well either.
- He was wrong in his earlier article that data is an incumbent advantage. One person with a strong set of LLM skills (skills as markdown files) can do amazing things without data. He allows that some applications may still need it.

chunks.heading: Urgency without chaos on AI
chunks.text:
- Jason pushes back on "chaos." Experiment and move with urgency, but don't overreact, because the tooling changes constantly (Claude Code ships updates daily, sometimes major ones, and "the way we're doing AI now is nothing like what we did six months ago").
- Since nobody knows what AI will look like in 6 to 12 months, he asks what there is to be chaotic about.
- The real risk is staying in the "chat with a model" mindset. That sees a dumb one-shot, context-free chat and concludes AI is dumb. Structured tools with skills, iteration and agents can be 5 to 10 times better in accuracy and productivity.
- Learn the stable concepts: prompting, then skills, then agents, then agent coordination. The details of a given agent setup will change.
- Start now to build the mindset. If you don't, you don't know when you'll start or how far behind you'll be.
- Much AI simply doesn't work, but when it does it is "magical," and a competitor who gets there first while you don't is "really bad." Anthropic overtaking OpenAI in revenue and growth because of Claude Code is something few predicted six months earlier.
