- Deep truths that held 10 or 20 years ago still hold. Use AI as a new tool to attack them, and drop ideas that are no longer relevant.

chunks.heading: Why startups usually fail, and what to do about it
chunks.text:
- Starting any company is net negative expected value, so applying probability to the decision means never starting one. Do it if you feel compelled, you have an idea, or "this is who you are."
- Failure is common because many things must each go right enough: the product works, you can build and maintain it, you find customers, it's cheap enough, customers convert, keep paying and find value, and you hold up against competition. Even at 70% each, the product of many is low.
- The model is not literally true, but it helps you find your weak or unknown areas. Then act on them:
  - Learn the skill.
  - Add a co-founder with complementary skills.
  - Test earlier so you find out in two months that it's a bad idea instead of twelve.
- Bootstrapped founders still have a shot. Most bootstrapped and VC-funded AI companies will fail, and too much money is going into AI.

chunks.heading: Using AI as a facilitator, and sharing ideas freely
chunks.text:
- Jason's book "Hidden Multipliers" (hiddenmultipliers.com) covers jump-starting growth with your current budget and team. It is strategic, not tactical, with no SEO or GEO tactics, only understanding how businesses work. Examples illustrate deeper concepts and shouldn't be copied exactly.
- ICP: write for one bullseye customer, because focus drives decisions and makes the homepage clear. Many people outside the bullseye still buy. Most buyers aren't your perfect customer, yet it stays your north star. His own ICP is a bootstrapped founder with about $2M ARR in SaaS whose growth has slowed or stopped and who doesn't know which of 10 options to pick.
- AI can't tell you who your perfect customer is, it would just generate something that sounds good. Where it helps is facilitation: it prods you, brainstorms and plays devil's advocate. You can't be your own devil's advocate, and a coach's value is facilitation, not answers. He built skills for each step of the process.
- He wants people to take and remix his ideas. His blog (18 years) has an RSS feed under "special links" with every article in markdown for ingestion. He isn't trying to make money from the ideas, only to cover the book's cost.
- Best way to learn from a book: read it, then build the skill yourself. "If you tell me, I forget. If I do it, I might remember, and if I teach it, I understand." Teaching the LLM gives you both understanding and efficiency. Pick which tasks to automate (those that don't matter to you) and which to stay engaged in (your company's strategy).

chunks.heading: Joy, craft and Claude Code
chunks.text:
- Jason finds Claude Code magical and fun to tune, but finishes days drained rather than energized, likening it to doom-scrolling. Other people report the same.
- Productivity gains are real: one thread is often faster, two or three threads accelerate things further, but beyond that he can't keep it in mind. Context switching is draining, and managing an AI that says "you're right" patronizingly is annoying.
- It's great for scaffolding and prototyping, but for tiny edits it's faster to open the file and change the number.
- He loved the craft of code optimization (reading how libraries implement cosine and sine, for example) and that part is gone. He says it's sad when a craft is lost, even when the technology is a net good.
- He is not going back to coding the old way, but he writes his book by hand because the human ideas and style are the product. He writes long, thoughtful sentences, not "fifth-grader" marketing prose, and articles take dozens of hours.
- Chess analogy: computers have beaten the best humans for 25 years, yet chess is more popular than ever, because the human struggle is the point. He thinks human expression is insulated, though AI changes styles and study methods. He clicks off YouTube videos that are clearly AI, and would rather watch a human do a bad job.

chunks.heading: Engineers need the non-code parts of business
chunks.text:
- Jason writes for engineers who only want to code. He has nothing new to say about writing code or unit tests, but as an engineer himself he can explain the non-code business work and persuade them to do it. His writing is about the structure of how businesses work, not ad-writing tactics.
- Background: Smart Bear (code review tool, started 2002, bootstrapped, sold 2007, he left 2009) and WP Engine (about 16 to 17 years old, bootstrapped first, then raised a small amount and later a lot, always proportional to its size; now 200,000 customers, 1,200 employees, profitable and growing).
- Advice from his mother: "always be your own advocate." Others, even good ones, are seeing many people and thinking about themselves, so advocate for yourself at work, in self-promotion and in your own care.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jason Cohen explains why he raised money for WP Engine after two years of bootstrapping, and why dogma on funding is unhelpful. He covers studying competitors' incentives to build a distinct strategy, hiring people better than you, and making consistent decisions, including how building in public forces a stronger strategy.

chunks.heading: Choosing funding: bootstrapping vs. raising money
chunks.text:
- Jason never planned to raise money. He bootstrapped Smart Bear and sold it while still bootstrapped; the buyer was Insight Venture Partners, who then put in more money and bought other companies.
- WP Engine, his fourth company, also started bootstrapped. About two years in, the market looked far bigger than he had thought, large enough that raising money was plausible and logical.
- He also had a different personal view by then: "maybe I want a different journey this time." He was a father and had already run the bootstrap path several times.
- The questions he says change the path:
  - Are you optimizing for profit or growth?
  - Is the constraint money or people?
  - How big a strategy can you make?
  - What kind of organization and impact do you want?
- Even with experience, he says every company is new: new customers, new market, new product. "You really have to have beginner's mind with each company."
- He credits "incredible product market fit" for making funding a viable option.

chunks.heading: No tribalism about investors or acquirers
chunks.text:
- Jason doesn't tie his identity to a funding approach. He identifies with the companies and ideas he builds, not with processes or decisions like whether to raise.
- Having done both, he says each has upsides and downsides, and there are bad actors in both places.
- Some investors helped hugely, including with culture and people. Others pushed the wrong pressures onto a company.
- As an investor in dozens of companies, he has seen founders who wanted to sell. Some investors tried to talk them out of it. He and others said "good for you, let us help you do that." The founders were burned out, so that outcome was good for everyone.
- He calls buyers like Tiny/SureSwift-style small-company acquirers (he is an LP in one) good for the world:
  - Founders get liquidity or relief from burnout.
  - Employees get leadership roles there was no room for before.
  - Customers get continuity instead of a company that dies when its founder burns out.
- He supports calling out bad investor behavior, but not the blanket claim that "investors are bad."
- Extreme positions are easy to follow, like a simple diet rule. They help you focus and go deep. The cost is a skewed picture of the world and missed ideas.

chunks.heading: Study competitors' incentives instead of demonizing them
chunks.text:
- Competitors may have raised money, or may simply be large. Either way, you need to know their incentives, culture and goals to build your own strategy.
- Example: a venture-funded competitor must prioritize growth. If you go heavy on personal customer relationships (reaching out to each new signup), they won't follow, "even if they could," because it isn't their culture or goal. That makes your strategy unique.
- Funded competitors almost need to spend money, because the point of raising is to spend it on growth or de-risking. Don't try to outspend them. Find a different way.
- "Part of what makes strategy good" is when you can say the other side won't follow you.
- Calling a competitor dumb or evil blocks objective analysis of their real strengths. You need to know where they are strong so you can go head to head or avoid them.
- A different set of constraints and goals than yours is "the Genesis of a good strategy."
- He distinguishes needing to do it your own way (healthy, gives you energy) from believing everyone else is wrong. Many founders, himself included, just need to do it their way without claiming they are right.

chunks.heading: Hiring people better than you
chunks.text:
- Founders who say "only I can do this" and won't hire often burn out. Jason's view is that the founder can't be replaced in everything, but hiring a developer or marketer doesn't replace all of you.
- Claiming no developer is as good as you is, in his words, "a personal failing," not something to be proud of.
- A leader's job is to make the organization better over time. So you hire people who are better than you at each function: "If you don't then the company will never get better than you personally are at every function, which is a complete failure of leadership."
- How to evaluate someone who knows more than you:
  - Ask how they would approach a problem you actually have (e.g. "we've exhausted our one channel, what do you do?"). If their answer sounds rational and compatible with your thinking, yet several steps ahead, they are likely better than you.
  - In reference checks, ask what environment the person thrives in and where they would fail. Don't reveal your own culture or expectations, so the answer stays honest.
  - Ask people in your network who know the function to help interview. Consider paying them a fee ("a grand, five grand, ten grand"), which may beat a recruiter who "just shuffles resumes and charges you a lot."
- He adds that it is fun and effective when others have ideas better than yours.

chunks.heading: Staying solo without burning out: keep decisions consistent
chunks.text:
- Wanting to stay solo is fine, but he says burnout is the most common outcome, and he burned out at Smart Bear too.
- His fix is a consistent strategy. Every other decision (customers, market, product, support, marketing, sales) must fit the choice not to have employees.
- Examples:
  - If it's just you, don't run 24/7 support or sell a product customers depend on around the clock. Four hours of downtime should be survivable for them.
  - Being the only person with a pager forever burns you out.
  - Alternatively, contract out support or the pager. Support is risky to outsource because those people talk directly to customers and become your brand. Technical on-call is less visible.
  - Or design the product with runbooks and rollbacks so you can outsource on-call once you are bigger.
- Inconsistent decisions "will kill you." You must decide what you really want, such as staying solo versus building a bigger company. You can also limit growth or close signups.
- Making hard tradeoffs produces a company aligned with what you chose and better-fit customers: "that's what strategy should look like when it's done right."

chunks.heading: Building in public
chunks.text:
- Benefits:
  - It forces you to evaluate yourself constantly, since you must decide what you think about each thing you post.
  - It brings feedback (which you still have to filter) and builds a network for questions like Stripe Atlas or design A vs. B.
- Costs:
  - It takes a lot of time and fragments attention. Context-switching hurts far more than the raw hours suggest, and he is skeptical of "five or ten minutes a day."
  - Mitigation: limit it to set times, like lunch or mealtimes.
- Strategic upside: if you build in public, secrecy can't be part of your strategy. For example, you can't pretend to be a big company ("we" on the About page) when you are one person.
  - That pretense promises 24/7 support or integrations you won't deliver, so it is a bad, inconsistent strategy.
  - Better to position as what you actually are. Customers who want to support the little guy will pick you, and those who need more should not buy.
- He also sees it as good for the world to show that many people try, fail and try again.

chunks.heading: Jason's own path and honesty as a personal brand
chunks.text:
- He doesn't plan another company. He has made enough money that a project doesn't need to earn any, so he'd pick something unique: writing, open source, or philanthropy. A full-time angel investor role wouldn't suit him because he needs to produce and create.
- He writes long-form strategy essays, posts about once a week, and says he earns nothing from it. Newsletter subscribers, RSS and Twitter followers are the "revenue" he wants. Sharing is how people can contribute back.
- On why founders restart after an exit: he is skeptical of tidy rationalizations and suspects people often simply need to build.
- Staying a person rather than a "persona" on social media:
  - He has written openly for almost two decades, so "this is who I am, take it or leave it."
  - Being upfront defuses situations. His Twitter bio ("keyword buzzword half truth adjective, hey look at me, founder of two unicorns") admits the brag before doing it, which resets expectations.
  - He says admitting a flaw ("I'm too hard on people about X, I'm working on it") takes the sting out of it in meetings too.
- He follows on Twitter as @asmartbear and writes at smartbear.com (his blog, ASmartBear).

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jason Cohen talks with Justin Jackson about why most startup advice is survivorship-biased and tied to the giver's goals. He covers how to decide among incomparable options with filters, the real time cost of bootstrapping, why "struggle porn" is a symptom, and a like/good-at/company-needs framework for deciding your role.

chunks.heading: Why Jason distrusts most startup advice
chunks.text:
- Advice is usually the giver talking to themselves. Jason says people "really are doing is giving themselves advice" and rarely ask about the asker's goals first.
- Good advice starts with questions: what are you trying to get out of this, what does good look like, do you want employees at all, do you want to be famous, or rich, or just independent.
- His own original goal at SmartBear was to "have my own job and no one tells me what to do" and make as much money as possible. After about 18 months he switched to raising money and going big. He says the two paths have different constraints and goals, and neither is better.
- He was CEO of WP Engine for four years and has not been CEO for the last five. At SmartBear that would have "sounded like hell".
- Survivor bias: a blogger with one or two wins may just have gotten lucky, since so many people try. Ask whether others did the same things and failed. If the behavior correlates just as much with failure, it proves nothing.
- Example: Jim Collins's *Good to Great* picked 11 outperforming companies and extracted a formula. Five years later 40% were bankrupt, and public-company peers did the same things too.
- Venture capitalists do nothing but try to pick winners and can't. Only about 25% of VC firms ever make money. His conclusion: "there's not a formula".
- You can't split test experience, so you can't tell whether a founder's choice caused their success.

chunks.heading: How to evaluate advice you receive
chunks.text:
- Check the giver's goals, motivations and context against yours. If they don't match closely enough, it may still be good advice, but you can't know. If the person is similar to you, started the same way and seems smart, weigh it more.
- It is fine to ask whether the advice resonates with how you feel.
- If competing advice (never use Twitter versus build a following on Twitter) can all work, pick the one you're most excited about. You will put in extra energy and wake up thinking about it, so you will likely execute it best.
- He is explicit that this is not "follow your passion", which he calls crap. It is a tiebreaker when you can't tell the options apart.

chunks.heading: Build something people love, not "beat the competition"
chunks.text:
- Jason scores high on competitiveness (StrengthsFinder) but thinks "how will I beat them" is probably the wrong mode. The better question is how to build a product you're proud of, and find customers who are excited about it.
- People buy for many reasons: best features, best product, culture, or purpose.
- Examples:
  - 37signals: early products weren't great, and the abandoned ones were bad, yet people loved the company, its ideas and its contributions.
  - Jason bought FogBugz from Joel Spolsky because he loved Joel's blog, not because it was the best bug tracker.
  - Patagonia: people buy for the culture and mission (company policy is to bail out employees arrested protesting for the environment).
  - Google won simply by being the best.
- You still must track competitors and keep features operational, but "you can't build a company by well, here's how we're not this other person". Decide who you are and execute.

chunks.heading: Tearing down a pitch, then filling it back up
chunks.text:
- On a podcast he called "Doctor Laura for startups" he critiqued ideas directly. He also does pitch practice with companies at Capital Factory in Austin.
- His method: shred the pitch honestly, then point out the real value the founder isn't telling you. Weak pitches focus on a feature (resizing an image) instead of what it does for people.
- Example: a tool that helps people earn money online can change lives. It gives an extra $1,000 a month to a single parent, a stay-at-home parent, an artist, or someone who wants to quit a bad job or lives where it's hard otherwise.
- Good criticism names specific problems (he might see three where everyone else said the idea was good) so the founder can work on them, and ends with what is compelling.

chunks.heading: How WP Engine's customers and motivation changed
chunks.text:
- At first he was excited that someone would pay for it, and that the engineering problems (optimizing, securing, caching) were fun for him. Signups were easy, a sign of product-market fit.
- Customers were often freelancers building sites, or business owners with a triggering event, ready to move from a $5 host to a $50 plan: an SEO person said the site was slow, a traffic spike took it down, or the site got hacked.
- Over roughly 18 months or more his motivation widened beyond money to what the company did for people. Example: a customer who makes guitars got press and a traffic spike, and her site survived her biggest sales day ever. WP Engine keeps one of her guitars in the support area.
- Employee impact also mattered to him. A third of employees have no college degree, which is unusual for a high-tech company, and the executive team has many women. His view: you have to measure diversity or you can't claim to care, and the door has to be opened but people still have to earn it.
- The cheapest WP Engine plan is now $35, down from $50 at launch.

chunks.heading: Bootstrapping honestly: time, money and the options
chunks.text:
- He pushes back on "work 10 hours a week and screw off the rest". Even 3 hours a day on a project means thinking about it all the time. A full-time job plus about 20 hours a week on a startup plus family is 100% of your time.
- His advice to a founder with about $4,300 MRR and 220 customers after 3 months: with nobody on it full-time, you can't act on big strategy, so you just need to get customers.
- Real options, all costly:
  - Salary job: least stressful, since the paycheck settles that anxiety, but time is very tight.
  - Consulting: spiky, "the hourly always wins" over product work, and when it drops you're stressed about money.
  - Raise money: includes newer bootstrapper-friendly sources (he names Earnest Capital and Tiny Seed). You give up structure, meaning equity or control.
  - Grind with your own time: burnout is a main reason these fail.
- Everything gives up something: equity or control, or your time. Co-founders already give up some control.
- On 37signals/DHH's side-project story: it was effectively four people part-time, about 40 to 60 hours a week total, funded by an agency, and took about two years. Be honest about that.
- He rejects "struggle porn": struggling means the business isn't working yet, which is a problem, not a badge. With a team of ten, 100-hour weeks signal a leadership failure. But it is also insulting to say you've failed for not having a $20K/month business after four months.
- Rule of thumb he agrees with: $20K a year in revenue after three years is probably not a good use of your time.

chunks.heading: Making hard decisions: filters, then one or two dimensions
chunks.text:
- The options aren't ranked good/better/best; they differ on multiple dimensions with incomparable units (more hours versus giving up equity), so you can't stack rank or use a rubric.
- Step 1: set filters, limits you won't cross. Examples: "I have four kids and a wife I'd like to keep, so nothing that jeopardizes that", a time you'll be home, or "I will never have an investor". Filters shrink the option set and let you stop second-guessing: you know why something is a no.
- Step 2: pick one or two dimensions to maximize (most money, or what excites you, or learning something) and decide on those, knowing you're trading off the rest.
- Wants change over time. He started wanting interesting work and customer payments, and later cared about diversity and culture. He notes Balsamiq's founder wanted a one-person company, and it grew.

chunks.heading: The like / good at / company needs framework
chunks.text:
- Check three things: what you like, what you're good at, and what the company needs. Each failure mode:
  - Like it and company needs it, but you're not good: fine when small, a failure at scale, since important things need real expertise.
  - Good and company needs it, but you don't like it: burnout.
  - Like it and good at it, but the company doesn't need it (e.g. he'd love to code): common for founders because nobody tells a founder to stop.
- He used it to decide he was not the right CEO for WP Engine at around 60 to 70 people. The company needed someone to lead large groups, hire an executive team and open global offices. That wasn't his strength and "sounds like hell", and it is the successor's favorite job.
- Everyone deserves roles where they like the work, are good at it and it's needed. He says he didn't invent it and similar frameworks exist.

chunks.heading: What is hard at scale
chunks.text:
- At around 600 employees, finding ideas that can make tens of millions a year is very hard; ideas worth a couple million a year aren't worth doing.
- Human events (births, deaths, marriages) happen constantly, and the company is small enough that everyone feels them. He says that is hard with no tactical fix.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jason Cohen and Rob Walling coach the founder of Drop In Blog, a bootstrapped $1M ARR product that has plateaued, on moving upmarket. Jason covers delight versus table stakes, positioning around the buyer's personal stake, using ads to learn messaging, focusing on agencies and BigCommerce, and organizing the team around a new initiative.

chunks.heading: Why Jason questions a new-segment push that only shows 5% of traffic
chunks.text:
- Jesse's big-company visitors were about 5% of traffic and converted at zero on the existing product. Jason reads zero conversions as "I don't want it", not as a hidden 5% pool.
- Capturing all of them on the current offer would add only about 5% growth. The bet only works if they pay roughly 10x more for a different package.
- His test for any new segment: what did you learn about what they want, and what would delight them, beyond covering their table stakes?
- He asks what made the early demos convert. Invoicing and POs, audit logs, and white-glove migration are table stakes. They remove fear but don't excite anyone.

chunks.heading: Delight versus table stakes, and what to say to marketers
chunks.text:
- Jason separates "I just have to have this" features (SSO, roles, audit logs, POs) from features that make a buyer tell others. Both matter, but only the second drives word of mouth.
- His example of delight is Linear: people rave about the design and speed and the product feels better than Jira. He says "there's no such thing as a product that shouldn't delight a customer."
- Enterprise users are still human. Keep the simple, polished UI that wins end users, and only add enterprise checkboxes where there is no choice. Don't let enterprise features degrade the design.
- For marketers at big companies, he'd position around keeping their job. A marketer who can tell the boss "I'm getting us into LLMs" is "saving my job", which is stronger than "you'll hate this less".
- He wants a pitch a marketer repeats in a Slack channel or alumni list ("dude, I just did this"). He says you don't need 100% of buyers to feel it. Even partial success lifts everything.
- Utility is the easy zone: "you need this and I make that" is true but weak.

chunks.heading: Find out who the buyer is, then test messaging with ads
chunks.text:
- Jesse's demos skew technical, but the marketer may hold the budget. Jason says the real answer may be "don't know", and finding out is critical.
- The marketer and the engineer need different messages. Engineers care about drop-in, migration and ongoing hassle. Marketers care about job security and AI visibility.
- Run separate ads and landing pages (even separate home pages) for each. Demos several clicks downstream won't reveal who was drawn in.
- Jesse's earlier $5-figure ad tests targeted SMB-style bottom-of-funnel intent with an unthoughtful message. Jason says that doesn't test this idea.
- Two ways ads can pay at the higher price point:
  - ROI: if the plan is ~10x the monthly price and lifetime value is higher, a campaign can pay even if SMB ads never would.
  - Learning: a fixed budget used to find the best 4-word hook and landing-page message in days. SEO takes too long and attribution is murky.
- The channel can be AdWords, LinkedIn or podcasts. Ask where the marketers actually are.
- Don't spend conference or sponsorship time on a fringe community (Laravel) when the fish are elsewhere (React). Budget it as fun and culture time, not growth.

chunks.heading: Pricing page: avoid a huge visible range
chunks.text:
- A single page showing $5-$20/month and $10,000/month leaves visitors unsure who the company is. Jason says buyers think "I don't want either one."
- His rough ladder rule with no other data: each tier about 2x the previous (sometimes 3x). At the time Jesse's plans were around $49, $199, $499 and $750.
- He called $500 and $750 too close to justify two tiers. The top tier mainly adds SSO.
- A $50 to $750 jump is segmentation, not growth. Nobody moves up because of a little more usage. He notes brand customers come in and stay flat.

chunks.heading: Pick the segments that scale: Big Commerce and agencies
chunks.text:
- Jesse's data: Shopify has more customers but is a worse cohort (high churn, support burden, app-store slop, many not real businesses). Big Commerce stores are real, old-school businesses, and the cohort loves the product. Jason praised this analysis.
- Big Commerce math from Jesse: 1/7 of 37,000 stores do over $400K a year. 5% converting to the team plan is about +$40K MRR. 5% on the business plan is about +$100K MRR.
- Jason's focus: "agencies and Big Commerce" over also chasing big brands generally.
- Why agencies: each averages about 3 customers over time. A direct brand pays once and stays flat, while an agency compounds. Jason calls it a parabola versus a flat line.
- Agency tactics:
  - Run a deliberate motion, not passive inbound.
  - Go back to existing agencies and ask about other clients who need a blog (content marketing, LLM visibility). The agency makes money on a new blog project.
  - Send agencies a monthly newsletter to stay top of mind.
  - Tier agencies: nurture the top ones regularly, treat the long tail differently.
- Some agencies want kickbacks, others are offended by them. He told WP Engine agencies "whatever you want."
- Where to meet them: events and podcasts, referral channels and online communities. At WP Engine he met agencies by going to WordCamps and chatting online.
- Look for existing podcasts rather than starting one. Hosts want good stories, and the AI visibility topic is current.

chunks.heading: Run it like a company initiative: owner, budget, separate metrics
chunks.text:
- Jason would not announce a "new strategy". It makes staff nervous. Frame it as expansion: "and, not instead of", the mission is unchanged, here are the green shoots, here's how every role contributes.
- Each initiative needs a single owner whose only thought is that area (an agency lead, a Big Commerce lead). Otherwise the existing business always wins every competing priority.
- Cordon off the budget and revenue for each so you can see its numbers and decide when to shift money between them.
- Metrics differ per track (SMB newsletter is for retention, agency newsletter is for growth), so measure them separately.
- If you've never done account-based marketing, hire or consult someone who has built it. Setting up the system is a different person than executing it.
- A ~$700/month plan can fund a lot; ~$400/month funds demos but not full ABM. He distinguishes enterprise-group selling from true enterprise sales like a $10M Workday install.
- Idea for a stronger presence: an online conference. At WP Engine in-person events were very effective but costly. When they moved online with pre-recorded talks, speakers chatted live in the room and live Q&A followed. It positioned them as the experts and gave a reason to reach agencies. Use 2-3 topics (e.g. "blogging in 2026").
- First-three-month plan: use ads and calls to learn the positioning that really lands with marketers (the scared, old-school marketer at a Big Commerce company), then scale.

chunks.heading: Not every plateau needs this playbook (Rob's framing, Jason's contribution)
chunks.text:
- Jason cites his own essay on the "elephant curve": everything plateaus, and at some point you change strategy (new product, new customer type, new big channel).
- A plateau at $5K MRR is a different problem from one at $1M+. Optimising existing channels has already been tried here, so the next lever is a new segment or channel.
- Jason's own book is Hidden Multipliers (hiddenmultipliers.com).

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jason Cohen argues that durable strategies come from interlocking decisions that include deliberate weaknesses, which create unique strengths competitors won't copy because nobody copies weaknesses. He uses Craigslist and Southwest Airlines as examples, then shows how to focus on the ICP and ignore out-of-scope customers.

chunks.heading: Why Craigslist wins despite looking terrible
chunks.text:
- Craigslist has barely changed its site in 25 years, and a Harvard Business School case predicted new entrants would beat it with a better user experience.
- Many tried, including OfferUp, which appeared in the original case. Several became multi-billion dollar companies, but none displaced Craigslist.
- In 2024 Craigslist did about three quarters of a billion dollars of revenue with 50 employees. Jason says it is 10 to 20 times more profitable per employee than very successful tech companies.
- The CEO's stated position: "creating a superior user experience is more important than making money." Harvard read that, plus consistency over innovation, as the obstacle to growth.
- Jason's explanation is that the apparent weaknesses create special strengths:
  - A minimal, stagnant UX means anyone can use it, including non-technical people. Craig Newmark has said part of the purpose was to help people get onto the internet.
  - No images means it is fast on slow connections and slow devices, so more people can use it.
  - More users means a big selection, which matters a lot for marketplaces.
  - Cheap servers, easy engineering maintenance and easy tech support keep costs low. Supporting 14 languages is easy because the product is simple and does not change.
- His key insight: it goes beyond "everything is a trade-off." Weaknesses enable strengths that would otherwise be impossible, and that is what makes the strategy unique and durable.

chunks.heading: Southwest Airlines: the same pattern in a different industry
chunks.text:
- Southwest is the low-fare airline in an expensive industry (planes, maintenance, airports, fuel, people). It is by far the most profitable US airline and has been consistently profitable.
- Jason notes it dipped the least during COVID and recovered the fastest. He also says every other US airline in history has gone bankrupt.
- Its deliberate weaknesses:
  - No meals.
  - No travel agent support. Many businesses require travel agents for pricing and expense systems, and American Airlines does multiple billions in revenue through them.
  - Limited passenger service: only short point-to-point hops, no long hauls, no international.
  - Secondary airports.
  - No connections with other airlines and no bag transfers.
- The strengths those weaknesses create:
  - Short hauls and a limited route variety allow a single aircraft type. That brings bulk discounts from Boeing and low maintenance costs, because engineers need one set of tools and spare parts and learn the aircraft deeply, so they diagnose and fix things fast.
  - Paying employees well and giving them stock looks like a business-model weakness. It produces a great culture, lean and productive ground crews, and frequent, reliable departures that customers value.
  - High aircraft utilization makes it very profitable, which funds very low ticket prices.
- The diagram comes from Michael Porter's 1996 Harvard Business Review article. Porter's point is that a good strategy is a network of interlocking decisions that reinforce each other, which creates coherence. Jason adds that the "weaknesses" are necessary to create the special strengths.

chunks.heading: Why these strategies don't get copied
chunks.text:
- Craigslist and Southwest have stayed profitable for about 30 years in competitive, commoditized markets, even though their strategies are not secrets.
- Jason's theory: when you see a competitor do something great, you talk about copying their strengths ("that new feature is great," "their pricing structure is great").
- Nobody says "let's pay all our employees 30% more," "let's give everyone stock," "let's drop travel agents and give up billions in revenue," or "let's only fly short hops to secondary airports."
- Competitors copy strengths, not weaknesses. But the weaknesses created the unique strengths, so a competitor unwilling to copy them cannot win on those strengths and may not be able to deliver them at all.
- Result: the weaknesses themselves make the strategy uncopyable.

chunks.heading: Strengths and weaknesses depend on the customer
chunks.text:
- Jason admits he "cheated" by labeling things strengths and weaknesses. Customers see them differently.
- Business traveler: no travel agent support and no connections are deal breakers, not mere weaknesses.
- Casual traveler (his example is a 20-something going to Vegas for the weekend): loves the low fares, does not care about travel agents, meals on a two-hour flight, which airport, or connections. Paying staff well is a positive. For this person there are no red items at all.
- Family traveling with kids in summer: likes the low fares, but multiple hops across the country is a negative, so they weigh a trade-off and sometimes pick Southwest.
- This gives a spectrum:
  - Ideal customer profile (ICP): sees no weaknesses.
  - Addressable market: from the perfect customer through people who see both sides and sometimes choose you as a trade-off.
  - Out of scope: people for whom your weaknesses are deal breakers.

chunks.heading: Tip 1: Focus everything on the ICP and show the trade-off clearly
chunks.text:
- Focus means everything: marketing, sales, the website, product development and features, aimed at the ideal customer rather than the whole addressable market.
- If the perfect customer lands on your site, they should immediately see "this is perfect for me." If they don't, "you are doing a terrible job explaining your product." You need to win that whole niche.
- He argues you won't lose the wider addressable market this way. Those buyers are making a trade-off, so they need to see your strengths clearly to know what they are trading. When the choice is clear, he says you "actually sign up more of the addressable market."
- He calls this how to maximize customers.

chunks.heading: Tip 2: Ignore out-of-scope customers, even when they sign up
chunks.text:
- This sounds easy but is hard, because out-of-scope people still become customers. Reasons he gives: they didn't realize it wasn't right for them, they hoped it would work, or (in business) someone else bought it and made them use it.
- They show up in tech support complaining, asking for features and integrations, reporting bugs, asking for UX changes, and leaving reviews.
- It is tempting to put all of it into the product management system and prioritize it. Jason says you must not.
- Know who your out-of-scope addressable customer is, and ignore their feature requests, bug reports and confusion. "They will drag you to a place that's not your strategy."

chunks.heading: The full recipe for intentional weakness
chunks.text:
- Your strategy is a set of interlocking decisions.
- Your unique strengths come from picking weaknesses that create them.
- Competitors won't copy the weaknesses, so the whole strategy is uncopyable.
- It also defines clear target markets: who wants this set of trade-offs and who doesn't.
- The question Jason ends on: "What intentional weaknesses are you going to put in your strategy to create unique and uncopyable strengths?"

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jason Cohen describes four sincere failed OKR attempts at WP Engine and names the "Precision Fallacy": the unfalsifiable claim that any framework failure is the implementer's fault. His fix is to treat frameworks like off-the-rack shirts, tailoring them through small experiments, and he shares how a self-chosen, controllable metrics framework worked instead.

chunks.heading: Frameworks fail without being wrong: "You didn't do it right" is an unfalsifiable excuse
chunks.text:
Jason tried OKRs four separate times at WP Engine (within one team, across a department, and across the whole company) and failed every time. The team read John Doerr's *Measure What Matters*, paid for training, gave presentations and coached people one on one. The experts' answer was always "You didn't do it right."

- He accepts that OKRs are a great framework, since plenty of organizations swear by them. He also says that if a framework is that hard to do right, it may be too hard to do.
- He sees the same pattern with Scrum (Ron Jeffries calls it "Dark Scrum"), jobs-to-be-done, Aaron Ross's prospecting/closing split for SDR teams, content marketing and Holacracy.
- Content marketing example: two years, two hundred posts, flat organic traffic, and the excuses never run out (not 10x content, no topical authority, no links, the algorithm changed).
- Holacracy example: at Zappos, 18% of the workforce took a buyout, and the company later reverted. He says the other companies he knows of that tried it also reverted.
- He has heard "You didn't do it right" about Scrum from teams that then succeeded with Kanban.

chunks.heading: The Precision Fallacy
chunks.text:
Jason names the fallacy behind the retort: the belief that a more precise understanding or implementation would have worked, where the precision is either undefined or so intricate that nobody can follow it.

- Its distinguishing property is that it can't be disproved. No matter how many sincere, capable teams fail, the answer is never "This isn't the right process for you" or "It's the wrong framework in these circumstances."
- That means the framework never gets boundaries for where it applies.
- He cites Karl Popper, who watched friends do this with Marx and Freud: "whatever happened always confirmed it." A theory that no evidence can disprove isn't a valid theory.
- Four sincere, well-trained failures at WP Engine are not evidence that OKRs are universally applicable. A team that went on to succeed with a different framework is not evidence that the first one was a poor fit for them.
- His conclusion: every framework works inside some context and not outside it, and he believes "not working" is the most common case.

chunks.heading: Try a framework on like clothes
chunks.text:
Jason uses a clothing analogy for adopting frameworks.

- Having no framework is like sewing a shirt from scratch when you don't know how. It will be a mess, which is why you went looking for a framework.
- A framework is a shirt off the rack. It's shirt-shaped and fits some people.
- Maybe 15% of the time it fits perfectly and you're done. These are the well-known successes that framework experts cite.
- The normal case is that it fits OK but is wrong in about three places. The answer is to tailor it: ask what you liked and didn't like, and adjust.
- Sometimes the fit is so wrong it can't be iterated into shape. Even then you've gained experience that helps you pick a different framework with more fidelity.
- Frameworks, like people and products, must match the culture, the people, the other processes and the collective desires of the organization. Even the creators and proponents typically don't know the conditions under which it will succeed.

chunks.heading: Roll out a framework as an experiment, not an announcement
chunks.text:
- Announcing to the whole company "We're switching to OKRs" creates instant detractors, and the rollout will probably fail.
- Instead say: "One team is going to try this for a quarter and find out what we like and what we don't."
- He says this isn't only a communication trick to get naysayers to try it. It's how you actually try it on, make alterations, or put it back and try something else.

chunks.heading: What worked at WP Engine: a self-chosen metrics framework
chunks.text:
OKRs never worked for Jason's teams. What did work was a metrics framework he created and then tuned through feedback (his Product KPI framework, written up in his product-metrics article).

- It wasn't "better than OKRs." People liked it because it held them accountable in a way they wanted to be held accountable.
- It did not hold them accountable for outcomes they influenced but didn't completely control. He calls that "the unlock."
- From his metrics article: "Whenever management requires a KPI that the team doesn't believe in, doesn't respect, doesn't care about, the team always wins."

chunks.heading: How he rolled out the metrics framework, step by step
chunks.text:
1. Start with one team.
2. Each person picks one metric, anywhere on the chart. He says it genuinely doesn't matter where.
3. Attach a goal to it. A very loose one is fine.
4. The only real requirement is that the person personally wants it: not because a manager asked, and not even because it's "good for the company." They should believe "we are not doing our jobs if this isn't true" or "we're failing at our craft if we don't accomplish this." It should connect to personal pride.
5. Track that one metric for a quarter.
6. Then ask what other metric belongs. Add one or two, not ten.
7. Grow outward from what the team has already accepted.

He closes without claiming it will work elsewhere: maybe it will, maybe some iteration of it, maybe something else entirely. "Just try something on."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jason Cohen argues that confidence scores in frameworks like RICE are noise: undefined, untrustworthy, and they bias prioritization toward small safe projects. He proposes uncertainty-proof techniques instead: bet on what is always true, validate with behavior, measure impact, invest in leverage, maximize optionality, and choose between portfolios and asymmetric bets.

chunks.heading: Why Jason distrusts confidence scores in prioritization
chunks.text:
- Frameworks like RICE ("Reach x Impact x Confidence / Effort") and RPS ("Reach x Potential x Solution Confidence") bake confidence into the score. Jason argues this is the wrong use.
- A small incremental feature he is sure he can ship and a large, high-impact, risky feature then score as equals. He calls that equality false.
- Teams are nearly always choosing between exactly those two kinds of project. They are confident about small ones and unconfident about large ones, "as well we should be."
- The result is that confidence systematically skews prioritization away from delivering as much value as possible, which he says is the opposite of what a framework should do.
- A sane use of confidence is as a tiebreaker only:
  1. Score the projects.
  2. If there is one clear winner, do it.
  3. If there is a tie, pick the one you are more confident in.

chunks.heading: Why he doesn't believe the numbers
chunks.text:
- **Ill-defined.** "30%" only means something if you track your confidence scores across all projects, compare them to outcomes, and compute how accurate you were. Teams don't do this. Teams that ship only a few major features a year lack the data to know, even in hindsight.
- **Always overconfident.** Projects are nearly always late and often have less impact, less quickly, than hoped, however confident the team was. They were at least "fairly confident" or they would not have agreed to a nine-month, six-team project.
- Hofstadter's Law: "It always takes longer than you expect, even when you take Hofstadter's Law into account."
- **Experienced PMs have stories.** Ask any experienced product manager about a feature they were certain would be well-received, backed by customer conversations, explicit requests or purchase commitments, that almost nobody used, including people who promised they would. Everyone has these stories, and that is his point.
- **Content creators see the same thing.** Hastily produced pieces they almost didn't publish often outperform work they spent dozens of hours on. He quotes the Twitter example of hours on threads with no traction versus 10 minutes on two tweets that each drew 15K+ followers.
- His two-by-two of confident/not confident versus loved/ignored has "lots of examples" in every cell.
- A mitigation for stated demand: ask customers to describe exactly how they would use a feature in their normal workflow, step by step. They often realize it would mean rewriting code or exporting to another system, and back off.

chunks.heading: Probability vs. uncertainty
chunks.text:
- Probability assumes you know the underlying distribution, like 100 fair coin flips landing between 40 and 60 heads.
- Almost nothing in a startup is like that. Strategies, features and startup success are unprecedented, too complex to model, or lack precision on inputs. This is Knightian uncertainty (Frank Knight, 1921).
- Bayesian methods don't rescue it, since they need numeric priors and conditional probabilities, which are unknowable and ill-defined.
- The question he asks instead: what actions are wise regardless of the probability distribution?

chunks.heading: Techniques for prioritizing under uncertainty
chunks.text:
**True always**
- Focus on what is true under any circumstance, in Bezos's sense of long-term constants (lower prices, faster shipping, fair and fast service).
- Example: users universally like fast, responsive software. At worst they don't care; at best (Notion, Figma, Miro, Gmail, Google Docs) performance is a differentiator.
- Mandatory-but-mundane items such as SOC 2 compliance are certain to be valuable when selling to enterprises.
- Caveat: your most innovative, differentiated ideas rarely fall in this "certain" bucket. Great products need both reliable improvements and leaps of faith.

**Quick discovery, quick recovery**
- Customer interviews can invalidate an idea before you build, saving months or years, but "you never really know until you build."
- Build an SLC (his upgrade of the MVP: simple but complete) to get experience instead of prediction.
- For existing products, keep a balanced portfolio of guaranteed wins and innovative bets, using different validation for each.
- "Dummy features": a button that says "This feature isn't built yet. Tell us how you'd use it." You get a count of interested users and interview candidates who showed interest through action. He says this gives 100x better signal than hypothetical survey questions: "Observed behavior beats stated intentions."

**Focus on customer impact instead of confidence**
- Majority rule: a feature most users use regularly is important.
- Passionate advocates: features a smaller segment says are the only reason they bought. These "magnificent delighters" drive purchase decisions, and users tolerate shortcomings elsewhere (the iPod's magic made people put up with iTunes).
- His quantified bar: a high-impact feature is either (1) regularly used by at least 51% of customers, or (2) cited by at least 15% of customers among their top three reasons for choosing or retaining the product.
- The bar is deliberately high because risky projects that may overrun need rewards that justify the risk.

chunks.heading: Leverage and optionality
chunks.text:
**Invest in leverage**
- Some areas of the business or product reward small changes with outsized results. He points to his book *Hidden Multipliers*, which covers eleven such areas of leverage with your current budget and team.

**Maximize optionality**
- If you can't know the future, make choices that keep the most options open. Examples:
  - Keep costs low so many pricing and packaging options stay profitable.
  - Choose established, actively developed, cross-platform UI frameworks.
  - Use a plug-in architecture so others can build things you can't imagine.
  - Use an API-first architecture to isolate teams and connect front-end, back-end and integrations.
  - Wrap vendor services so you can swap vendors that become unstable, expensive or laggy.
- Optionality costs work today (vendor-wrapping APIs add no value now). That suits mature companies that value stability over shipping a feature a month earlier, but may be wrong for early-stage companies that need velocity to beat incumbents.
- Company-level optionality comes from being a great company: healthy sustained growth, large and expanding gross margins, customers who love you (retention, upgrades, online chatter), employees who love you (longevity, advancement). Such a company can be acquired on decent terms, run as-is for a long time, raise money, never raise, go public, or be passed to employees or children.

chunks.heading: Portfolios vs. asymmetric bets
chunks.text:
**Portfolio of bets**
- Portfolios reduce variability at the cost of lower maximum upside: you are unlikely to have zero wins, but even a massive win is diluted by the losses. His example: buying Amazon at IPO and holding would have been best, but the same advice applied to other IPOs that year gives $0.
- They work regardless of the underlying distribution because of the Central Limit Theorem. Sample means converge to a normal distribution with the population mean and variance of 1/n of the population variance. A Lindeberg-type version holds even with different distributions per sample, if independence, finite variance and no dominant variable hold.
- Those conditions arguably fail for startups, since some power laws have infinite variance.
- Use portfolios when you want predictable, typical outcomes, such as prioritizing many smaller things for incremental reliable results.
- Don't use them to hunt outliers. He cites that 65% of venture/angel portfolios lose money and only about 10% generate returns high enough to justify the risk and illiquidity. Outlier hunting calls for all-in investments, not portfolios.

**Asymmetric bets**
- Portfolios give reliability; asymmetric bets give outliers. You don't predict whether it pays off. You take bets with limited, quantifiable downside and large upside.
- Example: if the worst case is "we lose two months" and the best case is "we're completely differentiated," the probability barely matters. The downside must be survivable and one win must pay for ten losses. "The exact probabilities are unknowable; the *shape* of each bet is not."
- At the feature level you usually have to construct the asymmetry. Software projects default to drifting from "two weeks" to "two months" to "we've spent so long we have to finish it."
- The mechanism is a budget written down before starting, for example "two engineers, three weeks, then we stop and look." The time-box is the bounded downside.

chunks.heading: What to use instead of confidence in a framework
chunks.text:
- Replace "confidence" with "how asymmetric." RICE asks for a probability you've already conceded you can't know.
- Asymmetry asks for two things you can estimate: the worst case in time and money, and the best case in customer value. Both are concrete and can be argued to a defensible number in a meeting.
- He recommends restricting all numbers to powers of ten when doing this.
- His closing line: "Stop pretending you can quantify confidence, or even define it. Instead, use techniques that work whenever the future is unpredictable. Because it always is."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jason Cohen argues you must hire people better than you at every role, or the company just gets bigger, not better. Since you can't assess domain expertise, he offers proxies: ideas you want to implement, learning from them, leadership breadth, a real problem test, and reference checks aimed at culture fit.

chunks.heading: Hiring above your own level means testing for signal, not expertise
chunks.text:
- Jason says that if you don't hire people better than you, "the organization gets bigger, not better." Without hiring up, organizations get worse with size: more overhead, more meetings, more communication cost, with no improvement in individual capability.
- He argues a great person is not ten times better than an average one. They are "infinitely better," because they come up with ideas and implementations a hundred average people never would.
- Early on, the CEO is the best person at some things (sales from passion, product from vision). By around a hundred people, if the CEO is still better than everyone at anything, the CEO has hired poorly and the company is suffering.
- The core problem: you hire a VP of Marketing precisely because you can't do the job, so you also can't judge whether the candidate can. Jason compares it to evaluating a pancreatic surgeon.
- Since domain expertise can't be assessed, he looks for other signals: ideas you want to implement, learning from the person, organization-wide leadership ability, and fit confirmed by references.

chunks.heading: Signal 1: you leave the interview wanting to implement their ideas
chunks.text:
- Test: after the conversation, do you think "Even if we don't hire them, we've got to do half of the things they said"? Maybe you start working on it right away.
- You can't verify that the advice is wise. But the feeling means the ideas connected deeply, which is at minimum a culture fit, and the ideas are plausible for your situation and constraints.
- Genuine expertise produces specific, actionable ideas that feel tailor-made to your context. People who "talk a good game" say impressive, broadly true things that leave you wondering "is that really what grown-up Marketing is?" instead of "Hell yes that's what I want this company to be like."
- Jason's heuristic: if they change how you think about your own company in an hour, imagine what they could do in a year.
- Red flag: a candidate who speaks fluently about frameworks but never connects them to the challenges you described five minutes earlier is parroting what they've seen. "ChatGPT can do that too." You want someone born for this job, not performing the generic version.
- Competitor test: if they went to work for your competitor, would you think "Uh oh, now we're dead?" Or "I'm not sure what they would do for that competitor?"

chunks.heading: Signal 2: you're already learning from them, and so would others
chunks.text:
- Jason reworks Zuckerberg's executive hiring rule, "you should only hire people to be on your team if you would work for them." He notes it isn't literally true of Zuckerberg, but the spirit is a good test.
- Weakest version: if you wouldn't be comfortable working for this person, you're hiring out of expediency, not quality.
- Better: would you learn from this person, and would others at the company? He says this is true of every great executive, and clear enough to tell in the interview because it has already happened. They said something you didn't know, you checked it afterwards, and fell down rabbit holes you never knew existed, ones the candidate already knew about.
- The "sabbatical test": if you took a six-month sabbatical and never checked in, would the department be measurably better under them when you returned? That means improved processes, a stronger team, higher output.
- He calls this "lift": the hire takes work away from you and builds a better department than you were building. "Your job isn't to also know all those things; it's to hire people who do."

chunks.heading: Signal 3: they will elevate the whole organization
chunks.text:
- Great leaders improve more than their silo. They are better at people issues, communication, decision-making, goal-setting, annual planning and org structure, which help everywhere in the company.
- Example: a great VP Marketing won't contribute to your TypeScript-specific `CLAUDE.md`, but will have theories on:
  - growing from three to thirty teams
  - setting annual goals while keeping people focused on the present
  - communicating difficult news to the whole company
  - knowing when it's time to adopt "big company" policies
  - structuring a two-day strategic retreat
  - handling a conflict between two employees
  - running performance management as objectively and humanely as possible
- You can test this in the interview by asking how they'd handle these situations, using ones you're facing now, just faced, or fear after reading a forum. Frame it as leadership in a company, not as their domain expertise.

chunks.heading: Interview tactic: give them a real problem from your company
chunks.text:
- Pose an actual challenge. Examples he gives: how would you implement goal-setting in a culture that's never had goals; how would you diagnose the cause of high churn; how would you figure out why turnover is high when people won't explain themselves.
- You're not grading the answer's details. You're watching how they think and what direct experience they have.
- Look for:
  - incisive, clarifying questions that show they understand what you're going through
  - acknowledging what they don't yet know
  - naming a framework and explaining how they applied it
  - any sign they did it themselves rather than parroting blog posts

chunks.heading: Reference checks: use them for culture fit, not expertise
chunks.text:
- Jason says standard reference checks are useless for expertise because candidates hand over friendlies primed to say nice things. They are powerful for judging whether the person will thrive in this company at this stage.
- He asks references three questions:
  1. "What is the ideal scenario under which this person thrives?" Construct the perfect circumstances (subject matter, goal, team or lack of one, direction or lack of it, incentives) where they are efficient, productive, happy, and make everyone around them happy.
  2. "Construct the scenario where they die inside, mess everything up, and piss everyone off." It's funny, easy to answer, and doesn't feel like negativity, since everyone has a personal hell.
  3. "What are their strengths that they're unaware of because they come so naturally to them?" These are abilities they don't realize are unusual; others do, and find them annoying and endearing.
- Example reading: a reference says the person needs a goal to know what success looks like, then needs you to get out of their way because they explore quickly. That yields attributes like "goal-oriented" and "craves exploration," which suggests an early-stage startup fits better than a mature product.
- Why focus on strengths: everyone has weaknesses. You're not hiring someone without weaknesses but someone with a few special strengths that your company needs right now. "Not just competence, but superpowers," which is the difference between "filling the seat" and making an impact.

chunks.heading: Handling mis-hires and accepting uncertainty
chunks.text:
- Jason has hired people who were great in interviews but couldn't do the job, and people who were unimpressive in interviews and "crushed it for ten years."
- Only one error is costly. A false negative costs a continued search. A false positive hurts the team, delays getting the right person, and hurts the hire, who may have quit a job. If it happens a lot, "you have to fix yourself."
- What you control is what happens after. Don't let it linger for a year, annoying your best people (who can most easily find other jobs) and delaying the department.
- Signs you hired wrong:
  - it feels easier to just do it yourself
  - your best people complain constantly instead of being inspired
  - things don't start improving immediately
- The team knows before you do, and only you can fix it. "Make the break cleanly. Act immediately; you're already three months late."
- Even a year later you won't know whether their strategy was optimal, since you never get the counterfactual. What you will know is whether they changed how you see your company, found problems you didn't know about, built things you didn't think to build, and made the people around them (including you) sharper. Those clues are available in the interview, and culture fit is available in reference checks.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Real strategy is a small set of macro-level choices between two genuinely good options, with all consequences accepted. Platitudes like "great design" are non-decisions. Good choices have real alternatives, explicit downsides, and reinforce each other so decentralized teams compound instead of dilute.

chunks.heading: Real strategy means choosing between two good options
chunks.text:
- Jason's test: a strategic choice is only real if the opposite is also smart. "Good design" fails, because "bad design" was never a sensible alternative. "All-in-one" vs "a small core, extremely extensible" passes, since many successful companies with great products have chosen each side.
- He calls this another form of the Opposite Test: checking that "the opposite" isn't trivial or nonsense is how you know you're saying something real.
- "Both" is not a sensible choice. Either the product is self-contained or it isn't; either support can answer questions about the whole product or it routes you to plugin vendors.
- Platitudes ("Customer-first," "Quality over shortcuts," "Great design over mediocrity") are non-decisions. Nobody says "our strategy is low quality and ugly design," yet mediocre products exist because companies chose other priorities (price, speed, extensibility, power, complexity) and the trade-offs showed up as low quality.
- "A strategy that never says 'no' is not a strategy. It should say 'no' most of the time; that's a signal that you are actually focusing."

chunks.heading: Why companies need a small set of strategic choices
chunks.text:
- Everyone making independent decisions is how you scale, whether you have three people or three hundred, but locally rational decisions can contradict each other across teams. Then the company goes nowhere even if everyone is productive.
- Autonomous teams still need alignment, not on weekly tactics or platitudes, but on a small set of macro-level decisions.
- When daily decisions conform to the strategic ones, "more people" actually produces "more results." Customers stop seeing dissonance between the homepage promises and what engineering built, and decisions compound instead of diluting each other.
- He borrows the term from Roger L. Martin (*Playing to Win*, 2013), whose definition: "Strategy is an integrated set of choices that uniquely positions the firm in its industry so as to create sustainable advantage and superior value relative to the competition."
- Your unique set of choices makes you "the best" for your target market.

chunks.heading: Write down the consequences, including the painful ones
chunks.text:
- A platitude feels good because it has no downside. If it's all good news, it isn't a real choice, or you aren't grappling with the consequences.
- Example, "great design" costs: talented designers (a larger team), engineers who chase every UI bug before the next shiny feature, design systems, slower features, saying "no" to features customers want if the design would worsen, and thrilling some people while irritating others who define good design differently.
- "A strategic choice is a package deal: you don't get advantages without weaknesses."
- Writing the consequences into the strategy makes the decision usable company-wide. It reduces individual interpretation and helps everyone align daily decisions.
- The list also lets you check the whole strategy for internal consistency.

chunks.heading: Make choices mutually reinforcing, not just consistent
chunks.text:
- Use the list of choice-consequences to find contradictions; conflicts often hide in second-order effects.
- Example: "small team" and "feature-rich" look unrelated, but a small team usually means a small, simple product because the team must build, maintain, support and evolve it.
- Resolution: add another choice. A small team can maintain a small core designed for third-party extensions, and a plugin/API ecosystem makes the product feature-rich. Now "small team," "small core," and "extensible ecosystem" interlock, each surfacing further choices.
- Better than non-conflicting is reinforcing: "extensible" helps "feature-rich"; a small team forces the core to stay small, leaving room for the ecosystem.
- Strong, reinforcing choices give the company a personality, "an opinion about How The World Should Be." Some customers won't share it, but those who do will love you more. "Love is how you win."
- Payoffs: you stop re-litigating trade-offs, marketing and sales stay aligned with product, and "coherence feels like competence."

chunks.heading: Converting weak pseudo-choices into real ones (facilitation)
chunks.text:
- When facilitating, people write weak choices that fail the Opposite Test. They already know their preferred side and make the other side obviously bad so theirs "wins," instead of struggling to decide.
- Jason's technique, ask:
  - "What are some successful and beloved companies that chose the 'bad' side?"
  - "What is the underlying reason why people love that company despite that flaw?"
- That thing people love is the actual other side of the strategic choice.
- Worked example: "well-designed UX, not bad UX" is fake. Why do beloved products have poor UX? Because a small core plus plugins lets third-party software "do anything," which is wonderful but costs UX coherence.
- Real-world case: Apple Notes and Bear are cohesive because they control the whole experience (no plugins, not even an API). Obsidian offers a huge range of downloadable functionality; people complain the UX is a hodgepodge but love building their own ideal system. The real choice is "all-in-one vs infinitely extensible," with design as one consequence.

chunks.heading: "Why not both?" The rule for when to take both
chunks.text:
- Everyone will "cheat" eventually: you build all-in-one, then customers love a competitor's plugins, so you explore plugins. Or "we should raise the price" or "we should slow down and polish this." These tempt precisely because the other side is also smart.
- Strategy exists so anyone can say: "Yes, that's a good idea in the abstract, but no, it doesn't fit the bundle of trade-offs we have chosen."
- The rule: "When in conflict, adhere to the strategic choice. When not in conflict, do whatever is best."
- Example: with a lowest-price strategy (which often implies lower quality), you still take quality wins that don't raise cost: better design choices, better suppliers, scale, great employees.
- Don't introduce a high-price offering "to get some of those customers" if you chose low price.
- The losing position is "it's a balance": not enough quality and design to earn loyalty, not enough power and breadth to win complex use cases, so you lose both markets.
- He cites the Agile Manifesto as the model: "While there is value in the items on the right, we value the items on the left more." It's a mechanism for consistency under pressure, a strict choice, "not a balance."

chunks.heading: Strategic choice pairs and their trade-offs
chunks.text:
Jason's examples (each side has real advantages and weaknesses):

- **Lowest price vs premium price.** Lowest price: biggest market, many competitors can never win on price; but you can't afford advertising and sales (word-of-mouth must carry you) and cost caps quality. Premium: high margins fund brand, polish and distribution; but a smaller market, and you must keep funding the brand or the premium collapses.
- **Cohesive all-in-one UX vs extensible ecosystem.** All-in-one: delight, trust, simple support and docs; but you own feature breadth and power users leave. Ecosystem: long-tail capability and partners as distribution; but the UX becomes "a quilt" and security, compatibility and support become a supply-chain problem.
- **Simple UX vs powerful capability.** Simple: short time-to-value, self-serve growth, less churn; but you lose complex workflows and checklist/RFP deals. Powerful: deep high-stakes workflows, high revenue per customer, switching costs; but onboarding needs training and specialists, and customers "operate" the product.
- **Minimal vs high-touch support.** Minimal: higher margins, forces ruthless usability and docs; but you can't sell to buyers requiring SLAs, and stuck users churn silently. High-touch: loyalty and a product discovery engine ("you hear the truth daily"); but expensive, hard to scale, creates 24/7 expectations.
- **Small-team simplicity vs enterprise complexity.** Simplicity: shorter sales cycles, low implementation burden; but you lose governance/audit deals and face constant "one more thing" pressure. Enterprise: passes procurement, big budgets, lock-in; but long sales cycles and bloat because every screen must honor roles and policies.
- **Cutting-edge speed vs rock-solid stability.** Speed: novelty differentiates and attracts early adopters; but bugs become part of the brand. Stability: trust is the moat for critical workflows; but you're slow and risk obsolescence.
- **Open vs closed source.** Open: lower trust barrier, community leverage; but monetization is hard and governance gets political. Closed: full control of roadmap, UX and pricing power; but slower adoption where transparency matters and you fund velocity yourself.
- **Fewer, better features vs more features.** Fewer: polish, retention, word-of-mouth, fewer bugs and tickets; but you lose checklists and under-serve edge cases. More: win procurement comparisons and upsell paths; but uneven quality, collapsing UX coherence, and exploding docs/support.

chunks.heading: Closing principle
chunks.text:
- "The weaknesses of your choices are painful to accept. The advantages of the opposite choices sound wonderful. Welcome to strategy, where you make hard choices."
- "If the choice wasn't hard to make, it wasn't actually a choice."
- Leaders should make the hard choices once, so everyone else is relieved of that burden and can decide independently and smartly.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jason Cohen argues that "focus" only works if you actually stop doing most things. Each thing you drop (bad-fit customers, generic marketing, minor metrics, parallel opportunities) frees time and energy to execute the few things that decide whether a company thrives or perishes.

chunks.heading: Doing less is a prerequisite for excellence, not a trade-off against it
chunks.text:
- Jason's core claim: stopping most activities is what gives you the time and energy to "fully, deeply execute the most important things", and those things "are the difference between thriving and perishing."
- He answers the objection that quantity sometimes beats quality, or that you should test a bunch of things, by arguing that spreading across everything leaves nothing executed deeply.
- He frames "Focus!" as the one piece of advice given to startups, to CEOs of large companies, and then passed down to their teams. His point is that the word is only useful once you define what you stop doing.
- He cites Sylvia Plath's fig tree passage as the cost of indecision: wanting every fig, choosing none, and watching them all rot and fall.
- His framing device is "create space." Every thing you stop doing opens room for something with higher return.
- He closes with: "We don't have unlimited time or energy, but we can better spend the limited time that we have." That is why: "Focus."

chunks.heading: Sales and customers: drop the bad fits to multiply the good ones
chunks.text:
- Stop selling to people who aren't a good fit. This creates space for "3x more sales pitches, each with 3x the close-rate."
- Help draining customers exit the business. This frees time for easy, happy customers who want to spend more every year and give you positive energy.
- Stop trying to win over everyone, so you can win over the right ones (the ideal customer persona).
- Stop trying to please every ill-fitting customer. That creates space to convert "satisfied" customers into "fanatics" who drive word-of-mouth growth, leave positive reviews, and never cancel even if something bad happens.
- Stop trying to win every battle with every competitor. Win the ones that matter most to the people in your ideal market.

chunks.heading: Product, metrics and differentiation: concentrate on the few things that matter
chunks.text:
- Stop chasing every metric and you can "attack the one metric that will transform the company."
- Stop maximizing every metric and you can maximize the few that matter most (his product-metrics idea).
- Stop trying to improve everything by 1% and you can "improve the biggest thing by 30%."
- Stop trying to shore up every weakness and you can leverage your strengths.
- Stop trying to do everything in a novel way (UX, coding, pricing, org structure) and you create space for "a few truly impactful modes of differentiation."
- Stop pursuing every opportunity and you can fully capitalize on the one with "the thickest intersection" of upside potential and your ability to execute.
- Stop trying to "find the balance" in everything and you can maximize the one choice that creates clarity and strength.

chunks.heading: Marketing copy: replace generic words with specifics
chunks.text:
- Stop using lazy, generic words in marketing. That creates space on the page to communicate what you actually do, who you actually are, or why anyone should care.
- His implication is that page real estate is limited, and generic phrasing wastes it.

chunks.heading: Time, management and teams: schedule less, control less
chunks.text:
- Stop trying to schedule all work and you create space for impactful work (his rocks, pebbles and sand idea: big priorities first).
- Stop checking email and social media "every 11 minutes" and you create space to get "enveloped in the flow of creativity and productivity."
- Stop trying to control every last detail. This creates space for empowered teams to flourish, and for you to work on things only you can do, or only you ought to do.
- Stop reading garbage so you can read something meaningful, useful, enjoyable, inspiring or refreshing.

chunks.heading: Relationships and life: fewer, deeper
chunks.text:
- End toxic relationships, personal or professional, for you and the teams around you. This makes space for healthy ones.
- Stop creating superficial relationships with every stranger on social media, to create "deep, mutual, caring relationships."
- Stop trying to "have it all" so you can deeply experience the few things that are most important.

chunks.heading: Endorsed framing: one priority makes decisions easy
chunks.text:
- Jason closes the essay with Derek Sivers' passage from *Hell Yeah or No*: "Decisions are easy when you have only one priority."
- The image: your destination is a huge mountain peak on the horizon. You say yes to that mountain and no to everything else, and "all paths go either towards that mountain or away from it."
- With your eyes on the horizon you step over obstacles undeterred, while most people look at the ground and get upset by every obstacle.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jason Cohen argues "mission" and "vision" are fuzzy terms and replaces them with three concrete tools: a Purpose bigger than the company, an N-year Vision (what you build, for whom, the insight), and a measurable Next Milestone. He also separates purpose-driven from purpose-derived companies, citing Smart Bear and WP Engine.

chunks.heading: Mission, vision and purpose: Jason's view on what is useful
chunks.text:
- Jason is skeptical of "mission" and "vision" as terms. Pundits can't agree on definitions, and he notes two nearly opposite meanings of "mission":
  - A higher purpose bigger than the company (Patagonia: "to save our home planet"; Tesla: "to accelerate the world's transition to sustainable energy").
  - A current execution goal (an army battalion's mission; McDonald's "to be our customers' favorite place and way to eat and drink"; FedEx's "superior financial returns for its shareowners").
- He says that in early-stage startups these are mostly irrelevant, because founders are busy making things and discovering customers wanted something else. In large companies they become marketing-written fragments on "About Us" pages that "no one reads and no one believes".
- He still sees real value: Khan Academy ("a free, world-class education for anyone, anywhere"), TOMS, DuckDuckGo and Patagonia (the founder put the company in a trust) take their words seriously.
- Because the terms are untethered, he prefers three plainer words: Purpose, N-year Vision, Next Milestone.

chunks.heading: Why a higher purpose can help
chunks.text:
Jason lists the benefits Simon Sinek (_Start with Why_) and other researchers claim, in his own words:
- Loyal, vocal customers who tolerate high prices and missing features because the company is part of their identity.
- Passionate employees with lower turnover.
- Differentiation against profit-only companies that consumers dislike.
- Resilience in downturns and bad publicity.
- Consistency in messaging, prioritization and goals.
- Easier fundraising from angels who expect you'll probably fail but want to make a difference.
