- Higher profits (he flags weak evidence: a study found "purpose + execution" beat the market but "purpose alone" did not; "purpose-washing" may hurt, though hindsight bias is possible).
- Legacy that outlasts any person or product.

He adds that you don't have to be mission-driven to succeed. Most successful companies aren't, and you can simply "make a dollar and get out of here".

chunks.heading: Purpose: the transformation bigger than the company
chunks.text:
- Definition: "The transformation in the world that is bigger than ourselves, that we hope everyone involved is excited to help bring about."
- Examples: Khan's "Everyone deserves a free, world-class education"; Tesla's "Accelerate the world's transition to sustainable energy."
- It is never fully achieved, so it is not an operational goal. It answers "Why are we doing this at all? Why should anyone else care?"
- It is about others, not about us or what we do, and it matters even if the company didn't exist.
- Others adopting the same purpose is an ally, not competition. Jason's examples:
  - Khan Academy gives away its AI teaching assistant to other educators.
  - TOMS shares sustainable-materials R&D with other shoe makers.
  - Tesla open-sourced its core battery patents.
  - Netlify coined "jamstack"; rivals adopted it and eclipsed Netlify in revenue.

chunks.heading: N-year Vision: a specific future state
chunks.text:
- Definition: "Our desired future state: what we will have achieved?" It must be different from today but not so far out that it isn't actionable.
- Rule of thumb for N: divide the company's age by 3 and round up. Smaller for new companies, larger for established ones.
- It must cover three things, in one or two sentences:
  - What we built (the product or service).
  - For whom (a subset of customers, can be larger than the ICP, never "everyone").
  - The insight (what makes this company "this company", in the product or how it gets there).
- His reductive examples:
  - Tesla: "Create the first high-performance luxury sports car for Americans that is powered only by batteries."
  - Patagonia: "Build the most durable, low-environmental-impact equipment for serious rock-climbers."
  - Amazon: "Create the largest and most affordable bookstore on Earth, by selling exclusively online with just-in-time inventory."
- Original audiences: Tesla started with rich Americans, Patagonia with serious American rock-climbers, Amazon with only 2,000 titles. Amazon's insight was operational: no physical stores and almost no inventory ("Your margin is my opportunity").
- Because it is over-simplified, it is the starting point for a fuller strategy document. The short version aids comprehension and communication.
- It should be clear, concise, declarative, specific, "bold, but plausible."

chunks.heading: Next Milestone: the specific, operational step
chunks.text:
- Definition: "The most important thing to achieve next, and how we'll know when we've arrived."
- Method: work backwards from the N-year Vision. Template: "If we're going to achieve [final result] by [far-future-date], we will have to accomplish [1-5 critical projects or results]. So, right now what we need to accomplish next is [near-term project], and we'll know we've achieved it when [objective observable]."
- Unlike Purpose and Vision, the Milestone is specific, tactical, decisive and metrics-driven or at least metrics-influenced. Not everything important is a number.
- Examples he gives:
  - Pre-raise founder: wants $1M in 10 months, needs 200 paying customers before raising in 6 months, has only happy beta-testers. Next milestone: 20 paying customers, "enough that it's not a fluke."
  - $5M ARR, stalled: customers cancel at 5%/mo, so he mathematically cannot grow; some cohorts cancel at only 2% and pay 5x as much. Mixture is 10/90 in the wrong direction. Next milestone: shift new customers to a 35/65 mix.
  - Burned-out founder (5 years in): hire a new CEO and manage the transition so he can stay ten more years. He was in this position at WP Engine and calls Heather Brunner "our late-joining co-founder."
  - Growth-stalled but healthy unit economics: brainstorm adjacent spaces and run five experiments, then pick one or two, before committing millions of dollars.
  - Indie game studio: needs $600K for an 18-month dream game; makes about $12K/month profit. Milestone: ship a small high-margin DLC in 4 months, lifting profit to at least $20K/month.
  - 35-person agency growing 15%/yr: wants recurring revenue at 40% of business in three years. Milestone: package the most repeatable service as a fixed-price subscription and sign 10 recurring customers, even at a steep discount.
  - Open-source project with 50,000 GitHub stars: launch a hosted premium version, 50 paying customers, $10K MRR, enough for two people to quit their jobs.
  - Acquired 15-year-old manufacturer: modernize operations, implement an ERP, cut COGS 12% in six months to fund e-commerce.
  - Series B AI startup at $12M ARR, 90% gross margins, custom solutions: extract common patterns, build a self-serve platform covering 80% of use cases, migrate 3 existing customers.
- To operationalize it, he points to his quarterly strategic planning method, Rocks/Pebbles/Sand prioritization, and a sensible set of product metrics.

chunks.heading: Purpose-driven vs purpose-derived
chunks.text:
- Purpose-driven: fulfilling the Purpose is the origin and number-one goal, shown by advancing it even at the cost of sales, share or profit.
- Purpose-derived: the Purpose is real and good for others but a by-product of success, not the driver. He believes most companies fall here.
- His own companies were derived, not driven:
  - Smart Bear began as an idea to data-mine a software project's history, then became a code review tool. Derived Purpose: increase software quality. Evidence: after he sold it over 16 years ago, it accumulated nearly a dozen quality tools, many open-source. He also wrote a free book on doing reviews well that didn't require buying the software.
  - WP Engine began because his blog crashed when it hit Hacker News's front page, and other bloggers said "if you find it, tell me." Derived Purpose: enable everyone to run a superior website (fast, scalable, secure), since 99.9% of business owners shouldn't become technology experts. Customers have told him unprompted that it matters.
- Apple sold computers to hobbyists and took 21 years to reach "Think Different." It was purpose-derived: Apple "did not, in fact, start with why. But it got there."

chunks.heading: Making it real
chunks.text:
- Words on an "About Us" page don't create a Purpose. You create one by:
  - Figuring out the positive difference you can make.
  - Writing it succinctly.
  - Building it into strategy, positioning and goals.
- Jason's test: on your deathbed you can honestly say "What I did, mattered."
- Best case is being driven by a higher purpose from the start and building a sustainable organization around it. He notes this is an era where "it's possible to do good as well as become rich."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jason argues that demographics and firmographics (company size, geography, age) usually misdescribe a market. Using WP Engine, where Google and big banks bought "SMB" hosting, he shows the real target is people who share needs and reasons for buying. He gives the testimonial test and a long list of better segmentation dimensions.

chunks.heading: Define the target market by use-case and shared traits, not demographics
chunks.text:
- Jason dislikes target-market definitions built on demographics and firmographics ("small businesses in the UK", "females 19-29"). For most companies these dimensions describe the market incorrectly.
- Demographic definitions both over-target and under-target. Most people in the named demographic never buy, and many outside it do. The real target is whatever the buyers share that non-buyers lack.
- Ad copy shows the real target. An ad for a TV show won't say "if you're a female 19-29, watch this." It appeals to the genre, the actors, the aesthetic, the writing style, or the kind of person who watches it. That appeal is the target market.
- Demographics are legitimate only when the product is inextricably tied to them. His example is back-office software for dentist offices under Norwegian law.
- An email client's target market has nothing to do with B2B vs B2C, company size, or geography. It depends on use-cases: people with hundreds of emails a day who need processing workflows, people whose assistants handle mail, people who get few emails, security-conscious people, outbound campaigners, or shared support desks.

chunks.heading: Why Google and other large companies buy "small business" software
chunks.text:
- At WP Engine, early on, the website looked like "a small company selling to SMBs." Mid-sized and large companies bought anyway, a little in the first two years and substantially in the next two.
- They bought the same product the small customers bought, not Enterprise-sized multi-million-dollar contracts.
- Many founders see Google, Facebook, Salesforce or Oracle become customers and ask whether to "go up-market" with a sales team. Jason's short answer: "No."
- Individual teams inside large companies buy things too. Not everything at Google is purchased top-down and forced on its roughly 27,000 engineers.
- Those teams buy for the same reason a small business's only team buys. That reason defines the target market, and in turn the advertising, positioning, pricing and features.
- The exception: if your software really is purchased top-down and forced on users, you are selling to the enterprise, and that belongs in the target-market definition.

chunks.heading: WP Engine's real target market: a worked example
chunks.text:
- Enterprise use-cases of WordPress hosting at WP Engine:
  - One of the world's largest banks let branches publish their own content.
  - One of the largest software companies ran its developer-relations portal.
  - One of the largest software development tools companies hosted its public technical documentation.
  - One of the largest fast-food chains published social content in small countries, where local agencies could get culture, language and color right.
- The target market was not "small businesses and individuals with WordPress." It was WordPress users who valued:
  - Enterprise-grade quality: speed, scale, security, 24/7 high-quality tech support.
  - A flexible, open-source, inexpensive-to-build platform where employees or agencies were easy to hire anywhere in the world.
  - Pricing 10x or 100x above "cheap hosting" but 1/10 or 1/100 of "enterprise CMS solutions".
- To go deeper, keep asking "why do they value those things?"
  - They valued enterprise-grade quality because the website mattered, unlike throw-away or fun sites where price is the issue.
  - They valued flexibility because they wanted to change things themselves or outsource anywhere.
  - Some chose WordPress because marketers already knew it from personal projects.

chunks.heading: Turning the definition into positioning
chunks.text:
- A segment of "mid-sized companies" would produce a home page like "WordPress for mid-sized companies": soulless, boring, and unclear about what "mid-sized" means.
- Naming what the customers value gives something like "Enterprise-Grade WordPress" or "Affordable Enterprise-Grade WordPress."
- He says it could be made more authentic and interesting still, but it is already an improvement because it is specific about strengths (affordable, reliable, high-quality).
- The chain of whys gives internal clarity and a path to effective marketing.

chunks.heading: How to find the actual target market
chunks.text:
- Customer interviews are part of this: find customers and interview them to learn how they view the problem, how they describe it, their constraints, and what would compel them to buy.
- Use that information to build an ideal customer profile and target everything at only them.
- Don't add company size, industry or geography unless it is tied to the nature of the product so that it truly can't be sold or used outside that boundary.
- Jason also points to his Needs Stack framework (where you sit in customers' hierarchy of needs) and his Love and Utility dimensions. The intersection of your personal motivation and what delights customers is the target market.
- Shortlist your best customers. "Best" means high retention, propensity to upgrade, a "10" NPS, proactive positive reviews and social advocacy, and engagement with beta-testing or feature ideation.
- Their shared characteristics define the target market. Ask which types of organizations and people would care about their testimonials.
- The customers may not know why they fit; it's your job to work out the defining characteristics through observation and interrogation.
- Then use those characteristics in marketing, sales identification and product optimization.

chunks.heading: The testimonial test
chunks.text:
- To check whether customer profile B belongs to the same target market as existing profile A, ask: would B be swayed by a genuine, effusive testimonial from A? The reaction he wants is "that person's situation is just like mine, so I'm interested, I'll give it a try."
- It can be tested directly: see whether testimonials in sales calls light up people's eyes, or whether adding them to landing pages increases conversions.
- It echoes Geoffrey Moore's definition in *Crossing the Chasm* (1991): a market is a set of actual or potential customers, for a given set of products or services, who have a common set of needs or wants, and who reference each other when making a buying decision.
- Moore's definition mentions no demographics or firmographics. Jason prefers a slightly looser version than Moore's, since Moore says two buyers who don't communicate are in different markets (a Boston doctor and one in Zaire). Jason thinks that is less true in today's connected world, especially in software.
- His summary: your target market is the set of potential customers your best customers self-identify with, in the sense that they would find each other's testimonials compelling.

chunks.heading: Better segmentation dimensions for the modern age
chunks.text:
- Old constraints that forced demographic segmentation are gone:
  - TV could only know gender and age, via a few firms like Nielsen.
  - Stripe, PayPal, Paddle and FastSpring made multi-country, multi-currency payments and tax compliance accessible, breaking geography and currency constraints.
  - AI support and translation may soon erode language barriers.
- Dimensions he suggests considering, though most won't apply and you should invent new ones:
  - Individual vs team (e.g. a free single-player mode that hooks people while teams pay, as with Asana or Notion).
  - Integrations and other software used daily.
  - Processes and workflows they use or aspire to.
  - Job-to-be-done success: which numbers they are held to, vital vs operational, satisfied vs maximized, what change would get them promoted or fired.
  - Personal success (their Needs Stack) and professional success (how they are evaluated and promoted; early-career priorities differ from late-career regardless of company size).
  - Corporate goals: revenue growth, revenue size, profit dollars or percentage, market share, Rule of 40, cost savings.
  - Role inside the company, title, and problem ownership (who owns the problem, and whether problem-owner and solution-owner are the same person).
  - Cultural attributes, such as productivity vs work-life balance, or external innovation vs internal efficiency.
  - *Crossing the Chasm* lifecycle phase: innovators (tinkerers), early adopters (take risks for competitive advantage), early majority (wary, want well-known vendors and support), late majority (dragged in by investors or market pressure).
  - Work style, technical acumen, risk tolerance (uncorrelated with company size), tech-stack philosophy, update cadence, communication culture.
  - Organization size (SMB is often bought by larger firms but not vice versa; it matters most for top-down sales or products like HR software), growth trajectory, regulatory environment.
  - Budget type, including whether a clear budget threshold changes the sale.
  - Sales process (top-down vs bottom-up PLG), decision cycle (hours, weeks, quarters), emergency vs deliberate buying, maker vs administrator, business model, learning style.
- Most answers will be "don't know" or "don't care," and that is expected.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jason Cohen introduces Max MRR (monthly new MRR divided by monthly cancellation rate), a leading indicator of where revenue will plateau. Using toy models and Buffer's public data, he shows why modest churn caps growth, why accelerating new MRR still yields linear growth, and why NRR at or above 100% is the next lever after retention.

chunks.heading: Max MRR: the growth ceiling formula
chunks.text:
- Jason defines "Max MRR" as the revenue level at which a SaaS company stops growing. It happens when dollars lost to cancellations equal new dollars added each month.
- Formula: Max MRR = New MRR per month ÷ monthly cancellation rate. Written out, MRR_max × c = MRR_new.
- Toy example: $1,000 of new MRR per month and 5% monthly cancellation gives a ceiling of $1,000 / 0.05 = $20,000. Starting from $0, such a company reaches about $10k MRR in 15 months and never reaches $20k, even after 60 months.
- Churn dollars grow with company size while new-MRR dollars stay flat. The churn rate is constant, but the absolute dollars lost keep rising, so growth slows.
- "New MRR" here includes new-customer MRR, upgrade MRR, and reactivated customers. "Cancels" includes cancellations and downgrades.

chunks.heading: Why startups plateau sooner than expected
chunks.text:
- Early growth is fast because there are few customers who could cancel. As customers accumulate, churn becomes the force slowing growth, not the size of the market.
- Jason says this explains the common founder surprise: growth tapers off while the target market is still "many orders of magnitude larger than the company."
- Max MRR marks both the maximum size of the company and the size at which growth starts to slow.
- Revenue follows an S-curve. Growth accelerates while there are few customers to cancel and a new channel is still ramping, then decelerates once marketing output levels off.
- Jason says the Max MRR curve predicts this "months or even years before it happens."

chunks.heading: Cancellation rate is the biggest lever
chunks.text:
- Cancellation compounds exponentially, so small changes in the rate move the ceiling a lot. Halving the cancellation rate doubles Max MRR.
- Toy example: new MRR fixed at $1,000/mo, cancellation at 7% for 20 months, then improving to 4% over 10 months. Max MRR jumps as soon as cancellation starts improving, while actual MRR looks "mostly linear but wavy." It is hard to see from revenue alone that the business model got massively better.
- Jason calls Max MRR a leading indicator and current MRR a lagging indicator.
- When MRR is near the ceiling, cancellation dominates growth. Lifting the ceiling makes new MRR the dominant factor again.
- Common misconceptions he has fought for years:
  - "7% cancellation is fine, especially for consumer businesses."
  - "As long as I keep adding $300/mo of new MRR every month, I'll build a real business."
  - Believing he'll keep scaling past a few million ARR by doing what he's always done.

chunks.heading: Accelerating new MRR still yields linear revenue
chunks.text:
- Toy example: new MRR rises by $100 each month for 60 months (100, 200, 300, ...) at 5% churn. Max MRR keeps rising alongside actual MRR, but actual MRR grows at "more or less a constant pace," roughly a line.
- The reason is that churn is exponential. Accelerating cancellations offset the acceleration in new MRR.
- Jason says even companies with accelerating new growth typically grow revenue only linearly.
- This scenario is still too optimistic, because marketing channels top out and tend to decline once mature.
- The typical real pattern is that a company unlocks a channel, then hits the channel's capacity for new sales each month. The result is accelerating growth followed by the ceiling.

chunks.heading: Buffer case study
chunks.text:
Buffer publishes its financials at buffer.com/metrics, which makes it a good case. Jason walks through four phases:

| Period | MRR | Cancel rate | What happened |
|:--|:--|:--|:--|
| 2012-2014 | $3k to $40k | 8% to 6% | Found product/market fit, brought cancellations under control, and accelerated new MRR. Max MRR rose and revenue accelerated. |
| 2014-2020 | $40k to $140k | 6% | Cancellations never improved. New MRR was accelerated through several "found a new channel... channel became saturated" events, visible as brief plateaus in Max MRR. Growth stayed linear. |
| 2020-2024 | $140k to $90k | 7% | Cancellation rose about a point. New MRR was still large, but Max MRR dipped below revenue, so revenue fell. |
| 2024 onward | $100k to $150k | 6% | New MRR rose substantially and cancellation improved slightly, so Max MRR shot up and growth restarted. |

- During the stagnation, Buffer had more new customers and upgrades than ever, but also more cancellations and downgrades than ever. The customer base was very dynamic yet flat overall.
- Max MRR reacted ahead of revenue and with much larger magnitude, anticipating both the good and the bad news.
- Jason's counterfactual: if Buffer had cut cancellation from 8% in 2014 to 3% by 2019, revenue would have doubled.
- He calls 6% "precarious." It requires forever-accelerating new MRR and quickly tanks revenue once new MRR stops keeping up, which it inevitably does.
- Buffer's 2023 fix, per CEO Joel Gascoigne's strategy letter, was to return to its ideal customer in its best target market (entrepreneurs and small businesses) and to a pricing model that works better for them (freemium). Those customers retain at higher rates, and cancellation fell, MRR rose, and Max MRR rose ahead of MRR.
- Jason adds: "Imagine what would happen with cancellation of 4%!"

chunks.heading: Max MRR vs NRR: after retention, push NRR to 100% or more
chunks.text:
- NRR (Net Revenue Retention) = (Upgrade - Downgrade - Cancel) / MRR × 12, converting MRR to ARR. It measures how revenue would change over a year with no new customers.
- When upgrades exceed cancellations and downgrades, revenue grows every month even with zero new customers. Max MRR then stops being meaningful, because with an infinite market you would never stop growing.
- Markets and channels are finite, so you still top out, but through market saturation rather than churn.
- Jason's rule: after high retention, the most powerful growth lever is NRR of 100% or more.
- Almost all public SaaS companies have NRR of 100% or more. Average NRR at IPO was 119% and average ARR at IPO was $255M (2022 data in his chart). Without it, the ceiling would be too low for their revenue goals.
- He says this is just as valid for solopreneurs, because NRR creates growth even with a limited marketing budget.
- It also signals that customers are growing with you, getting more value, and are "happy to share some of that with you" through price.

chunks.heading: Max MRR vs SaaS Quick Ratio
chunks.text:
- Quick Ratio = (New + Upgrade) / (Cancel + Downgrade).
- Jason's benchmarks:
  - 3-4 for a high-growth, early-scale company
  - 1.5-2 for a company at scale with healthy growth
  - 1 means no growth
  - Below 1 means contraction
- He says Quick Ratio is useful but "does not forecast revenue growth at all." Buffer's Quick Ratio fell sharply during its multi-year healthy growth and kept falling when growth stalled and reversed. It started recovering before the 2023 changes and still looked weak in 2025 when growth had clearly changed.
- Max MRR is predictive where Quick Ratio is not, and he finds it easier to rally a team around. Raising a "revenue ceiling" feels tangible, while "get our Quick Ratio from 1.4 to 1.6" does not.
- Caveat: no single metric tells the whole story, Max MRR included. It applies to companies of all stages and sizes.
- His closing advice: get cancellation rate under control first, then focus on NRR.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Time is zero-sum and you can do maybe 1-10% of what you "need" to, so Jason Cohen proposes a binary 10x / 0.1x framework: hunt for the few transformative tasks, and delegate, batch, automate or archive the rest. Then keep explaining the "not doing" list so the team doesn't lose faith while some fires burn on purpose.

chunks.heading: Time is zero-sum, so only a few tasks deserve your best hours
chunks.text:
Jason Cohen argues that time is a hard, zero-sum limit: an hour spent on one thing is an hour not spent on everything else, and every minute is a choice. He says there "isn't enough time for more than two big things" in your life. Because we can only do one thing at a time, whatever we're doing now is definitionally our "highest priority", so the real choice is whether it's thoughtful.

- Every company proves the point with its issue tracker: thousands of valid items accumulate (ideas, differentiating features, customer-visible bugs, design tweaks).
- Completing even 10% would be a miracle, and the ratio worsens every week as more items are added than removed.
- Listening better to customers, more creative teams and more hires all make the ratio worse, not better.
- He puts the fixed constraint at 1%-10% of what you "need" to execute, and says the fraction shrinks with scale.
- "Urgent, but not important" tends to win over "Important, but not urgent" if you aren't paying attention. Teams end up doing only the things that happen to have deadlines.

chunks.heading: The 10x / 0.1x prioritization framework
chunks.text:
Jason offers one overarching framework for any prioritization: sort work into 10x tasks and 0.1x tasks.

- A 10x task returns an order of magnitude more than you put in, even if you valued your time at about $1000/hour.
- Most other activities are worth far less than $1000/hour, even if mandatory. These are 0.1x tasks, to be minimized.
- If you don't know what your one or two 10x tasks are, "identifying that is your highest priority". Otherwise "the entire company is misusing their time."
- He recommends acting as if there were no 1x tasks, to force clearer decisions: "we must be ruthless, final, and precious with our time."
- He admits the binary is reductive. You will mislabel some 1x work as 10x and spend too much time on 0.1x work, but the forced choice helps you be ruthless.
- If you insist on a middle tier, he points to his Rocks, Pebbles, Sand framework, which segments work by size and prioritizes each size differently. He also credits Shreyas Doshi's LNO framework as another take on the same exponents.

chunks.heading: What counts as a 10x task
chunks.text:
Jason's examples of 10x work:

- The few features that win most sales. Rule of thumb: impactful features are actively used by at least 40% of customers, or are a critical reason-to-buy or reason-to-stay for at least 15%.
- Finding the marketing positioning and wording where ads convert 2x higher and home-page visitors buy 2x more often. He says "Not 10% higher", because you can't actually measure that.
- Finding the pricing model that maximizes profitable growth while staying fair to customers.
- Correctly identifying the next strategic objective or biggest obstacle. Working on the wrong thing is "a 100% waste of time, even if efficiently- and perfectly-executed."
- Hiring the next critical employee who raises throughput, work quality and decision quality, and adds a missing skill needed for the current obstacle or next objective.
- Applying energy where small changes have a large impact on growth or profitability.
- Addressing the single biggest drag on growth.
- Deciding how to expand into the next adjacency.

chunks.heading: How to test whether something is really 10x
chunks.text:
Jason says it's rare to have too many 10x candidates, and if you think you do, you're probably being too generous with the label.

- It must literally 10x a key metric, or be the difference between survival and bankruptcy.
- The upside must survive the usual misses. Work always takes about 2x longer and delivers about half the impact you expected. "To take that 4x hit and still have a great outcome requires starting at 10x."
- Treat 10x work as an investment: significant time, outsized expected return, real uncertainty. He has a separate Investment Criteria guide for this.
- If there truly are too many 10x choices with incomparable inputs, he points to his Binstack framework, built for maximizing impact when dimensions can't be compared.
- Easy is not the same as low-impact. Conflating effort with impact is a fallacy: easy things can be 10x, and complex things can have no impact on revenue or employee happiness.

chunks.heading: Minimizing 0.1x tasks
chunks.text:
Jason lists four strategies for tasks that are worth far less than $1000/hour:

- **Eliminate them** by structuring your life, product, target-customer selection or company strategy to avoid them.
- **Delegate**, even if the result is worse than you'd do yourself. His example: grocery delivery is more expensive and doesn't pick the apples you would have picked. You need to be "in command instead of in control."
- **Batch or automate**, accepting minor penalties. Examples: paying bills once a month and risking occasional late fees, or batching security patches since each one is unlikely to be exploited in the next few weeks.
- **Archive loose tickets older than 100 days.** More than 90% of ideas never get done, so these are already in that group, and deleting them helps you prioritize the rest. If something is truly important it will come up again. He says "archive", not "delete".

chunks.heading: "Life by a thousand sparks": when many small tasks add up to 10x
chunks.text:
Jason makes one exception to dismissing small tasks. In some regimes many small tasks sum to a 10x impact, which he calls "life by a thousand sparks" (a facetious inverse of "death by a thousand cuts").

- His example is great design. Amazing design isn't required for success, but some products win primarily because of beloved design.
- Great design is not one thing. It combines macro-scale architecture with many details: color choices, pixel-perfect layout, font and word selection, aspect ratios, white space, snappy interactivity, a design system for consistency, fixing every aesthetic bug, and harmony across website, product, emails and marketing, sales and support material.
- These tasks shouldn't be dismissed as individually 0.1x if they serve a 10x concept that is also the main way you win customers in a competitive market.

chunks.heading: The dog peeing on the floor: handling the fallout of ruthless prioritization
chunks.text:
Jason tells a parable he has retold many times at WP Engine. A dog pees on the floor of a lit living room while a man sits reading a book. An observer at the window thinks he's crazy. In fact he has the most important meeting of his career in an hour, and everything he needs is in the book. Cleaning up the pee is worth it.

The observer misjudges for two reasons:

- They don't know the complete story.
- They struggle to accept that something bad or stupid can still be the right decision because the alternative is worse.

The same thing happens inside a company that prioritizes ruthlessly:

- Important fires are intentionally left burning because the Most Important Thing matters more.
- Others see the fires and peeing dogs for months or years, lose faith in leadership, and lose morale. Loss of trust and respect leads to talent leaving, "which leads to the death of an organization."
- Prolific idea-creators complain "They never listen to my ideas." Jason says they're right in effect: you could mathematically never implement more than a few percent of those ideas. It's "inexorable math", not a failure to listen.

chunks.heading: Communicating priorities so the team keeps trust
chunks.text:
Jason's fix for the dogs-peeing problem is to tell the whole story, repeatedly.

- Share not just the few top priorities but why they are the top ones.
- Acknowledge the twenty other things that also deserve attention and explain why you're letting those fires burn on purpose.
- Keep a "not doing" list as an explicit part of the plan.
- Retell the dog parable and admit it feels bad to watch the dogs pee, especially when you know how to prevent it.
- The pee is tolerable only when people see it buys time for the most important things, which leverage "precious, woefully limited time, for out-sized results."
- He says this takes constant, repetitive communication, and that the full picture is what prioritization actually looks like, not social-media admonitions to "focus!"

chunks.heading: Jason's dislikes in prioritization frameworks
chunks.text:
Jason lists what he avoids when choosing or building a prioritization method:

- Rubrics or computed scores (he has a separate piece on why, "Fermi ROI").
- Any "confidence level", because "your confidence scores are bullshit".
- Models built for symmetry on consultants' slides rather than reflecting the messiness of real work.
- Anything that compares incomparable things, such as scoring "more growth" on the same made-up number as "don't run out of money" or "make employees happy."
- He adds that our ability to measure impact even after the fact is "laughably poor", and our ability to predict it is "even more pitiful."

His own frameworks, each for a specific job: Fermi ROI, Binstack (incomparable dimensions), Adjacency Matrix (expanding an existing product), Investment Criteria, Rocks/Pebbles/Sand, Satisficing vs Maximizing, Cleaving (separate upside from downside), Fairytale Quarterly Planning (work against strategic objectives and obstacles), and JIT streams (separate prioritization from work-planning).

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jason Cohen argues there are three viable pricing strategies: more for more, more for less, and less for less. Each carries consequences for product, marketing, hiring and funding that must be accepted together. The only wrong move is not choosing, which leaves a confusing message and a product that's right for no one.

chunks.heading: Three pricing strategies, pick one and commit to the consequences
chunks.text:
Jason argues there are three viable strategies in the interplay of value and price, and that each drags along a set of consequences you must accept:

- **More for more** ("the best"): luxury, advantage, high price.
- **More for less** ("high ROI"): everything you actually need at a reasonable price.
- **Less for less** ("incredible deal"): not much, but incredibly affordable.

The pattern holds across industries, consumer and business. In clothing: a cashmere sweater or Miu Miu cardigan is more for more, an L.L. Bean sweater is more for less, and a fast-fashion hoodie is less for less. The only wrong choice is not choosing. Then the market message is confusing, the product is a "Frankenstein," the pricing model is wrong, and "your product is the right choice for no one." Because all three are valid, he says to listen to your gut and pick the one that best matches your personal strengths and what you would be proudest to execute, since that is the one you will run best and find most fulfilling.

chunks.heading: More for more ("the best"): what it requires
chunks.text:
Being "the best" is good for profit and for enjoying your work: pride in craft, customers who love you, and a high price that funds further investment. But the best is an outlier. It is "special" and "different," not the average of what already exists, so your ideas must be substantially different from what is available.

- **Best at what?** It must be specific and customers must agree it is worth the higher price. Options include design (simplest, most pleasant, most beautiful), quality ("always just works"), a superior workflow, integrations with all the tools the customer uses, or personal tech support.
- **Best for whom?** Billions of people disagree on what "best" means. Founders go wrong by assuming "I built it for myself, I am the customer, so others will pay to solve it this way." Treat your initial insight as a motivation that is half right and half wrong, then interview potential customers and use a structured customer-development process to morph your definition of "best" to fit a specific ideal customer.
- **Who buys it?** Customers who care about something more than price: mission-critical products where failure causes outsized internal cost or reputational damage, urgent top priorities (emergency or strategic mandate), "toothbrush products" used at least twice a day, or things tied to personal identity. Luxury brands make being "far too expensive" the point. His WP Engine example: hosting eCommerce sites (all of the customer's revenue), media sites (slowness loses ad revenue), and corporate home pages (downtime loses leads and reputation). It can also be cover-your-ass buying ("no one ever got fired for buying ___").

Customers have their pick of options and every other product is a competitor, so the customer is in control. Hence the importance of being "the best" for some subset of the market.

chunks.heading: More for more: aligning the rest of the business
chunks.text:
Positioning as the best must shape every other decision:

- Marketing focuses on excellence and exclusivity, not affordability.
- The team is smaller and higher caliber, passionate artisans who celebrate perfectionism. Hire the top 1% and pay premium salaries.
- Support is measured in seconds, not hours, often white-glove with dedicated account reps.
- Product cycles may be slower, emphasizing perfection before launch and building without cutting corners regardless of cost.
- Because the number of customers is small and limited, market share matters and upgrading existing customers is vital for growth at scale. He notes many public enterprise software companies get the majority of revenue growth from upselling existing customers.

The high price tag funds all of this. If you pull it off it is the best outcome for you: fulfilling, validated by customers, and attractive to great employees. "Most products are not 'the best,'" but for those that are, it creates a virtuous cycle of excellence, satisfaction, and profitability.

chunks.heading: More for less ("high ROI"): the largest and most popular category
chunks.text:
Jason calls this the right value proposition for most things in life, especially business, where you need to get the job done as cheaply as possible "but not cheaper." Buyers have a budget and seek "the best that I can afford." Price is the primary constraint; within it they prioritize features by preference. The product's goal is not to be best on every dimension but to offer a set of trade-offs that enough customers prefer.

Apparel evidence he cites:

- Global apparel revenue is about $1,600B; more for less is about $1,200B, luxury about $250B, fast fashion about $150B.
- Profit margins: more for less roughly 5%-15%, fast fashion under 5%, luxury 20%-30% (Prada about 23% net profit). L.L. Bean is private, so its range is estimated from other retailers.
- Software can have much better margins than apparel, so reasonable prices plus the largest market segment is a great business model.

Where it fits best: back-end systems invisible to customers (no competitive advantage from being the best), areas where downtime is not disruptive in real time (a reporting tool can be down an hour; a customer support tool cannot), products where a missing feature like one chart type is not a deal-breaker, and products that just need to "tick a box" so requirements are lenient. Not being mission-critical is a cost but also gives leniency on quality and features.

chunks.heading: More for less: how to win the ideal customer and everyone else
chunks.text:
- **You can be "the best" for your ideal customer.** Target the "perfect" customer with marketing and features. They cannot believe they are getting a more-for-more product at a more-for-less price. If you cannot win them from your home page, "you're not doing your job."
- **Leniency gives you far more sales.** Jason says you will make 100x more sales than you expect, because for every ideal customer there are a hundred others who get most of what they want, hit no deal-breakers, and like the price. You get the specificity and emotional connection of talking to one ICP while still winning the broader market.
- **Position on value, not savings.** "Save money" is weak positioning; show how much value you generate. Even with a more-for-less pricing strategy, marketing should still be as strong as possible and emphasize that it is really more for less.
- **Marketing must be honest about trade-offs.** Make the "smart choice" feel obvious; do not waste money on useless branding. Do not claim to be best for everyone, which "quietly alienates everyone." Comparison charts should not be a solid column of green checkmarks but show where you are strong and where you are not the right solution.
- **Product rule of thumb:** build only features used by at least 50% of customers, or where at least 15% of customers buy you specifically for that reason. The price does not allow special exceptions or brittle integrations that only 5% use.
- **Team and costs:** hire people who excel at identifying and eliminating waste without sacrificing core value. Internal costs and decisions must match the external promise.
- **Against Porter.** Michael Porter's *Competitive Strategy* (1980) listed differentiated best, low-cost leader, and niche leader; later thinkers noted differentiated and niche are the same, differing only in market scope, leaving more for more and less for less. Jason argues customers have spoken: more for less wins most customers, revenue, and profit. It is not "a balance" between value and cost but a third, independent strategy to leverage fully.

chunks.heading: Less for less ("incredible deal"): why it works
chunks.text:
Jason rejects "never compete on price": many wildly successful companies, from solo bootstrappers to some of the largest, most profitable companies in the world, won on rock-bottom prices. His examples: Amazon, Walmart, Vanguard, Costco, Dollar General, IKEA, Southwest Airlines, H&M, Zara, Xiaomi, ALDI. "Sometimes, 'cheapest' is 'best'."

- **Why customers accept the trade-offs:** "the alternative is to not have the product at all." The choice is binary (any hoodie versus no hoodie), so no one quibbles over features, quality, or service. At $5 per month people expect crashes, no enterprise integrations, and knowledge-base-only support. A $2/month web host can have spam and slowness and tech support that can only reset a password.
- **Positioning:** extol democratization, participation, simplicity, affordability, and accessibility. The real mission behind the company, empowerment or exploiting desperation, shows in how it is run.
- **Consequences accepted:** low prices mean little money for marketing, sales, development, support, design, or culture perks.

chunks.heading: Less for less: making it profitable and surviving competitors
chunks.text:
The hardest internal challenge is profitability, since there is so little revenue to be profitable with. Costs must be extraordinarily, unconventionally low.

- **Scale helps:** bulk purchasing from suppliers, and structural effects like support per customer being lower at 100,000 customers than at 100, because most do not have a question in any given month. Still, it takes many $2/month customers to afford one support person.
- **Acquisition must be nearly free.** If a customer is worth $2/month and maybe $50 over their lifetime, you cannot pay much to acquire them: no heavy ad spend, no sales team. Rely on word of mouth and reviews, and encourage them. Affiliates and influencers paid only after you are paid are an affordable form of marketing. Organic marketing is slow at first but scales over time.
- **Funding:** revenue lags costs, so the company will burn cash from savings, friends and family, a loan, or investors. Annual billing helps a lot. Jason (and other pundits) tell bootstrappers to "raise their prices," which really means switching from less for less to more for less or more for more. "If you don't want to raise money, don't build a business that burns money on purpose."
- **You do not need exorbitant funding.** Each of the four case studies in his "never compete on price" article grew to multiple billions in revenue on only a small amount of raised money, because strategic decisions were aligned to low cost. VC-funded companies often assume "we can work the costs out later," but processes, technology, and culture solidify around what acquired customers, and change means layoffs, rewrites, and forced marketing and sales motions. Some bootstrapped companies never raised money thanks to an extreme cost advantage, such as being based in a very low-cost country and selling to the US and Europe.
- **Do not just lower the price.** Inexperienced founders think "my product sucks, so I'm not comfortable charging a lot." That is not a good reason, and you should not build a crappy product. Ask instead: how do I build a simple yet lovable product that a specific ideal customer would pay 10x more than I charge now, even with few features and occasional failures? He says that is what he did with WP Engine.
- **Biggest external threat:** a competitor undercutting you on price, because of newer technology, a different location or cost structure, or a larger company using a loss leader. His examples: Microsoft killed Netscape with a thousand-plus developers on a free Internet Explorer, and over a decade later Google killed Explorer the same way with Chrome. The antidote is constantly improving cost efficiency and possibly proactively lowering prices, as Amazon did in retail ("your margin is my opportunity") and later in cloud. He notes that once Microsoft and Google were the only other serious cloud competitors, all three stopped lowering prices at the same time ("Surely a coincidence?").

Less for less is "brutal," with relentless competition and no spare money, but it reaches the largest number of potential customers and can truly bring goods and services to people who could not otherwise afford them.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jason tells how, while selling environmental-monitoring hardware at ITWatchDogs, he found a hospital using a tiny bootstrapped product alongside HP OpenView. The lessons: price so procurement is a non-event, define the market by an individual's need rather than company size, ask customers about adjacent products to learn their life and channels, and land small then expand.

chunks.heading: Why enterprises buy a cheap second product that does the same job
chunks.text:
- Jason describes visiting a hospital's network operations center with a co-founder while selling ITWatchDogs, whose web-enabled hardware measured temperature, humidity, door status and power in server rooms. The hospital already ran HP OpenView, a multi-million-dollar monitoring suite.
- It also ran What's Up Gold, a bootstrapped, shrink-wrapped product with a silly name and an ugly logo, at about $500-$700.
- When they asked why, the buyer said: "What's Up Gold has a couple of features we like. There's this thing we do many times per day, and it's really quick with What's Up Gold. And it's only like five hundred dollars or something. We can just run that on our credit card without asking permission. So we just bought it."
- What's Up Gold never beat HP OpenView, IBM Tivoli, CA Unicenter or BMC Patrol head-to-head. It did not need to; it sold to the same customer anyway.
- Jason's point: a small product can sell into an enterprise that already solved the problem, if it adds even a little incremental value at near-zero cost to buy.

chunks.heading: Price for procurement pain, not buyer psychology
chunks.text:
- When selling to mid-sized and large businesses, Jason argues pricing is less about whether $49.99 feels cheaper than $50 and more about how much of a pain in the ass the purchase is.
- Procurement friction is the real price. "$500 is not the same as $499.99; it's the same as $0."
- He compares it to voting theory. Board shares of 7%, 16%, 17% and 60% give voting power of 0%, 0%, 0% and 100%, because the 60% holder always wins.
- Applied to price, $500 can be the same as $0 (a credit card, no approval), while $1,000 might be the same as $60,000 (it triggers the approval process).
- For What's Up Gold the product was effectively free, so any incremental value justified buying it.
- The price solved for procurement. It was "notably _not_ 'price to value' nor perception tricks."
- Jason notes this does not always work, and points to his essay on purgatory for the alternate cases.

chunks.heading: What a small product needs to win alongside an incumbent
chunks.text:
Jason lists what made What's Up Gold thrive:

1. A product with a few unique and delightful features. It was fast at one task the buyer did many times a day.
2. A price that solved for procurement.
3. A target market defined by the needs of an individual IT person, not "SMB" vs "Enterprise." The customer was an enterprise, but the buyer was one admin with a credit card.
4. A way to get the right person's attention, meaning distribution.

He adds that name, logo and website design clearly did not block the sale here.

chunks.heading: Distribution: find where the buyer actually pays attention
chunks.text:
- The IT admin said he probably saw the product in an ad "in the back of one of the ones in the bathroom," gesturing at a table of manuals, wires and CD-ROMs.
- Jason's takeaway: while you worry about SEO and AdWords positioning, it is easy to overlook the magazine the buyer reads for 20 minutes of solace.
- His team went to the bathroom to see which magazines were there, then advertised in them, and it worked.
- Sub-lesson from his footnote: always ask about adjacent products and behaviors. Wherever the buyer found What's Up Gold, he could have found ITWatchDogs too.

chunks.heading: Customer interviews: ask about their life, not just your product
Land and expand: shrink the first deal to fit the buyer
chunks.text:
- They walked in expecting to pitch a $10,000 package. After learning about the credit card, they changed the pitch on the fly: "You could just buy $500 worth of stuff from us today. See whether you like it."
- The hospital bought a little more each month, because the product was good and they could buy in a way that was convenient.
- The hospital was part of a larger group. After it worked well at one site, word spread internally, and the global IT center eventually placed orders of tens of thousands of dollars, going through real procurement.
- Jason's summary: enterprise sales is not always a large top-down deal. It "can start small, start accessible, start simple, start affordable, and then expand outward once you're a proven quantity."
- He acknowledges this is 20 years old, with SaaS, markets, budgets and AI all different, but says the fundamentals hold: learn from your customers and make things they want to buy, "twice."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jason Cohen explains why a product can pass the polite-interest test and still not sell. First, apply the Magic Wand Test: would they take it free, fully implemented? Then find the missing ingredient, urgency, by narrowing your target to customers who need it right now.

chunks.heading: Product Purgatory: why customers who love a product still don't buy
chunks.text: Jason describes "Product Purgatory": the prospect genuinely loves the product, wishes they could buy it, and still never does. He separates it from polite social white lies, where founders mistake kindness for validation because they "yearn so desperately for validation--nominally product validation but actually personal validation". Purgatory is the case where the enthusiasm is real. He gives two distinct causes: the product fails the Magic Wand Test, or it lacks urgency. They need different fixes.

chunks.heading: The Magic Wand Test: would they take it for free, fully implemented?
chunks.text:
- The test: "I have a magic wand, and when I wave it, our product will be fully implemented in your company. Everyone is trained. Other tools are integrated. Processes are changed. Security requirements are satisfied. And best of all, it is *completely free*! So! Do you want me to wave this magic wand?"
- Jason says the answer is often "No." Every product carries friction, risk, time and often ongoing cost, so value must "significantly exceed" this activation energy.
- Value only slightly above the penalty is not enough. Change is difficult and time is limited, so customers will not spend effort on minor impact.
- Founders "revel in all the value they generate, but don't see the penalties that they incur." Customers see the penalties.
- Even with a fair price, real costs remain: implementation, training, integration, and users being unproductive while they get used to a new interface and process.

chunks.heading: Why new companies fail the test even when free
chunks.text:
- A new company has no brand and no track record, which adds risk: it may be out of business in two years, or may not handle real-world use cases.
- His example is an Austin startup about twenty years ago, responding to news stories about employees leaking documents by email. It routed all corporate email through its servers to scan for sensitive material and return or flag questionable messages.
- It solved a real problem and still sold nothing. Putting a brand-new startup in the middle of all company email creates a security issue (a hackable startup, outsiders potentially seeing all email) and a bug risk that would be catastrophic for email. The value did not significantly exceed the penalty.
- He applies the same logic as a buyer. He won't use "the newest code library" for anything beyond throwaway projects, because he doesn't want to rip and replace in a few years, wants thousands of bugs already found and fixed, and wants to hire people who already know it.

chunks.heading: Urgency: the missing ingredient when the product passes the test
chunks.text:
- Even a product that passes the Magic Wand Test can stall. The prospect asks good questions, thinks the price is fair, hates their current tool, and still says "call back in nine months."
- Jason's diagnosis: at any time the buyer has one to three top priorities (in the quarterly plan, or an emergency that overrode it). The product is priority seven or ten. It is on the list, which separates this case from failing the Magic Wand Test, but not near the top.
- They won't displace a top-three priority, and the product isn't number four either, so it won't happen soon. The delay is their way of waiting until the top priorities are done.
- His conclusion: "You got so many things right... but there's no urgency, no reason it has to be done now. **Urgency is the missing ingredient.**"

chunks.heading: Example: accessibility at WP Engine
chunks.text:
- Jason's company WP Engine made its website and user portal accessible (screen readers, resizable text, semantic navigation, high contrast, image alt text). It generated appreciative messages and real sales from customers who chose WP Engine over competitors.
- It passes the Magic Wand Test, yet few people need the accommodations and implementation requires ongoing work. He says there are probably five other website projects that would drive more sales, so for nearly everyone accessibility is "priority number eight."
- The question is therefore not whether customers see value but which customers are ready to buy now: those for whom it is a top-three priority, driven by an emergency, a strategic decision, or company culture (as at WP Engine).
- When accessibility becomes a blocker: companies pursuing government contracts that require accessible vendors, companies being sued over accessibility, companies selling to audiences with accessibility requirements, and companies integrating with platforms like Walmart or Amazon that mandate it.

chunks.heading: Escaping Purgatory: narrow the market to "...and needs it right now"
chunks.text:
- The fix is to narrow the target market with the condition "...and needs it right now." Then aim all marketing, sales and new product features at that ideal customer profile.
- There is no product that is always valuable, always low-risk or always a top priority. There are segments where those things hold and segments where they don't.
- Questions to find pockets of urgency:
  - Who is the product critical to strategically, especially when tied to revenue? Examples: regulatory compliance, industry certifications, public strategy declarations, entering a new market, buying another company, a competitive shift, new fundraising or an IPO, modernizing legacy systems, customers publicly demanding new requirements.
  - What emergency would force a purchase? Examples: getting sued, executive turnover, a PR debacle, a negative analyst report, a loud competitor announcement, a significant employee leaving, a public security breach, a regulatory investigation, market-share decline, supply-chain disruption, a manufacturing defect, scaling issues.
  - What personal life changes trigger action (for consumer products)? Examples: becoming a parent, a child leaving for college, a serious diagnosis, inheriting money, losing a job, moving, retiring, starting or selling a business, divorce.
  - What competitive pressures create urgency? Examples: new entrants, competitors gaining share or announcing major features, trade publications highlighting what they lack, technology disruption, negative viral attention.
  - What financial pressures create urgency? Examples: budgets closing at a certain time of year, needing to "use up" budget, new fundraising bringing new expectations and budget, new teams, a change in profitability or financial goals.
- To locate such customers, he suggests watching: official announcements, CEOs and founders on podcasts, consistent complaints in reviews and social media, shifts in messaging, acquisitions, changes in job openings, Glassdoor comment trends, analyst reports, trade publications, venture capital allocations, regulatory change notices, new leadership, new departments or teams, and life events.

chunks.heading: When the segment is too small, and why a narrow focus still works
chunks.text:
- The answer may be bad news: there may be no target segment, it may be too small or too hard to find, or it may be disqualified by no budget or vendor lock-in. In that case the product may not be workable, but asking the question is how you find out.
- Even if the universe of "perfect customers" looks small, he says "for every customer who is in the center of that bullseye, there are 100x more who will find it useful enough to buy anyway." The reasoning is in his ICP article.
- Focusing on such a small surface area is scary, but he says it works, and "you have no choice, if you want to exit Purgatory."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jason Cohen argues EBITDASM (EBITDA plus S&M) is flawed because stopping S&M doesn't freeze revenue and it assumes efficient acquisition. He proposes SSEBITDA = EBITDA + S&M − COC, counting only the S&M needed to replace cancellations. A Profitable Growth Rate falls out of it, letting you justify "spend to grow" precisely.

chunks.heading: Steady-state profit as the test for "spending to grow"
chunks.text:
Jason's problem: a SaaS company that is "spending to grow" can't easily tell whether it is investing for future profit or running a model that will never be profitable. He wants an objective measure, not a story.

- Companies claim "we're unprofitable because we're growing" and many never become profitable.
- The question to answer: if you stopped spending on growth and just held the business where it is, would it make money?
- If yes, the extra spend really is "to grow." If no, the core model is broken.

chunks.heading: Rackspace's EBITDASM and why Jason liked it
chunks.text:
Rackspace, while scaling fast, asked what would happen if it stopped Sales & Marketing (S&M) spend. Their logic: CAC is small relative to LTV, so spend as much as possible on growth, but check that the underlying business is profitable.

- Metric: EBITDASM = EBITDA + S&M. This is the usual EBITDA with S&M also excluded.
- For small software companies with no amortization, depreciation or loan interest, it simplifies to "[your definition of profit] + S&M."
- Jason: "I like this model, and ten years ago we were using it at WP Engine."

chunks.heading: Two flaws in EBITDASM
chunks.text:
**1. Halting S&M does not mean revenue stays flat.**
- Revenue would fall from cancellations and downgrades, or rise from upgrades.
- The intent was to measure profitability assuming the company is neither growing nor shrinking. A company with revenue above costs that shrinks every month is soon dead, so it isn't truly "profitable."

**2. It assumes sales and marketing is efficient.**
- Rackspace's logic only holds if acquisition is efficient, and nobody can say how efficient is efficient enough.
- Jason's view: the metric should apply to every company. Sales and marketing efficiency matters but is a separate metric you can already compute. Don't cram multiple ideas into one metric.
- On thresholds: some say LTV/CAC of 3 (from a David Skok post), others 5, others 1. Jason says LTV isn't the right way to think about it and prefers payback period.

chunks.heading: SSEBITDA: steady-state profitability
chunks.text:
Jason's fix is **SSEBITDA**, which answers: "How profitable would we be, if we were spending only enough to maintain the current state of the company, neither growing nor shrinking?"

- Formula: **SSEBITDA = EBITDA + S&M − COC**
- COC (Cost of Cancellation) is the cost of replacing customers who cancel. Simplest form: CAC × C, where C is the number of customers who cancel in a month.
- It adds back all S&M, then subtracts only the S&M needed to replace churned customers. That keeps revenue flat.
- Because COC embeds sales efficiency (via CAC), the metric works for any company.
- It is "profit if we maintain the company as it exists today."

chunks.heading: Profitable Growth Rate: justifying "spend to grow" with precision
chunks.text:
SSEBITDA gives a self-funded growth rate.

- Formula: **Profitable Growth Rate = SSEBITDA / p**, where p is the cost of a dollar of revenue (defined in his COC article).
- Reasoning: if you recycle 100% of steady-state profit into growth, you spend p dollars per dollar of new recurring revenue.
- Example: SSEBITDA of 12% and p of 4 means the company can self-fund 3% growth per month.
- If it wants 8% per month, that's 5% beyond what it can fund, bought at p = 4, so it will be unprofitable by 5% × 4 = 20%.
- A company in that position is spending to grow responsibly, and "will result in a profitable business once the dust settles."
- Any growth beyond the self-funded rate requires a known, quantifiable loss, so "now we can justify 'spend to grow' with precision."

chunks.heading: How to use and read SSEBITDA
chunks.text:
Lessons from using it for years, including at WP Engine:

- **Negative SSEBITDA isn't automatically bad.** Early-stage companies spend a higher share of revenue on R&D. Mid-stage companies like WP Engine carry high G&A (office space, finance, legal, HR) until they grow into it. These eat into SSEBITDA but may not matter at scale.
- **Don't strip out other "growth" costs to refine steady-state.** It's tempting to say not all engineers do maintenance, but Jason says it's too much work and not really true. A product with no new features isn't in steady state because the market, customer needs, competition and technology (like AI) keep changing. Nobody knows how much new development "steady-state" needs, so don't invent an answer.
- **Diagnose from the components.** If SSEBITDA is negative because gross margin is low or COC is high, the model is unprofitable and you fix root causes. High cancellations and high CAC are actionable. Temporary R&D investment or a new office will correct over time. You can compute an "expected SSEBITDA after scale," for example assuming R&D plus G&A total 30% of revenue.
- **Treat it as a north star, with insight in the inputs.** "All the insights and actions come from backing out of the inputs."
- **Watch direction more than the absolute number.** At WP Engine they watched it move month over month from negative to positive and keep growing. A positive trend in the metric and its inputs, plus a roadmap to improve them, is healthy whatever today's value. "After all, your goal is not to actually be in a steady state!"
- **Once positive, percent growth matters less.** If SSEBITDA holds at 10% of revenue while the company grows, absolute dollars grow. It's reasonable to reinvest some for de-risking and growth rather than "maniacally" maximizing the percentage.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jason Cohen explains why "never compete on price" is right for commoditized markets but wrong when low price is the outcome of interlocking trade-offs, as at Costco, Southwest, Vanguard and IKEA. He covers the price-cut math, why weaknesses deter copycats, and seven shared traits that let bootstrappers pull this off.

chunks.heading: Why "never compete on price" is only sometimes true
chunks.text: Jason's core claim: "never compete on price" holds when low price is a tactic, and fails when low price is an outcome of a complete strategy. Companies like Costco, Southwest, Vanguard, IKEA and Amazon win on low prices and stay profitable.

chunks.heading: When competing on price is a trap
chunks.text:
- Two products solving the same problem for the same segment with largely the same features leave price as the only differentiator. He compares them to "two gas stations across the street from one another; the main difference is the number on the big sign."
- One cuts price 20% and wins share, the other matches, and the cycle repeats through special offers, permanent cuts, "branding" and influencer kick-backs until no profit is left.
- Both companies then can't invest in product development or customer service, so products stagnate and deteriorate. "Low price comes at a price, to consumer and company alike."
- Enterprise and SMB products usually differentiate on capabilities and user experience instead. An enterprise needs SSO, security, compliance and scale, which make software harder for small businesses to use.

chunks.heading: The math of price cuts
chunks.text:
- A 20% price cut needs a 25% increase in customers to keep revenue flat. Charging 80% at 120% volume yields only 96% of the revenue.
- Profit is worse. At a $100 price with $20 profit, a 10% cut to $90 leaves $10 profit, a 50% drop.
- This is why established companies can't match low prices on their main product, which is an Achilles' heel startups can exploit.
- It is also why he and other pundits tell bootstrapped founders to "raise your prices."

chunks.heading: Why new founders underprice
chunks.text:
- They don't know how to set prices and know the initial product isn't very good. Instead of making it simple and lovable and winning a fair price from ideal customers, they "sheepishly charge a low price."
- Low prices attract the worst customers: those who can't afford a proper solution but consume the most tech support.
- They also raise the number of customers needed before the founder can quit their day job, with no extra money for marketing, sales, design or development. He calls this "the wrong decision, made in fear and ignorance."

chunks.heading: Low price as an outcome of interlocking decisions
chunks.text:
- Successful low-price strategies treat price as one component of a comprehensive strategy. The decisions are unique, interlocking and self-reinforcing, and "lowest price" results from them.
- The decisions carry negative consequences that many customers hate. The winners built strengths by leveraging specific weaknesses.
- Competitors don't copy them because they "weren't willing to copy their weaknesses, which enabled those strengths."
- The product is ideal for a subset of customers, and for roughly 100x more it is a better set of trade-offs than the alternative. Targeting a subset lets you win more than that subset.
- Bezos's line: "Your margin is my opportunity."

chunks.heading: Four worked examples
chunks.text:
**Costco**
- Higher quality plus larger packages gives a lower unit price.
- A warehouse feel means a cheaper interior, and limited inventory gives flexibility.
- Drawbacks: unappealing interior, narrow selection, and an annual membership fee, which is pure profit and increases return visits.
- Margin is capped at 14% on all products to protect the low-cost brand, even though customers would pay more.
- Employees average $24/hr, roughly double typical grocery and retail pay in the same cities, which cuts turnover and raises productivity.

**Southwest Airlines**
- Many daily flights on a few short routes, with no long hauls, international flights, airline interconnection or bag transfers.
- Secondary airports are cheaper, so fares can be lower.
- A single airplane type gives pricing power over the supplier from large orders, plus one set of tools, spare parts and training.
- No first class, meals or travel-agency support.
- It stayed profitable through September 2001 and 2008 while other major US airlines went bankrupt. Copycats JetBlue, Spirit and Frontier were less successful, and two of three went bankrupt.

**Vanguard**
- In the late 1970s, mutual funds charged around 2% a year for managers and analysts. A 5% gain became 3% for the consumer.
- Vanguard offered index tracking with no human judgment and only de minimis trading fees.
- It appeals only to those who believe managers don't outperform the market after fees compound.

**IKEA**
- Customers assemble their own furniture, "often poorly, frustrated, and complaining."
- That enables flat-pack shipping and storage savings, efficient store layouts and less transport damage.
- The showroom-to-warehouse flow cuts staffing costs, and a globally standardized line avoids custom products per market.
- Trade-offs: not heirloom quality, a notorious assembly experience and limited selection per category.

chunks.heading: Low-price strategies don't need big funding
chunks.text:
Jason argues the SaaS playbook that low price requires hundreds of millions in venture capital isn't the only one.

- Costco: first warehouse in 1983 for $5M, public in 1985 with a $30M offering. Membership fees covered most fixed costs, and expansion came from operating cash flow.
- Southwest: founded in 1967 with $560,000, started in 1971 with three aircraft serving three cities, and funded expansion mostly from earnings.
- Vanguard: created in 1975 with about $2M and a client-owned structure that didn't need to satisfy external investors. Index funds needed minimal overhead.
- IKEA: Ingvar Kamprad started a mail-order business in 1943 with a small loan from his father. The first showroom (1953) was funded by mail-order profits, and global growth came from reinvested profits.
- His point: these are physical companies with inventory and buildings, so software companies "should be able to do the same."

chunks.heading: Seven common traits of winning low-price companies
chunks.text:
1. Trade-offs many customers find distasteful or a deal-breaker, accepted in order to dominate a subset of the market.
2. Weaknesses that were mandatory for the strengths, so copycats never replicated them.
3. Profitable after one store or a few products, not only at scale. In SaaS terms: profitable unit economics, gross margin above 70%, CAC payback under a year.
4. Profits reinvested in expansion rather than extracted as dividends, an area where bootstrapped companies often diverge from funded ones.
5. Innovation in operations, not just customer-facing features.
6. Narrow offerings and geographic footprints, expanded gradually.
7. A long-term vision with inviolable values and no short-term shortcuts.

His bottom line: being cheap is a lack of vision, while being affordable as a result of strategy is a winning one. "That's being cheap, not affordable."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jason Cohen argues that business models and frameworks, like physics theories, can be useful without being correct, but the useful ones try to capture the messy real world. Symmetric, tidy diagrams and round-number lists are red flags that a framework was built for slides and consulting pitches rather than reality.

chunks.heading: Useful models can be wrong about how the world works
chunks.text:
Jason argues that a model can be useful (it makes accurate predictions) while being incorrect (its explanation of why is false). His anchor example is the Mayans:

- Their cosmology was wrong: Earth at the center, thirteen tiers of heaven, nine levels of underworld, eclipses caused by spiritual beings consuming the sun or moon.
- Their priests still predicted eclipses with impressive accuracy. They knew eclipses happen roughly every 173 days, adjusted by a 405-month cycle and smaller corrections, and they refined the model over centuries.
- In his words, "their theory yielded accurate predictions, even though the theory's explanation of why was entirely incorrect."

He uses this to restate the bromide "All models are wrong, but some models are useful": the Mayan model was wrong in describing the universe and useful in predicting eclipses.

chunks.heading: Quantum mechanics shows the same tension in modern physics
chunks.text:
Jason uses Richard Feynman's view that "nobody understands quantum mechanics" to show that even modern physics wrestles with useful versus true.

- Feynman won a Nobel Prize for a model of how particles interact. It says all possible interactions happen simultaneously, each weighted by probability, and a measurement resolves one of them.
- Einstein ("God does not play dice") and Schrödinger both found this absurd. Einstein built the EPR paradox and Schrödinger built the cat thought experiment to show QM must be only a sophisticated Mayan-style calculation.
- Those experiments have been run many times over decades, and the model has been correct every time.
- Schrödinger said of the Copenhagen interpretation: "I don't like it, and I'm sorry I ever had anything to do with it."

The point he draws is that usefulness is judged by predictions holding up, not by whether the explanation feels sensible.

chunks.heading: Business models are far weaker than physics models
chunks.text:
Jason lists the models used for companies and markets: economics, management theory, strategy theory, product management (pain-points, delighters, JTBD, willingness-to-pay) and startup theory.

- They work some of the time and explain the past retroactively, but often fail to predict the future.
- A company is not an experiment with controlled variables and many trial runs, so these are arguably not "theories" at all.
- He says even the term "expected value" is a fallacy in this setting.
- He asks whether these models are like the Mayans (occasionally useful, not representative) or like QM (representative but noisy because of faulty or missing inputs). He also points to authors more interested in selling consulting off their HBR articles and books than in admitting the limits of simple models in an irreducibly complex world.

chunks.heading: The core test: does the model fit messy reality or a slide?
chunks.text:
Jason's stated filter for any framework: "Does the framework attempt to model the messy real world, or does it seem like a pretty fantasy that looks nice in presentations, HBR articles, and consultants' sales materials?"

- He trusts diagrams that are imbalanced, asymmetrical or even ugly, because they are probably trying to capture the truth rather than please the eye.
- His conclusion: "The most useful are the ones that genuinely attempt to model the real, complex, ugly, asymmetric world, not the ones made to look pretty on brochures for consulting services."

chunks.heading: Red flags that a framework is a pretty fantasy
chunks.text:
Jason lists concrete tells:

- **Perfect symmetry in a model of people.** He immediately disbelieves any human framework in a symmetric diagram with identical numbers of bullets and sub-categories. His example is the DISC personality assessment: four categories, each with exactly six subcategories, each with identical components. "No, that's never how it is with people."
- **Rotational symmetry as the goal.** A model seems to be built so the picture has 90 degree symmetry rather than to describe reality. He cites a marketing "periodic table of elements" graphic as an example.
- **Exactly 10 items on a list.** That is how many fingers we have, not how many things belong on the list.
- **People treated as fungible worker-units.** A model of organizations with predictable responses to stimuli, built by "a professor who has never managed a team beyond six sycophantic grad students."
- **One rubric for everyone.** Strategy as 2x2s and symmetric diagrams with the same questions for all companies, stages, industries and markets, instead of grappling with interacting, dynamic, partly unquantifiable systems (markets, customers, competitors, alternatives, employees, technology, products, global trends).

chunks.heading: What a realistic model looks like
chunks.text:
Jason's examples of models he trusts more, and how he builds his own:

- **Craigslist's category structure.** It has "however many" categories containing "however many" subcategories, which is how human activity actually organizes.
- **Plutchik's feelings wheel (1980).** He calls it quite useful for helping patients identify feelings. It is somewhat suspicious because every second-level category has exactly two third-level emotions, but the first-level categories vary in number.
- **Wardley maps.** They show which activities support growth and differentiation versus which are necessary but commoditized, so teams can invest appropriately.
- **Roger Martin's strategy slide.** It has "five boxes," but the instructions use however many questions are useful, and the order of operations is non-linear.
- **His own frameworks.** His lists on what goes into a great strategy and on deciding whether an investment is worthwhile contain however many items make sense. His analysis of why startups fail has imbalanced categories and unequal bullet counts. His system for product-market fit has steps of varying length and detail, and gives counter-examples to show it is "an interesting guide but not a law."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jason Cohen argues that the common "I had the problem myself" origin story hides seven assumptions, several false, which explains why most such startups fail. Treat your own problem as a spark and a starting theory, then interview real customers, validate the market, and build the non-code skills a company needs.

chunks.heading: Why "I had the problem myself" is only a starting point
chunks.text:
Jason argues that the most common startup origin story, "I had the problem myself, so I built a product," is also the most common origin story of startups that fail. It is a start, not a justification. For a company to succeed, a market must exist at an acceptable price, matching customers' willingness and ability to buy.
