Often left out of that list is the founder: the company has to be right for you, personally. His simplest test is "Why are *you* the right person to start and grow this company?"

He says the claim implies seven things: (1) I understand the problem, (2) I have an attachment and passion for the problem, (3) I know how to solve it, (4) I have the ability to execute it, (5) I understand my customers because I am one, (6) others have this problem and will choose my solution, and (7) I have what it takes. Some of these are true, and he calls that the trap: "Intermittent reinforcement is the strongest mechanism for conditioning," so because some are true, founders can't see why others are false. That blindness "consistently results in failure." Most startups may begin this way; most of those startups fail.

He backs this with others' warnings:
- Eric Ries: "You are not your customer."
- Evan Williams: "Be a user of your own product... But don't trick yourself into thinking you are your user."
- Cranky Product Manager: if the VP of Engineering or the VP of Marketing thinks the target customer is just like them, "you're doomed."

chunks.heading: You understand your version of the problem, not your customers'
chunks.text:
Jason says you do understand the problem, but only your version of it. Getting 1000 customers means solving a variety of related problems, even inside one niche. Sometimes the broader understanding is real: a consultant who has seen 13 variants, or an engineer with ten years across three companies. Even then, being an "expert" is its own form of blindness.

What to check through your customers' eyes:
- **Language.** Discord used to say "get a free community space," but kids were used to "setting up servers," so "get a free chat server" worked better. Their community spaces are still called "servers."
- **Variants.** Onboarding pain looks different by segment: Enterprise needs multi-phase, white-glove processes and training; small businesses need templates and ready access to tech support; consumer products need self-service options and wizards. Pick some to solve, or use features and language to show you address all of them.
- **Integrations** with systems you haven't heard of.
- **Budget.** Theirs might be 1/10th or 10x yours.

His fix: treat your initial understanding as a starting point and interview customers purposefully to get the full answer.

chunks.heading: Passion is real and necessary, but it won't carry you alone
chunks.text:
Jason says attachment to the problem is the item most likely to be true, and it matters. Passion gets founders through the hard times:
- constant rejection from customers, hires and investors
- friends, family, Twitter and Hacker News dismissing you
- bad reviews and cancellations
- engineering that takes longer than expected
- customer acquisition slower than dreamed
- watching others succeed while you struggle, especially a direct competitor

He notes that the day before a competitor goes out of business, all their social media and press is positive: hiring, growing, new features, happy customers. "Do not believe what you read."

Founders need some personal connection, loving the work or the problem, ideally both, because the company becomes an extension of who you are. "I solved my own problem" is a good motivator, but you must be strong enough to face what is coming, which means doing the other things he describes.

chunks.heading: Knowing how to solve it for one case is not solving it for the market
chunks.text: Jason says you know how to solve one facet of the problem: the exact configuration and constraints you had. Most things with computers can be solved, so he believes you can handle the other cases too. But there are cases where this is false, especially in AI, where demos look great and then immediately fail, not good enough often enough, in the real world.

chunks.heading: "It" is the whole company, not the code
chunks.text:
When founders say they have the ability to execute "it," Jason points out that "it" is everything a company must do to succeed, and most of that is not writing code. Questions he asks:
- Can you write a home page headline that attracts the right person in three seconds, or does it just say "______ doesn't have to suck" because you're a lazy writer who has never written a high-performing hook?
- Can you get dozens of qualified leads onto the pricing page, or have you never created a single successful marketing campaign?
- Can you interview twenty potential customers before they buy, or do you not know how to find them?

This doesn't mean you will fail. It means failing is likely if you ignore all this and "go back to writing code," assuming that because you have something working, the rest of the company will unfold naturally.

chunks.heading: You are not like your customers
chunks.text:
Jason is blunt: "You are absolutely not like your customers." You were so frustrated with current solutions that you built your own instead of buying and implementing something that existed. So you are like "exactly none of your customers."

Customers have day jobs. You're lucky if this problem is in their top three right now, and those top three are what they have budget and time to solve. His prescription is to find and interview potential customers to learn what they are actually like, using your own experience as the initial theory, and iterate until you actually understand them.

chunks.heading: The #1 failure: assuming others have the problem and will buy your solution
chunks.text:
Jason calls this fallacy "the #1 reason why companies fail when they start with 'I solved the problem for myself.'" The problem and solution may be real, but many other things must go right before there is a market that can sustain even a solo entrepreneur. Enough people must:
- have the problem, and
- know they have it, so they search for a solution, and
- have a budget for solving it, and
- prefer buying from you over a competitor, and
- stay longer than a couple of months.

Existing solutions may be "good enough" to customers, who won't risk switching to a new product from a new company that lacks features, doesn't lack bugs, and might not exist in two years. His line: "There are a hundred times more legitimate problems in the world than there are markets to buy solutions to those problems." Believing "where there's a problem, there's a company" will almost always disappoint.

chunks.heading: You don't have what it takes yet, and neither did any successful founder
chunks.text:
Jason encourages founders: you don't know what you're capable of until you try. Today you probably don't have what it takes, but that was true of every successful first-time founder. Don't give in to impostor syndrome, but expect an emotional gauntlet. Almost everything you need, you lack yet: knowledge of customer, market, marketing, sales, finance and skills.

He uses himself as evidence: even second-time founders typically fail, and after four successful startups, two unicorns, both bootstrapped and funded, "still most of my initial ideas about most things are wrong." So everyone needs a Beginner's Mind and should use their pivot points to win in their own way. His closing line: "Your current idea is the spark; the right idea is still out there. You have to go get it."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jason Cohen argues your first marketing channel should sit at the intersection of where your customers already are and what you are naturally good at or genuinely want to master. Go deep on one channel, even a small one, and expand later from strength. If the overlap is empty, change the business or partner with someone for whom that channel is a superpower.

chunks.heading: Pick the channel at the intersection of two constraints
chunks.text:
Jason argues that a brand-new company has far fewer viable marketing channels than the "dozens" on offer. Constraints of time, money, brand, reach and specific knowledge about customers rule most of them out. He turns those constraints into the selection method: your first channel must sit where two things overlap.

- Where your customers already are.
- What comes naturally to you.

He frames this as a Venn diagram. If a channel is outside either circle, it is not your first channel.

chunks.heading: Constraint one: fish where the fish are
chunks.text:
Jason treats customer location as something you do not control, so it is a hard constraint. You go where customers already engage rather than trying to pull them elsewhere.

His examples:

- Accounting software: customers are mostly on LinkedIn, some on Twitter, occasionally Threads, maybe Facebook for an older audience. Not Pinterest, Snapchat or TikTok.
- Miniature-alpaca yarn for weavers: Facebook, Pinterest and possibly Threads, plus weaving clubs (a better target than selling to consumers one by one), magazines (even print) and popular influencers.

Questions he says to ask beyond social networks:

- Which keywords do they search when they hit the problem you solve?
- Which podcasts do they listen to?
- Which YouTube channels do they subscribe to?
- Which consultants do they already pay for problems like yours? (Some answers will be "none".)

chunks.heading: Constraint two: what comes naturally to you
chunks.text:
Jason pushes back on the usual advice to leave your comfort zone and become an "expert" in a hundred hours of coursework. His view: "Doing something unnatural, that you despise, will fail."

- You can spot impostors on any network you like: people who don't understand the medium and exploit it for selfish marketing. It's awkward, gets no engagement, and the algorithm silently buries it.
- You will also hate using a platform you disdain, and that disdain leaks onto the page and makes the work less effective.
- His own example: he doesn't understand Pinterest (boards, sharing, even what they're called), so he'd be bad at it and hate it. "Ineffective and unhappy--is this why you started a company?"

The practical step is to take stock of your Pivot Points and consider only marketing options you are naturally good at or genuinely wish to become great at. Pick your first channel from that subset.

chunks.heading: A smaller channel you're good at beats a bigger one you aren't
chunks.text:
Jason says to operate where customers are and where the work comes naturally and joyfully, and that practice then moves you from good to great. That is unlikely if you pick a poor fit.

This holds even when the channel is low-volume. His example: customers are mostly on LinkedIn, but you don't get LinkedIn (it looks like AI, seems fake), while a small, vocal community exists on Threads.

- "It is better to be one of the top three creators on this topic on Threads than to be the 200th biggest creator on LinkedIn."
- Algorithms don't promote the 200th-biggest thing; they do promote the 3rd-biggest.
- You can be 10x or 100x more effective in your messaging, so a smaller audience can still produce success.

chunks.heading: Expand only after you're powerful on one channel
chunks.text:
Once you are powerful on one medium, you can expand to adjacent ones. With a foothold on Threads and revenue that can pay for consulting, tools or a part-time marketer, you repurpose your Threads content in the style of LinkedIn. You enter the second channel "from a position of strength."

Jason's standing rule: pick one marketing channel and go deep. Don't spread across several channels, none of which work well.

chunks.heading: When the intersection is empty
chunks.text:
Sometimes your customers are only on Facebook and you despise Facebook. Jason offers two outcomes:

- **This may be the wrong business for you.** If you're so different from your customers that you can't relate to them, you may not be the right person to run it. The business might be great for someone else.
- **Partner with someone for whom the channel is a superpower.** He describes a Facebook wizard who does in a month what takes others a year. You then focus on the parts of the business that are your superpowers while they bring in new customers daily. He says this could be the team that maximizes the chance the company works.

What he rejects is forcing yourself to figure out the channel you hate. You could, since it's your life and company, but you're adding risk to a venture that is already very risky, and that is "not the right way to solve the equation."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jason Cohen models startup success as a chain of "ands" where any single failing factor is fatal, so failure is the default outcome. He lays out moves to improve the odds: crush a few areas, pick the easiest market for you, build a complementary founding team, design out your weaknesses, play asymmetric games and attack the highest risks first.

chunks.heading: The core model: a startup is a chain of "ands" that fails by default
chunks.text:
Jason argues that "why do startups fail" is the wrong question. Startups fail by default, so the useful question is why any survive. He borrows the Drake Equation (Frank Drake's 1961 estimate of how many alien civilizations we should see) as a model. In marketing terms: "The galaxy produces many warm leads, but every step of the conversion funnel is brutally leaky."

- A startup faces a chain of risks, a chain of "ands", and the failure of any one is terminal.
- He estimates perhaps 999 out of 1000 side projects drop off the chain before becoming a real business.
- Factors in his list:
  - A product people (really!) want to pay for
  - Getting their attention amid the noisy internet
  - Pricing they accept that is substantially above costs
  - Being competitive and distinctive enough to be chosen
  - Being able to build what the home page promises
  - Sustained value delivery so customers stay and keep paying
  - Funding, through early profits or fundraising
  - Working well with co-founders
  - A repeatable, profitable acquisition process
  - Attracting and retaining talent
  - Psychologically handling years of effort, stress and pain
  - Luck (capture good luck, dodge bad luck)
- He gives example failures for each factor, such as the non-technical founder who outsources to a consultant, or the technical founder who builds forever without validating.
- Two takeaways:
  1. Spend more time identifying and addressing the biggest risks.
  2. Reason in terms of "reducing risk" or "increasing chances" rather than "best ideas", "unique strategy" or "changing the world".

chunks.heading: Completely crush a few areas so they overcome your weaknesses
chunks.text:
No startup is low-risk everywhere, but a few areas can be pushed to 100% or beyond, which then compensates for deficiencies elsewhere.

- A top-1% engineer largely removes the "can we build it" risk.
- A founder of a successful open source project with a community gets a competitive and marketing advantage that covers missing unique features or advertising skill.
- Teaming up with an influencer who already has distribution can be worth 50% of the equity, because it far more than doubles the likelihood of success.
- Being a renowned expert in a market lowers market risk, as a marketing advantage and through insight others lack. Entering a market you know nothing about, your education may prove fatal. He also warns that your experience can blind you.
- A singular winning attribute gives both focus and a higher chance of success, "even when you're terrible at everything else".
- Be extreme in the difference, not merely different: "Not just a minimal UI, but so minimal it works on the command-line." Great design so remarkable people buy it only for that. An algorithm that uncovers things no one else does, even at the expense of missing things others catch.
- You can't be extreme at everything; even one extreme attribute is already powerful.

chunks.heading: Pick the easiest product, market and customer for you
chunks.text:
Jason suggests swapping the success-oriented question ("Who would be delighted by this product?") for a risk-oriented one: "What would be the *easiest* customer segment for us to target?"

- "Easy" includes profitable, not just doable or fun.
- Negative example: indie hackers like selling to other indie hackers, but they have no money and usually go out of business in under a year.
- Better example: stable small businesses like dentist offices have large budgets, rarely change software and last for decades. He notes the catch: dentists are hard to get on the phone and aren't usually shopping for software. "Nothing is easy!"
- Large, growing markets are easier still:
  - Many niches to start in
  - Many adjacencies to expand into
  - Incumbents fight over new customers rather than worrying about small new entrants
- The "for us" part matters. A one-person company can't deliver the integrations, governance protocols and professional services even one Enterprise customer demands, so Enterprise is a risky segment for them.
- He likes the word "easy" because it keeps things personal. If you think it will be easy, you're wrong (harder than you think but possible). If you already think it will be difficult, it's worse than you fear: impossible.

chunks.heading: Use the founding team to zero out risks
chunks.text:
- A top-1% engineer co-founder takes execution risk close to zero (except in AI, where he says normal rules differ).
- A top-1% growth marketer co-founder, if the market exists, takes getting-attention risk to zero.
- This is why investors like two founders: "one to build it, one to get rid of it" (a line from his ITWatchDogs days). The value is not just double the work or a partner to commiserate with, but dramatically improving two different variables in the equation.
- Two technical co-founders is "far less interesting".

chunks.heading: Design out weaknesses instead of fixing them
chunks.text:
Rather than becoming good at seven different things, make strategic choices that make your weaknesses irrelevant.

- **Limited time (day job, toddler):** serve an audience that doesn't want tech support or accepts a 48-hour response time. That shapes product complexity, intuitiveness, expectations and price. It is a superior strategy, not just a constraint: higher margin (no support cost), sellable worldwide (language and timezone are no barrier), and a product so delightful that communication is asynchronous praise on Reddit. This works at scale too (Gmail, Facebook, Twitter, most hardware).
- **Bad at design:** don't build for designers or marketing agencies. He says he is a terrible designer and sells to infrastructure engineers or backend Enterprise systems managers.
- **Bad at marketing:** build a collaborative product where people must invite others to use it. It is hard to start, but even poor marketing can then grow a healthy company.
- **Can't code but good at selling:** run a productized service, using internal workflows, spreadsheets and no-code tools that only need to be good enough for your own staff, for low cost and high profit.
- Acknowledge weaknesses as fervently as you're proud of strengths, then embrace the knock-on implications. He points to his Pivot Points article for detail.

chunks.heading: Play asymmetric games
chunks.text:
The probability of success is typically unknown, so some failures are expected. What matters is whether the magnitude of the few successes exceeds the failures.

- He notes that in most startups "most things are mostly a disaster most of the time", and new hires often say, "I can't believe you're doing ______ and yet you're still in business!" That shows a few powerfully positive things can overwhelm deficiencies.
- Jeff Bezos quote he cites: "I've made billions of dollars of failures at Amazon.com. Literally. But a few big successes compensate for dozens and dozens of things that didn't work."
- Asymmetric marketing examples:
  - Fixed-cost, fixed-upside efforts like paid ads (you pay whether or not someone signs up)
  - Fixed-cost efforts that can bring customers for years, like reputation (social media, community forums) or media (successful SEO)
- Asymmetric markets have many ways to win: many niches, routes to customers and expansion paths. Avoid stagnant or shrinking markets where every sale is a scrap against desperate, monied incumbents.
- Rule: "Pick games where the downside is 1x but the upside potential is 10x or 100x." If the realized benefit is "only" 3x, the game is still a success.

chunks.heading: Attack the highest-risk areas first
chunks.text:
Applying the Risk-First Heuristic: tackle high-risk items first.

- Starting with low-risk tasks guarantees early success but leaves the big risks unresolved. Nine months later you may find the venture unworkable, or have to rework everything.
- After designing your market, product and strategy to avoid risks, circle what remains and address it first.
- Examples:
  - **AI in the product:** make sure it works in real life first, because usually it doesn't.
  - **Unsure what customers will pay for:** find out before writing code, since people often have a problem but won't pay to solve it.
  - **Never marketed a new product:** build ads and landing pages leading to a waiting list, to confirm you can get attention before building something no one will see.
  - **No reputation for talking to customers:** do things that create those conversations.
- Even with this model, most startups will still fail. But articulating the risks, reducing some through the team, choosing the market and product right for you, crushing one or two areas, designing around weaknesses and attacking the remaining risks first dramatically improves the odds.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: A sarcastic essay where Jason Cohen lists the worst startup habits as if they were winning tactics. Read in reverse, it argues for talking to customers early, shipping imperfect v1s, validating willingness to pay, treating marketing and sales as the hard part, raising money after traction, and focusing on a differentiated niche.

chunks.heading: Why "stealth mode" is a bad startup strategy
chunks.text:
Jason's essay is sarcasm: every "strategy" in it is one he argues you should do the opposite of. This section covers the stealth-mode core of it.

- He opens with "The last thing any startup needs is people finding out about it," meaning the reverse is true: you want customers and attention early.
- He mocks the fear that a competitor launching at the same time kills you. A head start of "a full 4 months" is no moat against "two Stanford kids with $9,000,000 in funding."
- Secrecy blocks customer conversations, so you never learn what people want.
- He mocks refusing to talk to potential customers who pay "$20/mo" because they might copy you. Their feedback is worth far more than the risk.
- He mocks avoiding entrepreneurs and advisors who "have trod this path before." His point is that mentors and people vetting ideas are valuable and almost every founder story includes them.
- He links this to his customer development essay (talk to customers early).

chunks.heading: Ship an imperfect v1 and gather feedback
chunks.text:
- The sarcastic advice is "Get it right the first time": hold the release until there are no bugs, "even if that means years."
- He points out the obvious counterexample: if products shipped finished, "feedback gathering" tools and bug trackers wouldn't exist.
- The "ounce of prevention" proverb is a trap here: waiting for perfection costs time and learning.
- The implied principle is to release a simple, lovable but imperfect v1 (he links his SLC essay) and let real feedback guide the next steps.

chunks.heading: Ask people if they'd pay, and don't assume the math sells itself
chunks.text:
- The mocked belief: "Of course they'll pay," because the ROI math is obvious. His example: a tool that saves 45 minutes a day, at $20/hr and 20 working days a month, saves $300/mo against a $20/mo price, so it looks like "a money-printing machine for customers!"
- He argues buying decisions are not "cold, rational, and based on micro-economics 101."
- So verify willingness to pay directly. Don't skip it because the value calculation looks obvious.

chunks.heading: Founders do work hard, and obsession is normal
chunks.text:
- Sarcastic claim: great founders have "30-hour work-weeks," and Jobs, Gates, Zuckerberg and Tim Ferriss (4 hours a week) are cited as examples of not working constantly.
- He mocks the idea that the 2,000 founders interviewed on Mixergy are all lying about their intensity "to keep potential competition at bay."
- He mocks "A startup is a job just like any other" with "leave work at work."
- His real view, from the linked essay on sacrificing your health for your startup, is that startups demand a level of effort and obsession most jobs don't. The essay itself doesn't give details here.

chunks.heading: Don't just write code: selling is the hard part
chunks.text:
- Sarcastic advice: "Write the code first." Coding is what you know best, so you double down on it, and attention and sales are "easy."
- He lists what he mocks as easy: getting people to a website (with "1,317,681,984 other websites clamoring for attention"), converting them, getting consistent media attention, and landing reseller deals.
- The reality: "The world isn't littered with failed startups with decent products but only four customers." A great product does not sell itself.
- The fix is to "face your fears now": work on the part of the business you least understand early, namely distribution, marketing and sales. He links his essays on startup biz-dev and on code being your enemy.

chunks.heading: Raising money before you have customers is not the default
chunks.text:
- Sarcastic claim: "Every successful startup raised a big pre-pre-pre-pre-seed round before they had customers or revenue."
- He mocks giving away control early ("Who cares if you already gave away control?") to fund ten engineers building something trivial like "dark mode."
- He mocks the easy-money story: a Figma mockup, a "$48B TAM justification," pitch competitions and "three cocktail events on Sandhill Road," with no questions about customers or revenue.
- The implied lesson is to get customers and revenue first, and keep control.

chunks.heading: Don't copy competitors, and don't sell to everyone
chunks.text:
- Copying: he mocks copying a competitor's feature list ("or just 70% of it"), their pricing, and being "20% cheaper." Competitors' pricing isn't necessarily optimal, and they target different segments with a different brand.
- He mocks skipping customer conversations because "the competitors obviously did all that research already."
- On differentiation: "forget about differentiation. Just match their features but 20% better and 20% cheaper" is the mocked advice. Better and cheaper means little if "better" is undefined.
- Targeting: he mocks "sell to everyone" and writing "everyone" on the home page. Products make different trade-offs in features, usability, integrations, design and price, and people buy from competitors for reasons.
- The fix is to pick a specific segment (he links his ideal customer persona essay) and differentiate on purpose.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jason Cohen argues that hitting product/market fit demands a radical shift from "Explore" (figure out what works) to "Execute" (become excellent at what works, at scale). The founder belief that "what got us here will get us there" is the trap. Roles, quality bar, risk, predictability and even which people fit all change, including the founder.

chunks.heading: Explore and Execute are two different business modalities
chunks.text:
- Jason defines **Explore** as "figuring out what works, as quickly and flexibly as possible."
- He defines **Execute** as "becoming excellent at doing what works, while scaling."
- He prefers "Execute" to the standard term "Explore vs Exploit". Exploitation means extracting value at the expense of someone else. He wants capitalism to create more value than it consumes, so that both parties are better off.
- Execute means operationalizing what was discovered: making it repeatable, teachable, higher quality and automated, and building teams that improve and grow.
- After Product/Market Fit (PMF) the company needs a "radical shift in working style" from Explore to Execute. Applying the wrong modality fails in either direction.
- "Scaling too soon" is a common cause of startup failure. It means switching to Execute before exploration is complete, while you still don't know:
  - which customer segment to target,
  - what price to charge,
  - why someone should pick you over a competitor.

chunks.heading: Why founders resist the switch after PMF
chunks.text:
- Founder arrogance peaks right after PMF. The logic runs: "We achieved our success *because* of the way we've run the company... we will continue to be successful because of those things."
- Jason says most honest founders are "scared shitless". He finds that founders who are deeply certain their success is assured are the most likely to fail, because they are disconnected from reality. "Reality wins."
- The company's needs change dramatically after PMF, and so must everyone at the company, including the founder.
- The result is tumult, frustration, chaos and sometimes irreparable disaster. He calls the period after PMF but before maturity the most difficult part of the journey. "Being hard doesn't make it the hardest. What's hardest, comes next."

chunks.heading: What breaks when growth outpaces the company
chunks.text:
- The company suddenly grows faster than it can manage. For example, support requests exceed capacity, queues grow without bound and service quality plummets.
- Small-company care and personal attention is often a differentiator against larger competitors, and it is the first thing lost.
- WP Engine example:
  - PMF hit in January 2012.
  - Twitter feedback went from "Best support team in the world!" to "Wow, what happened? They're crap now."
  - It was 2013 before there were enough people and process, covering both the science of metrics and the art of culture and empathy.
  - Over the next decade WP Engine became known for the best service in the industry, winning many awards, with a CSAT of 98% and an NPS of 64.
- Hiring is slow. A person contacted today takes about six months to become productive: interview, notice period, a week off, training with no materials while everyone is overloaded, then ramp-up. This applies to engineering, design, product, marketing, sales and finance.
- Because it happened suddenly, "there's quite literally no time in which to fix it," and digging out makes it worse.
- Many facets of the business break at scale, not only software and infrastructure but also people, processes and workflows.

chunks.heading: The Explore vs Execute shift, item by item
chunks.text:
| Explore | Execute |
|:---:|:---:|
| experiment | standardize |
| fail fast | fail never |
| speed | reliability |
| creativity | stability |
| learning | leveraging |
| gathering evidence | data extrapolation |
| manual labor | automation |
| discontinuous jumps | continuous optimization |
| question assumptions | leverage assumptions |
| short-term tactical planning | long-term strategic planning |
| low quality buys speed | high quality buys safety |
| new | valuable |

- **Explore** is for answering the pre-PMF questions:
  - the problem solved,
  - the target market and perfect customer,
  - why they buy,
  - which few features make them buy,
  - which distribution channel works,
  - the right price,
  - the biggest risks.
- In Explore you try, test and fail quickly, because you are running out of time and money.
- In Explore you look for big shifts rather than subtle changes that are too small to notice, since there isn't enough data to measure them.
- Explorers are "confident about nothing", question everything and seek difficult truths.
- Exploration follows no timeline and no single path, though well-researched patterns can improve the odds.
- Once PMF is reached those questions are answered. "All that work, all that worry... none of that is relevant now. In fact, it's getting in the way of what needs to be done, which is to execute."

chunks.heading: Execute mode: hiring, fixing shortcuts and de-risking
chunks.text:
- **Hiring and managing, not building only.**
  - Executives move from building things to building teams that build them.
  - Anything important must be done by a team, for quantity of work and so that illness or departures don't halt a function.
  - Team building is its own skill set: organizational design, hiring managers rather than individual contributors, new communication methods, being "in command instead of in control", prioritization, coordination, and balancing organizational against individual needs.
  - Knowing how to code or design a website doesn't mean you know how to interview a manager, set priorities or run a meeting.
- **Fixing shortcuts, not new features only.**
  - The simple, lovable, complete (SLC) product and the tech debt taken on to ship fast was the right trade in Explore.
  - Customers now hit those bugs and UX issues. They contact support or click "Cancel Subscription".
  - The debt must be paid down. You also need automation, test suites, CI/CD, auto-scaling infrastructure and separate support prioritization and channels.
  - None of that counts as "new features". It is needed because of a growing product and a growing team coordinating work inside it.
- **De-risking, not new innovation only.**
  - Pre-PMF, the likely cause of failure was not having a working business model.
  - Post-PMF, the likely cause of failure is operations: bad tech support, a buggy product, load failures, marketing that can't keep up, hard-to-track finance, security emergencies, taxes and legal.
  - De-risking is a completely different mentality and skill set from adding features.

chunks.heading: Execute mode: scale, predictability and measurement
chunks.text:
- **Rare things become common.**
  - A bug affecting 1% of customers didn't matter before. Now it causes 5 support tickets a day and angry Twitter complaints.
  - Rare problems are hard to detect and hard to solve.
  - Quality becomes a priority, addressed with requirements and processes. Those ideas are new to the company and likely counter-cultural.
- **Predictable processes.**
  - Hiring takes at least six months from deciding to open a position to a trained, productive person.
  - So you must know what the company needs in six to twelve months, which means the business has to become more predictable. This applies to support, sales, engineering and new departments like finance, HR and account management.
  - Predictability requires playbooks, documentation, measurement and processes that keep output steady under variable input.
  - These guardrails also help new people get up to speed in your new way.
- **Stalls in growth.**
  - You are underwater serving customers, hiring, lacking documentation, adding processes and changing culture all at once.
  - Meanwhile growth can stall because you lag on features, competitors and marketing.
- **Measuring success.**
  - Execute lends itself to measurement: sales leads, closed-won rate, sprint velocity.
  - Measuring Explore is difficult or impossible. If you expect to fail at least half the time, "we learned something" is hard to verify, and "learning" probably can't be measured.
  - Still, "an explorer who wanders for years and never finds anything, is not succeeding."
  - Teams that have only known Explore often resist the specific measurement of Execute.
  - Jason doesn't think sprint velocity should measure productivity. It becomes meaningless once management watches it, because teams subconsciously inflate point values. He says it should be a private team metric for honest self-management.

chunks.heading: People and culture have to change, including the founder
chunks.text:
- Explore suits someone who doesn't want a map, happily throws work away when an assumption proves wrong, and ships at 50% quality and 50% completion.
- Execute suits someone who wants a clear goal and constraints, designs a way to complete the mission, then executes it.
- "These aren't the same personalities. It's probably not the same person." Some people can make the transition and some can't. This is hard to manage, especially when they were critical to early success.
- It is hardest when that person is the founder: "It's most difficult when that person is you. And it always is."
- The change is a fundamental shift in attitude, skill sets and company culture, not only daily tasks.
- Things you were proud of were right for discovering what to make, but now hold you back from scaling it. "It's time to be proud of something else."
- It means letting go of "the things that got us here", sometimes even the people who got you here, and sometimes realizing you yourself no longer fit. "This is going to be hard."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: A practical menu of ways to get customer-development interviews when you have no brand, product or audience. Jason Cohen covers ground rules (talk only to your ICP, frame it as asking for advice, make scheduling trivial) and tactics from referrals and LinkedIn to forums, ads, influencers and events, drawing on how he got interviews for WP Engine.

chunks.heading: Interview ground rules before any outreach
chunks.text:
- Jason says to interview only the ICP. Family and friends will say "that sounds cool" but cannot say whether real potential customers will pay. "Go where the ICPs are."
- "Good enough is good enough." An hour-long interview is best, but a partial one is fine. If the person seems interested, always ask for a follow-up, because that is "10x more valuable."
- Frame the request as asking for advice. People hate being surveyed but love being asked their opinion. Flatter them honestly ("because you're an expert", "I've really loved your article on ...").
- Make scheduling trivial: send a calendar link with many open slots and minimize back-and-forth.
- Expect a low success rate. Cold outreach is "soul-crushing" for you and annoying for them. A 10% response rate would be fantastic. Don't take rejection personally.
- He does not need many methods: "You only need one or two methods to work," especially if each interview yields new referrals. The goal is to either invalidate the idea or change it until it is validated.
- What won't help: building software, adding features, and "yapping about nothing on social media."

chunks.heading: Referrals: the compounding source
chunks.text:
- Ask your whole network to introduce you to ICPs. The network has almost no ICPs itself, but it probably knows some. Use a tight ICP description so people immediately think of the right person.
- At the end of every interview, ask who else you should talk to. Try to get two or more.
- Recruit them into the journey instead of just asking for names: "I'm trying to have 20 conversations like this, to give this product a real shot. It's my dream to create something people genuinely love. It would mean the world to me if you could help me by intro'ing me to a few other people who are [my ICP]."
- If you average one referral per interview, "you have an infinite supply of interviews."

chunks.heading: LinkedIn outreach (the WP Engine playbook)
chunks.text:
- For WP Engine, Jason used LinkedIn to find people with the target title and industry (web developers using WordPress) and asked for an hour to discuss a new startup concept for which they were the ideal customer.
- Result: out of 50 requests, 40 agreed, and 30 eventually became customers.
- Why the hit rate was so high:
  1. He offered payment: "I will pay any fee you feel is fair for an hour of your time. I'm not asking for a donation; I'm genuinely interested in your expertise and opinion." Only 1 of 40 asked to be paid. "Reciprocity works."
  2. He researched each person briefly (who their business serves, location, anything in recent blog posts to comment on), so the outreach was personal.
  3. He tried to get an intro from a mutual connection, and wrote the InMail for the connector. It was polite, did not over-sell, and sounded like a normal person, not a robotic marketer.

chunks.heading: Communities, complaints and people asking for help
chunks.text:
- **Forums (Reddit, Discord, Slack, Facebook Groups):** Selling is a no-no, but customer development is not selling; it is learning about people's lives. Post one question per post and don't flood. Answers are disconnected, but good for surveying and honing hypotheses.
- Lurk to learn when the community is most active. Give high-quality answers to others first, because communities are "give-and-take, not just take." Treat it as a long-term relationship, not hit-and-run.
- Hacker News, Quora and Craigslist are possible, but they are general forums where ICPs are hard to target and long-term relationships are nearly impossible. Small independent community sites may welcome a new member or sell cheap, tasteful ads. Don't dismiss old-school Facebook Groups, even for modern software.
- **Complainers:** Set up searches for your problem area and competitors across social media (including YouTube comments), forums, and review sites (G2, TrustRadius, Capterra). When someone complains, find them on LinkedIn and reach out, referencing their review.
- Best signal: people who have taken action (evaluated other products, switched, or built workarounds). "It's free to complain, but expensive to act, so they must really mean it."
- Feedback and voting sites are informative for trends, but caution applies: your product, segment, goals and maturity differ. Verbose posters are more likely to want to talk.
- **Help seekers:** Use keyword monitoring for "How do I ______?" posts, actually help them, then ask for a call.

chunks.heading: Landing pages, influencers and content
chunks.text:
- **Buy traffic to a one-page landing page** asking for interested people. Bid on low-competition keywords; you want a few targeted visitors, not a scalable channel. A/B test ads and page. AdWords is the most sophisticated for targeting and testing, but Twitter, LinkedIn or Facebook may fit where the audience is. Tim Ferriss used AdWords to test titles and positioning for The 4-Hour Work Week.
- Clicks are a positive signal on positioning but not an interview, so collect emails from people willing to talk. Offer something (an Amazon gift card, a charity donation, "first year free").
- Bonuses: add web chat so a visitor sees a real human; offer a fee to those unconvinced; gate content the ICP cares about behind an email; put a scheduler link on the page, or make the scheduler itself the landing page, including the participant fee (as John-Paul Anderson did).
- **People who already talk about the problem:** Bloggers, newsletter writers and social posters like discussing it. Engage thoughtfully first, then offer a chat and to share your aggregate findings. "It doesn't matter how many followers they have"; smaller ones are more likely to engage and later promote you, including via affiliate links.
- Guest posts work only if significantly better than their median post, and better on multi-author sites than single-author blogs.
- **Influencers:** Don't ask them to spam their audience. Offer value: share your findings summary for a post, a revenue split on promotion later, a useful report from your prototype, or a truly great guest piece.

chunks.heading: Paid sources and investors
chunks.text:
- **Pay for meetings:** User Interviews (and maybe Fiverr or Upwork) has people who talk for money. Use a strong ICP filter; your ICP may not be there.
- **Expert networks** (GLG, Third Bridge) connect you with verified operators, including Directors, VPs and C-level people, for candid talk about budget, decision-making and competitive dynamics. They cost more than most options.
- **Angels and VCs:** They talk to founders for a living and have broad industry perspective. Treat their input as "ideation" not "validation," because "ultimately they don't know any more than you do. If they did, they wouldn't have such a large failure rate." Their real value is introductions to actual ICPs.
- **Professionally engaged people:** Job postings reveal pain points (read the requirements and responsibilities patterns); contact hiring managers. Look for backers of similar products (Kickstarter prepayers, ProductHunt voters). Newly funded startups (via Crunchbase, AngelList) may enjoy talking to another founder.

chunks.heading: Build in public, micro-tools, podcasts and cold outreach
chunks.text:
- **#buildinpublic:** Twitter was the main place; Bluesky is growing, with some on Threads. LinkedIn "isn't very good for this." Comment usefully on others' posts, then ask for referrals. Beware that other early-stage founders are almost certainly not your ICP.
- **Free micro-tool:** Build something SLC (simple, lovable, complete). It serves both early conversations and a permanent inbound funnel. HubSpot pioneered this; at $2B revenue it still works, with 30+ tools.
- **Podcast:** Pitch an episode where you interview the podcaster on the topic (they must be an ICP). Or run your own: Steve McLeod's podcast, described as being for his ICP, now has a waiting list of people wanting to be interviewed.
- **Cold outreach (email, DMs):** Low conversion but cheap. A/B test a tight message and offer a reward.

chunks.heading: Physical places, PR and events
chunks.text:
- **Waiting people:** Approach people in lines, airport terminals, between conference sessions, or in live-stream comment sections. Gifts help: Nick Basile used free donuts with university students; Karsten Duus Wetteland found people in his own building (future encounters make them friendlier). If you work in the target industry, interview coworkers.
- **Early PR:** Usually late-stage, but if you are an expert with interesting insights and good at interviews, it builds credibility and inbound conversations. "You have 'given first,' and now you can 'take.'" Stunts count: Brian Chesky's "Obama O's" and "Cap'n McCain's" cereal at the 2008 DNC; Alexis Ohanian's personalized Reddit luggage tags to the first few hundred people mentioning Reddit.
- **Conferences and networking events:** The event must attract your ICP. People love talking about themselves; prepare 3-5 questions. Bonus: earn a speaking slot for instant credibility. Noah Kagan gave his speaker fee to the audience ($50 each) at FinCon.
- **Make your own events:** Giff Constable's example: a founder targeting mothers of young children failed at pickup zones, got a few minutes at playgrounds, then succeeded by hosting evening events at a spa with pedicures and wine. Jitpal ran an industry panel with experts and C-suite; costly, but it led to many ICP conversations and initial sales. A local Meetup.com group takes time and works best in a large city, but can last for years and become a brand fixture, and you need no existing following.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jason Cohen defines "brittle points" as single dependencies (a platform, marketing channel, big customer, key employee, or the founder's whole identity) whose failure kills an otherwise healthy company. He borrows redundancy from server engineering and argues you fix them serially, one at a time, with each fix costing money and sometimes creating new brittle points.

chunks.heading: Brittle points: single dependencies that can kill an otherwise healthy company
chunks.text:
Jason Cohen defines "brittle points" as places where a sudden change makes the company fail catastrophically, "regardless how wonderful everything else is." The product works, customers pay, sales are picking up, and then one component breaks. His examples:
- **Platform changes.** An app drops to zero downloads after Apple builds the feature into iOS. A Google Workspace add-on drops to zero sales after Google builds it into Docs. A Twitter tool breaks when Twitter removes API functionality.
- **Channel saturation.** The first marketing channel saturates fast, and growth stalls at a low but non-zero rate.
- **Channel wipeout.** Large bidders triple cost per click, Google's SEO algorithm changes, the big industry event stops, the hot blog loses its traffic, or the magazine running the ads closes.
- **Customer loss.** One big customer representing 80% of revenue leaves. Signing that customer wasn't a mistake, because it funded the company.
- **Key-person loss.** An early 10x person can mint the company but may be irreplaceable. Finding, convincing and ramping a replacement takes too long when pay is almost nothing.

He notes that all young companies, and some mature ones, have dependencies like these. You have to rely on outside technology, vendors and people.

chunks.heading: The engineering analogy: redundancy buys robustness, at real cost
chunks.text:
Jason borrows how engineers harden a single server.
- A power supply, strip or cord can fail, so data centers add a second set of each. "In short: redundancy"; "It's twice as expensive, but it buys robustness." He says airplanes do the same.
- City power can fail, so data centers keep gas generators, stockpile gasoline, and test and maintain the units weekly. They often run several generators.
- The whole data center is itself a brittle point, so clouds add identical servers in a physically separate data center with different power and network vendors.
- That requires a smart traffic-routing system, which "becomes--you guessed it--a Brittle Point."

His takeaway: fixing brittle points adds cost and complexity and sometimes creates new brittle points. "Reliability is expensive." The same pattern applies to every business failure above.

chunks.heading: Neutralizing each type of brittle point
chunks.text:
**One platform**
- Be multi-platform. At WP Engine, they run on all three major clouds (AWS, Google, Azure).
- A Twitter listening tool could add LinkedIn, Threads and Bluesky. Extra features then double as risk mitigation.
- Or build only on platforms whose owners are committed to never competing with their ecosystem. Ideally the platform promotes the ecosystem so it becomes a growth vector. He says Salesforce is currently the best at this.

**One marketing channel**
- Find additional channels so variation in any one isn't fatal.
- This is a "double-win" of growth plus risk mitigation, which makes it especially worth investing in.

**One big customer**
- Get a long-term contract with a serious breakup clause, as insurance while you win replacements.
- Prioritize sales until that customer is a smaller share of revenue.
- Take up-front payments, so you have cash to invest in that growth.
- Charge more than you originally calculated, for the same cash-flow cushion.
- Wrong attitude: "We now have a large customer, so pour extra money into development to make sure we don't lose it." Right attitude: use that money to win other customers.

**One key employee**
- They may leave, and they will inevitably get sick or take vacation.
- He pushes back on the startup refrain that everyone must work 70+ hours a week to the exclusion of everything else: "Talk about brittle!"

chunks.heading: How to prioritize: keep a list, attack one at a time
chunks.text:
- "Solving these things takes time and money." You can't just hire three great developers or snap your fingers and find three new marketing channels.
- Maintain a list of these risks and periodically ask: "Which single one is best to attack right now?"
- Example: experimenting with new marketing channels is cheaper and easier than finding, interviewing, convincing and managing a second developer. A second channel also generates revenue, which lets you afford the second developer. So put all your energy into getting a second channel working.
- Manage risk rather than trying to eliminate all of it at once. Tackle one or two items at a time.

chunks.heading: Brittleness scales up with the company: the HubSpot example
chunks.text:
- As you grow, the "chunks" that create brittleness grow too, creating new risks and new investments.
- In 2016 HubSpot had $260M revenue, was growing about 60% a year, and had about a thousand employees. It was not brittle in any of the ways above.
- But Jason says it was a single-product company, which at that scale is a brittle point. A sea-change in the inbound marketing software market could be fatal, and a maturing, saturating market limits long-term growth.
- The redundancy was to become a multi-product company. The second product had to scale at least as well as the first, because it's still brittle if one product is 95% of revenue.
- In his words, HubSpot attacked that problem, and "in 2024 it's clear that they succeeded."

chunks.heading: The biggest brittle point: the founder's whole identity
chunks.text:
- Jason says almost all founders, himself included, suffer from the largest chunk: "the entire company."
- This is one reason founders are often sad, sometimes permanently depressed, after a successful sale. The company was their identity and life for years. They may have no hobbies or close friends left, and may have sacrificed family or health.
- The fix is not two companies or two jobs. That's burnout, and a lack of singular focus creates worse outcomes.
- Instead, realize there were things you loved before and there will be things after, perhaps different ones. "You are inside a chapter in the book of your life."
- He frames it as robustness "not in many things simultaneously, but in things serially."
- Rediscovering who you are is rarely easy, simple or fast. He hopes the successful sale "has literally bought you time."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jason Cohen explains how stopping A/B tests when they look conclusive (p-hacking) and running many tests at 80-90% confidence produces a flood of false positives, which is why stacked "wins" never add up. His fix: rerun tests, don't stop early, chase large effects, and design each test to validate a theory of the customer.

chunks.heading: A/B testing false positives and p-hacking
chunks.text:
- Jason argues that roughly half of the A/B tests marketers call "successful" are false positives.
- A test at 90% confidence is wrong about 1 time in 10, and many teams use 85% or 80%, which makes false positives more common.
- Some teams never pick a confidence level or a sample size N. They "run the test until we get a result that looks conclusive."
- He calls stopping whenever a result looks conclusive "p-hacking," a fallacy statisticians have documented since the 1950s.
- It fails because at small N, random fluctuation often looks like "90% confidence of a positive result." If the experiment continues, the data drifts back to a negative result.
- Jason says, "Before you shake your finger at them, shake that finger at yourself." He is comparing marketers to scientists who publish a single lucky result.

chunks.heading: The coin-flip example of multiple testing
chunks.text:
- Jason's example: flip a coin 270 times. If the coin is fair, 90% of the time the result lands between 45% and 55% heads, per the binomial distribution.
- If you get 57% heads, you can say "biased" at 90% confidence.
- Now test 10 coins and get 9 "fair" and 1 "biased." That result is exactly what you'd expect even if all 10 coins are fair, because 10% of tests wrongly say "biased."
- The `9 / 1` result is also the single most likely outcome if 9 coins are fair and 1 is biased.
- So the result can't separate the two cases. His conclusion is that "this procedure is insufficient" and needs to be augmented, not that you've found a biased coin.
- He says marketers make exactly this mistake with A/B tests: run a batch, see about one in ten "win," and call that a success.

chunks.heading: How pharma and social science fake results with real experiments
chunks.text:
- To get a useless drug approved, a company can run the same study 15-25 times until a false positive appears, then publish only that result.
- Pharma used to do this. The FDA now requires pre-registered studies and publication of all results.
- Jason notes companies are still sometimes approved on a subset of trials and later found ineffective. His example is the decongestant phenylephrine, with nearly $2B in annual sales, which an FDA advisory panel unanimously concluded is ineffective.
- Social science has the same problem as the Replication Crisis. One small study, often on college students, produces something "interesting," and journals publish it without waiting for replication.
- Even Nobel Laureates have admitted the fallacy debunked their own work and called for "replication rings."

chunks.heading: The evidence from real A/B testing programs
chunks.text:
- A study of more than 2,100 real-world A/B tests across Optimizely's customer base found a 40% false positive rate. The software declared those tests "significant," so marketers had no way to know.
- Shopify's Growth Team (600 people) tracks results at 2-8 weeks and again at 12 months.
- Of tests that showed statistically significant improvement in the short term, 35% had the effect disappear over the long run. Jason cites this from Archie Abrams, Shopify's VP of Product and Head of Growth.
- He describes a pattern many testers recognize:
  1. Run tests and keep the winners.
  2. One is 10% better, another 20%, another 10%.
  3. That should compound to about 45% overall.
  4. Looking back months later, there is often no improvement at all.
- His explanation is that the improvements didn't add up because they were false positives.

chunks.heading: Practical fixes to stop fooling yourself
chunks.text:
- Run the test again. If false positives are 1 in 10 at 90% confidence, a real effect should reproduce in a second test.
- Don't stop tests early. His blunt advice: "I know you're excited. Just wait."
- Decide how much N you need before the test starts, and pick a confidence level up front.
- Seek large effects, such as double-digit changes in conversion rate.
  - Large effects are unlikely to be caused by randomness. Small fluctuations are far more likely to be false positives.
  - Large effects also matter to the business, and small ones don't.
  - This may mean testing drastic changes instead of incremental ones.

chunks.heading: Form a theory, test it, extend it
chunks.text:
- Jason says many A/B tests are just "throwing shit at the wall," excused by "no one knows which headline will work." He calls that thoughtless, and says you learn nothing whatever the result.
- His alternative is to create validated learning. Form a theory of the customer, then design variants that would win if the theory were true.
- Example theories he lists:
  - Visitors at this point are ready to buy, so send them down a restricted purchase funnel.
  - Visitors here want to learn more, so let them explore features rather than pushing a funnel.
  - People are on the fence, so use more forceful, confident language.
  - People can't see well on mobile, so use higher contrast and less text.
  - Pictures beat paragraphs, because people hate reading and half don't speak English natively.
  - People click buttons more than links.
  - Visitors from channel X are in a Y state of mind and excited by Z.
- Write down the theories that come to mind first, then build designs that would perform better if each were true.

chunks.heading: Reading negative and positive results against a theory
chunks.text:
- **Negative result:** the theory isn't disproved yet, because your implementation may not have been extreme enough or had other issues. Run a new experiment.
  - If you still get nothing after a few iterations, you've accumulated evidence the theory is wrong. Jason calls that "learning," and it wasn't happening when you threw things at the wall.
  - Then invent a different theory and test that.
- **Positive result:** the theory isn't proven, since positive tests are often false. Lean further into it with a more extreme version or a different form of the same concept.
  - If the theory is right, it works again, maybe better. If it reverts to nothing, it wasn't real.
  - Once validated, extend it: ask what else is probably true and design to exploit it. This can give multiple leaps of improvement instead of random changes.
- Jason says most theories won't be right, or won't be impactful enough, and most tests will come up negative. That's true even for world-class testers like Shopify's Growth Team.
- He frames this as the route to being a marketer AI can't replace, since AI can generate random phrases but isn't a good marketer.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jason Cohen argues the case for retention, growth, profit, sales efficiency, LTV, Rule of 40 and NPS in turn, then shows the real lesson is that no one metric is always the most important. Metrics are tools for your stage and goals, so narrow to a few that the whole company aligns on.

chunks.heading: The metric you pick depends on stage, circumstance and goals, not on a universal ranking
chunks.text: Jason Cohen's essay answers "what is the single most important SaaS metric?" by arguing that the question itself should be un-asked. He makes a strong case for seven different metrics, then says all of them are true "for some companies, at some times, in some stages, in some industries, in some markets." His larger point is that "companies are more complex than 'a single most important metric.'" A metric is a tool in service of your goals, timeline, size, circumstance and even philosophy, "not a master that you thoughtlessly obey."

chunks.heading: Retention and top-line growth: why each can be called the most important
chunks.text:
**Retention.** Jason argues cancellations signal a lack of Product/Market Fit, whatever the cause (price, features, severity of need, duration of need). If that can't be fixed, the business is a failure even with otherwise stellar metrics, because customers are rejecting the product.
- At scale (past Product/Market Fit, into tens of millions in revenue), cancellation grows with total customers, so it scales exponentially.
- New-customer growth scales only linearly with sales and marketing cost.
- So cancellation necessarily and always outgrows inbound activity, and growth stops.
- Retention matters at every stage.

**Top-line growth.** High revenue growth implies many other things are going well, even unmeasurable ones: Product/Market Fit, ability to reach and retain customers, and a large addressable market.
- Tech market dynamics follow a "winner take all" power law, and the only way to be the biggest is to grow the fastest.
- Fast growth proves every other part of the company is healthy, or at least healthy enough not to be fatal.
- High-growth companies keep all options open: stay independent, raise money, or sell.
- It is also the biggest determinant of equity value, because it maximizes both revenue and the revenue multiple.

chunks.heading: Net-profit growth and sales efficiency: the counterweights to growth-at-all-costs
chunks.text:
**Net-profit growth.** Jason says the era when equity value was determined almost entirely by top-line growth "died in 2015." Public and private markets now reward profitable growth.
- Profitable growth means building sustainable, value-creating companies, not companies that "grow like a virus," without purpose and possibly killing the host.
- In his words, unicorns are dying "not for lack of revenue, but for lack of profit."

**Sales efficiency.** If acquiring new revenue is expensive, the product is being stuffed into the market rather than embraced by it. That means you are growing artificially and haven't found real Product/Market Fit and longevity.
- Merely replacing natural cancellation becomes too expensive, which caps your maximum size.
- Too much of a customer's lifetime revenue is spent on costs before they write the first check, so long-run profit is hard.
- It suggests you are "buying customers" rather than building a product people organically want, enjoy and talk about, which questions the product's fundamental value.

chunks.heading: LTV and Rule of 40: combined metrics that avoid optimizing one number at a time
chunks.text:
**LTV.** Looking at component metrics individually never gives a complete picture.
- High growth fails if margins are too low for a profitable business at scale.
- High retention fails if MRR is so low that meaningful revenue needs too many customers.
- Optimizing one number in LTV often moves the others the wrong way. Example: raising price increases MRR but also increases cancellations because people can't afford it.
- Only combining the metrics gives a true picture of the business model's health.
- To critics who say LTV isn't valid because the future is unpredictable, he replies that this is "exactly why it's so important to try."

**Rule of 40.** The sum of year-over-year revenue growth rate and bottom-line profit margin.
- A company either needs to grow fast (so being unprofitable now creates long-term value) or be very profitable (value is cash coming out of the business over many years).
- He calls it the "super-metric" covering both the growth and profit phases of a successful company's life.

chunks.heading: NPS: customer satisfaction as the root of other metrics
chunks.text:
Jason presents NPS as the ultimate measure of value creation, which feeds every other important metric.
- **Growth:** only high-NPS customers spread word of mouth, the cheapest form of marketing and one of the few that keeps scaling with the business.
- **Retention:** high NPS implies customers stay.
- **Intangibles:** brand quality, Product relevancy, and customers who love you even when you screw up.
- **Scope:** it covers Product Management, Tech Support and every other function.
- His framing: "The customer is the fundamental unit of the company, and NPS measures customer health."

chunks.heading: How to choose: focus on what matters right now, then simplify
chunks.text:
Jason says focusing on one thing is valuable because it creates focus, especially in a young company that doesn't have time to maximize multiple goals. Larger companies like WP Engine can have three or four, "but still not many."

His process:
- Figure out what is most important right now.
- Find what's on fire.
- Identify what matters most for reaching the company's next milestone.
- Lean into what is working well.
- Then simplify and clarify the few goals and metrics the entire company should align on.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jason Cohen pushes back on the habit of calling common biases "fallacies," arguing that maximizing expected value is itself the fallacy for one-shot, high-stakes decisions. He walks through ten biases and shows why each can be the right call for founders and startups.

chunks.heading: Jason treats common "fallacies" as heuristics that can be rational
chunks.text:
- Jason rejects the "back on the Serengeti, this made sense, but now it's a fallacy" narrative. He says "not all heuristics are 'fallacies.'"
- He argues that calling something a fallacy implies it breaks "cold, hard, scintillating, pure, perfect logic," and he disagrees with some of that logic.
- He objects to the lizard-brain framing and to buzzwords like "first principles," "maximize expected value" and "Bayesian priors" used to look enlightened.
- His closing advice is to use ideas and tools that fit each person's circumstances, think for yourself, and run your own experiments instead of believing "models and theories with more exceptions than examples."

chunks.heading: "Maximize expected value" is the real fallacy for one-shot, high-stakes decisions
chunks.text:
- Jason believes maximizing expected value is "rarely the correct way to make a decision."
- He notes that economists who push it cannot predict major economic metrics or markets, yet call everyone else irrational.
- Thought experiment: a fair coin flip where heads doubles your life savings and tails loses all of it.
  - Expected value is zero (sum of outcomes weighted by probability), so EV says playing and not playing are equivalent.
  - People with little in the bank might play. Most people who spent years building a nest egg would not.
- Change it to 55% win and 45% lose-everything:
  - EV becomes positive (+10% of savings, so $10,000 on $100,000).
  - Very few people would change their answer, because losing everything at 45% is essentially as bad as at 50%.
- Jason calls the "Expected Value Fallacy" using statistics that only apply if you play the game a million times and keep the average, then applying them to a single play.
- Losing everything is the point: the outcomes are not symmetric, so averaging them is the wrong lens.

chunks.heading: Loss aversion and the endowment effect are not irrational
chunks.text:
- **Loss aversion** (valuing loss pain above gain joy):
  - It took "a lifetime of pain and sacrifice and luck" to build what you have, so protecting it more than you chase more is rational.
  - This matters most when the loss is catastrophic.
  - If the loss is immaterial (an experiment with 1/1000th of your money), people happily play. So the "fallacy" only gets invoked when the loss is important.
- **Endowment effect** (valuing a thing more because you own it):
  - Owning something carries real value: emotional investment in the decision, identity ("a person who would have this object"), how others perceive the ownership, and sentiment that grows over time. He says economic theory is wrong if it treats sentiment as worthless.
  - Concert-ticket example: a $200 ticket, per a study he cites, wouldn't be sold for less than $300 to $400. Jason's explanation is that you bought it because you value going to the show, so selling the ticket means selling the experience, which is worth more than face value.

chunks.heading: Sunk cost, confirmation bias and status quo bias have a startup upside
chunks.text:
- **Sunk cost:**
  - In long-term projects, commitment can lead to eventual success, while "fail fast" can ensure failure.
  - Emotional and financial investment drives perseverance when there's little apparent hope, which can be the key to overcoming obstacles.
  - He says sometimes people claim to avoid the sunk cost fallacy when "really we're justifying bailing out when times got tough."
- **Confirmation bias:**
  - Constant self-doubt leads to inaction, and frequent plan changes confuse people.
  - A leadership team that keeps shifting priorities will confound the whole organization. "A strategy that constantly changes, cannot be executed."
  - A strategy that never changes is also wrong. There is a time to reevaluate, but that time is not "always."
- **Status quo bias:**
  - Stability and consistency build reliability and trust.
  - A startup thrusts constant change on its people, so keeping some things constant gives everyone something to hold on to.
  - If you put real thought into a decision, changing it should take even more thought. It's not a bias to honor your former self unless new information would have changed the decision.

chunks.heading: Availability, recency and overconfidence bias are how startups operate
chunks.text:
- **Availability bias:**
  - Startups (and even scaled-up companies) often lack comprehensive or statistically significant data, and extensive research is impractical.
  - You must act on what's in front of you under uncertainty rather than fall into analysis paralysis. "It's not a bias, it's life."
- **Recency bias:**
  - Early in a startup almost everything is being done wrong, so reacting quickly to what's in front of you is how you iterate to doing it right.
  - "This is how we did it at my last company" doesn't matter when that company was 400x larger, 50x older and in a different industry.
  - Agility is one of a startup's few advantages, and "reacting to the latest information is the definition of agile."
- **Overconfidence:**
  - He cites that 93% of drivers believe they are above-average drivers. That is mathematically wrong, but it gives them the confidence to act, and constant second-guessing would make them worse.
  - "Founders must be over-confident." The most likely outcome is failure, so you need overconfidence to stay optimistic.
  - At the beginning, successes and failures look the same, so you need it to push through.
  - Before product/market fit you can't know whether or when you'll hit it, so you need it to keep trying things and treat everything as an experiment, not a failure.
  - Overconfidence is not blindness: "Being confident in the vision, but skeptical about every detail, is how you find the truth."

chunks.heading: Survivorship bias is real, but copying successes still beats avoiding failures
chunks.text:
- Jason has been pointing out survivor bias in business advice for more than 15 years.
- He concedes several points:
  - Successes are lucky, not just good.
  - Failed companies often do the same things as successful ones, so those things may not have caused success.
  - Often one or two most important things caused the success despite everything else, not because of it.
- He disagrees that "you learn more from failure than from success." Failure shows what didn't work, but that doesn't point to what does.
- His test: which is more likely to work, copying everything about a success or avoiding everything about a failure? The success, because "not all of it was luck."

chunks.heading: Herd behavior: be different in one place and conventional everywhere else
chunks.text:
- Your product and company should differ in one way your target customers believe makes you the best in the world (for them).
- In every other way, "surprises are bad." His examples of unwanted novelty:
  - A unique pricing model where the customer can't work out the bottom-line price.
  - Bizarre controls built because the team didn't want to use menubars.
  - Non-standard icons for things like copy and paste, chosen to be creative.
- Adhering to norms provides "safety, understanding, control, and ease," which are desirable in products and companies except where you make a genuine improvement.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jason Cohen replaces "strengths/weaknesses" and SWOT thinking with "Pivot Points": non-judgmental facts about a person or company that you build around. He gives prompts to find personal ones, a reverse-engineering workshop for a company's, and nine ways to apply them to strategy, positioning and ICP, plus a rule for when changing one is worth it.

chunks.heading: Pivot Points: the core concept
chunks.text:
- Jason's "Pivot Point" is a non-judgmental fact about a person or company that is neither a strength nor a weakness. It is a strength in some situations, a hindrance in others, and irrelevant in still others.
- He dislikes "strengths" and "weaknesses" (in personality tests, SWOTs and similar tools) because they assume the context for judging is already known, and often it isn't.
- Example: his own third-ranked StrengthsFinder trait is "Competitive". It helps in sales calls and in closing a candidate who has other offers. It hurts in team meetings meant to help each other, and when self-worth is based on others' accomplishments.
- The name comes from the "pivot foot" in basketball, lacrosse and Ultimate Frisbee. One foot is stuck, and the rest of the body can go anywhere subject to that constraint. Pivot Points are the constraints you build around.
- Example: if you hate managing people, don't become a manager, and don't build a company that will eventually require a team (or at least don't be its CEO).
- Pivot Points can change, but not often and not capriciously. Short-term planning should treat them as fixed. Long-term planning, especially about where to invest time and money, can ask "What new Pivot Points do we want?"
- This matches the Lean Startup "pivot": you keep what is correct or immutable and pivot the rest of the company around it.
- He doesn't like the term "enabling constraints" because people get hung up on "constraint". Pivot Points are facts with consequences that you leverage or design around.

chunks.heading: Finding your personal Pivot Points
chunks.text:
Jason says honest self-knowledge is hard because we are biased, carry baggage, and can't get outside our own heads. His approach uses fill-in-the-blank prompts plus outside input.

**What drives you** (sample prompts):
- "Even when I was a kid, I would ______, and I still find myself drawn to it."
- "When I'm on an extended vacation, I get itchy to ______."
- "Whenever I ______, I get lost in the work, and feel energized (not exhausted!) when the work ends."
- "I asked a few people who know me, and who I trust to be thoughtful and observant, and they said my special strengths are ______."

**What hinders you.** Jason notes it is sometimes easier to avoid what you hate than to construct a life of what you love ("always invert"). Sample prompts:
- "When I'm faced with ______ I physically feel the 'pit of my stomach' falling."
- "If my job starts requiring me to ______ with even 10% of my time, I would at least think about changing jobs."
- "Whenever I ______ all day long, I know I do great work, but I'm absolutely exhausted."

He says to be honest even if "society" won't like the answers. Wanting money or fame is a legitimate motive, and he quotes Orwell's "Why I Write" on desire to seem clever.

chunks.heading: Outside-in questions for personal Pivot Points
chunks.text:
Jason asks others about "strengths and weaknesses" because that language helps them generate answers, then untwists the answers into non-judgmental Pivot Points. People are rarely fully honest, even anonymously.

His favorite reference-check question, because candidates only refer friendlies who give sanitized praise:
- "What is the ideal scenario, under which this person thrives?" Construct the perfect set of circumstances (subject matter, goal, team or lack of one, direction or lack of it, incentives) where they kill it, are efficient, productive, extremely happy, and make everyone around them happy.
- The opposite: "Construct the scenario where they die inside, mess everything up, and piss everyone off." It's funny, easy to answer, and doesn't feel negative.

Example of extracting Pivot Points: "give them a goal so they know what success looks like, then get out of their way because they explore quickly" yields "goal-oriented" and "craves exploration". That means R&D (not goal-oriented) or a mature product (needs execution, not exploration) is a poor fit, while an early-stage startup is great.

A third question: "What are my strengths that I'm unaware of because they come so naturally to me? Where I don't realize other people aren't like that too?" These are the most natural, powerful Pivot Points and constitute your "edge". You can't see them yourself, so ask others.

chunks.heading: Finding your company's Pivot Points
chunks.text:
- Pretend you are an outside consultant hired to reverse-engineer the business: not what people inside think it is like, but what is actually going on. Observe behaviors and results.
- Don't interview people about why they took actions, because they will rationalize or defend. The goal is discovering, not judging.
- Start by "write-storming" (brainstorming in writing, in isolation, then pooling) observations about what is special or peculiar about the product and company.
- Write-storming avoids bias toward the fastest, loudest voice, supports slower thinkers and non-native speakers, and uses background processing. He cites Leigh Thompson's *Creative Conspiracy*: "I was shocked to find there's not a single published study in which a face-to-face brainstorming group outperforms a [write-storming] group". His optimal process is write-storming to maximize creativity, then meeting to synthesize.
