- He does not claim it is fail-safe: "Even in chess. The rest of the game does matter."
- His summary: when so much risk is removed by avoiding avoidable things, with frameworks that spell out what "not blundering" looks like, why wouldn't you? "80% winning is not blundering."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jason Cohen argues that success-through-perseverance and failure-through-obstinance look identical at the moment of decision, so nobody can know in advance which one they're in. The job is to decide decisively, measure honestly, and use practical questions (timeboxes, existence proofs, sounding boards) to find out fast.

chunks.heading: Treat the decision to persist as an unknowable bet, and optimize for finding out fast
chunks.text:
- Jason frames two scenarios. In S1 you start an AdWords campaign, it's "obviously not working" at time B, you keep going, and by time C it works. In S2 you do the same, and at time C it's still failing and you've wasted more time and money.
- At time B the two are identical. Persevering is only wise in S1 and stopping is only wise in S2, and you can't tell which one you're in.
- He says the usual labels are convenient rationalizations: S1 becomes "success through perseverance" and S2 becomes "failure through obstinance." Both sets of platitudes (winners never quit; doing the same thing expecting different results is insanity) are backward-looking.
- It applies to AdWords, product design, a company's vision, and the market you hope to create around it. "It all looks the same at point B."
- Even venture capitalists, who decide this for a living, can't tell. He notes most VC portfolios lose money.

chunks.heading: Why stopping isn't the safe default
chunks.text:
- Stopping at B can look smart, but "either way you've failed" to achieve something useful.
- "Stopping is sure failure while persisting is at least possible success." If you stop, you never create something great.
- He argues you also can't reliably say you "learned something" from the outcome. You made choices and observed results, and that may be all there is.

chunks.heading: Treat uncertainty as liberating
chunks.text:
- Accepting that you can't know which scenario you're in lets you decide with less second-guessing in the moment and less guilt afterwards.
- It also means taking less credit when things go well.
- The job becomes to "find out which one it is as quickly as possible." In practice:
  - Stop dithering and make a strong decision.
  - Keep your eyes open and measure what's happening as objectively as possible.
  - Hope for S1 but allow for S2.
  - Don't feel guilty if you guessed wrong or cocky if you guessed right.
- His closing advice: "just shut up and get going," and when done, don't look back too much, "just shut up and get going again."

chunks.heading: Guiding questions for whether to keep going (reader-contributed, lightly edited and endorsed by Jason)
chunks.text:
- **Timebox:** set a hard deadline for how much longer you'll work on it without seeing improvement.
- **Enjoyment and learning:** are you still enjoying the project and learning from it?
- **Rate of progress:** is it slowing or accelerating?
- **Existence proof:** if others achieved a similar outcome, don't stop, especially if their solutions are bad and they're still making money.
- **Noticeably better:** is the product better than market alternatives, or will it be soon? If no to both, consider stopping.
- **Run out of ideas:** if the team has run out of ideas and conviction, consider pivoting. If it has run out for pivoting too, do a full reset or quit.
- **12-month test:** can you see yourself doing this in 12 months? If not, you might as well stop now.

chunks.heading: Guardrails against self-deception
chunks.text:
- **External sounding board:** use one to keep you honest. Numbers often won't say left or right, and even when they do, we dismiss them as "outliers" or "this time is different."
- **Sunk cost:** don't let it decide.
- **Fear:** don't decide out of fear. If the outcome scares you a little, stick with it.
- **Penny in the air:** take a long walk and listen. Often you already know but "don't want to admit it to myself."
- **Go back to "The Why":** if you now have more information about whether the original reason is credible, re-assess. If the information and belief are unchanged, press on.

chunks.heading: Weigh the stakes and alternatives
chunks.text:
- **Opportunity cost:** are you missing opportunities because you're fixated on this?
- **Consequences:** what's the downside of not finishing, and what do you get if you succeed? Are there smaller wins along the way?
- **Worthwhile, fixable, energy:** is it worthwhile, is it fixable, and do you still have energy for it?
- **Self-checks:** am I enjoying it, do I have room to improve, am I willing to do the work, am I marketing it as well as I can, and would my time be better spent on a new project?

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jason Cohen argues AI breaks the normal David-vs-Goliath playbook. Incumbents are embracing AI, already have the tech, data and talent, and "the AI market" is really existing markets with tougher competition. Startups need a strategy built on rapid differentiation and distribution, not the old assumptions.

chunks.heading: Why AI startups can't rely on the usual David-vs-Goliath playbook
chunks.text:
Jason argues that the standard startup-versus-incumbent dynamics held in the internet and mobile revolutions but do not hold in AI. He lists five lost advantages: risk-aversion, innovation gap, data, talent, and the "market" itself. His conclusion: "If an AI startup has a strategy that looks like a strategy a non-AI startup had five years ago, that may very well be the wrong strategy."

- Startups normally lean on specific advantages over incumbents to overcome mature products, distribution, brand, trust, optimized organizations, and cash.
- In AI, many of those advantages are unavailable and some become disadvantages.
- He notes blockchain is not comparable: it has had almost no business effect despite billions of dollars over more than a decade.
- Typical strategies are wrong because they assume the David-against-Goliath advantages. If strategy is "how we will win," the "how" must be different in AI.
- It is easy to create an AI startup, gain attention, and generate excitement. It is much harder to compete and win. He expects most AI startups that ignore this to fail.
- He still says all new startups probably need to include AI. The point is that they need a different view of how they will win.

chunks.heading: Disruption Theory does not apply to AI
chunks.text:
Jason says the Innovator's Dilemma is not a dilemma this time, because incumbents are not ignoring the new technology.

- Disruption Theory: new technology is (a) better in some ways, (b) worse in others, and (c) cheaper. (a) plus (c) can overcome (b). Over time the technology improves and disrupts incumbents who thought they were safe.
- His example is the transistor radio. Sound was far worse than furniture-sized RCA radios, but it was portable and cheaper. "A radio at the beach that's staticky and tinny is a lot better than not having a radio at all." Sound later improved and the incumbents were disrupted.
- In AI the conditions are absent. Incumbents say the technology is groundbreaking, that they will become irrelevant if they don't embrace it, and that shareholders demand they invest huge percentages of annual revenue.
- Startups that normally depend on incumbents ignoring new technology and new markets cannot count on that. They compete directly with well-funded incumbents selling to existing customer bases.

chunks.heading: Incumbents already have innovation, so distribution is the startup's hard problem
chunks.text:
Jason reframes the Alex Rampell idea that the race is "whether the startup gets distribution before the incumbent gets innovation."

- In AI, incumbents already have the innovation, via closed APIs or open source.
- Startups struggle as hard as ever to find distribution, arguably harder, because every market is over-saturated with new startup competitors, some with massive funding.
- The "hard tech" is the same for everyone: LLMs rented from OpenAI, Anthropic, Cohere and others, or open source such as Llama, Bloom and Mistral. This is a level playing field, not a startup edge.
- Differentiation exists in prompt engineering, problem break-down and use of vector databases. But startups have no edge there, such as willingness to take more risk. At best it is neutral.
- Simply matching established players' capabilities is not a winning strategy. A startup needs differentiation and distribution "even more quickly and dramatically than is normally required."

chunks.heading: There is no AI strategy without a data strategy
chunks.text:
Jason says data is needed for training, testing, benchmarking and features, and incumbents have it or can afford it.

- Incumbents have data because they have customers. They can use customer data to train models and tune algorithms, so long as they maintain secrecy and privacy.
- Examples he gives:
  - Intercom's AI strategy builds on hundreds of millions of customer interactions, an advantage over a newcomer building a chatbot from scratch.
  - Google has an advantage in AI video because it owns the YouTube library.
  - GitHub's Copilot benefits from its vast code repository, including changes with human-written explanations.
- Incumbents can also pay for data. He cites Axel Springer licensing news to OpenAI for tens of millions of dollars, and Reddit striking a deal with an unnamed AI provider for $60M.
- AI will keep getting cheaper, better and faster. Access to huge training data will not; the opposite, since data owners have learned how valuable it is.

chunks.heading: Top talent is happy at incumbents
chunks.text:
Jason says startups traditionally attract talent with autonomy and wealth potential, but AI changes that.

- Top AI and software engineering talent can get above-market pay at incumbents, with a large budget, all the data, and a built-in large customer base that will use what they build.
- They avoid sales, marketing, support, accounting and fundraising. For pure computer and data scientists, "This is heaven for many."
- Many people still want to create or join startups, but startups have no inherent talent advantage. At best it is neutral.

chunks.heading: "The AI market" is not a market
chunks.text:
Jason rejects "AI will be a multi-trillion-dollar market, so there's enough for everyone."

- A market is a set of buyers with sufficiently similar needs, constraints and goals that the same product can be sold to all of them.
- The real AI market is companies like OpenAI and Cohere. Unless you compete directly with them, you are not in it.
- A chatbot is in the chatbot market and an SEO tool is in the SEO market. It is the same market as before, now with stiffer competition.
- "AI is in the solution-space, not the problem-space." The customer problem is unchanged. For chatbots it is still talking to customers 24/7 in any language. AI enables new solutions.
- AI can reignite growth in existing markets. Customers may pay more for better chatbots that defer more contacts from humans, support more languages and answer more questions. Companies that rejected chatbots as bad customer experience may enter the market.
- The right analysis is: "Here is how AI will transform this existing market," then "Here's how we fit into that growth."
- Even so, an incumbent with a trusted brand, customers and data has the easier path. A startup is at a special disadvantage, especially when entering a new niche or a market that is organically large and growing.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jason Cohen argues that every big-company advantage (scale, brand, process, profit centers) creates a weakness a startup can exploit. He lists ten attack vectors: unquantifiable risks, niches below the materiality threshold, non-scalable work, founder-led support, new tech, drastic change, personality, non-zero-sum channels, being worse-but-acceptable, and low-cost against a profit center.

chunks.heading: Taking risks that incumbents can't quantify
chunks.text:
Jason argues a startup beats a large incumbent by doing "things that incumbents cannot or will not do." Big-company advantages (money, brand, customers, sales) come with weaknesses, because things at scale are "super-linearly more difficult."

- Incumbents approve risk by asking whether ROI (potential revenue divided by cost) is good and whether the chance of failure is low.
- ROI analyses are usually wrong. Projects run late and over budget, and outcomes come in worse than expected, so both sides of the fraction are off.
- Projects that look low-ROI on paper are unlikely to be pursued by incumbents, even though some are genuinely good. Easy-to-analyze ideas get chosen over better ones.
- Fear of failure motivates more than the desire to innovate. The core business is going well, and no one wants to preside over a multi-million-dollar failure. "Let's gather more data" and "let's wait for consensus" feel safer.
- Startups can pick high-risk or unknowable-risk ideas with large upside, and incumbents are unlikely to follow.
- He applies the same logic to work planning: big "Rocks" should be chosen on potential outcome, while "Pebbles" should be chosen on ROI.
- His blunt aside: the incumbent can buy you later at 10x revenue.

chunks.heading: Going after a niche that fails the incumbent's materiality threshold
chunks.text:
Incumbents can't afford niches because new bets must be material to their revenue.

- Rule of thumb: a new market or product should add at least 10% to overall revenue (the "materiality threshold"), and the bar rises with perceived risk or investment. For a company with hundreds of millions in revenue, that means a product with a good chance of making $50-100 million, or they won't try.
- He quotes Warren Buffett: "Given our size, we only see a few good things [to invest in]. If we were smaller, then we'd see lots of good things."
- There is also a P&L ratio. Software companies at scale spend around 20% of revenue on R&D. A fully loaded team (assumed: 8 engineers, a PM, a designer, a manager, in the US) costs upwards of $2 million a year. At 20% of revenue, that team must generate at least $10 million a year, even if it owns a small add-on.
- A founding team of two plus one employee doesn't need $10 million. A $1 million niche is a win.
- A startup can pick a niche and ICP the incumbent can't afford to target. The bigger the incumbent, the less the startup has to worry about competition.

chunks.heading: Doing things that don't scale, and not needing to operate at scale
chunks.text:
Jason uses WP Engine's launch of LetsEncrypt support as the example.

- WP Engine had around 100,000 customers who could use it on day one. Before release it had to be built to scale: components split into queues, monitoring and human alerts when a queue stayed broken, at-scale tests with 1,000 simultaneous requests and random failures.
- Hundreds of support reps and hundreds of salespeople had to be trained, marketing had to craft messaging, and the feature needed near-zero bugs. If 10% of thousands of users hit a bug, support gets crushed and people complain on Twitter.
- It took the team most of a year. On launch, thousands of users adopted it on day one and tens of thousands in the first month, and people praised the company on Twitter.
- The upside of scale: 1,000 users on day one, 10,000 by day 30, and $1M or even $10M ARR quickly. A startup can't do that.
- A startup can launch in a few weeks and iterate. Incumbents won't spend a couple of years getting to $1M ARR, a couple more to $5M, and a couple more to $20M. That is too slow to reach material revenue and doesn't use their at-scale assets.
- That ramp is a "highly successful growth rate" for a startup. Nobody knows you exist, which is bad for sales but good for iterating without harming your reputation.
- Heuristic: a product that is naturally easy to scale from day one is easy for an incumbent to copy. One that is naturally hard to scale from day one is ideal for a startup.

chunks.heading: Unsurpassed customer service from founders and engineers
chunks.text:
Jason handled support tickets himself every day at WP Engine until the company had around 35 people.

- Talking to customers when things go wrong is the best way to learn how people use the product. It produces feature ideas, ways to streamline the product, and ways to improve retention.
- Customers are impressed by the quality of support and the range of problems you can solve, which a company with a thousand support reps can't match.
- Great support builds love and loyalty. Love brings forgiveness during outages or security incidents, and word-of-mouth advocacy, so it produces inexpensive growth. His line: "Love is the best form of 'willingness to pay.'"
- The advantage fades as you scale. WP Engine objectively still has world-class support (a dozen Stevie Awards, 98% CSAT), but it's not the same as personal attention from the founder.
- Option: never grow that large, optimize for profit and efficiency over revenue and scale, and make support a permanent competitive advantage. Either way, it is a great way to get started.

chunks.heading: Using new technology and making drastic changes
chunks.text:
New technology is risky for incumbents, but the startup's constraints differ.

- Incumbents are right to avoid new tech. It may lose support in five years, be hard to hire for, have security problems (he says it will "certainly" have many), not work at scale, or be hard to coordinate across thirty developers.
- A startup is more likely to die from the things that block product/market fit: customers are hard to find, there is no budget for the problem, competition is tough, or it runs out of money. The tech stack is rarely the cause.
- New technology often creates advantage by making things efficient or possible that weren't before (AI is his current example).
- Worst case, if the startup survives, is a rebuild on a different platform five years later, possibly pausing features for a year. If that penalty "buys" a successful company, it was worth it.
- Incumbents struggle to change anything with 100,000 paying customers. Even a slight UI change brings angry tweets, clogged support, and docs and screenshots to update. Customers don't wake up wanting a different UI, and they have workflows to accommodate. Brand positioning, pricing, architecture, integrations and partners are locked in.
- A startup with 100 customers can change any of that drastically and pivot toward market reality and its own strengths. When the market shifts (AI today, mobile before), incumbents can't adapt quickly and the startup can adapt immediately.
- Part of why "big companies are dumb": they can't change even when they know they're doing something dumb.

chunks.heading: Having an opinionated personality
chunks.text:
Large companies rarely express a personality, and startups can win on it.

- A big company addresses a large, diverse market, so by speaking to everyone it speaks to no one in particular. It relies on brand trust ("No one ever got fired for hiring IBM"), which means impersonal but solid language.
- Customer communication is spread over hundreds or thousands of people in support, sales, marketing, product and design. A thousand people can't share one genuine human voice, so they default to generic, professional language.
- Startup founders often have strong personalities and views on what's good and bad, which is partly why they started the company.
- Some customers will be attracted and some repelled, which is true of anything "wonderful and different and powerful."
- When a big company injects personality it feels contrived. A startup's feels genuine because it is. He says you will directly win customers because of it.
- Some buyers only want the market leader and nothing a startup says on its home page will change that. Ignore that segment and target customers who want to buy from a plucky upstart that has something to say.

chunks.heading: Playing non-zero-sum games
chunks.text:
Incumbents win zero-sum games because they can apply money and expertise, and can even overspend at a loss to make a channel worse for competitors.

- Zero-sum channels arise from power laws or exclusivity:
  - SEO (the top positions get more traffic than all others combined)
  - AdWords (same)
  - Affiliates (the top few produce more leads than all others)
  - Retail shelf space
  - Exclusive distribution deals
  - Government fiat
- Non-zero-sum channels, where an entrenched incumbent can't stop others from winning:
  - Social media
  - Newsletters and content marketing
  - Collaborative promotions
  - Ecosystems like Salesforce and the Apple Store
  - Consumers who buy multiple products (3D animators often use several tools)
- Markets can be zero-sum too. Stagnant or shrinking ones are, because winning one customer means a competitor can't have that revenue. Growing markets have a stream of new dollars, so many competitors can grow. He says startups should target growing markets, whether the goal is a small profitable company or a unicorn.
- Startups needn't never play zero-sum games, but those are harder and sometimes impossible. Invest in the non-zero-sum ones.

chunks.heading: Being worse but acceptable on most dimensions, and low-cost against the profit center
chunks.text:
Most customers don't care about most things, so a startup can choose one or two dimensions to care about and win the segment that cares about the same.

- Uptime example: "99.9% uptime" sounds excellent but equals 44 minutes of downtime a month. Most hosting providers promise only 99.9-99.95%. Getting to 99.99% takes an order of magnitude more spend, software and process, yet looks little different on a pricing page.
- Incumbents must invest in these dimensions because "at scale, rare things become common," and because it wins segments (WP Engine has enterprise customers whose policies demand 99.99% uptime).
- Startups don't have the rare-at-scale problem and can pick customers without extreme demands. They should actively avoid customers with myriad difficult demands.
- Dimensions where incumbents must care and startups needn't:
  - **Security:** WP Engine spends tens of millions a year (internal teams, policies, training, SOC and ISO compliance, vendor reviews) because security is a selling point. Most products and customers don't demand it.
  - **Quality:** An entire product that is low quality in every dimension is just a bad product. But a SaaS tool used in one geography's working hours can tolerate an hour of downtime in the middle of the night.
  - **Scalability:** Without "big data," build with simplifying assumptions: PostgreSQL instead of BigQuery, SQLite instead of PostgreSQL, Python instead of Erlang, reading into memory instead of streaming, batch jobs instead of queues and auto-scale groups, off-the-shelf libraries and vendors instead of bespoke.
  - **Compliance:** Internal policies (data access, device management, IP ownership, enterprise and government requirements) win multi-million-dollar three-year contracts but slow everything and raise cost and price.
  - **Legal:** Startups often (unknowingly) don't comply with all laws, such as taxes and acceptable-use policies. He doesn't advocate breaking laws on purpose, but notes it doesn't hurt sales and may speed them. Uber's growth by ignoring regulation is his example.
- Incumbents must charge more to pay for multi-dimensional excellence at scale. A startup can charge less for something objectively "worse" in many dimensions and stay profitable.
- Incumbents can't change their business model. The costs of a global sales team, white-glove onboarding, expensive infrastructure, vendors and shareholder expectations of rising profits mean they can't drop prices, so they can't match "a 'lite' version for 1/10th the price."
- This is a softer version of Disruption Theory (The Innovator's Dilemma): incumbents retreat to their most profitable segments and let the startup thrive.
- "Whatever generates the most profits for the incumbent, is the thing they are least able to change."
- Caveat: incumbents will defend profit centers heavily, but not on price. They might overspend on AdWords to ruin that channel, but can't stop a great content marketing strategy.
- Summary: "The only mistake is for a startup to go head-to-head with an incumbent where the incumbent is strong. Attack where you are strong, and they are weak."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jason Cohen argues expected value misleads for one-shot, all-in investments like a career path or startup, since a guaranteed $1M and a 10% shot at $10M are not equivalent. He offers a framework: outsized payoff, accumulating value, stable conditions over ten years, alignment with global trends, a personal edge, and fit with your long-term vision.

chunks.heading: Valuing a long-term investment: why expected value fails
chunks.text:
Jason defines an "investment" as a big commitment of time, money and reputation over months or years, for a large payoff in the far future, under real uncertainty. You can only do 1-2 at once because you are "all in." This is different from short experiments like a poker bet, an A/B test or a brochure to test demand.

His framework for judging one has these parts:
- Mandate an outsized payoff.
- Value must accumulate over time.
- Success conditions must stay stable for ten years.
- Align with global trends.
- Have an edge.
- Match your long-term vision.

chunks.heading: Why "expected value" is the wrong tool
chunks.text:
Jason says expected value (payoff times probability) is almost always the wrong tool for evaluating investments. His example:

- Investment A: spend $50,000 and a year. The payoff is $1,000,000 with 100% probability, like a signed contract with cash in escrow. Expected value is $1M, a "20x."
- Investment B: spend the same $50,000 and year. The payoff is $10M at 10% probability and $0 otherwise. Expected value is also $1M, also "20x."

The math calls them equivalent, but B almost certainly wastes a year and $50k, while A is a guaranteed life-changing sum. Unless you already have many millions, you would not pick B.

It is worse in practice because you rarely know either number. Even experts can't predict probability or outcome, so you end up multiplying garbage numbers together.

Expected value does work for a portfolio of bets: a VC with twenty companies, 100 newsletters and 1000 tweets, or 1000 poker hands. Winners and losers roughly balance. The bets must be uncorrelated ("as goes one, so very likely goes the other" breaks it). Single big commitments like your next job or the startup you spend your savings on are not like this.

chunks.heading: Mandate an outsized payoff, estimated to a power of ten
chunks.text:
In the success case the payoff must be enormous, because the risk is unknown, both whether it pays and how much. If it can pay 10x or 100x, or be life-altering, then falling short (3x, or merely life-improving) is still worthwhile.

How to size it:
- Use Fermi estimation: estimate to the nearest power of ten. It is easy and needs little research, unlike detailed estimates that tend to be wrong.
- Example: a career path earning 50% more for ten years is about 10x more earning power over the career. A startup in a small, stagnant niche might be worth $1M, versus $10M for a small software company in a larger, growing space.
- Don't round up. Errors typically run toward the investment being less valuable. If your goal is to maximize earning power, "50% more" is not good enough; look for a route that potentially doubles your trajectory. Jason notes 2x for 10 years is 20x, but he rounds down to 10x since it may not be exactly 2x and may take years to ramp.
- Large personal investments are the "Rocks" in his Rocks, Pebbles, Sand prioritization framework.

chunks.heading: Value must accumulate, ideally with a feedback loop
chunks.text:
For a large payoff, value has to be reliably addable and must not erode quickly. At minimum it accretes; ideally growth begets growth.

- Social media and SEO: more writing brings more interaction, links, attention and traffic, which makes more attention easier. Writing consistently also improves your writing.
- Recurring-revenue product companies: revenue grows as long as more customers start each month than stop, which holds if people truly want and love the product.
- Consulting, accounting and law firms often don't accumulate. Work for one client doesn't automatically apply to others. Jason says such firms are often valued around 1x revenue or less, while SaaS companies with similar growth rates are valued at 5x-10x revenue.

He warns the investment doesn't need to be exponential. People often think "viral products" are exponential when they are not, and exponential is probably a red herring for most ventures.

chunks.heading: Bet on what stays stable for ten years
chunks.text:
If you spend 3-5 years investing and expect payoff in the following 5, the world must still value the thing in years 5-10.

Jason endorses Jeff Bezos's 2012 point that people ask what will change in ten years but rarely what will not, and that "you can build a business strategy around the things that are stable in time." Customers will always want low prices, fast delivery and vast selection, so effort there keeps paying off. "When you have something that you know is true, even over the long term, you can afford to put a lot of energy into it." Jason notes that ten years later this analysis proved correct.

chunks.heading: Align with a global trend
chunks.text:
If a stable thing isn't available, pick something aligned with a trend that has enough momentum to not change soon. A dependable trend is either:
- (a) so large today it would take a decade to change significantly, or
- (b) growing so fast (at least 5x in the next 5 years) that it stays strong even if your growth estimate is badly wrong.

For startups, he favors a large, growing market:
- More niches where you might find traction, without triggering a large incumbent.
- More marketing channels you can use.
- People already spend money, so you answer "why buy from me" rather than "why allocate budget at all," "that's a problem but not a priority," or "I never heard of that problem."
- The pie grows even if your slice is small.

Trends he cites: distributed workforces, aging populations, physical delivery and online shopping, global demand for health care, education and energy, and AI unlocking new product capabilities.

chunks.heading: Have an edge, and a vision
chunks.text:
An edge answers "why should you make this investment, not someone else?" A good investment you can't execute with excellence isn't good for you.

- Edge in investing often means evaluating risk better, but that is rare. Jason notes the majority of VC funds lose money and angels do worse.
- More likely your edge is in execution. You don't need to be unique.
- Two routes: be top 0.1% in the world at one thing (rare), or be top 25% at a few uncorrelated things, which together make a special edge. Math plus programming is correlated and not special; artistic plus great at programming is a much more elite group.
- Example: Scott Adams was a decent illustrator, a decent humorist and held tech jobs, and the intersection of those is what is unique.
- Passion is part of an edge, not enough. It gives motivation through hard times, but doesn't mean the risk is low, the market good, or the career lucrative.

He also says the payoff must match your long-term vision. If it won't make you proud, happy, fulfilled or rich (whatever your goals are), it's not a good investment. "If you run quickly in the wrong direction, that's not progress." He admits he often lacked a vision and wonders how much of his path was luck: "Best not to leave it to luck."

chunks.heading: Good investments are rare
chunks.text:
Jason says few investments pass all these filters. Most startups fail, most VC portfolios lose money, and 80% of day-traders lose money. That is why adhering to the criteria matters: most investments aren't right for you, and you don't want to spend five years on the wrong one.

You'll never know if you made the best choice, even in hindsight, so the goal is an excellent choice: "To invest wisely, with the information you have."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jason Cohen lists apparent mistakes that are actually expected side-effects of good decisions, such as pivoting a fresh strategy, removing then re-adding features, or shipping buggy early. Each is a signal you're culling, learning fast and holding to strategy and values rather than over-engineering or waiting for perfect.

chunks.heading: Re-adding things you cut from the backlog is a sign you're culling enough
chunks.text:
- Jason argues that a backlog grows without bound unless it is culled. "1000 tickets is the same as 100 tickets, except that you haven't identified which 10% are most important," which means you aren't working on the most important ones.
- If you delete feature requests or bugs and later find some of them were needed after all, that is a sign you're handling the backlog well.
- His rule of thumb: "If you're not adding back feature-requests or bugs you cleaned out of the backlog, you're not cleaning out enough."
- He recommends keeping multiple backlogs, except for the work being done right now.

chunks.heading: Pivoting a strategy right after writing it is expected
chunks.text:
- Jason says a strategy that never changes is wrong, and the most likely time to find out it's wrong is just after you wrote it down, because you have the least practical experience with how it meets real life.
- Not pivoting a wrong strategy costs the company months or even years of useless work, followed by rework. That can put the whole future of the company at risk.
- Strategies are released with fanfare (documents, presentations, speeches, reorganized teams), so saying "just kidding, we were wrong about something important" feels costly. He says you have to take that risk, because executing the wrong strategy is far worse.
- His communication tactic: say it out loud to everyone. Explain that a new strategy is unlikely to be right the first time, that you're putting the company first, and that no one should be doing work you secretly know is the wrong work.

chunks.heading: Refactoring infrastructure after 10x growth means you didn't over-engineer
chunks.text:
- If you're not refactoring your infrastructure after a tenfold increase in growth, you over-engineered the original.
- Jason scaled WP Engine to millions of websites serving tens of billions of requests daily. His lesson: you don't know what will break under scale until you're already scaling, because you must handle things you can't even measure yet.
- Over-engineering for massive scale up front means you aren't shipping your SLC (simple, lovable, complete product) fast enough. He calls it a form of premature optimization.

chunks.heading: Release early and expect a pile of bugs afterward
chunks.text:
- If you're not fixing lots of bugs after a major release, you released too late.
- He says releasing garbage is a bad policy, but waiting until "everything's perfect" is also bad.
- Example: Windows 95 shipped with tens of thousands of known bugs (an entire book explained how to work around 1000 of them) and was still heralded as one of the most successful product releases of its time.
- Contact with customers shows which bugs matter most to fix next, and reveals bugs you would never have found on your own.

chunks.heading: Keep support and sales in-house longer than feels natural
chunks.text:
- If you held onto support and sales rather than hiring a team, you learned a lot about your customers and about how to do support and sales.
- Scaling either too soon is a classic funded-startup mistake. Without a system (materials, knowledge bases, scripts), new hires don't know how to do the job, and distributed work makes this 10x harder.
- "The second you put someone else between you and a customer, your pace of learning and understanding falls off a cliff."
- His rule: wait until it's breaking for lack of scale, then scale. Once the company is truly at scale, this rule no longer applies, and he says you're mismanaging the company if you still follow it.

chunks.heading: Letting someone go soon after hiring is a good outcome
chunks.text:
- If you kept someone on when you knew it was never going to work, you did a disservice to that person, the team, the company and yourself.
- Don't do it capriciously, but dragging it out has costs: good people leave because they don't want to be on that team, meetings, complaints and side-conversations multiply, morale drops, and competent people cover for the incompetent, lowering productivity.
- Face the truth and act quickly. If it happens a lot, fix your hiring process, but the rule still applies in the meantime.

chunks.heading: Ignore most competitor moves, and reject lucrative deals that don't fit
chunks.text:
- **Competitors:** "If you're not ignoring most of your competitor's moves, then you're playing their game, not yours." Stay focused on your unique value proposition. His example: when a major competitor launched a similar service at a lower price, Dropbox stayed the course on user experience and brand loyalty rather than fighting a price war.
- Sometimes ignoring a move turns out to be wrong. He says the signal to react should come from customers: asking for features "because so-and-so has it," or cancelling and going to a specific competitor. React then, because you're seeking what's best for customers, not reacting to everything competitors do.
- **Deals:** "If you're not rejecting lucrative deals that don't align with your strategy, then you don't have a strategy." The same goes for relationships that conflict with core values.
- He admits money is tempting and is a main reason to build a company, and that it's often wise to say "yes" so long as there's enough money in it. But money can't outrank strategy or values, or you're saying you have neither.

chunks.heading: Messaging and removed features: the other "good errors"
chunks.text:
- **Terse messaging:** If you're never adding words back because messaging got too terse to understand, your marketing is too verbose and fluffy and probably doesn't know what it's trying to say. He says it's "100x more likely" that messages aren't punchy or specific enough than that they're too brief. People don't read: tweets, Google Ads and email titles are short, and visitors bounce off home pages in three seconds. He notes ChatGPT prompts can get you 80% of the way to tighter copy.
- **Removed features:** If you're not adding back features you removed, you're not removing enough. Products that never remove features aren't weeding the garden, learning what customers really want, or admitting when they got it wrong. Occasionally a removed feature turns out to matter, which is a natural consequence of weeding.
- **Overall frame:** Not all errors signal progress (some are negligence or bad luck), but these are by-products of good decisions. Celebrate them, because they mean you have a strategy and the ability to make tough, wise decisions.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jason Cohen argues you cannot speak to everyone, so write for one perfect customer (Carol) with vivid, specific messaging. Because buyers decide by trade-offs, a Carol-focused message also pulls in 10x-100x more people with similar preferences. He shows how to separate ICP data from noise and why turning down non-ICP revenue marks a seasoned founder.

chunks.heading: Why speaking to "everyone" fails and the ICP is the fix
chunks.text:
- Jason argues most companies make the home page speak to "everyone" (buyers, users, existing customers, large and small companies) for fear that a narrow message makes everyone else bounce.
- He says the result is generic positioning like SAS's trademarked "The Power To Know®". The Penny Group uses the same trademarked line, so there is no defensible differentiation and no information.
- By not speaking to a specific customer, you say nothing to everyone, and everyone bounces and never thinks of you again. "If your ideal customer doesn't know you're selling to them, who will?"
- It is also impossible to speak to everyone at once. Developers want to hear about the extensible API, corporate buyers want to hear it makes them more money, large companies want configurable workflows and reports, and small companies want simplicity. You want to look professional to big buyers without looking "too corporate" to small ones.
- His conclusion: be evocative and specific, you can't speak to everyone, so speak to one type of customer.

chunks.heading: How to define "Carol", the perfect customer
chunks.text:
- Pick one concrete perfect customer, "Carol", at a concrete company similar to one of your existing thrilled customers. Give her an official title and say what she does.
- Carol has all the problems your product solves, knows she has them, already has the budget, and is already looking for how to spend it. Write the problems down in her words, as she'd complain to a friend over lunch.
- Carol needs exactly your competitive advantages and has the attributes of people who love you and who keep paying forever.
- Where to find these answers:
  - Sales team: the thing a prospect says that means "we're going to close the sale".
  - Support team: which customers ask great questions and say they love you.
  - Retention data: who stays forever, even if you think they shouldn't.
  - Customer interviews using the Iterative-Hypothesis method.
- Jason says to skip invented back-stories like "Carol has two cats and loves Mahler". They are irrelevant and inaccurate. Stick to professional attributes: what she's interested in, why, why she's looking for a new solution now, how she decides, and her budget.

chunks.heading: The 3-second test for ads and home pages
chunks.text:
- You get about 3 seconds to grab Carol's attention and another 5-10 to convince her. A paragraph won't do. Communicate in a picture and a few words.
- Ways to do it:
  - A before/after she can relate to.
  - Three features that make it plain.
  - Your best competitive advantage.
  - A provocative question she identifies with.
  - A phrase she'd laugh at because "that's so true".
- The test, in his words: "If your ad can't grab Carol's attention--your perfect customer--why do you think it will grab anyone else's attention?"
- If you say it's impossible to communicate your message in 5-10 seconds, no one in the world will get it. Simplicity matters in positioning as much as in strategy.
- Examples he cites of speaking to a specific audience:
  - Twilio targets developers even though the buyer isn't one, and the campaign was effective enough to become a book.
  - Dollar Shave Club was unabashedly "cheap but good" and ignored Gillette-style sleek advertising.
  - Subaru knows it isn't cool and highlights its positives.
  - Porsche's message is differentiated from Subaru's.

chunks.heading: Why targeting Carol makes the market 10x to 100x larger, not smaller
chunks.text:
Jason's bullseye model, using Subaru. Strengths: low-cost, reliable, safe, rugged. Weaknesses: low performance, not sporty, not cool, ugly.

- **Carol (center):** values everything on the strengths side and actively doesn't want the weaknesses side. She'd never be caught in a Porsche, so the weaknesses are strengths to her.
- **Diana (next ring):** values your positives or is indifferent to them, and isn't dissuaded by the weaknesses. Jason's own example is driving his daughter to school and to work, wanting safe and reliable, and not caring about performance. "There are 10x more of those people than there are of Carol."
- **Eddie (outer ring):** weighs trade-offs differently, may care about looks or not care about off-roading, but still decides this trade-off set is the best available. He supposes about 1/10th of the people in that ring pick you over competitors, and that there are about 100x more of them than of Diana.
- Net effect: the effective target market is at least 10x larger because of Diana and more like 20x-100x larger because of Eddie.
- Why it works: targeting Carol makes the message clear, compelling and emotional. People buy on trade-offs, and because you were clear about yours, you paved the road for many people to make that choice.

chunks.heading: Case study: Subaru in the 1990s
chunks.text:
- Sales were declining, so Subaru researched which segments were most likely to buy. It found five: teachers, healthcare professionals, IT professionals, "outdoorsy types", and lesbians. Lesbians were the strongest, four times more likely to buy.
- This was risky then. When Ellen DeGeneres came out in 1997, advertisers including Chrysler pulled out, and Ikea received bomb threats after running an ad with a gay couple. Jason quotes Buffett: "Be greedy when others are fearful."
- Result: the campaigns were a hit, and Subaru grew faster over the following ten years than any other car company founded before 1990, measured as a share of total sales volume from 1995 to 2005.
- The vast majority of Subaru buyers were still straight, buying for the affordable, safe, rugged attributes and caring more about those than about sleek, sporty, high performance.
- His takeaway: target Carol and your positioning is strongest and you win where you deserve to win, but far more people buy because they share similar purchasing preferences.

chunks.heading: Separating Carol from the noise in your data
chunks.text:
- Cancellations: unless the customer stopped their project or went out of business, a cancellation signals a gap between what marketing promised and what the product delivered. This is most urgent when the customer is Carol, since you declared her perfect. Either the product must change or your definition of Carol must change.
- Diana's cancellations deserve the same scrutiny. Eddie's are less clear. Eddie may cancel because of attributes you shouldn't change, since they align with Carol and Diana.
- If you treat every customer as Carol and every cancellation as vital signal, "we lose track of building for Carol and we end up building for nobody."
- Some customers aren't even Eddie. They are off the bullseye yet signed up, which happens all the time. Identify them and ignore their data, because the noise pushes you off course.
- Tactics:
  - Identify who is a Carol right from onboarding, with a few questions or activity indicators.
  - Measure Carol's cancellation rate, "the only rate you care about", and spend extra time finding out why she cancels.
  - The extra time comes from the time saved by not pursuing and interviewing other customers.
- Segment Carols from everyone else everywhere: activation funnel, trial or freemium conversion, feature usage, conversion to monthly active users, and tech-support requests for bugs and features. "It's always about the Carols; everything else is noise."

chunks.heading: Prioritize Carol over revenue: turn down the big non-ICP deal
chunks.text:
- Typical failure mode: your biggest customer, whom you desperately want to keep for the revenue, constantly occupies support and feature requests. You build features just for them, telling yourself larger customers will want them too, yet they stay unhappy and are obviously an anti-Carol.
- They eventually leave in a huff, having been very unprofitable despite high nominal revenue. You should have recognized they were never in your bullseye and helped them leave early.
- The opportunity cost: you could have been finding and onboarding more Carols, who would still be paying you profitably.
- His marker for doing this right: you turn down a sale, even your largest ever, because the buyer isn't your ICP. He cites Daniel Zarick of ArrowsHQ, who rejected a $48,000 sale for that reason, and John Doherty of EditorNinja.
- "This separates first-time founders from seasoned founders." Both Zarick and Doherty had made the mistake before and avoided it the second time.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jason lays out the eight-step process that took WP Engine from idea to unicorn: personal fit, market fit, customer interviews, shipping an SLC, marketing before code, retention-driven product work, ruthless prioritization, and managing founder psychology. He admits Smart Bear only half followed it, and warns that most founders retreat to coding instead of doing the uncomfortable work.

chunks.heading: The PMF roadmap Jason used at WP Engine
chunks.text: Jason lays out an eight-step progression from idea to Product/Market Fit: personal fit, market fit, customer fit, ship an SLC, marketing and sales, retention-driven product, ruthless prioritization, and managing psychology. He says it took WP Engine from an idea to a unicorn. It is repeatable, but not a guarantee. "Exceptions are not repeatable, and therefore they may not be teaching you anything useful."

chunks.heading: Personal fit: passion plus a unique edge
chunks.text:
- "Do what you love and the money will follow" is false. Most artists and the roughly 80% of failed startups had real passion.
- Passion is required as the motivator through dark times: depleted savings, constant rejection, impostor syndrome. It is not a competitive edge, since every founder has it.
- The edge is leverage: big output from little input, drawn from your mix of talents, taste and experience. Unique leverage is the source of differentiation.
- Uniqueness usually sits at an intersection. He cites Scott Adams, who is a decent illustrator, a decent humorist and has tech jobs. That intersection is unique, not being top 1% at any one thing.
- He prefers "different" to "better", because being better for some people means worse for others.
- Leverage plus your chosen path forms the kernel of strategy. The test question: "Why are *you* the perfect person to build *this* company?"

chunks.heading: Market fit: a plausible theory of why they will buy
chunks.text:
- Product/Market Fit means fitting the market, not building something fun, interesting or ego-enhancing. Most "indie hacker" and "AI is cool" startups fail because they began as a fun project, not a plausible business.
- "I had the problem myself" is the most common origin story, and all his startups began that way. But your own view of the problem is less likely to be a real business than you think: "You are, in fact, not like your customer."
- Passion projects sometimes become businesses anyway (Smart Bear), but that is luck. The framework exists to reduce reliance on luck.
- Test the market on six traits, answered with Fermi estimation:
  - Plausible: do 10M people or 100k companies have the problem?
  - Self-aware: do they know and care?
  - Lucrative: is there substantial budget?
  - Liquid: can they buy now?
  - Eager: do they want to buy from you specifically?
  - Enduring: will they still pay a year later?
- Write a one-page strategy on "how we will win". Have a specific, falsifiable theory so you can notice when reality contradicts it and pivot. Smart Bear, Slack, WhatsApp and Flickr all found their winning idea this way, by noticing what customers wanted instead of the original idea.

chunks.heading: Customer fit: talk to customers and find the ICP
chunks.text:
- "There's only one source of truth for what customers will buy: Customers." Not advisors, analysts, Twitter polls, past data or competitor behavior.
- Customers' "yes" is a "maybe", but their "no" is a "no", which can save months or years.
- Interviews reveal:
  - where customers look for products, so you know where to advertise
  - the language they use, to copy into marketing
  - how their budgets work, for pricing and packaging
  - what they use today
  - the trigger moment when they decide "today I'm going to buy ___" (Bob Moesta's framing)
- Founders avoid this because building is the fun part. Building first doesn't make customers easier to find, and means you never learn what people want.
- How he got WP Engine interviews: he used LinkedIn to find web developers working in WordPress and asked for an hour to discuss a new startup concept they would be the ideal customer for. He offered to pay any amount they wished. Of 50 requests, 40 agreed, only one asked to be paid, and 30 eventually became customers.
- He uses his Iterative-Hypothesis customer development method. About 17 years ago it invalidated an analytics startup idea he thought was good and validated the idea that became WP Engine.
- Find the ICP: a segment "almost comically over-specified" so that the product is the obvious best choice. Aim all messaging at it: website, ads, terminology, writing style, pricing. The ICP should see in three seconds that "you get them".
- Targeting only the ICP doesn't shrink the market. For every ICP, he says 10x more people make similar buying decisions and 100x more take more convincing but still buy. The clear message also earns attention and loyalty.

chunks.heading: Build and ship the SLC, then focus on marketing and sales
chunks.text:
- SLC is his alternative to MVP: Simple (so you ship and learn fast), Lovable (love overpowers bugs and missing features), Complete (a v1 that does the job, not a v0.1 that is broken).
- Real learning starts only when customers use, or don't use, the product. Six months of building without customer use is not progress: "What you've done is proved what you already knew--you can build software."
- Founders drift toward what they enjoy, so push yourself to do marketing and sales until it feels like "too much". Daily question: what can I do today to (a) bring more target-market visitors, (b) convert more of them to try, (c) convert more of those to buy?
- The answer is sometimes code, such as a better new-user experience to lift try-to-buy. But more often it isn't, and several steps happen before the person touches the product. His line: "The code is actually your enemy."
- He cites examples of founders whose growth took off after hiring a marketer, such as ProjectionLab going from not enough to quit a day job to a team and $1M ARR, and Pallyy not growing until marketing started.

chunks.heading: Retention-driven product work
chunks.text:
- A customer who noticed your ad, tried the product, paid, used it and then cancelled means "You made the right promise, but didn't keep it." Marketing finds the promise; retention shows whether you keep it.
- Low retention can't be offset by growth. Growth slows and halts sooner than expected, and if users don't want the product, the growth is "fake news" and not real fit.
- When building features, build things that increase retention.
- Churned customers rarely talk, though paid interviews (gift cards, charity donations) can help. Better is to spot struggling customers by in-product activity and reach out while they are still in the struggle.
- Look for patterns in unsuccessful customers that successful customers do not share. If feature X predicts success, unsuccessful users may not know about it (promote it) or can't use it due to workflow (add integrations). Sometimes the fix is tuning the ICP by industry, geography, company size, buyer title or use case.
- Retention is a lagging, multi-factor indicator: good as a high-level check but not as a day-to-day operating metric.
- At WP Engine, years passed with no new features because engineering time went to scale, speed and uptime. This produced best-in-industry retention for 16 years, which fed word of mouth and reviews (87% of 1,007 Trustpilot reviews are 5-star).

chunks.heading: Ruthless, systematic prioritization
chunks.text:
His system combines Fairytale Planning with Rocks, Pebbles, Sand:

1. **Next milestone:** one thing, written down and read every morning. Examples: finding a business model, public launch, 20 paying customers, trial conversion from 1% to 5%, cancellation from 7%/month to 4%, $10k MRR to quit the day job.
2. **Current obstacle:** why the milestone is hard, slow or expensive. Pick the uncomfortable, existential one, not the comfortable one. Examples: only 15% use it again, 17 Product Hunt customers but no repeatable channel, can't get interviews.
3. **Split work into Rocks, Pebbles, Sand.**
4. **Pick one Rock** that attacks both milestone and obstacle (use Binstack). If none is good enough, brainstorm with friends or customers rather than commit three months to a mediocre plan.
5. **Schedule Pebbles sparingly,** using an ROI framework.
6. **Make almost everything only "good enough".** "Almost everything you do will not determine whether the company is successful." Satisfy most metrics rather than maximizing them, and design matters less than people think. Exception: obsessive details that give a new customer an amazing experience, so pick your battles.

His rule: "Don't stray from the system. You don't have the time."

chunks.heading: Managing psychology, and the trap of comfortable work
chunks.text:
The journey demands:

- facing the truth about your abilities, customers and market
- finding yourself
- making clear decisions: ICP, milestone, what you're not good at
- tolerating constant rejection: 99% of visitors don't act, customers leave, employees and investors say no
- changing course fluidly, and telling an anomaly from a real learning
- acting under uncertainty while feeling like an impostor

He calls it a "gauntlet of pain", possibly the hardest thing you'll do, though also the most exciting professionally.

The common failure is retreating to comfortable work: building a fun feature, learning Rust, building with AI (a technology, not a customer problem), while avoiding ad managers, asking for the sale and customer calls. Posting "$1600 MRR after 18 months" while framing it as perseverance is the trap. "Perseverance is a virtue, if you're doing the right work, with the right goals. It's a vice if it means you're moving diligently in the wrong direction."

chunks.heading: Smart Bear: only half the roadmap
chunks.text:
- Smart Bear (founded 2002, sold 2007) began with Code Historian, a personal project built to learn .NET, on an assumption (version-control history has value) that sank every product built on it.
- He did not talk to customers beforehand. After they paid, he learned many were using it for something else. He built Code Reviewer, which half-fit the need but had the wrong architecture, then rewrote everything from scratch as Code Collaborator, which made millions.
- He admits interviews up front would likely have stopped everything cold, and he wouldn't have known what to ask. So interviewing isn't the only road.
- Still, he credits steps 1, 4, 5 and 6 (specific passion-driven idea, shipping, marketing and selling, learning through retention) and says skipping those would have failed. He values getting product into customers' hands over conversations.

chunks.heading: WP Engine: the roadmap followed exactly
chunks.text:
- **First idea (invalidated):** a marketing analytics tool with a real-time event dashboard, retroactive goal-setting, and capture of partially filled web forms, all via one line of JavaScript. About 20 interviews showed it wasn't strong enough, so he avoided wasting years.
- **Second idea (validated):** managed WordPress hosting, born from his own blog crashing when it hit the top of Hacker News. Bloggers he asked said, "I don't know, but if you find it, tell me." The same interview method showed the need, what people would pay, and how to find them.
- **Market:** WordPress powered 11% of the top 10 million sites then, and 43% in 2023, so large and growing. He knew WordPress as a user and loved code optimization.
- **SLC:** he built the first version in 30 hours. It survived a Hacker News traffic day with almost no server load. It had no customer dashboard; he took cards via the credit card service's default page, and the rest was plain WordPress. The early site was spare, and a later version showed database errors on the home page, which he says shows the market need was overwhelming if customers still paid.
- **Marketing before product:** he did marketing and sales before there was even a login screen and launched with 30 paying customers. His asks to his advisory group in 2010 were for marketing and sales help, not product or engineering.
- **Results:** $1M ARR in 18 months. True Product/Market Fit, a sudden shift to hyper-growth that never slowed, came in early 2012. He credits the right promise, market and product, plus hard work, craft, a large growing market and luck.
- He cites Simon Hoiberg's FeedHive as a bootstrapped example that echoes the roadmap: a large growing market, a focused ICP, an SLC, and marketing and sales over features.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jason Cohen argues that "Top 10" is an arbitrary number, and that the right count of items on a list depends on its purpose. He walks through cases (1, 3, 5-7, one per team, a full audit checklist, bankruptcy) and concludes that fewer is usually better.

chunks.heading: The right number of items depends on the list's purpose, and it is almost never 10
chunks.text:
- Jason's opening argument: if people had evolved with nine fingers, there would be "Top 9" lists, so "a 'Top 10' list probably doesn't have the correct number of things."
- His test for any list: ask "What is the purpose of this list?", then ask whether that purpose calls for more or fewer items, and whether there is "a _good reason_ why this the right number of things."
- His default: "Usually, fewer is better, and the right answer is almost never '10.'"

chunks.heading: One item is the best choice when speed and focus matter
chunks.text:
- Jason calls it "reductive to say only one thing is important," but a single item "ensures that it gets done, as quickly as possible."
- He links this to his maximized-decision idea: one priority gets full attention and the fastest completion.
- Applied per team: with 17 teams, 17 items (one each) is arguably a repeat of the "one thing" rule at the team level.
- Caveat: 17 is still arguably too many if projects span multiple teams.

chunks.heading: Three items work because people like threes and can remember them
chunks.text:
- Humans across the globe have always liked things in threes.
- Three items are small enough that you can remember all of them.

chunks.heading: About seven items is the memory limit, and the real number may be nearer five
chunks.text:
- Jason cites one of the most-cited psychology papers, "The Magical Number Seven, Plus or Minus Two": seven items is what the average person can hold in their head at once.
- His rule of thumb: "If you can't keep it in your head, even when you're trying very hard, it's too many items."
- He jokes that post-COVID brains are now 5 ± 2, and says plainly he has no data for that claim.

chunks.heading: A long list is justified when the goal is to finish every item
chunks.text:
- Example: a security audit with 132 flags can have the goal of addressing all of them.
- Why 100% completion is powerful:
  - It is a clear statement to make: every item in a specific set is done.
  - It works like "1: Focus" with sub-items, where a checklist shows progress as the team works through it.
  - It explains why there are 132 items: that is the audit's count.
  - It gives a clear state change at the end. His example: "We pass this audit, and then [large customer] renews for three years."

chunks.heading: Declare bankruptcy on huge backlogs
chunks.text:
- Example: an inbox with 402,302 unread emails is effectively the same as an empty inbox, except that the number looms over you.
- His advice: declare "bankruptcy" on the email inbox or the Jira backlog and archive it all. "The important things will come back."
- He says archive rather than delete, because disk space is close to free and you still have the items if you really need one.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jason Cohen shows how to build a quarterly strategic plan using the fairytale story structure: Objectives, Obstacles, Actions, Measures, and Not Doing. He argues most planning time belongs on defining obstacles, picking a few big "rocks," and stating out loud what you are choosing not to do.

chunks.heading: Strategic planning with the fairytale structure: why it works
chunks.text:
- Jason says fairytale structure is "a cheat code for effective communication" because "our brains are pre-wired for fairy-tales".
- The structure: once upon a time there was an unsuspecting hero; every day, the way things are; but then, one day, a change that motivates action; adventure begins; it was almost impossible because of obstacles; until finally victory; and forever after, the world is different.
- He uses it for sales calls at WP Engine. A under-a-minute case study of a food blogger whose site crashed on Thanksgiving, their busiest day, costing thousands of dollars in revenue and hundreds of newsletter sign-ups. They moved to WP Engine, it never happened again, and they now just focus on their business.
- He also applies it to presentations, fundraising and product proposals.
- His less obvious use: a strategic plan, meaning analyzing the current situation and deciding what to do. For a single team, this means being in command of the most critical things to do right now.
- He builds WP Engine quarterly department plans this way. Over about two years, he and a few product teams refined the "Fairytale Plan". The process resembles the Double-Diamond design process, and the final result matches the fairytale structure.

chunks.heading: The five-part Fairytale Plan
chunks.text:
1. **Objectives:** what we're trying to get, and what happens if we don't.
2. **Obstacles:** what stands in our way.
3. **Actions:** how we overcome the obstacles while advancing the objectives.
4. **Measures:** how we'll know we've been successful, and when we're finished.
5. **Not Doing:** the important things we've chosen not to do so we can achieve the above.

- Guiding question for objectives: "If we weren't encumbered by roadblocks, with no distractions and no interruptions, how would we advance our strategy right now?"
- Guiding question for actions: how do we overcome the obstacles while advancing the objectives, with the people and capabilities we currently have?
- Unlike a real fairytale, where surprising the hero with obstacles is fun, the plan must clarify obstacles up front.
- The final plan is clear and simple, and hides the complexity of the process that created it.
- Every team and the company needs one. Without it you're probably not working on the right things, and not communicating what must be done in a way everyone can implement.

chunks.heading: Objectives: strategy vs. plan
chunks.text:
- "If you run very fast in the wrong direction, you fail." Objectives name the right direction.
- Objectives shouldn't summarize the whole strategy. Link to the strategy document and highlight 1-3 objectives that make sense to advance right now.
- "Right now" is the difference between plan and strategy. Strategy is the long-term vision and main ways to achieve it. The plan selects specific next steps that materially advance the strategy while delivering results needed today, typically revenue growth, cost reduction or an internal transformation.
- Expect fluidity between exploring the problem space and solution space. If you can't invent a working solution later, you may need different objectives, or decide that "eliminating obstacles" is all you can do right now.
- It's fine for objectives to stay the same for a few quarters; it gives stability and focus. To test whether you're sticking too long, ask how the world is different. If there are good answers, you're making progress.

chunks.heading: Obstacles: the most important section
chunks.text:
- Jason cites Einstein: "If I had an hour to solve a problem, I'd spend 55 minutes thinking about the problem and 5 minutes thinking about solutions." This is where most time goes.
- Resist jumping to solutions or saying "we've already talked about this." Without fully exploring the problem space you don't know the goal of the solution space, you repeat mistakes and avoid difficult truths.
- Generate many options first. The team benefits from clarity on what to tackle and what they're allowed to leave alone "even though it's on fire".
- Obstacle types to explore:
  - Difficulty executing the strategy (novel builds, algorithms, scale, pivots, repositioning).
  - Team challenges: skills, experience, motivation, burnout, headcount.
  - Competitive pressure.
  - Customer retention.
  - Interruptions (interrupt-driven vs. planned work; reduce via automation or rejecting work types).
  - Too many bugs.
  - Dependencies and coordination.
  - Process bottlenecks (step-changes in productivity, not nice-to-haves).
  - Market evolution.
- Narrow to the 1-3 most critical. The test: which few issues, if you took a huge bite out of them and let all others fester, would substantially improve velocity, competitiveness, team dynamic or retention? Versus issues that, left untreated, would block the objectives even if five others were fully solved.
- His order of precedence when several serious problems exist, picking whichever comes first:
  1. Retention (if customers are leaving, the business model and product aren't working)
  2. People (must have the right team)
  3. Throughput (can't do enough strategic work per month)
  4. Growth
  5. Competition
  6. Health of the code base
  7. Execution risk
- His rule of thumb for a "good" monthly cancellation rate: 3%/mo consumer, 2%/mo small business, 1%/mo enterprise.

chunks.heading: Choosing main activities
chunks.text:
- Finding the crux is the emotionally hardest part; deciding what to do is the intellectually hardest. No framework makes you creative.
- Start in "generation mode," coming up with as many ideas as possible, then switch to "selection mode". Draw on idea queues from around the company, and use Extreme Brainstorming if stuck.
- Select a few large, impactful things ("Rocks"). Otherwise you chip away at incremental work, believing you're progressing because you're "agile", without tearing down obstacles or achieving objectives fast enough.
- The Herbie parable, from Goldratt's *The Goal*: a hiker who keeps falling behind blocks the group reaching the summit. Three options, which map to solutions:
  1. Leave Herbie behind: let that problem burn or ignore work you assumed "must" be done.
  2. Help Herbie get better: do extra work that mitigates the problem.
  3. Decide you won't reach the goal: change the objectives to something achievable.
- Best solutions often synthesize several ideas. At WP Engine, an idea that speeds customer websites often also cuts costs, since it takes less CPU time or fewer bytes transferred. Even a bonkers idea may combine with a practical one into a great solution.
- For final selection he recommends the Binstack method. Objectives and obstacles act as natural filters, eliminating anything that doesn't address them, with a few secondary prioritization dimensions allowed.
- He says not to use ROI analysis for the critical work. ROI suits smaller activities where the goal is the "best use of time". For critical work the goal is "to maximize your impact on the most critical things".
- He points to his Rocks, Pebbles, and Sand framework for covering all work types, including medium-sized work where ROI is appropriate.

chunks.heading: Measures and indicators
chunks.text:
- It's easier to avoid accountability by believing hard work and high throughput equal impact. "Focus on inputs, not outputs" is true when executing but false if it means you don't get the outputs you need.
- Don't measure against metrics you don't believe in, and don't insist everything important reduces to a number.
- Ideal numeric measures are objective, well-defined, measured daily, with a clear stopping point where you can declare victory. Use his KPI framework as a checklist for a good metric.
- For non-numeric concepts, capture the essence in crisp writing understandable inside and outside the team. He notes AI can turn a rambling audio description into a pithy statement. Examples: "Be revered as the most innovative product in the category"; "Have the best social media content."
- Such statements are powerful even if people later disagree on progress; that debate is the point of metrics, since it sorts out how things are going and whether to change.
- Test for sticking with objectives too long: the "how will the world be different" answers show progress even when objectives repeat.

chunks.heading: Not Doing: saying no out loud
chunks.text:
- Guiding question: what do we really want to do but must wait on so more important or urgent things can be done?
- Decisions are about saying "no" even more than "yes". Without articulating the no's, the team is less focused, decisions less clear, and stakeholders wonder whether you know about the problems you skipped.
- Deciding on a few things means deciding against dozens. "Not for now" is mostly "not ever", since you always have 10x more ideas than time, as every Jira backlog and prioritization spreadsheet shows.
- Unstated, it looks like you don't know those things exist. "Perception is reality." Saying it out loud also steels your team to stand firm on "no" when a big customer complains about something you intentionally ignored.
- Revisit the list next quarter. Many items will seem less important; some will now be right.
- At WP Engine it is a simple one-line-per-bullet list of topics, without reasons. You could add reasons, or a Now / Next / Later roadmap.
- His preference is "Now / Likely / Maybe", which signals confidence the ideas are even right. If you get to under 50% of "Later" items, they're "merely a possibility".
- It's not a random bucket of 100 feature requests. It's the important, even urgent, things that barely missed the cut, the difficult decisions.
- Quotes he uses: Buffett ("really successful people say no to almost everything"), Derek Sivers ("You can do anything, but not everything"), Steve Jobs ("Innovation is saying no to 1000 things").

chunks.heading: Worked example: Tesla
chunks.text:
- **Objectives:** accelerate the world's transition to sustainable energy via EVs. Invent desirable, high-performance, safe battery-powered vehicles; create scalable, cost-effective production lines to be profitable; generate excitement and loyalty by bucking the view that EVs are impractical and low-performance.
- **Obstacles:** intrinsic difficulty of inventing new batteries and production lines; market skepticism; manufacturing scale; lack of charging infrastructure causing range anxiety.
- **Activities:** battery innovation ("the insight is that the battery is the key"); direct-to-consumer sales to bypass dealerships; Gigafactories ("factories are not just a necessary step but strategically vital"); Supercharger network.
- **Metrics:** battery cost per kWh and discharge rate; units sold and EV market share; fully completed cars per day per Gigafactory; new Supercharger stations; non-numeric consumer delight ("never wanting a gas-powered car again").
- **Not doing:** safety and practicality (solve batteries and performance first); affordable models (start as a luxury brand until scale and costs improve); expanding to China (needs a popular working car first).

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jason Cohen defines PMF as a felt shift from push to pull, backed by three tests: sudden sustained growth, low churn, and critical mass. He shows the same linear-then-steeper-linear curve across bootstrapped, VC-funded, viral and media businesses, and argues high churn means no fit.

chunks.heading: What Product/Market Fit actually looks like, in numbers
chunks.text:
Jason defines Product/Market Fit (PMF) as all three of the following being true at once:

1. **Easy growth (pull, not push):** the growth rate suddenly spikes up and stays at the new rate. You often don't know why.
2. **High retention:** cancellation under 3%/mo for B2B, or under 5%/mo for B2C.
3. **Critical mass:** at least $20,000/mo in revenue, or weekly active users growing by at least 200/mo.

He built this from building several companies himself and angel-investing in dozens of others, with a wide range of outcomes.

- The critical-mass rule exists because anyone can grow 1000% month over month from a base of 7 customers. Seven customers is not evidence of "fit."
- A single huge customer shows fit for one customer, not for a market. He calls that consulting, not product.
- If you're not sure whether you have PMF, you don't. He says "there is no doubt when you have it."

chunks.heading: The lived experience: push turns into pull
chunks.text:
Jason treats the subjective experience as the starting point.

- Before PMF, "every day it's a struggle to get customers." After it, "every day it's a struggle to keep up with demand."
- The momentum flips from fighting for each customer one at a time to a flood of signups you can't explain. The question changes from "how do we get more customers" to "how do we handle the influx of demand?"
- It is not all good. Complaints outrun your ability to ship fixes. You feel behind in every department at once, and you can't interview and hire fast enough.
- Brand damage follows. A public review might say "I heard they were good but it took them a day to answer my support question."
- He calls it the best problem to have, but says it doesn't feel good in the moment.
- It matters because it decides whether the company is sustainable. It changes what you build, who you hire, how you plan, and whether you start tackling scale.

chunks.heading: The characteristic growth curve: linear, then a bend, then linear again
chunks.text:
The recurring shape is slow linear growth, often for about two years. Then a sudden bend, then continued growth that is still linear but much faster.

- He stresses that the new growth is **not exponential**, even though people often say it is.
- Bootstrapped examples he cites: Pallyy (revenue linear for about two years, then a visible turn upward), ConvertKit (about two years of bumping along, then fast linear growth), and Tally (celebrating $6M ARR).
- ConvertKit founder Nathan Barry personally reached out to ideal customers one by one and onboarded them manually, to get both the sale and the testimonial. Jason calls it a brilliant playbook to copy, and also the definition of hard-scrabbling for customers.
- Jason himself was one of those early ConvertKit customers, and his newsletter is still on ConvertKit.

chunks.heading: The pattern holds across funding models, business models and product types
chunks.text:
- **VC-funded:** Beehiiv raised a small round and shows almost the same curve. Jason's company WP Engine started self-funded and became VC-funded two years later. It eventually raised more than $300M and had a decade of hyper-growth, yet showed the same two-year slow preamble and linear segments. You can't tell from the chart when funding rounds happened.
- **Other examples:** a Y Combinator company chart shared by Paul Graham, and Balsamiq Mockups with one-time (non-SaaS) revenue, shared by Peldi Guilizzoni in 2008.
- **Second products:** HubSpot grew linearly for about twelve years, then changed to a new but still linear slope around 2021, when its second product line reached its own fit. Jason says the slope can change again when a company adds a second successful product, enters a lucrative new market, or changes its business model.
