- **Viral products:** Slack and Facebook also grew linear, then bent, then linear again, not exponentially. Facebook bent in early 2009, around the embeddable "like" button. Airbnb bent in late 2010, around the realization that professional photography was key to matching customer expectations.
- **Media:** a successful YouTube channel and Lenny Rachitsky's newsletter show the same curve. When asked what he changed in July 2022, Lenny's answer was "Not sure TBH." A year later his subscriber chart showed nearly perfect linear growth for two years after the bend.
- **Hyper-growth benchmark:** he cites "2T3D" (revenue triples, triples, doubles, doubles, doubles after $1M in annual revenue, reaching close to $100M five years later). WP Engine did that and more, starting with 5x.

chunks.heading: What it felt like at WP Engine in 2012
chunks.text:
Jason remembers the exact flip to PMF.

- There were only five people and the company was completely sustainable. Then everything changed.
- Support fell behind, because "the founder does Zendesk tickets" doesn't scale. They also couldn't keep up with their free white-glove site-migration service for new customers.
- Hiring made it worse in the short term. Finding and interviewing candidates takes time, and he didn't want to hire the wrong person just because they were moving fast. After hiring there was no documentation or training, so people learned by osmosis while the team fell further behind.
- Customers complained on Twitter that service was declining, and "they were right." They blamed the funding round, but the company hadn't spent a dollar of it.
- His stated error: not spending the money on hiring ahead of need, to cushion the impact of a growth increase.
- They recovered later that year and went on to win service awards and maintain 98% CSAT.

chunks.heading: High cancellation means there's no fit
chunks.text:
Jason calls cancellation the one killer metric that stops growth even when the curve looks right.

- Founders often think 5-7% monthly cancellation is fine if new customers keep arriving. He says they are mistaken.
- Churn at a percentage grows in lock-step with total size. Marketing and sales do not automatically grow just because the company is bigger, so cancellations always win that race and growth tops out.
- **Buffer:** it had the linear-bend-linear curve (2012-2014, then 2014-2020), then growth levelled off in 2020 and never returned. Churn was higher during the slow period, then fell to 5%/mo, which allowed faster growth. But 5% was still too high. New MRR naturally tops out, while cancellation grows forever in absolute dollars.
- **SparkToro:** it adds about the same new MRR per month, but cancelled dollars keep growing, so at current size cancellation "wins" and growth goes flat. He praises Rand Fishkin's vision of building a great, profitable company with happy employees, customers and investors, and says this is not an indictment.
- His core point: "It's not actually about finances; it's the fact that customers are choosing to leave." The numbers are only the objective measure of that behavior.
- Hence the thresholds: cancellation above 3% for B2B or 5% for B2C indicates a lack of fit.
- Easy inbound growth with heavy churn means the promise and price were right but the product didn't deliver, or the customer's need was too brief to sustain a recurring-revenue business.
- He rejects the labels "a fit, but not sustainable" and "a fit, with limited upside." In his words, "if customers are leaving, it's not a fit." His advice is to pay attention to customer behavior, not dollars.
- He points to Twitch founder Michael Seibel's Socialcam story. It got 60M downloads in 4 months and a top-5 App Store ranking, but almost no users were retained after 10 days, so it was not PMF.

chunks.heading: If you haven't hit it yet
chunks.text:
- Slow growth doesn't mean you failed. It means you haven't hit that success curve yet.
- Possible outcomes he lists: you may never find PMF but grind out a profitable company anyway; growth may be so slow that the best move is to face facts, stop, work out why it was too hard, and try something else; or your growth spurt may start today. He says it's impossible to know.
- He offers a roadmap to PMF, the system he used to build a unicorn. He also notes that his previous startup used only half of those techniques, and "no one knows; that's life."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jason Cohen argues that some enticing metrics can't be measured even after the fact, so you shouldn't predict them or turn them into goals. Examples: single-feature revenue impact, incremental churn initiatives, risk probabilities, brand value, culture ROI. Use KPIs that measure specific aspects of your systems instead.

chunks.heading: Why some metrics can't be measured, even in hindsight
chunks.text: Jason's core rule: if a metric cannot be measured in retrospect, with all the facts and months of analysis available, it cannot be measured now, and you certainly cannot predict it or set a goal on it. He says many of these metrics are so tempting and seemingly important that teams try anyway, which is "a frustrating waste of time" that ends in failure. His fix is to learn the pattern and stick with KPIs that measure specific aspects of your systems.

chunks.heading: Revenue impact of a single feature
chunks.text:
Jason argues you cannot attribute revenue to an individual feature, even after the fact and with hundreds of thousands of customers (his example is WP Engine).

- Some WP Engine features get genuine excitement in sales pitches but are rarely used after the sale. Low usage does not mean no revenue contribution, because the feature may have helped close the deal.
- A frequently used feature is almost surely valuable, but how much it "earns" is unclear. If ten features are all used often, does each earn 10% of revenue?
- If the feature is also heavily used by people who cancel, it wasn't keeping them. But it may have been, and something unrelated caused the cancellation.
- Many other reasons customers are willing to pay have nothing to do with that feature.
- His takeaway: use a variety of KPIs, only one of which is "usage." Product teams should celebrate widely used features, but usage is not the same thing as revenue.
- Side point: this is why you should listen to customers rather than copy competitors, since you don't know what is really driving results over there.

chunks.heading: Measuring the impact of a single activity on churn
chunks.text:
Jason says churn is one of the most valuable things to work on, because retention compounds. All the profit from a SaaS customer arrives in the later years, after they have paid back sales and marketing costs, gotten past the higher initial support load, and after gross margins expand with scale. Churn is also a lagging indicator that customers don't want what you sell.

But measuring what any single initiative did to churn is folly. Even a year later you won't know, unless the effect was enormous and immediate. He gives four reasons, which he says apply well beyond churn.

- **Signal is swamped by noise for rare events.** If churn is 3%/mo, a big 10% improvement only gets you to 2.7%/mo. Random variation can exceed a 0.3-point difference. Example: some months have 15% more weekdays than others, so if most customers churn on weekdays, churn can swing 15% from that alone.
- **Lag between action and reaction.** A customer who churns today has likely been struggling and researching alternatives for weeks or months. Larger customers may try for a year, then run a multi-month evaluation. Something you start today won't change the path of people who already decided and only today pushed the button.
- **Many causes of one result.** People leave because they never got hooked, got mad at support, gave up waiting for a feature, were never the right fit, or simply forgot they had the product until a spouse asked about the card charge. Any one action is incremental and hard to see in that fog.
- **External forces larger than your control.** Market, competition and the economy have a big, unmeasurable effect. Growth and churn rates can map onto the stock market or inflation, and sometimes that is the largest factor.

He adds one exception: when churn is especially bad (anything over 3%/mo is "scary"), large improvements are sometimes possible and measurable.

chunks.heading: Probabilities of risks on a "Risk Slide"
chunks.text:
Executives rightly ask for the probability and magnitude of each risk, since probability decides whether you mitigate, monitor, or ignore it. Jason argues these probabilities cannot be measured even after the fact.

- Each risk is independent and one-off. It happens or it doesn't, and you may not find out for months or years.
- If a risk listed at 30% happens and one listed at 70% doesn't, the numbers weren't necessarily wrong, because 30% is not 0% and 70% is not 100%.
- Contrast with weather forecasting: across hundreds of days with a "30% chance of rain" forecast, you can check whether it rained about 30% of the time. If it rained 34% of the time, the forecaster is doing great; if 70%, they need work.
- A Risk Slide has only a handful of complex risks that have never happened before, so no such calibration is possible.
- His advice: don't put probabilities on the slide at all. List only the risks important enough to merit action or awareness.
- If you do give probabilities, use numbers, not "medium" or "low." He has a separate piece on how to talk about probabilities properly.

chunks.heading: Other things not to try to measure
chunks.text:
Jason lists more examples of the same trap.

- **Small design choices (color, typography, layout, word choice).** They matter, but noise overwhelms signal in small iterations, and surveying users on a font preference doesn't work. Any UI change also initially lowers satisfaction scores because people dislike change.
- **ROI of company culture or values.** A strong culture with a specific direction creates a healthy organization of people alike in the ways that matter and diverse in all other ways. But measuring the impact of a specific value or culture initiative doesn't make sense.
- **Value of brand.** Techniques like unaided awareness or brand recall may work for the largest companies in the world. Otherwise you can't look at winning specific deals, competitiveness or growth and say how much was due to brand. This includes brand-focused marketing such as company-sponsored events.
- **Value of fixing bugs proactively or good engineering practices.** You can't measure the impact of a bug that never shipped or a practice that is simply how you work. There is no counterfactual.
- **Willingness-to-pay or "value delivered."** Even raising prices and watching new-customer counts or cancellations doesn't measure value or willingness. You also can't run that test often, and it is often destructive to brand and customer relationships.
- **Efficacy of employee compensation or retention programs.** Overall retention is easy and important to measure, but it is multi-factored and the rules change over time, so it is like measuring a feature's impact on product retention.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jason Cohen explains why founders can't run a 500-person company like a 50-person one. Two forces drive it: rare things become common, and complexity exceeds human comprehension. He walks through consequences for team robustness, predictability, materiality thresholds, recruiting, communication, infrastructure and risk.

chunks.heading: Why a 500-person company can't run like a 50-person one
chunks.text:
Jason argues that idealistic founders believe they can scale without becoming a "typical big company": no dumb rules, no meetings, no "average" hires. He says they never succeed because two forces are unavoidable. Everything else about scale follows from them.

- **Rare things become common.** At scale, events that were rare happen daily, so manual handling stops working and new processes become necessary. Example: with 1,000 servers, one failure per server every three years means one failure per day. That hits DevOps, customer support and social media every day, and automation helps but doesn't solve it.
- **Complexity beyond human comprehension.** "Complicated" systems can be split up, built and tested in parts, and handled by specialists. "Complex" systems have components that affect each other, often in cycles, so most of the difficulty is in the interactions. Jason says that difficulty "grows non-linearly" as the company grows and never stops being difficult. He cites the Cynefin Framework for the terminology.
- **Large companies are not small companies × 100.** He calls the difference "not a bad thing or a good thing. It's a different thing."
- **Org structure doesn't fix it.** None of his examples depend on organizational structure, so Holacracy and Teal Organizations do not solve these problems. The forces are universal.

chunks.heading: Robustness costs productivity: the trade-off in teams and systems
chunks.text:
Jason's line: "a team of one is fast, but brittle."

- A one-person team has the highest output per person: no meetings, instant decisions. Small companies need this speed, because it counters the things constantly about to kill them: no customers, no attention, missing core features.
- The brittleness: one illness takes velocity or quality to zero. If the person leaves, you lose about six months, or twelve months or a rewrite if nothing was documented. If it was a co-founder, it can be fatal ("founder trouble" is a leading cause of startup death). He notes data also show solo-founder companies fail more often, and says the choice comes down to temperament.
- At scale, with 15-25% annual employee turnover plus illness, vacation and family, people are out every day. Keeping the tiny-company attitude becomes "disorganized and irresponsible."
- His rule of thumb: no project can have fewer than about three dedicated people, plus management and possibly product or project management. A team of 4-5 is not 4-5x as productive as one person. "Per-person productivity goes down in exchange for robustness and continuity."
- The payoff: the small company loses 9 months to a key departure or implodes, while the big company "adds thousands of customers per month like clockwork and wins the race."

**Software robustness works the same way.** His worked example:
- One server at 99.9% uptime sounds good but means over 500 minutes of downtime a year.
- Two servers cut simultaneous failure to 0.1% × 0.1% = 0.0001%, about 30 seconds a year. Each server must still be big enough to carry all traffic alone, so there are no savings from smaller machines.
- You then need a load balancer, plus a shared database moved to its own server, plus two of those. That is four servers and a load balancer, "more than 4x the original cost."
- Caveats: real failures are correlated or cascade, and the load balancer itself can fail.
- "Robustness always carries a cost." You trade local inefficiency for whole-company continuity.

chunks.heading: Predictability becomes a requirement, not a nice-to-have
chunks.text:
- A small company has no need to predict ship dates, so it should "optimize myopically for speed-to-market."
- A large company's advantage is coordinated execution. When WP Engine launches a product, a well-funded set of teams hits press, events, campaigns, social and newsletters at once, getting more attention in one week than a small company gets in a year. It also sells immediately to about 200,000 existing customers plus thousands of new ones per month, adding more revenue each month than a small company earns in a year.
- That requires predictability, and predictability requires going slower: estimation, coordination, planning, documentation, and re-planning across teams when reality differs.
- **Hiring lead time example (support team):** recruiting, interviews, the new hire's notice and a week off, orientation, classroom training, then pairing with senior staff. That is four to six months from deciding to grow the team to having people up to speed. So support demand must be forecast four to six months ahead.
  - Under-estimate: staff are overwhelmed and customers suffer.
  - Over-estimate: you pay a cost penalty. This is the better failure mode, but both are sub-optimal.
- Against "the future is inherently unpredictable": he says that is partly a self-fulfilling prophecy, because insisting on it means skipping the work that makes things more predictable. Small companies lack the data, customers and experience, so they are usually right that they can't predict, but that is "impossible for *them*," not impossible in principle.
- At scale it is required, "not because Wall Street demands it" or investors do, but because it's critical for healthy scaling.

chunks.heading: The Materiality Threshold
chunks.text:
- Definition: the minimum contribution a project must deliver to materially affect the business.
- Google example: a new product earning $10M/year is a failure, because the same tens of millions of dollars spent making the existing operation just 0.01% more effective would earn more. At over $100B/year in revenue (when written in 2017), Google could only consider products with potential of at least $1B/year as an absolute floor, up to $10B/year if things go well, such as YouTube, Cloud and self-driving cars. An editor's note says that by 2023 Google's revenue was nearly $300B, reinforcing the point.
- A small business's threshold is near $0. A feature that lands a few customers, or a campaign that adds two sign-ups a week, counts as success.
- A modest-sized company needs millions in revenue from new products, maybe tens of millions. Very few products reach that; most startups never hit a $10M/year run-rate, even with decent products and dedicated teams.
- So a Product Manager at a mid-sized company has a "tough job": inventing, designing, implementing and nurturing exactly those products, which most entrepreneurs never achieve.

chunks.heading: Recruiting changes at scale: employee #200 is not employee #2
chunks.text:
- Employee #2 joins for the experience, stories, influence, potential, thrill, control and camaraderie, even with a pay cut and even if the company likely fails. Employee #200 has a different risk profile, won't take a pay cut, and wants different problems to solve (scale problems rather than "why 7 people bought and the next 3 didn't").
- Small companies see cheap amazing hires as an advantage. But Jason says hundreds of people at WP Engine are much more skilled in their area than anyone he met at a small startup, including his own.
- Why experienced people join larger firms:
  - They are in a life phase where they want a predictable, larger paycheck and a well-defined job, so they can still tuck their kids into bed at night.
  - They enjoy applying advanced skills in a larger environment (for example, marketing techniques that make no sense for a small company). They'd hate going "back to Kindergarten" as Jeff Bezos quipped, scratching out a $2,000/month AdWords campaign or being called a "growth hacker."
- Implications: compensation, where you find talent, and why someone picks you over a company that pays a bit more. It is critical to have a genuinely important mission, meaningful and interesting work, and to connect everyone's work to something bigger. "These matter even more at scale, because it's the reason why talent will join and stay."

chunks.heading: Communication: repeat simple messages
chunks.text:
- With 4 people, everyone can know everything, and a 5% chance of misunderstanding rarely matters. With 400 people, that 5% means 20 confused people, and that assumes they even read or listened.
- "Slack" is not the answer and "Email" is not the answer. The answer is **repeating simple messages.**
  - Repetition answers "I didn't see it": repeat in different formats, at different times, by many leaders. It approaches 100% asymptotically, with collateral damage for people who read everything and tire of hearing it.
  - Simplicity answers "I didn't understand / remember it": accept that people don't read, don't remember, have other things on their minds, and that you wrote less clearly than you hoped.
- Consequence: you cannot communicate anything complex to 1,000 people. "Scale is hard."

chunks.heading: Technology, infrastructure and risk mitigation at scale
chunks.text:
**Technology**
- Managing 10,000 virtual servers sounds easy ("automate everything"), but it never works like that. Examples he cites: Reddit took 18 months to get "number of likes" working at scale, StackOverflow took 4 years to convert to HTTPS, Wired did the conversion in 18 months.
- Patterns behind this:
  - Rare things are common, and hard to predict, identify or reproduce.
  - Compatibility with existing technology. New companies start from scratch, but at-scale companies must transform, and the cause of the difficulty may also be generating $100M in revenue ("Instead of 'legacy code' we call it the 'revenue code.'").
  - Bottlenecks. Small scale can be fixed by adding capacity; eventually something forces re-architecture.
  - Hickam's Dictum: problems in complex systems usually have more than one root cause. Example: a software upgrade breaks seven customers undetected. Causes include no failure detection, missing tests, undocumented code, and inadequate code review. Five Whys and Occam's Razor don't apply, so analysis and decisions are complex.
- Result: entire teams for infrastructure, scaling, deploys, cost management and dev process, none directly customer-visible but necessary.

**Risk**
- A small company's likeliest cause of death is "suicide": starvation (not enough customers paying enough for long enough), founders splitting, no traction for the next round, going back to a day job.
- At scale the risks differ. At WP Engine, the risk of failing to sign thousands of customers this month is very low, but other risks are likely and must be addressed head-on. Example: an Amazon data center down for a week. How fast could all customers be restored while thousands of other businesses also spin up servers? Could you communicate quickly and simply so support isn't swamped with tens of thousands of angry customers?
- Risk mitigation can drive growth: serious customers want vendors who manage risk. That is why enterprise suppliers like WP Engine promote SOC 2 and ISO 27001 compliance. Small companies mock these, "while they're busy making that point, the larger companies are busy signing three-year multi-million dollar deals."
- Early on you don't need a disaster-recovery plan, since it won't kill the business and customers understand young-company risk. Later it becomes critical.

chunks.heading: What founders must do: change the details, keep a few values
chunks.text:
- Many founders believe "what got us here is what's important and unique about us, and thus we should preserve *all* of it," and that other companies fail because they act like big companies. Jason says: "But they're wrong."
- Keep a few constant values, otherwise "none of it means anything," but the details "must change."
- Scaling is hard, foggy, lasts years, may need a different set of people, and "no one emerges unscathed." Struggling with these forces is not a sign of disaster. Everyone does.
- Disaster is when leaders don't appreciate these forces, don't work constantly to reshape the organization, don't bring in experienced talent, and assume they can figure it out alone.
- Instead, expect new people, roles, values, processes, recruiting, stories, constraints and opportunities.
- Many founders can't make the shift, which always hurts the company and sometimes kills it, an avoidable waste of sometimes hundreds of person-years of effort.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jason Cohen argues "fail" is almost always the wrong word for setbacks because it is final and suggests no next step. He maps different situations (experiments, innovation, learning, optimizing, problem-solving, major errors) to more precise vocabulary that points toward action, reserving "failed" for true shutdowns.

chunks.heading: Why "fail" is the wrong word
chunks.text:
- Jason argues "fail" is almost never the right word for what is happening. It is "so final, so negative, and it's a dead end: What do you do after a failure? Mope?"
- He says words should do two jobs: explain what is really going on, and suggest what to do next. "Fail" does neither.
- He rejects "fail fast" and "fail forward" too: "It's not fail fast. It's not fail forward. It's not 'fail' at all."
- His fix is to pick a more precise word for the situation, so you understand it better and are pointed at the next step.

chunks.heading: Exploring new territory: it's an experiment, not a failure
chunks.text:
- Building a business or product is like solving a maze (he links the "idea maze" concept). When a path doesn't work, you haven't failed, you've backtracked.
- This usually takes the form of an experiment. The result is evidence for or against the hypothesis, and neither outcome is a failure.
- A/B testing is a good practice even though most tests won't find an improvement.
- Words to use instead: experiment, test, bet, learning, investigate, trial, retry, probe.
- He cites Fermi: if the result confirms the hypothesis you've made a measurement, and if it contradicts it you've made a discovery.

chunks.heading: Revolutionizing: you haven't found the breakthrough yet
chunks.text:
- If you're building something nobody has done before and it doesn't immediately transform the industry, you haven't failed. You just haven't found the breakthrough.
- Innovations often need many trials before the right solution appears. If the answer were obvious, it wouldn't be an innovation.
- Words to use: backtrack, iterate, trial, attempt, step, miss.
- He cites Edison: "I have not failed. I've just found 10,000 ways that won't work."

chunks.heading: Learning and iterating
chunks.text:
- **Learning a skill:** stumbling, getting lost, or sliding backward is growth, not failure. No good teacher gets mad at a student for not learning instantly. The learning curve is well understood and is not a straight line.
  - Words to use: practice, cultivate, acquire, develop, learning curve, learning moment, progression, evolve.
- **Iterating on something that already works:** this is optimization. Not every improvement attempt has the hoped-for effect, but you shouldn't call yourself a failure when things are basically fine as they are.
  - Words to use: refine, calibrate, optimize, polish, hone, correct, fine-tune, dial-in.

chunks.heading: Solving problems: setbacks are normal
chunks.text:
- When you hit a minor problem particular to your current circumstance and your high-level strategy and plan are still right, that is not failure.
- In a complex space, whether a one-person startup or a thousand-person organization, you cannot have innovation and speed and also no setbacks, complications or false starts.
- Words to use: iterate, adapt, adjust, course-correct, tweak, revise, morph, refactor, amend, fix.
- He endorses Churchill: "Success is not final, failure is not fatal: It is the courage to continue that counts."

chunks.heading: Major errors: name the nature of the mistake
chunks.text:
- Jason grants that a complete misjudgment, a wrong strategic decision, or months of work by dozens of people proving useless is a big deal, and saying "we failed" may be justified.
- Even then, the word doesn't explain the nature of the problem and doesn't point toward a solution, which is the constructive thing to do.
- Words to use: pivot, evolve, migrate, overhaul, revamp, transform, reconstruct, repurpose, reimagine, redesign, recreate, reinvent, reengineer, remodel, rebrand, realign.
- He includes Sumner Redstone's line: "Success is not built on success. It's built on failure. It's built on frustration. Sometimes it's built on catastrophe."

chunks.heading: When "fail" is the right word
chunks.text:
- Jason says there are moments of true, irrevocable, fatal failure, and then you should say so. His example: a company that has to shut down, especially before achieving meaningful success.
- Otherwise, find a better way to describe what's happening so you understand the situation and are pointed toward what to do next.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Using chess openings as an analogy, Jason argues that an objectively worse but unusual strategy beats a popular, objectively better one, because opponents are prepared for the popular one and not for yours. Startups should fight on their own terms, pick an extreme difference, and accept that many customers won't want their game.

chunks.heading: Positioning against incumbents: pick a "worse but unique" strategy
chunks.text:
Jason argues that an objectively "worse" strategy can win if it leverages something unique or unexpected. Startups can use this to beat incumbents.

- The chess analogy: the Queen's Gambit is popular and objectively good, but beginners are better off playing a refuted opening like the King's Gambit.
- At beginner level the King's Gambit isn't refuted, because neither player has memorized the branching sequences of moves and counter-moves, and nobody can find the best move in the moment.
- Games at that level are decided by "stupid blunders," not brilliant tactics.
- His conclusion: "Worse, but unique," is in fact "better."

chunks.heading: Why fighting on popular ground backfires
chunks.text:
- Because the Queen's Gambit is popular, your opponent has likely studied it. They may know the defense better than you know the attack.
- As you progress, this gets more likely. The question becomes whether your preparation beats your opponent's preparation.
- Jason says that is not "the sort of 'luck' you want to depend on" and "not a good strategy."
- The fix: learn a refuted-but-not-completely-atrocious opening. Almost no one has prepared a defense, because "no one plays that." The opponent reacts for the first time, while you have memorized a few of the best moves. That gives a clear advantage even as a beginner.

chunks.heading: Applying it to startups and leverage
chunks.text:
- He ties this to his definition of leverage: it produces a superior strategy for products and companies even if many things about your team, product and company are "worse" than the competition.
- A startup is a "beginner" in the market. Its "opponents" have varying preparation and skill: age, capabilities, customers, brand, funding.
- A startup needs to fight "on its own terms, not attack where the opponent is already strong."
- "Playing on your own terms changes the game."
- On a personal level, he applies the same idea: use your leverage to do and be something special, at the intersection of what is special, enjoyable, and what the world needs. He quotes Oscar Wilde: "Be yourself. Everyone else is taken."

chunks.heading: Accept that many customers won't want your game
chunks.text:
- Many potential customers won't want to play your game. You'll feel bad losing them to a competitor, and they may say mean things about you, your product and your decisions, especially publicly on review sites and social media.
- Jason's take: "don't worry, you weren't going to win them anyway." They're just not into you.
- The customers who do want your game will see you're the best at it, even if you're two people facing a dozen competitors, from well-funded, media-covered startups to old-but-reliable incumbents.
- Pick a different game and you can be the best at it and become extremely successful.
- Example from his own company: WP Engine powers as many substantial websites as Google Cloud or Digital Ocean, yet has only 2.3% of that market. So 98% of potential customers are not customers, and WP Engine is still a unicorn.
- That is also why he says to seek large markets.

chunks.heading: Be extreme in your difference
chunks.text:
Jason says that being extremely different beats merely being different. Examples he gives:

- Not just a minimal UI, but one so minimal it works on the command line.
- Not just great design, but design so remarkable people buy the product only for that, and it gets written up on designers' blogs.
- Not just a new algorithm for an old problem, but one that uncovers things no one else does, even at the expense of missing things others catch.

Tactics and reasoning:

- You can't be extreme on every aspect of the product and business. Even one extreme dimension is already powerful.
- Extremity is how you maximize the power of the few things that make you special.
- Competitors cannot play your game as well as you. They can't make every choice you made, so they are definitionally not the best at your game.

chunks.heading: Don't be deterred when others say your strategy is refuted
chunks.text:
- Jason's closing advice: "Play your King's Gambit. Don't worry if others claim your strategy is refuted. It's not refuted for you."
- His final point: the fact that competitors think your approach is refuted is why you will win.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jason Cohen argues that strategy is simply "how we will win," and that most documents titled strategy are vague wishful thinking. He lays out six traits of great strategy (simple, candid, decisive, leveraged, asymmetric, futuristic), with examples like Craigslist, Zappos and Amazon, plus tell-tale signs of bad strategy.

chunks.heading: Strategy is "how we will win," and most documents titled "Strategy" aren't
chunks.text:
Jason defines strategy as "How we will win." The format does not matter (a four-sentence master plan, a few dozen bullets, a six-pager, an eighty-pager, Salesforce's V2MOM, a Lean Canvas). Its only job is to communicate how the company wins. He says most so-called strategies are "vague, wishful thinking, written once and never seen again."

He lists six traits of great strategy:
- **Simple:** reshapes complexity to be manageable and actionable.
- **Candid:** spotlights the most difficult truths.
- **Decisive:** asserts clear decisions and accepts their consequences.
- **Leveraged:** magnifies strengths into durable competitive advantage.
- **Asymmetric:** higher upside than downside, so it beats uncertainty.
- **Futuristic:** solves for the long term.

Without these, the "strategy" is at best a plan and at worst "wishful thinking masquerading as 'vision.'"

chunks.heading: Simple: omit detail so people can remember and use it
chunks.text:
- "No one reads anything... No one remembers anything. Certainly not an 86-slide PowerPoint." A strategy has to be simple, even "simplistic," to be read and remembered.
- Strategy lives in weekly meetings and prioritization sessions. A simple narrative lets teams move quickly and independently with little coordination while still supporting one theory of how the company wins.
- Long supporting documents are useful as optional reading. They explain and justify, and they inspire conviction even in people who don't read them. Tesla's 39-word Master Plan was preceded by 1,200 words of justification.
- A simple strategy may look obvious, and obvious may look uninsightful. Jason treats obviousness as a sign it is easy to communicate, execute and believe. Its job is to specify what matters most. X, Y and Z may all be "obvious," but choosing X and not Y or Z creates focus.
- Simplicity can become reductive, overlooking complexity and landing on wrong conclusions. The process of creating strategy must tackle real complexity. The output is like a street map, which omits detail to show the important routes. Simplicity that comes from having processed the messy world is elegant.
- Signs of a strategy that is not simple: pages of detail, slides with more than 20 words, a litany of numbers with no narrative, diagrams with 20 boxes, too many points to recall from memory, and key concepts with no short phrase people can use as daily shorthand.

chunks.heading: Candid: expose the scariest facts, as present-tense threats
chunks.text:
- Strategy must "lay bare the most frightening, embarrassing realities." If it doesn't expose and then solve the most brutal facts, "the strategy is wrong." Existential threats matter most.
- Lazy threats could apply to any company: "Google could copy us," "a new startup could get huge funding," "a security breach could cause half our customers to leave."
- Real threats are happening now or are at least 70% likely. They are specific and backed by data, such as a shrinking market, a competitor with accelerating share, or cancellation rates showing even paying customers don't value the product. They are written in the present tense, not with "could" or "might."
- If someone might leave when they hear how scary things are, "maybe they should leave the company." He quotes Nick Saban: "Great players want the coach to tell them the truth."
- Example from Jim Collins's *Good to Great*: A&P and Kroger both had data showing their 1960s grocery model was becoming obsolete. Only Kroger faced it and changed strategy. Though half the size of A&P, Kroger increased its value 100-fold while A&P shrank and then went bankrupt.
- Sign of a non-candid strategy: nothing that makes the reader say "Oh wow, what are we going to do about that?", and a reader who finishes thinking "we're still ignoring the elephant in the room."

chunks.heading: Decisive: choose, and accept the negative consequences up front
chunks.text:
A strategy asserts justified, self-consistent decisions on:
- Which market subsets to target, and which to ignore.
- Which customer personas to delight, and which will dislike the product (their feature requests get a quick "won't do").
- How to position against competition, including where competitors are stronger.
- What the company values (quality, service, speed, design, compatibility, lock-in) and what it gives up.
- What to build and what not to build.

Key arguments:
- Customers outside the target segment will buy anyway, then complain about features, UX, integrations and price, drag down NPS and star ratings, and cancel at high rates. Without a strategy that names these consequences, teams log the complaints and start prioritizing them. With one, the team can say "we expected that."
- Fluffy language like "leverage synergies to create unique solutions" is a hallmark of indecision.
- The **Opposite Test:** the opposite of a real decision must also be a rational choice made by successful companies. Open source versus closed source passes. "Customer-first" fails, because no successful company is "customer-last."
- Decisions must at least be self-consistent. A low price conflicts with white-glove service, and top design conflicts with out-shipping competitors, unless you accept extra constraints that resolve the conflict.
- Better than consistent is **mutually reinforcing**. Few features plus amazing design works because customers forgive less functionality when the design is delightful, and great design is easier to deliver with a simple product.
- Strong decisions make you say "no" to most things, including reasonable ones. He cites David Allen: "You can do anything, but not everything."
- Signs of non-decisive: "for everyone" targeting, headings that use "and" to expand scope, unclear what you're not doing, and conflicting decisions.
- Example, Craigslist: it values a consistent experience over great design and accessibility over monetization. Pundits have predicted its demise for 25 years, yet it remains one of the most-visited sites in America, with revenue of $1,000,000,000 in 2020 and a staff of about fifty.

chunks.heading: Leveraged: play to strengths and build moats
chunks.text:
- "If Sandra is a great singer, and Peter is a great pianist, then... Sandra [should] sing and Peter... play piano." Great strategy leverages the organization's strengths. Bad strategy asks it to act unnaturally, often "under the cover of 'overcoming weaknesses.'"
- Leverage means a large effect from small effort, and you know you have it when others are amazed at how much you did in so little time.
- Most organizations spend their energy making weaknesses "less weak," which never makes them strengths. Putting the same energy into strengths has a much larger effect, and it is more fun.
- Strengths are better when differentiated from competitors, and better still when durable. Software and business models are easy to copy, so decide which one or two moats to build and name them in the strategy.
- Example, Zappos (1999): when few people bought shoes online, it combined postage-paid returns even 364 days after purchase, legendary support (including buying pizzas for customers) and a culture of employee empowerment. Each depends on the others. Competitors laughed, press was constant, and it reached $1B annual revenue before its tenth birthday.
- Signs of non-leveraged: it would apply equally to a competitor or another industry, no moats are being built, and it demands overcoming more than one or two major deficiencies.

chunks.heading: Asymmetric: bets where upside far exceeds downside
chunks.text:
- Jason's metaphor is a sailboat, which always moves forward because its shape resists moving backward and eases moving forward. Strategy should amplify the positive and mute the negative, so setbacks and bad luck don't stop progress.
- Activities should have upside far above cost, so that even if you "took 2x longer to achieve 50% of what you expected," you still win.
- A bad sign is when success requires everything to go right. A portfolio of asymmetric bets (VC-like convexity) lets the successes make the failures moot.
- Forms of asymmetry he names:
  - **Large, growing markets:** budgets, pricing and channels already exist, and optionality means many niches and many ways to succeed.
  - **Compounding processes:** retention, upgrades, employee retention, word of mouth and viral products. Most don't grow exponentially, which is still fine.
  - **Reseller channels:** growing resellers by N brings N × M potential customers.
- Intuit example: it made QuickBooks easy for CPAs, who then required their clients to buy QuickBooks, so few CPAs produced many sales.
- Threats are asymmetric too. With ten competitors, only a few need to break out. He cites the IRA's line after the Thatcher bombing: "we only have to be lucky once. You will have to be lucky always." A portfolio of bets means you don't need to be lucky always.
- Example, Amazon: it kept taking bets (electronics, warehouse and logistics products, Kindle, phones, cloud). Many failed and failure was expected. Bezos is quoted: "A few big successes compensate for dozens and dozens of things that didn't work." Per Andy Johns, Bezos assigned the Kindle to the executive running physical books: "Your job is to kill your old business with a Kindle."
- Signs of non-asymmetric: upside less than 10x cost, linear risk/reward, and several hard things that must all go right at once.

chunks.heading: Futuristic: choose the mountain, aim three years out
chunks.text:
- Agility is good for climbing a mountain shrouded in fog, but strategy picks which mountain. An agile team climbing the wrong mountain wastes everything.
- Strategy looks further out than anything else at the company, and data tells you about the past, not the future.
- If a problem can be solved in a month, solve it, but it is not strategic. Anything buildable in three months is not a moat.
- Distinctions he draws:
  - Features or timelines make a **roadmap**.
  - Teams, roles, hiring or processes make an **operational plan**.
  - A strategy specifies market and business outcomes, primary decisions and secondary consequences, and what takes the whole company together.
- Strategy is where you pick the "high-hanging fruit" (important but not urgent, in the Eisenhower Matrix), which are the Rocks in Rocks/Pebbles/Sand.
- The **vision** describes what the world looks like when you win. Examples he lists: Stripe's "Increase the GDP of the internet," YouTube's "Give everyone a voice and show them the world," WP Engine's "Power the freedom to create online." It is often the first sentence of the document but the last thing written, because you can only summarize the future after understanding challenges, courses of action and desired results.
- Example: after Google bought YouTube, it set a goal of a billion daily views. This drove architecture demands, debates about licensing TV and film, and billions invested in fiber and data centers.
- Signs of non-futuristic: the "vision" describes what the company already does, it specifies teams or timelines, it solves quarter-sized problems, and it relies primarily on data to predict the future.

chunks.heading: Bad-strategy checklist and what is not strategy
chunks.text:
- Generic statements that fit almost any company are not strategy: grow faster, lower attrition, hire the best talent, delight customers, beat the competition.
- Also not strategy: aspirations without a "how," financial goals instead of how to win competitive markets, plans that live only in someone's head, and written documents not referenced when making plans.
- Jason's closing: a sailboat always moves forward, but without a destination it ends up somewhere you didn't want. "A mediocre strategy is still better than no strategy," so don't wait to write one.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jason Cohen argues that control is impossible but command is achievable. A leader who is in command still has bugs, missed metrics, mistakes and threats. What sets her apart is that she has expectations, watches the right metrics, writes down her thinking, and reacts honestly when reality diverges. The essay lists what command looks like across metrics, hiring, strategy, sales, backlog and decisions.

chunks.heading: Being "in command" versus "in control"
chunks.text:
Jason argues that being "in control" of a business is impossible and perhaps not even desirable. Being "in command" is the ideal: "honest, introspective, agile, aware, and proactive." When a founder, CEO or team leader is in command, he doesn't worry about that business, whatever its challenges.

- In command does not mean meeting every expectation. It means you *have* expectations of yourself and your team, and when you miss them it bothers you and you react.
- In command does not mean being in control of everyone and everything. It means "proactively seeking the truth, working rationally, and communicating."
- The payoff is "autonomy, coupled with accountability, with realistic expectations."

chunks.heading: Metrics, bugs, backlog and prioritization
chunks.text:
- **Metrics:** Healthy or moving the right way is not the test. You have already thought about what to measure and you watch the things that really matter. When metrics go awry you are the first to spot it, and you act in proportion to their importance and how far off the mark they are.
- **Bugs:** A product can have a list of 100-1000 bugs. The sign of command is that you are working on the top three that matter most.
- **Backlog:** A long backlog, most of which you will never get to, is fine. You have identified the few "Rocks" that are your bets on how to win strategically, and you have a system for prioritizing the rest, which also means doing almost none of the rest.
- **A/B tests:** Not every test succeeds. You run them and honestly assess the results, so you improve over time.

chunks.heading: Strategy and changing your mind
chunks.text:
- Great strategy means you have one, it is written down, a normal person can understand it, and people genuinely try to follow it.
- Being in command does not mean the strategy is completely correct. When flaws become apparent, you write those down too, work on one or two at a time, and update the strategy "calmly but purposefully."
- A mind that never changes is very likely wrong. You write down what you think so it is more obvious when your mind needs to change, then communicate the change, both what and why, even if just to yourself.
- He quotes Paul Samuelson, Nobel laureate in economics (1970), who was criticized for "not being able to make up his mind" as his models of wartime inflation shifted: "Well when events change, I change my mind. What do you do?"
- Surprises still happen. When they do, it is not due to negligence: something actually changed or an important new fact surfaced. Even better, you were intentionally seeking new information and thus seeking surprise.

chunks.heading: Customers, sales and feature requests
chunks.text:
- **Customer knowledge:** You do not know everything about your target customer. You actively seek out what they say and do, so you can understand them and decide better.
- **Churn from missing features:** Customers may leave because of lack of features. You have identified which features fit your strategy, which lead to the ultimate benefits the customer is seeking, and you are working on one or two of them right now.
- **Wins and losses:** You do not win every sale. You look for patterns in wins and losses. Where a pattern intersects your strengths and strategy, and thus where you *should* win, you make changes so you can win the next such deal.
- **Stakeholder and executive requests:** You do not do everything they ask. You listen with curiosity and empathy, use a system to reject bad requests and prioritize good ones, and communicate the result and the rationale.

chunks.heading: Team, hiring and not doing others' work
chunks.text:
- **Great team:** You are not always the smartest person in the room. You have hired great people who challenge you and bring diverse perspectives.
- **Problems with team members:** Problems may exist, but you have already talked to the person and are working with them to change, either changing and staying, or changing by leaving. You proactively and intentionally solve for fulfillment of the whole team, yourself included.
- **Editor, not writer:** You are not constantly telling people what to do. You act as an editor rather than a writer, unless writing is necessary to make progress. If you are constantly doing the writing, you change the team so that it stops, which might mean changing someone else or changing yourself.
- **Whose fault it is:** "If you're constantly having to do someone else's work, that's your fault." Either you hired incorrectly, or you hired correctly and are not allowing them to do their job.
- **Unpopular decisions:** You are not always popular. You make tough decisions, even if poorly received, because they are in the best interest of the customer, the team and the business.

chunks.heading: Mistakes, threats and overwhelm
chunks.text:
- **Mistakes:** You still make them. You are proactively on the lookout for them and call them out when you find them, so you can rally many people to find solutions and make a change.
- **Existential threats:** They may loom over the business. You have articulated what they are because you sought them out and faced them head-on, and you mitigate the more likely ones with a few logical actions.
- **Overwhelm:** You still feel it. You recognize it, take steps to manage your stress, and seek support when needed.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jason Cohen proposes mapping product metrics as a value chain across time (leading to lagging) and across hidden, internal, external and strategic domains, so every department sees itself in the result. He pairs this with a checklist for good metrics, including plain-language definitions, causing action, and signal at least 2x stronger than noise.

chunks.heading: Product metrics as a value chain
chunks.text:
- Jason maps product metrics as a chain of events across time, by actor (team, customers, peers in other departments), and by type of value.
- Every box on the map gets one or more metrics showing "it is happening" or "we're making progress". Arrows can carry funnel or conversion metrics, but he notes too many arrows make a "dizzying bird's nest".
- The map lets every department "see themselves" in it: executives want financial outcomes, strategists want systemic impact, managers want team accountability, teams want credit for work, planners want progress, ops wants stability.
- He used to believe in "one true metric" plus operational indicators, but now prefers this more comprehensive system. He argues it gives the team a view of everything they do and everything they affect.
- Color the boxes by what you are maximizing versus satisficing. Maximizers are critical to success; satisficers are operational indicators that can't be ignored but shouldn't distract day to day.

chunks.heading: Satisficing KPIs and SLO-style thresholds
chunks.text:
- At WP Engine, satisficing KPIs are tracked continuously using Google's SLO approach. The team acts only when a KPI slips into "violation" territory, instead of fielding requests to invest in improving it.
- The violation threshold is pre-agreed with stakeholders in periodic meetings, outside "high-emotion catastrophes". Everyone can then soberly decide when high-value work will be interrupted for a critical problem.

chunks.heading: Leading vs lagging: the axis of time, immediacy and control
chunks.text:
- Some events happen before the product team's activity, some after. Some team activity is measurable immediately and fully in the team's control, so the team should be held directly accountable for it.
- This resolves the conflict where executives ask "why isn't the team more focused on increasing revenue in the next 60 days" and the team says "other people don't understand that we're doing a lot of important work".
- Work is measured sprint by sprint. Revenue is a "multi-input, lagging indicator". The product team is responsible for it but is not the only contributor, and individual features often can't be directly linked to revenue.
- Revenue stays potentially the most important metric. It just lags by months or years. Example: Blackberry's revenue kept growing for two years after the iPhone launched, while other KPIs changed far faster.
- If the work is succeeding but financial impact isn't, the conversation becomes diagnosing that disconnect. If the work isn't completed, or built features aren't used, those are immediate and within the team's control.
- Teams must measure both direct results and lagging outcomes, and are accountable for all of it. Not yet achieving the outcome is "not a complete failure" but a learning that shapes the next two weeks of work.
- He argues the world is unpredictable, not all work yields a large outcome, and outcomes need execution plus luck, so expecting every idea to produce the desired outcome is wrong.
- Quote he endorses (Fermi): "If the result confirms the hypothesis, then you've made a measurement. If the result is contrary to the hypothesis, then you've made a discovery."

chunks.heading: Internal vs external, visible vs hidden work
chunks.text:
- Draw a bright line between internal (engineering, infrastructure, security) and external (product, design, support, sales working with customers) activity. Use the right metrics for each.
- Internal work splits into customer-near (releasing features) and customer-far (security patches). If all work is invisible, customers see a stagnant product, competitors look faster and sales has nothing new to say.
- If only visible work is valued, you get tech debt, unhappy engineers and slow delivery from an under-invested foundation. The diagram honors both.
- Strategic outcomes are often distant from the product team. A team controls "satisfaction" more than self-motivated customer "advocacy", yet advocacy is the ultimate measure and drives efficient growth. Teams should own creating those outcomes without letting lagging metrics be the only progress measure.
- The most valuable outcome is the customer achieving their own ultimate goal (the Needs Stack). If the customer's business doesn't thrive, they stop paying regardless of software quality.
- You can't control that, but you can notice attributes of customers who thrive and aim marketing, sales and features at that subset. He says this yields higher growth, retention and likely profitability.

chunks.heading: Checklist for great metrics, part 1: definition and intent
chunks.text:
- **Normal language:** "Customers are using feature X" works. A precise formula like unique IPs firing events P, Q or R over rolling 14 days divided by total unique IPs is too hard to scan.
- **Precise too:** Also keep the technical definition. Writing it often reveals you can't get the exact metric, or need engineering work first. Terms like "cancellation rate" or "cost to acquire a customer" can be defined many ways, and different precise definitions can suit different metrics in one company.
- **Matches the intent:** Example failure: intending "User Portal usage" but measuring "User Portal logins", which only fires when a session expires. Proxies can be fine if they truly measure the intended concept.
- **Causes action:** If the metric moved, would you re-plan the next sprint or interrupt the current one? If not, it doesn't belong on the main board. It may belong on an operational board as explanatory.
- **Obvious what good looks like:** Not every metric needs an explicit goal. "Not changing" or directional ("usage increasing") is enough.
- **Measures "what is happening", not work:** Metrics are "the dials on the airplane dashboard", not the pilots' actions. If a metric can only be moved by one course of action, it measures work and presupposes solutions. Exception: metrics explicitly measuring volume or quality of work completed.

chunks.heading: Checklist for great metrics, part 2: practicality and trust
chunks.text:
- **Measured easily:** Best is automated, second-best is manual-but-trivial. Hard-to-get metrics stay un-updated in spreadsheets.
- **Measured frequently:** Daily is best. "Rolling N days" can update daily while still thinking in weeks or months. Slow-moving numbers needn't be measured often.
- **Stable definition and applicability:** Stable definitions ensure changes come from deliberate actions or environment shifts, not changes in measurement, enabling month-to-month comparison.
- **Common definitions when possible:** Standard definitions enable benchmarking and make it easier for others to understand. Custom definitions can hide signal or be used for deception. His examples: revenue recognition, classifying costs in or out of COGS/GPM, and conveniently leaving costs out of EBITDA. He says "Don't do that."
- **The team actually cares:** When management mandates a KPI the team doesn't believe in, "the team always wins". Six months later it is likely not even tracked. The team must want to depend on it, look at it at least weekly and change behavior at a threshold.

chunks.heading: Signal at least 2x stronger than noise
chunks.text:
- Metrics vary for reasons unrelated to the underlying signal. Monthly revenue example: calendar months vary in days by ±5%, daily numbers can differ 2x between weekday and weekend, and months vary in weekdays by ±10%.
- So a real 10% change in new revenue per month is the same size as the noise and can't be detected.
- Fix noise via definition: "new revenue over rolling 28 days" removes both factors and approximates a calendar month. Multiply the trailing 28-day figure by `52/48` to approximate an average calendar month.
- For infrequent noise, use median or 95th percentile to ignore outliers.
- If you don't know how much of a metric is noise, "it's probably a bad metric".

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jason Cohen argues that words like "unlikely" or "probable" mean wildly different things to different people, even after training, so they should not be used for risk or strategy. He recommends a few crisp numeric probabilities (Fermi-style), rounded by context, with teammates estimating independently.

chunks.heading: Why probability words fail
chunks.text:
- Jason argues that words like "unlikely" and "almost certainly" don't communicate probability, because people read them very differently.
- In the study he cites, the median intended probability of "likely" is 70%, but "unlikely" is 20%. Since one is just the negation of the other, he says you'd expect a symmetric 70/30 or 80/20 split, but the numbers are biased.
- "Probable / improbable" is worse, at 70% vs 10%. "Probable" and "probably" are both 70%, yet "probably not" is 25% while "improbable" is 10%.
- He notes this causes confusion in analytical settings such as risk analysis or debating a strategy.
- He points to the literature on our bias about rare and common events. People are surprised how often 5% things happen and how often 95% things don't. Examples: Taleb's *Black Swan*, and getting upset when a "10% chance of rain" rains out a picnic.

chunks.heading: Individuals disagree more than the words differ
chunks.text:
- Jason's central point: "the differences between individual interpretations are larger than the differences between the words themselves."
- One person's ratings in the study: "probable," "probably" and "likely" were each scored only 50%. "Probably not," "we doubt" and "unlikely" were each 20%. "Improbable" was a flat 0%, while "highly unlikely" was still 30%.
- He sympathizes with that rater. If the consensus is that a project is "improbable" to finish on time, he would *act* as though the probability were 0%.
- Conclusion: give up on using words to describe probabilities.

chunks.heading: Why assigning numbers to words doesn't work either
chunks.text:
- The CIA tried to fix this with the "Sherman Kent Scale," published in 1964. For example, "probable" was defined as 75% and "almost certainly not" as 7%.
- When officers were assessed against the scale, fully half the time they failed to stay in range.
- Even with official numeric definitions and trained, competent people, words still fail.
- Jason says the CIA's mistake was continuing to use words. Their categorical probabilities were already Fermi-style:
  - Certain 100%
  - Almost certain 93% (range 87-99%)
  - Probable 75% (63-87%)
  - Chances about even 50% (40-60%)
  - Probably not 30% (20-40%)
  - Almost certainly not 7% (2-12%)
  - Impossible 0%

chunks.heading: The solution: Fermi-style probabilities
chunks.text:
- Rule one: force numbers and never use vague words. He says this alone improves communication.
- Writing precise probabilities is hard, because we usually can't know the true value. The world is unpredictable even with expertise and data, so we need fuzzy ranges to gesture at our intent.
- Saying "unlikely" can seem more accurate when the true figure could be 10% or 40%. But given how differently people read "unlikely," the range isn't communicated anyway.
- Borrowing from Fermi estimation (as used for impact and time estimates), he says haggling over "20% or 30%" is unproductive. Nobody knows the true number, and you need crisp signals to make decisions.
- His formula for a Fermi-style probability:
  1. Use numbers, not words.
  2. Select from a small set of options.
- His recommendation: "use just a few raw numbers, without words," with instructions for rounding off that depend on context.
- Example: when estimating whether a project finishes on time, things are more likely to be late than early, so round toward the lower probability.

chunks.heading: Where to apply it
chunks.text:
- **Risk slides:** use Fermi probabilities to force yourself to decide what you think the risk really is, so everyone can decide whether to act.
- **Strategy:** put a Fermi probability on each assertion, so people know what is more or less likely to change as the team learns.
- **Work prioritization:** put Fermi probabilities on the "value" or "estimate" metrics used for decision support.
  - Have everyone supply their numbers independently.
  - Where numbers disagree, discuss. Where they agree, move along and save time.
  - He adds a caveat: sometimes probability isn't even applicable to such things.

chunks.heading: Why people avoid numbers
chunks.text:
- Jason's view: we use wishy-washy probability words because we don't actually know the probability, and rather than admitting that, we glide past the challenge. He calls that "the worst reason of all."
- His closing instruction: "Be brave, and put a number on it."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jason Cohen argues effective strategy rests on three nested layers of leverage: strengths, differentiated strengths, and durable differentiated strengths (moats). He says to sidestep weaknesses rather than fix them, and shows how interlocking choices (Southwest) and competitor lock-in create lasting advantage.

chunks.heading: Leverage means a large effect from small effort, and strengths are the source
chunks.text:
Jason defines leverage as generating a large effect from a relatively small effort by riding natural abilities or hard-won assets, rather than fighting a battle you are ill-equipped for. Whatever makes others wonder how you got so much done with so little is leverage, not just a "strength."

He ranks three tiers:
- Leveraging strengths is the only way to do great work, not "fixing weaknesses."
- Leveraging differentiated strengths means you beat the competition.
- Leveraging durable differentiated strengths means the win lasts.

He treats the near-term, accessible forms of leverage as worth using. They are not a substitute for a moat, but he warns against ignoring them while waiting for one.

chunks.heading: Why fixing weaknesses is the wrong strategy
chunks.text:
Jason notes that company success stories are always about one or two things done amazingly well, never the 47 complex details or a 28-page strategy document, and never about "shoring up weaknesses."

- Netflix pivoted to streaming. Snap had disappearing messages in a uniquely simple interface. The iPhone had unparalleled design. Tesla solved both EV performance and safety. Google's PageRank was an order of magnitude better than anything else and beat thirteen major search companies that had a head start.
- Twitter's 140-character limit created an addictive communication pattern and worked on cheap devices and cheap cellular plans. It kept growing through years of the Fail Whale because of that experience.
- Facebook beat MySpace on its strengths in hypergrowth, not stable infrastructure. It later changed its motto from "Move fast and break things" to "Move fast with stable infrastructure."
- Downtime and security flaws must be fixed, but that is an operational necessity, not a strategy.

His summary: "Reversing weakness is hard, painful, likely to result in something merely neutral, not great, and is at high risk of failing completely." "How we will win" is the entire purpose of a strategy.

Corollary on tools: the best answer to "what tool/language/framework/process should I use?" is usually "the one you already know," because it leverages your most limited resource, time. Slack was built in PHP, a language derided as passé at the time, because that is what the founders knew. Facebook used PHP too and later wrote its own version when it needed performance. Companies that never get off the ground never earn the "good problems to have" of scaling.

chunks.heading: How to handle weaknesses: avoid them, accept them, or fix at most one
chunks.text:
- **Rarely fix a strategic weakness.** Occasionally you must change "who we are" because you keep losing deals to a competitor over a major product or positioning gap. A good strategy explains why this risky, expensive, unnatural journey is the best way to win. There should be probably no more than one, because you can't afford the time, people, or energy for more.
- **Avoid weaknesses through target market, persona, and product decisions.** If you can't offer 24/7 support, position as a "boutique" where customers get incredible interactions with experts available at limited times. If you have a small team that can't build millions of features, build for users with simple needs who appreciate simple, well-built software that "doesn't have all that crap I don't want."
- **Manage threshold weaknesses (like uptime) with SLOs.** Jason says WP Engine had great success with the SLO system from Google's SRE Book. It works for anything that should be satisfied rather than maximized:
  1. Define a metric for the effect (for example "uptime in past 28 days").
  2. Define the acceptable threshold (for example 99.5%).
  3. While the metric exceeds the threshold, do not try to improve it, since that over-invests in a weakness that will never become a strength.
  4. If it drops below the threshold, the team addresses it.
  - A cross-functional team agrees on the threshold quarterly. When downtime hits and everyone is emotional and demanding that "something must be done, so this never happens again," you go back to the previously agreed decision rule and defuse the discussion.

chunks.heading: Other sources of leverage: business model, tooling, and passion
chunks.text:
- **Near-zero marginal cost business models.** Software and content (blogs, newsletters, podcasts, videos, books, courseware) cost a lot to create the first copy and almost nothing to sell the next. A newsletter written for 100 people takes the same effort as for 100,000, yet the latter can generate 1000x more revenue. A self-funded content company is hard at first (all effort, no income, no compounding) but can be extremely profitable if it takes off.
- **Supporting tools and systems.** AI can draft a simple blog post, with factual errors, no personal examples, and a plodding style. But it can draft ten articles, and a human can edit those many times faster than writing from scratch, which greatly increases output. A great strategy may call for a specific supporting system that makes the team 10x more efficient, which becomes a new form of leverage.
- **Passion.** It magnifies strengths through sheer will and carries you through the emotional pain and drudgery of challenges. "Follow your passion" is correct but incomplete. He quotes Teller: "Magic is just someone spending more time on something than anyone else might reasonably expect."

chunks.heading: Differentiated strengths: separating yourself from competitors
chunks.text:
The strengths above are shared by competitors (many organizations have talented, passionate engineers, and all content companies have a leveraged model). The more strategic strengths are the ones that separate you from others. These are the familiar "differentiated competitive advantages" or "unique selling propositions."

- It is hard to invent differences that are non-trivial and also apply to most of your target audience. That is why they must be identified in the strategy; you won't stumble onto them during day-to-day work.
- **Technology and design trade-offs.** Every architecture makes some capabilities easy and others hard or impossible, and every design makes some use cases delightful and others annoying. Great strategy names the trade-offs, shows how they fit the target market and persona, and exploits them. Competitors who made different trade-offs can't follow without extreme cost and time.
- **Accept the downsides of your trade-offs.** The limitations that result are not "bugs." Trying to fix them takes inordinate effort, won't yield a fantastic product, blunts your strengths, and takes time away from magnifying them.
- **Heroku example.** It mandated trade-offs many Rails developers initially hated: Bundler (when it was bad), PostgreSQL instead of MySQL (when MySQL was about 10x more common), and no writing data to disk. Together they enabled a new way to develop, test, stage, deploy, and scale apps. Today nearly all SaaS apps follow 12-factor principles, and Heroku won the Rails market for a decade.

chunks.heading: Differentiating through hard engineering problems and secret insights
chunks.text:
**Solving a very hard engineering problem**
- Upside: success can create a moat (Google search, Tesla cars, OpenAI).
- Downside: it likely fails by taking too long, costing too much, not truly solving the puzzle, or not doing enough of what the customer needs.
- His advice: be surgical about which subset of the software is hard. Pick something that creates a moat and leverages existing strengths or assets.
- Example: Google Wave pioneered fast multi-user simultaneous editing, a precursor to Google Docs. It was so difficult that it failed. Co-founder Lars Rasmussen said that even redoing it with the same team and all the knowledge gained, it would take years and probably still not work. That means competitors would have failed too, so success would have been durable leverage.

**Insights (Thiel's "Secret")**
- An insight is an important truth you understand while the rest of the world does not, especially if the world confidently believes the opposite. Their disbelief prevents competition. Once proved true others follow, but by then the strategy has already succeeded.
- Examples he lists: "People will buy shoes over the internet" (Zappos), "People will take rides from strangers" (Uber, Lyft), "People want to sleep in stranger's houses" (Airbnb), "Rockets can be reusable" (SpaceX), "The highest-performing sedan can be battery-powered" (Tesla), "Large enterprises will put customer data in the cloud" (Salesforce), "Open source copycats will defeat multi-billion-dollar incumbents" (RedHat).
- Differentiation erodes: secrets become known and almost anything in software can be copied. He doubts patents protect software companies. The most valuable differentiation is the kind that takes decades to erode, if ever.

chunks.heading: Durable differentiation: moats and exploiting a competitor's ossified structure
chunks.text:
A durable differentiated advantage is a moat. Jason describes it as: "I have something that you don't, and furthermore, you either don't have the ability to acquire it, won't invest enough to achieve it, or in the case that you try, you would have to make an incredible investment of time and energy and possibly brand adjustment to do it, which is unlikely to succeed, and even if it does succeed it will take years, by which time we've already won."

He highlights an often-overlooked form: exploit an ossified structure in a competitor that prevents them from reacting even if they wanted to.
- **High cost structure.** A competitor with high costs must charge high prices, so "40% of the features at 10% of the price" is a position they can't match. This is a simple form of Innovator's Dilemma disruption.
- **Simple product, no tech support.** That competitor can't win complex clients, so "Enterprise offering at Enterprise prices" stays differentiated.
- **Publicly espoused values.** A competitor can't act against its stated values, so a strategy built on contrary values stays differentiated. A company that values sustainable sourcing can't price-compete with those who don't, and sustainability-minded consumers will pay the premium.
- **Platform trade-offs.** A competitor invested in a core platform can't change its trade-offs for years, if ever, so choosing different trade-offs yields different features and liabilities that stay differentiated.
- **Loss-leader attacks.** A competitor whose profit depends on one product can't cut prices when someone builds the same thing free to power another business:
  - Netscape (browser revenue) was killed by Microsoft's IE, a loss-leader for Windows.
  - For-profit smartphone operating systems were killed by Google's Android, a loss-leader for Google's services. Apple is the exception, remaining because of hardware; 87% of global handsets are Android.
  - Twenty proprietary Unix operating systems were killed by RedHat's Linux, a loss-leader for RedHat's Enterprise Services (later sold for $34B).
  - He quotes Satya Nadella on Bing: "There is such margin in search, which for us is incremental. For Google it's not, they have to defend it all."

chunks.heading: Mutually reinforcing structures: durability from a combination of choices
chunks.text:
In a crowded space no single thing may be unique or durable, but a combination can be both, if the pieces form a mutually reinforcing, cohesive structure. A competitor who copies only a fraction still won't have a similar product.

- **Southwest Airlines example.** It stayed profitable through September 2001 and the 2008 Great Recession, when every other major US airline filed for bankruptcy at least once. It has no single unique element a competitor couldn't copy, but its combination of decisions, strengths, and weaknesses has been durable for sixty years. Michael Porter diagrammed it in 1996 and the analysis was still accurate twenty-plus years later.
- Some attributes are customer strengths (low fares, frequent reliable departures) and some are weaknesses (no meals, no baggage transfers, no connections to other airlines, no long-haul routes). They all support one structure: no amenities allows lower prices, and short hauls on standardized aircraft cut costs and also produce frequent, reliable departures.
- He quotes Roger Martin: "Strategy is a set of interrelated and powerful choices that positions the organization to win."
- It is not strategic to claim "our peculiar set of features makes us unique" unless they form a mutually reinforcing network that includes the weaknesses. It is not durable leverage unless a written strategy explains the network, so the company keeps reinforcing the whole thing and accepts the weaknesses instead of treating them as bugs. "Otherwise, it's just a pile of features."

chunks.heading: What a winning strategy must say, and what happens without each tier
Summary
chunks.text: Jason Cohen explains the Needs Stack: every customer need is a means to a higher need, and a product serving a higher level makes lower-level products obsolete. He shows how to use it for positioning (features at the customer's current level, benefits one level up), for competitive attack, for choosing metrics, and for finding higher purpose.

chunks.heading: Jason's Needs Stack framework
chunks.text:
- Jason says every customer action sits in a "stack" of needs. Each lower item is a means to a higher end. - Example: Charlie buys AWS infrastructure only to get a WordPress site, which is only for a personal website. That website is for a book deal, which is for becoming a famous speaker. - He notes that Charlie "never wanted to set up infrastructure, and still doesn't." - Format: "★ top need
→ next need down → ... → bottom need." - He distinguishes it from Jobs to Be Done and Five Whys. His point is the competitive insight: a product at a higher level makes the levels below it obsolete. - Moral: "You need to understand the Needs Stack of your target customers", not just your market, product, or immediate job.

chunks.heading: Competitors you don't see: higher-level products make lower levels vanish
chunks.text:
- WP Engine sets up a WordPress site in about one minute, with no infrastructure to think about. It handles monitoring and WordPress-specific support. Charlie buys it and "disappears from the cloud infrastructure market."
- AWS would name GCP, Azure and Digital Ocean as competitors. Jason argues WP Engine is also a competitor for Charlie's business, even though it buys infrastructure from AWS, GCP and Azure.
- The same applies up the stack:
  - Wix and Squarespace skip "get WordPress."
  - Substack skips "build a website" with tools for long-form writing, a mailing list and social promotion.
  - Speaker bureaus and services like SpeakerMatch skip the website, years of writing and the book deal.
- You always want to stop at the level you operate on, "but there's always another level."
