- Lower-level businesses survive. WP Engine is 16 years old and healthy, and AWS posted $5.2B profit in one quarter. Jason says higher-level products only win customers who value speed over flexibility.
- Data he cites: 43% of the top 10M websites use WordPress, with Shopify next at 4%. Over one million sites run on WP Engine.

chunks.heading: The core tradeoff: speed up the stack, flexibility down the stack
chunks.text:
- "Up the stack, customers achieve their end-goal faster; down the stack, customers have more flexibility and customization."
- Substack vs WordPress example:
  - WordPress is far more configurable, so sites can look unique, while Substack newsletters all look alike.
  - WordPress has far better long-form tools, such as drag-and-drop layouts that differ for phone, tablet and laptop. Email newsletters can't do that.
  - If the customer values those things, WordPress is still right.
- Rule: if ease of reaching the need matters more than customization, the higher-level product makes all lower levels obsolete.
- WP Engine doesn't let you customize infrastructure, so customers who need that still buy from AWS.

chunks.heading: Messaging: features at the customer's level, benefits one level up
chunks.text:
- Jason resolves "sell benefits, not features" with the stack. A customer thinks at one level at a time, so an engineer shopping for a database wants specs, and someone shopping for a socket wrench wants "a 5/16" lock nut" and "has a mounted light."
- Google searches are "a good proxy for 'what level of the stack are potential customers operating at right now?'" Charlie might search "best way to publish online," then later "how to get a WordPress site."
- Tactic:
  - Meet the customer where they are and talk features there. For "get a WordPress site," that means showing how you are the best way to get one.
  - Sell the benefit one level higher: "Become famous online with our turn-key, customizable WordPress website."
  - Substack can't say "customizable," but can say "Grow your own audience with our turn-key newsletter platform."
- Jason notes Substack's homepage leads with higher-level benefits ("be independent," "get paid for writing") and lists same-level features lower down.

chunks.heading: Positioning: make the levels below you irrelevant
chunks.text:
- Fight at the level where you win. Substack would lose a "get a website" fight, so it fights at "build an audience."
- Message: "While others just give you a website, we help you build a following." It won't work on businesses that need a website, but it can suit the aspirational speaker.
- WP Engine does this to cloud services. They say "click 17 times to make a server," then install server software, configure WordPress, set up a paid caching network, add plugins, patch security and learn SSH. WP Engine says "You don't want infrastructure, you want a WordPress site, and in less than one minute, you'll have exactly that."
- WP Engine adds that it is faster and more secure than doing it yourself, and has a support line cloud services don't.
- Summary: "make 'infrastructure' irrelevant by focusing on the next level up."

chunks.heading: Moving up the stack yourself: barriers and partial strategies
chunks.text:
- Jason says you can disrupt yourself and competitors by moving up, but companies "almost never" overcome the barriers:
  - **Different product and business.** You must rebrand, build expertise and build the product. Pricing may change, such as from per-gigabyte to per-site monthly, pay-for-performance subscribers, or a percentage of speaking fees. Mature companies may buy the product to trade cash for speed.
  - **The next level may not be possible.** Software can't guarantee an audience or force people to subscribe.
  - **A smaller market.** Few people share Charlie's exact stack. WordPress sites serve many personas (individuals, brands, media, ecommerce, communities, non-profits, governments), each with a different level above. Narrowing is a tried-and-true strategy but may not suit an established broad brand.
- Partial strategies:
  - **Sub-brands or products:** keep the original business, launch vertical or niche products that use the parent's scale, and treat each as its own startup.
  - **Add-on features:** an extension aimed at personas sharing that next level, without fully committing to it.
  - **Better marketing:** educate without promising results, with field guides, content ideas, partner promotion and customer success stories.
- Successful full transitions he cites are the "Emotional vs Functional" case studies in Blue Ocean Strategy: Cemex selling "build an addition to your house, for your family" instead of cement, and Starbucks selling a lifestyle experience.

chunks.heading: Metrics and purpose from the levels above you
chunks.text:
- Measure three layers:
  - The bottom of the stack tells you whether you're operating well.
  - The level the customer is actively thinking about tells you whether the product delivers its direct promise.
  - The very next level up is strategic for predicting long-run happiness. Not too far up, or it's hard to measure and external factors dominate.
- Shopify example:
  - A customer can create a store (the product works) but get no sales and churn.
  - Jason cites only 34% sticking around for even one year, with huge cancellation rates that "would sink most companies." Shopify survives because inbound volume is high and survivors grow a lot.
  - Shopify's primary success metric is GMV (gross merchandise value, the total customers sell through their stores). It reports GMV to Wall Street right after revenue, in the same large font.
  - GMV measures the next level up, which Shopify can't control but can measure and help with, via marketing articles and features like ShopPay to reduce cart abandonment.
- Purpose: direct goals like signups, activation, churn and costs create no higher purpose. Purpose lives in the upper stack: helping someone build a career, win respect, be a hero in their organization, raise money for a cause, or speak truth to power.
- Jason's advice is to tell those stories on the website and internally, and celebrate when it happens for a customer.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jason Cohen splits willingness-to-pay into three sources: Love, Utility and Coercion. Each one changes growth, retention and exposure to competitors in a different way. His conclusion is that even a cold-blooded investor should build WTP through Love and Utility, and treat Coercion as the weakest base.

chunks.heading: Utility vs. Love vs. Coercion: three kinds of willingness-to-pay
chunks.text:
Jason argues that "willingness-to-pay" (WTP) is the maximum price a customer would have paid, and that economists treat any transaction as proof that WTP > Price. The gap between WTP and price is "Consumer Surplus." The gap between price and cost is "Profit." His ideal business "delivers $4 of value, charges $2, and costs them $1 to do it."

He dislikes the word "willingness" because it hides intent and ability to pay. Examples he gives:
- Martin Shkreli raised Daraprim from $13 to $750 per pill (treatment cost from about $1,000 to $63,000). Patients had no choice, which isn't really "willing."
- Gas prices rise at once when oil rises and fall slowly when oil falls.
- Cable TV bundles exist because consumers are not "willing" to pay for every channel.
- "Willing" is not "able": many people would be willing to pay $1,000 for a top phone, but few are able.

Genuine willingness does exist, and he says it "creates the best, most durable, most profitable businesses." Customers are happy to pay more, become evangelists, and ignore competitors who compete only on features and price.

chunks.heading: The Love category: what builds allyship
chunks.text:
Jason's first category of WTP is Love. The result is "allyship": customers are glad to do business with you, root for your profit, advocate publicly, don't consider competitors, and would accept a small price rise.

Drivers he lists:
- **Mission:** supporting a change bigger than the customer.
- **Reciprocity:** giving before taking, exceptional service, being deeply human.
- **Exceptional design and quality:** joy in use, and relief from reliability.
- **Personal identification:** the brand becomes part of the customer's own brand.
- **Culture:** treating employees and vendors well (counter-examples: Walmart and Amazon).
- **Transparency:** Buffer is the extreme case, sharing salaries, strategy and monthly revenue.
- **Social or environmental impact:** fair, sustainable practices.
- **Community:** members teach, support each other, and form a tribe.
- **Ecosystem:** members earn more money or prestige than they would outside the group.

Examples he uses:
- He pays more for Anker chargers and power strips because of their quality, with no lock-in and no recurring revenue.
- TOMS (One for One shoes) and Patagonia win on authentic missions. Patagonia has a formal policy to bail out employees arrested while protesting peacefully.
- Skechers copied TOMS exactly, including the style, a name ("BOBS") and the altruism. Consumers were outraged and Skechers cancelled the line after 24 hours. His point is that the strategy was individual to TOMS, so being publicly visible and copyable didn't matter. TOMS has weaknesses (poor service, shoes developing holes) but wins on its individual story.
- Hollow Knight (released 2017, made mostly by three people) is sold at $15 with four free expansions. Fans beg them to charge more and they don't. Jason says rabid fans generate millions of purchases, and that impact is far larger than closing the WTP/price gap.

chunks.heading: The Utility category: fair exchange of value
chunks.text:
Utility WTP gives a "fair exchange of value": the product is useful and not excessively painful, and it is "easier to stay than to leave," with no particular desire to leave. Drivers he lists:
- Cheap, even if functionality is low.
- Integrations, system-of-record status, and training investment (each makes switching costly).
- Market-share leadership as social proof.
- Location (airport coffee) and convenience (grocery delivery).
- Simplicity, quality, and risk reduction.
- Unique functionality.
- Onboarding experience: he cites ProfitWell data that ease and reciprocity in onboarding raise WTP.
- Familiarity with a workflow.

Utility grows existing customers and is neutral-to-positive on attracting new ones. Organizations buy more seats and more infrastructure as they grow, and at scale that internal growth outweighs new-customer growth. But a customer buying ten more JIRA seats isn't advocating for it on forums, and may still try a new competitor. His example is Linear, which built a rabid fan base on UX: JIRA users could imagine switching to Linear, but "it's laughable" to imagine a Linear user pushing to switch to JIRA.

chunks.heading: The Coercion category: why it leaves you exposed
chunks.text:
Coercion keeps customers paying against their will, and the result is "adversarial." Jason's list:
- Contract lock-in and data lock-in.
- Effective monopoly (including purchased ones, like Uber subsidizing rides for tens of billions to drive out rivals, then raising prices) and effective price-fixing.
- Middle-man positions, such as ticket resale at 10x.
- Bundle-stuffing: packing in things the customer doesn't want to charge more.
- "Scale Anti-Pricing": raising prices once an installation is at scale, because switching cost is so high.
- Predatory pricing: pricing below cost, funded by another business unit or VCs, until competitors are gone.
- Patents used to block normal competition.
- Corporate policy (the only approved vendor) and government fiat or regulation.

Consequences he describes:
- Coerced customers are "allied with competitors." They say "just give me an excuse," and will build a case that switching pays for itself ten-fold.
- Renewal time is when "you should be very afraid."
- When someone asks on Twitter what to use, your customers answer "we use X, but don't make the same mistake."
- You are exposed to disruption "even by mediocre competition."

chunks.heading: How Love drives growth
chunks.text:
Love produces "inexpensive, non-linear growth" because customers are allies:
- Repeat purchases with no extra marketing or sales cost.
- Word-of-mouth: fans answer "what should I buy?" questions, and the product ranks first on review sites. The effect compounds as the customer base grows.
- Retention against better or cheaper competitors. There is a limit (the product eventually has to be good enough), but it carries you through ordinary one-upmanship.
- He points to retention as growth: look at the growth curve of any startup that went from 7%/month cancellation to 2%/month.

chunks.heading: Create more WTP, then split it with the customer
chunks.text:
Jason quotes Michael Mauboussin: when you raise WTP, "you're adding value for the consumer, and then figuring out how to split that with the consumer." His order of operations is to create value first, and only then decide how to share it, either by keeping Consumer Surplus for advocacy, retention and growth, or by raising prices.

- Value created via Love or Utility is both sustainable and profitable. Value created via Coercion is "temporary at best."
- The strongest organizations use all three. Apple creates Love (design, personal brand, privacy), Utility (familiarity, convenience, being the center of photos, files and notes) and Coercion (no export from Notes, older devices slowing after mandatory OS upgrades, changing cable connectors every 5-10 years). Apple's net profit margin ranged from 21-26% from 2010 to 2022, which he reads as increased WTP split with customers.

chunks.heading: Why the cold-blooded investor should still pick Love
chunks.text:
Jason's thought experiment: two companies identical in product, market, customers, price, costs, revenue, profit and WTP. Company 1's WTP comes only from Love. Company 2's comes only from Coercion. Which grows faster and is the better VC investment over five years?

- He picks Company 1. Its customers help it grow efficiently while competitors can't convert them even with unique features and lower prices.
- Company 2's customers are trying to leave, hoping for a competitor to rescue them, and publicly warning prospects away.
- Company 1 can add Utility or even Coercion later. It is much harder for Company 2 to generate Love from where it is.
- He is clear that Coercion isn't banned: like the Agile Manifesto's "working software over comprehensive documentation," it means the other two are better places to spend your energy.
- His conclusion: "Love beats Coercion, even as cold-blooded, money-grubbing capitalist investor," and it also makes the world better. "So choose Love."

chunks.heading: Related frameworks: moats, engagement and buyer utility
chunks.text:
- **Moats:** raising any type of WTP strengthens your ability to capture and keep customers. Network effects appear in all three types: Love (community and ecosystem), Utility (eBay as a functioning marketplace people used because it was useful), and Coercion (insurance "preferred vendor" networks that force you to switch doctors when you switch insurers).
- **Start with Why:** a strong, permeating mission is "impossible for a competitor to destroy." Buffer has a relatively undifferentiated product and pays lower salaries than many can get elsewhere, yet its culture and transparency draw people. TruthSocial has downtime and slow innovation but a rabid fanbase because of mission and community.
- **Kano model:** Love maps to "Delight," Utility to "Performance," Coercion to "Inverse."
- **Blue Ocean buyer utility:** productivity, simplicity, convenience and risk map to Utility; fun & image and environmental friendliness map to Love. He says "customer productivity" is too broad because it's "an order of magnitude more important to increase value" than to save cost.
- **Engagement metrics:** in a multi-year Facebook experiment, sending fewer, higher-quality notifications first lowered app usage but raised satisfaction. After a year, usage rose above its prior level and stayed higher. His takeaway is that real satisfaction produces more long-run engagement, and traditional growth hacking did not find that solution.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jason Cohen explains why many startups fail despite a real problem and a working product. He lays out a chain of filters (Plausible, Self-Aware, Lucrative, Liquid, Eager, Enduring) and a multiplicative Fermi-estimate score to test viability, plus exceptions and how niching can fix a bad score.

chunks.heading: Why solving a real problem is not enough
chunks.text:
- Jason says many startups fail after finding a real problem and building a product that solves it. The founder talks to three people, they agree the problem exists (and they're correct), the founder builds the product (and it works), then sales stall and the company dies within 6-24 months.
- His claim: "solving a problem is--perhaps surprisingly--not nearly enough to build a successful company."
- He models the path from "Problem" to "Viable Business Model" as a chain of ANDed conditions: Plausible, Self-Aware, Lucrative, Liquid, Eager, Enduring. Each can be a deal-breaker even when the product is excellent.
- He says there is an exception to every rule, but you have to really want that harder path and have a specific answer for the weakness.

chunks.heading: Plausible: market size math (10M consumers or 100k businesses)
chunks.text:
Jason uses Fermi estimation to show how big the market must be, even for an indie company:
- Impression to visitor converts about 1%. A very good AdWords campaign gets about 2% click-through, display ads 0.3%-0.5%, and a top SEO position 3%-5% (almost impossible for a competitive keyword).
- Visitor to paid converts about 1% for a typical successful product website (sign-up or trial forms show 2-5%, of which only a fraction pay).
- So 10,000 impressions gives about 1 paying customer, and 10M impressions gives about 1,000 paying customers.
- 1,000 paying customers is his minimum for a sustainable small company, at roughly $30-$100/mo. Below that price you need more customers; above it you need fewer, but they're harder to find and convert.
- It takes about two years, 10M impressions, and luck. WP Engine, which hit $100M ARR fast and now has over 200,000 customers, took two years to get its first 1,000 customers. Competitors that started later took that long too. It's a rule of thumb: some founders take 52 hours, 6 months, 4 years or forever.
- Consumer products need about 10M people with the problem. Business products need about 100k, because there are far fewer businesses but they pay orders of magnitude more and convert better.
- Exceptions: a high-price product in a small niche, or a frugal solo business making about $100,000/year post-expenses post-tax. He notes 80% of small businesses do this and it's valuable; there are two kinds of companies, those replacing a salary and those trying to become huge.

chunks.heading: Self-Aware: they must know and care they have the problem
chunks.text:
- People who don't believe they have a problem won't search for a solution, and you can't get them to pay to fix it.
- Website security example: everyone has the problem, since hackers want your server for spam, ad-click fraud, remote-controlling visitors' browsers, or hiding their tracks. But millions think "I'm nobody," so they don't search for or buy security software. WP Engine blocks hundreds of millions of nefarious requests daily.
- Second version: they know but genuinely don't care because it's their ninth priority. Accessibility is his example; many agree they have the problem but few act.
- Timing matters. Instacart worked after 80% of Americans had smartphones; WebVan had the same idea before the market was ready.
- Sam Altman on Loopt (raised $30M, failed): "The market wasn't there. You can't force a market."
- Exception: founders who are natural evangelists on a mission to educate and create the market. He calls it difficult (changing minds is almost impossible), expensive and slow, because you create demand then fulfill it.

chunks.heading: Lucrative: a substantial allocated budget
chunks.text:
- Typical objections: needs someone else's approval, budget closed for the year, the internal team says they don't need help.
- College-student startups at Capital Factory: in 17 years none of them worked, even though the problems were real. Students have no money and don't buy SaaS, and the businesses serving students charge low prices so they have no budget for new ideas.
- Large companies fund only their top few problems each year. They also add compliance approval, vendor comparison and pilots, and internal teams may resist outside tools that make them vendor-managers. Target companies that already outsource the problem.
- Consumers pay little even for high-value productivity apps. Examples he cites: Bear Pro at $15/year, Remember the Milk at $40/year, and an Evernote user leaving over a rise from €29 to €43/year.
- Consumers "pay" with attention and data, so he argues self-funded companies should target businesses, which spend money to solve problems and to make more money. He flags this as a personal bias: he doesn't build or invest in B2C because he doesn't understand that customer.
- Exception: a huge number of customers, extremely low cost basis (no direct support, little infrastructure, near-zero acquisition cost, tiny team, low switching costs), a simple product, ideally against poor, expensive incumbents. You then need far more than 10M customers.

chunks.heading: Liquid: able to buy right now
chunks.text:
- Blockers: contract not up for 15 months, the problem is already covered by an all-in-one like Workday, deep integrations with other systems, or a one-time need ("I'll let you know when I get married again").
- At WP Engine, Jason's own team cancelled several SaaS products because Workday did it all in one system.
- Lock-in forces include contracts, hard data extraction, retraining thousands of employees, and re-implementing integrations, workflows and reports. "All these forces have nothing to do with your product or its price," yet they can overwhelm the best product at the best price.
- Flip it into strategy: how will you create lock-in so competitors can't kick you out of your customers?
- Temporary-need products struggle. From his Smart Bear days, founders of code profilers and load-testing tools struggled to keep even small companies alive: customers didn't have the problem, then suddenly needed it right now, then didn't again.
- Exceptions: pay the customer's contract-breaking penalty (if still profitable), do the migration as a service or for free (common in WP Engine's market), target buyers who can't afford Workday so it isn't a competitor, or offer a cheap or free way to stay on while not using the product.

chunks.heading: Eager: they want to buy from you specifically
chunks.text:
Two hurdles:
- **Trust:** that the product works, that you'll be around for years, keep up development pace, avoid security issues, deliver real support, and scale as they scale. Typical objections: "only a year in business," "will you handle 100x growth," "SOC 2 required."
- **Differentiation:** being unique isn't enough. If only 10% of the market cares about your feature and 30% cares about a competitor's feature you lack, you lose.
- Over-serving: with ten features where the market cares about three, the simpler or cheaper product wins even if your feature matrix looks more complete.
- A sales team helps by building trust and positioning so the customer accepts your mix of pluses and minuses. He points to "Love" and "Utility" willingness-to-pay as the best way to overcome both.
- Exceptions: build a product that needs little trust (no private data, not time-critical, local, or for freelancers who like supporting startups); mitigate with open source; compete on price (works but hurts margin and customer quality); specialize in a niche in a large market; or sell into a small market with few competitors. A mission bigger than the company can differentiate, mostly in consumer products. His example is Patagonia, bought for its conservation spending and treatment of employees.

chunks.heading: Enduring: churn kills the business
chunks.text:
- Jason has seen countless indie developers reach $15k MRR and stall at 7% monthly cancellation, with many thinking 5% would be a success. It isn't: at 5%/mo only half of customers remain after a year.
- The deeper issue is that customers don't want the product enough: it lacks features, has bugs, lacks integrations, is too expensive for the result, or the problem isn't important.
- The math: top-line growth is linear (or quadratic in hyper-growth), but cancellation is exponential because it's a percent of the base, so it catches up with new sales.
- Worked example: $15k MRR, adding $2k/mo of new customers (a healthy 15% per month), at 7% churn. A year later MRR is about $27k and growth has stopped, since $27k × 7% ≈ $2k cancelling each month. Each of those new customers cost money to attract, sell and onboard.
- One-time-revenue businesses still need repeat revenue, from customers buying again and from happy customers referring others.
- Even Unicorn goals are impossible with high churn. He cites Gainsight CEO Nick Mehta on launching a second product to avoid the inevitable stall.
- Exception: Shopify has about 8% cancellation (only 34% of new customers last one year) and still wins, because (a) survivors grow forever and super-linearly, (b) the market is huge and growing, and (c) people cancel because their own business failed, not because the product is bad. If the product itself is the problem, he believes there is no exception.

chunks.heading: The viability scoring model and worked examples
chunks.text:
Jason's Fermi-style score multiplies seven inputs (power-of-ten only where noted), scored for one specific target market, buyer, problem, trade-off set and price:
- **Plausible:** potential customers with the problem (1k to 1B).
- **Self-Aware:** 0.01 few agree or care; 0.1 thought-leaders evangelize; 0.5 industry standard practice; 1.0 almost no one doesn't care.
- **Lucrative:** annual allocated budget, net revenue ($1 to $1M). Net revenue means after pass-through costs, not after marketing, support or infrastructure.
- **Liquid:** purchase-decision frequency: 0.01 every few years; 0.1 annual; 1.0 always in the market.
- **Eager (identity):** 0 cannot buy from you; 0.1 structural challenges; 0.5 indifferent; 1.0 mission-level desire to choose you.
- **Eager (comparative):** 0.1 no differentiation; 0.5 some features good enough for some buyers; 1.0 one-of-a-kind.
- **Enduring:** 0.01 one-off without loyalty; 0.1 one-off but repeat and referrals; 0.5 recurring revenue from recurring problem; 1.0 strong lock-in.
- Multiply, because the conditions are ANDed, then divide by 625,000. A score of 1 is the indie-startup threshold; 2 or more suggests a scale-up. (625k comes from 100M × 0.5 × 0.1 × 0.5 × 0.5 × 0.5, with 100M being 10M consumers at $10/mo or 100k businesses at $1000/mo, e.g. dentist practice management.)
- He warns it's "dangerously close to a silly quiz": use it as guidance, since "having to think through the answers and trade-offs is most of the value."

Examples:
- **WP Engine:** 100M × 0.1 × $100 × 0.01 × 0.5 × 0.5 × 1.0 = 2,500,000, so score 4, a scale-up (as happened). Market logic: 334M businesses, 71% with websites, 43% of sites on WordPress.
- **ConvertKit** (email for creators monetizing newsletters): 10M × 1.0 × $100 × 0.01 × 0.5 × 0.5 × 0.5 = 1,250,000, score 2. A good model, bootstrapped to large scale though not a Unicorn. Focusing on higher-paying customers (1M people, $1000 budget) gives the same score but is a different product and market.
- **Consumer security software:** 1B × 0.01 × $10 × 0.01 × 0.5 × 0.1 × 0.5 = 25,000, score 0.04. A bad model.

chunks.heading: What to do with a negative score: niche down or move on
chunks.text:
- Re-score a narrower target. Security for high-net-worth individuals: people fall to 1M, but willingness to solve rises to 1.0 and budget to $100 or $1000.
- Security for mid-sized businesses: fewer organizations than consumers, but very high willingness (policies, fear of incidents) and substantial budgets.
- His rule: "targeting a niche often results in a better business model," because it can raise several other numbers even as it cuts customer count. It works whether you stay in the niche forever or use it as a beachhead to expand later.
- If no target scores well, "your business idea might simply not be viable." Facing that early is better than spending years on it.
- This path isn't the only factor: you still need reach, attention, cost-effective acquisition, manageable costs, skills and runway.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jason Cohen shows that even elite experts fail at forecasting markets, sales, winners and products, then lays out how to build strategy anyway. Have a strategy, follow customer behavior (especially product "abuse"), and use moats, optionality, hedges and bets on what won't change.

chunks.heading: Strategy is required even when the prediction is wrong
chunks.text:
Jason argues that experts fail badly at predicting the future, so "skate where the puck is going" is less reliable than it sounds. His evidence:
- Goldman Sachs analysts missed T-Bill rates, oil receipts and solar installations for about 25 years, often not even directionally right. Solar installation forecasts were about 3x too low for two decades.
- McKinsey studied 1,700+ new-drug sales forecasts across 260 drugs: almost two-thirds missed peak revenue by 40% or more. Follow-on drugs were no better.
- The base-rate method (start from what similar companies did) is also shaky. In 2015 the base rate said no company of Tesla's size had exceeded 40% CAGR over 10 years, and the average was under 3%. Tesla's actual CAGR since then was 55%.
- Chess and World Cup favorites lose to long shots (Giri at 10% or less won Tata Steel; Argentina won the 2022 World Cup).

His conclusion: you still need a strategy, because "a strategy gives you a direction. A direction creates something interesting." Even a wrong strategy attracts early fans and surfaces the real answer. Slack came from Game Neverending, then Glitch. Flickr (sold to Yahoo for $25M in 2005) was the byproduct of chat and image sharing.

He also says that "making a decision and moving forward is often more effective than extended deliberation," provided the company is willing to face the truth when the strategy proves wrong. He tells founders to "dispense with the idea that there is One True Solution."

chunks.heading: Follow customer behavior to upgrade the strategy
chunks.text:
Jason sees no contradiction between holding a strategy and following customers. The initial strategy is known to be wrong, so customers are how it gets corrected.
- A feature request is not the new strategy; the intent behind it might be. "Push notifications for my status updates" in WhatsApp really meant "circumvent SMS." The winning strategy became "SMS, but free."
- The strongest signal is when customers abuse the product to do something else, because they want it enough to use the wrong tool.
- His own example: Smart Bear's first product, Code Historian, visualized a codebase's history and few paid for it. Users abused it for peer review, asking to "package up what's on my screen and send it to someone else" and "write directly on a line of code and send it back." That became Code Collaborator, which "within a few years represented 97% of the revenue of the company."
- Stewart Butterfield wrongly believed "yet another chat" wouldn't sell. Slack became one of the fastest companies ever from $1M to $100M ARR anyway.

He notes some strategies are right from the start (Google, LinkedIn, Amazon, Apple, WP Engine). For WP Engine he used a customer-development system to discover what mattered before building.

chunks.heading: Build optionality: have more than one way to win
chunks.text:
Jason says a plan where many things must all go right ("and") is a bad bet, since it assumes you can predict many components. He lists the "ands" of a startup: an insight, a compelling product, reachable customers, cost-effective acquisition, a price customers accept, being better than competitors for a segment, keeping a key team member, and no global economic failure. A resilient plan is built from "or":
- Reach customers through social media or paid ads or influencers or channel sales. A product sellable several ways beats one sellable a single way.
- A very low-cost product has many pricing options, so it is more likely to find one that works.
- A product in a large, growing market has many niches, personas and channels to try.
- Some indie developers build several small products and pour effort into whichever takes off.

He cites Taleb: with optionality "you don't have much need for what is commonly called intelligence, knowledge, insight, skills... you don't have to be right that often."

chunks.heading: Leverage your assets and build a moat
chunks.text:
- **Leverage:** Jason cites Sun Tzu ("strike where you are strong and the enemy is weak"). Founders often chase lucrative ideas outside their competence. At minimum, use your capabilities, knowledge, network, professional friends and accumulated assets. That may mean a very different company, product or market, which is the point: pick the battle you are best suited to win.
- **Moat:** A long-term, durable, structural advantage others cannot disrupt is resilient to market volatility. He points to a companion article on moats.

chunks.heading: Stay reactive, and hedge with "insurance"
chunks.text:
**Intentionally reactive.** If you can't predict, don't spend time planning. React to what you see, using judgment and a long-term strategy. He is blunt that people say "iterate fast" but then take four months for one feature or 18 months to "launch." He wants constant delivery, feedback and learning loops, quick updating of prior decisions, no ego about who was right, and treating all doors as two-way doors, encoded into the organization's DNA. Frameworks he names: building in public, the OODA loop, iterative hypothesis testing, Continuous Discovery and Continuous Delivery.

**Hedged bets** work like life insurance: you come out ahead either way but pay a tax and cap your upside. Examples he gives:
- Multiple vendors for the same service, shifting workloads on price and performance (it also strengthens price negotiations). Wrap third-party APIs in a proxy layer, use multiple clouds and banks.
- Multiple brands, created or acquired, each finding a different niche.
- Multiple simultaneous solutions: Apple had the iPod team grow its OS while the Mac team shrank theirs to fit mobile, which caused in-fighting but picked the right path for the iPhone.
- Redundant systems ("Two is one, one is none").
- Disrupt thyself: Bezos told the new Kindle leader, who ran the book-selling business, "Effective tomorrow, your job is to kill your old business with a Kindle."

chunks.heading: Reduce exposure to the unpredictable: novelty, coalitions, simplicity, constants
chunks.text:
- **Extreme novelty:** Zappos, Airbnb, Uber, SpaceX, Tesla, Bitcoin and OpenAI created categories others thought impossible. They avoided competitive unpredictability, since "it doesn't matter what's happening at Amazon if you can return shoes for free even after 364 days." The upside must be immense for the risk to be rational.
- **Coalitions:** Massive objects resist being moved. Examples: open source projects, industry standards (HTTP, HTML, SSL) that let members build for decades without hedging, and peace treaties. He adds that price collusion also works but is unethical and illegal.
- **Stay simple:** More tasks, dependency arrows and intricate analysis make estimates less believable. A simple product with a simple value proposition in a simple market has fewer dependencies to predict.
- **Bet on what will not change:** Bezos cites low prices and fast delivery. For WhatsApp, people want to chat and not pay. For WP Engine (founded 16 years ago), people want sites that are fast, stay fast under traffic, and are secure.

chunks.heading: Map futures, but don't stall
chunks.text:
Jason recommends mapping possible futures (a "futures cone," extended with "unknown unknowns") rather than predicting one. This does not let you predict, but it helps you mitigate plausible problems and notice sooner when an "improbable" thing is happening. He recommends the pre-mortem: "It's 12 months from now, and the project is a disaster. What went wrong?" The goal is to pick a few things to mitigate intentionally and leave the door open for the rest.

His closing lessons:
- Have a strategy and decide quickly.
- Follow customer behavior, treating product "abuse" as a strong signal.
- Include a moat or two and create optionality, so single failures aren't fatal.
- Leverage existing strengths.
- Either keep it simple, form coalitions, or go completely novel.
- Bet on what won't change.
- Do your homework, but avoid analysis paralysis.

He ends with the 2024 chess World Championship: Gukesh was the overwhelming favorite, Ding won game one, pundits flipped to 50-50, and a pundit said "there's a 1% chance Ding doesn't draw" a dead-drawn final game. Five minutes later Ding blundered and Gukesh won.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jason Cohen presents a framework for fulfillment at work: you need Joy, Skill, and Need together, and any two without the third create a predictable trap (useless flow, indulgent failure, or burn-out). He used it to step aside as CEO of WP Engine and become CTO, and pairs it with Pink's motivation model and Sinek's "Start with Why."

chunks.heading: Fulfillment needs Joy, Skill and Need together
chunks.text:
Jason's framework for what makes work (and a life) fulfilling, which he built about ten years ago when deciding to step aside as CEO of WP Engine, the company he founded. He still uses it and recommends it to others. Fulfillment sits where three circles overlap:

- **Joy:** You love doing it. You forget to eat and pee while doing it, and at the end of a long day you still want to keep doing it.
- **Skill:** You're great at it. Your work is good enough that even you are proud of it, others notice, and people who don't see the effort call you "a natural."
- **Need:** The company needs it done. It's a top-three priority, doing it well makes a critical part of the strategy succeed, and not doing it is crippling.

He stresses that all three are required, and that any two without the third create a specific, common trap. The traps matter because it can feel good to be inside them.

chunks.heading: The three traps: Useless Flow, Indulgent Failure, Burn-out
chunks.text:
**Joy + Skill − Need = Useless Flow.**
- This is "being in the zone." It is intoxicating and recharges the batteries, but it is unproductive because the company doesn't need it.
- Nobody is willing or able to tell a founder to their face that they aren't contributing, so they stay in their happy place.
- The classic example is the technical founder writing code instead of making sales, fixing the website, handling accounting, or hiring the next great team member.

**Joy + Need − Skill = Indulgent Failure.**
- Example: the company needs to start advertising. You've never done AdWords but always wanted to try it, and you tell yourself you can't hire or manage someone without understanding the job.
- You waste three months, and may wrongly conclude "AdWords doesn't work" because that is easier than "I don't know what I'm doing."
- Then you tell yourself that three months of flailing makes you an expert, so now you can hire.
- As founder, no one contradicts you, so the company falls further behind.

**Skill + Need − Joy = Burn-out.**
- You do the work all day and feel drained rather than energized. You do it because the company needs it and you're undeniably great at it.
- You take it on yourself to "protect others from the drudgery," or because you think they can't do it as well, or because you can't afford to hire.
- Because the results are great, it doesn't look like a problem to you or your team. But you grow to resent it, eventually can't face it, and you're finished.

chunks.heading: Why Joy is the missing piece in Pink's model
chunks.text:
Daniel Pink argued that carrots and sticks are poor, often counter-productive motivators, and that internal motivation comes from three conditions:
- **Autonomy:** deciding what to do and how. Counter-examples are micro-management and command-and-control; positive ones are self-managed scrum teams, work-from-anywhere schedules, and agreeing on goals rather than dictating details.
- **Mastery:** the chance to do great work around others doing the same. Experts like deploying expertise; eager novices like learning.
- **Purpose:** being part of something bigger, from a noble cause to genuinely helping another person (for example world-class customer service).

Jason agrees with this and says it matches his own experience. His point is that it is possible to have autonomy, to use your expertise, and to be proud of the cause, and still "dislike every day of your existence." Moving from Pink's question (what motivates people?) to his own (what is fulfilling?) requires adding Joy.

He explains how his framework relates to Pink's:
- It adds the missing Joy and reinforces Mastery under the label Skill.
- It lacks Autonomy, probably because he built it for founders, who by definition have autonomy, even to their detriment.
- "Need" is more tactical than "Purpose"; it is really about being useful.

chunks.heading: Why founders stay stuck: ego and the CEO myth
chunks.text:
Jason says burn-out creeps up like boiling a frog. He quotes an anonymous founder who spent months fantasizing each morning about working at WalMart or as a grocery bagger because it "seems so stress free," and who locked himself in the bathroom with the shower running to cry.

- The ego says "being the CEO is the best," and Silicon Valley says the founder being CEO is the only way. That makes it hard to let go of the role even when it creates unhappiness.
- He notes the usual examples cited (Apple, Facebook, Amazon) ignore counter-examples like Google, LinkedIn and Intel.
- He burned out at his previous company, Smart Bear, and says even selling the business didn't immediately fix it, though it was the start of the answer.
- He used the framework to change roles at WP Engine from CEO to CTO, so that both the new CEO and he could operate in the center of their Venn diagrams. He says the thousands of people who have since worked there agree it was a fantastic decision for both of them and for the business, which is now a unicorn.

chunks.heading: Hiring and delegating around the framework
chunks.text:
Several lessons follow from the traps:
- Don't hold onto a job you hate to "protect" others. He notes no one wants the boss doing all the drudgery, especially if the boss visibly hates it, and some people actually like what you hate. By keeping it you prevent them, and yourself, from being happier.
- Don't delay hiring for a skill because you want to learn it first when the company needs results now. Playing with it yourself can cost months.
- Be wary of a company where nobody will tell the founder they aren't contributing to what the company needs.
- To decide what to keep and what to hand off, ask of each task whether it gives you Joy, whether you have the Skill, and whether the company has the Need. Give away what fails any of the three, and move yourself toward the center.

chunks.heading: A higher purpose helps even mercenary leaders (Sinek and ikigai)
chunks.text:
Jason ties the framework to a higher purpose and recommends identifying it, then fulfilling your own part at the center of the three circles.

- **Simon Sinek's "Start with Why":** companies that produce fanatics, not just customers, have a clear, simple, compelling reason for being that they won't contravene even if it hurts sales or profit. Employee turnover is low and productivity high, so every part of the business is stronger.
- **Examples he gives:** Patagonia (saving the Earth, with a formal policy to bail employees out of jail if arrested protesting peacefully), SpaceX (a multi-planetary species), the Gates Foundation (eradicating malaria), Apple's "Think Different," Salesforce's "1-1-1," WP Engine's "Engine for Good," and Rackspace's "fanatical support," which turned customer service from a cost center into the honor of serving others and a differentiator in a commoditized market.
- **Not just a Gen Z thing:** those companies were created and run by Gen X and older. Even a skeptical, cold-blooded leader should see that having a higher purpose is more useful than not having one, since the freshest talent skews younger.
- **Ikigai (生き甲斐):** the Japanese concept of a reason to be alive, and the shokunin (craftsman) ideal of mastering a craft while bettering the community. He frames this as already covering two of Pink's three: Mastery and Purpose.
- **Purpose can be small:** being useful, needed or wanted by one person can be enough.
- Quote he cites from Sinek: "When people are financially invested, they want a return. When people are emotionally invested, they want to contribute."

chunks.heading: Why this matters for managers and leaders
chunks.text:
- Managers ask the question because the Great Resignation showed that people are more mobile than expected when insufficiently motivated. He calls your best talent "volunteers" who can always cross the street for more money.
- Enlightened leaders ask it proactively, because intrinsically motivated people do great work that is as fulfilling for them as it is productive for the company. He calls this "capitalism on its best day."
- Creating a work environment where others can find fulfillment already improves the world substantially, and caring enough to learn what fulfills each person helps it materialize.
- The closer you are to your own center, the better you can serve others.
- For working out what drives you and what stops you, he points to a separate system he has used for himself and others (his "pivot points" essay), which he also uses to figure out who a whole product or company is.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jason Cohen lays out a five-step interview method (goals, written hypotheses, open-ended questions, iterating, stopping when it's boring) used to vet WP Engine and reject other startup ideas. The aim is to disconfirm assumptions and learn how customers live, not to pitch or ask what to build. He adds tips on discussing price, segmentation, and using customers' exact words.

chunks.heading: Validate customer problems by iterating written hypotheses, not by pitching
chunks.text:
Jason Cohen's customer development method exists to uncover truth about potential customers, not to sell. He has used it for 17 years, and says it led him to reject some startup ideas, pick the idea for WP Engine, and choose the right features in its early years, which led to hyper-growth and a unicorn.

- The most common mistake he sees as an interviewee is the founder spending the hour pitching. A kind interviewee will say "yeah, that sounds pretty good," and the founder has learned nothing.
- His test: "If you don't come away knowing something new and actionable at the end of the interview, you've wasted your time and theirs."
- The mindset should be "What does this person know, that invalidates something I thought was true?" Seeking confirmation means you see confirming evidence, miss disconfirming evidence, and end up believing wrong assumptions, which is worse than wasted time.

chunks.heading: Start with learning goals, and never ask customers what to build
chunks.text:
He lists goals first because they drive the interview content. For a B2B product solving an existing pain, his goals are to learn:

1. What the "perfect customer" (PC) looks like.
2. What outcomes PC must deliver in a typical month (Jobs to Be Done).
3. What PC does in a typical day (tools, workflows, loves, dreads).
4. What pain points PC has today.
5. How PC copes today (competition, including DIY).
6. How much PC would pay, and how PC can budget and execute payment.
7. The triggering moment that makes PC decide "today's the day I'm going to buy something" ("no one randomly switches vendors").
8. What makes PC resist or fear buying (habits, anxiety of change, implementation risk and cost).
9. Where PC goes to discover and buy products like this (distribution channels).
10. The exact words PC uses and their tacit assumptions.
11. PC's higher-level goal.

Not on the list: asking the customer what to build, or whether they would buy a specific feature. Jason says this has happened to him dozens of times: he asked "Would you buy if we build ______?", heard "Yes", built it, and they didn't buy. Every seasoned PM has the same story.

He dismisses the Henry Ford "faster horse" quote: a faster horse is often a wonderful product, sometimes you should invent the car, and Ford never said it (the Henry Ford Museum doesn't list it, and it first appears over fifty years after his death). The point stands that you can't decide what to build by asking customers; you learn what their current life is like.

chunks.heading: Write down hypotheses before interviewing
chunks.text:
Step 2 is to write your current best guesses, at least one per goal, in the first column of a spreadsheet, one per row, mapped to goals.

- Reason one: research on predictions shows people are more objective when forced to record bets. Otherwise we retcon our beliefs or discard new information (confirmation bias).
- Reason two: hypotheses generate good interview questions.
- Example WP Engine hypotheses from 2009: bloggers with over 100,000 page-views a month struggle with speed; blogs with over 10,000 RSS subscribers have traffic bursts that take sites down; all bloggers worry about being hacked; a blogger with 50,000 page-views per month will pay $50/mo to fix these problems; bloggers need to try software before buying; bloggers call themselves "bloggers" and their site a "blog."
- After dozens of hours of interviews, about half the hypotheses were wrong, the correct ones needed tuning, and new attitudes surfaced that weren't on the list.
- List even the most mundane assumptions. Jason says "We're all wrong, at the beginning," even experts.

chunks.heading: What the WP Engine interviews overturned
chunks.text:
- **Security:** Most bloggers would not pay extra for it. Selling security to bloggers is like selling backup software: until you've had a failure, you won't pay $30/mo, and afterward you sign up for any service promising full backup. Mid-sized companies differ, because they run a formal security policy.
- **Free trial:** Bloggers like trials for most software, but moving a site is such a disruption they treat hosting as permanent. "Free migrations" was more compelling than "free trial." WP Engine tried a free trial anyway; conversion was over 90%, and removing the trial didn't reduce signups at all.

chunks.heading: Write open-ended questions, one per hypothesis
chunks.text:
Step 3: in the second column, write a question per hypothesis (one question can cover a few related hypotheses). Questions must:

1. Confirm or negate the hypothesis.
2. Not hint at a specific answer.
3. Invite a specific answer.
4. Invite more information, including answers to questions you didn't know to ask.

Leading questions get a polite "yes" and tell you nothing about what visitors will think of your ad, home page or pricing page.

| Hypothesis | Bad question | Good question |
|---|---|---|
| Bloggers call themselves "bloggers" | Do you consider yourself a "blogger?" | When you meet someone new, how do you explain what you do in a few sentences? |
| Serious bloggers publish 4+ times a week | Do you publish often so Google ranks you high? | How often do you publish new content? Why at that rate, what led you to that decision? |
| Some spend thousands on consultants for speed | Would you spend $2000 on a consultant if it made your blog faster? | How valuable is the speed of your website? Have you ever spent money to improve it? If so, how much, what did you do, did it work, were you happy with it? |

On security, the good version was: "Do you ever think about website security? If so, how do you think about that? Do you do anything about it today?"

chunks.heading: Run the interview, iterate, and know when to stop
chunks.text:
- Take notes in a third spreadsheet column beside each question. Straying from the script is fine if it teaches something.
- Treat surprise as the signal to dig deeper: "Surprise means you're learning." His trick is to say "Tell me more about that."
- After each interview, check what supported or contradicted each hypothesis. Don't alter hypotheses after just a few interviews unless there's a pattern. Add new hypotheses and questions from new learnings, even if they don't map to a goal.
- Stop when it's boring, meaning surprises have stopped and learning has stopped. Then move to a proof-of-concept, high-fidelity demo, MVP (or SLC), or other method.
- A typical mistake is stopping after three interviews because "I'm not learning anything." He compares it to a marketer testing two AdWords variants and quitting.
- If there are truly no patterns, you may be fishing in the wrong spot: no pain point that more than a few people have and will pay for. Then you need different ideas.

chunks.heading: Segment emergently and discuss price in the interview
chunks.text:
**Emergent segmentation.** Customers may cluster, such as marketing departments at large companies thinking about security while independent bloggers almost never do.
- Write hypotheses and questions that determine the segment and ask them at the top of the call.
- Keep a separate hypothesis spreadsheet per segment.
- Then target one, some or all segments with clarity about each.

**Discuss price.** He disagrees with those who say to avoid price in early interviews.
- Price is tied to what the product means to the person, and it determines the company's business model, so it shouldn't be "figured out later."
- In early WP Engine calls, near the end, he floated $50/mo for a faster, more scalable, more secure service with genuinely good support. Reactions were immediate and vehement. One group was shocked at such a high price and would never pay near it. Another said they'd buy only if it were much more expensive, because otherwise it couldn't possibly deliver. These became emergent segments, which told him how to price and for whom.
- Pricing insights were also how he invalidated an earlier startup idea, which made room for WP Engine.
- Pricing questions can be open-ended ("How much would you expect to pay for..."), but he thinks quoting a specific price is an acceptable breach of protocol. A specific number draws a visceral reaction, the same one people will have on your pricing page.
- Tie price to other topics to test real value. For security: "Would you pay extra for a security package that really worked, or do you not really worry about being singled out for getting attacked by a hacker?" Most bloggers said security mattered but admitted they wouldn't pay extra.

chunks.heading: Interview tactics that surface the truth
chunks.text:
- **Expect contradictions.** People differ in goals, values, experiences, roles and projects, so data is noisy. Some hypotheses will turn out to reflect variation or no pattern, which is still learning, since it stops false assumptions. Real patterns stand out from the noise, and there may not be much of it, which is "all the more reason to highlight it."
- **Ask for step-by-step usage.** Customers say they have the problem and would buy, then don't. Ask them to describe in painstaking detail how they'd use the product: when they'd open it, how it fits their workflow, which features they'd invoke, how outputs move to other systems. Thinking it through exposes blocking barriers like missing integrations or unconsidered features.
- **Use customers' exact words for positioning.** Discord calls rooms "servers" because founder Jason Citron found kids were setting up servers for audio or chat, so the early pitch was "Get a free server!" even though "we create communities" sounds better to investors. Record the calls and note exact phrases.
- **Ignore "market guru" mode.** Almost every interviewee starts speaking for others ("I wouldn't pay $50/mo, but a lot of people would"). They don't know what everyone else wants, and neither does he, which is why he interviews. Politely thank them, reinterpret "everyone wants X" as "I want X" or discard it, and redirect to their own situation. Successful companies find an untapped aspect of the market (Zappos: human touch wins; Geico: it doesn't matter), and even experts may have missed it.
- **STFU.** "If you're talking, you're not learning." Talk only to clarify, dig deeper, or open a new vein.

chunks.heading: Where AI helps and where it doesn't
chunks.text:
Jason says half the value of the exercise is thinking it through yourself. The "aha" moments, such as finding contradictions, realizing you didn't believe something, or seeing which hypotheses are wrong, come from wrestling with the details.

- He advises against using AI for the core thinking.
- Fine uses: cleaning up transcripts so they take less space, double-checking your thinking after you've done it (and maybe suggesting new ideas), and summarizing your own thinking to be pithy and clear.
- Possible but secondary uses he lists: scanning conversations for themes or for evidence contradicting a set of hypotheses.
- He names Rob Fitzpatrick's *The Mom Test* as probably the single best book on this topic and compatible with his method.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jason Cohen argues that one big ordered backlog conflates prioritization (what is most important) with work-planning (what we do next), and forces comparison of incomparable things. His fix: keep separate prioritized lists per stakeholder group, customer journey stage or other category, then pick from the top of each list just in time when planning work.

chunks.heading: Prioritization is not work-planning
chunks.text:
- Jason argues product managers conflate two questions: "What is most important?" (prioritization) and "What will we work on next?" (work-planning). A single big backlog encodes the second answer well but is the wrong tool for the first.
- "Important" means many different things: calming a customer threatening to leave, catching a competitor on a feature, opening a new market segment, satisfying security policy, cutting the top cause of support tickets, cutting the top cause of cancellations, refactoring for engineer productivity, improving profitability, or long-term strategy with no next-quarter revenue.
- Sorting one list of epics fails for two reasons. The items are incomparable, since each has different motivations and impacts measured differently, so there is no metric to order them by. And stakeholders are left unsatisfied: Sales lacks context on why engineers need a month to "clean up a mess, which by the way, they made themselves."
- Work-planning rarely matches ideal priority, so one list can't serve both purposes.

chunks.heading: Why actual work order diverges from priority
chunks.text:
Jason lists reasons the work-planning order differs from the importance order:

1. Hard deadlines, often external (a zero-day security patch, functionality needed for a live customer event).
2. No current capacity on the teams able to do the high-priority item.
3. Missing skillsets.
4. Dependencies: A is very important, B is not, but A can't happen without B.
5. Unknowns needing a spike or proof-of-concept before work can even be planned.
6. Amount of work or risk means it shouldn't be tackled yet.
7. Shipping smaller wins alongside longer work helps throughput and morale and is more agile.
8. Blockers on other work or other teams.
9. Starving: low-priority things put off so long they effectively become higher priority.
10. Holidays and seasonality (don't kick off a huge initiative on December 15th).

His solution: prioritize items in separate, actually-comparable streams, and keep that effort cleanly separate from work-planning.

chunks.heading: Build one prioritized list per stakeholder group
chunks.text:
- Sit down with each group (Sales, Sales Engineering, Support, Engineering) and ask them to generate and then prioritize the things they believe would be most impactful. Tell them to ignore other departments' needs; this list is just for them.
- A single ordered list is fine here, because it's one group answering one question (e.g. "what would best increase sales, via win-rate or average transaction size"). Ordering becomes a forcing function for clarity.
- Sales ideas may come from the last lost deal (insight or noise), from critical causes of lost sales (bonus points if tied to specific lost deals; motivating for Engineering too), or from gut feel ("I know I could sell the piss out of X"). He says not to dismiss gut feel, since "multi-billion-dollar startups have been built atop experience-informed gut-instinct."
- Test whether a group has a consistent sense of impact by watching whether priorities swing dramatically quarter to quarter.
- Forcing prioritization creates empathy for the PM's job and stops everything being Priority #1. Later, when Sales complains "you still haven't made feature X," you can point out it was number seven on their own list. People can change their minds, so run the process several times a year.
- You are not promising to do everything in their order. You are promising to take the list seriously.
- Sales Engineering has a distinct, more technical view, closer to users than buyers.
- Support often knows the product best and has the best data on what causes confusion. Fewer support contacts means a happier, more loyal customer, not just lower support cost. He cites research that "needing Support less" correlates with loyalty (The Effortless Experience).
- Engineering needs its own list: refactors, library replacements, spikes, CI replacement, neglected test automation, systems outgrown by scale. These concern operational excellence, not growth, so they are easily never prioritized, which breeds resentment and grinds velocity to a halt. Engineers also have more ideas than time and must prioritize.
- No single list is correct. Like the blind men and the elephant, each has truth but not the full picture; the PM's job is to deduce the elephant. Keeping inputs separately ordered makes that easier.

chunks.heading: Add customer lists, split by persona, space or journey step
chunks.text:
- The customer is the star but is handled by PMs, designers and UX researchers rather than internal stakeholders.
- Simple products may need one customer list. Products with distinct functional areas or personas can have one list each, e.g. small versus large companies, or first-time users versus power users.
- Another option is one list per customer-journey step: trial users need quick success, paying customers need continuing value, and the highest-revenue power users need reasons to stay and grow. Priorities within each are not comparable across categories.
- Jason notes this resembles Story Mapping (Jeff Patton) and Opportunity Solution Trees, and argues Story Mapping is the same idea of independent lists, extended beyond customer topics to Sales, Support and Engineering.

chunks.heading: Alternative ways to split the lists
chunks.text:
- **Kano Model:** one list each for Delight, Performance and Must-be. Don't starve any. It's tempting to say Must-be goes first, but products shouldn't supply only basics; unexpectedly Delightful items are often why a customer stays despite failings. Separate lists, none fully starved, counter that.
- **Jyoti Bansal's "Four Lists"** (summarized by Adam Thornhill): customer engagement, sales intelligence, technical debt, and vision for the future.
- In all cases every list matters and none can be ignored forever. You can't move every needle at once, and items within a list are different in kind, so prioritize them separately.

chunks.heading: Cross the streams only at work-planning time (JIT selection)
chunks.text:
- When people actually do work you need a clear answer to "what's next?" without more meetings. So select work from the streams into an ordered backlog, at the last possible moment, hence "JIT" (Just In Time).
- Waiting to compare incomparable things keeps prioritization clear. It also lets you handle work-planning puzzles (deadlines, dependencies, capacity) separately, which is divide-and-conquer.
- You are picking from each team's top items, not from everyone's 1000 ideas. Picking from about 12 is far easier, and "on average all 12 are probably decent ideas."
- It's more explainable afterward. Example messages: Sales's first item is impossible now, but their second is also Support's number four and fits a multi-month journey project. Or: "We knocked out two of your top items recently; we've been starving the engineering list so we're going to hit a few of those in the next few months, then resurface."

chunks.heading: Metrics and side benefits of separate streams
chunks.text:
Jason says the structure keeps the PM honest and makes reporting easy:

- How much of each kind of work are we doing?
- What is the age of the top three items on each list (are we starving something)?
- How much of this sprint addresses someone's "top 3"?
- How much work is internal rather than customer-visible?

It also surfaces better ideas:

- Trends seen across every function that should inform strategy.
- New product ideas that hit several top-three items at once and so have outsized impact.

He adds that the more primary work-planning principle is to schedule rocks, then pebbles, then sand. Separate streams help identify which rocks and pebbles to consider scheduling at all.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jason Cohen extends Covey's jar analogy into a practical system. Rocks (3+ months) maximize strategic impact and need deliberate decisions. Pebbles (1-4 sprints) maximize ROI and are decided by the PM. Sand (up to 1 sprint) maximizes throughput with minimal process. He also gives a sprint-planning order and fixes for common failure modes.

chunks.heading: Rocks, Pebbles, Sand: three work types need three different prioritization mindsets
chunks.text:
- The geology-in-a-jar lesson (from Stephen Covey) says to schedule big things first or they never fit. Jason says the common misreading is that this is about *size* of work. He argues it is about *impact*: not letting easy or urgent things crowd out strategic things that take years to unfold but "are more important than everything else combined." "A thousand 'quick wins' do not create durable advantages or fulfill a long-term vision."
- A second mistake is stopping at "revenue growth first, then maintenance." Each type needs its own decision framework, goal, and traps. Ignoring this gives a team that commits lots of code and looks productive, but feels it isn't progressing fast enough, lets competitors catch up, and can't see how its work connects to strategy.
- He says doing this right takes no extra time: "smarter, not harder."

| | Rocks | Pebbles | Sand |
|---|---|---|---|
| Effort | 3+ months | 1-4 sprints | 1 sprint or less |
| Maximize | Impact | ROI | Throughput |
| Outlook | Long-term, strategic | Short-term, tactical | Immediate |
| How to decide | Deliberate | Analytical | Intuitive |
| Exec role | Decider | Observer | None |
| PM role | Driver | Decider | Decider (engage devs) |
| Beware | Insufficient impact | Over-estimating ROI | Over-thinking / over-planning |

chunks.heading: Rocks: maximize impact, not ROI, and set the bar higher than feels necessary
chunks.text:
- Rocks are nominally 3-6 months but realistically 3-12, because they are the most complex, have the most unknowns and dependencies. He cites Hofstadter's Law: "It always takes longer than you expect, even when you take Hofstadter's Law into account."
- A team might finish one Rock a year, certainly no more than three. "If you can do only one big thing this year, that thing had better be extraordinary."
- A Rock must deliver dramatic, measurable impact, not "incremental improvement." It must be strategic: attack your most important challenges, advance the company down its unique path, leverage existing advantages, and build new durable advantages others can't easily follow.
- Big projects over-run on time and often under-deliver on impact (occasionally they over-deliver by an order of magnitude or two, which is the usual after-the-fact story of a successful company). Because predictions are inaccurate, demand an enormous impact so that even an under-achieving Rock was still worth the time.
- Controversially: "Do *not* maximize ROI" on Rocks. A less impactful but quicker idea is the wrong choice. When things go worse than planned, "less impact" becomes "incremental impact," and you can't spend half a year on something trivial.
- Hofstadter's Law applies to the impact estimate too, so the bar must be higher than you think. "Over-shooting is the antidote to Hofstadter's Law."
- Don't just pick the best idea on a weak list. "Good" is the enemy of "Great." If no truly great idea exists, the real problem is a lack of one; solve that while the team does Pebbles and Sand and helps create and validate better ideas. If ideas aren't coming, also check whether the strategy is too vague.

chunks.heading: Rocks: decide deliberately, act as if it's a one-way door, and let PMs drive
chunks.text:
- Rocks commit so much of the team's life that the decision is strategic, not "agile." Pick the mountain deliberately; then be agile in how you climb it. "If you're climbing up the wrong mountain in the first place, being 'agile' doesn't help; the result is a team self-managing themselves into a mediocre, unfulfilling result."
- Aborting a failing project is smarter than sunk-cost plodding, but cancelling a months-long project is demoralizing and ruins trust. So treat a Rock as a one-way door (Bezos's framing).
- For the decision he recommends his Binstack framework, which makes impact the top priority, lets other dimensions participate without dominating, and produces a clear explanation.
- Execs ultimately own strategy and make the final call. In a healthy setup the PM is in command of the ideas and discussion, and the exec acts as coach and Devil's Advocate who signs off on a well-thought-out proposal.

chunks.heading: Pebbles: tactical wins that maximize ROI, and why ROI rubrics are fragile
chunks.text:
- Pebbles are not a "balance" between Rocks and Sand. They are tactical wins landing in the next few months, aimed at current challenges or a feature that can surprise customers sooner than expected. They take 1-4 sprints (multiple stories) and, unlike Sand, must have a measurable impact.
- They maximize ROI (value divided by effort): modest value in a short time or more value over more time are both fine. "What you cannot do is deliver little value but still take a long time."
- Impactful things tend to explode in effort. Anything over four sprints must be treated as a Rock. If a Pebble expands, either cut scope so it fits, or move it to Rocks. Either way you often find the impact is no longer big enough, meaning get more creative or drop the idea.
- Estimation error swamps ROI. His example: estimated impact 60, effort 4, ROI 15. Actual: 20% less impact (48) and 50% more time (6), giving ROI 8, "half the ROI than we originally thought." Many items' ROI fall within that error, so noise exceeds signal and a naive rubric is useless. He points to his ROI rubric framework to avoid this.
- PMs decide Pebbles. It's a judgment call synthesizing customer needs, competitors, strategy, company metrics and customer delight. One mind should make it: the one closest to customers, product, competitors and market. Not a drive-by manager decision, and not "a hostage negotiation with engineers who would rather rewrite a whole module from scratch." With self-management comes responsibility for results, so there should be a sensible justification and an objective measure of impact.

chunks.heading: Sand: maximize throughput and strip out administration
chunks.text:
- Sand items need no breakdown, take at most a sprint (sometimes under an hour), and "just need to be done." Examples: UI tweaks, corner-case unit tests, performance optimizations, small bug fixes (some customers never hit), small refactorings for tech debt, security patches, library upgrades, documentation tweaks. Even most edits to a piece of writing change a single sentence.
- Individually unmeasurable, together they make software feel "really well-done." Ignoring them means never reaching greatness even with the best strategy.
- Goal is throughput: how many are done per sprint. Don't try to measure or prioritize impact; it's too small. Fixing ten bugs in a sprint is a good accomplishment. (If a rare item has measurable impact, just do it.) High throughput is also energizing: "Do not discount the importance of the *feeling* of productivity and usefulness."
- Administrative overhead is the main enemy. Debating, writing user stories, filling JIRA fields, re-prioritizing across sprints and balancing assignments, multiplied by meeting attendees, can cost more than the work. "If you're using the same processes to prioritize and define Sand as to define Pebbles or Rocks, the process is wrong."
- His example: a JIRA ticket with Type, Priority, Estimate, Story, Linked Goal, Risks, Testing Considerations and Acceptance Criteria to upgrade the npm package `minimist` from 1.2.2 to 1.2.3. It could be a one-liner and takes minutes (change one line in `package.json`, rerun unit tests). Engineers usually already know what and why, so formalities are waste.

chunks.heading: Sand: prioritize by intuition and desire, and let the team schedule it
chunks.text:
- Complex prioritization systems produce nothing meaningful for Sand. Since delivered value per item is near zero and timing rarely matters, let people pick what they have energy for. That raises morale and quality, and "you get 'productivity for free,'" which lifts throughput.
- Teams should schedule their own Sand rather than debate it with executives. If management is constantly engaged in Sand scheduling, "it's always the manager's fault": either micromanaging, or having hired wrong or failed to build an environment where the team understands customer, market, technology and work.
- Small requests from around the company are normal, but if you're debating with spreadsheets and virtual sticky-note boards, it has gone too far.

chunks.heading: A simple sprint-planning order and how to handle common failure modes
chunks.text:
Schedule in this order, skipping a tier if capacity is insufficient to make significant progress or stories aren't ready:
1. Time-critical items regardless of size (security patches, bugs actively hurting customers, launch work with an immovable date).
2. One or more stories from the current Rock.
3. One or more stories from the current Pebble.
4. Sand.

Common problems:
- **Time-critical work eats everything:** the meta-problem (too little effective time) becomes the top priority, above the Rock, because no Rock will finish. Diagnose causes (individual productivity, too many owned things, architectural dependencies, domain needing more people, missing skills, not saying "no") and schedule sprint time to fix it.
- **Starving the Rock:** one story per sprint causes context switching and slow calendar time. The PM should address it; the team is likely falling for the Eisenhower Matrix fallacy of doing urgent over important. Maybe pause the Pebble.
- **More than one Pebble:** no time for two at once, and context switching hurts morale and productivity. Exception: a Pebble nearly done or blocked for at least a week.
- **Always Rock, never Pebble:** may be fine if the Rock is valuable enough; call it "the theme of the next four months." After a first complete version, do Pebbles with incremental Rock updates instead of starting another Rock right away.
- **Zero Sand:** leads to a poor product and unhappy engineers. Tone down other stories, pause the Rock or Pebble for a sprint, or run a Sand-only sprint, which is fun and gets a lot done.
- **Starting a new Rock or Pebble too soon:** after shipping, you still need field learning, deferred small items, and follow-on functionality, so keep the Rock or Pebble around longer. This is another reason estimates are subject to Hofstadter's Law.
- **Trying to balance every sprint:** unnecessary. Balance over several months matters; intentionally imbalanced sprints give more focus and less context switching.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jason Cohen argues that weighted rubrics fail for multi-dimensional decisions because scores are imprecise, incomparable and tie easily. His Binstack method replaces scores with binary "material or not" judgments against a stack-ranked list of attributes, producing a clear winner and an easy-to-explain decision.

chunks.heading: Binstack: picking the single most impactful option
chunks.text:
- Jason's technique for "multi-dimensional maximization": choosing one best option when each is better on a different, incomparable dimension.
- Examples he gives: which major feature to build in the next six months, which candidate to hire, which marketing campaign to test.
- Goal: pick the best option, and be able to explain the decision to people who wanted a different outcome. He says not to undervalue "crisp explanation."
- Binstack asks whether an option has a material effect on each attribute (yes or no), then stack-ranks the attributes by importance. It is meant to maximize impact, not ROI or efficiency.
- Jason says to use a separate ROI rubric if you want to maximize impact per unit of effort.

chunks.heading: Why weighted rubrics fail
chunks.text:
- Adding up scores often produces ties. His example: Player P (Health 8, Strength 5, Speed 2, Endurance 5) and Player Q (5, 7, 6, 2) both total 20.
- Adding weights doesn't fix it. Weighting Strength 2.0 and Speed 0.5 gives 24 vs 24. Even weights rigged to favor Q give only 20.5 vs 17.5, which is not a decision anyone can feel confident about.
- Real-world scores are imprecise guesses, such as "potential new revenue" or a 1-to-5 scale. Multiplying by weights compounds the error, so "differences in the final results are more error than signal."
- Attributes aren't comparable. Adding them implies they are. Saying the weights out loud exposes it: "Every $150k of additional ARR is exactly as valuable to us as 10% more customer satisfaction... Really?"
- A tie broken arbitrarily can't be explained to anyone.
- His general rule: complex decisions are hard because we've avoided making smaller decisions first.

chunks.heading: Step 1: Binary materiality
chunks.text:
- Drop values, weights and scores. An option either materially affects an attribute or it doesn't. "Materially" means the effect is large enough to measure easily.
- Examples of material thresholds he gives:
  - Revenue: at least a 10% bump so the curve visibly changes.
  - Retention: a 20% decrease in cancellations tied to a specific cause.
  - Usability: a 40% decrease in support tickets on a topic, or a 50% increase in interface success rate.
  - Profitability: gross profit margin improves by 1%.
