  - Word-of-mouth growth beats marketing-driven growth on cost per customer and because it scales automatically with the company, so work on building it into the product rather than leaving growth to marketing.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Using a pilot's lesson (stuck fuel gauges, checked with a wooden stick), Jason argues that important business metrics must be derived two different ways, because some data is always lying. Redundancy catches errors and also gives a fuller picture of what is driving the numbers.

chunks.heading: Redundant instruments: "Who's lying?"
chunks.text:
- Jason takes the pilot's rule "Who's lying?" and applies it to business metrics: some instrument is always wrong, so important numbers need independent cross-checks.
- Origin story: on a long flight with a pilot friend, Gerry, both fuel gauges still read "full" after four hours. The needles stick to the glass.
- Gerry had "stuck" the tanks before takeoff, meaning he dipped a wooden dowl into the tank through the top of the wing to judge fuel by the wet line. Jason's takeaway: "Sometimes the simplest technology is best. Wooden sticks don't run out of batteries."
- Usually your instruments are right. The danger is not knowing when one is wrong, like running out of gas without realizing it.

chunks.heading: Redundancy must be different in kind, not just doubled
chunks.text:
- Having "two of everything" is not enough. Two gauges that both depend on electricity both fail when the power goes out, and that was exactly the case with the two fuel gauges.
- The second source must be implemented differently, using a different source of energy or method. Example: a stick versus a gauge.
- Aviation example: a magnetic ball compass floating in liquid works without power but bounces with vibration. A second compass runs on suction (air pressure differential), which stays stable in turbulence. Each covers the other's failure mode.
- Gerry's check: ask "Who's lying?", and cross-check suction-based dials against electric ones.
- Jason cites "Trust, but verify" as the principle.

chunks.heading: How metrics silently go wrong
chunks.text:
Jason lists failures he has seen in real companies:
- A spreadsheet with a subtle formula bug.
- Analytics JavaScript accidentally left off one page.
- A survey email not sent to every customer in the cohort.
- A database query that did or did not filter something important.
- A nightly update script that had not run for three months.

chunks.heading: Cross-check the same number two ways
chunks.text:
Jason's method is to derive the same figure from two different systems:
- **Revenue:** billing system versus cash flows in bank statements. He once discovered his credit card processor was delaying cash receipts.
- **Active customers:** Stripe versus the user portal, because sometimes a cancellation in one system fails to cancel in the other.
- **Web traffic:** Google Analytics plus another analytics tool, or your raw web server logs. Five analytics tools will give five different numbers. This could be differing definitions of "visit" and "session," but he asks: "is that truly all it is?"

chunks.heading: Redundancy also improves understanding
chunks.text:
- Beyond catching bad data, computing the same thing twice gives a better grasp of the forces behind it, and so better analysis of how the company operates and how the market is changing.
- Web traffic example sources: analytics on where traffic originates (imperfect, especially as browsers and extensions block or obscure data), ad click-through data, your own raw server logs, and industry-wide data such as Google Trends on search volume for your keywords.
- Each tells a different story, none has the full picture, and all are biased. Together the picture is more complete, and biases can cancel through averaging or by heeding only the clearest, most consistent trends.
- His rule of thumb: "If four different sources agree that a trend is happening, then it's definitely happening."

chunks.heading: When to double-check a metric
chunks.text:
- Criterion: if a metric is important enough to watch every day, and to act on when it deviates from expectation, it is important enough to be double-checked.
- Reasons: accuracy and completeness of comprehension.
- His closing warning: if your dashboard isn't redundant, you will never know "who's lying."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jason Cohen argues that breakout startups don't fix their many weaknesses. They deliver one thing so compelling that customers tolerate everything else. Using the iPhone, Heroku and Basecamp as examples, he says founders should pick the one thing they can obsess over for years and let other fires burn.

chunks.heading: The Important Thing: one overwhelming strength overrides every deficiency
chunks.text:
- Jason argues startups win despite crushing disadvantages: "No brand, no features, no customers, no money, no distribution, no search engine rankings, no efficient advertising, no incredible executive team, no NPS, no strategy."
- They do not win by solving all those problems, or solving them quickly. He gives two answers:
  - Pick battles where the startup has advantages over incumbents.
  - Get one thing to go really, really right, enough to overcome the torrent of things going wrong.
- He calls this universal pattern **The Important Thing**: break-out products deliver something so fantastic, game-changing and important to the customer that it overrides the deficiencies of the rest of the product and company.

chunks.heading: What The Important Thing buys a startup
chunks.text:
When the one thing is compelling enough, it neutralizes the usual startup weaknesses:
- **No marketing:** people tell their friends or force colleagues to use it.
- **No operational excellence:** they use it even if support is slow and releases have bugs.
- **No brand:** they are excited to support a promising new company instead of worried about depending on a wobbly one.
- Net effect: despite lacking brand, service, features, stability, integrations and social proof, the startup can still beat the incumbent.

chunks.heading: Case study: the first iPhone
chunks.text:
- The first iPhone launched with a mountain of issues. As a phone it was worse than a cheap Nokia flip-phone, which everyone agreed was "ten times better at being, you know, a *phone*."
- It had no copy/paste in its operating system.
- Its Important Thing: you could use the real Internet, with full websites. The web worked (even if slowly), and email worked, in your pocket.
- That was compelling enough that all the other problems didn't matter.

chunks.heading: Case study: Heroku
chunks.text:
- Early Heroku was full of deal-breakers developers complained about, and the complaints were valid:
  - Forced use of Bundler, which was broken half the time.
  - No changing the filesystem at run-time, forcing algorithm changes.
  - No MySQL support, so queries could break.
  - Slow websites.
- Its Important Thing: type `git push production` and the site goes live. A knob on a web page sets how scalable the site is (also connected to your wallet). You never see a server, think about backups, or worry about stashing API keys, and you always get a staging area to test in a real server environment.
- DevOps became a thing of the past for a large class of applications.
- The evidence of its power: developers changed their workflows and code around Heroku and "12-Factor" apps; Heroku did not change to suit developers.
- It has been the dominant way Ruby on Rails developers launch public applications for more than ten years.

chunks.heading: The Important Thing isn't always a feature
chunks.text:
- Jason's examples of non-feature Important Things:
  - **Reputation and values:** Fogbugz was never the leading bug tracker, but he used it for most of the 2000s because he was a fan of Joel Spolsky's blog. Using a product from a company whose values and behavior he respected and learned from felt good. The same happened with Basecamp and the 37signals blog.
  - A **lifestyle** the product enables, such as remote-work or with-kids-work.
  - **Solving a problem in an industry others overlook:** "any solution, even with problems" beats no solution.
  - **Culture that resonates with an audience,** for example an informal voice in an otherwise formal market.
  - **A cause or higher purpose,** so customers are supporting a movement rather than just buying a shirt or software. His example is Patagonia: a company policy to bail employees out of jail if arrested for peaceful protest, and only 4% annual employee turnover.
- Feature example: disappearing messages with Snapchat.
- On Basecamp, he rejects the idea that 37signals' work-style explains success. Their many later products used the same work-style, people and even code base, yet were dramatically less successful and have all been discontinued. The company was renamed "Basecamp" to emphasize that only the first experiment worked. (Editor's note, 2024: they now seem successful with hey.com.)

chunks.heading: How to apply it to your own business
chunks.text:
- It is easy to be overwhelmed by your many inadequacies. Attacking all of them at once, "with no weapons," leads to burn-out and a company that is excellent on no front.
- "You don't need to solve all those problems. You need to solve almost none of them."
- Focus on the one thing (maybe two) that is your Important Thing: the thing where, if you are extraordinarily good at it, customers overlook everything else.
- Pick something that meets three tests:
  - You *want* to obsess over it for the next five to ten years.
  - It gets your customers excited.
  - You have at least a possibility of executing it.
- Then do that, maybe only that. Let the other fires burn.
- If you become excellent at it, the other disadvantages still exist but are not fatal. In his words, that is all you can hope for at the beginning, "And all you need."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Startups need many things to go right at once, and multiplying those probabilities makes success unlikely. Jason Cohen argues you can improve your odds by reducing the number of "and" dependencies and building in many parallel "or" paths, because optionality is strength.

chunks.heading: Why startups need luck, and why "and" kills the odds
chunks.text:
Jason argues that luck always plays a role in startups, because success requires many things to go right at once. His list includes:
- A marketing channel that works.
- The right mix of features and usability to trigger product/market fit.
- Employee number one working out.
- A competitor not making a fatal move.
- Enough money in the market.
- Appropriate pricing.
- Market forces not shifting the rules of the game.

He notes this comes on top of the luck of where and when you were born. His conclusion: it is obvious why startups fail so often, because they need a lot of success in a lot of areas.

He opens with a story. As a kid he won a fake stock market competition in elementary school by putting all his money in a few penny stocks. Prices moved in multiples of 1/8, so small moves were large percentage swings. Some days he had the worst portfolio, some days the best, and the contest happened to end on an up-day. That was "high risk, high reward."

chunks.heading: The math of "and": probabilities multiply
chunks.text:
Jason's core point: a list of requirements joined by "and" is bad, because each has a probability of success and the total is their product.

- "No matter how optimistic you are about those probabilities, the end product is a small number."
- 70% multiplied by itself six times is only 12%.
- Most of the things on the startup list are below 70%, and more than six have to go right.

He states it plainly: **"'And' is bad!"** Needing a good channel and killer features and great early employees and a healthy market means stacking multiplied odds against yourself.

chunks.heading: First technique: make explicit choices that raise each probability
chunks.text:
Before using "or," Jason says you can raise the odds of individual "and" items by choosing deliberately:
- Pick a large, growing, healthy market so the risk of "no one wants to solve this problem" goes to zero.
- Compete in a niche where incumbents don't care or can't move quickly.
- Hire someone you've worked with before, or build something sustainable without hiring.
- Generate Love rather than only Utility or Coercion, to overcome your deficiencies.

He points to a separate long list of common blunders and how to mitigate them. Even so, he says there will be plenty of challenges, which is why a second technique is needed.

chunks.heading: Second technique: leverage "or" instead of "and"
chunks.text:
Jason's rule: **leverage "or" instead of "and."** When only one of several options has to work, the combined odds rise even if each option is unlikely.

Marketing channels are his example. Your first few hundred customers could come from any of these:
- Google Ads
- Facebook ads
- Affiliate sales
- Targeted outbound sales
- SEO
- Guesting on podcasts and newsletters
- Partnering with a high-profile reseller
- Great press about your unique brand and message

"Only one of these needs to work! So although the probability of success for each one of these is low, the probability that *something* will work is higher."

He says the same logic applies to product features, website copy for conversions, and the avenues for exiting the company years later.

chunks.heading: Optionality is strength
chunks.text:
Jason's general rule: **"optionality is strength."** When there are lots of ways for things to go right, that is a strong position even if you haven't actualized any of them yet.

Practical reading of the idea:
- Structure the plan so success can come from many independent sources.
- Don't bet the company on one channel, one feature set, or one exit path.
- Each added "or" is another way for luck to land in your favor.

His closing line: "Set yourself up for luck!"

chunks.heading: Why marketplaces are the cautionary example
chunks.text:
Jason uses marketplaces as the converse: businesses with extra "and" clauses, even more than usual. He says they almost never succeed. When they do, they are often durable and profitable, which makes them a smart bet for a venture capitalist with a diversified portfolio of attempts. For the individual business, he says it is a tough road.

The "and" chain for a marketplace:
- It must thrive with sellers and buyers.
- It can't be too expensive to build up both sides.
- Both sides must realize value.
- It must not be easier, cheaper, or preferable to transact outside the marketplace.
- Many only deliver value at scale, so they must also "scale down," so the first 100 buyers and sellers also see value.

His takeaway: accumulating "and" requirements lowers the probability of success, while stringing together possible solutions with "or" increases the number of ways luck can smile on you.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: A technical essay on a hybrid logical clock with skew correction that orders events across independent replicas without central coordination or vector clocks. The takeaways for builders are about design constraints: bound the error, keep memory constant, avoid central points, and favor simplicity.

chunks.heading: A hybrid logical clock for decentralized event ordering
chunks.text:
Jason (writing on his long-form site, 2019) presents "Distributed Logical Time" (LT). It is a decentralized, constant-memory way for independent replicas to timestamp events so that anything that happened before something else is always ordered correctly. It needs no master server, no leader and no join or leave announcements. He frames it as an alternative to two options most teams can't use:
- Custom infrastructure such as Google TrueTime, which is unavailable in browsers, laptops and non-Google data centers.
- Vector clocks, which have unbounded memory and leave "conflicts" that are resolved arbitrarily or not at all.

His closing point: "Simplicity is a core requirement for scalability and truly bug-free code."

chunks.heading: Requirements Jason sets for the clock
chunks.text:
He defines RT (omniscient real time), PT (the OS clock, the only time a replica can read) and LT (the synthetic clock). The requirements:
- **PT is arbitrary.** It can move backwards, repeat values, update rarely, be unsynchronized between replicas and be off from RT by any variable amount. It only generally increases over the long run.
- **LT always increases** on every request, regardless of PT.
- **Bounded error window `e`.** If two events on different replicas are more than `e` apart in real time (`e` being 1-2 seconds, a small constant), LT orders them correctly. Inside `e`, order is best-effort.
- **`e` must be a constant**, not proportional to any state or configuration.
- **Happened-before is always preserved.** If A happens, the replicas communicate, then B happens, `LT{B>A}` always holds, even inside `e`.
- **A skewed clock must not skew the collective.** A fast replica shouldn't automatically "win", and a slow one shouldn't be unable to write.
- **Constant memory:** a fixed number of bits, unlike vector clocks.
- **Fully decentralized:** no leaders, no peer list, any communication pattern.

chunks.heading: Single-replica algorithm
Preserving happened-before across replicas
chunks.text:
If replica P sends event A to Q and Q then creates B, Q must produce a strictly larger LT. That is automatic when Q's PT is ahead of P's. If P's PT is ahead (his example: one minute), Q's LT would be far behind and `LT{A>B}` despite `RT{A<B}`.

The fix: every message carries the sender's LT. The receiver takes the larger of its own and the peer's, then increments the counter:

```go
func UpdateLTFromPeer( LT_Peer ) {
	LT_Local = GetLT()
	if LT_Peer > LT_Local { LT_Local = LT_Peer }
	Counter = Counter + 1
	SaveState(LT_Local)
}
```

- Q's `PT_LastSeen` may now sit ahead of its own PT. That's fine; it uses its counter until its own PT catches up.
- Jason notes this is the Hybrid Logical Clock (HLC) from a 2014 University at Buffalo paper, which contains the correctness proof.

chunks.heading: Skew correction: making `e` small and bounded
chunks.text:
HLC alone breaks the bounded-`e` requirement. In his example, Q's PT is a minute behind P's. Q must keep using its counter while P keeps advancing via PT, so every event on P in that minute outranks every event on Q, regardless of real order. The error window equals the clock skew (a minute, or an hour) and persists even after Q syncs.

One answer is to mandate small skew, for example with NTP (tens of milliseconds). Jason rejects it as the sole fix because browsers, laptops and VMs aren't under your control.

His algorithm extension:
- When P sends its LT, Q computes `s = PT{P - Q}` as the skew.
- If `s` is positive, Q stores it and uses `PT + s` as its physical time from then on.
- If `s` is negative, Q ignores it, so clocks that are already ahead don't get further ahead.
- `s` always under-estimates true skew by the one-way transmission delay `d`. With real skew 60 and `d`=1, the computed skew is 59.
- `d` is bounded by network time (about 1ms in a data center, 100ms across a country, 1000ms across the world), not by skew or system state. So `e` is on the order of `d`, which meets the "small constant" goal.
- If all clocks are well synchronized (NTP, or GPS-synced phones), the computed skew is negative and `s` stays 0. Skew correction vanishes when it isn't needed.
- A replica that is very early develops a large forward skew. A replica that is very late pulls the other replicas' skews to align with it.
- To stop skews from creeping upward as replicas keep nudging each other, his implementation adds another 500ms to the effective `d`.

chunks.heading: Simulations from his Golang implementation
chunks.text:
- **Staggered PT:** replicas start 10 seconds apart and one-way-sync a random pair each second. LT increases monotonically and all converge on the replica with the latest LT.
- **Variable-rate PT:** clocks run at different speeds relative to RT. All replicas converge close to the one with the fastest clock.
- **Far-future replica joins, then leaves:** the others converge on the far-future LT. After it leaves, their skews stay put and do not creep up.

chunks.heading: Known problem: start-up
chunks.text:
A freshly started replica probably needs skew correction and should fix its LT before using it for anything meaningful.
- Best fix: talk to any live replica, which sets an appropriate skew.
- Alternative: persist LT state, including the skew, between runs. This is weaker because PT behavior or the group's skew may have changed.
- Skipping both is still legal and consistent, but its events will look older than they really are relative to other replicas' events at the same real time.

chunks.heading: Anti-objectives and trade-offs
chunks.text:
- **Uniqueness is not provided.** LT is unique per replica but not globally. Collisions are realistic when PT updates coarsely and `d` is tiny. His example: PT refreshed once per second and `d`=0.001, so two synchronized replicas that generate an LT in the same real-time second can collide.
  - Fix: append least-significant bits that are a unique replica ID, or enough random bits. This also lets LT serve as an event name in logs or databases.
- **Keeping PT close to RT is not required.** Disabling skew correction keeps PT provably close to RT (per the HLC paper), but you get a large `e` and mis-ordered events. To keep both, use NTP or a similar service alongside the algorithm.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jason argues decisions should default to fast, because speed accelerates action and learning. He lists the conditions that justify slowing down: irreversibility, huge effort, unfamiliar decision types, unmeasurable progress and imperfect information. He frames these as honest questions, not a scorecard.

chunks.heading: Default to fast, and slow down only when specific signals say so
chunks.text:
- Jason's premise: startups should usually decide quickly, because fast decisions speed up action, which speeds the loop of production and feedback. That is how you "outpace and out-learn a competitor, even one that already has a lead."
- Some decisions deserve slow, contemplative, data-driven treatment: a key executive hire, pricing strategy, whether to raise money, whether to invest millions in a new product line, whether to enter a new market.
- He frames it as a set of questions rather than a rubric: "important decisions aren't a Cosmo Quiz." Don't score items 1-5 and add them in a spreadsheet. Answer honestly, and the quick, light-touch decision stays the default unless several signals point the other way.

chunks.heading: Signals that you'll decide better later, or can't take it back
chunks.text:
- **You'll make a much smarter decision later.** "Today we know the least that we're ever going to know." Waiting doesn't always add information, but sometimes it does. Before launch you can't judge which features come next; launch and learn from customers. Don't even think hard about it now, and make no firm decision, when you know a better one is coming.
- **Can't undo.** This is the one-way versus two-way door distinction. If a decision can't easily be reversed, invest more effort in analyzing the upsides and risks.
- **Can't measure incremental success.** If you can objectively see whether things are going well after implementation starts, course-correcting (or reversing) is easy. If progress will be invisible or subjective, you could sink person-years before knowing, so build confidence in the path up front.

chunks.heading: Signals about effort, urgency and cost of deliberating
chunks.text:
- **Huge effort.** Some things take less time to implement than to estimate or debate (his "Sand" category). Two engineers for a week might be cheaper than a team debating for a week. This is why small teams without process can out-produce larger teams with process. If implementing costs less than deciding, "just knock it out." If you're picking a path that takes six months to yield results, research up front is worth it.
- **No compelling event.** If the status quo isn't bad, there may be no reason to decide quickly, or at all, so more deliberation is justified. With time pressure, the opposite holds: every extra day deciding is a day less for implementation and surprises, so dragging it out adds risk.

chunks.heading: Signals about your team's experience and information
chunks.text:
- **Not accustomed to this kind of decision.** Online marketing teams throw creative things at the wall daily, so they don't agonize over trying a campaign on a new social platform or which headlines to test. Most organizations have never made decisions like a pricing change or an acquisition, and most founders don't know how to hire a great executive. They also don't know when to shift from "just throwing something out there and iterating" (right at the start of a company) to a deliberate multimillion-dollar product bet. First-time decisions are riskier, so add research, data, debate or outside advice.
- **Don't know how to evaluate the options.** If strategy is clear and detailed, relevant data is at hand, goals are clear and the team is confident, the decision can be fast. If not, deliberate to clarify those things. Tools he points to: Fermi Estimation to simplify evaluation, and Binstack to find the best option among many.
- **Imperfect information.** Buying a house is nerve-racking because it's expensive, hard to undo, and you know little about the goods (what the seller isn't telling you, what you'll discover a year later). When more information is obtainable, buy it, such as reports or experts, as with a house. When objective data is impossible to get, the opposite applies: don't burn time debating subjective points. Decide from experience and gut, since that's all you have, and "experts are often wrong."

chunks.heading: Cross-team decisions and what to do with the answers
chunks.text:
- **Multiple teams that haven't worked together.** At WP Engine, Jason notes, the company is extremely collaborative across support, sales, marketing, engineering, product and finance, which avoids solving one department's goals at another's expense. But it makes decisions harder, because good solutions need compromise and creativity, and that takes time. If the teams or members lack rapport, common language and shared experience, give the decision more time. You're really giving people time to build relationships and find good solutions, which is a long-term investment in organizational intelligence.
- **Use problem signals to guide next steps.**
  - If "Can't undo" is the problem, rethink the decision so it can be undone: apply it to one segment only, invest more in planning, create a disaster recovery plan, or split the decision so part of it is undoable.
  - If "No compelling event" is the problem, the best answer may be to "not decide." Some people will be disappointed, but it's better to honestly say "we can't figure out the answer right now" than to make a rash decision that does more harm than good, or to spend time on a decision that doesn't need making at the expense of work that does.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jason Cohen argues that pricing is driven by positioning and perceived value, not cost analysis. Using a hypothetical AdWords tool, he shows that a "generate growth" pitch is worth a multiple of a "save money" pitch, both in value created and in the share of it customers will pay. Frame your product in the way your customer already measures value.

chunks.heading: Pricing on growth value, not savings: the 8x repositioning
chunks.text: Jason argues that pricing is "much more about positioning and perceived value than it is about cost-analysis and unconvincing ROI calculators." The same product can command a much higher price depending on how its value is framed. His worked example is a fictional tool, DoubleDown, that doubles the cost-efficiency of AdWords campaigns, so a marketer gets the same conversions and lead quality for half the ad spend. Repositioning it from "saves money" to "creates growth" lets him raise the price eightfold.

chunks.heading: The "saves money" pitch caps your price at a fraction of the savings
chunks.text:
- Jason's baseline: a customer spends $40,000/mo on AdWords. DoubleDown halves that, saving $20,000/mo.
- The customer cannot be charged more than the savings, so he assumes a vendor can charge about 25% of the savings and still find many willing customers. That is $5,000/mo.
- The customer keeps 75% of the value ($15,000/mo) and the VP of Demand Gen can boast to the CMO about it.
- His footnote on the 25% figure: there is data supporting it. Charge less and you are not monetizing enough. Charge much more and you leave too much space for a competitor.

chunks.heading: Why growth is worth more than cost reduction
chunks.text:
- Marketers' paramount goal is growth. Even brand, events and PR support growth indirectly.
- "Increasing growth is much more valuable than decreasing cost." He says it is "always 10x more valuable for a business to grow faster than it is for the business to save money."
- The contrast he uses, a CMO reporting to the CEO:
  - "I reduced costs 20% this year": the CEO is happy, then asks how to use the savings to grow faster.
  - "I increased growth 20%, but it also cost 20% more": the CEO is thrilled. Company value rises non-linearly, the extra revenue more than pays for the extra marketing cost, and the follow-up question is "Can we spend even more?"

chunks.heading: The repositioned pitch: spend more, get more at the same unit cost
chunks.text:
- Same customer: $40,000/mo yields 200 quality leads, so $200/lead.
- New pitch: use DoubleDown to double leads to 400, still at $200/lead, for $80,000/mo total.
- The customer already accepts $200/lead, so it doesn't matter how the $80,000 splits between AdWords and DoubleDown. The goal is not "save money on AdWords" but "generate more growth at a similar unit cost."
- Value created becomes $40,000 instead of $20,000, and the customer is willing to hand a vendor 100% of it rather than 25%. Both numbers move up, which is how the price goes from $5,000/mo to $40,000/mo (8x).

chunks.heading: The rule: sell the value in the customer's own metric
chunks.text:
- Both the amount of value created and the share the customer will pay are "a multiple higher" for the growth pitch than for the savings pitch.
- His instruction: when you want to describe your product as a way to "save time" or "save money" or "be more efficient", don't.
- Instead, work out how the product creates value in the way the customer already measures value, and position the product as a way to accomplish that.
- Check for the equivalent in any market: identify the metric the buyer is judged on (for a marketer, growth and lead volume at an acceptable cost per lead), then frame the product as producing more of it.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jason Cohen argues the MVP is a selfish process that hands customers unfinished, embarrassing products. He proposes SLC (Simple, Lovable, Complete) as the first version: small enough to ship fast, loved enough to win customers, and complete enough to stand alone. Delight can be prioritized over utility from day one.

chunks.heading: Simple, Lovable, Complete (SLC) beats the MVP as a first version
chunks.text:
Jason argues that the MVP ("Minimum Viable Product") is a selfish process: it treats customers as test subjects so the team can "learn". His alternative for the first version is SLC: Simple, Lovable, Complete, pronounced "Slick". He coined it years ago and uses it at WP Engine ("We don't build MVPs at WP Engine").

- He agrees with the MVP's motivation: build something small so it is quick and cheap to test, get it to real customers fast because real learning only happens with a real product, then trash, hard-pivot or invest.
- His objection: "Customers hate MVPs." Nobody wants an unfinished product its creators are embarrassed by (he cites Reid Hoffman's "launch early enough that you're embarrassed by your v1.0"). Customers want great products they can use now.
- His summary: MVPs are "too M and rarely V". What is bad for customers is ultimately bad for the company.
- The test question: "What's the 'Slick' version of your idea?"

chunks.heading: The three SLC ingredients
chunks.text:
- **Simple:** complex things can't be built quickly, and you must ship quickly to learn quickly before you run out of money and willpower. Customers forgive a simple product as long as it never claimed to do more than it does. Early Google Docs had about 3% of Word's features but did its core job (simplicity and real-time collaboration) well.
- **Lovable:** crappy products are insulting, and you didn't start the company to make crappy products. Love overpowers the fact that the product is buggy and feature-poor. Products that do less but are loved beat products with more features that are disliked. The "Darwinian success loop" of a product is a function of love, not features.
- **Complete:** products exist to accomplish a job. The customer should want to use it as-is, as "version 1.0 of something simple", not "version 0.1 of something complex" or broken. Simple is good; incomplete is not.

chunks.heading: Simple and complete is possible: examples
chunks.text:
- First versions of WhatsApp, Snapchat, Stripe, Twilio, Twitter and Slack were small but complete.
- Some later grew complex (Snapchat, Stripe, Slack); some kept simplicity as a permanent value (Twitter, WhatsApp).
- Virgin Air and Southwest Airlines each started with one route. Southwest is the most profitable US airline in history.
- Snapchat v1: a screen where tapping anywhere took a photo you sent to someone, and it disappeared. No video, filters, social network, comments or storage. The "no storage" insight was critical, and the simple interface plausibly was too. Video, filters, stories and camera sunglasses came later.
- WhatsApp started with only a status message ("What's up?"). Chat was added after people were found abusing it to avoid SMS fees.
- Dropbox started with one folder that would eventually sync across devices.
- Twitter had only 140-character messages. Replies and retweets were invented by users by convention, then folded into the product.
- Starting SLC does not preclude becoming complex later.

chunks.heading: Many ways to generate love (it is not only UX)
chunks.text:
- Design: elegant UX and delightful UI (the current-in-vogue way).
- Company attitude and culture: Buffer's blog with open salaries and corporate metrics; MeetEdgar's blog genuinely helping entrepreneurs; HubSpot's blog, which early on was at least as instrumental to customers' success as the product.
- Connection to the customer's psyche: Heroku filled its homepage with command-line examples instead of benefit statements, instantly connecting with its geeky target customer.
- He points to his "WTP" (willingness to pay) essay for many more forms of love. His advice: "Pick some." "Minimum" and "viable" are definitely not among the ways.

chunks.heading: Life after SLC: better options than an MVP
chunks.text:
- An SLC needs no ongoing development to create value. "An MVP that never gets additional investment is just a bad product. A SLC that never gets additional investment is a good, if modest product."
- If it succeeds, you have already delivered value and have several futures, none urgent. You can build a v2 with more time to decide, and ask existing happy customers what v2 should be rather than alpha-testers who just want a broken thing fixed.
- Or you can leave it alone: "Not every product has to become complex. Not every product needs new major versions every two quarters."
- SLC can still fail, as can an MVP, because either is an experiment.

chunks.heading: Why Maslow's hierarchy is the wrong model for product
chunks.text:
- Jason says Maslow's hierarchy has weak empirical support (no evidence at original publication in 1943; a 1976 review found little for the ranking or a definite hierarchy) and is wrong for product too, though teams act as if it were true.
- His product pyramid, bottom to top: Useful (solves a problem), Reliable (always works as promised), Easy to use (effortless; makes tech support obsolete), Delightful (exceptionally wonderful, eliciting strong positive emotion, likely surprising), Meaningful (identity, belonging, higher purpose, impact, legacy).
- A classic MVP follows Maslow: minimally useful, ignoring every other level until Useful is satisfied.
- Mature enterprise software maximizes the bottom layers, because the buyer isn't the user.
- SLC instead leads with Delight to win hearts even though the product is less useful and reliable than it will become, then rewards already-happy customers with features. Differentiation comes from more than feature bullet points.
- Another framing: SLC is Delightful and Useful on day one, but the scope of "Useful" is narrow enough to be Complete.
- "Products that prioritize delight win over products that don't." It is a decision to prioritize Delight over Utility, since utility is what the customer's budget is allocated to and delight needs insight and great design.

chunks.heading: Meaning as the top of the pyramid
chunks.text:
- Starting with delight can reach Meaning: products people tie their identity to. His examples: Linear honoring the developer rather than the project manager; Basecamp and the culture of 37signals; Moleskine and the romantic ideal of the brooding writer; Patagonia as an environmental badge; Vim vs Emacs as a badge of geekery.
- He says almost no company tries to create meaning for customers, and the proof is that they track no metric for it: "out of sight, out of mind."
- You can build large, even great, companies without it (most do), but if you care about it, SLC is the right way to start.
- SLC is "another way of prioritizing the customer: the human being, not just their 'job to be done.'"

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jason Cohen argues that everyone wants change but nobody wants to change, yet the right choice is almost always to change because it reflects new facts or a shifting environment. Leaders must recognize that change is exhausting, watch for burnout, and manage it with kindness while still holding organizations accountable for striving to improve.

chunks.heading: Change is usually the right call, but it's costly and needs kindness
chunks.text:
Jason argues that nearly everyone wants things to improve, yet almost no one wants to change. Customers demand a better UX but complain when it changes. Team members want consistency but resist policies. Developers want efficiency but don't want to change how they work. Strategy fails if it's constantly in flux, but a strategy that ignores new information is wrong.

- "The right choice is almost always 'change.'" Change is a reaction to new facts, getting smarter, or a shift in the environment.
- He says death awaits any organization that picks the comfort of the familiar over the discomfort of change.
- His summary of top workplace complaints: (1) the way things are; (2) change.

chunks.heading: Change is exhausting, so leaders must watch for burnout
chunks.text:
Even people who love change, who brag that "it's hard but every day is different," hit a breaking point after years of adaptation. Jason notes that constant learning is simply tiring.

- Even the most stoic, change-loving people sometimes need a break from change. His analogy: "it's a marathon" but sometimes you need to walk a mile to catch your breath.
- Leaders should look for signs of burnout or decision fatigue and address them proactively.
- This matters for everyone in a startup, not only managers, because constant change can feel like management has no plan and no strategy.
- It takes careful consideration to tell a rudderless company from a culture of self-reflection and improvement.

chunks.heading: Not all change is an improvement, and it's harder to verify than code
chunks.text:
Sometimes an attempt to fix a problem makes it worse, such as when making code faster breaks it.

- Code has safety nets: slow code is objectively visible in a profiler, changes can be wrapped in unit tests and code reviews, you can iterate before shipping, and in the worst case revert to the previous version.
- Those safety nets don't exist when the change is happening to a whole team, a major product release, or a cross-departmental strategic initiative.
- Sometimes it's objectively impossible to know ahead of time whether a change is right, and you have no choice but to place a bet.

chunks.heading: Deciding what to change is hard, and success creates two opposite traps
chunks.text:
Jason describes two ways successful companies stall out:

- **Forgetting why they won.** They lose sight of the fundamental reasons for their success: the key insights and UX of the product, or the key culture and values that attracted their first hundred or thousand employees.
- **Dogmatism.** They cling to their strategy or "non-consensus but correct" ideas, so when the world changes around them, or scale breaks their previously correct notions, they fail to adapt.

His conclusion: it is not generally true that "what got us here will get us there," which means deep change is required.

chunks.heading: The mindset for handling it: be kind
chunks.text:
Jason's prescription is a single word: "Be kind."

- Don't judge too harshly when your organization tries to improve one thing and breaks another, or takes too long to implement a change.
- Don't judge too harshly when a teammate needs to work on something easy for a few sprints or take a vacation.
- His example: Edison tried thousands of materials before finding the one that made lightbulbs practical. Would you have judged him for "thrashing?" He says invention is often frustrating.

chunks.heading: When to judge harshly instead
chunks.text:
Kindness has a limit. Jason says you should judge harshly if nobody is thinking about change at all.

- If nobody cares whether there's change or not, if there's no rhyme or reason to the company strategy, or if everyone is expected to act and feel happy and productive all the time, then you should definitely judge.
- "An organization that isn't striving to improve, will rot and disintegrate."
- His closing view: there are no straight paths in life or startups. All you can do is keep being introspective and keep attempting the right sort of change.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jason Cohen separates maximizing (finding the best option) from satisficing (taking the first acceptable one) and argues you must pick deliberately for each decision. Speed is a startup's edge, so satisfice almost everything, and save maximizing for slow, foundational calls like product and business strategy.

chunks.heading: Maximizing vs. satisficing: pick the goal per decision
chunks.text:
Jason defines two decision-making goals.

- **Maximizing:** finding the best solution. It takes exploration and analysis to make sure "the best" option wasn't overlooked, and confidence in how the options were evaluated.
- **Satisficing:** picking the first, easiest or cheapest option that meets the requirements. It prefers a faster decision to the best one, avoids paralysis from chasing "perfect," and rarely yields the very best outcome.
- People lean one way or the other, but it depends on the subject. His example: you might maximize your career and satisfice your diet.
- Studies he cites show maximizers make better choices, but satisficers enjoy their choices more, and they spend less time and feel less stress deciding.
- His core instruction: "You must choose when to Maximize, and when to Satisfice." Pick the right goal for each decision and communicate it clearly.

chunks.heading: Why speed usually means satisficing
chunks.text:
- Jason calls speed "one of the greatest competitive advantages," and says it partly explains why small upstarts beat large incumbents.
- Speed requires satisficing, not maximizing. It can seem that maximizing is best, especially when smart teams are available to do it, but he says that is often the wrong move.
- Startup strength comes from shipping. Benefits arrive today instead of theoretical benefits in the future.
- Use customer reaction and real data to decide your next move, rather than planning many moves ahead, which he says you can't do anyway because the future can't be predicted.
- Satisficing is also the right mode for "sand" in his Rocks, Pebbles, Sand analogy, where deliberation is the enemy.

chunks.heading: When to maximize: product and business strategy
chunks.text:
- Maximizing is best for decisions that should be made slowly.
- His main example is Product & Business Strategy, which he calls "a slow obsession." Approach it from many angles:
  - Pound it with devil's advocacy.
  - Question every assumption.
  - "Sleep on it" repeatedly.
  - Repeat pieces of it to customers, strangers, and anyone who might have a useful reaction.
- Reason: strategy isn't something you want to change often, since whole teams and careers get built on top of it.
- For the most important decisions, he recommends maximizing with his Binstack method.
- For almost anything else, he says satisficing is likely wiser.

chunks.heading: The perfectionist trap
chunks.text:
- Jason warns that the same perfectionism that makes you "a force to be reckoned with" also drives impostor syndrome.
- That same trait will lead natural perfectionists to maximize too often.
- Default to satisficing, and reserve maximizing for the few high-stakes, slow decisions like strategy.

chunks.heading: Set an objective threshold for "satisfactory"
chunks.text:
- For satisficing activities, he says to define an objective threshold for "what is satisfactory."
- Tie it to a metric. When a metric is below its threshold, investment is warranted.
- Once it is at or above the threshold, you "must not" keep investing in it. By definition it isn't valuable enough to deserve more attention.
- Redirect that investment to areas that are below their own thresholds, or to things worth maximizing.
- This turns "good enough" from a feeling into a rule that stops over-investment.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jason Cohen reflects on being credited with creating WP Engine and reframes the founder as only the seed of a tree that hundreds of people sustain. He argues a company's purpose lies in the journey and in what each person gains from their time there, not in the founder's glory.

chunks.heading: Founder as seed, company as oak tree
chunks.text:
- When visitors to WP Engine's building meet the founder in his small office, they say "You must be so proud of what you created." Jason answers "What *we* created," and says it isn't false humility.
- He didn't create what exists today. Over four hundred people were building it as he spoke, and he hadn't been CEO for more than a decade.
- His metaphor: "WP Engine is an oak tree. I was the seed." The seed mattered and holds a permanent place in the history of the tree, but nothing you see today is the seed.
- He says a founder's job is to start the thing and then work with amazing people who collectively create the result.
- He frames this as the answer to "How does it feel to have created two unicorns?" He says he only knows what it feels like to start them, not to build them alone.

chunks.heading: The unglamorous work is what keeps the company alive
chunks.text:
- Jason splits a company into what outsiders can see and what they can't.
- Visible: sales calls, trade-show booths, product launches, an incredible tech support experience.
- Invisible: the 3am security upgrade, the start of a long-term new product category and brand strategy, collecting accounts receivable, quarterly financial reporting.
- He gives a quality example. A widespread but unreproducible bug was caught before it was ever deployed, because of a mature quality practice.
- His conclusion: "It is all vital to the life of the tree." Branches, cells, leaves and roots all matter, not just the externally obvious parts.

chunks.heading: Employees are acorns: people will leave, and that is healthy
chunks.text:
- Jason says each person at WP Engine will eventually leave. He hopes not for years, since "we have so much more to do," but he calls it inevitable.
- He compares departing employees to acorns. Some birth their own trees. More often they join another tree to strengthen it and grow in symbiosis.
- Some alumni started companies, not just in tech but in salsas, comic books and consulting.
- Some joined niche small companies, others the largest resume-enhancing big-tech names.
- He treats people leaving as a normal outcome of a company that develops its people, not as a failure of retention.

chunks.heading: What the company does for people's lives
chunks.text:
- Jason lists outcomes he sees as part of a company's real impact:
  - Some employees used their success to be the first in their family to buy a house.
  - Some were the first in their family to travel internationally.
  - Some were the first in their family to attend college.
  - Some arrived with one career and left with another, with more responsibility and making 10x more money than they thought possible.
- He treats this career and life growth as a core part of what a company is for, not a side effect.

chunks.heading: The test of whether a company was worth it
chunks.text:
- Jason says it is up to all of us to make sure each person looks back on their time at WP Engine as well spent.
- The questions he wants people to answer yes to:
  - Were they proud of the work they did?
  - Did they grow as a person, as well as professionally?
  - Did they have an impact on others' lives, helping the next generation thrive as they were helped?
  - Were they gratified by the important role they played in customers' lives?
  - Did any of it matter?
- He says if the answers are yes, "it was all worth it."

chunks.heading: Companies are mortal; the purpose is the journey
chunks.text:
- Jason says the oak tree drops acorns for decades if not centuries, but is eventually returned wholly to the soil.
- "All mighty trees inevitably dissolve into their base elements, to be recombined by and for the next generation."
- He applies this to both companies and lives: their purpose "resides in the journey, not in the end."
- Implication for founders: success is measured by the people helped, the customers served and the work worth being proud of, not by the company lasting forever or by the valuation.
- He says he rarely talks about this future with strangers, preferring to talk about what exists now.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jason Cohen argues that building in public isn't a risk to your moat but a forcing function. Public code gets judged so quality rises, and if copying is easy you must build non-technical, permanent advantages. Open pay and transparency push you toward a culture of autonomy, growth and purpose.

chunks.heading: Building in public as a forcing function for quality code
chunks.text:
- Jason's premise: if you had to put all your proprietary, "secret-sauce" code in a public GitHub repository, you would be judged by peers on file and class organization, documentation, tests, removing reliance on "security by obscurity," tracking to-dos, and the artful quality of "you know it when you see it."
- The force at work is "Ego--your desire to impress others."
- His conclusion: "building in public would force you to create quality, artful code."

chunks.heading: Building in public forces non-technical competitive advantage
chunks.text:
- The objection is that competitors can copy you if they see your code and growth rate. Jason's answer is that this pushes you to build a non-technical [competitive advantage](https://longform.asmartbear.com/moats/) into the business.
- Etsy example: if Etsy open-sourced its entire stack, a competitor still couldn't overtake it. Etsy has built a marketplace, and the presence of buyers and sellers is its primary asset, not the software behind the website or payments.
- Facebook example: it open-sourced its entire data center infrastructure, and that doesn't make it easy to overtake Facebook as a social network. The value in these companies "cannot be replicated with money," which is why they are valuable.
- Technical advantage can be permanent in select cases (he points to a case study of Amazon AWS), but this is rare.
- Typically a technical advantage is fleeting because most technical things can be replicated, often faster and more cheaply than the original inventors did it. "First to market" often doesn't equate to "winning the market."
- His conclusion: "building in public forces you to create permanent competitive advantages."

chunks.heading: Public salaries force a culture-driven talent strategy
chunks.text:
- Building in public also applies to organizations and people, not just software.
- If you publish the salary formula for everyone at the company, you can no longer compete for talent on compensation alone. You can't add an extra $10k/year to win a critical employee with especially germane experience.
- He acknowledges it can be weird for everyone to know what everyone else makes, but says that for many people "it's not weird, it's fantastic."
- The constraint forces you to build a company where great talent wants to work, with people there for culture and mission rather than as mercenaries.

chunks.heading: Three ingredients of a culture that attracts and retains talent
chunks.text:
Jason names three elements common to frameworks for building such an environment:

- **Autonomy:** freedom to explore, plus control and empowerment to invent solutions to problems and prove their quality through implementation, in exchange for accountability for the result.
- **Growth:** working on interesting puzzles, personal or professional, along a fulfilling journey.
- **Purpose:** why the company should exist, why it's worth busting your ass to see it thrive, the culture and values, and the joy of working with people you admire.

His conclusion: "building in public forces you to create a company with exceptional culture and an organization of empowerment and purpose."

chunks.heading: Why this produces durable companies
chunks.text:
- Writing code you can be proud of, building permanent competitive advantages, and creating a culture that attracts talent "for reasons beyond legal bribery" are critical ingredients of durable companies.
- Durable companies keep their growth and brand unhindered by the "onslaught of well-funded, hard-working, intelligent upstarts" that inevitably join any market big enough to be interesting.
- Building everything in public forces you to do "what's most valuable" and "what isn't easily copyable," whether that is the quality of workmanship, the fortress of the business model, or a talent magnet.
- He allows that operating in secret is still possible and occasionally advisable, but says "sunlight isn't just the best disinfectant, it's a great way to forge durability."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jason Cohen argues that a "10x rule" is a useful default assumption across startups. Best products, channels, people, products-in-a-portfolio and decisions tend to outperform the rest by roughly 10x, so you should hunt for the one 10x truth instead of fiddling with a hundred variables.

chunks.heading: The 10x rule of thumb
chunks.text:
Jason argues that startup outcomes follow 10x patterns often enough that "10x" should be the default assumption until proven false. He admits people love stories and see patterns in noise, but claims this one holds up as "an excellent rule of thumb."

- Things are not always exactly 10x.
- Some 10x properties last for years but can evolve until there is no other 10x left.
- The practical advice is to assume a 10x truth exists and spend your time finding it, rather than fiddling with one hundred variables, almost none of which matter.

chunks.heading: 10x in products, people and decisions
chunks.text:
- Winning products have at least one attribute that is 10x better than all competitors. It is not necessarily design, though it can be.
- Great people are more than 10x better than average.
- For multi-product companies, one product often earns more than all the others combined. At Smart Bear and 37signals, the largest product was 10x larger than all the others combined.
- One or two decisions or principles are 10x more important than all the others combined.
- Companies do not naturally 10x their size or quality. That takes intentional focus and investment.
- Scale is 10x harder than operating small, because complexity is non-linear.

chunks.heading: 10x in markets and venture outcomes
chunks.text:
- SaaS returns in a market follow a power law, and the winner can take 10x the profits of the next. His examples: eBay ≥ 10x Etsy, Google ≥ 10x Bing, Facebook ≥ 10x Twitter, Salesforce ≥ 10x the rest of its market.
- VCs must invest in 10x winners, so they push every portfolio company toward that outcome, even at the cost of more risk and sub-optimal cash use.
- Business models change with pricing in roughly 10x increments.
- Warren Buffett earned $77.4 billion of his $77.7 billion net worth after his 50th birthday.

chunks.heading: 10x in marketing
chunks.text:
- Your best marketing channel is often 10x as productive as the next best. This is also true within content marketing.
- One article or tweet often outperforms all the rest by 10x.
- The implication is to find and concentrate on the one channel or piece that works, rather than spreading effort evenly.

chunks.heading: 10x in customers
chunks.text:
- About 1/10th of customers are likely gross-margin unprofitable. Jason says this does not mean you should "fire" them, but the calculation is worth understanding and measuring.
- Changing a policy or product to shrink that unprofitable set can be a quick, strategic way to generate profit.
- About 1/10th of customers generate 10x more support calls than the rest. Some of that is fine, but it can signal a problem with the product, with those customers, or with who you are selling to.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jason argues that worry actively causes the bad outcomes it fears, because it injects second-guessing and fear into the moment of execution. The antidote isn't apathy but preparation: long-term deliberate practice and short-term visualization, then clearing your mind and executing. He applies this to the many worries founders carry.

chunks.heading: Worry is self-fulfilling: it injects the failure it fears
chunks.text:
- Jason argues that worrying causes the thing you're worried about to happen. "Worry" breaks things which aren't broken. It doesn't lead constructively to solutions, it only creates problems.
- Backstage before a performance, mounting anxiety injects second-guessing and fear into the performance itself. His fix is to recognize that the practice is already done, and that mistakes don't matter much because "No one is counting except you."
- At a pool table, a tennis serve or a golf swing, thinking through everything you're supposed to do while executing inevitably ruins the shot.
- His conclusion: worry is "worse than unhelpful--it's destructive." It might even be better to be blissfully ignorant than to worry.

chunks.heading: The opposite of worry is preparation, not apathy
chunks.text:
- Jason says the opposite of "Worry" isn't "Apathy". The opposite is "Preparation".
- The recipe: tackle the root of the worry constructively, prepare as best you can, then "just proceed."
- Preparation replaces anxious rumination with something that can actually change the outcome.

chunks.heading: Long-term preparation: purposeful repetition and season planning
chunks.text:
- He points to what great athletes do: they pummel themselves with purposeful repetition of specific skills, to the point of boredom.
- They plan energy output and practice schedules across an entire season so they peak at the most important meets.
- This is the slow version of preparation: build the skill and the schedule ahead of time, so the big moment is not the place where you try to figure things out.

chunks.heading: Short-term preparation: visualize, then clear your mind and execute
chunks.text:
- Right before execution, Jason recommends visualization. He notes it is common to all sport and its efficacy has been verified by a robust set of experiments.
- Examples he gives: Olympic downhill skiers, gymnasts and ice skaters with eyes closed, mentally running their routines and routes, swaying with muted motions.
- Billiard players visualize the motion of the cue ball before they strike, but clear their minds as they actually strike.
- The sequence for a high-stakes moment: visualize ahead of time, clear your mind, then execute using muscle memory. Do not think while doing.

chunks.heading: Applying it to startups: what founders worry about
chunks.text:
- Jason says the lesson is generic and applies to all of life, including startups.
- Business worries he lists:
  - How to make payroll.
  - How the competition will hurt you.
  - What someone said about you on Twitter.
  - Whether the visual design isn't compelling.
  - Whether you'll close the customer on this call.
  - Whether you're optimizing for the right metric.
  - Whether you don't know the right way to do things.
- Each of these gets the same treatment: find the root, prepare, proceed.

chunks.heading: Worry turned inward on yourself
chunks.text:
- He calls out a worse form, "turning the gun on yourself": worrying that it's just too hard, that you're not following good advice, that everything you do is unsatisfactory.
- Also worrying that others are so much better than you, and therefore that you have no business doing any of this in the first place.
- He describes startups as a crucible and these as among the symptoms, pointing to his related essays on startups being emotionally draining, feelings of inadequacy, impostor syndrome and being yourself.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Circular debates happen because pros and cons are mixed together. Jason Cohen says to split upside from downside, decide and invest based on upside, use downside only as a veto, reduce the choice to at most three dimensions, then pick a process and move on.

chunks.heading: Separate upside from downside before deciding
chunks.text:
Jason argues that complex decisions stall because people argue in logical circles, with every point true but none converging. His example is "should we build feature X?":

- Feature X makes the company unique in the market.
- But the company is behind on feature Y, which three competitors have.
- But once Y is built, those competitors will have Z.
- But deals are being lost today for lack of Y.
- But a competitor with Y could copy X.

All of those statements are true, which is why no decision comes out of them.

His fix is to split "how could this go right" (upside) from "how could this go wrong" (downside) and state the outcome of each in a line:

- Upside of X: unique market position leads to deals won through differentiation, plus some less measurable brand benefit.
- Downside of not building Y: deals lost to one specific competitor.

Building Y also wins more deals, but only in a subset of sales calls and with no brand benefit, so X looks better.

He adds a caveat: if you can quantify it, quantify. If the company is losing $10m/yr without Y and expects to gain $1m/yr from X, Y wins. Even without data, which is common for early-stage startups, the separation still gives a clear and sensible answer.

chunks.heading: Decide on the upside, use the downside only as a veto
chunks.text:
Jason applies this to hiring a senior leader such as a VP Marketing. The "perfect candidate" (vision, strategy, operations, people, org structure, internal and external communication, speed, mentorship) is mythical, so it is easy to go in circles.

His rule: hire on exceptional strengths, then fill weaknesses through the rest of the team. "Only through exceptional strength will the person make an impact on the business."

He tests two questions:

1. For the most critical problems this leader is expected to solve over the next year, is she world-class at solving those particular problems? If not, it is a no-hire, however much you like the other upsides or ignore the downsides.
2. Do you know her weaknesses (otherwise you can't plan for them), and are they either low-impact or something you or she can concretely mitigate? Everyone has weaknesses. If any is impossible to ameliorate, it is a no-hire. Otherwise, that is the plan.

So the primary decision rests on the magnitude and likelihood of the upside, and the downside is only a veto when it is unworkable. He adds that it is your job to fill the company with people much better than you at every position.

chunks.heading: Over-invest in strengths rather than shoring up weaknesses
chunks.text:
Jason says people naturally focus on weaknesses ("we're getting killed for not having F," "customers complain we're bad at E," "20% of customers leave because we're bad at D") and spend time and money bringing them up to neutral. His argument: "developing a 10x strength is far more valuable than shifting a weakness to neutral." This holds personally, professionally, and in product.

His examples:

- **iPhone v1:** it mattered more to be 10x on strengths (form factor, browser and email experience) than to fix weaknesses (no copy/paste, poor call experience).
- **Engineers:** you are more effective being very deep in one language, framework or problem domain than passable at ten.
- **Heroku:** it won Rails developers by being 10x better at deploy/stage/production, so developers (begrudgingly) accepted a read-only file system, having to use Bundler, having to use PostgreSQL, overpaying for CPU, and tying their fate to a platform.
- **Counter-example, WP Engine:** web design was a weakness, so the company invested and "got zero return," because words and product/market fit turned out to be 100x more important than design.

Practical rule: invest most in your greatest upsides and strengths. Treat downsides as constraints to design around, or as a veto in extreme cases. He suggests running the same exercise on your own personal strengths and weaknesses.

chunks.heading: Deliberately over-simplify to at most three dimensions
chunks.text:
Jason says the feature X/Y summary ("both increase sales, but only one also increases differentiation") quietly ignored many real factors, such as implementation time, team fit and likelihood of failure. That is intentional. "If you don't intentionally over-simplify, you will never reach a firm and clear decision."

He compares it to voters in the 2016 US presidential election. There are too many issues to weigh (climate, taxes, trade, war, education, civil rights and more), no candidate matches on all, and it is unknowable which few issues will actually change. So voters pick a few issues they care about most and decide on those. He says this kind of reductive simplification is logical and necessary, and links it to his writing on SaaS metrics and on great strategy.

Why it is safe: if you treat all the considerations as important, you end up with a set of good options. Any one of them is objectively good, so almost any process for picking among them is acceptable. His guidance is to decide using one, two, or at most three key dimensions.

He points to two frameworks for doing this as a group:

- Binstack, for multi-dimensional choices.
- Fermi ROI, a better way to run rubrics or "ROI" calculations.

chunks.heading: Ignore the social pressure of the options you did not pick
chunks.text: Jason warns that whichever option you exclude, people with a vested interest (even just that it was their idea or they got attached) will push back with "how is your choice really better?" He says they are right, because you had several equally good choices, and someone will say it whatever you do. His conclusion: do not include this "social pressure" in your decision.

chunks.heading: Decide how to decide, then move on
chunks.text:
Jason's closing rules:

- Making decisions quickly is valuable, because you can usually make a different one if the first proves wrong. If you can't reverse it, that is a reason to spend more time evaluating.
- Pick a process, use it, and move on.
- Separate upside from downside, clarify the choice with one to three dimensions, base the decision on the magnitude and likelihood of the upside, and use the downside to veto untenable options.
- Use Binstack or Fermi ROI as frameworks that guide a group to a joint, explainable decision.
- "Defining the conditions of the decision is 80% of the decision," so spend your time there.
- Don't be too hard on yourself afterwards even if it goes badly. Life is an experiment with little predictive power, no control group, and N=1 that cannot be re-run.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jason Cohen argues that no company 10x's forever, and that tech's obsession with growth multiples eventually stops being the right question. Once a business has likely peaked, he says its true impact comes from applying its success to betterment (jobs, working conditions, community) rather than only biggerment.

chunks.heading: Peaking is not failing: growth multiples fade for every company
chunks.text:
- Jason argues that the "how do we 10x" question is right for a young startup but cannot be the right question forever. "No company 10x's forever. Not even Google."
- He points to Google as proof: it became a Berkshire Hathaway-style conglomerate of separate companies, each of which could potentially 10x on its own.
- His opening questions are what-ifs: Dropbox is a great file-sharing and backup service but not a universal key/value storage API. OpenTable is a perfect reservation system and nothing more. Yelp has ratings but can't solve food-delivery logistics. Twitter never 10x's its user base but stays a critical communication and news system for a decade.
- Facebook is his example of a plateau: it can make $20b/yr in advertising, but with teens and the social media elite gone it may never make $200b/yr.
- A 2024 editor's note checks the predictions. Dropbox, OpenTable, Yelp and Twitter all proved true. Meta projected $160B for 2024, about $100B of it from Facebook, so the Facebook call was half-right: 5x over 8 years, not 10x.
- The note adds that Facebook's attempts at a virtual currency and chat monetization failed, that the Instagram and WhatsApp acquisitions were critical for growth, and that Metaverse and AI efforts burned tens of billions with no substantial results. Jason says this shows "how difficult it is to '10x forever.'"

chunks.heading: Why growth-multiple valuation distorts how tech companies are judged
chunks.text:
- Jason notes that in tech, "growth" is treated as the prime determinant of a business's value. Valuations are usually quoted as a multiple of revenue, and higher growth earns a higher multiple.
- If growth dips below the level of "rivets rattling out of the plane," revenue multiples plummet. The press then writes the company off as a has-been, ripe for disruption by startups 1/1000th its size that are "growing exponentially."
- His example: Microsoft made more cash profit in 2015 than Facebook made in revenue, yet was worth only 12% more in Enterprise Value. The market was pricing in the chance that Facebook could keep adding ads, invent a virtual currency or monetize chat users.
- The point is that a profitable, durable business can be valued far below its cash generation purely because its growth rate is lower.

chunks.heading: You can't know whether you're done 10x'ing, but plan for the possibility
chunks.text:
- Jason concedes that you can't know right now whether you've finished 10x'ing.
- His argument is conditional: if another 10x is not a plausible outcome, you should redirect attention instead of keeping all effort on growth.
- He treats "just ploughing back into a 10x growth objective" as an optimal strategy only up to a point. After that it is no longer the best way to make a "dent in the universe."
- The practical test he implies is to ask honestly whether a further 10x is plausible, rather than assuming growth is the only acceptable path.

chunks.heading: What to do instead: apply the company to betterment, not just biggerment
chunks.text:
- Jason lists what a company could focus on once relentless growth stops being the right goal:
  - Create more jobs and better working conditions.
  - Be a catalyst for employees' personal growth.
  - Give back to relevant communities.
  - Use its logistics, technology, infrastructure and cost savings to do something important with the success it has earned.
- He says it is exactly when a company is applied to "betterment instead of (only) biggerment" that its true dent in the universe is determined.
- He frames this as a legacy question and closes with "What will be your legacy?"

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jason Cohen explains how to grade probabilistic forecasts like lead scoring or churn prediction. Accuracy alone is gameable, so you also need discernment, and you judge both against the baseline of just guessing the average. He shows the math with a weather example.

chunks.heading: Why accuracy alone fails: the climatic-average trap
chunks.text:
Jason's starting point is a probabilistic forecast like "30% chance of rain". A single outcome tells you nothing about whether it was good. The correct reading is: gather every day the forecaster said 30%, and check whether it rained about 30% of those days. Forecasts are "bucketed" by predicted value (0%, 10%, 50%...) and each bucket is compared with what actually happened.

- **Accuracy Error** is the squared difference between the predicted probability and the actual rate in that bucket. Example: A always predicts 32%, B always predicts 25%, and it really rains 30% of the time. A's error is (0.32-0.30)^2 = 0.0004 and B's is (0.25-0.30)^2 = 0.0025, so A is more accurate.
- He squares errors instead of using absolute values for two reasons: squaring exaggerates items that are very different, and the math of squared differences is far more tractable (it can be factored and used with calculus, which is how least-squares linear regression is derived).
- The trap: a forecaster in a region that rains 110 of 365 days (30%) can predict "30%" every day. Her accuracy error is exactly zero, yet she is "not forecasting at all", just "regurgitating the climatic average".

chunks.heading: Discernment: rewarding forecasters who stick their necks out
chunks.text:
Jason adds a second concept, *discernment*: the forecaster actively segments days and takes a strong stance on which will rain, instead of copying the overall average.

- Discernment is computed like accuracy error, but compares the **actual rate in each bucket** to the **climatic average** (not to the prediction). It measures how far the buckets depart from the average, so how much the forecaster is "saying something specific".
- Worked example, forecaster B (100 predictions): 8 times he predicted 0% (actual 10%), 12 times 100% (actual 90%), 80 times the 30% average (actual 30%).
  - Accuracy error per bucket: 0.01, 0.00, 0.01. Weighted by bucket size: (0.08 + 0 + 0.12) / 100 = 0.002.
  - Discernment per bucket: (0.30-0.10)^2 = 0.04, 0.00, (0.30-0.90)^2 = 0.36. Weighted: (0.32 + 0 + 4.32) / 100 = 0.0464.
- Predicting the average earns zero discernment points. A confident 100% call earns many, because it is a bigger departure from average.
- B has slightly worse accuracy error than a forecaster who always says 30%, yet Jason says you should prefer B, "even though he has more error". When B is very sure, he is usually right. So discernment is "a fundamental component of how 'good' a forecaster is".
- Naively comparing the two numbers (0.0464 vs 0.002) and calling the forecaster good is not valid. They need a proper way to combine.

chunks.heading: Discernment Error: how much discernment is even possible
chunks.text:
Jason argues it is unfair to ask "how discerning is the forecaster?" without asking how much discernment the environment allows.

- Antofagasta, Chile gets rain about five days a year (1.7 millimeters annually). Any varied prediction would necessarily be wrong, since reality isn't varied. There is "no space" for discernment.
- Portland, Oregon rains 164 days a year (about 45%) with no rainy season, so a world-class forecaster has lots of room to be discerning.
- Maximum possible discernment given climatic average c is **c(1-c)**. It peaks at 0.25 when c = 50% (a coin flip) and shrinks as c nears 0% or 100%.
  - At c = 30%: 0.30 x 0.70 = 0.21. B's 0.04 is "not too impressive", though still better than a no-discernment forecaster.
  - For the desert (5/365 days), only about 0.0128 is available.
- Derivation: maximum discernment occurs when forecasts are only 0% or 100% and fully accurate. The positive bucket contributes (1-c)^2 for Nc cases, the negative bucket c^2 for N(1-c) cases, and the weighted average simplifies to c(1-c).
- **Discernment Error = Maximum Discernment - Discernment.** Lacking discernment is its own kind of error.

chunks.heading: The Forecast Error score (Brier score) and the baseline
chunks.text:
Jason's combined metric is simple addition:

- **Forecast Error = Accuracy Error + Discernment Error = Error + Maximum Discernment - Discernment.** Lower is better, as it is a total error.
- Baseline: always guessing the climatic average gives zero accuracy error but maximum discernment error, so a score of **c(1-c)**.
- Forecasters deviate from the average to cut discernment error, but must be right. The best ones reduce discernment error by more than the accuracy error they add.
- It is possible to do worse than the baseline (making bold guesses and being wrong). That shows when total error exceeds c(1-c).
- Equivalent normalized version: divide Forecast Error by c(1-c). Then **1 = same as baseline, 0 = perfect, and the distance from 1 shows proportionally how much better or worse** the forecast is. The reader doesn't need to know c(1-c) to interpret it.
- Credit: this is the Brier score (Glenn Brier, 1950). The three-component breakdown was found by Allen Murphy in 1973.

chunks.heading: Diagnosing a model with the two components
chunks.text:
Jason says the total is useful, but the components show what is going wrong:

| Accuracy error | Discernment | Meaning | Explanation |
|---|---|---|---|
| High | Low | Failure | Not segmenting, and still worse than guessing the average |
| Low | Low | Useless | Accurate only because you guess the average |
| High | High | Try Again | Strong predictions, but wrong |
| Low | High | Ideal | Strong predictions, and correct |

chunks.heading: Business uses and how to apply it
chunks.text:
Jason lists where better probability forecasts pay off:

- **Lead scoring:** predict the chance a new sales lead converts, and its dollar value.
- **Predicting churn:** if you can predict a given customer's chance of churning in the next 30 days, you can act proactively and perhaps avert the loss. Doing this enough puts you "on the road to Product/Market Fit".
- **Predicting upgrades:** know which customers are amenable to an upgrade and focus internal messaging accordingly.
- **Risk assessments:** better probabilities on risks lead to more intelligent investments.
