His advice: build forecasting models to better understand customers and prospects, then use this score to know whether each iteration of the model is actually improving. He says the whole calculation is simple enough to do in Google Spreadsheets.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jason Cohen argues that every creation, from Edison's light bulb to a band's gig, rests on enormous hidden drudgery. We see only the finished result, so we feel bad about being mid-journey, and quit. Those who succeed are the ones who plodded through the failures.

chunks.heading: The journey is the whole book, and most of it is drudgery
chunks.text:
- Jason argues we "skip to the last page of other people's books" and forget they took the whole journey, so we feel bad when we're only on "Chapter Four" and ask when we get to the good part.
- The visible success is a small fraction of the effort. For musicians, he says there are "a hundred hours of toil behind each visible hour of glory": practicing in spaces that aren't sufficiently isolated, landing gigs, setting up stages, and getting more than four people to show up.
- His claim is that invention in every field, not only engineering, is mostly drudgery rather than inspiration.

chunks.heading: Edison: roughly three years of trial and error before a salable product
chunks.text:
- Edison spent 18 months of trial and error producing the first workable light, which lasted only 13 hours before the carbon fiber filament burned out.
- He spent another 18 months of trial and error before finding that a carbonized bamboo filament lasted 100x longer, which made a practical, salable light bulb.
- Jason quotes Edison: "I have not failed 10,000 times--I've successfully found 10,000 ways that will not work."
- Lesson: persistence through many failed attempts is the mechanism of invention, not a detour from it.

chunks.heading: What drudgery looks like when you build a product
chunks.text:
Jason lists the unglamorous work that fills most days:
- Fixing bugs your unit tests "proved couldn't exist".
- Tying off loose ends of development that never stop arising.
- Planning, estimating, communicating and post-morteming.
- Taking the wrong path and backtracking.
- Planning the launch, the training, the targeting, the positioning and the alpha testers.
- Losing five hours on a problem that, on another day with different luck, might have taken five minutes.

chunks.heading: Why people quit, and why that's the trap
chunks.text:
- Products have no clear end the way a book does, and it's often unclear whether to continue or quit. He describes the early stage as chaos where you can't tell if you're on the right track.
- People quit the job, thinking the next company will be much better, or quit the startup because it "apparently" isn't working. He acknowledges tiredness is real and "life's too short" is a fair thought.
- His point: it is the drudgery itself that tempts people out, and it is exactly the stretch that has to be endured.

chunks.heading: Who eventually succeeds
chunks.text:
- Those who succeed are the ones who "plodded through the 5,999 filaments that didn't work", put in the 10,000 hours to master a craft, and fought through the overwhelming pile of challenges and drudgery that "is always required to create something great".
- Success is not found by avoiding the grind; it is the result of getting through it.

chunks.heading: Luck, credit and meaning
chunks.text:
- When you finally succeed, you can say "I really *did* something". That is also the cue for others to dismiss it as mostly luck, and Jason concedes: "They're not altogether wrong."
- He acknowledges it may seem crazy to do all this for a fleeting feeling of accomplishment, but suggests "maybe it's the meaning of life."
- Practical takeaway: expect the work to be mostly drudgery, don't read your own Chapter Four against someone else's final chapter, and don't treat the absence of glory mid-journey as a sign you're on the wrong path.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: "Survival of the fittest" means most prolific, not best. When growth rate is the only measure of fitness, profitability and betterment of humanity go unsolved. Cohen argues founders should let their values drive growth, citing Buffer, TOMS and USAA as examples.

chunks.heading: Founders carry two jobs: win on growth and win on "best"
chunks.text:
- Jason separates "survival of the fittest" from "survival of the best." "Fittest" means "most prolific at becoming grandparents." The grandparent test is the only one: offspring that can't reproduce don't count (a horse-donkey cross makes a sterile mule).
- Nature has no ethics. "Bad" things can be as fit as "good" ones. Viruses are amazingly fit: they spread at prodigious rates and are hard to stop once numerous.
- He argues it is the founder's responsibility to solve for both growth and the betterment of the world, because the market will not do the second job on its own.

chunks.heading: "Growth at all costs" turns companies into viruses
chunks.text:
- Jason is not against obsessing over growth. In winner-take-all markets, "growth is objectively the correct goal."
- His complaint is "growth *at all costs*." Investors and founders hold up viral growth as the best kind, since exponential curves overwhelm all others. Once the mechanism is stable and the company is big enough to be noticed, competitors can hardly catch up.
- A virus colony grows with no care for the host, and can destroy the host and itself.
- His rule: "When 'growth rate' becomes the *only* important metric for company 'fitness,' other metrics are left unsolved."
- Winning the market this way proves you are "an excellent virus in a Darwinian sense," not that you have "an excellent business model."

chunks.heading: Profitability is the metric most often left unsolved
chunks.text:
- Many companies that won the growth battle never convert from a virus into a business.
- Jason names companies he sees as already past the point of "can never be profitable unless something drastically changes": GroupOn, Zynga, SoundCloud.
- Others continue on massive investment, and he says the jury is out on whether they ever produce profits: SnapChat, Pinterest, WeWork, InstaCart, Square, FourSquare, and Twitter, which has impressive revenue but has never been profitable.
- His read: some will find a business model and some won't. Either way, their market-winner position came from growth, not from a proven model.

chunks.heading: Betterment of humanity is the second unsolved metric
chunks.text:
- Jason says it is the entrepreneur's duty to build companies that leave the world better than they found it, or at least not worse.
- He says it is also employees' duty to put most of their waking hours and most productive years into companies that make the world better, "not just 'hit a number.'"
- He gives examples of market-winners that do make the world better:
  - Biotech advances, which have extended and improved life.
  - WordPress (25% of all domains), which made owning your website orders of magnitude cheaper.
  - Amazon's cloud services, which enable products and services that were impossible a decade ago, for startups and 100-year-old companies alike.
- He also lists winners that are a mixed bag:
  - Uber turns under-paid employees into so-called "entrepreneurs," but they are still indentured and still under-paid.
  - Twitter connects people and ideas but kills attention spans and stokes hate more than debate.
  - Google puts the world's information at our fingertips but destroys personal privacy in ways more insidious than most people want to know.
  - Self-driving cars will solve traffic, help the environment, serve people who can't drive, and make parking lots obsolete, but will destroy millions of transportation jobs, many well paid relative to the holders' formal education.
- Darwinian growth wins by definition. He says there is no use crying about it, and regulation would only shift where the winners are located.

chunks.heading: Make values drive growth instead of trading growth for values
chunks.text:
- Jason asks founders and employees whether growth is *sufficient*, and whether the company will treat other values as "*also* inalienable and unassailable," letting them drive the most important decisions and requiring growth to be compatible with them.
- His framing: "The real question is not how to retard growth in submission to other values, but rather how to use our insistence values to drive growth."

chunks.heading: Three examples of growth driven by values
chunks.text:
- **Small, Buffer:** a 5-year-old company, profitable and growing, in the overcrowded "Social Media Tools" space with a product Jason calls not particularly special or unique. Talent still beats down the door to work there, even knowing they'll take a pay cut, because salaries are set by a formula. The pull comes from complete transparency and positivity, honesty about struggles and successes, and care for employee health and well-being.
- **Mid-sized, TOMS shoes:** a massive success due to a viral story people want to support and retell, "exactly because its mission is so commendable and pure," not because of a superior product.
- **Large, USAA:** a company with the boring homepage title "insurance, banking and retirement solutions." It is the 49th most valuable company on Earth, with $24 billion in annual revenue and $3 billion in profits. Its customer-service NPS runs consistently between 75 and 80, among the highest in the world. It is known as one of the best places to work, even in traditionally low-paying, low-formal-education roles like customer service, and for its unwavering commitment to US Armed Forces families.
- Jason's conclusion: you can "grow and be profitable exactly because of goodness and love." He points to his willingness-to-pay essay for ways to do it.

chunks.heading: The takeaway: build the virus with beneficial effects
chunks.text:
- A virulent company is wonderful only if it carries beneficial effects: customers who love the service, employees who enjoy spending most of their waking hours at work, and net-positive effects on economies, communities and societies.
- His closing line: "When you build your unstoppable company, make it an unstoppable force for good."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Using a web-server analogy, Jason Cohen argues that running people and teams near full capacity makes them brittle. Variation and interruption are inevitable, so teams need slack and should reserve high-gear surges for short, justified periods.

chunks.heading: Why 90% utilization makes systems brittle
chunks.text:
- Jason argues that running any system near full capacity removes the slack that absorbs normal variation. His framing: "Your non-linear problem of 90% utilization."
- Server example: a server at 50% has spare resources when traffic spikes. Traffic arrives "in spurts and occasionally large spikes," not smoothly.
- If someone says "it costs the same at 90% or 99%, so drive it into the 90s," even normal fluctuations exceed capacity. Response times "skyrocket" and requests get dropped all the time, not just in unusual events.
- His label for the result: "The system is now brittle." It is bad for cost, product quality and customer experience.
- The point is non-linear: the cost of the last 10-40% of utilization is far higher than the benefit.

chunks.heading: The three-server trap: pooled capacity still fails
chunks.text:
- Three servers at 70% each look like a happy medium between 50% (wasteful) and 90% (brittle). Total load is 2.1 servers (3 x 70%).
- When one server crashes (data center power cut, network flooded with garbage traffic), two servers must carry 2.1 servers of traffic. Each runs at 105% and the system breaks.
- Lesson: spreading load across a team does not remove the need for spare capacity. Headroom has to cover losing a member, not just average load.

chunks.heading: This is really about people and teams
chunks.text:
- Jason says "This isn't really about servers; it's about you and your teams."
- People have a capacity, measured in hours, energy or focused attention. Instead of web requests they get "life-requests": emails, Jira tickets, Zendesk tickets, Salesforce leads, co-worker requests, friends, and family who need time and attention.
- A hectic, always-busy team can still be slow. Everyone works hard yet accomplishes a fraction of what seems possible.
- He treats burnout as the obvious cost (sleep, health, friends, family) but says the bigger miss is lower productivity and output: "You're trading that for super-human productivity, right?" The implied answer is no.

chunks.heading: Context-switching and interruption: the Twin Enemies of productivity
chunks.text:
- At 90% utilization, work is constantly interrupted. Jason calls frequent context-switching and interruption "the Twin Enemies of productivity."
- Work-completion drags out, and some work is abandoned.
- You also don't get "outsized professional gains" as a reward for the sacrifice.

chunks.heading: The cascade effect when everyone is at 90%
chunks.text:
- In many organizations everyone is at 90%, which behaves like the three-server system. One person's hiccup ripples to several other people or projects.
- Because those people are also over capacity, they cannot absorb the spike. They pass the problem on, creating "a cascade like the run-away chain reaction of an atom bomb."
- Variation is "inevitable": illness, death, people leaving or changing, errands, and small work nobody mapped out weeks ahead. Real emergencies also deserve to interrupt work.
- He says you can't "architect out" variation. Build a system, and personal and team work-style, that assumes variation and interruption and is resilient to it.

chunks.heading: What the healthy pattern looks like
chunks.text:
- Target: most of the time in the safe zone, with occasional surges into high gear "for a short period of time" and "for good cause."
- Examples of good-cause surges:
  - A new product launch, with extra time fixing bugs, especially post-launch when real customers hit issues that everyone agrees should be fixed swiftly.
  - A clear-and-present danger to the company that needs a special, time-bounded rally.
  - Infrequent, brief surges used in a fun way: a Hack-a-Thon, a Bug Squash Competition, or a Ticket Kill Day.
- His conclusion: "We're erring on the side of over-utilization." Instead of competitive advantage from higher productivity, it creates "needless turmoil and lower productivity." His closing advice: don't let yourself or your team fall into the trap.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jason Cohen refutes the claim that every acquisition is a failure. Companies change constantly whether independent or acquired, most startups fail either way, and a well-chosen sale can create liquidity, jobs, and opportunity for founders, employees, and products. He argues the useful question is when acquisition is wise.

chunks.heading: Acquisitions are not inherently failures; companies change either way
chunks.text:
Jason Cohen's 2015 essay rebuts Jake Lodwick's claim (PandoDaily, "An acquisition is always a failure") that founders either failed to achieve their goal or failed to dream big enough. He calls that "the false wisdom of those who haven't experienced the alternative."

- Superlative framing ("always a failure") spreads because the media runs on what people click and share, not because it is accurate.
- He argues the better questions are "When is acquisition wise?" and "What are the conditions under which acquisitions are likely to be good for all parties?"
- He objects to the framing because it insults everyone who chooses to join a larger company while providing liquidity for employees who also took a risk.

chunks.heading: "Youthful energy" doesn't last just because you stay independent
chunks.text:
Lodwick lamented that the "youthful energy that created so much value was siphoned off" by the sale. Jason calls this classic founder naïveté.

- Companies are constantly changing. Cool companies stop being cool, new products stop being new, and a slow-growing startup with a great idea gets eclipsed by a faster-growing one with weaker ideas.
- A fast-growing startup, by definition, changes so quickly that year over year it is unrecognizable to the people inside it.
- Example from WP Engine: he and his colleagues laugh about how drastic the changes are. The company still has "youthful energy" for new innovations, but also all the challenges of a fast-growing company with hundreds of employees, which he says "is part of success."
- A company won't stay "a band of six people doing whatever they want forever, whether you sell or stay independent." He says expecting otherwise is foolish.

chunks.heading: A founder's unhappiness after a sale is not proof the sale was wrong
chunks.text:
Jason says the author's evidence is weak: he judged the sale a failure because he didn't like being an employee at a larger company.

- More likely this is the "typical postpartum depression that naturally follows even the most successful of exits" (he links to his own essay on identity and sadness after selling).
- A founder leaving and returning to founder-style work does not prove the acquisition was the wrong choice at the time, for the founder, the employees or the products.

chunks.heading: Judge an acquisition by what happens to the employees, not only the founders
chunks.text:
Jason argues the "failure" view ignores everyone except the founders.

- Questions to ask: did employees get new opportunities they lacked before, better compensation and benefits, greater job stability and peace of mind?
- Most people don't have a founder's temperament for independence and risk. Some of them wanted those jobs.
- Investment by an acquirer can create more jobs, faster.
- He knows of quite a few acquisitions where nearly everyone stayed for years, where it was the right call in retrospect, where being part of a larger company opened growth and enhancement opportunities, and where employees made good money both at the acquisition and in compensation afterward.

chunks.heading: Bad outcomes happen at independent companies too
chunks.text:
Jason concedes some acquisitions go badly: the product is ruined, the culture is annihilated, jobs are destroyed, or it is "an unmitigated disaster."

- But all of those things also happen at independent companies.
- People quote statistics that most acquisitions fail, but forget that most independent startups also fail, or at least cease, over the same span of time used to measure acquisitions.
- The fair comparison is acquisition versus the real alternatives, not acquisition versus an idealized independent company that stays beloved by employees, customers and shareholders.

chunks.heading: Examples where acquisition was good
chunks.text:
Jason asks whether these were "really bad for everyone there":

- Google's acquisition of DoubleClick.
- Google's acquisition of YouTube.
- eBay's acquisition of PayPal.
- The hundreds of small companies that weren't "killing it" as much as their hype and Twitter feeds suggested, but whose people now sit on solid teams with nice stock options in successful tech companies.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jason Cohen argues that a big, profitable incumbent is a better target than it looks, because defending its revenue stream stops it from matching a cheaper, just-good-enough upstart. The exception is attacking a loss-leader, where the incumbent can outspend you and has nothing to lose.

chunks.heading: Why a large, profitable revenue stream is a competitor's weak point
chunks.text:
Jason argues that a big company with a large, growing, profitable revenue stream is easier to attack than it looks. "The profitable revenue stream is a prison." It is the "Achilles heel that allows the little guy to win."

A big profitable business also tells a startup three useful things:
- The market is large (otherwise the revenue wouldn't be large and growing).
- Customers will pay far more than cost for this product (otherwise there would be no profit).
- The abundance will probably last a while, because big profitable businesses usually die a slow, sagging death rather than disappearing overnight.

chunks.heading: Why the market is ripe for Innovator's Dilemma-style disruption
chunks.text:
- Jason says this combination invites disruption of the kind described in The Innovator's Dilemma.
- A startup with a new cost structure, new technology and new ideas can compete at 1/2 or even 1/10 of the incumbent's price.
- The product only has to be "just-good-enough" at that price.
- The startup's advantage is structural. It starts from a much lower cost base, so it can stay profitable at prices the incumbent can't match.

chunks.heading: Why the incumbent can't just cut prices
chunks.text:
Jason's core argument is that the incumbent's goal is to protect the profit stream at all costs, even at the expense of innovation or speed.

- Valuation rests on continued growth of revenue and earnings. He notes how fast a stock drops when Wall Street thinks future earnings are in jeopardy.
- Small top-line changes cause large profit changes. A company with a 20% profit margin that cuts prices 20% doesn't see its costs fall 20%, so profit drops to 0%.
- Even a 10% price cut halves profit, for an effect (slightly lower prices) that won't materially change the price conversation with customers.
- So when a startup cuts prices 50% or 80%, the big company cannot chase.

chunks.heading: How the incumbent actually responds
chunks.text:
- Jason says the incumbent asks: "If we're going to lose on price to the low end of the market, how can we charge *even more* on the top end, to make up for that lost business?"
- That strategy might work for the incumbent.
- Either way, the startup can grab 1/2 of the big company's low-end market share and still be profitable, because it began with a lower cost structure, new tech and a new business model.

chunks.heading: Why "growth over earnings" doesn't hold for big companies
chunks.text:
- Jason says sacrificing earnings for growth is a young company's game, played when the goal is to dominate a market before someone else does and set up decades of profitability.
- In real, at-scale companies, valuation is about total future earnings.
- Growth matters only because it leads to more earnings, not "growth for growth's sake."
- So a large incumbent is unlikely to burn profit to fight off a startup.

chunks.heading: The exception: never attack a loss-leader
chunks.text:
Jason warns that all of this applies only if you attack the product line that generates the profits. "If you're attacking a loss-leader, the situation is reversed."

- Big profitable companies often run unprofitable lines that the profitable unit funds.
- Examples he gives: Google's profitable search business funds Gmail. Amazon's retail business funded AWS, which he says was closing in on $10B in annualized revenue with 20% profit margins and now funds other projects.
- Attacking a loss-leader is a terrible strategy because the incumbent can use all its power and orders of magnitude more dollars, without needing a direct business model to justify it. He calls this "lots of resources and nothing to lose."
- Microsoft made Internet Explorer a loss-leader against Netscape and destroyed the company. This started only after Netscape was large and winning, so Jason says it wasn't Netscape's strategic error but a demonstration of what a profitable company that doesn't care about making money in a market can do.
- The reverse case: Google built a $1B business-applications line ("Docs") against Microsoft, because Office is the profitable line Microsoft can't cut prices on.

chunks.heading: Takeaway for picking a fight
chunks.text:
- Jason concludes that competing against a large, profitable, growing business "might be the smartest thing you can do."
- The condition is to hit them "where they're fat, not where they're able to beat you with their size."
- In practice: target the incumbent's profit-generating product line, undercut on price with a leaner cost structure, and avoid products the incumbent treats as loss-leaders.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jason Cohen argues that channels like AdWords and top-ranking SEO are zero-sum: winners lock out others, cost top dollar, and are capped in volume. Startups are better off investing in non-zero-sum channels like social, content, long-tail SEO and resellers, where success depends on yourself and the ceiling is the market itself.

chunks.heading: Zero-sum vs non-zero-sum marketing channels
chunks.text:
Jason defines a zero-sum channel as one where one company winning a piece of it locks competitors out of that piece.

- AdWords: "the price is set by the highest (dumbest?) bidder." The few companies in the good slots get the vast majority of clicks. The rest cannot get enough clicks to materially affect their sales.
- SEO for head terms: the top three results get nearly all the traffic. Even holding 10 slots ranked 11-30 doesn't add up to a fraction of what the winners get.
- Counter-example: social media. If company P has an awesome Twitter feed, company Q can have one too. P's great content doesn't stop Q from earning attention the same way.

chunks.heading: Why winning a zero-sum channel is usually a bad deal
chunks.text:
He acknowledges the tempting logic. Winning a zero-sum game has "double" value: you get the sale, and your competitors don't.

He argues the cost outweighs that, especially in auction-style channels:

- Winning means paying top dollar.
- Available inventory is limited (the top few slots in AdWords or SEO).
- So even if you win, growth in that channel is capped and expensive.

chunks.heading: Invest in non-zero-sum channels instead
chunks.text:
His recommended alternatives:

- Social media
- Long-tail SEO
- Brand-building
- Content
- Value-added resellers
- Cold-calling

Because these channels aren't winner-take-all, "the limit of the channel is closer to the limit of the market itself, rather than the sliver of the market which might reach you via a single advertising channel."

chunks.heading: Control: success depends on you, not a platform or a competitor
chunks.text:
Jason says that in non-zero-sum channels, "your success is dependent almost exclusively on yourself." It does not depend on:

- how an advertising platform works
- how much money a competitor is willing to lose

chunks.heading: Why this matters most for small companies
chunks.text:
- Smaller companies lack the money, consultants and in-house expertise that large or funded companies bring to "gladiator-style kill-or-be-killed arenas of zero-sum games."
- In the other games, "there's nothing the big guys can do to prevent you from shining."

chunks.heading: Focus on what you control
chunks.text:
Jason notes there are few things in startups a founder controls. He names three of them:

- The product
- Your culture
- Your voice online

His advice: "Take advantage of those when you can!"

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jason Cohen argues that founder-style "delegation" (do it, understand it, then hire someone to do it your way) yields a team no better than the founder. Real scale comes from hiring people better than you at every role, trusting teams to own outcomes, and building teams that themselves attract greatness, even replacing yourself as CEO.

chunks.heading: Delegation does not scale a company; hiring people better than the founder does
chunks.text:
- Jason argues that "delegation" does not scale a business. What does is "creating a team that is better than the current team. Including you."
- Founding a company is a selfish act, fueled by youth and energy. Founder skills (coding, design, salesmanship) are "probably right enough" early on.
- Those skills do not help build a 100-engineer team balancing quality and speed, an international sales team, a consistent global brand, or cash-flow management once the P&L is "(in millions)".
- Jason's job definition for any founder or manager: "hire people who are better than you at every position," because only then is the organization increasing its strength and abilities.

chunks.heading: Why the "do it myself, then hire someone to do it my way" model fails
chunks.text:
- The common founder pattern Jason says he followed himself when young and naïve:
  1. First I'll do it myself.
  2. Then I'll understand it.
  3. Then I'll hire and instruct a new person to do it the right way (my way).
- The result is "a team that is not materially better than the founder, at anything." The company is then never very good at more than one or two things.
- That is bad for the company, employees, customers, and ultimately the founder.
- He ties this to the idea that if you think a position isn't useful, it is because you have never worked with greatness in that position.
- Hiring someone who knows what you know and works like you work gets you a substitute for your own not-world-class performance. You are lucky to even get that; you might hire worse.

chunks.heading: Micromanaging hires is always bad management
chunks.text:
- Jason's logic: if you hire and then micromanage, or constantly "fix" what others do, you are a bad manager.
  - If the person is incapable, you hired the wrong person.
  - If the person is capable, you are getting in their way and wasting your time.
  - If the person isn't better than you, you aren't improving the organization.
  - If the person is better than you, micromanagement destroys that improvement, their morale, and your schedule.
- In every case, "it's bad management, and it's your fault."
- He quotes Steve Jobs: "It doesn't make sense to hire smart people and then tell them what to do. We hire smart people so they can tell *us* what to do."

chunks.heading: Delegation vs. team-building
chunks.text:
- Delegation: you still own the outcome, and someone else does the work. You assign away lesser jobs so you can be even more heroic, so it is still about you.
- Team-building: the team is trusted to own the work and its obligations, figures out and executes the details, and is responsible for raising its own expectations of itself.
- Jason's line: "You're still in charge, but the team is in command."
- At larger scale the goal is building teams that themselves grow and create greatness. The founder is not attracting, identifying and retaining greatness alone; the founder builds teams who do that. Jason calls this the best definition of "team-building."
- His conclusion: "Delegation isn't team-building, and thus it doesn't lead to scale, nor to greatness." Hiring "up" creates greatness and the space for scale.

chunks.heading: Bottlenecks and resilience
chunks.text:
- Under delegation you are still the bottleneck, just with a slightly wider neck.
- Team-building removes the bottleneck because the team can be as wide as needed. The best teams measure their own necks and decide how and when to widen further.
- It also derisks the company by moving it from brittle to resilient:
  - With delegation alone, if one person gets sick a deadline is missed, and if someone leaves a strategy is not executed.
  - With team-building there is group knowledge, so illness or departures are baked into the plan.

chunks.heading: Applying the rule to yourself, including stepping down as CEO
chunks.text:
- No one is exempt. A technical founder will readily agree she is not the best person to build a global sales organization.
- The harder test: even where she is excellent, it is still her job to find people who are more excellent, not just at individual tasks but at building entire teams.
- Jason did this multiple times at WP Engine, including no longer being the CEO.

chunks.heading: Managing people who are better than you
chunks.text:
- Jason acknowledges the consequence: leaders manage a set of people, all better qualified than the leader to do their jobs.
- He admits this is difficult (how you argue with them, how you earn their respect and confidence), but says it is the leader's job, because anything less "is by definition holding the company back."
- His bar: if you can't handle that, don't be a manager, a leader, or the CEO. The company and its employees deserve a real leader.
- The end state: convert the selfishness and egocentrism needed to start a company into an "egoless, outward facing, empowering, team-growing organization," where you are never the most knowledgeable and experienced person in the room because you've surrounded yourself with greatness, who each do the same.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jason argues resolutions fail and suggests asking yourself sharp, stage-specific questions instead. For bootstrappers, consultants, new startups, post-PMF and scale-phase companies, he lists the levers that matter: price, retention, marketing, focus, ICP alignment, hiring and unit economics.

chunks.heading: Self-questions beat resolutions, and the questions differ by company stage
chunks.text: Jason argues that New Year's resolutions don't work (he cites studies saying so). His alternative is to ask yourself good questions you haven't taken the time to ask, and to match the questions to your stage. He posed them in a December 2014 essay.

chunks.heading: Bootstrapper questions: double take-home profit without new hires
chunks.text:
- Core question: "How could you double your take-home profits without additional hires?"
- His hint for the usual answer:
  - Increasing price, not cutting costs.
  - Increasing retention, not expanding to new markets.
  - Better marketing, not more features.
- Saving money is wise, but not so much that it hurts the business. Ask what the single most impactful thing is that you could spend non-trivial money on.
- Example: you may be able to spend more than you think on paid marketing.
- Thought experiment: what would you do with an extra $50,000 in cash?
- If the answer is truly game-changing, consider making it real through crowd-funding, customer prepayments, or an angel investor "who won't drive you nuts".

chunks.heading: Consultant questions: force a doubling of rates
chunks.text:
- Core question: "If I forced you to double your rates, what would you have to do to justify it?"
- Prompts he gives:
  - How would your website be redesigned or rewritten?
  - Would you become more impersonal/corporate or more personal/boutique?
  - Would the service itself change, in what you deliver and when?
- Follow-up options:
  - Make some of those changes and actually raise rates.
  - Make some of them without raising rates, and win more business.
- Some changes may be relatively easy and enough to raise your rate by 50%.

chunks.heading: Small agency questions: avoid the consulting-company financial trap
chunks.text:
- Jason asks how a small agency can avoid the trap of being bigger than a single-person consultancy but still small.
- He points to ideas at the end of his article on consulting company accounting.

chunks.heading: Brand-new company questions: validate with money, honestly
chunks.text:
- Core question: "How can you get 20 people to give you $50?" He says to make sure you're asking that now.
- Be completely honest about what the market is saying, including price in the discussion.
- Work out the key thing that makes people buy.
- Consider whether you can position the same product better.
- Decide whether you're going broad/cheap or deep/expensive, and think through the implications.
- Check whether you're aggressively going after the first few customers or hanging back doing the easy stuff (product, coding, social, events).

chunks.heading: Post-product/market-fit, pre-scale questions: one focus and retention
chunks.text:
- Are you focused on the single most important thing that gets you to early scale, and do you know what it is?
- Is the whole company aligned to it, with no exceptions? His test: ask any employee what the one thing is that the company must do to succeed, and they should all give the same answer.
- Have you clarified your target customer and aligned marketing, sales, and product around it?
  - That may mean saying "no" to other interesting opportunities, including one-off features or consulting work.
- Are you aggressively discovering and removing barriers to sale?
- He adds that you should probably be doing something to increase retention.

chunks.heading: Scale-phase questions: what breaks in six months
chunks.text:
- Focus on the most important things. What is minor today will be trivial in three months. What is important but only a minor irritant today will become critical and massive in three months.
- Identify the "Rocks" that will move the needle and organize teams around them.
- Are you spending a seemingly disproportionate amount of time sourcing and hiring, finding "10xers"?
- Are you driving toward the unit economics needed to eventually be profitable?
- Ask: "What is going to be broken in six months and thus needs to be addressed today?"

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jason Cohen argues that comparing your startup to Instagram, WhatsApp or Slack, or even to averages, breeds needless depression and bad decisions. The better question is what the best move is for your own company given your specific challenges, and whether a metric change is the right trade for you, your customers and your employees.

chunks.heading: Comparing yourself to other startups is the wrong yardstick
chunks.text:
Jason argues that measuring your company against other startups produces envy and bad decisions, because the comparison set is always distorted. His example is the run of headline exits and valuations around 2014:

- Instagram sold for a billion dollars with 13 employees, about $77,000,000 per employee, after roughly two years and with $0 in revenue.
- WhatsApp sold for 19 billion dollars with 55 employees, about $345,000,000 per employee, after four years.
- Slack was valued at over a billion dollars less than a year after launch, adding more than a million dollars of annual recurring revenue every month.

He notes that each new headline made founders feel worse, and that even Instagram's founder was told by pundits he had "totally missed this wave" once Instagram was said to be worth "$15B today minimum."

chunks.heading: Why outliers and extremes are useless as a benchmark
chunks.text:
- Jason says you "mustn't judge yourself with the yardstick of other companies, particularly not against the rarefied few who dwell in the extremities of reality."
- Comparing your worst fears (exaggerated negative) against the public façade of other people (exaggerated positive) and against media darlings guarantees you look bad.
- This leads to depression about your own results and, in his words, is "not a path to finding good answers."

chunks.heading: Why averages and medians don't fix it either
chunks.text:
- Measuring against the average or median is no better. Knowing the "average" company is at `P` while you're at `Q` tells you little.
- For any metric where you look worse, Jason says he can show another company in an even worse position on that metric that is extremely successful for other reasons.
- Founders then envy each other's strengths while ignoring their own, and get increasingly discouraged. He sums it up: "Sometimes, benchmarks aren't healthy."

chunks.heading: The better question to ask
chunks.text:
Instead of "how do I compare," Jason says to ask: "What is the best thing I can do for my company, with the specific challenges and benefits that I have in front of me?"

This applies to every metric he lists:

- valuations
- growth rates
- retention rates
- NPS scores
- early-stage uncertainty
- ratio of revenue to employee
- CAC
- cash burn
- LTV
- gross margin
- selling your company

chunks.heading: A decision test for any metric
chunks.text:
Rather than asking what the average or extreme is at some other company, Jason reframes it as: "Am I happy with this metric, and if I change it at the expense of other metrics, or of innovation, or of my lifestyle, or of my happiness, is that the right trade for me, for the company, for my customers, and for my employees?"

- Change a metric only if the trade is right for you, the company, customers, and employees.
- If you can answer yes across all of those, "you have your answer."

chunks.heading: Learn to reason about your own situation
chunks.text:
- Jason says that if you aren't sure how to reason this way, "that is your next big challenge."
- Without confidence in reasoning about yourself, you have no choice but to fall back on comparing your fears to others' public image, which he ties to impostor syndrome rather than good decision-making.
- His closing frame: you're the captain of your ship, navigating your own waters. "Don't forget it."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jason argues early startups should not spread thin across many marketing channels. Successful companies find one channel that works and exhaust it before adding others. Pick that channel from the few you personally use and understand, because social channel success depends on natural resonance with its culture.

chunks.heading: Go deep on one marketing channel you already understand
chunks.text:
Jason argues early startups win by concentrating on a single marketing channel, not by spreading across many. Founders who spread thin rarely get off the ground.

- Successful founders almost never say they ran many channels that each "worked a little bit" and added up to a river.
- Spreading "precious money and even more precious time over many channels doesn't get a company off the ground."
- The usual pattern is that a company finds **one channel that really works**, then plumbs it to its maximum inventory before layering on additional channels.
- The goal on that channel is to double the business, not to dabble.

chunks.heading: How to pick the one channel
chunks.text:
Jason says "spray and pray" is a poor way to find the answer. Start instead with the handful of channels you personally use and understand.

- If you are a Twitter person, spend a few months building a corporate Twitter presence and buying Twitter ads. This holds even if you rarely use Facebook and can't see the appeal of Pinterest.
- If you think Twitter is "all trash and politics" but find Pinterest full of appealing visuals, build shareable images and buy Pinterest ads.
- Test the channel for a few months, focused on one channel at a time.

chunks.heading: Why personal fit with a channel matters
chunks.text:
Jason's reasoning is that success in social marketing channels comes from resonance between your personality and the norms and language of that channel.

- The best chance of resonance is when it arises naturally.
- Resonance doesn't come from A/B testing a persona. His example is agonizing over whether to be "more humorous and sarcastic or more serious and profound" on Twitter.
- If a channel's culture baffles you, you won't just jump in and develop a presence that resonates with people you are "predisposed to despise at worst and just not understand at best."
- His example is someone who finds Facebook culture fake: people pretending to be "thoughtfully happy and thoughtlessly witty" while privately feeling they fall short of their friends.

chunks.heading: Stay in your comfort zone, but don't spread thin
chunks.text:
Jason's summary rule: "stay with what you know, where you're comfortable, and focus on doubling your business on that channel."

- "Sometimes, getting outside your comfort zone is wrong."
- "Spreading yourself thin is even more wrong."
- Add further channels only after the first one is exhausted (see his related essay on low-budget marketing and maximum inventory).

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jason Cohen applies the Lindy Effect to startup growth: however big you are, you can probably double by doing what you already do, but 10x needs new channels, innovation, or hyper-growth. He explains why early tactics don't scale and why investors fixate on fast growth.

chunks.heading: Growth doubles by assumption but 10x has to be proven (the Lindy Effect applied to startups)
chunks.text:
Jason borrows the Lindy Effect: for non-perishable things like technology, companies, books and ideas, the expected remaining lifespan is about twice the current age. Applied to a project with an unknown endpoint, "on average, you're halfway there." He ties this to Tom Cargill's line: "The first 90% of the code accounts for the first 90% of the development time. The remaining 10% of the code accounts for the other 90% of the time."

His startup version of the rule: "However large you've gotten, you can probably double it." If you have 10 customers, you can probably get another 10 the same way. Most companies that reach 10 customers never reach 2000.

- Doubling sounds plausible because you've done it once and can do it again, even faster.
- 10x or 100x is not obvious at all.
- "You get 2x by assumption but 10x you have to prove." If you're raising money, you actually have to prove it.

chunks.heading: Why 2x is easy but 10x needs innovation
chunks.text:
The actions that got you the first 10 customers are probably not enough to get 100, though they can probably get another 10. His summary: "You can probably double your size by doing what you're already doing, but 10x will require innovation."

Examples of tactics that don't scale 10x:
- Scratching and clawing through your social network for the first 10 customers does not scale to 100.
- Converting customers one at a time through hour-long Zoom calls does not mean you can convert 100 no-sales-touch customers via Google ads.

The alternative to innovation is time and luck. Time means waiting a long time for the existing mechanism to keep working. Luck means nothing stops the slow, predictable growth: the channel doesn't saturate and get worse, no new competitors arise, market conditions don't make the product less desirable, and the economy doesn't slow. He calls this possible but unlikely in the fast-moving world of tech.

chunks.heading: Marketing channels have limited inventory
chunks.text:
Jason's channel version of the argument:
- If one marketing channel got you to 1000 customers, it can surely produce another 1000.
- It's unlikely that channel holds 10x the inventory to reach 10,000 customers.
- You will need other channels to work, which is hard, and to reach 10x you'll probably need multiple new channels.
- Possible, but not with the confidence you have in 2x.

He links this to his separate essay on exponential growth and channel inventory.

chunks.heading: Hard ceilings on 10x
chunks.text:
At some point 10x is strictly impossible.

- **High end:** market size limits and running out of acquisition channels. Facebook has 2B users and there aren't 20B humans. GoDaddy's customer growth rate was 13% per year since 2009 (per its SEC filing); at that rate it would take 18 years to 10x, assuming market size and conditions even allowed it.
- **Low end:** maybe there is no market, or the market doesn't want the product at a profitable price. You can squeeze out some early sales, but it can't get substantially bigger.

**2024 editor's note on GoDaddy:** annual revenue in 2014 was just under $1B and in 2024 is about $4B. It did not 10x, and did not even 5x, over ten years. GoDaddy also expanded into several additional product lines; had it done "what we've always done," growth would have been even lower.

chunks.heading: How to prove 10x: very fast growth
chunks.text:
Jason's first answer to "how do you prove something we agreed is unlikely" is very fast growth.

- If you're doubling every six months, you clearly have line-of-sight to more than 2x. The trajectory shows intense market demand coupled with an ability to find and serve it.
- If the underlying market is large or growing, you have a good case that 10x is within reach, and innovation could potentially get 100x or 1000x.
- Companies that showed this growth at "interesting size" went on to 100x or 1000x thereafter.
- "Interesting size" does not mean going from 10 customers to 20 in six months and being proud of "rapid growth." Going from 1000 to 2000 in six months is more like it.
- Example: his company WP Engine experienced hyper-growth after hitting $1M ARR and reached 100x that six years later.

This is why investors, and founders who want to build enormous companies, fixate on hyper-growth. He says it's the only way to have even the potential of building something enormous. He adds that "exponential growth" is a misnomer for it.

chunks.heading: How to break the Lindy Effect: change something substantial
chunks.text:
Jason's second answer is to change something substantial, which he thinks of as expanding into an adjacency.

- Keep one foot planted in the areas where you're already strong.
- Expand into something new and risky, with much higher upside than incremental improvement on the existing business.

He notes that not everyone wants to build a company serving a million customers or expand just for growth, and they shouldn't have to. Even so, the Lindy Effect helps you see what will be easy (doubling with what you already do) and what will require something new (10x and beyond).

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jason Cohen argues price isn't an afterthought but core business design, tied to brand, product, buyer, and go-to-market. He walks through each order of magnitude ($0 to $100,000/mo) and what it forces on support, sales, funding, and product, and says to discuss price in customer interviews.

chunks.heading: Price is business design, not an afterthought
chunks.text:
Jason argues that pricing "cannot be 'figured out later,' because it determines your business model today." He sees price as "inextricably linked to brand, product, and purchasing decisions" (by whom, why, how, and when). It is not a supply/demand curve slapped on after the product exists. It shapes the nature of the product and the structure of the company that builds it.

- Price is as important as any feature in deciding product/market fit.
- Typical failures he lists: people say "it would be great if someone did X" but won't buy at $700; app reviews hung up on $0.99 vs $1.99; users stuck on an inferior product they can't afford to upgrade; users stuck on freemium who refuse to pay anything; buyers stuck with an expensive, inferior product bought on salesmanship ("expensive must mean it's better") rather than craftsmanship.

chunks.heading: Bring price into customer development interviews
chunks.text:
Jason disagrees with the common advice not to mention price in customer interviews. That advice says price diverts talk to budgets and away from the customer's day-to-day pain. He wants price discussed like any other feature.

Questions he suggests asking:
- What do they expect it to cost, and why?
- Who would write the check, and who would need to approve it?
- Would an ROI argument be welcomed or scoffed at?
- What would need to change (if anything) to justify doubling your price? If there is an answer, maybe you should double it.

He closes with: "Price is not an afterthought, it is essential business design."

chunks.heading: $0/mo and $1/mo: growth over revenue
chunks.text:
**$0/mo**
- The goal is to maximize growth (trust and usage), not revenue.
- The product has natural tripwires that trigger other pricing (freemium), or the business model is "left as an exercise to your future self."
- Typically needs venture funding because there is no income, and success demands lots of people and tech.
- Even efficient outliers raised tens of millions: WhatsApp (sold for $19B with 55 employees) and Instagram (sold for $1B with 13 employees).
- Often B2C, since value is in quantity and there are 100x more consumers than businesses.

**$1/mo**
- You can't afford customer service, and running the technology must be nearly free. So the product must be simple enough to be self-service.
- Marketing and sales spend is nil, at least initially. It needs a reason to spread by word of mouth, ideally virally as a natural result of using it, or via vocally passionate early users, perhaps galvanized around a mission.

chunks.heading: $10/mo: the slow bootstrapped slog
chunks.text:
- Customers see you as a cheap version of something else, yet still expect a phone number (his example: GoDaddy).
- Bootstrapped businesses can make it work (e.g. most shared hosting companies), but only make interesting money at scale. By his math, it takes over 8,000 customers to make just $1m/yr.
- You can reach tens of millions in revenue, but it takes about 10 years.
- To scale faster you need venture funding, because revenue is anemic and you can't afford to advertise.
- Bootstrapped companies at this price often boast of having no marketing or sales departments. Jason says the truth is they can't afford them, so they grow slowly and are often eclipsed by competitors who can grow 10x faster. In a huge market there is still room for everyone.
- Upside: people forget they have a $10/mo service even if they don't use it. That "free revenue" can be substantial at scale, as with shared hosting.

chunks.heading: $100/mo: the sweet spot for bootstrappers
chunks.text:
- Customers expect to be able to call support. If a competitor is substantially better, switching is probably worth the effort.
- Almost exclusively B2B unless it's a "luxury" item.
- Big companies buy it with little consideration. Small companies need to understand the value, so you may need sales material and a demo.
- Jason says he loves this zone for bootstrapped companies: low enough to address a broad business market, high enough to become "nicely profitable" with a reasonable, achievable number of customers (e.g. 200-300), and you can afford to spend money acquiring them.

chunks.heading: $1,000/mo: mid-market and the sales burden
chunks.text:
- Only medium to large companies can afford it. They have buying processes: annual budgets, approvals, ROIs, demos.
- You'll be compared to alternatives and weighed, and you'll be asked for a discount.
- You need to be part of that conversation: a real sales force, sales materials, impressive logos, case studies, referenceable customers.
- Features may need to include big-company requirements like role-based access privileges and LDAP integration.
- He calls it a "surprisingly difficult zone to become profitable in," because the sales, marketing, and engineering costs match those of much larger deals without the attendant revenue.

chunks.heading: $10,000/mo and $100,000/mo: enterprise
chunks.text:
**$10,000/mo**
- Larger companies only. The product is unlikely to be sufficient out of the box, so you may need in-house professional services or consulting partners to build the "Whole Product" (Geoffrey Moore's term).
- If something goes wrong, they'll cancel and won't pay out the rest, "no matter what your contract says; what are you going to do, sue your customers?"
- Mid-sized companies can reach this price if it's usage-based (his examples: ZenDesk, JIRA, Box, Slack) or performance-based (e.g. marketing optimization). Then the product must create and demonstrate value to earn it.

**$100,000/mo**
- Global 2000 only. Large projects need multiple departments to decide and approve.
- Sales cycles run 9-18 months, which requires a massive cash outlay while you wait.
- Likely starts as a pilot or proof of concept, ideally paid, and it must succeed convincingly, perhaps against another vendor's pilot.
- Needs on-site visits even in the video-conferencing era.
- Examples: WorkDay (much of its revenue is consulting) and IBM.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jason Cohen uses the Ship of Theseus and Lao Tzu to argue that everything in a startup changes except its values, so values define its purpose. Written values, lived and signed by everyone, let any employee act like an owner without approval chains. Financial success is the means, not the end.

chunks.heading: The "ship of Theseus" test for startups: what stays constant is the essence
chunks.text:
- Jason argues that nearly everything about a startup changes over time: product features, marketing copy (molded by A/B testing), team composition, metrics (by orders of magnitude), logo, name, and office space.
- He uses the Tao Te Ching's "emptiness creates function" idea and the ship-whose-boards-all-rot-and-get-replaced puzzle to frame it. The "emptiness" a ship, a person, or a company creates is its essence.
- His example: is a company of 2 people and 150 customers the "same company" as one with 150 people and 25,000 customers? Tangibly no, but "in its emptiness lies the essence and purpose" of the people in it.
- The founder's key question: "What is constant? What doesn't change as we grow, and thus what binds us together in this journey?" Whatever the answer is "defines the startup and its purpose."
- That answer also resolves why anyone, employees or customers, should join the founder and share this "very personal responsibility."

chunks.heading: Core values as the constant: WP Engine's "inviolable constitution"
chunks.text:
- At WP Engine, Jason calls the constants "values", described as an "inviolable constitution". When a tough decision comes up, the values determine the outcome.
- Concrete examples he gives:
  - If a choice is between losing money and doing what's right for the customer, WP Engine does what's right for the customer.
  - If someone is exceptionally skillful at their job but dishonest, or works for himself instead of the team, WP Engine will always fire that person.
- Values are the tiebreaker for hard tradeoffs, not decoration, so they must be able to override short-term money and individual talent.

chunks.heading: Values are how you empower everyone to act like an owner
chunks.text:
- Jason says a clear agreement on core values "is how you empower everyone in the company to act like an owner."
- Example: can someone in their first week of tech support decide to give a customer a large refund, or spend extra hours going above and beyond to fix something? If the values clearly point to that being right, they can decide without approval chains, meetings, or debates.
- He treats this as the definition of empowerment and as part of the solution to scaling, since decisions no longer have to route through founders.

chunks.heading: Write the values down and get real buy-in
chunks.text:
- Jason says it is "so important to encode your company's values on paper."
- At WP Engine they literally put the values on the wall and everyone signed it, like the US Declaration of Independence.
- Agreement must go beyond a condition of employment or values memorized because of an external requirement. The goal is that people "in their bones" already embody the values, so they naturally keep propagating them to those around them and to those who follow.

chunks.heading: Culture is the output of living your values
chunks.text:
- Jason defines "Company Culture" as "the output of living your values."
- It's never perfect, for individuals or the organization. At any moment the company falls short on some aspect of its culture while aspirationally trying to live up to its own expectations. He says that is healthy.

chunks.heading: Financial success is the means, not the end
chunks.text:
- Jason's first three companies, before WP Engine, were "successful enough", yet he never thought about culture or values and calls that a mistake. Two still exist and have kept growing for nearly two decades.
- His critique: without a higher purpose, a truly important mission for customers, and dedication to employees, "maybe who cares?"
- He questions what that success actually created: were people happy and empowered, mentoring and being mentored, building careers they're proud of, feeling their time wasn't wasted? He admits he doesn't know, and calls that sad.
- His position: "Financial success is the means, not the ends." Financial success is absolutely necessary because without it the company isn't sustainable, but money doesn't make you happy or other people happy, and doesn't lead to a fulfilling, meaningful life.
- He closes by saying you've done something important with your life, and for others' lives, if you answer what does create fulfillment through your culture and values, and he asks founders: "What is your emptiness?"

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Using Depeche Mode's Rose Bowl peak as a cautionary tale, Cohen argues that tying success to a single outcome (an exit, a metric, a funding round) almost guarantees failure and unhappiness. Keep score with metrics and money, but make the years of building the point. It also helps recruit people who want to join the journey.

chunks.heading: Success comes from valuing the journey, not hitting a peak outcome
chunks.text:
Jason argues that startup success cannot be guaranteed by any specific result. It can only be guaranteed by how you define success. His claim: "If you value the journey, your 'success' is guaranteed."

- The Depeche Mode story is his proof. The band sold out the Pasadena Rose Bowl (capacity 60,000) on the 101st show of their 1988 tour. Critics expected humiliation, and the band themselves hoped to sell only the 10,000 floor seats. Instead it sold out, with paid attendance above any Rose Bowl event in the prior eight years.
- Backstage, singer Dave Gahan cried because he didn't know if the group could ever do anything this great again. Jason notes they never did, despite more hits, albums and tours.
- His lesson: "reaching the peak means by definition your next steps must be downhill." The peak is fleeting and often unhappy.

chunks.heading: Why a single "moment of success" is a trap
chunks.text:
- The same pattern hits founders. Jason cites well-documented sadness and even depression right after an exit.
- The mistake is believing "the goal is to achieve a single moment of success": a big sale, an IPO, or passing the company to your daughter.
- His reframe: "it is the building, not the result of that building, that matters."
- The math: about 99.99% of your time is the journey and 0.01% is basking in "success" (a sale, ringing the bell at an IPO). Often that moment never comes, so it is 100% journey.

chunks.heading: How to define winning
chunks.text:
Jason's test is a retrospective one. You win if you can look back and say:

- It was a wonderful time and you'd do it again.
- You'd change some things, but you're proud and stronger and wiser than ever.
- You created terrific jobs where great people were empowered to build important things together.
- They were comfortable and safe, shared in whatever upside you could muster, and would say they're personally fulfilled too.

chunks.heading: The cost of outcome-based definitions of success
chunks.text:
- If success is tied to metrics, money, growth rate, headcount, whether you exited, how much you raised, or how many users you got, "mathematically you're almost guaranteed to fail."
- The failure comes only from your own definition of failure.
- You end up spending years in nervous agony chasing an outcome you think will make you happy, instead of "making all those years be the years you are happy."

chunks.heading: Keep score, but don't confuse the game with life
chunks.text:
- Jason is explicit that he is not anti-money. He made plenty from previous startups and hopes to make more at WP Engine, where all employees are shareholders, as are the investors.
- Honoring metrics is part of building a high-performing team and a huge, sustainable enterprise. There is nothing wrong with using metrics and money to keep score.
- The rule: "Keep score, so long as you can distinguish between the game and life."
- Enjoy the journey alongside the score: generating happy customers, launching unique products, and gathering the energy and brainpower of brilliant people tackling interesting problems.

chunks.heading: Journey focus solves the hiring and recruiting riddle
chunks.text:
- Jason paraphrases Peter Thiel: the first employee joins because it's the ground floor of an exciting startup, but why will the 20th person join? Or the 200th?
- His answer: "To be part of the journey."
- So valuing the nature of the journey is also what makes a company attractive to the people it needs to hire as it grows, and it is why the founder should be there too.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jason Cohen explains why startups' "win-win" distribution proposals get ignored by larger companies: a one-time revenue sliver is immaterial and costs the big company its reputation. Good biz dev brings the big company new customers in its existing business model, or generates material, repeating revenue (2%+ of top line).

chunks.heading: Why startup biz dev proposals fail: the "1% for one month" math
chunks.text:
Jason (founder of WP Engine, which serves millions of websites for hundreds of thousands of paying customers) gets weekly emails from startups proposing a "win-win" deal. In his words, "approximately zero have resulted in a successful deal."

- The standard pitch: the startup has fresh product, the big company has distribution. Trade innovation for distribution.
- The big company emails its customer base, generates "easy sales at no cost," and the revenue is split.
- Jason says this is never accepted. The startup's equation leaves out a cost to the big company: its reputation.

chunks.heading: Why distribution-for-innovation pitches look attractive but aren't
chunks.text:
- Jason defines distribution as "getting in front of potential customers," and calls it the hardest thing for a young startup.
- Big companies have solved distribution (his proof: 100,000 paying customers). They struggle with innovation because scale makes it hard to keep building things people love while delivering quickly with extra requirements.
- Each side's weakness maps onto the other's strength, which "feels like the kernel of a deal."
- The startup assumes big companies are hunting for excuses to up-sell their base and lack up-sell material. That assumption leads to the doomed proposal.

chunks.heading: The WP Engine math: a plugin sale is worth roughly 8 hours of revenue
chunks.text:
- Typical inbound pitch: a WordPress plugin or theme maker with a $20, $50 or $200 product wants to market it to WP Engine customers, framed as a service to those customers.
- Jason runs deliberately optimistic numbers: 1% of the customer base converts, and WP Engine gets $50 per sale (higher than the typical offer).
- WP Engine's 2014 plans ran from $29/mo to $99/mo or more, so he assumes an average of $50/mo (the true average is higher; this keeps the math simple).
- Result: 1% of customers each give one extra month of revenue. That is a 1% revenue boost for one month only. The next month there is no boost.
- "By definition a company earns 1% of their monthly revenue in about 8 hours." A one-time 8-hour revenue bump isn't interesting to a company of any size. It's "not enough to even discuss or negotiate."
- The price of that bump is spamming the customer base.

chunks.heading: The test: grow the big company the way it already makes money
chunks.text:
Jason's core question for any biz dev proposal:

- "How can the smaller company make money for the larger company *in the manner that the larger company already makes money?*"
- Restated: how can you grow the larger company in a way that matches its existing business model?
- Applied to WP Engine: how can you create new hosting customers for WP Engine?

chunks.heading: Worked example: send your customers to the big company
chunks.text:
- Instead of selling to WP Engine's customers, the plugin or theme maker asks their own customers whether they'd like hosting too, maybe with a limited-time discount.
- A couple of dozen new hosting customers per month can "move the needle." The reason is not the size of overall growth. It's that the revenue repeats month after month.
- Even a small customer may refer others, and Jason says WP Engine can see that value even if it doesn't track it.
- That arrangement makes it easy to justify announcing to WP Engine customers that there is a new partner "optimized for our hosting platform, both in code and in business," worth serious consideration.
- His summary: bring customers to a big company, even a few, rather than "milking their existing customers for a sliver of revenue."

chunks.heading: Criteria for a deal that can actually work
chunks.text:
- Pursue a deal that brings the big company new customers, or one that produces material revenue in a way that fits how it already earns.
- Jason's threshold for "material": 2% or more of the larger company's top-line revenue, and repeating, not one-time.
- He admits this is hard to find, "that's why most biz dev deals don't work."
- Meeting these criteria is what makes a real win-win possible, and might "mint your company."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jason Cohen uses WP Engine's 1,000+ servers to show that scale turns rare failures into daily events and strains how you handle them with customers. Automation helps but cannot replace human support or forensic engineering, so founders projecting growth must budget well beyond linear costs.

chunks.heading: Scale turns rare events into daily events
chunks.text:
- Jason's core claim: "scale causes rare events to become common." Things that happened once in a blue moon with 50 servers happen every week or every day with 2,000.
- Worked example from WP Engine, which ran over 1,000 servers hosting hundreds of thousands of websites in 2014 (he later notes it now runs about twenty times as many).
- Suppose a server suffers one fatal failure every three years (kernel panic, both power supplies failing). That is normal, not a quality problem to "fix."
- Three years is about 1,000 days, so with 1,000 servers there is one fatal server error every single day.
- On top of that come about 10 minor incidents with degraded performance, DDoS attacks in the data center, and other events that set pagers buzzing and mobilize Customer Support.
- A shrug and a manual reboot every six months is an appropriate "process" at small scale. At large scale the same event needs a real process.

chunks.heading: Scale changes how you handle problems, not just how many you have
chunks.text:
- A dozen minor and major events a day means 20-50 customers affected every day.
- Notifying 50 customers a day breaks down quickly. Some contact emails are out of date, so those customers are not told.
- Some of those customers notice anyway, create extra support load, or post on Twitter that their site was slow or down and WP Engine "didn't even know it."
- The social media team then has to piece the story together, respond, and perhaps arrange a special phone call.
- Affected customers are more likely to leave a bad review. The 99.99% who had no incident have no reason to decide "today is the day I will go to a review site and leave a good review."
- So rare events create far more downstream work than operational fixes alone suggest.

chunks.heading: Fast onboarding makes every incident a first impression
chunks.text:
- With 1,000 new customers a month, any given server issue probably hits a customer who has been around only a month or two.
- That produces a "bad first impression," which is harder to repair than an incident for a three-year customer who has "built up a bank account of patience."
- Customer age mix is therefore part of how scale amplifies problems.

chunks.heading: "Automate everything" is true but incomplete
chunks.text:
- Jason calls "automate everything" a knee-jerk response with truth in it. Without automated monitoring you are blind, and without automated problem-solving you are overwhelmed.
- Some things cannot be automated:
  - A knowledgeable, friendly customer support team.
  - Responding to a complaint on social media.
  - Recruiting, training, rapport, culture and "downright *caring*" in teams awake 24/7/365, from support chat multitasking to clear phone communication to logging into servers and fixing issues fast.
- Rare things cannot be fully automated away, even technical ones. They are hard to define, so hard to monitor, and hard to repair without the forensic skills of a human engineer.

chunks.heading: Better per customer, harder in aggregate
chunks.text:
- Any one customer has fewer problems per year than a year earlier, because processes, automation, hardware and human service keep improving.
- The difficulty shows up across the whole company: the effort needed to manage the worst-case experience grows non-linearly, not just the average experience.
- This explains why people complain about a company daily on Twitter while you have never had an issue with it. "Rare" means you probably never saw it, but at scale someone experiences it every day.
- Jason says this is no excuse for high-scale companies to have problems: "if we're not constantly improving on all fronts, the scale will catch up and overtake us."

chunks.heading: Budgeting for growth in early-stage companies
chunks.text:
- A projection of 5x growth against 5x costs (or 3x costs, assuming savings at scale) is "guessing low."
- Plans that show 5x growth without budgeting for new hires in security, technical automation and specialized customer service areas are "heading for an ugly surprise."
- He also says to hire managers and executives who have been down this path before, "battle-hardened" with playbooks for tackling these problems.
- With high growth the surprise arrives quickly, and recovery means acting twice as fast again to climb out of the hole and then get ahead of it.
- His summary elsewhere: scaling is hard.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jason argues that a normal 24-hour day leaves room for roughly two time-consuming "Big Things" (job, kids, spouse, social life, major hobby, startup). Trying to hold three means one or more suffers, and you can't escape the limit by cutting sleep or by believing you're an exception.

chunks.heading: You have a fixed time budget, so only two Big Things fit
chunks.text:
- Jason's rule: "You can have two 'Big Things' in your life, but not three."
- The reason is time. The 1950s-style split of a 24-hour day is 8 hours for work, 8 for home and commute, and 8 for sleep and ablutions. Work and home are the two things that can each take 40+ hours a week.
- That 40+ hours a week is what it takes to tackle something huge: a career, a parent, a startup.
- Weekends, vacations and sick days don't add up to enough concentrated time to carry off something like a startup without making work or home suffer.
- "Work" and "home" are placeholders. If you're unattached, "home" doesn't occupy significant time, so something else can take that slot.

chunks.heading: What counts as a Big Thing
chunks.text:
- Job
- Kids
- Spouse
- Social life
- Major hobby (his examples: building a boat in the garage, becoming a chess master, a video game addiction)
- Startup

He lists kids and spouse separately. Young kids strain marriages because there isn't enough time to invest in the kids and also be there for each other.

chunks.heading: What happens when you try for three
chunks.text:
- Founders who run a startup on the side while holding a day job: "your family will never see you. You might even lose your family. It happens."
- This is partly why Jason says it's easier to start a company before you have a family or even a spouse.
- A job plus a social life works only if your spouse is fully integrated into, and agreeable to, that social life. Otherwise there's strife ("Going out with the guys *again?*").
- People of both genders try to "have it all", but "it's never true." At most two function well and the rest do not.
- More often, one thing gets most of the energy and the rest suffers.

chunks.heading: Why sleep is not a lever
chunks.text:
- Sleep takes the same kind of time commitment, but it isn't on the list of options.
- Cutting sleep doesn't work, because then you can't function at a high level at anything.

chunks.heading: Don't assume you're the exception
chunks.text:
- Jason's line: "No, you are not an exception. That's egotistical self-deception." He applies this both to sleep and to the number of Big Things.
- His test: ask the people around you whether they think you're failing at one of your Big Things.
- His conclusion: "Time to decide which two."

chunks.heading: Decision rule for founders
chunks.text:
- Before starting a company, count your current Big Things. A startup is one, so it leaves room for only one other.
- If you already have a job, a spouse and kids, a startup makes three and something will break, usually family or the startup.
- If you're single and unattached, a startup plus a job (or a startup plus a social life) is workable because "home" takes little time.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jason Cohen argues that investors are right to say "raise more than you think you need." Any deviation from plan, whether revenue grows slower or faster, requires more cash than the base plan. Since you can't predict finances 18 months out, raising only the planned amount creates a cash crunch 9-12 months in.

chunks.heading: Cash needs are always higher than the plan says, and deviation in either direction is the reason
chunks.text:
Jason argues that a business always takes more money than you expect, even when you account for that fact. He frames it as a version of Hofstadter's Law: "It always takes longer than you expect, even when you take into account Hofstadter's Law." His version: "A business always takes more money than you expect, even when you take this fact into account."

- He says the standard investor advice, "Always raise more money than you think you need," is correct, and that it is not a ruse by greedy investors chasing extra equity.
- The only way you need exactly the amount you planned for is if everything over the next 18 months goes exactly to plan.
- A deviation in either direction, better or worse, means you need more money.

chunks.heading: How the original funding number is built, and why it is a floor
chunks.text:
Jason describes what a founder has on day one: a business plan with a plausible growth trajectory (neither too conservative nor too optimistic) and a cost structure for driving signups and serving customers.

- It costs money to acquire a customer, but the monthly revenue takes time to cover that cost. Costs therefore rise faster than revenue, and a cash investment funds the gap.
- The plan yields a projected cash low-point of $X. You then raise $Y, which covers the operational cash requirement and also de-risks the company with additional investments you couldn't otherwise afford.
- That $Y is built on one plausible scenario. It is a floor, not a buffer.

chunks.heading: Scenario 1: growth is slower than planned, so you need more money
chunks.text:
Jason walks through what happens if revenue lags the plan nine months in.

- You have already signed a 5-year office lease and hired support, sales and engineering. You have also brought in training, a comptroller and a business operations person.
- Marketing is over-spending to try to kick-start growth, so you burn more than expected.
- His position is that the correct move is to forge ahead and let revenue catch up, "not fire half your team and retreat."
- Holding that course costs more cash than the plan assumed.

chunks.heading: Scenario 2: growth is faster than planned, so you also need more money
chunks.text:
Success also consumes cash, which Jason treats as the counterintuitive half of the argument.

- You scramble to hire ahead in support, sales and engineering. You trade money for speed through recruiting, contractors, office space and finance.
