- Customer on-boarding costs arrive faster than planned. Over the long run the revenue more than makes up for them, but right now these unexpected new customers cost much more than their revenue contributions, and cash reserves plummet.
- If sales and marketing is working, you want to spend more on it too (he links this to his annual prepay essay).
- Both outcomes end in the same place: "you'll need more money than you planned."

chunks.heading: Why under-raising is irresponsible
chunks.text:
Jason's point is that no one can predict a startup's finances 18 months out with precision, and that this is fine because founders aren't supposed to.

- The failure is denying that uncertainty. Not raising "more than enough" money means "you're denying that reality."
- The result is a time-pressured cash crunch for yourself 9-12 months from now, which he calls irresponsible.
- Practical takeaway: size the raise to cover plan variance in both directions (slower growth and faster growth), not just the plan's projected cash low-point.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jason Cohen argues that builders default to coding because they love it, yet startups fail on attention, marketing, positioning and selling, not code quality. He says to attack the high-risk, poorly understood business problems first: interview 50 customers and get daily website traffic.

chunks.heading: Builders build; businesses are built elsewhere
chunks.text:
- Jason argues that a technical founder's strength is also their weakness: love of creation. Builders wake up thinking about what to make, not how to sell, and open the editor before the to-do list or CRM.
- Most startups fail despite excellent coding and design. They fail because not enough people reach the home page, visitors don't try or pay, acquisition costs too much, nobody tells friends, or the product isn't solving a pain people know they have. None of those is "whether the code works or whether it looks good."
- He frames startup success as a Drake Equation of many things that all have to go right, and code is only one factor.
- Jason has "made millions of dollars on companies with hideously ugly websites and buggy code." Customers don't buy based on unit test coverage or font choice.
- He says coding and design are necessary but insufficient. He tells builders to force themselves out of their comfort zone and *mostly* do the other things that create a valuable business, while still doing some coding and design.

chunks.heading: Talk to fifty potential customers before building
chunks.text:
- Jason's first test of whether you're working on the right thing: have you talked to 50 potential customers? He means "*fifty*, not a dozen."
- Small samples mislead. After the first 10 interviews on one idea he thought he was onto something, but later interviews were less clear. The early people had been selected with accidental bias, obvious only in hindsight.
- Another time, everyone said it was a great idea and it wasn't. That only became clear after dozens of interviews.
- If finding that many people is hard, he says it will still be hard after you've built the product. At that point you've likely built the wrong product and wasted months. Solve the hard problem now.
- Vet the price in the same conversations and make sure people will actually buy. Otherwise the interview doesn't count.

chunks.heading: Get daily traffic before polishing the product
chunks.text:
- Jason's second test: are people coming to your website every day? Getting attention is "much harder and much more outside your control than building software."
- He poses a CTO choice: a company with 1,000 daily new, unique, qualified visitors and a buggy product, or one with a clean, stable product and 10 unique visits.
- His answer: you know you can fix the buggy product in the first case; nobody knows whether the second will ever be a real business.
- Staying nose-down in the code instead of getting attention builds the second case. He asks whether you're sure the market even exists.

chunks.heading: Attack the high-risk part first, like a hard module
chunks.text:
- Jason uses a coder's analogy. On a large development project you tackle the high-risk, poorly understood modules first, because you understand the rest and need time to pivot and re-plan if the unknowns fail.
- In a business, attention, marketing, positioning, selling and defining the problem are the high-risk, poorly understood part.
- All the coding and design is low-risk and well understood by comparison, so it should not get the first and biggest share of your time.
- His one-line prescription: "Put down the compiler and talk to customers."

chunks.heading: Peers still make the same mistake
chunks.text:
- Jason notes that the essay dates from 2013 and was used as a pep talk to kick off a Three-Day Startup challenge event.
- In 2024 he points to a tweet from Rob Walling and many successful bootstrapped founders agreeing that engineering founders still don't listen. He presents it as confirmation that the lesson is correct.
- He describes the pattern as a rite of passage that developers learn "in blood" by finding out for themselves. He asks whether you can learn it today, "just this once," without paying for it.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jason Cohen argues the "10x developer" idea understates reality: a great person in any role (developer, designer, writer, manager, support, product, sales) produces ideas and results that 100 average people never will. Because of this, he says you can't afford to hire anyone less than great.

chunks.heading: A top performer is infinitely better, not 10x better
chunks.text:
Jason rejects the saying that a great developer is 10x as productive as a mediocre one. He argues the real gap is larger, because great people produce ideas and work that no number of average people would produce.

- His test: "You can't put 100 average designers on a committee and get a fabulous design, right?"
- A great developer or designer is "better than an infinite number" of average ones, since they come up with ideas and implementations that 100 others wouldn't.
- He calls this "universal, timeless, human rule" and says it holds in every role, not just engineering.

chunks.heading: The same rule applies in every function
chunks.text:
Jason gives one example for each role, contrasting the great person with a crowd of average ones:

- **Writing (content marketing, social media):** a great writer versus 100 average bloggers.
- **Management:** a great manager who develops the careers of their people versus several average managers who are "glorified project managers."
- **Customer support:** a great rep thrilling customers and causing love on Twitter versus 100 others "answering tickets" who never evoke an emotional reaction.
- **Product management:** a PM who consistently drives brilliant output based on salability, instead of under-the-hood technical gymnastics.
- **Design and development:** the original case, where committees of average people cannot reproduce one great person's output.

He says that if you think any position at your company doesn't follow the "better than 10x" rule, "you've never worked with greatness at that position."

chunks.heading: Great salespeople are not revenue-acquisition robots
chunks.text:
Jason pushes back on modeling sales as robots with a "zombie-like drive to make phone calls," where a slew of barely productive closers may be financially inefficient but still gets the job done. He says that if you see it that way, you shouldn't be responsible for building the sales group.

What a great salesperson does instead:

- Produces "cheerleader customers" who are actually thrilled and referenceable after the sale.
- Excites the whole company about what's possible with growth, "the engine that makes everything else possible."
- Brings along people at every position and shares the corporate culture, rather than building a separate roost that feeds on leads bagged by marketing.

He says that if you think sales can't work this way, "you are the one with incorrect expectations," and he cites WP Engine as living proof that it can.

chunks.heading: Hiring conclusion: you cannot afford to hire less
chunks.text:
Because of this rule, Jason concludes that you can't afford to hire anyone less than great.

- If a competitor has the intent, the money and the story needed to hire great people and you don't, you must work out how your business will thrive anyway.
- He allows that this might be possible, but calls it "a special sort of optimization" and not one he would be excited to execute.
- His own preference is to work with the best, do amazing things together, and learn new things every day from them.
- His closing line: "Life's too short, and high tech moves too fast, to mess about with mediocrity."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jason Cohen argues the LTV metric blends three unstable variables (MRR, gross margin, cancellation) into one falsely precise number that drives confident but bad decisions. He recommends payback period and tracking MRR, cancellations, GPM and CAC individually, since those are short-horizon and actionable.

chunks.heading: Why Jason distrusts the LTV metric
chunks.text:
- Jason says a metric packs many causes and processes into one number. That makes it powerful for reasoning about complex systems, but it also hides error and uncertainty behind false precision.
- He argues the dangerous outcome is "the illusion of knowledge": you think you understand something you don't, and make bad decisions with confidence.
- His verdict: "For many SaaS businesses, the incorrectness of the LTV metric outweighs the value it supposedly confers."
- He says the rubric-style number always gives "8 decimal places" of precision even when those digits are all error and uncertainty.

chunks.heading: How LTV is defined and used
chunks.text:
- LTV is the total gross profit a customer will generate over its lifetime.
- Gross profit means income after the costs required to deliver the product (tech support and infrastructure for SaaS, cost of materials for physical products). It excludes sales and marketing, development and other costs of running the business.
- Formula: LTV = MRR x GPM x lifetime in months. Since lifespan is usually estimated from monthly cancellation, this becomes LTV = (MRR x GPM) / monthly cancellation rate.
- It is commonly used to cap customer acquisition cost (CAC). If CAC exceeds LTV, the business is unprofitable even at scale over ten years. If LTV = 3 x CAC, the business is unprofitable at first (months of revenue are needed to pay back CAC) but profitable in the long run.
- Jason notes that using LTV for a decision like this implies lifetime gross revenue is knowable today, and it isn't.

chunks.heading: Why the inputs to LTV can't be trusted
chunks.text:
Every component changes over time:

- **MRR:** moves with how systematic you are at upgrades, cross-selling, customers growing or shrinking, per-use charges, and the mix of customer segments.
- **GPM:** for small companies it can change by 30% in a year, and even large stable companies can move about 1% per year.
- **Cancellation rate:** hopefully shrinks as you improve the product and service, but over years it can swing with new competitors, a shrinking market, new technology, or a new customer mix when you grow into adjacent markets.
- Example: HubSpot famously had a low LTV that rose 3x in 18 months (documented in David Skok's SaaS metrics overview). That is a big swing in a metric meant to summarize the next ten years.
- His point: "Three variables, all changing, unpredictably, which you multiply together and.... you expect the result to *mean* something?"
- If LTV can vary 2x in a year through normal business activity, rules like "an LTV:CAC ratio of 3:1 is healthy" can't be trusted either. You may believe you're acquiring customers efficiently, then find your growth is capped or that you're not profitable even at scale.

chunks.heading: What to use instead: payback period
chunks.text:
- Every insight LTV promises can come from metrics that avoid long time horizons and point to actions you can take.
- For "what is a reasonable CAC?", he replaces "LTV/CAC should be at least 3, and 5 is very good" with payback period: p = CAC / MRR, the months until a single customer has paid back its acquisition cost.
- He prefers p = CAC / (MRR x GPM), which also accounts for the cost of serving the customer.
- Rule of thumb for payback:
  - 6 months is fine.
  - 3 months is fantastic.
  - 12+ months is poor, unless there is indirect strategic benefit (e.g. branding), efficiency is improving so you want to stick with it, or it is a mature company or one with larger business customers where you can justify assuming 5-10 years of revenue per customer.
- Payback period also explains why annual prepayment is smarter than it looks, and feeds other metrics he uses: COC (Cost Of Cancellation), showing how cancellation affects the cost of growth, and Max-MRR, showing how cancellation caps your maximum size. He says LTV leads to none of these insights.

chunks.heading: Why you need the components, not the blended number
chunks.text:
- A common defense is that LTV measures long-run dollars earned and should rise over time. Jason says that in practice you always need the individual components to know whether the company is healthy.
- Example 1: LTV is steady, but GPM is improving through cost-cutting while cancellations rise. He says this is not good: "Your customers are pissed."
- Example 2: MRR rises because you land larger customers, but GPM falls because you're inefficient at serving them. That is both good and bad news. It means you need efficiency work now, or you need to raise money so you can stay devoted to growth for the next few years.
- His conclusion: always measure MRR, cancellations, GPM and CAC individually. Combining them into one number "only serves to hide data, hide insights, not help 'get a handle on the business.'"

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: A reflective essay on the magic of landing the first customer and how founders become hooked on growth metrics. Cohen argues that obsessing over customer and employee happiness is the right path to financial results, but metric optimization can blind founders to bigger, truly innovative opportunities beyond the incremental.

chunks.heading: The first customer as "magic" you can't fully explain
chunks.text:
- Jason describes a new customer signing up as an almost impossible chain of improbable events: a frustrated person searching Google, landing on a site at position #7, being caught by a headline "for reasons he himself could not articulate", hovering over screenshots, weighing a missing "hard requirement" against a clever feature, and sizing up the "professional, yet approachable" About Us page.
- The buyer is often too annoyed with his current provider to worry much about pricing. He then has to pry a company credit card from a gatekeeper and get through a long payment form that "assumes he's guilty of fraud until proven innocent".
- Jason says that at WP Engine events like this happen "with the constancy of the sand-falls of the beach", and each is as magical as the first.
- He quotes Arthur C. Clarke's idea that magic is what you call something until you understand it. His point is that no amount of preparation or effort removes the unbelievable, inscrutable feeling of the first customer.

chunks.heading: Why founders get hooked on growth metrics
chunks.text:
- Jason argues the first sale is the most exhilarating moment, more than the first feature. Even tech founders who refuse to think of themselves as "sales people" feel it.
- He compares each new customer to another "hit off that pipe", with none as sweet as the first.
- Single hits stop being enough and you need a "biggest ever" to feel the rush. Founders then become "slaves to the mantra of %MoM growth", push more sophisticated metrics into acceptable ranges, and chase ever more abstract calculations that together get called "scale".

chunks.heading: Obsess over customer and employee happiness, not just financial ratios
chunks.text:
- Jason says obsessing over metrics is not wrong, as long as founders obsess over customer happiness and employee happiness at least as much as the "self-serving financial ratios".
- He trusts that customer and employee happiness are the most efficient and personally fulfilling path to the financial results. He links this to his essay on legacy.

chunks.heading: Metric optimization can block bigger opportunities
chunks.text:
- Jason says that even a "right-minded" obsession with metrics too often blocks an even greater calling.
- To fulfill the promise of entrepreneurship, meaning what founders can do for customers, communities, employees and the top and bottom lines, visions must "lift beyond the incremental metric and the hourly order rate". Those are "necessary and just, but incomplete".
- He names the cost of staying inside optimization: there is little room for true innovation and exploration in "a land of metrics optimization". He asks how you realize you can move vertically when "your compass measures only two dimensions".

chunks.heading: The crab metaphor: fighting over scraps while the ocean goes unexplored
chunks.text:
- Jason uses the image of three crabs fighting over a scrap of seaweed on a beach full of it, which is effectively infinite to a crab.
- He says he goes back to the office the same way, "fighting the other crabs for seaweed", forgetting the wider beach and the ocean and foreign lands beyond it that are "begging to be discovered, explored, won".
- The takeaway is that day-to-day competition over incremental gains hides much larger, unexplored opportunities beyond the current market.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jason Cohen introduces COC (Cost of Cancellations) = payback period × monthly revenue churn, the share of revenue a SaaS company must spend each month just to avoid shrinking. It shows churn alone is a third of the story and that CAC, ARPC and net negative churn matter just as much.

chunks.heading: COC: the cost of cancellations as a percentage of revenue
chunks.text:
Jason introduces COC (Cost of Cancellations), a SaaS metric for the share of revenue spent each month just to replace cancelled revenue and avoid shrinking.

**Building blocks**
- `CAC` is the all-in cost to get one customer in the door: Sales and Marketing spend, including fully-loaded salaries and commissions, divided by new customers added that month.
- `ARPC` is average monthly recurring revenue per customer: MRR divided by number of customers.
- `p` = `CAC / ARPC`. This is both the cost to acquire one more dollar of MRR and the payback period in months. Example: $80 CAC on $10 MRR means 8 months to payback.
- `c` is monthly cancellation rate in terms of MRR (4% means `c = 0.04`).
- Each month `MRR × c` dollars stop recurring, and replacing each one costs `p`.
- **`COC = p × c`**: "The percentage of our revenue we'll have to spend this month, just to keep from shrinking."

**He notes a full payback definition should also include gross profit margin.**

chunks.heading: COC examples across SaaS models
chunks.text:
- **SMB SaaS:** 3%/month cancellation and a 7-month payback gives `COC = 0.21`. That is 21% of revenue every month just to stay level. His example of a 7-month payback: Google Ads at $2 per click, 1% conversion to sale, $30/month average sale price.
- **Enterprise SaaS:** 1.5%/month cancellation and an 18-month payback gives 27% of revenue spent replacing cancellations. He says many public SaaS companies have stopped net customer-count growth and grow mostly from upgrades because replacement is so costly (example cited: Fastly).
- **No-touch, word-of-mouth SaaS:** a prominent business he knows has a 2-month payback and 5%/month cancellation, so 10% of revenue to stay even. Half of its revenue cancels within a year, yet the low acquisition cost keeps it healthy, and another 10% of revenue on marketing buys reasonable growth.
- **What fails:** 5% cancellation with a 12-month payback burns 60% of revenue to stay even. Profitable growth is nearly impossible and the business may shrink.
- These figures exclude support, infrastructure, 3% credit card fees, engineering, and growth spending.

chunks.heading: COC can be as big as R&D or G&A
chunks.text:
- COC is often as large as R&D or G&A, which means the business model stays unprofitable even at scale.
- A SaaS business must work constantly to reduce COC.
- Reducing COC means lowering cancellations and lowering `p`. Lowering `p` means decreasing `CAC` and increasing `ARPC`.
- He argues typical metrics literature "focuses only on reducing cancellation rate, which is only a third of the story."
- After product/market fit, cancellation rate is often hard to shift compared with the other two levers.
  - Reduce `CAC`: smarter campaigns, optimized landing pages, self-serve sales and onboarding.
  - Raise `ARPC`: tiered features to segment customers by budget, a la carte add-ons, price scaling with usage.
- A great payback period can overwhelm a bad cancellation rate. The 5%-cancellation company above has a better COC than a typical enterprise SaaS business.

chunks.heading: Applying COC at WP Engine
chunks.text:
- WP Engine's cancellation rate is under 2% per month, low for hosting.
- When customers who cancel after 90 days are polled, the most common reason is "project ended," which product changes can't affect.
- So Jason focuses on payback period instead.
  - CAC is already very low thanks to strong word-of-mouth; he suggests doing more to increase word-of-mouth while continuing to optimize paid ads.
  - For revenue per customer, WP Engine started selling SSL certificates to customers who want secured sites. This adds revenue and improves the experience because WP Engine handles installing and renewing them each year.

chunks.heading: Zero net churn beats both CAC and ARPC
chunks.text:
- Upselling existing customers offsets cancellations. If cancellations are 2%/month but upgrades, extra seats, add-ons and premium support add 1%/month, effective loss is 1%.
- So `c` should really be net churn: cancellations plus downgrades, minus upgrades. The strongest SaaS companies have negative net churn.
- If `c = 0`, COC is 0. Replacing losses costs nothing, and `p` (therefore CAC and ARPC) stops mattering for the "not shrinking" headwind. They still matter for cash flow and efficient growth.
- He concludes that getting to zero net churn is the strongest thing you can do for COC. Since cancellation rate has a floor, you must build paths for upsells.

chunks.heading: Using COC as a standard metric
chunks.text:
- The conventional claim is that growth rate diminishes as a SaaS company scales while cancellation rate doesn't, so you need zero net churn to build a large, profitable SaaS company.
- Expressing this as COC measures how big the headwind is and what it costs every month, so you can set goals and track progress.
- It balances the headwind of cancellation against the tailwind of low CAC, which helps decide where to spend time improving the business.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jason Cohen explains how cash-strapped startups should choose among marketing channels. Decide whether to optimize a channel by how much untapped inventory remains, abandon channels that fail out of the gate, optimize the website before any single campaign, and chase only large effects because small-sample data is mostly noise.

chunks.heading: Maximum inventory decides whether to keep optimizing a channel
chunks.text:
Jason treats "should I optimize this channel?" as a question about inventory, not "it depends." In advertising, inventory is all the available ad space; in AdWords it is the maximum clicks available to you across all relevant keywords. Being #1 for a keyword means you already have the max inventory for it.

- If you sit in lower spots on most keywords you care about, or aren't bidding on other relevant keywords, there is likely a lot more inventory to take.
- Optimizing an existing campaign is easier and cheaper than starting a new one, and can even lower cost per signup.
- His rule: "If you think there's 2x or more inventory you could go get, I say go get it."
- Example at WP Engine: #3 on AdWords and #3 organic for "WordPress Hosting", and #1 for "Managed WordPress Hosting". Traffic on related keywords drops off fast, so they estimated less than 2x inventory left. Even with heavy spend and losing money on every sale, it wouldn't be a significant growth area.
- Once you approach inventory limits, look for other campaigns that can double the business.

chunks.heading: Cut a campaign that fails out of the gate; don't give it the benefit of the doubt
chunks.text:
When a new channel utterly fails, the temptation is to keep spend low and iterate (better phrasing, better design, lifting click-through from 0.1% to 1.0%). Jason says this line of thought is usually wrong.

- Basis: his experience across 100+ campaigns over 11 years at Smart Bear and WP Engine, with no hard data. Campaigns that were bad out of the gate tended to stay bad.
- Possible reasons he gives: by the third campaign your messaging is decent, so early failure points to a bad channel rather than a bad message; iteration gets you incrementally better, not drastically better; failure may mean you don't understand the channel at all, which iteration won't fix.
- Example scenario he describes: $600/mo of banner ads yielding two signups in a month, and an affiliate program with $50 per signup where 100 affiliates joined but most sold once or never, and two produced about five signups a month.
- Advice: "cut out early and go find another channel."

chunks.heading: Optimize the website before individual campaigns
chunks.text:
Website optimizations beat per-campaign optimizations because every campaign leads to the site.

- A 10% improvement in bounce rate off the pricing page means 10% more revenue across all campaigns: paid, organic and word-of-mouth.
- Landing-page learnings can be shared across campaigns. The exact text can't, but layouts that raise click-through, a form that captures an email instead of signing up directly, or a message for a customer segment that flows through multiple campaigns can be reused.
- Early-stage sites often have large-effect problems: missing or weak testimonials or demo page, testimonials not on all pages, a home page that would triple click-through if it were long-scrolling and well designed, no strong call to action, a confusing pricing page, or a main hook and product description that turns people away.

chunks.heading: Only chase large effects when your data is small
chunks.text:
When you're small, almost no data is statistically significant, so most variation is random noise, even if you use tools that claim to handle the statistics.

- Seek large effects, not incremental improvements.
- Example: at one signup a day, a "10% improvement" is still one signup a day. You need two a day, and "you'll know if you get a change that drastic."
- Changes should be drastic but also based on a theory, not "throwing shit at the wall." Otherwise A/B tests can be wrong even with a positive result.
- He made a video explaining why small samples mislead.

chunks.heading: Low-budget and high-budget marketing are opposite playbooks
chunks.text:
Jason's advice is explicitly for cash-strapped companies. Large-budget marketing works differently.

- High budget: try as many channels as possible, as fast as possible. Hire experts to accelerate or de-risk. Find what works quickly, then ramp to full inventory immediately. For channels like affiliate programs where a big check doesn't make them work, build a whole team to extract value.
- Burning cash on things that don't work is "exactly the trade-off you want": accelerated cash burning for accelerated learning.
- VC-funded companies should do this to grow faster. Even bootstrapped companies might, if they adopt annual pricing.
- Low-budget summary: use inventory limits to decide whether to push a channel, exit bad channels quickly, optimize the website before channels, and don't get excited by tiny, immeasurable results.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jason gives a pre-data formula for bootstrapped SaaS founders deciding how much to pay per click. Assume 20-month customer life, CAC at one fifth of LTV (four months of revenue), and 1% visitor-to-paid conversion. That gives max CPC = ARPU/25, which also argues for charging more.

chunks.heading: Bootstrapped CPC rule of thumb: max bid = ARPU / 25
chunks.text:
Jason's pre-data shortcut for how much a bootstrapped, profit-seeking company should pay per click on campaigns like Google AdWords. It is built from four assumptions that chain together, and he says to tune the numbers if you disagree with them.

- Funded startups can "bid as much as possible" to buy customers and data quickly ("pay to find out").
- Bootstrapped companies cannot, and need a reasonable return reasonably quickly.
- In the first year there is no data. Even after 100 customers, half are serendipitous one-offs and the sample isn't statistically significant.

The end formula is CPC = ARPU / 25. Example: if the average customer generates $50/month, you can spend $2 per click.

chunks.heading: LTV = ARPU x 20: the pre-data customer lifetime
chunks.text:
- ARPU (Average Revenue Per User) is the average monthly charge across all customers, including mixed tiers and add-ons.
- LTV (Life-Time Value) is roughly ARPU x expected months a customer stays. With data, expected months = 1/c, where c is the monthly cancellation rate.
- A more correct LTV also multiplies by gross profit margin (support, servers, payment fees). He skips it because small bootstrapped companies usually have very high margins.
- With no data, his rule of thumb is 20 months, based on his experience and an informal survey of some of the ~100 startups at the Capital Factory co-working space in Austin.
- If real lifetime is under 20 months (cancellation above 5% per month), that is a "dangerously high" rate for almost any SaaS business. Fix the business issues before acquiring more unsatisfied customers. Use surveys and one-on-ones to find out whether the cause is technical failings, missing features, missed expectations, bad service, or not hitting pain points.
- Assume a low LTV early. Early adopters and non-ICP customers meet the product at its worst (fewest features, lowest quality), so don't inflate LTV to where it might be later.
- He dislikes LTV as a metric in general because it is hard to compute for small companies and impossible for young ones, but it is the common tool for this question.

chunks.heading: CAC = LTV / 5: the acquisition budget
chunks.text:
- CAC (Cost to Acquire a Customer) is total acquisition cost divided by customers acquired. It includes direct costs (AdWords spend, affiliate payouts, affiliate system fees) and indirect costs (consultants and your own time).
- "A surprising number of startups have CAC > LTV." They justify it by ignoring indirect costs, promising to fix it later with higher prices or other revenue, or calling it a "land-grab."
- "Profit-seeking bootstrapped companies cannot afford those delusions." CAC = LTV is not enough either, because you still have to cover other expenses and make a profit.
- Funded SaaS companies commonly target CAC = LTV / 3. This echoes his IT WatchDogs co-founder Gerry Cullen: "A third to build it, a third to get rid of it, and a third to keep." (Build cost, acquisition cost, then overhead, development and profit.)
- Jason urges profit-seekers to be stricter and use LTV / 5. His reasoning is that early on you should be able to find a few efficient channels, even though those saturate over time.

chunks.heading: CAC = ARPU x 4: payback period
chunks.text:
- Combining the two rules: acquisition cost should be no more than four months of revenue, i.e. a four-month payback period.
- If you collect the first month's revenue immediately (for example via annual prepay), it is effectively three months of cash float.
- Companies with large budgets accept 12-month paybacks, and very high-volume businesses like shared hosting accept 24 or 36 months. A bootstrapped company's cash flow can't, even if the long-run math works.

chunks.heading: Conversion rate = 1%: from CAC to cost per click
chunks.text:
- Conversion rate here is the percentage of website visitors who become paying customers. In practice it should be data-driven and segmented by customer type, channel and landing page, and A/B tested. With no data and too few visitors to measure, you take a guess.
- He uses 1%, based on his informal survey and formal surveys, where a large number of bootstrapped SaaS companies report about 1%. In his words: "You need 100 visitors to make 1 sale."
- So if a sale can cost at most CAC, each visitor can cost at most CAC/100, which is the maximum CPC.
- Substituting CAC = ARPU x 4 gives CPC = ARPU / 25.

chunks.heading: Customized formula and the "charge more" corollary
chunks.text:
- With your own numbers: CPC = ARPU x r / (5c), where c is the monthly cancellation rate and r is the visitor-to-purchase conversion rate for that paid source.
- Corollary: "you should charge a lot more than you think." Higher ARPU lets you pay more per click, opens up more marketing channels, and lets you outbid parsimonious competitors whose low LTVs rule out competitive ad spend.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jason Cohen argues freemium is a marketing cost, not a product strategy. Free users cost more than expected, convert poorly, and skew your feedback away from paying customers. Charge the marketing department the true per-user cost and compare the ROI against AdWords, SEO and other channels.

chunks.heading: Freemium is a marketing expense, not a business model
chunks.text:
Jason argues that freemium is best understood as a customer-acquisition channel and should be accounted for like AdWords. In his 2013 essay, "Freemium means high costs, low conversion, and customer feedback dominated by the non-ideal customer. Treat it as a marketing expense to ensure ROI." Founders often adopt it because it sounds easy, and it "usually crushes companies, not only because of direct costs, but because the founders didn't realize the business model itself caused them to make incorrect strategic decisions."

- The free tier is lowest-priced, free-forever, with trip-wires arranged so "real users" getting "real value" start paying.
- It can work wonderfully, but the costs are routinely underestimated.
- Retool expectations: it is "a *marketing cost.* It's more expensive than you give it credit for, but it could very well be the best marketing strategy."

chunks.heading: Freemium users are not customer development
chunks.text:
A common belief is that 1,000 active free users will teach you what to build next (feature usage stats, votes on the roadmap). Jason says this misleads you.

- "Those freemium users are not like those who will actually give you money." Features paying customers want often never show up on freeloaders' radar.
- Almost no freeloader converts, even to the lowest tier. Charge $1/mo and most would quit, because their need is not pressing enough for even a pittance.
- People who pay $10/mo or $100/mo differ "in kind," not just in scale.
- Free-tier users are not your ICP. Some ICPs sit among them, and price works as a sieve to let those rise up over time. "95% will never rise up."
- Free users outnumber paying customers 20:1 or even 100:1, so in feedback forums "they drown out the voices of those who actually matter."

chunks.heading: Why freemium conversion makes marketing expensive
chunks.text:
Jason shows the math on funnel conversion.

- A really good free-to-paid rate is 4%, as Dropbox achieved, and that took a ton of work from one of the most successful freemium products ever. Normal is closer to 1%, since most free users neither convert nor stay active.
- He informally surveyed a dozen small startups that do not use freemium. On average they saw about 1% of web traffic convert straight to purchase.
- Visitor-to-free-tier conversion is higher than visitor-to-paid, but only to about 3%-5% (10% at the extreme). Then only roughly 2%-5% of free users pay (outliers like Slack and Spotify are around 30%).
- Compounded, the visitor-to-money rate can be many times worse than non-freemium startups.
- Benchmarks he cites: OpenView data (458 respondents) gave 6% visitor-to-freemium and 5% freemium-to-paid, about 0.3% overall. FirstPageSage's 2025 report gave 13% and 2.6%, again about 0.3% overall.

Consequences:

- Paid advertising and most other marketing channels become uneconomic for driving growth unless you accept big losses to get started.
- You essentially have to build a viral product, which is very hard and still needs seeding, so the marketing expense problem remains.
- The clear freemium winners also raised tens or hundreds of millions in funding, partly to get over this hump.
- Annual pre-pay might help, but "it's a huge hill to climb."

chunks.heading: The hidden cost of free-tier tech support
chunks.text:
Jason walks through why every support policy for free users has a price.

- "Just point them to forums" ignores that people emailing support want a response, and that other customers may not want to be your support team.
- Refusing support for free users makes them less successful, which cuts conversion and word-of-mouth. Spreading the word is one of freemium's main benefits, so this could be fatal.
- Lesser-grade support forces each rep to decide "how much to help." That is awkward for the customer and demoralizing for reps who intentionally help people less, day in and day out.
- Expect people who say "If you help me through this, then I'll pay." He asks whether you are hard enough to shut the door, knowing they probably still won't pay.
- Great support is one of the few true competitive advantages a small startup has, and good support also drives sales and reputation. Segmenting who gets treated well undermines that.

chunks.heading: The real advantages of freemium
chunks.text:
Jason acknowledges four benefits, and notes that all of them are marketing, not product utility:

- **Easy to start.** Even a 30-day free trial or money-back guarantee is a much bigger barrier than "free." Getting a visitor to stop perusing and start using is a critical step.
- **Easy to upsell.** Users already use the tool, so special offers, pricing changes, or outgrowing a tier all become paths to payment.
- **Stats for selling.** "Join 10,000 happy users" is social proof, like a newsletter's subscriber counter. It also proves to bigger customers that you scale technically and in training new users.
- **Not using the competition.** One more user for you is one fewer for them. Market share has its own value, especially in zero-sum games.

chunks.heading: How to charge the marketing department
chunks.text:
Jason's technique is to bill freemium to marketing exactly like AdWords or any lead-gen campaign, measuring total cost of acquiring each new paying customer.

1. Treat freemium as a theory: spending money to support freeloaders builds an efficient path to paying customers. Revenue could come from AdWords, SEO, social media or other channels, so compare ROI against them.
2. Compute the free tier's effective "price": imagine charging free users only enough to recoup costs (infrastructure plus tech support), amortized per user, with no profit. That amount is what marketing "reimburses" the rest of the company.
3. Deduct the value of the other benefits (a competitor not getting that customer, word-of-mouth from a larger market share). Ask: "What would you be willing to pay, per customer, per month, only to prevent them from being a customer of a competitor?" The answer is probably more than $0 but not infinite. If you truly have no money, freemium probably isn't your model.
4. Make sure the net cost per acquired customer is far below total lifetime revenue. Many startups fail this equation because they don't honestly count the total cost to acquire.

His bottom line: "You have no excuse to not be measuring this net cost-per-user" so you run freemium knowing the costs and compare it to other marketing.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jason Cohen explains why nearly every founder feels deep sadness after selling, even after a big win: the startup is the founder's identity, not a job. He argues selling can still be right, and that founders should decide based on the CEO role they want as the company matures, not on money.

chunks.heading: Selling a startup feels like losing your identity, not just a company
chunks.text:
- Jason says almost all founders feel deep, prolonged sadness after selling, even after an outrageous success. He felt it himself while faxing page 34 of 72 of the Smart Bear sale paperwork, then "sadness. A profound sadness," like "the punch-in-the-stomach of discovering your dog was hit by a car."
- His explanation: a barista who sells art on Etsy says "I'm an artist," because that is who she really is, and the barista job is just a means. **A startup founder lacks this distinction between personal identity and work identity.**
- A startup is an obsession, not a "necessary evil" en route to what you really want to do. It is the thing you think about before sleep, the thing that won't let you sleep, and the first thing in your head in the morning. He started a second and eventually a fourth startup "because it's in my DNA and I have to do it."
- Selling is therefore "less like selling your baby and more like selling your own identity. Now you have to find a new one," and there is no guarantee a new one exists.

chunks.heading: Evidence that the post-exit blues are the norm
chunks.text:
- Famous cases he cites: Vinay Hiremath (sold Loom for nearly $1B, nearly died in the Himalayas, lost his girlfriend) and Markus "Notch" Persson (sold Minecraft to Microsoft for over $2B, then melted down on Twitter, directionless and socially distant).
- A Columbia Business School study of 22 entrepreneurs who sold: every one of them felt this effect. Some refocused on a new venture, but most took years to find something that replaced the excitement and the identity. Many never found it, many wished they had their companies back, and a few bought them back.
- The same pattern shows up in Olympic athletes ("post-Olympic blues"), and anyone who devotes their identity to a cause that suddenly ends.
- A brain-imaging study (Halko et al., 2017) found entrepreneur-parents' brain activity looking at their own company's brand resembled activity looking at their own children. Jason takes this to mean the attachment, intensity and worry are real.
- He doesn't call it identical to baby blues, but the shared element is a "feeling of loss and mourning": "A piece of yourself has been eviscerated, irrevocably."

chunks.heading: Money and an exit won't answer "what do you really want to do?"
chunks.text:
- Selling forces a hard question: if you could do anything, what would you do? What do you really want to be when you really grow up?
- The trap: the startup already was that thing. It's a grinding, risky, irrational adventure nobody picks as the easy path, so you wouldn't have done it unless it was what you wanted.
- Jason warns founders to resist believing millions of dollars will make them fulfilled or happy: "Money doesn't make you happy" is cliché because it's true. You need to understand how to be fulfilled regardless.
- Guilt compounds it: you can't complain about not knowing what to do with time and money most people only dream of.

chunks.heading: Selling is still often right, even when it hurts
chunks.text:
- Jason does not conclude that selling is the wrong choice. Like ending a bad relationship with someone you love, "just because it's painful doesn't mean you don't need to do it."
- It's easier to decide if you're saying "I can't wait to start the next thing." It's riskier if your thought is "I don't know what I'll do with myself."
- His honest answer to "what should I do?" is often "it depends," or "every choice is a path of pain."

chunks.heading: The job changes as the company grows, whether or not you sell
chunks.text:
- Building a company in year one is completely different from year seven (when he left Smart Bear) or year fourteen (when he left WP Engine). The CEO's job description changes, and so does the company.
- Questions he asks founders to test whether they want to stay:
  - Are you OK with innovation taking a back seat to scalable, mature processes?
  - Are you OK releasing day-to-day control to managers, then releasing the managers to an executive team?
  - Are you OK getting out of Visual Studio, AdWords, the website, live chat and sales calls, and not becoming the meddling micro-manager you hate?
  - Are you OK carrying the livelihoods of dozens or thousands of families instead of "pulling 90 hour weeks" to push code out with a co-founder?
- Successful startups grow into businesses: sustainability, risk-avoidance, HR law, strategic planning, executive meetings. The founder-CEO still steers, but it's "a different sort of ship."

chunks.heading: How Jason's own choice differed at Smart Bear and WP Engine
chunks.text:
- At Smart Bear he didn't want to lead a huge company, give up Eclipse and the ability to check in code, manage managers, or work out what hiring, strategy, products, marketing and sales it would take to reach $100M/year.
- So he sold at a good point: before he needed a C_O, but when the company was big enough to produce enough money to cross his "Freedom Line."
- At WP Engine (written early 2013) his ambitions were different. He was the CEO managing managers, setting vision rather than running day-to-day operations, worrying about culture, without SSH access to all the servers, and driving toward a company he believed could generate $100M/year.
- Editor's notes: Heather Brunner joined as CEO later in 2013 and was still leading 10 years on, which he calls a "late-joining founder." WP Engine did reach that revenue at hyper-growth velocity, and by 2023 revenue was many times the $100M figure.
- His takeaway: he will always love writing code and taking a company from $0 to $1M/year, but at that point in his life, running the larger company was who he was, "for reasons unknown even to me." He later developed a personal framework for avoiding burnout and staying with a company long-term.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jason Cohen recounts how Smart Bear broke every conventional rule for selling to enterprises (silly name, no traditional sales force, slide-free demos, amateur design, human voice) and still reached millions in revenue. His point: conventional wisdom describes what works for most, but you can choose your own way if you go in eyes open and accept the harder road.

chunks.heading: Founders can ignore "how it's done" if they accept the cost
chunks.text:
Jason argues a founder should not let "that's not how it's done" settle a decision on its own. He sold to large enterprises at Smart Bear with choices "They" said would fail:

- A silly company name ("Smart Bear")
- No traditional human sales force and no Salesforce
- Selling over GoToMeeting, with a live demo, no slides, and no webinar, from a geek
- Amateur design and a small-company, human voice

He did all of it and ended up with millions of dollars of revenue, largely from enterprise customers.

chunks.heading: "They" are not wrong, and tried and true is fine
chunks.text: Jason does not claim conventional wisdom is mistaken. He says "They" describe how most successful companies sell to The Enterprise, and "Nothing wrong with 'tried and true.'" The problem is only when the standard playbook "doesn't happen to jibe with you."

chunks.heading: Reasons to break from convention come from who you are
chunks.text:
He lists personal reasons a founder might not follow the standard path:

- You can't bear to hire a traditional "enterprise sales guy."
- You can't stand content-free language and choose honesty over formal "corporate" language on your website.
- You prefer excitement over ROI-style selling.
- You would rather compete with big companies than become one.

He says he wasn't trying to be "disruptive," "innovative" or a "maverick": "I just *couldn't do it*." Departing from convention can come from inability or distaste for the standard way, not from a strategy to stand out.

chunks.heading: The cost: a harder road with no safety net
chunks.text:
Jason is clear that ignoring "Them" has a price:

- It leads to gut-wrenching awkwardness.
- You exit "the safe and well-travelled road," so when you hit an unusual problem you can't rely on conventional wisdom to get you out.
- You must go in with your eyes open to address the special challenges you are creating for yourself.

chunks.heading: Being different can be enough, if it's for a good reason
chunks.text: His upside case is modest: "at least you'll be different," and "Sometimes just being different is enough, if it's for a good reason." His closing stance is that "it's not done that way" should not win an argument by itself: "Maybe it *should* be done your way."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jason argues that "better" has no meaning without a specific market segment, so "we can do it better" is not a real idea for a business. Defining who your product is better for turns a vague claim into an actual proposal. It also tells you how to advertise, what to build, and who to interview.

chunks.heading: Why "better" is never a valid business idea
chunks.text:
- Jason says "we can do it better" is "always an invalid 'idea' for a business." Founders say it constantly, and he thinks they should be thinking something like it. But it isn't an idea until it says who the product is better for.
- "Better" is "always in the eye of the beholder," so he asks one question: "Better for whom?"
- His analogy: a home builder says "I looked at all the other houses in this city and thought, 'I can do better.'" Better for a 19-year-old bachelor who never cooks and has no money? A millionaire with a wine collection? A family of six? A family of rats?
- His conclusion: "there's no such thing as 'better.' There's only such thing as 'better for a specific market segment.'"

chunks.heading: Spotting the empty pitch in crowded categories
chunks.text:
- The trigger for the essay was a founder in project-management (PM) tools who said they looked at the existing products and thought they could do it better.
- Jason notes why this is tempting: almost everyone dislikes some aspect of their PM tool, which may also explain why there are so many of them.
- A typical empty pitch is "All the things you love about Microsoft Project, but none of the things you hate." His reaction: "Uh-huh. Who's 'you?'"
- If your product were inferior in every way to even one incumbent, there would be no reason to build it. Saying it is better only restates that baseline and defines nothing.

chunks.heading: What a real "better for whom" pitch looks like (PM tool examples)
chunks.text:
Jason says he doesn't know whether these are good ideas, but each is an actual proposal because it defines "better":

- **Accidental PMs:** Existing tools assume you already know project management. A tool for people thrust into a PM role who need help with nomenclature, process, best practices, and getting the most from the tool and team.
- **Large, complex projects:** Modern tools follow the 37signals and Lean Startup mantra of building the simplest possible thing, so they fail on large, complex, distributed, multi-user projects. Older tools understood that use case but are clunky install-only products where online collaboration, mobile and even the Mac are bolt-ons. The pitch is a tool for large, complex projects with modern technology requirements.
- **iPad-first:** Existing tools were built in the installed or web-based eras. A tool built from the start for the iPad is best for managing projects from meetings and on the go.
- **Open, large-scale projects:** Existing tools are built for a small, fixed set of workers. A tool for distributed, open projects with thousands of members that still need central management.
- **Constantly changing requirements:** Existing tools assume tasks, goals and projects are fairly fixed. A tool for open-ended projects where requirements change constantly and the tool changes with them, and even measures the change.

chunks.heading: Defining the audience tells you what to do next
chunks.text:
Once you can say who it's better for, the next steps in the business follow:

- **Marketing:** You can run targeted advertisements, go to specific conferences, and even cold-call people on LinkedIn.
- **Messaging:** You know what words to put on your homepage and what to highlight to differentiate from competitors.
- **Product:** You know which features will especially tickle that audience's fancy.
- He frames this as the usual benefits of identifying your ideal customer, applied to the product rather than to the customer's identity.

chunks.heading: Using "better for whom" at the ideation stage
chunks.text:
- If you're still working out the idea, the answer becomes the basis for customer development.
- It tells you where to find potential customers to call.
- It also tells you what you're verifying once you have them on the phone.
- His closing test: "Surely your product is 'better' than the rest... for someone. Whom?"

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jason Cohen argues there is no map to startup success. Every piece of advice has successes and failures on both sides, and successful startups are by definition outliers that statistics can't predict. Treat frameworks and famous origin stories as a candy store for inspiration, not laws, and find your own way.

chunks.heading: Why frameworks aren't maps: "A compass is not a map"
chunks.text: Jason argues that startup advice tells you how to move, not where to go. A compass "tells you **which way is north, not whether you should be heading north**." He says there is no map to startup success, and that this is fine: "There's no map. That's OK. Keep moving."

chunks.heading: Frameworks and famous startups are not laws
chunks.text:
- Jason treats Lean Startup, 37signals' habits and the origin stories of favorite startups as examples, not rules.
- He points out that most startups failed before Lean Startup and most still failed after it, so he questions whether it is strictly necessary.
- When an entrepreneur said he disliked Lean Startup and asked if he was cut out for startups, Jason noted that Elon didn't use Lean Startup to build Tesla, though he added that most founders aren't manufacturing cars.
- He criticizes founders who justify every decision with "37signals does it" without explaining why it applies to their situation, or whether 37signals did it when they were still the founder's size.

chunks.heading: For any advice P, the 2x2 is full
chunks.text:
- For any piece of advice `P`, there are many successes and failures among startups that did `P`, and many successes and failures among startups that did the opposite.
- He gives examples: one startup got 300 customers from a TechCrunch launch article while another got 0; some built loyalty on Twitter while another grew revenue 20% month-over-month without having reserved their Twitter handle; some credit spectacular design while another successful startup has "never hired a designer (and it shows)".
- His question to the reader: if all four boxes are full, what does that tell us about `P`?

chunks.heading: Why startup "rules" fail: survivors are anomalies
chunks.text:
- Besides survivor bias, the core problem is that "by definition the successful ones are anomalies."
- "Trends don't predict outliers." Statistics show trends, but they can't determine the outcome of an individual case, in startups or anywhere else.
- Nothing predicts which startup becomes an outlier. A successful startup looks a lot like an unsuccessful one at the start.

chunks.heading: Lessons are not traction
chunks.text:
- Jason questions pitch decks that boast about mistakes made and lessons learned when those lessons haven't produced paying customers.
- The open question he poses: is it time to give up, or does that knowledge and introspection position the team for rocket-ship growth? He doesn't claim a rule settles it.

chunks.heading: How to use startup advice
chunks.text:
- Use advice "for sparks of inspiration, for brainstorming, as a candy store where every item has its own merits but you must pick and choose what to put into your basket."
- Don't confuse frameworks, dogma or your favorite startup's origin story with laws.
- Find your own way: "Decide what makes you the best version of who you already are."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Using Rock, Paper, Scissors as an analogy, Jason Cohen shows how trying to outguess what competitors know and think leads to endless recursive fakes. His startup takeaway is to stop reacting to rivals and instead focus inward on building something you're proud of for your customers.

chunks.heading: Competitors are mostly unknowable, so build for your own customers
chunks.text:
Jason uses the Rock, Paper, Scissors literature as an analogy for second-guessing competitors. A new study (via the Telegraph and New Scientist) says rock is the most popular first throw. That produces an endless chain of counter-moves, and he draws a startup lesson from it.

- If neither player knows the study, an opponent throws rock too often, so you should throw paper.
- If the opponent has read the study, he expects you to throw paper and will favor paper himself, so you should throw scissors.
- If he knows that you know that he read it, he flips back to rock. "Double-fake!"
- If you know all of that, you can double-fake too, and the chain has no stable end.
- His takeaway on the game: people with more information win more often.
- Another game tactic he describes is to announce what you will throw and then throw it, on the theory that the other person won't believe you. If A says "rock" and B disbelieves, B's best reply is scissors and second best is rock, so A ties or wins.
- That tactic also stops working once B knows the strategy.

chunks.heading: Don't try to outwit competitors; focus inward
chunks.text:
Jason compares the guessing game to trying to work out what your competitors think, what they know, what they think they know, and whether they will react to your knowledge of that guess.

- His conclusion: "screw it, just build the best company you can, for you."
- He argues you are wrong about most of what you think about competitors anyway, "both the good and bad".
- So stop reacting to them and focus inward. Build something you're proud of.
- His framing of the ideal: "Even better than trying to outwit the competition, is to not react to them at all, and just do your best, directly for your customers."

chunks.heading: When information advantage matters, and why it's a trap in business
chunks.text:
Jason notes that in the game, more information wins. He does not carry that over to competitive strategy.

- In RPS the payoff structure is symmetric and the counter-move chain is endless, so each extra level of reasoning only helps until the other side matches it.
- A company that spends effort modeling competitor reactions enters the same regress, with worse data than a game player has.
- His alternative is to put that effort into customers and the product, where the work compounds and does not depend on guessing the other side's next move.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jason Cohen argues that investors and press reward growth and "shareholder value" while ignoring sustainability, producing companies that look successful and then collapse. He contrasts Groupon, Zynga and serial-exit founders with HubSpot, Rackspace, Freshbooks and SEOMoz, and says growth is necessary but not sufficient.

chunks.heading: Sustainable growth versus "successful" unsustainable companies
chunks.text:
Jason argues too many companies funded and celebrated as "successful" are unsustainable. His summary of the pattern: "Build up a business, create impressive 'shareholder value,' then it fails." Growth alone is not the measure of a lasting company: "Growth is necessary, but not sufficient."

- He says the press and the Valley reward companies that raise money and create shareholder value, even when the business later collapses.
- He asks founders to be honest about what "lasting" means before they decide what to build.
- If the goal is a flash-in-the-pan, like a cool mobile app, he says that is fine too, as long as the founder knows that is what it is.

chunks.heading: The Bill Nguyen case: investors acting rationally on a track record of exits that later failed
chunks.text:
Jason uses serial entrepreneur Bill Nguyen (from a Fast Company profile) to show how a "successful" track record can hide unsustainable companies.

- Color, his seventh startup, raised $41m for a mobile app before launch. The launch failed and it went bankrupt.
- Jason says the investors backing Nguyen are "acting rationally": before the house of cards tumbles, private equity investors get a tidy return, and Nguyen knows how to keep the magic going long enough for the payday.
- Track record as Jason lists it: Forefront (IPO'd 1995, parent stock fell 85% in 1998); Freeloader (sold for $38m on $3m invested, shut down in 1997); Support.com (IPO'd at $32/share in 2000, now about $2); OneBox (sold for $850m on $60m invested, 18 months after launch); Seven (still private, cancelled IPO); Lala (sold to Apple for $80m on $35m invested, shut down in June).
- He rejects blaming the acquirers: they are not all stupid. His own sold companies did well afterward: Smart Bear grew revenue and profit every year for five years after the sale, even through 2008/2009, and IT WatchDogs did the same after its 2005 sale.
- He treats Nguyen's persuasion ("the Jedi," in a quoted colleague's words) as a skill that keeps the funding flowing, and asks whether such a person is driven by truth or deception.

chunks.heading: The bigger problem: companies everyone honestly believed were sustainable
chunks.text:
Jason says the bigger issue is not deceivers but what Dan Lyons calls unsustainable companies that people honestly believed were sustainable.

- **Groupon:** a product everyone called brilliant, with 1,000 copy-cats. Heavy investment in growth and a sales force had no long-term payback, and the product's value to small businesses was lower than claimed. He says simple customer development (asking any restaurateur) would have revealed this. It IPO'd at a $13b valuation, fell month over month to about one-fourth of that, and appeared to be in "constant pivot mode" seeking product/market fit again.
- **Zynga:** financially successful at a certain scale, but individual game successes are fleeting and he doubts they can keep innovating enough games to justify their size. They bought Draw Something for $200m and it lost 5m active users a month after the purchase. Stock was $2.43 against a $10 IPO price under a year earlier.
- These were not like Color. They had real, growing revenues (not just "active users"), a repeatable, scalable business model, ownership of a large market, and had survived the operational challenges of rapid growth.
- His two candidate explanations: the markets were more short-lived than assumed ("Facebook games" a fad rather than an industry), or executives and investors over-valued growth versus sustainability. Groupon's engine that turned capital into revenue growth was "a form of force-feeding rather than building a product."
- He flags this as hindsight-based armchair speculation.

chunks.heading: What sustainable high-growth companies look like
chunks.text:
Jason names companies that grow fast and remain sustainable, and what each does:

- **HubSpot:** a revenue curve "as predictable" as a plot on a TI-90, while obsessing over customer satisfaction and retention.
- **Freshbooks:** an enviable corporate culture plus an unflagging revenue curve.
- **SEOMoz:** insistence on TAGFEE wins over employees, customers and investors, giving consistent growth even in the tumultuous SEO tools market.
- **Rackspace:** a "maniacal obsession" with excellent customer service lets them charge premium prices and sustain about 30% annual growth at $1b in revenue.

Financing path does not decide it. Some were bootstrapped, some bootstrapped and raised later, some had huge funding from the start: "It's not about the financing path, it's about what you've decided to build."

chunks.heading: WP Engine's model for sustainable growth, and questions Jason asks founders
chunks.text:
Jason states his goal to put WP Engine among those excellent companies. At the time of writing it had thirty employees and millions in revenue, and he describes it as experiencing fantastic growth that he believes is sustainable. He borrows a trait from each exemplar:

- A Rackspace-like commitment to customer service (more WordPress experts per 1,000 customers than anyone).
- An SEOMoz-like commitment to honesty and transparency.
- A HubSpot-like obsession with introspective measurement, covering customer happiness and retention, not just marketing and growth.

Questions he poses for any founder:

- Is your company building something of lasting value?
- Are you valuing growth over sustainable growth?
- Are you articulating and then living up to company cultural values that attract and retain the right people, who then create the right product and service?

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jason Cohen explains why ROI and cost-savings arguments never closed a sale at Smart Bear, even when the math was sound and customers asked for it. Savings are unmeasurable and budgets are siloed, so he advises building value so obvious it needs no calculation and pricing by willingness to pay and budget structure.

chunks.heading: Why "ROI" fails as a selling argument
chunks.text: Jason sold Smart Bear's Code Reviewer, a tool that helps developers review each other's code, for seven years. He tried to sell it with a "saves you money" argument, and some customers demanded an ROI spreadsheet. He says the argument "never worked, not once," even though the reasoning was sound and customers asked for it.

chunks.heading: The ROI math he used, and why it was correct
chunks.text:
- Premise: Code Reviewer cuts code review time roughly in half by eliminating busywork. It led the one-page leave-behind, because in 2004 sales calls were in person.
- Calculation:
  - Two developers each spend an average of 30 minutes on a review, once a day, which is 20 hours per month.
  - At a fully loaded developer cost of $150/hr, that is $3,000/mo.
  - Halving it saves $1,500 every month.
- Price: Code Reviewer cost $499 per developer, one time. That was the pre-SaaS "lifetime" licensing era, with maintenance and upgrades sold in later years at 20% of the original price. Payback came within the first month.
- Despite that, the deal did not close on the spreadsheet.

chunks.heading: Why savings are invisible to buyers
chunks.text:
- Better, higher-volume code is valuable, but it is "essentially impossible to measure, and is in fact not measured." The savings are real but invisible to the customer.
- Budgets are siloed. The "Salaries" budget is separate from the "Tools" budget.
- In seven years of selling software, at deals from 10 seats to 2,500 seats, Jason never saw a company turn a saving in the Salaries budget into an increase in the Tools budget.
- Customers bought because they genuinely believed the tool made their team more productive, even though they could not quantify it. His conclusion: "Spreadsheets are worthless. They either believe, or they don't."

chunks.heading: What to do instead: create value so large it needs no calculation
chunks.text:
- Make the value so obvious that nobody has to compute it. If payback is under a month, it is evident.
- Change a workflow so drastically for the better that people can't live without it, whether or not it saves money.
- Improve a customer's marketing campaigns so obviously and drastically that they don't need a spreadsheet to see the value.
- He treats "value" as broader than cost savings. His list: more leads, more sales, faster code, efficiency, time-savings, cost-savings, delight, corporate brand, personal image, societal impact.

chunks.heading: Price to ability and willingness to pay, not to "value"
chunks.text:
- Set price according to the customer's ability and willingness to pay and the structure of your business model, rather than as a direct function of so-called value.
- A software development department has a tools budget, and different companies have different ways of arguing internally to expand it. Your price has to match those constraints.
- Example: a marketing department might be willing to pay for services but not for tools.
- Bottom line: a simple "cost savings" equation is rarely how you win sales or set prices.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jason Cohen borrows Pascal's Wager as a decision rule: when you act on scant knowledge, pick the stance that holds up in every outcome. Using WP Engine tech support as the example, he argues that assuming you are ignorant and asking for help beats accusation, and he challenges readers to try humility for a week.

chunks.heading: Pascal's Wager as a decision rule: assume humility, because it cannot fail
chunks.text:
- Jason takes Pascal's Wager (act as if God exists, because the downside of being wrong is tiny and the upside is huge) and reuses only its structure: choose the behavior that does well in every possible world.
- He is clear it is not a valid argument for God's existence. Substitute any God humans have worshipped and it "proves" belief in that one, so it is "both invalid and irrational". He keeps it as a tool for choosing between assumptions, not as proof of anything.
- Its link to maximizing expected value: some assumptions pay off in all outcomes, others only sometimes. Pick the first kind.
- He notes this is not how to size large bets. It is for choosing a default posture.
- The core claim: "Being humble cannot fail; being arrogant can."
- Founders decide from scant knowledge. In a startup essentially every decision is an educated guess, but "not terribly educated". That is why the humble default beats the confident one.

chunks.heading: Contacting support: open with curiosity or helplessness, not accusation
chunks.text:
- Example from WP Engine tech support: customers often open from a posture of accusation ("I didn't *do* anything!"), implying the company screwed up. Jason says that is occasionally true, but usually it is ignorance, someone else on their team, or the customer themselves, hoping to be rescued. (He says support will rescue them.)
- Support staff are human, not "mechanized automatons" immune to rude language or assumed incompetence. They chose a field where they "help people" for a living, which he calls a noble profession, and they get little thanks call after call.
- If you open from helplessness or curiosity, people are inclined to help even when it is your fault.
- If it turns out not to be your fault, the person is even more sympathetic: you are "the nicest person on Earth, blaming themselves from the get-go", and yet it was their fault. They will personally fight to fix it.
- The usual behavior is the opposite. Customers are angry and take it out on the one person who is their only link to a fix. Support has metrics that punish it if they don't do their job, but anger is still not the way to get the most out of people.
- His test question: "is that the way to get most out of other people?"

chunks.heading: The assumption to adopt: you are ignorant and missing information
chunks.text:
- "You can't fail if you assume you're ignorant, that you're missing information, that you're ready to learn, that you need help to understand."
- Humility is a default assumption about your own state of knowledge. It is not politeness or a tactic layered on top.
- If you are right anyway, the humble approach costs you nothing. If you are wrong, it saves you from acting on a false premise.

chunks.heading: Where it applies: any channel, especially email
chunks.text:
- It is not specific to support. It applies anywhere, any time: tech support, vetting a new idea (he links to customer development), arguing with a spouse, or exchanging emails or tweets with a stranger.
- It matters most in email and other text where emotion is hard to convey and text gets misread.
- Misreading is common: people read things that do not exist "in-between lines that aren't the lines you thought they were".
- For vetting ideas, the same posture means going in assuming you are missing information, not defending the idea.

chunks.heading: A one-week experiment
chunks.text:
- Jason's challenge: act humble in every situation for a week and observe.
- Questions to watch for:
  - Do you discover you are wrong more often, and about more things, than you thought?
  - Do you find you misread, or read something that was not there?
  - In the cases where you are correct, do people respond more positively, learn too, and go out of their way to make things better?
- His framing: "Could the simple act of being humble be life-altering?"
- His closing argument: "You have nothing to lose and everything to gain by trying. Like Pascal."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jason Cohen reflects on his daughter's birth and colic to argue that a startup, like a child, is a crucible that pushes you past your limits. Reading about the founder roller coaster doesn't prepare you; living it changes you permanently, even if the company fails. A personal essay with little tactical content.

chunks.heading: Startups as a crucible, not a roller coaster
chunks.text:
- Jason calls a startup "a crucible -- a fiery place that tests your limits, not by probing them but by violently exceeding them, all of the time."
- He says the same is true of raising a baby. His daughter had colic: she screamed 12 hours a day for three months, and a newborn feeds every three hours.
- He says the startup is one of the few times in his life he has been taken to the brink, physically and mentally. Colic was the other.
- He argues that the pithy tweets about the "roller coaster o' emotions", the thought of quitting your job, and books like The Dip are "only words". They "don't help much, not really. *You* have to *live* it."
- He argues that you can't understand it until you do it.

chunks.heading: What a startup does to the founder
chunks.text:
- Jason says that even if you "fail", you come out "stronger, wiser, ready for the next thing, never able to go back to being a cog, eyes opened."
- He says the change "can never be undone, forever changing who you are and how you interact with the world."
- He has "never met a person who tried a startup, failed, and said they wouldn't have done it all over again. Never."
- He treats that regret-free pattern as a signal worth thinking about: "What does that mean?"

chunks.heading: Startups and children: where the comparison holds and where it breaks
chunks.text:
- Jason lists the similarities:
  - Both spend the first two years of life "trying to kill themselves" while you frantically work to prevent it.
  - Both are a mix of your own creation and their own direction. They are malleable in some ways and stubborn in others.
  - Each one is different, even when made by the same parents, and needs the freedom to find its own way with loving guidance.
  - Both pass through predictable macro-level stages, which are obvious to anyone who has walked the path before. Both also have micro-level stages unique to each one.
  - Both take all of your time and all of your patience.
- He says they are not actually that similar. A kid grows up pretty much no matter what. A startup usually dies regardless of the founders' actions, and often because of them.
- He thinks drawing such comparisons is "not only unnecessary but useless". His test: even if the two were similar, "so what? What would you do differently tomorrow?"
- The one thing he says both share is the crucible effect.

chunks.heading: Needing to improvise without knowing what to do
chunks.text:
- Jason describes bringing his daughter home with no training, and says it matters less than you'd think that you don't know what to do next.
- He says each day can feel like "an interminable mixture of necessary drudgery and constant invention", and that the same is true of a startup.
- The work is "boring and inevitable and yet precious and impossible".
- He says eventually they "don't need you anymore, or so they claim."

chunks.heading: Finding your own crucible
chunks.text:
- He asks where your "child-like combination of wonder and determination" is. He means the thing that is so difficult you're sure you can't do it, "and yet, you do it".
- He argues that this is "how you really live a life, instead of watching life elapse."
- He closes with a quote from Omar Khayyám: "Awake my little ones, and fill the cup, before life's liquor in its cup be dry."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Using Feynman's physics lectures as an analogy, Jason Cohen argues a real startup idea converges: the deeper you dig in customer interviews, the more people agree on the pain, the solution and the price. A false idea diverges into contradictory advice. He contrasts a divergent first idea with WP Engine, where 30 of 40 interviewees agreed to sign up.

chunks.heading: How Jason tells a truly great startup idea from polite "sounds good" feedback
chunks.text: Jason's test is whether the answers you gather converge or diverge as you dig. He borrows the idea from Feynman's Lectures on Physics, where the same contrast separates a real law from a coincidence. The aim is to know when an idea is real and when to give up.

chunks.heading: The problem: people say nice things but aren't buying
chunks.text:
- Jason's complaint is that people "say nice things to your face, but really they're not buying", even after twenty systematic customer interviews.
- The usual advice is contradictory. He lists "trust your gut", "trust data", "don't give up", "if it's hard it's not a fit", "don't listen to the haters", "haters have something to teach us".
- He says no formula settles it, because the formula "doesn't know what to do with the answers".
- His answer is a way of reading the answers you already have, not a new set of questions.

chunks.heading: The physics analogy: a coincidence versus a fundamental law
chunks.text:
- The drag force on an airplane is approximated as F = Cv², proportional to the square of velocity. That is astonishing given how chaotic the airflow is.
- Jason says it is "not a law at all". It is a "tenuous coincidence".
- It breaks in new situations. It is inaccurate at slow speeds and at very fast speeds. The constant C changes dramatically with small wing perturbations. Removing one wing changes the drag on the other.
- Conservation of Energy behaves differently. Friction seemed to break it, but the lost energy showed up as heat, in exactly the predicted amount. Heat was then explained as the kinetic energy of jiggling particles, and the predictions held again. It survived Relativity and Quantum Mechanics.
- His rule: with the drag equation, "the deeper we dug the more we discovered that the 'law' doesn't encompass much truth". With energy, "the closer we look the more powerful the law becomes". The second case is the mark of a real fundamental law.
