chunks.heading: "Truth in startups converges or diverges in the same way"
chunks.text:
- A real idea gets stronger as you probe it from more angles, and answers from different people point to the same place.
- A false idea gets blurrier. Each new conversation sends you in a different direction.
- Jason says to watch for "multiple areas of inquisition lead[ing] to a common destination instead of leading to different planets".
- He admits it is not an immutable law. It is "something that behaves like truth".

chunks.heading: Divergent example: the startup idea before WP Engine
chunks.text:
- During customer development for an earlier idea, everyone said "That's a great idea, you should do it!"
- Digging into each person's answer, the "truth" diverged:
  - One said to target enterprises, charging $1000/mo and selling through consultants.
  - One said to go freemium and convert 5% to $5/mo.
  - One said to charge a minimum of $50/mo to cut out moochers who email support but don't pay.
  - One said the small-to-mid-sized business market was the untapped niche.
  - Use cases split three ways: measure online ads and forget about leads; feed leads into Salesforce and forget about ads; or reveal general marketing efficacy without closing leads.
- He describes the result as a "blotchy Venn Diagram with twenty lobes of dissonance and no discernible center", with no clear steps forward. It was intriguing and exciting but not fundamental.

chunks.heading: Convergent example: WP Engine
chunks.text:
- The more people he spoke with, the more they agreed on the pain, on whether his solution was acceptable, and on what they would spend.
- The converged offer was $50/mo for a WordPress site that is fast, scalable and secure. Tech support should answer the phone and be knowledgeable about WordPress. Add a staging area and backups and "it's a done deal".
- Thirty of forty people agreed to sign up during their interview. Twenty of those thirty later did, and WP Engine launched with a total of thirty customers.

chunks.heading: Use the test honestly, and don't delay the answer
chunks.text:
- There is "no rubric" for deciding whether an idea is tenable or when to give up. But the feeling of convergence or divergence is "very strong" if you are introspective and honest with yourself.
- He says "your hardest battle is indeed with yourself". You are tempted to bias the evidence toward validation, and you fear learning that your cool pet idea "is not a business", meaning people won't give you money for it.
- The cost of staying ignorant: "You will meet the same, bitter end, only after a significantly larger investment in time, money, heart, and reputation."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: After running a hundred ad campaigns at Smart Bear across paid search, trade shows, mailers, newsletters and print, Jason Cohen concluded he could not predict which would work. His fix is to rank options by measurability, speed of learning, low cost and personal comfort, then start and test rather than agonize over the "right" channel.

chunks.heading: Jason's rule: you can't predict which advertising channel will work, so pick for fast, cheap, measurable learning
chunks.text:
Jason ran about a hundred campaigns at Smart Bear: paid search, trade shows, postcard mailers, newsletter sponsorships, and print magazine ads. His conclusion: "I learned I have zero ability at predicting which campaigns would produce."
- The only way to find out is to put accurate measurement in place and try it.
- He negotiated a lower "first time" rate for the trial.
- He eventually built a system that measured campaign efficacy with pinpoint accuracy, even for print.

chunks.heading: How Jason chooses where to start advertising
chunks.text:
Of a dozen options, he picks the one that maximizes these, in this order of precedence:
1. **Measurable.** You must know objectively whether the value to your company exceeds the money spent. Online is generally easier to measure than offline, but not always (e.g. contests, special offers, secret landing pages can make offline measurable).
2. **Quickest** to learn whether it worked. Fast learning gets you to a working advertising model sooner.
3. **Cheapest.** At this stage the goal is learning what advertising works, not maximizing total revenue. Once you know how to spend money to make money, pour money on it as fast as possible.
4. **Comfortable.** Pick something you like, such as a news site you already read, because your gut isn't useful for prediction anyway. Knowing the site's culture lets you build an ad suited to its audience.

His examples: he was particularly successful on StackOverflow (he was an early beta user) and on Coding Horror (he was a long-time reader).

His closing advice: don't fret over picking the "right" campaign, because you can't. Make sure these key things are in place and "just go."

chunks.heading: Campaign quality changes over time, so keep re-measuring
chunks.text:
Jason's Dr. Dobbs magazine ads show how results decay.
- He started with a 1/4-page ad in the back (what he called "in the zoo", over the ad salesmen's objections to that characterization of their remnants).
- It worked great, and a full-page ad worked better.
- Over the years it became less and less effective, "like clockwork", and he kept demanding a lower price.
- Three years before the magazine died, it had been one of his top lead sources.

Lesson: "Things change. Can't predict." Past performance of a channel doesn't guarantee its future performance.

chunks.heading: Be skeptical of ad salesmen's arguments
chunks.text:
Jason describes the standard pitches he heard when pushing for lower rates:
- "Our readership is increasing," backed by BPA stats. He calls BPA a third-party "auditor" who always certifies strong growth and a monied readership.
- "You'll lose credibility if you stop advertising. People will wonder whether you've disappeared."

He didn't let these override his own measured results. The magazine went under a few months after that conversation.

chunks.heading: Be wary of lead-gen lists
chunks.text: Jason is dismissive of typical "lead-gen" offers: CSV dumps of contact information for so-called "pre-qualified" people who were tricked into downloading a whitepaper. He asks whether any such channel is actually good at generating sales, and his answer is that you can only tell by measuring.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jason Cohen argues that mid-sized companies combine large-company bureaucracy and slow sales cycles with small-company budgets, so the reward rarely justifies the effort. He also says "mid-sized" isn't a real market segment, and uses his early WP Engine thinking to show why focusing on one end of a market lets you optimize the whole business.

chunks.heading: Why the mid-market is the worst of both worlds
chunks.text:
Jason argues that selling to "mid-sized" companies (his example is around 400 employees) looks like the best of both worlds and is actually the worst.

- The pitch he hears: small businesses have no money, large companies already use Entrenched Competitors X and Y, so "the opportunity is in the middle."
- Startup graveyards are "littered with companies who tried to target this seemingly alluring market segment": customers supposedly nimble and open to new technology, yet big enough to spend real money.
- He calls it "a tar-pit" and his reaction to anyone "selling to middle" is "Yuck."
- There isn't necessarily an opportunity there. Incumbents may have already figured out that the middle isn't cost-effective to sell to.
- If you do it anyway, he hopes you have "extenuating circumstances that truly makes you the exception to the rule."

chunks.heading: Mid-sized companies are not nimble, but they have the same bureaucracy as big ones
chunks.text:
- At about 400 employees they have already built much of the "lumbering process and bureaucracy" of companies ten times their size.
- Budgets and internal politics shackle them. Technology changes require expensive coordination and retraining, and "fear of change trumps potential rewards from improvement."
- The result is an arduous sales process like a large company's, without a large company's budget. There is no big reward for getting through the "painful, Herculean sales adventure."
- Why it happens, in his words:
  - Possibly a parsimonious small-business founder still "straightening used staples to save pennies" (he includes himself).
  - Even a few dozen people split into teams, departments and roles. Communication limits and tribal behavior produce semi-autonomous isolation, which gets paired with formal processes for command-and-control. A bureaucracy is born that is "self-generating and largely inescapable."
  - Some of the reasons are genuinely good ones.

chunks.heading: The numbers argument ("look how many there are") falls apart
chunks.text:
- There are 220,000 US businesses with 50-500 employees and only 18,000 with more than 500. This is the usual argument for targeting the mid-sized.
- The average mid-sized company has 119 employees; the average large one has 3,100.
- If you sell a seat to everyone inside a company, you must sell about 30 mid-sized companies for every large one.
- Total employees: about 26M at mid-sized companies versus 60M at large ones.
- Sales effort is roughly the same whether you sell 75 seats or 750, so the mid-market means much more work for the revenue.

chunks.heading: "Mid-sized companies" isn't really a market segment
chunks.text:
- Size says little. Industry, the problem being solved, and the manner of solving it matter far more.
- Example: a 100-person tech startup has a particular mix of developers, QA, tech support, sales and HR. A 100-person plastics manufacturer has a very different mix: no developers, probably not tech-savvy, and IT run by a Windows "power user" who runs Exchange, has never used Google Apps, and doesn't know how to open a firewall port that "my Cisco guy" installed.
- For something like server monitoring software, everything differs between the two: how you find them, what pain you solve, and what the user wants to see in the interface.
- Both monitoring 100 computers is only vaguely "the same." There are more differences than similarities.
- He points to defining your target market by the problem instead (linked from the essay as a better way to choose a market).

chunks.heading: WP Engine: the squeeze in practice
chunks.text:
- His initial WP Engine idea was to target the "mid-market" of WordPress: blogs and sites too big for cheap hosting on speed, scale and support, but too small to afford full-time WordPress experts or Automattic's "WordPress VIP" program at $2,500/mo and up.
- The segment had the classic problem: small-blogger budget meets big-blogger problems.
- Trade-offs he weighed:
  - A $50/mo blogger has many of the same problems as a $2,000/mo blogger but can afford 40x less.
  - Many $50/mo bloggers never call and never have problems, so profit margin is great even if absolute profit is smaller.
  - A $2,000/mo blogger constantly hits new speed and scalability challenges, because even small configuration changes are magnified by 10,000,000 hits a month. Expensive expert human time vaporizes the supposed profit.
- His conclusion: pick one end or the other and optimize hiring, automation, marketing and sales around it. His 2012 note adds "(Narrator: They did.)"
- 2024 editor's note: WP Engine did intentionally expand into mid-market and even enterprise, but only once it could spend tens of millions of dollars on marketing, sales, service, account management, compliance and other things that made it work.

chunks.heading: Takeaways for choosing a segment
chunks.text:
- Don't treat "the middle" as an opportunity just because small is too poor and large is taken. Ask why incumbents skipped it.
- Choose one end and build the whole company (hiring, automation, marketing, sales) around that customer.
- Segment by industry and problem, not company size.
- Count revenue per sales effort, not number of companies. Seat count per deal matters more than total business count.
- Expanding into the mid-market can work later, but only with the resources to fund the sales, service and compliance machinery it demands.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jason Cohen answers a founder torn between raising money and staying bootstrapped. When both options are valid, outside advice can't settle it and delay is costly, so use your own fulfillment as the tiebreaker. Ask which kind of company sounds most fun to build.

chunks.heading: Choosing between two good options by asking which is more fun to build
chunks.text:
Jason treats a choice like "raise money or keep bootstrapping" as a case where neither answer is wrong. His advice is that once both options are valid and rational, you should stop analyzing and pick on a different basis. He also says to never let anyone make you feel guilty for not choosing the other path.

- He says "there's no wrong answer" doesn't answer the question, so a tiebreaker is needed.
- He applies this to a founder with thirty paying customers, bootstrapped so far, who sees a big opportunity to raise money but could also continue as is.
- That founder already knew the pros and cons. Jason does not re-list them.

chunks.heading: Why outside advice can't settle a major business decision
chunks.text:
Jason argues the answer cannot come from other people.

- While bootstrapping WP Engine, he constantly heard that he was hamstrung by not taking investment.
- After raising a Series A, a different set of people were disappointed that he had "sold out."
- His verdict on who was right: "Both. Neither." That is why you cannot look externally for the answer.
- Other people can still help by asking you more and better questions. But "only you can decide the answer."

chunks.heading: Indecision has a daily cost
chunks.text:
Jason's case for deciding fast:

- Every day of delay costs you. Dithering moves you toward neither goal.
- It drains time and energy.
- It blocks other decisions: spending money, hiring, lifestyle, stories for the press, features, "everything."
- Since you need a fast decision and others can't give you the answer, that "leaves you, alone."

chunks.heading: The tiebreaker: which company sounds like the most fun to build?
chunks.text:
Jason's yardstick is fun, enjoyment and fulfillment. He suggests asking yourself:

- Do you like working alone or with a very small team? Does hiring ten people in the next 12 months sound exhilarating or depressing?
- Do you like having a hand in everything, or would you rather be evangelizing and leading?
- Do you enjoy slowly growing a backyard garden, or would you have more fun "strapping on an afterburner" to see how much impact you can have?
- Do you like being good at what you're good at now, or do you want to learn a completely different kind of business?

chunks.heading: Test your feelings about bootstrapping versus funding
chunks.text:
Jason offers a gut-check on identity:

- Are you proud of bootstrapping? Do you enjoy telling a funded founder you're in control, don't need help, and have a product so good people actually pay for it?
- Or does bootstrapping make you feel small, knowing you're not growing, reaching or earning as much as you could?
- Whichever reaction is stronger points to your answer.

chunks.heading: Fulfillment is undervalued in company decisions
chunks.text:
Jason's broader point is that most founders let joy and fulfillment barely enter the calculus, and that is a mistake.

- His question: why build a company, or anything else, if it's not fulfilling?
- A choice between two valid options lets you pick on something "we all really ought to be valuing" but often lack the means or courage to value.
- He tells the reader: "But you can."

chunks.heading: Hindsight won't tell you which was right
chunks.text:
Jason also offers a way to take the pressure off:

- Five years later you still won't know which option would have been "right."
- Even if your chosen path "failed" in some objective sense, you can't know the other would have been better, whether in money, fulfillment or happiness.
- So optimize for the choice you can enjoy making and living with now.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jason Cohen compares two companies with equal revenue: 1,000 customers at $10/mo versus 10 at $1,000/mo. For raising money and maximizing growth, the many-customer company wins on market proof, market risk, time-based improvement and pivot data. A small, happy company is better served by the few-high-price model.

chunks.heading: Many low-price customers (A) vs few high-price customers (B): the framing
chunks.text:
Jason frames the choice with two companies that each earned $10,000 last month in recurring revenue. Company A has 1,000 customers paying $10/mo. Company B has 10 customers paying $1,000/mo.

- He rejects "which is better?" as a bad question. Better questions: which would you rather own, what problem should each solve, under what conditions is each interesting.
- He settles on one test: which company would be easier to raise money for?
- He uses fundraising as a lens even for founders who don't want to raise. In his words, "raise money or not" is a decision everyone must make, and exploring it answers the other questions too.
- He cites the real-world origin: guest posts on his blog compared selling many cheap eBook copies against selling about 1/6th the units at a higher price, which brought in more revenue.
- He calls this "a choice that every startup founder must make."

chunks.heading: Market size and what 1,000 customers prove
chunks.text:
- If the total addressable market is small, A runs out of room to grow and B wins by extracting more from a limited pool. Investors dislike small markets, though.
- In a large market, B isn't necessarily bad, but A shows far more potential.
- Companies at low price points can raise prices over time and extract more from different customer segments, so A has more revenue potential.
- Most important, A shows that a large market exists at all. If you've found 1,000 customers there are likely 10,000 and then 100,000. With only 10, there might be 10,000 out there, but you have no evidence, which is riskier.

chunks.heading: Market risk is the biggest startup killer
chunks.text:
- Jason says many more companies die because they can't find enough people to pay than die because the product sucks, lacks features, or has no staff designer.
- Finding customers involves many variables: locating prospects, getting them to the site, getting them to read and click, getting them to sign up, getting them to accept the price. With that many variables it's hard to get right.
- 1,000 customers paying any amount is irrefutable progress on this front. It's harder than adding three features, because features are "a matter of time and money" while customer acquisition is largely out of your control.
- Getting 10 people to pay, even a large amount, isn't that hard. A co-founder with an industry Rolodex would likely find 10. That doesn't prove a repeatable, scalable way to find customers, or that more exist.
- One way to reduce market risk is to build a B-type company that doesn't need many sales to hit its goals. "The risk is low when the bar is low." He says this isn't an insult and that far more companies should have this attitude.

chunks.heading: What improves with time and what doesn't
chunks.text:
Over years, Jason says to expect two trends:

- **Customer acquisition cost falls.** You get organized around marketing metrics, campaigns get optimized, landing pages and drip campaigns improve, and word of mouth brings sales "for free."
- **Average revenue per customer rises.** Better pricing tiers segment customers, prices go up as reputation grows, you add add-on products and services, and business development creates new revenue.

What does not automatically happen is unlocking big growth drivers.

- Many companies get stuck at a positive but slow growth rate that burns too much money on the way to cash-flow positive, and produces uninteresting profits afterward. Such a company still creates jobs and could unlock something later, but investors aren't interested in that outcome.
- A has already unlocked one growth driver. Where 1,000 customers came from a shoestring budget, other drivers likely exist. B has not shown that.
- So A's weaknesses matter less. If $10/mo seems too low, revenue per customer tends to rise. If it costs $60 to acquire a $10/mo customer, that cost tends to fall.
- Investors care about where you'll be in two years, and worry most about problems that don't self-correct with time.

chunks.heading: Pivotability and learning speed
chunks.text:
- Jason says early-stage startups should actively probe the market, not just watch for pivots. That means interviewing customers and non-customers, attending industry events for real conversations (not "quipping to each other on Twitter"), and studying website, marketing and product-feature metrics.
- A common answer to "what made you successful" is "we decided to stop X and do Y." Collecting data on what customers actually pay for and where the valuable gap actually is ranks among the most valuable things a company can do.
- A has about 100x the quantity and range of customers to interview and analyze, likely correspondingly more website traffic, and can split its user base to test four ideas at once.
- Citing Lean Startup, he says learning is proportional to how fast theories can be tested. He argues this holds whether or not you take investment.

chunks.heading: When Company B is the better choice
chunks.text:
Jason concedes investors generally prefer A, but lists cases where B wins:

- Support costs are high: A's support load kills profitability.
- Customer acquisition cost is 10x monthly revenue, or monthly revenue is 1/100th of what the company needs to sustain operations. "It gets better over time" fails because it's hard to justify orders-of-magnitude improvement.
- The human cost of scaling A exceeds that of B, so at scale B may be much more profitable.
- The company is staying small. B is almost always cheaper and more fun: less spent on marketing and acquisition, less time training customers, more time making customers love you (less churn), and product work for a handful of customers with homogeneous needs instead of thousands who can't agree.
- The market is small and only a few customers are reachable, so you need B's model to extract the most from the pool.

chunks.heading: Freemium is not Company A
chunks.text:
- Jason often hears founders and investors use the arguments above to claim a company with 100,000 free users is worth more than one with 1,000 paying customers. He disagrees.
- Many startups had great products, marketing, growth and large user bases yet couldn't convert enough free users to paid, or couldn't get conversions to pay enough.
- If there is a conversion rate, the earlier logic applies again: conversion rates rise over time, so if the absolute number of paying customers is interesting and growth is strong, it's good. It can be better than A because there are more levers (conversion, other products, pivots).

chunks.heading: Which to choose
chunks.text: His one-sentence summary: "If you want happiness and fulfillment from a small company, strive for B; if you want to maximize growth, influence, and financial value, strive for A."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jason Cohen uses Erica Douglass's self-doubt after selling her company for $1M to show why driven founders torment themselves with comparisons. Businesses are asymmetrical in time, market, team, location and everything else, so comparing yours to another is comparing the incomparable.

chunks.heading: Why Jason says driven people feel inadequate (and why the comparison is invalid)
chunks.text:
- Jason uses Erica Douglass as the example. She bootstrapped a hosting company (Simpli) and sold it for $1M, which is success by any definition.
- After watching WP Engine's marketing push for a few months, she concluded she "must have really sucked at growing my business" because WP Engine was growing faster than her company had.
- Jason says "all driven people do this to themselves, and it has to stop." He frames it as a problem for himself and for the reader, not just for her.
- Arguing that her definition of success is wrong (growth rate and gross margin versus happiness or fulfillment) wouldn't help. Type-A obsessive people don't respond emotionally to that argument, even when they accept it intellectually.

chunks.heading: Self-flagellation is rationalization, not cause
chunks.text:
- Jason points out the criteria are gerrymandered. Erica values "growth rate" but not "monthly cash loss," and values "gross profit margin" but not "percent ownership."
- He argues you could credibly say she is intentionally selecting only the metrics that make her feel inadequate and ignoring the rest.
- His conclusion: her stated explanation "is a rationalization rather than a cause." The real source is Impostor Syndrome, which he says is well documented in studies.
- He notes that by definition, high achievers using self-invented, impossible yardsticks "always come up short."

chunks.heading: Even on a pure money-and-power definition, the comparison is wrong
chunks.text:
- Jason concedes there's nothing wrong with defining success by money, power and speed of accumulation. His point is that the comparison fails on those terms too.
- His thought experiment: start WP Engine in 2002, alongside Erica's Simpli, with WordPress around v2.5 (circa 2008) to give his company a boost.
- Why it would have gone badly:
  - WordPress was far less prevalent, so customers couldn't be found "in droves."
  - No global network of WordCamps to reach potential customers.
  - He's not a hardware geek, and cloud hosting didn't exist, so he'd have to build, configure and maintain hardware, with false starts and legacy configs.
  - He'd be in Austin, not San Jose, with roughly 100x fewer customers at meetups.
  - No Twitter or Facebook, and little blogging culture, to let zealous fans spread the word.
  - No prior startup successes or moneyed contacts from blogging and speaking, so no way to raise money the way WP Engine did.
  - A post-bubble recession, with companies not paying a premium for WordPress-specific hosting.
- Likely outcome: failure, or painfully slow growth at about 1/10th the income, while holding a day job. He'd then claim to be profitable and to have Product/Market Fit, eventually realize that's a cope, and write a blog post about feeling inadequate next to someone like Erica.

chunks.heading: Businesses have no symmetries
chunks.text:
- Jason borrows the physics idea of symmetry: an experiment gives identical results if you move it elsewhere, provided all influences move with it. He notes that constant linear motion symmetry, combined with the constant speed of light, gives rise to special relativity, which he describes as "half of modern physics."
- Physics symmetries aren't always obvious. Rotation is symmetric at a fixed angle but not under continuous rotation. A mirror is almost symmetric, but not quite.
- For businesses, "where two businesses are symmetrical: Nowhere!" They differ in time, location, market, features, founding team, talents and gaps, investors, money raised, social following and everything else.
- If there were even near-symmetries, you could use them to predict success and failure. He says even professional investors manage that so rarely it's hard to say they "predicted" anything.

chunks.heading: Humans invent symmetry, and how to use it healthily
chunks.text:
- People expect, seek and invent symmetry, craving patterns and connections. Pitches like "We're Netflix for art" imply a symmetry that rarely holds: same site structure, pricing and delivery in a new market.
- In detail, each company has its own execution, route to market, margins, opportunity, competition, technology and strengths to leverage, so each is a new, unpredictable challenge.
- Healthy use: apparent symmetry can spark an idea ("That's a creative marketing campaign, maybe we could try something similar").
- Unhealthy use: seeing symmetry that doesn't exist, then building a straw man to fuel self-loathing.

chunks.heading: The practical takeaway
chunks.text:
- Jason says "stop comparing yourself to others and just be as good as you can" is wise but useless for high achievers, who can't follow it.
- His substitute advice: "Stop comparing yourself to something that is objectively incomparable." In his words, doing otherwise "is just irrational."
- He credits Erica for being willing to admit this publicly to help others suffering from the same delusion.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jason Cohen argues that copying style (not plagiarizing) is one of the best ways to learn a craft and discover your own voice. He shows how copying Seth Godin and James Altucher taught him what he likes and can do, and applies the same idea to racquetball, chefs and Picasso.

chunks.heading: Copying is a legitimate way to learn a craft, as long as it's a means to an end
chunks.text:
- Jason argues that American culture treats all copying as evil because it prizes creativity, uniqueness and "innovation". Plagiarism (using someone else's words) is bad, but he thinks the culture throws out the baby with the bathwater.
- His position: "copying is one of the best ways of learning, growing, evaluating, and exploring." It is "a valid tool so long as we regard it as a means to an end."
- The goal is not to match the person you copy. After he imitated James Altucher's style, he said the point was not "being as good as James at James' style" but to "learn and grow as a writer."

chunks.heading: Copy style, not content
chunks.text:
- Jason separates plagiarism (lifting someone's words) from copying style: structure, pacing, tone, how an essay opens and closes.
- His examples:
  - **Seth Godin style:** the 160-word post "Hello, I'm 1074018628" (2008). One simple point, a specific example that runs straight to an overarching lesson, and an inspiring ending.
  - **Steve Almond:** a satirical piece about Joel Spolsky whose construction was "100% lifted" from the first essay of Almond's *Rants, Exploits, and Obsessions (not that you asked)*.
  - **James Altucher:** a personal story up front, short sentences, admitting embarrassing things about himself, and an almost trivial conclusion that still leaves a sense of the larger point.
- He still does this after finding his voice, with 65,000 subscribers at the time of writing.

chunks.heading: What copying teaches you: what you like and what you can actually do
chunks.text:
- Imitating a style shows you what you like and what you have some ability to do.
- Lessons from copying Seth Godin:
  - He likes evocative examples.
  - He dislikes leaving the reader with no framework for finding a solution. A post that says "be the opposite of shitty" gives inspiration but no tools, like "full of expectation and no answers."
  - He can't explore an interesting thought in only 160 words.
  - He likes leaving the reader on an up-note.
- He applied these lessons directly in a later article, "Be Yourself", which exemplifies each of them.
- Lesson from copying Almond: the structure was fun to do, but inventing structures like that is beyond his ability.

chunks.heading: The same technique works outside writing
chunks.text:
- Racquetball: Jason was the inter-mural racquetball champion at the University of Texas. It took lots of practice, but he learned by watching the good players and copying their swing, where they ran and where they placed the ball.
- Chefs: he asks rhetorically whether any great chef did not, at points in her career, intentionally learn styles from various cultures.
- Art: even Picasso, "one of the most creative, innovating artists in history," first learned his craft by copying the styles of the Great Masters.
- He calls the technique "useful in almost any pursuit."

chunks.heading: Copying helps you find your own voice
chunks.text:
- Jason's claim: "Copying ironically helps you discover yourself."
- The method is to try things on like clothes and see what fits: "Bits and pieces of you are already reflected in the things around you, so pick up handfuls of other creations and see which bits you want to keep."
- This is how you learn what you value, what you're good at and what you believe.

chunks.heading: Why school writing instruction didn't teach him
chunks.text:
- He says High School English III "doesn't teach you how to write prose in the real world any more than a college CS degree teaches you how to write code in the real world. English III teaches you how to write things that English III teachers want to read."
- In class, nobody understood the Eudora Welty story. When he honestly said he didn't know what it meant, the teacher was disgusted and never told them the answer.
- The class ended up memorizing a textbook commentary in case it was on the test, which taught nothing about writing persuasively or with entertainment and interest.
- Having never learned to write well that way, he taught himself by copying.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jason Cohen argues that our emotional baggage defines who we are but also creates blind spots. Using a hosting-cost example from WP Engine, he shows how bootstrapper habits can misallocate time once a company is funded. His fix: define core values, build a company that fits them, and seek compatible outside counsel.

chunks.heading: Scars can be a defining strength and a blind spot at once
chunks.text:
Jason argues that the emotional baggage and past experience that make a founder unique also act as blinders. He cites examples of people whose strong opinions are really scars showing:

- The guy a little too steadfast that "VCs are evil."
- The founder who says she doesn't need to talk to customers before a $200,000 development project because "customers don't know what they want until you show it to them."
- The developer who is sure that "Java sucks."

He says dwelling on our peculiar trauma is a comforting way to develop uniqueness, and most advice says to embrace that uniqueness and own it. His caveat: some of that baggage is a hindrance whether or not it is also "defining me." Even if you know your scars, embrace them, and can rationalize every decision as correct for you, a decision can still be wrong.

chunks.heading: Bootstrapper scars at a funded company: the $1000/month hosting example
chunks.text:
Jason says he still sometimes runs WP Engine like the bootstrapped startup it was for its first 18 months, instead of the funded growth machine it evolved into.

- Last week he spent about 10 hours saving about $1000/mo in hosting costs.
- The financial case looks good: 10 hours to earn $12,000 over the next year means his time was worth over $1000/hour.
- He says that is "not no matter what." The same 10 hours could have gone into making the website speed report (speed.wpengine.com) easier to share.
- His estimate for that alternative: 1000 people try it over the next year, 10 move their WordPress site to WP Engine, and a few consultants put 20 of their clients on it. At $50/mo, that is 30 × $50 = $1500/mo in direct new revenue, plus side benefits in marketing and branding.

chunks.heading: When cash now beats growth later, and when it doesn't
chunks.text:
Jason's rule for choosing between saving money now and investing in growth depends on whether you have money in the bank:

- **Bootstrapping:** getting the $1000/mo right now is the better choice. Money is scarce, time is precious, and "$1000 today is better than $5000 next year (which you might not survive to see)."
- **Money in the bank:** it is "just the opposite." The point of an investment is to turn money today into long-term value, meaning a growing, profitable, predictable revenue machine.

The lesson is that the right call depends on your company's stage and funding, not on what your instincts (your scars) are comfortable with.

chunks.heading: Step one: define your core beliefs
chunks.text:
Jason says to decide your inalienable tenets, the things you want to live by no matter what, even if holding them means:

- making less money
- increasing risk
- hurting your brand or your feelings
- limiting your fame
- closing doors
- losing relationships

These beliefs are strong enough that if a relationship contradicts them, the relationship is what's wrong and it's good that it dissolves. If a way of making money contradicts them, you don't want to make money that way. These are your core values and also form the basis of your company's cultural values.

chunks.heading: Step two: build a company where the right decisions come naturally
chunks.text:
Jason says to make sure your startup journey conforms to your values and to your natural strengths and weaknesses. Decide to build a company in which the correct, consistent decisions are the ones you'll naturally take:

- If you love optimizing the last dollar out of the process (as he apparently does), build a bootstrapped company.
- If you don't like working with people, be a Micropreneur like Rob Walling and Patrick McKenzie.
- If you want to leave a mark on the world with big ideas, lots of people and lots of money, seek advice from people who have walked that path. Find advisors who help you become a better version of yourself, rather than pushing you to be something "rational" but unnatural.

chunks.heading: Step three: surround yourself with trusted advisors to find your blind spots
chunks.text:
Jason says that once you have defined yourself and made decisions consistent with it, you still have to find where you are wrong, ignorant, or doing the wrong thing by your own definition of "right." You can't do that alone, "almost by definition," because otherwise you would already have fixed it.

- Surround yourself with trusted advisors.
- Be completely and continuously honest with them.
- Then actually listen and learn.

He applies this to himself: he knows he is naturally a bootstrapper, a "get to the first $10M in ARR, but only after seven years, and then what?" type, so he needs constant course corrections. He stresses that you "cannot know you're wrong," even if, like him, you are proactively introspective, have escaped Impostor Syndrome, and have a few successful startups behind you.

chunks.heading: Summary principle: you are your scars, but more than that
chunks.text: Jason's closing guidance is to embrace your scars and let them lead you to who you are and what you believe. Construct your life, relationships and organizations around them. Then, on that solid foundation, seek compatible guidance on how to execute despite the weaknesses, blind spots and flaws those same scars create. His last lines: "You are your scars. But you're also more than that."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jason Cohen argues founders should value their time at roughly $1000/hr, not their consultant rate. Working for a startup is like a client paying in four years with a high chance of never paying. That price forces focus, delegation, and spending money to save time.

chunks.heading: Why Jason says a startup founder's time is worth $1000/hour
chunks.text:
Jason argues that founders undervalue their time. Consultants know their rate ("what the market will bear"), but a founder in a startup is working on very different terms. His claim: "Your time is worth $1000/hour, and you need to act accordingly."

- Valuing yourself at a consultant rate ($150/hr in his example) is a mistake once you are in a startup.
- The reason is that the math of a startup is not the math of a consultant.

chunks.heading: The thought experiment: a client who pays in four years
chunks.text:
Jason builds the $1000/hr figure from a hypothetical.

- A consultant who normally charges $150/hour meets a client who says: "I can't pay you now. I promise to pay you four years from now, at which time I will pay everything I owe in one lump sum."
- The rate must go up for the delay alone. 4% interest isn't the whole story, because you can't live off money you don't have, so you also have to work for other clients to cover your expenses. That inconvenience demands a hefty premium.
- The bigger problem is the risk the client never pays. If the client is an early-stage startup, even a funded one, the most likely outcome is that it dies and stiffs you.
- He assumes a 25% chance the company exists in four years and pays its bill.

chunks.heading: Why 1/odds isn't enough
chunks.text:
- The naive fix is $150 ÷ 0.25 = $600/hour.
- Jason says this "merely brings you back to break-even."
- Test: split your time across four companies on these terms. Probably all but one fold, and the survivor pays 4x your rate. That leaves you where you'd be charging $150/hour on standard terms, without the risk and without waiting four years for cash.
- Like gambling or investing, steeper odds require a bigger upside. To be worth the risk you must charge a premium over break-even, so he lands on "more like $1000/hr."

chunks.heading: Founders are already accepting those terms
chunks.text:
- Jason says this isn't hypothetical: it is "exactly the terms you're accepting for yourself when you create a startup."
- Because the risk is high, the financial reward must outweigh it, so "you have to value your time at least $1000 per hour."
- Platitudes like "my time is worth what the market will bear" don't apply.

chunks.heading: What valuing your time at $1000/hr changes day to day
chunks.text:
- Skip projects that have potential only for small, incremental results.
- A personal assistant is worth the money.
- Focus on a few things that really matter, the ones worth that hourly rate, and delegate far more than you think.
- Follow the rules of finding product-market fit: talk to customers rather than assuming you know what to build, and work on marketing and sales at least as much as the product.
- Spend money on a bookkeeper and CPA instead of messing with receipts, QuickBooks and taxes. Pay for help at home with cleaning and chores.
- Build things more valuable than money, ones that generate customer Love.
- Work harder than is healthy, and obsess about your own productivity.
- Be smart at prioritization, and make sure you are actually doing it.

chunks.heading: The filter for how to spend your hours
chunks.text:
- Jason's summary: stay in the intersection of your zone of maximum excellence and the zone of importance.
- "Because at $1000/hr, you can't afford to do anything else."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jason Cohen argues that being "first" is rarely a real advantage: it implies a buggy v1 and legacy baggage, and lets later entrants copy your public mistakes. First only wins when paired with relentless innovation and fast expansion that builds a moat, as with Amazon, McDonald's and Ford.

chunks.heading: Why "first" is not a competitive advantage (and when it is)
chunks.text:
Jason argues that being "first" sounds like innovation and leadership, but it is not a tangible benefit a customer can experience. He treats it as history, not an advantage. This position came from competing at WP Engine, where a rival's pitch was "We started the trend" in Managed WordPress Hosting. Jason's view: that line does not make the rival better.

- "Being 'first' isn't an end in itself": it is not an advantage, not a feature, not a benefit.
- It can be a means to one of those ends, if levered into market dominance with persistence and the right strategy.
- Otherwise it can be a manacle that lets newer competitors accelerate past you.
- He says to be proud of being first at something, but like being "disruptive," it is not necessarily desirable.

chunks.heading: Most market leaders were not first
chunks.text:
Jason's evidence is that the leaders are rarely the originators:

- Google was not the first search engine.
- The iPod was not the first MP3 player.
- Dropbox was not the first cloud filesystem.
- Excel was not the first spreadsheet.
- Dell was not the first PC manufacturer.
- Facebook was not the first social network.
- Cisco did not invent the router.

He notes they are nonetheless the market leaders and their markets' greatest innovators. Early MP3 players did not get huge traction and were not creative in hardware or design, which left Apple room to innovate in design while the market was still largely up for grabs.

chunks.heading: "First" implies the faults of version one
chunks.text:
Being first implies innovation, but also the flaws of a v1 product.

- His example is the first electric car: short-range, sluggish, unattractive, and constantly in the repair shop.
- In software, "v1.0" implies "buggy" and "incomplete." He asks: "Who wants their business to depend on a v1.0 product?"
- His framing for WP Engine: "We're not the first electric car; instead we're Tesla."
- A footnote concedes that Tesla was also first at some things: good-enough batteries, realizing "performance" was non-negotiable, and using EV engineering constraints to build the safest sedan ever made.

chunks.heading: Compete on tangible advantages, not on history
chunks.text:
Jason counters the "first" claim with measurable differences, as WP Engine did in 2011:

- Uptime: the competitor had 40 minutes of downtime in a month, WP Engine had 0, per Pingdom, an unaffiliated third party.
- Speed: WP Engine was 30% faster at delivering HTML (also Pingdom).
- Security: WP Engine guaranteed cleanup of any hacks, while the competitor only claimed it had never been hacked. WP Engine had found malware in customers who switched from them.
- Support: more responsive and knowledgeable, because WP Engine employed more WordPress experts per 1000 customers than anyone.

His point: "Those are tangible competitive advantages; being 'first' isn't."

chunks.heading: How being first becomes a shackle
chunks.text:
Jason lists the costs of being first:

- You are stuck supporting the legacy of version one.
- Features you thought were important but are not now, and maybe never were, a journey new competitors skip.
- Grandfathered customers who are no longer profitable.
- Architectural choices you wish you could change, which competitors can avoid.
- A reputation that is hard to revamp even if the company has changed.
- You made all the mistakes in public. Newcomers swoop in with your hindsight on pricing, positioning, marketing, features, and design, and get a running start without your baggage.

A footnote example: years later, founders of a competitor that did not exist at the time of writing told him how they set pricing: "We figured you'd already done the research and tested different things, so we just copied y'all."

chunks.heading: When being first is a massive advantage
chunks.text:
Jason says first-mover advantage is real when two conditions hold:

- You are first and also able to expand fast and keep innovating.
- Fast expansion creates a moat that prevents late-joining competitors from catching up.

Examples he gives:

- McDonald's and Ford kept their leads because they never stopped innovating in process and product, constantly driving down costs while adding desirable features, and using the lead to fund stronger growth.
- Amazon in cloud infrastructure: "first, but relentlessly innovative." It did not just put cloud computing on the map, it kept lowering prices while expanding the depth and breadth of service. He saw no one overtaking it as long as it continued, though at least four multi-billion-dollar companies were trying.
- A 2024 note says this held true, even after Amazon stopped lowering prices, and points to strategic moats as the explanation.

He adds that this usually takes a well-funded startup, a stellar team, and a bit of good fortune. Most small companies are not in that position, and it is often not the best risk/reward anyway.

chunks.heading: Hindsight on the WP Engine bet
chunks.text: A 2024 editor's note says that when the piece was written WP Engine was one and a half years old. By 2024 WP Engine was a unicorn, while the competitor's growth leveled off many years earlier at less than 1/30th WP Engine's size, and it was then folded into a much larger company. Jason says the predictions in the article proved accurate.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jason Cohen explains how to make the first startup hire: write a personality-filled job post, filter hundreds of resumes with a free-form writing test, avoid bounty recruiters, and hire constantly by building a company good people seek out. He treats the first hire like a marriage, not an HR exercise.

chunks.heading: Hiring employee #1 means choosing between a lifestyle business and trying to get big
chunks.text:
Jason says the first hire is a big decision, because what you're really deciding is whether to keep a lifestyle business or attempt to "cross the chasm" and maybe get rich. He treats employee #1 as a culture-setter, not "any old programmer or salesman".

- Employee #1 helps set the company culture and has to mesh with the founder's personality "100%".
- You'll put in long hours together. If they don't get your jokes, "it's not going to work".
- He compares it to "getting married" more than hiring an underling. The rules of HR don't apply, except the law.
- His closing advice is that going with your gut is not wrong.

chunks.heading: Hire for comfort with startup chaos, not for big-company habits
chunks.text:
Jason argues startups are chaotic, rules change, and there is no "job description". The founder already lives by this "Code of Turmoil" because they have no choice. Most people abhor chaos and are used to big companies, so the hire must be comfortable with the bedlam.

- Someone leaving IBM is a fit only if they left over bureaucracy, tolerated incompetence and no visibility into what customers want.
- Red flags in an interview: asking how often you do performance reviews, or saying "I thrive in environments with clear requirements, written expectations, and defined processes". His advice is to run away.
- It's better to make a strong decision that turns out wrong, and admit it, than to plan ahead or wait for instructions.
- Prefer people who favor potential earnings (stock, performance bonuses) over guaranteed earnings (salary, benefits).

chunks.heading: Put your personality in the job description to filter candidates early
chunks.text:
Jason says not to wait for the interview to test personality fit. Make the job description funny and reflective of your company's uniqueness.

- He points to the WP Engine jobs page for examples, covering culture, code quality and customers. Quoted lines:
  - "Being transparent about our strengths and weaknesses wins us sales"
  - "You think using a profiler is fun, like a treasure hunt"
  - "Whether or not you sleep at night is directly proportional to whether you've made something thrilled or pissed off that day"
- The test shows up in the cover letters. If someone still sends a generic cover letter after a posting like that, they're not for you. If they respond in kind, it's a good sign.

chunks.heading: Don't use recruiters on a bounty; their incentives are opposite to yours
chunks.text:
Jason quotes Bryan Menell: "If you find yourself wanting to hire a recruiter, hit yourself in the head with a frying pan until the feeling goes away." He says you need an absolute superstar, and recruiters aren't in the business of finding superstars.

- Recruiters work like real estate salesmen. They earn the same amount whether it takes four days or four months.
- Every extra day, resume or interview lowers their income per hour. So the longer you take to find the right person, the more they push you to settle for someone you already rejected.
- The exception is a recruiter who works by the hour instead of a hiring bounty. These are hard to find, and he's had luck only in that case.

chunks.heading: Treat resumes as conversation starters, and require clear communication from everyone
chunks.text:
Jason says resumes are useless for judging fit, since your own resume likely has nothing that qualifies you to run a company. They're useful only as talking points on a phone call: probe past experience and test claimed technology knowledge.

- Trick: dig deep on one detail. Pick the weirdest technology or an odd bullet from two jobs ago. Don't accept "It's been a while"; if they can't talk about it, they can't claim to bring that experience.
- Everyone must communicate clearly, even someone who will spend 60 hours a week writing code or solving differential equations.
- Reasons: in a modern startup everyone writes blog entries, tweets and posts on whatever comes next, and there's no layer between employees and customers.
- Everyone needs to be able to talk to customers and even sell to them. He reminds readers that "tech support is sales".
- Because everyone must decipher each other's nuances, part of the interview must include free-form writing.

chunks.heading: Screen applicants with a short writing test instead of reading resumes
chunks.text:
When you post on large sites like Monster or Craigslist, expect a torrent of resumes (100 in a day isn't unusual). Jason says screening resumes is not an option, so he sends an email template asking for a few paragraphs on each question.

- His example questions:
  1. Why do you want to work at [company]?
  2. Describe a situation in your work-life where you failed.
  3. Describe a time when you accomplished something you thought was impossible (work or personal).
- Expected results: most people never respond ("Good riddance!"). Some give lazy answers like "I want to work at your company because I saw you are hiring" or "I have never failed at anything".
- He says to resist replying "You just did", because that's what assholes do.
- Roughly 10% actually answer. In two minutes you can tell whether the person can communicate, and whether they seem fun, intelligent or interesting.
- Exception: if a cover letter is truly wonderful, it's a rare great sign and you can skip to the phone interview.

chunks.heading: Hiring a good person takes 3-6 months, so hire constantly and be a place good people seek out
chunks.text:
Jason's rule of thumb is that it takes 3-6 months to hire a really good person. If you start when you really need someone, it's too late.

- Why so long:
  - Good people are rare.
  - They change jobs at most about once a year, more likely every 3-4 years, so you must catch their window.
  - They get lots of offers, so by the time you finish the writing test, phone interview, in-person interview, compensation talk and written offer, they may have accepted elsewhere. He says this happened to him all the time at Smart Bear, and was happening at WP Engine.
- Good people choose where they work: they hear about a cool company and call you. So the company must be a place they seek out.
- His ideas for that:
  - Build a blog and Twitter following with a steady stream of readers.
  - Attend local meet-ups and user groups, and meet the organizer, who knows everyone worth knowing.
  - Sponsor a meet-up at your office, or co-sponsor with a company or co-working space if you have no office.
  - Example: OtherInbox sponsors the monthly Austin on Rails group and the annual Lone Star Ruby Conference, so the best Ruby developers in Austin already want to work there.
  - Ask friends for resumes of people they liked but didn't hire.
  - Make your Jobs page rank in local search, e.g. "java programmer job in austin tx", not "java programmer".
  - Take everyone you know to lunch and ask about candidates. In person brings out more than email, and sometimes the person you ask is interested himself (it's happened to him a few times).

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jason Cohen argues that tearing apart any business idea is trivial and useless, since the entrepreneur's job is to build, learn and stay humble rather than be right. He also warns against dismissing criticism wholesale, and suggests asking whether a sting hides a truth you don't want to face.

chunks.heading: Criticism is cheap, but dismissing it is just as costly
chunks.text:
Jason argues that explaining why any business will fail is easy, and that being "right" is the wrong goal for an entrepreneur. He takes a hard stance against reflexive skepticism and a softer one against ignoring critics. In practice, that means building with humility and listening with "half an ear".

He also shows how easily a good business can be torn apart. His Netflix example, written in 2011 when Netflix still shipped DVDs, makes the point.

chunks.heading: Why armchair criticism is easy and useless
chunks.text:
- Jason says he can "rip any business idea to shreds."
- His Netflix takedown: inventory logistics costs, millions of non-technical customers, the Postal Service, wear and delivery losses, no browsing gratification, movie duplication angering publishers, and Blockbuster copying the model and undercutting on price.
- The outcome: Blockbuster, which did copy the model, went bankrupt. Netflix turned a profit of $60m in the latest quarter, more than Blockbuster earned at its peak.
- If your goal is to be *right*, you should bet against every startup and every novel idea. You will be right far more often than wrong.
- He calls this "Right, but useless": it guarantees nothing new or great gets created.

chunks.heading: What the entrepreneur's goal actually is
chunks.text:
- "The goal of the entrepreneur is not to be 'right.'" At least not about everything, all the time, from the start.
- The job is to construct with humility, hold strong opinions while seeking better ones, and infect customers and employees with your "peculiar disease."
- Live to fight another day, and acknowledge being wrong before the fault turns fatal.
- Even a "failed" venture never really fails. Jason has never met a "failed" entrepreneur who didn't say they were better off: new skills, clarity about what excites them each morning, a view of their limits, and more confidence in what they can do.

chunks.heading: Learning over being right: experiments and Francis Crick
chunks.text:
- He ties this to the Lean Startup movement (the book came out the same year), which values learning and experience over being right and frames the work as "running experiments."
- He quotes Francis Crick, Nobel winner for the discovery of DNA: "The dangerous man is the one who has only one idea, because then he'll fight and die for it. The way real science goes is that you come up with lots of ideas, and most of them will be wrong."
- Real science is mostly being wrong while staying vigilant and honest enough to keep going until you aren't. Dating and startups work the same way.

chunks.heading: Every craft wants to be "right" and has to temper it
chunks.text:
- **Designers** want to be right but must temper that with analytics. The true masters treat metrics as an incontrovertible goal while keeping the aesthetics, creativity and philosophy that make design an art.
- **Programmers** want to be right but must temper that with building and shipping, even before it's ready and even with bugs. They should build what customers actually want, including features customers truly love rather than ones that are rationally calculated.
- **Advisors and pundits** (he includes himself) want to be right but should aim to inspire people to be a better version of themselves rather than indoctrinate them with their own biases, since their experience contains "unknown quantities of luck."

chunks.heading: Listen to critics with half an ear, and don't dismiss them either
chunks.text:
- "As a founder, you still need to listen to critics with half an ear." Sometimes you have been blind, and critics are showing you the truth.
- Jason admits he resists opposition to his ideas more than he should: "I still hate being wrong."
- A founder must be negatable. Otherwise you are pig-headed.
- As founder of WP Engine, he says most days hold more contradictions than construction: balancing customer needs with internal costs, following your nose against what competitors do or say, and staying true to the vision while flexing as you learn what the market and you want.
- Dismissing criticism without consideration is "just as easy" as criticizing, and "equally hazardous."

chunks.heading: A test for criticism that stings
chunks.text:
- Ask whether it stings exactly because it contains an element of truth you don't want to face.
- His rule: ignore the messenger, ignore the emotion, and see whether it's "a gift of truth, poorly wrapped."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jason Cohen relays Noah Kagan's advice that a startup can focus on only one metric and should ignore the rest. Using WP Engine, he shows why shaving cancellation rate from 3% to 2.5% pales next to doubling or tripling sign-ups, even if cancellations rise. Small optimizations can wait.

chunks.heading: Focus on one metric and ignore the rest
chunks.text:
- Jason relays Noah Kagan's rule: "A startup can focus on only one metric. So you have to decide what that is and ignore everything else."
- He says this is not the usual "startups need focus" platitude. The point is to pick the single number that matters most and let everything else go.
- It took him 15 years, and a side comment at a group meeting, to understand it.
- At WP Engine the metric he chose was growth in sign-ups. He still thinks cancellation rate matters, but he narrowed in on the one thing whose movement would change the business.

chunks.heading: Only do things that can move the business "that much"
chunks.text:
- Jason's starting priority at WP Engine was cancellation rate. Dharmesh Shah had told him it was the key number.
- His case for it: it shows whether the service is genuinely valuable, and it drives customer LTV. Example: $50/mo for 30 months is $1,500 in lifetime revenue.
- Kagan asked what would change if cancellation fell from 3% to 2.5%. Jason said LTV would rise about 15%, so they could spend more on ads, and he admitted things wouldn't change that much.
- Kagan's rule: "You should only be doing things that can be 'that much.'"
- Jason's takeaway: "At a little company there's no time for small changes achieving small goals."
- Example: lifting conversion from 0.9% to 1.1% is meaningless if only 100 people visit the site a day. Getting 1,000 visitors a day is what matters.

chunks.heading: Why a worse cancellation rate can still be a win
chunks.text:
- Jason's objection to doubling sign-ups: he could do it by spending 5x on AdWords, but lead quality would drop and cancellations would spike.
- Kagan's counter: don't assume they'll cancel at a ruinous rate. If sign-ups triple and cancellation rate doubles from 3% to 6%, "you'd still be growing almost three times faster."
- Jason ran the experiment. Cancellation rate went up only a little, "and it doesn't matter."
- General lesson: a big gain on the primary metric can swamp a modest loss on a secondary one. Don't let a secondary metric veto a large move on the main one.

chunks.heading: Leave incremental optimization for later
chunks.text:
- Jason: "You can always optimize that little stuff later." Squeezing out 0.1% or 1% more conversion is mechanical, doable and in your control, and there are plenty of people you could hire to do it.
- Early on, spend effort on big needle-moving levers. Examples he gives: doubling revenue, solidifying the funding story, pushing the viral coefficient above 1, and building the asset of an active user base.
- Small incremental work can wait until there is spare time.

chunks.heading: What counts as big stuff, and how strict to be
chunks.text:
- Part of "only do big stuff" is knowing what big stuff is, and that requires choosing one metric.
- With one metric chosen, you can pursue actions that could move that needle regardless of the other numbers.
- He says this kind of focus tends to break you out of incremental changes and into a major change in the business's trajectory (a link to his "local minimum" post).
- Kagan is strict: no A/B testing, no AdWords copy tweaks, no landing page optimization.
- Jason admits he is less disciplined and takes a softer line. 15% lifts from small tweaks are real, and "you can still do the 15% thing."
- The trade-off he frames: hours iterating to a 15% lift versus pouring time, emails, social media, creativity, new features, marketing, ads and measurement into a 2x or 3x change in the Most Important Number, which is an order of magnitude better.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jason Cohen argues that expertise makes founders skip customer conversations and miss what has changed. A founder certain about pricing learned more in one week of quick vendor calls than in a year. Use experience for hypotheses, not decisions, and test every assumption with real customers.

chunks.heading: Assuming you know your market blocks the learning that kills bad assumptions
chunks.text: Jason argues that expertise hinders learning, and that insight comes from curiosity, not certainty. The worst case is the self-declared "expert," who is least likely to challenge his own assumptions. He says the goal is to leverage expertise without being blinded by it.

chunks.heading: Test the "I know my customers" claim by asking them
chunks.text:
At a startup incubator, a founder dismissed several mentors' pricing advice with "I know our industry, I know how our customers think."

- Jason asked whether the last dozen prospects had all said "Heck yes" to her pricing. She hadn't asked them, because "I know what they're going to say."
- He did not argue. He asked her to include the pricing scheme in her pitch at the next week's convention, since she was sure it would be well received.
- She expected an "I told you so" moment, and so did he, because she was the expert.
- She was wrong. She emailed: "In the past week of quick phone calls to vendors, I've learned more about this market than I did in the past year."
- Her earlier "lean" discovery had been hour-long calls, relationship-building meetings and vague answers to poorly formed questions.
- His takeaway: "whenever an assumption is kicked out from under you, that's when you learn the most." Betting on an assumption that is actually tested is what exposes it.

chunks.heading: Resist pitching in customer calls
chunks.text:
Jason says the defect is human nature: thinking we know more than we do, and so missing chances to learn. He still struggles with it.

- In every customer call he consciously restrains himself from pitching.
- He asks questions instead and tries to understand what customers mean, rather than mapping their words onto what he wants them to say.
- Experts' "laws" about what makes their market unique are largely based on feeling, not fact.

chunks.heading: Markets change faster than your experience
chunks.text:
Fifteen years of experience in a sector is not a defense, and Jason applied this to himself too: "I built a company and forged dozens of customer relationships in the software development tools sector; I know exactly how to sell into that market." He gives several reasons it fails.

- You can't rely on five-year-old information about customers, even in stodgy big-company markets and especially in mass-market consumer ones.
- Non-technical people now use iPhones and Facebook. Industries built on controlling process and information, such as real estate and book publishing, are now out of control.
- Methods of reaching consumers change yearly, for example SEO or AdWords strategy in 2003 versus 2010.
- Expectations also shift constantly: what software should do, what it should integrate with, whether data can live on someone else's server, whether it must work from a cellphone.
- Old experience can cloud judgment. A competitor not shackled by old ideas can beat you with innovations they achieve because of that freedom.
- Jason's 2024 editor's note on AdWords: in 2003 at Smart Bear he was often the only bidder on a keyword at $0.05/click, which let him bootstrap the company with AdWords. By 2010, at WP Engine, AdWords was too expensive to start with anything but long-tail phrases. It became a staple only once the company could afford it, and was still one of the lowest-ROI marketing activities. By 2024 many bootstrappers call advertising prohibitively expensive, partly from inexperience with paid ads, but also because AdWords ROI keeps worsening.

chunks.heading: Selling a different product into the same industry is a different market
chunks.text:
Experience selling one product to a market doesn't transfer automatically to another product in that market. Jason's example is an entrepreneur who had sold a standard medical device to doctors for years and had an idea for practice-management software.

- He assumed his Rolodex let him line up ten alpha testers before writing code, but he hadn't done it.
- He didn't know whether doctors could install new software, since he had sold hardware.
- He had never asked whether the software could depend on an internet connection inside a secured hospital.
- He assumed that because doctors pay a lot for the device, software would fetch a lot too. Jason doubted that front-office software budgets relate to device budgets.
- Zero people had said they wanted this software, even for free, and that didn't worry him.
- Jason's point: you aren't starting from scratch, but you need an attitude of re-learning and questioning everything.

chunks.heading: How to use expertise without being blinded by it
chunks.text:
Jason says combining special knowledge with an open mind could be unbeatable. It won't happen unless you force it.

- Set your ego aside and explore anew with a "child-like" mind.
- Use your Rolodex to set up meetings and sales calls, but don't assume you know what prospects will say.
- Use experience to generate plausible theories, not to make decisions.
- Some prior experience is invaluable, an unfair advantage worth leveraging, but the old assumptions in it should be treated as hypotheses to test.
- His closing line: "After all, you're the expert."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jason Cohen argues that "be yourself" must include being a person who strives and keeps improving. He uses his own fight with procrastination to show why you shouldn't just accept faults. He also lists the common entrepreneur side effects of that internal "motor" and how to manage them.

chunks.heading: Striving is part of who Jason is, so "be yourself" does not mean accepting your flaws
chunks.text:
Jason takes Lady Gaga's "be yourself" ("I was born this way") as sound advice. The upside is fulfillment, happiness and often success. Natural excitement leads to "merry obsession", which leads to hard work and long hours in a field that fits your talents. Even total failure was fun and was your own life. He adds that being yourself is necessary but not sufficient: many other things also have to be true for a venture to succeed.

His tension is self-improvement. It is sensible to work around your faults, but should you also tackle them directly? A person afraid of public speaking could pick a career that avoids stages, or take a stand-up comedy class to beat the fear.

chunks.heading: How Jason's relationship to being "the best" changed over time
chunks.text:
- As a kid he needed the blue ribbon, the gold medal and the first-place trophy in everything.
- In high school he accepted there will always be people smarter and better. His new rule had two parts: (1) be the best at one thing (telling a computer what to do), and (2) keep improving at everything else.
- He measured against himself, not others. He didn't need to beat the top student on the Math Team, but he beat his own scores in national competitions year over year. He didn't need to outpace piano prodigies, but he played harder pieces as well as he could.
- Over time, responsibilities pile up and even "improving" is too much work. For hobbies he dropped it: he runs a few 5ks a week untimed and learns new piano pieces for enjoyment, not progression.
- That relaxed stance doesn't work for a career or startup. You can't say "I suck at selling stuff, and I don't care!"

chunks.heading: Procrastination: why the usual excuses are bullshit
chunks.text:
Jason says he struggles constantly with procrastination, and that everyone does to some degree. You invent logical-sounding reasons to avoid something. His list, with his rebuttals:

- "I don't have time for X right now." Time always exists; you're choosing to spend it on something else.
- "It's more efficient to do X with Y and Z." Someone is waiting on X, and you've been delaying Y and Z too.
- "I'm not in the mood, and it'll go twice as fast when I am." If you dislike the task you'll never be in the mood, or you haven't been for weeks.
- "I forgot because I don't have a good system." There are 100 organization systems, plus blogs, books and videos.
- "I have better things to do." Then delegate or delete it instead of leaving it on the to-do list.

He rolls deadlines over to "tomorrow" and so out-wits his own to-do software. He has used GTD for years ("yes, it works") and been inbox-zero for years ("it changed my life"). He still has "temporary surges of success and guilt-ridden lapses of ineptitude". He even wrote a post arguing procrastination is useful for running a startup, and half jokes that this was a coping mechanism.

chunks.heading: Jason's decision: keep fighting, because "I'm a person who strives"
chunks.text:
He chose to keep fighting procrastination because it means getting more done in less time with less stress, and optimizing for the long run instead of the easy moment. The deciding factor is another fact about who he is: he is a person for whom "good enough" isn't.

Examples he gives:
- He won't let a 5k stay at 26:06.
- He lectures that blogging success is about content and time, not looks and plugins, yet wrote his own plugin to control how the "retweet" link behaves in the RSS feed.
- He couldn't just make peer code review software. He made it a "real company", created the modern theory around it, wrote a book, and pushed it into 70,000 people's hands.
- He couldn't just read Joel Spolsky and Jason Fried. He wrote his own blog, got better at writing and promoted it, "for no reason or reward other than pure ego".
- After two Mixergy interviews with Andrew Warner (already an honor), he pushed for a third so he could interview Andrew on Andrew's own show.
- After selling Smart Bear he couldn't stay retired. New ideas "foisted themselves" on him, so he ran through bad ones until he found a good one and started that company.

chunks.heading: The "motor" and why serial entrepreneurs repeat
chunks.text: Jason sees this attitude in most successful entrepreneurs. He cites Adam Carolla's term "motor": an internal, unstoppable force that keeps you going from wake to sleep for decades. It explains serial entrepreneurship. His line: "You do the third one for the same reason you did the first one, because you are compelled to."

chunks.heading: The four problems the motor creates, and how to manage them
chunks.text:
The motor causes problems for most entrepreneurs regardless of age or success:

- **"Spread too thin":** you're interested in and good at many things, so you join too much. Nothing gets enough time, and most things end up worse off than if you'd stayed out, because others could have planned around your absence instead of relying on you.
- **"Shiny new thing":** you get bored when a project moves from the "mostly creative" childhood to the "mostly execution" adolescence, so projects don't get the lasting attention they need.
- **"Work all the time":** it works better when young, but you burn out. Jason did, and says many famous workaholics have, though they rarely admit it. Andrew Warner publicly admits he sold his company for less than he should have because of burnout. Jason's verdict: "Pulling 70-hour weeks catches up to you. Period."
- **"Not good enough":** perfectionism or control-freak tendencies make nothing ever feel done. If you also believe others will find out you're inept, you have real impostor-syndrome problems.

His remedies:
- Acknowledge each syndrome and act accordingly.
- Learn to say "no" to new projects, which lets you stay healthily obsessed with a few.
- Take a trip without the laptop so you have no choice but to be "unproductive". Do it once for a week and you'll be so struck by the gain in productivity, energy and happiness on return that you'll never doubt the tool again. He says this as a workaholic.

chunks.heading: Being yourself in business, and the closing principle
chunks.text:
- Don't "vomit out some stupid marketing prose" on your website. Decide what you believe, then run your company accordingly and publicly, and you'll be more proud, more fulfilled and likely more successful.
- You can't fight every foible, nor should you.
- Never compromise your ethics or your sense of taste and awesomeness, because those are among the few things that differentiate you and your company.
- Don't stop striving, improving, learning and developing "who you are". His closing line: "Feed your motor."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jason Cohen tells Startup Weekend builders that code and design won't win; judges and customers reward a clear pitch, validated pain, a plausible business model and evidence of demand. He urges working outside your comfort zone on those things instead of defaulting to building.

chunks.heading: The core claim: Startup Weekend is a startup contest, not a code or design contest
chunks.text:
Jason told Startup Weekend teams in Austin that the code does not win. He had judged the previous event, and tech and design had nothing to do with the decisions. Judges don't ask "which had the best algorithm" or "which had the cleverest logo."

- Everyone in the room can code an app and make a clean home page, so that output cannot separate teams.
- He extends this to real life: customers don't pick companies for code difficulty, unit test coverage, or which typeface is on the home page.
- He says he has made "millions of dollars on companies with hideously ugly websites and buggy code."
- Builders have a natural weakness: they do the work they like and are good at, then end up with "a curiosity, a hobby, some trivial code and a typical website." That makes a website, not a company.

chunks.heading: Sharpen the pitch until it is brutally short
chunks.text:
Jason's first non-coding priority is a pitch so clear that a customer sees you are relevant to their pain and might solve it. Other intelligent people, such as judges or investors, should see the same.

- The verbal pitch should be under 60 seconds.
- The home page should entice in three words and explain in under fifty.
- The value is in the choices: what you're building, why, who cares, and what they'll pay. A short pitch only forces those choices.

chunks.heading: Get five strangers to react before you build more
chunks.text:
Jason's second priority is feedback from 5 strangers, even if only as interviews and without a prototype.

- Validate the pain, the minimum needed to address it, and what they would pay.
- Even if they disagree, or you change your story each time, you learn what is critical and what is unresolved.
- His ranking: "A concept validated by five people is far more valuable than a working application that no one has critiqued."

chunks.heading: Build a plausible business model in a simple spreadsheet
chunks.text:
Jason says to build a business model, not a business plan: a simple spreadsheet.

- Include the pricing model, how money flows in and out in normal operation, and customer acquisition cost.
