- From that, work out how many customers you need to break even on operating costs, and how many more to cover human costs.
- He notes it is surprisingly hard to build a company where revenue beats marketing, salaries, and operations, even at scale. Showing yours can work puts you ahead of the group.

chunks.heading: Find evidence that people are already looking for a solution
chunks.text:
Jason says too many companies build cool tools that nobody in particular wants. Counter this by producing evidence of potential customers already searching.

- Examples of evidence: people complaining on Twitter, asking on forums, musing on blogs, or paying too much for poor alternatives.
- This shows need and also hints at how to reach those people.

chunks.heading: Need beats product: a landing page with 50 emails beats a working app nobody asked for
chunks.text:
Jason argues that identifying a need is the scarce skill, because a team that finds a need can build the solution, but a website cannot create interested people.

- A landing page that describes what the company will do and asks for an email, with 50 emails collected, is "far more of a real company" than a working product no one requested.
- Teams that make real progress on even one or two of the points above are the likely winners and the likeliest to have a viable small company.

chunks.heading: Practice what you're not already good at
chunks.text:
Jason's closing advice is to push out of the comfort zone. You can write code or make logos any time, so use the weekend to get better at the other skills every startup needs.

- Do some coding and design, but force yourself into pitch, validation, and business-model work.
- His line: "You can go back to building things for the sake of building things on Monday. This weekend, build a company."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jason Cohen shows that a full WP Engine redesign didn't move bounce rate, time-on-site or conversion. Smart Bear and ITWatchDogs grew fast with ugly sites, while Hipmunk won on design alone. His conclusion is to decide whether design is core to your identity and act consistently. If it isn't, nail something else harder.

chunks.heading: Design is a strategic choice, not a universal requirement
chunks.text: Jason redesigned the WP Engine website in 2011, going from a site with database errors and CSS blowups to a sleek, themed design (a grayscale 1950s automotive motif built with CSS3/HTML5). He used the result to ask whether design really matters, and concluded that it depends on whether design is core to your strategy.

chunks.heading: The WP Engine redesign did not move the metrics
chunks.text:
- After the redesign, customers emailed things like "Thank God you fixed that horrible website. I was embarrassed when referring you to my clients."
- The team said they were "soooo glad" the site was fixed, because they had been embarrassed by it.
- But the same customers were still customers and were still referring clients.
- Jason checked Google Analytics before and after the change. Home page bounce rate, average time-on-site and sales conversion rate (weekly signups) all showed no visible change at the redesign date.
- His reading: "Looks like the data are objectively saying 'design doesn't matter.'"
- He still values the soft evidence. Customer emails and team morale matter even when the dashboards are flat. He is glad they did it, "if not for objective data, then for the subjective feelings."

chunks.heading: Design as a signal of maturity in sales
chunks.text:
- After the redesign, WP Engine landed a large customer who said they could tell from the website that, among competitors, WP Engine was more mature and ready to handle a bigger customer.
- Jason notes that WP Engine was not objectively particularly more mature, and that this customer would probably have been fine with a competitor.
- He says the design "could be" what gave the edge, and "Didn't hurt, anyway."

chunks.heading: Companies that won with bad design
chunks.text:
- **Smart Bear:** an "eye-melting" website, yet the company doubled revenue and profit every year for half a decade.
- **ITWatchDogs** (his second company): an old homepage with calliope-colored menubar, two broken images above the fold and a chaotic layout. It grew every month, made millions of dollars, took business from competitors with billion-dollar market caps and professional-looking sites, and had a successful exit.
- His conclusion: this does not prove design doesn't matter, but design may not be the deciding factor.
- At ITWatchDogs, the culture and message were "low-cost, friendly, approachable, regular people, who understand exactly what you worry about, exactly what your budget is, and we nail it." Competitors had slick corporate sites; the messy site matched customers' own offices, full of "assorted hardware corpses and solder stains."
- He rejects the retort that "that's design too," since no designer would have created that site because it looks "relatable."

chunks.heading: Counter-examples where design is the business
chunks.text:
- **Hipmunk:** does the same thing as Orbitz or Travelocity. The only difference is design, which makes flight search pleasurable and usable. It lacks better data, branding, name, SEO or money, so design was its quantum-leap advantage.
- **Amy Hoy's time zone tool:** Jason uses and recommends it only because it is "just nice to use and look at."
- **Mint:** many credit its success to design. Given how many features were broken for how long, Jason finds it hard to argue otherwise.
- **37signals:** documented with data that Highrise signup page design and headline changes produced more credit-card-swiping customers.

chunks.heading: How to decide: pick a position and act consistently
chunks.text:
- Decide whether design is core to your startup's identity, then act consistently.
- If design is how you win (how you acquire and retain customers, earn referrals and stand out in the market), it can be the most important thing, as with Hipmunk.
- If design is core, build a consistent culture that values design "through-and-through" starting now.
- If design is not important to you, decide what is, and "nail those things all the harder." Competitors will use superior design to cover up weaknesses in those areas, so your superiority "must shine through regardless."
- It is not strictly either-or. WP Engine did fine before and after the redesign.
- Editor's note added in 2025: with the consumerization of enterprise software and product-led growth, design has moved to the fore in business software, and consumers will pick and pay more for great design, so it is no longer clear one can hold that "design doesn't matter."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jason Cohen reflects on why he answers spam and pandering offers politely: fear of offending famous or soon-to-be-famous people. He asks when a blogger earns the right to say what they think and argues that social-media "honesty" is mostly performance. Reflective and personal, light on tactics.

chunks.heading: Calling out spam and disagreeing in public: why Jason stopped being polite
chunks.text:
Jason gets a steady stream of "special" offers, guest-post requests, pleas for attention and mild bribery because of what he calls his "moderate, only-in-bubble fame". Most are sincere, and even the blatant marketing pitches (for example, "review this fantastic new book that's so relevant to your readers") are professional, direct and arrive with a gift, often just a free book.

- His default reply was always well-mannered, even to obvious spam. Example: thanking someone for the chance to "e-interview" a celebrity they represent, then declining because the book was not directly relevant to his audience.
- He now thinks the real reason for that politeness is "terrible": he was afraid of annoying someone famous, or someone who might become famous, who might then refuse to work with him or say something bad about him in public. He calls this "Pathetic."

chunks.heading: What finally pushed him to stop being nice: a guest-blogger scam
chunks.text:
The trigger was what he calls the worst solicitation to date, titled "Guest Blogger Proposal--An Interesting Twist." It ran 729 words, nearly the length of his own article.

- It used the standard lines ("We are only looking for a handful of sites... and don't want you to miss out") and heavy exclamation marks ("saving you time and effort!!").
- It asked for "our own restricted login (preferred)" so the senders could publish articles directly to his blog without review.
- It guaranteed the posts would carry sub-headlines and bullets on "how to...", "7 tips for...", "5 reasons..." topics.
- It left out that the senders were affiliate marketers, and that the auto-published articles would push products for them to monetize.
- His view: letting strangers publish anonymous, self-serving, product-pushing posts on his blog would pollute it and betray his readers.

chunks.heading: The reply he sent, and why it mattered to him
chunks.text:
He replied bluntly instead of declining politely. In summary, he called it a "fascinating scam," said he would tell everyone he knew about the offer to "pollute my blog with garbage," and asked them to send more contact details so he could post them online for people to send "a token of their appreciation."

- Jason says the recipient surely couldn't care less. What mattered was that he "finally grew the stones to say what I feel even if it pisses someone off."
- He admits he wrote it after two "poor-man's martini's" (three ice cubes dropped in, swirled, no shaker). He cites the ancient Macedonian practice of making important decisions only when drunk: with the societal filters and self-doubt lowered, you think and act as your true self, so supposedly more truthfully and "correctly."

chunks.heading: Social media "honesty" is mostly performance, and Jason includes himself
chunks.text:
Jason argues that although social media is supposed to be about "honesty," "being human" and "genuineness," most of it isn't.

- Bloggers "fluff their feathers," coming across as more confident, smarter and more sure than they are. He includes himself, though he says he at least tries to reveal the "emotional underbelly" (he links his posts on impostor syndrome and how emotionally draining startups are).
- Twitter users retweet, follow and pander to minor celebrities, hoping the lesser deity will retweet them someday, or accept their email as non-spam because they have already "joined the conversation." He includes himself here too, and says he "still" does it.

chunks.heading: The deeper question: when do you earn the right to say what you think?
chunks.text:
Jason asks whether he dares to publicly disagree with the well-known figures he respects, and what he fears would happen if he did.

- Disagree with Seth Godin, and he might not be considered for Godin's Domino project.
- Disagree with Jason Fried, and Fried might lay into him the way he did with Mint.
- Make fun of Joel Spolsky, and he might not be invited back to Business of Software (he had written a satirical "letters to Joel Spolsky" piece).
- He asks: "When do I earn the right to say what I think?" and "Why do I think I need to 'earn' that right?" He also asks how many RSS subscribers or Twitter followers it would take before it feels fine to rail against asinine offers or gently disagree with luminaries he does respect.
- His answer is deliberately flat: "This many." The implication is that there is no threshold. The permission is one he has to give himself.
- He closes with lines from Amanda Palmer about not wanting to be the person you want to be, and possibly dying before you see that you already are that person.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jason Cohen resolves the tension between startup focus and experimentation by never refusing outright, but attaching terms to "yes" so strong that acceptance funds your real goals and rejection costs nothing. He illustrates with $100/hr consulting, WP Engine's large-blogger deals, and $2,500/day code-review trips at Smart Bear.

chunks.heading: Qualify "yes" instead of saying "no"
chunks.text:
- Jason argues that "focus" says to refuse most things, while experimentation says to try new ideas. His way out is to never say "no" and to carefully qualify "yes." He wants new ideas explored without losing the plan.
- He frames it as: "Never say 'no,' but rarely say 'yes.'" Every "yes" is conditioned so it only happens when it is clearly worth the distraction.
- He expects most qualified yeses to be rejected, and he counts that as a fine outcome.

chunks.heading: The two-sided test for a qualified "yes"
chunks.text:
Set the conditions so that:

1. **If they say "yes," you're happy.** The terms or money are so good they more than compensate for the distraction, and may fund the thing you really want to do.
2. **If they say "no," you're happy.** It wasn't a worthwhile return on your time and effort anyway.

If a deal fails either side of this test, the terms are wrong.

chunks.heading: Price the "yes" to fund something you want
chunks.text:
- Jason calls "funding the thing you really want to do" the single best way to decide how to qualify a "yes."
- Example conditions he lists:
  - "Yes" if it pays for an entire additional person.
  - "Yes" if it extends the startup's runway by at least three months.
  - "Yes" if it completely funds development you'd like to do anyway.
  - "Yes" if it means a co-founder can quit her day job.
  - "Yes" if it pays for three new marketing efforts.
- He treats the money like another form of funding: "Funding is always a distraction from actually running your business, so the amount of money you get must be transformative to the business."
- If a deal wouldn't move the needle, he is fine losing it.

chunks.heading: Early example: $100/hour Mac Java work
chunks.text:
- In the mid '90s, at 17, Jason did Macintosh contracting at about $25/hour.
- A company with a new Java product that was broken on Mac called him. Their investor wanted a Mac demo. He didn't want the job: Java was new and buggy, and he was a C/C++ person.
- On the advice of an older, wiser friend, he showed up and quoted $100/hour instead of declining. He expected to be laughed out.
- They agreed. Everything was working in about an hour and a half, for roughly $150. He says the difference was "all in how I phrased 'yes.'"

chunks.heading: WP Engine: big bloggers and the "pays for a developer" rule
chunks.text:
- Early in WP Engine's life (about a year in), large bloggers wanted to move over. They had tens of millions of monthly page views, traffic spikes, custom code, perfect uptime and 24/7 support needs.
- The stated target was the "middle market": people who outgrew free blogs and don't want to run servers, but aren't huge.
- Saying "no" might close the door on a pivot, since serving 100 large blogs could beat serving 1000 medium ones. Saying "yes" could hurt a blogger, bring bad press, or create an unprofitable "albatross."
- Solution: quote high enough to be sure of good money, enough to partially fund something else, such as a big ad campaign or another WordPress expert.
- For one especially large customer, the deal had to cover operating costs with a reasonable profit and also pay a full developer salary (a low, bootstrapped one). The customer would eat much of that person's time, and the remaining time came "for free."
- Many of those qualified yeses were rejected. Later, with more large customers, WP Engine could say a plain "yes" to the same bloggers, for example one with 30 million monthly page views.
- Editor's note in the essay: by 2023 WP Engine was 13 years old with 200,000 customers, and hosted more large WordPress sites than anyone.

chunks.heading: Smart Bear: $2,500/day consulting trips
chunks.text:
- Customers flew Jason out to help implement peer code review. Often "management" wanted him to convince the team and invent a painless process.
- It was a poor use of his time: they already owned the software, so it sold no new seats. Counting a travel day on each side, the time could have landed a customer or gone into the code.
- He first said "no," then reframed to "yes" at $2,500/day including travel days, which he calls unheard of since travel time is usually unpaid and only expenses are reimbursed.
- That cut out most trips. The remaining ones brought in about $10,000 for a week of easy work, often combined with a long weekend with his wife. He adds that those clients "really wanted me there," which made the work more enjoyable.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jason Cohen argues that markets work like single-elimination tournaments, so the "undefeated" winner proves less about repeatable skill than we assume. He urges skepticism toward "be more like Google/Apple/37signals" advice, learning from companies at every rank, and striving to become a better version of yourself rather than a clone of #1.

chunks.heading: Why "undefeated" and "#1" prove less than we think
chunks.text:
Jason argues that finishing as the #1 team or company is partly a product of the tournament system itself, not clean proof of superior skill.

- A single-elimination tournament always produces exactly one undefeated team, even if every match is a coin flip.
- The number of teams reaching each round, and the fact that one goes undefeated, is dictated by the system regardless of how random each contest is.
- He says being "undefeated" is "merely a result of the system itself, not necessarily proof that the winner is in fact better than other top contenders."

chunks.heading: Skill versus luck is unknowable, in sports and in business
chunks.text:
Sporting results mix skill and luck in "unknowable proportions", which is why underdogs can win on any given day.

- Statistically replaying a match until a significance threshold is reached would reduce luck, but it is neither fun nor practical.
- Business works the same way: a mix of skill and luck in unknowable proportions.
- The market and economy act as a tournament that decides how results are distributed, and it is an experiment that can be run only once.
- Long-tail distributions are common across industries, which Jason takes as evidence of systematic effects outside the usual "luck versus skill" debate.

chunks.heading: Why fixating on the leader misleads
chunks.text:
People fixate on whoever is #1 and tacitly assume the contest (marketing, sales, product) is mostly skill, so the marketplace must have picked the rightful leader.

- Jason says he is not sure the skill/luck proportion is known.
- He does not assume the market picks #1, or #2 or anyone else, according to a "repeatable, codify-able law."
- He asks which decisions actually caused success, and notes that this is hard to know.

Questions he poses to challenge the assumption:
- Does a pitch contest winner have a better shot than the #7 finisher who learned from it and is redoubling his efforts?
- Does McDonald's have all the answers, or can the #12 largest fast-food chain also teach something?
- Is the #4253 largest company in the world not still a success story with its own lessons?
- If the Google founders had published the PageRank paper at MIT instead of Stanford, without being plugged into the Silicon Valley system, would Google have existed?

chunks.heading: How to respond when told to "be more like" a famous company
chunks.text:
Jason lists reasons to be skeptical of advice that points at a famous example.

- "More like Google": the person may be citing the only company they know to compare to.
- "More like 37signals": almost no successful companies are like 37signals.
- "More like Apple": the person probably does not know what really goes on inside Apple or whether it resembles your company. He also asks which Apple is meant: today's, or Apple at 3 years old doing hardware with a late-1970s mindset.

chunks.heading: A better kind of role model
chunks.text:
The more interesting comparison, in Jason's view, is a little-known company that someone says you resemble.

- You visit its website and try the product, and it resonates.
- It feels like a "finer, more mature version" of yourself.
- It reinvigorates you because it inspires you to become a better version of what you already are, not because of its revenue or celebrity status.
- His conclusion: it is fine to muse about being #1, but not everyone should strive to become just like #1.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jason Cohen argues the single best writing advice for marketing copy, pitches and humor is to be specific. He walks through a workshop that replaces generic words, tightens accuracy, adds named examples, and shows how specificity is the easiest route to funny.

chunks.heading: Be specific: the core rule of Jason's writing advice
chunks.text: Jason's single best piece of writing advice, for marketing copy, blog posts, sales pitches, investor pitches and humor, is: "BE SPECIFIC." He argues you make text clear, powerful, engaging and even funny by swapping generic words for specifics. His method is to demonstrate with a worked example rather than preach.

chunks.heading: Step 1: remove generic words
chunks.text:
Jason defines generic words as ones that span broad concepts instead of conjuring a specific image.

- In his sample sentence, the generic words are "usage," "many," "effort" and "better."
- He calls generic words "a sure sign of lazy writing." You say "usage" because you can't be bothered to describe what people actually do on Twitter, and "many" because you won't quantify the number of industries.
- Generic words are boring, and different readers interpret them differently, so you can't be sure what message arrives.
- Worked fix: "usage" becomes "people increasingly make buying decisions based on Twitter conversations," "many industries" becomes "non-technical industries," and "better spent" becomes "a higher return on your time investment."

chunks.heading: Step 2: move from truth to accuracy
chunks.text:
After the generic words are gone, some words are still technically correct but add too little meaning or persuasion. Jason's example is "expert."

- When he thinks of Twitter experts he thinks of Chris Brogan and Tony Hsieh. They aren't merely knowledgeable; they promote Twitter and teach others to become experts.
- That distinction matters because experts in other fields often aren't evangelical. An expert classical guitarist may not teach or care about getting millions of people to pick up a 12-string, and few of the thousands of physicists at CERN have YouTube channels teaching high-schoolers.
- So "evangelist" is more accurate than "expert" for the point being made (that they promote Twitter without qualification).
- Other swaps: "higher return" becomes "profitable," and "people" becomes "consumers."
- Result: "Twitter evangelists insist that consumers make buying decisions based on Twitter conversations. But Twitter hasn't made inroads in non-technical industries, so traditional marketing channels might be more profitable."

chunks.heading: Step 3: add concrete examples
chunks.text:
Jason says examples are bloat only if brevity is your primary goal. Otherwise they help persuasive writing in five ways:

- They clarify abstract arguments.
- They make arguments more believable.
- They make arguments harder to counter.
- They make it easier for readers to apply your points.
- They make it easier for readers to do their own research.

Applied to the sample, he names the evangelists (Chris Brogan and Mike Volpe), names the industries (agriculture, construction, retail) and names the alternatives (direct mail and resellers). He notes that putting a name to the evangelists makes the claim tangible even for readers who have never heard of them.

chunks.heading: Specificity is the easiest way to be funny
chunks.text:
Jason says almost any statement becomes funnier just by being specific, with specific nouns, verbs and adjectives. He lists several techniques, each with a rewrite of the same dull sentence:

- **Exaggerate to extreme:** "Evangelists wet their pants every time someone uses Twitter to find a coffee shop."
- **Exaggerate to banality:** evangelists proudly point to Twitter enabling "people of every creed, color, persuasion and nationality to join the global conversation on what they had for lunch."
- **Invent an example:** "Farmers looking for a deal on a new tractor aren't peeling iPhones out of their Wranglers and thumbing out tweets through work gloves."
- **Highlight the absurd thing:** Twitter as a way to gather "advice" culled from the stray comments of millions of strangers and bots.
- **Blow something out of proportion:** customers are mostly "twittering about how to twitter," most of those people are bots, and the human non-twitters are "missing out on this incredible exchange of knowledge."
- **Transfer the concept to another context:** the principle behind his satirical post on the "rules" of social media, which he says demonstrates all of these techniques.

chunks.heading: Quick checklist Jason's approach implies
chunks.text:
- Hunt for vague words ("usage," "many," "better," "effort") and replace each with what actually happens or a number.
- Ask of each noun whether it is merely true or actually accurate (expert vs. evangelist).
- Add named people, industries and tools wherever a claim feels abstract.
- To add humor, pick one specific detail and push it to an extreme, a banality or an absurd image.

He points to Naomi Dunford, Joel Spolsky and Amy Hoy as writers who use these techniques well.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jason Cohen separates what money can fix (execution, ads, code, QA, runway) from what it can't (finding great people, authority, knowing what to build, learning). He argues exploration can't be bought while execution can, and shows how to use this when pitching investors or competing against better-funded rivals.

chunks.heading: Money accelerates execution, not exploration
chunks.text:
Jason separates what money can fix from what it can't, and argues the second list holds the most valuable things. "What can't be solved with money, are the most valuable things." Concepts, behaviors, knowledge and process can't be fabricated with money, and probably can't even be accelerated. Once a founder knows what to do, or knows how to learn quickly, money becomes an accelerant.

His shortest version, using explore vs execute: execution can be solved with money; exploration cannot.

Why he cares even if you aren't raising: if you're good at the things money can't buy, you stay competitive against a well-funded competitor. And if you have no money to waste, you need those skills even more.

chunks.heading: Team: money helps only after you find the person
chunks.text:
- Finding good people is "almost impossible." Jason has a blog, a Twitter following, local attention and social favors to call in, and it's still nearly impossible.
- Great people always have options: an existing job, other excellent offers, the freedom to not work for a while.
- If someone handed him a million dollars it wouldn't help him find an awesome person; they're scarce.
- Once he finds someone, money helps a lot: large salary requirements, relocation, a signing bonus, a leased car, whatever makes money "not the issue."
- Raising rule: an investor knows $200,000 won't assemble a team you don't have. If the team exists but works only in spare time because day jobs pay the mortgages, that's a good reason to raise. Don't raise money if you haven't assembled the core team.

chunks.heading: Marketing: money buys volume, not authority
chunks.text:
Most marketing can be solved with money:
- Spray ads everywhere.
- Try 20 campaigns even if most utterly fail.
- Try 50 titles, descriptions and landing pages through AdWords until one converts decently.
- Fund a freemium offering.

The big exception is anything that needs authority, like blogging and social media. You can't buy the kind of attention where people listen because they want to, interact because they respect your opinion and enjoy your style. If your business depends on "tell-your-friends" social-media punditry, you have to do that without money.

If marketing is just pouring more dollars in the top to crank out more revenue at the bottom, Jason calls that a machine investors like to invest in.

chunks.heading: Paired examples: what money buys vs. what it doesn't
chunks.text:
- Writing more code, faster: yes. Knowing what to write: no.
- Acquiring more leads: yes. Knowing how to convert them: no.
- A prettier website: yes. What text to put on it: no.
- Leeway to make mistakes: yes. A philosophy of learning from mistakes to improve: no.
- A QA team to improve quality: yes. Knowing when a bug isn't important enough to block shipping: no.
- Time to outlive a recession: yes. Making something people want to buy even during a recession: no.

chunks.heading: How to use this when raising money
chunks.text:
1. Emphasize how spending money will improve specific things that are broken or missing today only because money is lacking.
2. Show proof you've mastered what money can't buy: your ability to learn, change and improve.
3. For things money accelerates and where you've spent a teeny amount, show how well that went. It's easy to imagine more money bringing more results.
4. For things money can't solve and you haven't mastered, raise them before investors do, with a clear, plausible plan that shows self-awareness. If you don't have that plan, don't raise yet.
5. Don't raise if the core team isn't assembled.

chunks.heading: Demonstrate adaptability, don't claim it
chunks.text:
Jason is unimpressed by claims like "I'm in love with A/B testing," "I'm not afraid to admit when I'm wrong," "I listen to my customers," or "I'm a big fan of Eric Ries." Everyone is now a Lean Startup expert, so founders must show evidence. He wants to hear:

- How and why your pitch changed after vetting the idea with potential customers.
- A walkthrough of an app screenshot, with the customer feedback behind each part.
- Your company dashboard of the numbers that matter: why each is there, what you expect it to do, and what you do when it doesn't.
- Your first idea that turned out wrong but led to the second, and how much easier the second was to sell.
- What happened at different price points, and why you settled on the current one.
- Which parts of your landing pages improved with A/B testing and which needed old-fashioned creative thought.
- Why customers are willing to pay, in their own words.

What this really shows is that you know how to think, overcome roadblocks and figure out what to do. Those are the things money can't buy, and combined with money they make companies most likely to succeed.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jason Cohen argues most small startups fail because founders stop, often from emotional exhaustion. He tells how a bullying enterprise procurement manager made him want to quit, even though the man had no real power. His point: you don't need to be stoic or confident, just keep going.

chunks.heading: Startup pain never fully goes away, and the answer is to get through it
chunks.text:
Jason argues that most small startups fail because the founders stop working on them, and the usual reason is that the work is emotionally draining. He says "I don't care who you are or how strong your ego is, you *will* have these moments," and he describes nearly closing Smart Bear many times.

- The pain is not only at the start. Paul Graham and Trevor Blackwell's rollercoaster has despair in the middle and calm at maturity, but Jason says it persists years later despite revenue, profit, daily customers and a great team.
- He was four years in, with several decently paid employees (hard for a bootstrapper), a product people bought and roughly a million dollars a year in revenue, when the worst episode hit.
- His advice is to normalize it. Other founders feel it too and often only admit it in private rooms, so commiseration helps.

chunks.heading: The $200,000 enterprise deal that hit him hardest
chunks.text:
Four years into Smart Bear, Jason was negotiating his first true enterprise sale, about $200,000 of one-time revenue and the company's biggest order to date, for 400 seats.

- He does not believe in price negotiation, even for enterprise. Pricing was on the website and bulk discounts were already built into the invoice.
- The counterpart was a procurement manager, not the end user or anyone in the buyer's chain of command. Jason calls such roles "terrorists" because "they use fear tactics to get their way, yet they have no power other than fear."
- The manager demanded 30%, said he had worked with 47 other vendors who all gave at least 20%, and was told "There's always a first!"
- The manager escalated to "You have no business selling anything to anyone," then said he would recommend never working with the company in any capacity, even if given a discount.

chunks.heading: Why the traditional enterprise discount dance exists
chunks.text:
Jason explains why vendors and buyers keep playing the same game.

- The ritual: the vendor asks too much, the client feigns astonishment and calls it a deal-breaker, the vendor drops 30% in exchange for a three-year maintenance contract the client wanted anyway, and the deal is struck.
- The incentives are perverse. The salesperson sometimes gets away with a high price, which pads her commission. The procurement manager shows his bosses how much he "saved."
- He grants that big companies need a defender against vendors who overcharge ("They can afford it!") or sneak things into invoices, but this procurement manager felt like an attack, not a parry.
- Jason was the one refusing the "mating ceremony" and trying to skip straight to the wedding night, so he expected pushback. The personal attack was what he did not expect.

chunks.heading: Feelings don't yield to logic
chunks.text:
Jason expected his stoic, confident-entrepreneur self to shrug it off. He felt like throwing up instead.

- He felt like a "baby geek playing in the adult's house," with naive ideas of how the world should work, now exposed to people he had worked hard to earn trust from.
- He fretted for days and questioned whether the promise of money (he was bootstrapping with no regular salary) justified feeling inadequate. He asked himself why he didn't just write code and let natural salesmen handle sales.
- After days the despair turned to anger at the manager. He was angrier at himself for letting the manager make him feel bad.
- He says the moment where reasoning defeats irrational emotion "never came." He still carries the experience, because "that's how emotions work."

chunks.heading: The threat was empty
chunks.text:
The procurement manager turned out to have no power to stop the deal.

- When Jason's actual buying contact joined a call and asked what was holding up approval, the manager said "Nothing, just some paperwork, we'll have it done by Friday."
- Days of angst were for nothing.
- Years later, meeting the man in person, Jason "still felt small." The lesson is that a bully's bluster can be empty while your reaction to it is still real.

chunks.heading: Living through it, not beating it
chunks.text:
Jason's conclusion is that you don't need to be confident, stoic, smart, right or wise to get through a startup.

- You don't need to match the emotional stability of big bloggers, which he says is "mostly a façade" anyway.
- "It's not even about 'overcoming.' Maybe you don't overcome, you just get through." He has never "beaten" that procurement manager emotionally, if he is being honest.
- He frames it as "living through it, not beating it" and calls it your crucible.
- He is clear that tenacity isn't all it takes, but without it you stop. Stopping is easy, there are many reasons to stop, and it is how most little startups actually fail.
- He later (a 2022 follow-up) says he avoided burn-out and tamed these thoughts with a framework he detailed in a separate article on fulfillment.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jason Cohen shows that an employee's true cost per billable hour is about double their nominal rate once holidays, taxes, non-billable time, downtime and training are counted. He then covers the levers for consulting profit (charging more, billing more hours, subcontractors, treating a product like a client) and why scaling or launching a side product rarely works.

chunks.heading: Why hiring a consultant at $30/hour barely pays
chunks.text:
Jason argues that the "nominal" cost of an employee is far below the real cost per billable hour. He walks through a $60,000/year hire (2,000 working hours, so $30/hour nominal) and adjusts step by step:

- Subtract 10 US federal holidays (240 working days instead of 250): about $31/hour.
- Add roughly 15% employment tax (Medicare, Social Security), taking the annual cost from $60,000 to $69,000: about $36/hour.
- Employees bill about 36 hours a week, not 40, which loses roughly two days a month (18 working days/month): about $40/hour.
- Dentist visits, waiting for the A/C repair person and a sick day cost about two more days (16 working days/month): about $45/hour.
- Gaps between projects: at least 10% of time, often 2-3 weeks of downtime between large gigs (14 working days/month): about $51/hour.
- Career development (conferences, open source, learning new tech) is another 10% (12 working days/month): about $60/hour.

His conclusion: "The true cost of an employee is double the nominal cost." Billing a "$30/hour" employee at $60 only breaks even. You need roughly $100/hour to make any profit.

chunks.heading: Why you can't just re-bill at a higher rate
chunks.text:
- Clients don't do the math above. They judge "fair" by the person's nominal rate plus a bit of profit for you, which caps what you can re-bill before they feel ripped off.
- Even at $100/hour you earn about $40/hour, or $80,000/year, on that employee.
- Jason's counter: if your employee can bill at $100/hour, you could bill at $150/hour yourself. Working 20 hours a week on average at that rate clears $150,000 a year with no hiring or managing.

chunks.heading: Scaling a consulting company is worse than it looks
chunks.text:
Five employees looks like $300,000/year in profit, but scaling adds time and cost:

- Keeping 3-6 projects running year-round is a full-time pipeline job that falls on the owner.
- Turnover means you are permanently hiring, and it is hard to time new hires with departures.
- Six people need office space, or a real travel budget for quarterly get-togethers.
- You can no longer also manage projects, client relationships and internal product work, so you need a project manager, salesperson or office manager, paid out of profit.
- None of the new work is fun or creative. "It's drudgery, and it's all on you."

The so-called $300k often shrinks to about $150k, and you are now doing things you hate.

chunks.heading: Charge more, and watch discounts
chunks.text:
- Any extra amount you charge goes straight to profit, so even a small rate increase matters at year end.
- Charging much more usually pushes out your existing client base. The new clients tend to be bigger, more dysfunctional companies with 47-page Master Service Agreements and shifting requirements, which is a different life from fun projects for entrepreneurs.
- Discounts cut the other way. A 10% pre-pay discount comes straight off the bottom line.
- Better pre-pay tactic: raise prices by P%, then offer a P% discount for pre-payment. Cash-rich customers pay the same as before, and others pay more in exchange for delayed payment.

chunks.heading: Bill more hours
chunks.text:
- Billing even 5 more hours per week significantly increases profitability.
- Employees see extra hours as unpaid overtime on a fixed salary, so give them a reason. Jason's suggestion is to split overtime billings with them: it is pure profit to you and a meaningful bonus to them.
- Review hours weekly so nobody consistently falls behind 40 billable hours.

chunks.heading: Why a consulting firm's side product usually fails
chunks.text:
Jason notes that 37signals, Fog Creek and Pivotal Labs grew products out of consulting, but hundreds if not thousands of firms never ship theirs. Reasons:

- Turning an internal tool into a user-friendly product means drudgery (onboarding, docs, UI, installers, password reset, fixing 200 workaround bugs), and it is no one's job.
- No one markets or sells it, and a roomful of consultants may lack the skills. Hoping "social media word of mouth" delivers users does not work.
- Attention is spread across five kinda-cool projects, so none gets finished. "Lack of focus kills."
- Billable hours always beat product work, so the product stays second-class.
- Assuming a market exists because the tool is "great for us." Usually there isn't one.

His fix is to treat the product as a client:

- List it as a client alongside the others.
- Give it a budget, even a separate bank account (maybe a separate corporation), with the project paying consulting fees (perhaps at cost rather than full rate).
- Schedule and prioritize its hours like any other client.
- If potential income can't justify the cost, stop rather than limp along as a money-losing project.

He still says "ultimately, it's just hard."

chunks.heading: Subcontractors instead of employees
chunks.text:
- Paying only for hours you re-bill avoids employment tax, 36-hour weeks, vacations and project gaps. It is simple time arbitrage.
- But subcontractors charge a lot more per hour, for exactly the reasons above. The same person as a consultant would charge $60/hour instead of $30, so profit is unchanged; you have moved the costs onto their P&L.
- Still worthwhile for less headache: simpler taxes, no vacation bargaining, no prodding for 45-hour weeks. Psychologically it is easier to give up $60 when you charge $100 than to pay a "day's work" when there is no work.

chunks.heading: Is consulting still worth it?
chunks.text:
- Jason calls consulting a great way to earn a living and a smart way to self-finance a startup, if you avoid these traps.
- Most consulting companies don't make much profit, and only about one in a thousand has the discipline to launch a successful product in off-hours.
- You need to be "serious, disciplined, and relentless," and set up incentives such as employee profit sharing.
- The payoff: a self-financed startup, a nice living, less risk than a product-only startup, and a great team.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jason Cohen argues that building a business on a platform you don't control (Twitter, the App Store, SEO) is risky, using TweetUp and Ad.ly as cautionary tales. Choose stable platforms or ecosystems, or diversify across many acquisition channels so no single rug-pull kills you.

chunks.heading: Platform dependence is a business-model risk, so pick stable platforms or diversify
chunks.text:
Jason argues that building a startup on a volatile platform can kill the company overnight, and that bootstrapped companies have no cushion to survive it. His two defenses: choose platforms with this risk in mind, or diversify so no single platform can sink you.

- Platform risk applies to the *entire-company* case. Using a platform as one part of the business is fine.
- "All technology depends on 'platforms'" (operating systems, browsers, libraries, even customer prejudices). The danger is a platform still "undergoing tumultuous change", especially when the whole company rests on it.
- He closes with: "At least don't pick a rug that's already moved around the house three times."

chunks.heading: Twitter's 2010 ad ban killed the paid-tweet startups
chunks.text:
Jason uses TweetUp and Ad.ly as the cautionary case.

- Twitter once allowed unlabeled advertising tweets. TweetUp and Ad.ly acted as liaisons between advertisers and popular tweeters, e.g. an advertiser paying about $3 for someone with 10,000 followers to tweet about a widget. He calls it "AdSense for Twitter".
- In May 2010 Twitter launched its own ad platform and barred "any third party" from injecting paid tweets into a timeline on any service using the Twitter API. The Terms of Service now explicitly prohibit it.
- TweetUp renamed itself PostUp and ended up with vague marketing-buzzword copy and no clear product.
- Ad.ly survived by pivoting to matching celebrities (e.g. Mandy Moore) with major brands (e.g. NBC).
- Both had millions in funding and could afford to flounder. "Bootstrapped companies have no such luxury."

chunks.heading: Apple's App Store and SEO as unpredictable platforms
chunks.text:
Jason treats these as two examples of platforms whose rules shift without notice.

- **App Store:** famous for "screwing innovators without notice", with scandals almost weekly about apps inexplicably banned or allowed (one telephony app banned, the next sanctioned). Flurry went from awesome analytics platform to being called out by name by Steve Jobs.
- Rule of thumb: an iPhone app as a useful addition that wouldn't hurt if it vanished is fine. A company built entirely on an iPhone app is in critical danger.
- **SEO:** in his opinion it is "an ever-shifting landscape of shit you chase without ever really knowing what the rules are."
- SEO as one of ten tactics for getting people to your site is fine. Betting the entire business on search traffic is not, since "at any moment a competitor or the platform itself could oust you."

chunks.heading: Platforms that look like lock-in but aren't: the Heroku test
chunks.text:
Jason offers a test for whether a platform dependency is truly dangerous: can you leave and keep the business alive?

- Heroku (managed Ruby on Rails hosting: "git push" deploys across redundant servers) looks like scary black-box lock-in.
- It isn't, because the stack is still Rails and Postgres, with free tools you already run on your laptop.
- If you had to leave: get a server, "git clone" the code, install a database, restore from backup. It would be painful, with downtime and refactoring, but that's true wherever you host, and the company survives.
- His conclusion: "you're exploiting Heroku as a tool; your business's success does not depend on them."

chunks.heading: Ecosystems like WordPress and Salesforce are safer than single-owner platforms
chunks.text:
Jason distinguishes an ecosystem from a platform controlled by one company. His company WP Engine depends on WordPress.

- An ecosystem is a guild of hundreds of thousands of agencies, products, companies and power users who depend on each other for revenue, attention and credibility.
- WordPress is open source, so Automattic couldn't kill the community "if they tried". He also cites five years of evidence that Automattic supports it, including a deal with WP Engine that landed both on TechCrunch.
- Contrast: Twitter doesn't care which clients are popular, and Apple "rule[s] with an iron fist no matter the consequences".
- Salesforce is a model ecosystem curator. It intentionally leaves "obvious" features out of the base product so as not to harm companies that make money adding them. It is the shark that knows the remora fish must survive.
- Positioning aside, people call WP Engine "The Heroku of WordPress", which he loves, though most WordPress people don't know Heroku, so it isn't a good home-page message.

chunks.heading: The fix: avoid dynamic platforms or diversify your channels
chunks.text:
Jason gives two ways to avoid platform dependence.

- **Don't base the company on something dynamic and outside your control.**
- **Diversify.** Keep doing SEO for lead generation, but not as the only source. If it disappears, "you still have nine other ways to get people to your website."
- If you've tried nine things and none work, "the problem is with you, not the ten platforms!"
- In the end you have to depend on *something*, and the rug can always be pulled. The goal is to pick a stable one.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jason Cohen launched WP Engine to 18,000 blog subscribers and got just two signups, far below his 10-50 estimate. The audience's real value was recruiting a cofounder-caliber team member, and the first 50 paying customers came from other work. Fame helps, but startups stay hard.

chunks.heading: Reputation gave Jason far less launch traffic than people assumed
chunks.text:
- Jason announced WP Engine, his WordPress hosting company, to a blog audience of about 18,000 RSS subscribers, plus similar page-hit volume from Twitter and HackerNews.
- Readers called it an unfair advantage: "You're starting with 18,000 prospects. How convenient."
- The announcement produced two new signups. He had expected 10-20 at minimum and hoped for 50, so he was wrong by an order of magnitude.
- Eric Sink, a well-known writer on software business, got a similar result with Winnable Solitaire. He had sold six copies after one month, and the product eventually sold for a small sum on $216 of revenue.
- Jason cites other well-known founders and creators who reported the same pattern: a large following does not turn into launch sales.

chunks.heading: Where the first 50 customers came from
chunks.text:
- Before the announcement post went live, WP Engine already had 50 paying customers, not prospects.
- Most paid $49/mo. A few paid over $1000/mo (large blogs with serious traffic).
- His conclusion: whatever the company did without the blog's help mattered far more for the first customers. He promised to explain exactly how in later posts.
- The blog was still instrumental, but not by pushing hosting onto 18,000 subscribers, a.k.a. 1000 "true fans." Its real contribution was building the team.

chunks.heading: Why a famous-person team is worth more than a mailing list
chunks.text:
- Jason says the team is a critical factor in a startup, yet there is little advice on how to assemble a stellar one.
- The usual answers ("we went to school together", "we worked together", "we met at StartupWeekend") boil down to putting yourself where capable people are and hoping for a social fit.
- WordPress hosting was already a commodity, with offerings at every price point: $0, $5, $15, $40, and even $500/mo plus $200/hr consulting.
- His rule: "In a mature market you need severe points of differentiation" or moats, and he felt one of them had to be the team itself, a team that "would itself be an unfair advantage."

chunks.heading: The Aaron Brazell hire as the real payoff
chunks.text:
- Aaron Brazell is a WordPress core contributor and author of WordPress Bible (Wiley), recognized enough that strangers at WordPress conventions ask him to sign their copies.
- Jason expected value from Aaron in several forms:
  - a network of WordPress-community followers as a source of free leads
  - instant credibility transferred to the company
  - press connections (WordPress.com, CopyBlogger's media group, ProBlogger, Mashable, TechCrunch) for traffic spikes and legitimacy
  - deep knowledge of WordPress internals and roadmap, for a technically better service
- Aaron was charging a high hourly rate for consulting in Washington DC, but wanted the startup life. He accepted less money now for possibly more later, and for building something lasting instead of fixing hacked WordPress installs.
- Jason says "we got Aaron, and it's because of this blog." Aaron could have joined or started many startups, but wanted to start one with Jason because the blog showed his attitude, perspective and credentials.
- Aaron moved to Austin and was already instrumental to the company's success.

chunks.heading: Takeaways on fame, expectations and startup difficulty
chunks.text:
- Fame helps in important ways, enough to deserve the label "unfair advantage," but it showed up in recruiting, not in direct sales.
- Startups remain hard and unlikely to succeed regardless of who leads them. Eric Sink's failed experiment is the case in point.
- Jason's own revenue was orders of magnitude above Eric's, but his expenses were too, so having advantages does not make it easy.
- He frames the difficulty as part of the point: "if it were easy it wouldn't be worthwhile."
- In 2023 he adds that WP Engine went on to become a unicorn and is still growing and profitable. He also notes that his launch forecast was an example of why you cannot predict the future.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jason Cohen argues that generic tactics like A/B-tested AdWords, SEO and Twitter followers are not a marketing strategy, since every startup lists the same ones. He offers ways to stand out: radical transparency, virality built into the product, a real story, a paid-acquisition machine where cost to acquire is below lifetime revenue, and borrowed credibility from relationships.

chunks.heading: Why "build it and they will come" fails, and what actually cuts through
chunks.text:
Jason's core claim is that most technical founders have no real marketing strategy, only a list of tactics every other startup also lists. He says "A/B tests and accumulating Twitter followers is not a marketing strategy, just as 'we'll use salt and cheese' isn't a recipe."

- He asks founders how people will find their product and usually gets silence, then a recited list: A/B-test AdWords, A/B-test landing pages, "we're better at SEO," a friend who knows Twitter, blog reviews, starting with their own network, an affiliate program, a "Retweet" button in the product.
- His objection: every new startup says the same things. These are as undifferentiated as "we'll have a website" or "we'll have an email address." Millions of others do them too, so you stay invisible.
- The question he poses instead: how do you rise above the noise of the internet? His answers follow in the sections below.

chunks.heading: Radical transparency as a marketing engine (Balsamiq)
chunks.text:
Jason holds up Balsamiq Mockups (founder Peldi) as a ludicrously popular wire-framing tool. He credits its success to the founder's startling transparency rather than to feature selection or bug-free releases.

- Peldi published revenue figures even when they were still pathetic.
- He pledged loudly and eagerly to give away lots of free copies to non-profits.
- He revealed all his marketing strategies, which were remarkably effective, even though competitors would learn them too.
- Jason's distinctions: "He didn't just have an 'authentic voice,' he made public promises. That's compelling." And: "He didn't just 'tell it like it is,' he gave up his marketing secrets and opened his company books. That's newsworthy."
- It is almost too much honesty, like answering "how's it going?" with a detailed account of a weird pustule on your toe.
- Rule: everyone is "joining the conversation," so you must truly bare your soul to compete on transparency. It is not for everyone, but if you use it, "don't half-ass it."

chunks.heading: Make virality part of the product's DNA, not a bolt-on
chunks.text:
Jason's example is Calendly, which lets people book meetings in your open time slots without seeing your calendar.

- The customer sends the Calendly link to other people, perhaps many times a month. Those recipients must use the product to schedule the meeting.
- That is the viral step: having used the tool, the stranger may adopt it herself, and so on.
- He says this works so well that smaller bootstrapped competitors like YouCanBookMe and SavvyCal compete with Calendly despite it being large, well-funded, profitable and growing.
- He knows of no company that went viral because of a "like on Facebook" or "Retweet" button. Buttons are fine and cheap to add, but they do not make a product intrinsically viral.
- Not every product needs to be viral. But if it is not, you still need a killer method of finding customers. If it is supposed to be viral, "it better be encoded in the DNA of the application, not bolted on as an afterthought."

chunks.heading: Lead with a story, not a description of what you do
chunks.text:
Jason says the number one mistake founders make when trying to get press is talking about what the company does rather than telling a compelling story.

- His contrasts: Twitter gets press for helping Iranians fight an illegitimate government, not for a new internal IT process to increase uptime. Apple wins hearts through its obsession with design, not its development APIs. 37signals has over three million users because it motivates designers and entrepreneurs through its writing and philosophy, not just because the software is "better."
- Without a powerful narrative, he says, the chance of big press and enthusiastic users who spread the word approaches zero.
- His own progression at Smart Bear took years:
  1. "Smart Bear makes data-mining tools for version control systems." Accurate, but esoteric enough that not even a hardcore geek would know what it is or why it matters.
  2. After refocusing on code review software and eliminating the other 5 products: "You know how Word has 'track changes'... We do that for software developers." Better, but still no press, because it described what it is rather than why anyone should care.
  3. A story tuned to each audience. For journalists, the angle is that software developers traditionally review code in isolation, and Smart Bear brings the age-old benefit of peer review (which journalists know is how another person finds problems you can't see yourself) to an industry that needs it but where it was too hard to do.
- Tactic: write a different version of the story for each category of listener, and make the reason for excitement explicit instead of leaving the reader to infer it.
- It took him five years to realize he needed a story and to find what it was. His verdict: "one story beats a pile of AdWords A/B tests."

chunks.heading: Paid advertising still works if customer acquisition cost is below lifetime revenue
chunks.text:
Jason pushes back on the idea that marketing is now only "relationships" and "authenticity," which cost time but not money. Advertising is not dead; you can still buy eyeballs.

- The model: average cost of acquiring a customer is C (advertising, sales, support, demos) and lifetime revenue per customer is R. If C < R, you have a business.
- Ways to drive C down: cheaper ads, better lead quality, a more efficient conversion rate, and straightforward trials with minimal tech support.
- He warns that many business plans he has seen unintentionally omit real acquisition costs, so it is less simple than it sounds.
- He is not describing arbitrage tricks like buying AdWords that link to a page of ads. Most companies on Earth do not rely on "joining the conversation" to acquire customers.
- He recommends Sean Ellis's VentureHacks interviews on finding a repeatable, profitable model where C < R, and only then optimizing and growing. He notes they lean toward huge VC-style companies.

chunks.heading: Use an existing network and reputation as an unfair marketing advantage
chunks.text:
Jason says celebrity endorsement or personal reputation can be an untouchable competitive advantage and a way to burst out of the noise of internet marketing. He says he is "no Seth Godin," then shows what he could do as a co-founder of a new software development tool company:

- Relationships with CEOs and influencers at hundreds of software development companies: they would brainstorm during ideation, be guinea pigs in beta, and some would become paying customers after v3.0.
- Relationships with editors of nearly all software development publications, online and off, with whom he has already published articles: some would vet the stories, some would publish the company's articles.
- He has bought ads in every major and many minor software development websites, magazines, newsletters, conferences and webinars, so he knows the right message for each audience and could probably cut a deal.
- A few mentions on his blog, read mostly by software developers, might beat $10,000 of A/B-tested Google AdWords.
- His prior success would get initial meetings with investors and raise the odds of funding.
- The contrast: while others set up a new blog, blast their LinkedIn network with pleading emails, and pay to test AdWords variants, he would be "years ahead in the marketing war."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jason argues that the minimum proof for a startup idea is ten real people saying they'll pay. He dismantles the common excuses (scratching your own itch, mock-ups don't work, a great product sells itself, friends like it) and says to attack the riskiest non-code parts of the business first.

chunks.heading: Ten buyers, not opinions, are the validation test
chunks.text:
Jason's core rule: if you cannot find ten people who say "If you build this, I'll give you $X," your company is "bullshit." He saw hundreds of pitches at the Capital Factory incubator in Austin, Texas, and almost none had found even ten people willing to pay. Founders were ready to quit jobs, burn savings, risk their reputation and work 70-hour weeks without that evidence.
- He wants hard evidence that customers exist in your "future light cone," not mantras repeated at Lean Startup meetings.
- He says founders resist because they fear being proved wrong, especially after telling friends and family.
- He points to his own guides on how to find customers to interview and how to run customer interviews.

chunks.heading: "I'm scratching my own itch" is a starting spark, not validation
chunks.text:
Jason rejects the idea that being your own target customer means you already know what to build.
- By definition, a startup founder is not the typical customer. A typical customer rarely has the observation, creativity, persuasion and passion needed to spot monetizable pain, invent a product, recruit free help and quit a job.
- All three of his companies started by scratching his own itch, "but it's only that--the start." In his words: "the spark of inspiration, not the strategy. It's the grain of sand tickling the oyster, not the pearl."
- He cites Evan Williams: be a user of your own product, "but don't trick yourself into thinking you are your user."
- He challenges readers to find one founder of a real business who says "I'm the customer" is the only market validation needed.

chunks.heading: "There are millions of customers" makes ten easy to find
chunks.text:
Jason counters the argument that ten opinions don't matter when the market is huge.
- If there are millions of potential customers, finding ten who say they'll buy is trivial. If you can't find ten, either the millions don't exist or they aren't interested in you.
- Businesses start with one customer, then ten, then a hundred, then a thousand. "But most don't get past ten."
- If you haven't got ten people to even say they'll buy, he asks where the hubris comes from to claim thousands actually will.

chunks.heading: You don't need a product to sell the concept
chunks.text:
Jason rejects "my customers can't understand mock-ups, so I have to build it first."
- If you can't describe the concept to someone in your target market in 30 seconds at a cocktail party, it is too complex or you don't understand it yourself.
- WP Engine example: he got thirty people to say they'd pay $50/mo before he had a company name, website, product, co-founder or employee. He notes he had earlier ideas that proved to be "crap," so it wasn't just easy for him.
- Your first customers are early adopters who are fine with alpha software. If you can't find a few and get them excited, maybe the product isn't exciting.

chunks.heading: A great product does not sell itself, so attack the riskiest part first
chunks.text:
Jason argues against "I suck at sales/marketing, so I'll build something so compelling it sells itself."
- His guess for the top Twitter clients (150+ existed in 2010): about 80% are decent software that works, about 5% earn any revenue, and under 1% earn enough after hosting and marketing to let the owner skip a day job.
- Conclusion: if the goal is a business rather than a hobby, "building charming, novel software isn't enough."
- Founders default to coding because they love it. He says to do the opposite: attack the part you are least sure of and least qualified for.
- He frames it as project risk management. In a big software project you tackle the high-risk, ill-defined work first. For a startup the "high-risk unknown" is everything that isn't code: finding customers and getting them to open their wallets.

chunks.heading: Whose opinion counts: only people willing to pay
chunks.text:
Jason dismisses feedback from friends, family and dentists.
- Non-entrepreneurs don't understand product/market fit, tight budgets or how customers actually spend time. As he puts it, "Your mother thinks you're smart and good-looking, but that doesn't mean I do."
- Even real entrepreneurs matter only slightly. They may lack expertise in your domain, hold outdated notions, be biased against certain ideas or technology, and carry baggage from good and bad experiences shaped by timing and luck.
- "The only thing that matters is that people are willing to give you money!"
- Example: experts could argue that buying shoes online makes no sense, but while people give Zappos $1 billion per year, it doesn't matter.
- "When ten people say they'll give you money, that's the only validation that counts."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Anything that can be copied will be copied, including features, copy and pricing. Jason Cohen argues the only real competitive advantages are those that can't be copied or bought: insider knowledge, an obsessive hard One Thing, personal authority, a dream team, the right celebrity endorsement, and existing customers. Build toward them on purpose.

chunks.heading: Unfair advantages are only the things that can't be copied or bought
chunks.text:
Jason argues that anything that can be copied will be copied: features, marketing copy, pricing, and anything read on popular blogs. Being passionate, hard-working or "lean" is not an edge. He says investors' question about big companies copying you is really a prompt to ask what you are doing now, knowing copying will happen.

- Other scenarios to plan for: a funded, TechCrunch-featured startup copy, four free open-source competitors, or employee #2 leaving with code, roadmap and customer list to sell at one-tenth the price.
- His warning: "Almost no one I talk to has good answers, but they think they do." That belief is fatal because it stops them working on a fix until it's too late.
- His rule: "The only real competitive advantage is that which cannot be copied and cannot be bought."
- Advantages he lists: insider information, a hard One Thing, personal authority, a dream team, the right celebrity endorsement, and existing customers.
- He says almost no one has an unfair advantage at the start (he didn't at Smart Bear), but you can build one intentionally.

chunks.heading: Insider information as a legal unfair advantage
chunks.text:
Jason says deep knowledge of an industry and its specific pain points is a legitimate, hard-to-replicate advantage.

- His example is Adriana, a psychiatrist of 10 years who moved into leading software product teams. She knows both the pain of existing practice-management software and the customers first-hand.
- She can exploit modern shifts, such as web apps replacing installed software and new interpretations of HIPAA that allow web apps to store medical records.
- Her position: an industry expert who can "geek out" with customers and can also lead a product team. A rival would struggle to find or assemble anyone with that integrated knowledge.
- Copiers can only copy after the fact, and by then she has moved on to version two.

chunks.heading: A single-minded obsession with one hard thing
chunks.text:
A unique feature alone is not an advantage, since it is easily duplicated. Jason says most of Smart Bear's code review innovations were already duplicated by commercial and open-source competitors. The advantage is "unwavering devotion to the One Thing that is (a) hard, and (b) you refuse to lose, no matter what."

- Apple compromises everything for design. Jason notes the products are overpriced, buggy and have poor tech support, yet "their stuff looks and feels nice."
- Google's search algorithm was simply better, which won eyeballs and then monetization. It remains the company's biggest focus a decade on, backed by hundreds of millions of dollars.
- Photodex (an Austin image browser maker where he worked in the 90s) competed only on speed, not on stability, formats or features. It now makes tens of millions of dollars a year and still won't compromise on speed.
- 37signals earns millions of customers by refusing to compromise on simplicity, transparency and owning their company. Competitors could build equally trivial software, but "without the single-minded obsession it's just software with no features."
- The One Thing must be difficult to achieve to stay un-copyable. Google's search plus the infrastructure to query trillions of pages in 0.2 seconds took Microsoft and Yahoo years to match. 37signals' blog (131k followers) and best-selling book are nearly impossible to build even with a team of writers.

chunks.heading: Personal authority converts into sales and can't be bought
chunks.text:
Jason cites Chris Brogan ($22,000 for a day of consulting in a field where the information is free) and Joel Spolsky (millions from bug tracking, a crowded market). He says authority cannot be purchased: VC money can't buy it in a year, big companies can't decide to be thought-leaders, and smart geeks don't get it just by coding well.

- He was not an authority when he started. He had no blog, column or lectures, and wasn't an expert in code review or even development processes. He built authority over years, and Smart Bear became the leader in revenue and ideas in peer code review.
- It costs years of effort plus luck, and that is exactly why it works as an advantage.
- Conference example: competitors pay thousands for a booth, then thousands more to lure passersby who are bombarded by other pitches. As a known authority, he gets an entire hour with about 100 self-selected people.
- After a talk, 5-20 people typically want one-on-one chats; some go to the booth for demos, and some get private demos on hallway sofas. "It's not unusual to get $10,000-$50,000 in sales over the next three months from people who saw me at that talk."
- Other effects he points to: a blog read by tens of thousands, and writing the book that serves as the modern authority on code review.
- He hopes his blog authority will help launch his next venture, though that isn't why he blogs.

chunks.heading: The dream team and the right celebrity endorsement
chunks.text:
Jason says a strong founding team is hard to duplicate and reduces startup risk, though it doesn't guarantee success. He cautions that famous pairs (Gates & Allen, Page & Brin, Fried & DHH) are easy to see only in retrospect, which is "a terrible teacher."

- ITWatchDogs, which he helped bootstrap and sell, had three elements: varied skills (Gerry, an experienced startup and sales person; Jason, software; Michael, hardware), a common vision to build a product and ultimately sell the company, and insider knowledge (Gerry's prior startup in the space, Jason's embedded software experience, Michael's decades building cheap circuits).
- A team member who is already successful, with a big blog, a prior startup win or a huge Rolodex, is a proxy for advantages that can't be bought.
- He was building a new startup whose main advantage was a dream team (details to follow).
- Endorsement example: Hiten Shah's KISSMetrics entered a crowded marketing-metrics market with hundreds of competitors. Its advantage was advisors and investors who are celebrities in that exact market: Dave McClure, Sean Ellis and Eric Ries, who promote it on blogs, Twitter and in appearances.
- Those people are "taken," and there are only a limited number of respected authorities in any field. Their endorsement turns a feature gap into a pitch: these experts say the extra features are distractions.
- Jason says that kind of jump-start can't be bought for millions, because buyers trust Hiten through people they already trust. He adds that investors like a co-founder or advisor who has succeeded before, since "the VC game is more lemming-like than most care to admit."

chunks.heading: Existing customers and staying willing to change
chunks.text:
Jason says everyone you've sold to, including trial users who abandoned, holds the most valuable market research, and a new competitor will not have it. He admits "I listen to my customers" is now as hollow as "we're passionate," so the advantage only holds if you keep learning and keep moving.

- Momentum cuts both ways. Smart Bear has 35,000 users, so a drastic UI or workflow change would mean too much retraining, even if the result were better.
- Even "agile" 37signals is trapped by its "do less" philosophy. For example, Highrise doesn't suit traditional sales organizations with more than a few salespeople, which need pipeline reports, geographic territories and campaign management. He calls those features necessary rather than unnecessary complications.
- An entrenched company still has more money, brand recognition, happy customers to spread the word, employees to build with, and more experience of what customers actually do and need. "Any new competitor would kill for just one of these advantages. If you're not using them, how silly is that?"
- He quotes Zoho's view that "Companies don't get killed by competition, they usually find creative ways to commit suicide." If Zoho stops innovating it dies anyway, with or without Office 2010.
- His closing advice: find something they could never beat you on, "hang your hat on that and don't look back," and be intentional about building it.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jason Cohen argues customers now expect providers to try hard, care, and treat them well when things inevitably break, and they forgive sincere human error but turn adversarial toward sterile corporate behavior. He offers practical ways to find your voice and warns that a strong persona will alienate some people while making the rest love you.

chunks.heading: Authenticity beats polish: why customers forgive humans and refund corporations
chunks.text:
Jason argues the expectation of customers has shifted. They no longer demand "those assholes better not ever screw up." They expect a company to try hard, care, and treat them well when it inevitably does screw up.

- His example: a customer said of a hosting company, "I want someone else making sure the server doesn't go down. Or, if it does go down, I want someone to apologize to me."
- Ten years earlier, he says, the same sentence would have ended "someone to scream at" or "give me a refund."
- His summary: "People readily forgive sincere human error, but become adversarial and distrustful with the typical, sterile customer/provider relationship."
- He says small startups are especially suited to exploit this, and incumbents cannot.

chunks.heading: What earns forgiveness (and what doesn't)
chunks.text:
Jason says this is not a free pass to abuse customers and then publish a faux-heartfelt "open letter from the CEO." Three things have to be true:

- **You're doing your best by customers**, shown continuously in all communication (blog, tech support, website), not just after a crisis.
- **You're learning from mistakes**, shown by problems trending toward the esoteric and by apologies that explain what steps prevent this and similar classes of error.
- **You're doing everything in your power to be the best**, shown by a culture of awesome employees and new ways to make customers successful, so mistakes read as ordinary human error, not negligence or indifference.

He adds that the apology itself isn't the point. No one is convinced by an insincere, legally-vetted "official apology" that fixes nothing. What customers really want is to work with people who behave like real people, who are obviously trying, and who respond to problems earnestly and quickly.

chunks.heading: Why "be human" is hard advice to follow
chunks.text:
Jason jokes that "be human" and "be authentic" are standard advice that nobody explains how to apply ("Compared to what, being feline?"). "Just be yourself" is equally vague, since Thales said the hardest thing is "Know Thyself" (and the easiest is "To Give Advice").

He rejects the heavyweight route of synthesizing your life experience and ten-year goals into a four-word home page philosophy ("I can't even decide what to have for lunch"). He offers three practical ways to discover your point of view instead.

chunks.heading: Three practical ways to find your voice
chunks.text:
- **Criticize others.** When you love someone's slogan, ask why: funny, clever, specific, unwavering, simple, confident, ballsy? When you loathe an "About Us" page, ask why: too personal, not personal enough, too formal, childish, arrogant? Complete the sentence: "I absolutely [love|hate] that because ...."
- **Decide what you are not.** Corporate behavior that annoys you tells you what to avoid and what to do instead. Examples he gives: "I hate companies who use formal language," or the opposite, "I hate companies who think it's funny and clever to use informal language; I'm going to instill confidence by showing that we behave like grown-ups."
- **Copy something you love.** You love it because you identify with it, so copying gives a head start. Treat the original as "a rough draft that needs extensive editing but whose heart is in the right place." The goal is mimicry, not theft; influence, not carbon-copy. Over time it morphs into something unique.

chunks.heading: Strong choices alienate some people, and that's required
chunks.text:
Jason says every strong decision will alienate many people while thrilling others. His examples:

- Informal style: some find it refreshing, others find you untrustworthy.
- Proactively announcing bugs: some gracefully tolerate problems, others are "shocked" and tweet that you sell shoddy software.
- Admitting the company is two people: some expect primo customer service, others flee because you might not be around next year.
- Cursing on your blog: many click "Back," others laugh and click "Subscribe."

His conclusion: be "strong, specific, and honest." Turning off some people is the price, and the remainder will love you more and tell their friends. He says this wins far more customers than people think.

chunks.heading: The case against having no persona
chunks.text:
Jason frames the alternative bluntly: with no persona, "why would anyone get excited about you? Why would they put up with your faults? Why would they tell their friends about you?"

- A persona is what makes customers tolerate faults and spread word of mouth.
- His closing line: "Is your goal to become a soulless corporation? No? Well then, do whatever it takes to be soulful."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Incremental A/B testing tends to get stuck in a local optimum, like water pooling in a backyard instead of reaching the sewer. Jason argues you should always test a radically different version next to the small tweaks, because a discontinuous change in message, value proposition or audience can pay off far more than polishing the current page.

chunks.heading: The local-minimum trap in A/B testing
chunks.text:
