- Jason compares incremental A/B testing to water in a backyard. Water picks whatever direction is lowest in its immediate vicinity. It never surveys the yard, so it pools in a "cesspool" (a local minimum, or watershed) instead of hopping the fence to reach the sewer, the true global low.
- His point: "Maybe your A/B tests are missing the forest for the trees too."
- A typical incremental test starts from a baseline, changes one thing, and picks the winner. Example: the title "Souring on Sour Cream?" vs "Don't know when Sour Cream Goes Bad?", then another variation like "Is this Sour Cream Good or Bad?".
- Inching along this way, you believe the small gains will "add up to real money". Often they don't.

chunks.heading: Recognizing when you've hit a local minimum
chunks.text:
- The sign is that small changes stop doing anything.
- This is hard to see by eye, so Jason says to (horrors!) use math to decide empirically whether anything is actually happening, with proper statistics rather than gut feel.
- He warns that you might be tempted to give up at this point, "but that's wrong too". The page is stuck at a local optimum, not at the best possible result.

chunks.heading: Jump the fence: try radically different variants
chunks.text:
- Escaping the cesspool means completely changing your perspective, which can reveal "an entirely new, discontinuous, non-incremental change".
- Things worth radically changing:
  - Message
  - Layout
  - Value proposition
  - Colors
  - Target audience
- His line: "The real fun is in the sewer; you need to jump over the backyard fence."

chunks.heading: Run radical and incremental tests together from the start
chunks.text:
- Looking in completely new places has far more potential than incremental improvement, so "you need to be looking for discontinuous results from the start". Don't wait until incremental tests stall.
- Recommended technique: do both.
  - Instead of running only A vs incremental-change A2, also run a B version that's radically different from A.
  - You reap the straightforward benefits of incremental improvements while also searching for something that could radically improve revenue.

chunks.heading: A radical win should change more than the test
chunks.text:
- If a radically different message gets massively better results, perhaps all your messaging should change accordingly.
- It may also shift your idea of what customers want, and potentially the whole business: "Maybe your entire business can change for the better."
- His closing advice: stop making minor variations when you could be "toying with new ideas and new identities". In his words: "Play!"

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Humans see patterns in randomness, and slicing analytics or A/B test data many ways guarantees some "significant" result appears by chance. Jason Cohen argues you should form a theory first, then test that specific theory, rather than hunting through combinations after the fact.

chunks.heading: Pattern-seeking in noisy data produces false insights
chunks.text:
Jason argues that humans are bad at telling patterns from randomness, and that marketing data is full of "insights" that are actually noise.

- Gilovich's 1985 study recorded basketball hits and misses as strings like `HMHHMMMMHMMHH` and found players were not "streaky": a coin flip produces the same runs. Pundits and fans stayed unconvinced.
- When shown strings with varying real streakiness, pundits and fans could not classify which were streaky and which were random.
- He notes that a later critical analysis suggested the hot hand might exist and the debate is inconclusive. His takeaway is that it is extremely hard to know whether something is random, even for statisticians.
- Humans also fail at the dot-field test: asked which dot set was placed randomly, we pick the wrong one.

chunks.heading: How picking the sample window hides data
chunks.text:
Jason uses baseball announcer stats to show how a framing choice inflates an observation.

- "This pitcher has retired 5 of the last 7 batters" implies that batter 8 got on base, and so did the one before the window. Honestly, it is at least "5 of 9," which sounds less impressive though it is the same data.
- Choosing the cutoff after seeing the data builds the pattern into the claim.

chunks.heading: Seeking combinations until something shows up
chunks.text:
The core fallacy is combing through a mountain of data until a pattern appears.

- Announcers cite things like "Rodriguez is 7 for 8 against left-handed pitchers in asymmetric ballparks when the tide is going out during El Niño." Someone examined millions of combinations and reported the one that sounded impressive.
- Jason says this "is the epitome of Pattern-Seeking."
- The Bible Code: strip out non-letters, arrange the letters in a grid, and look for words at regular row and column intervals. With any grid size and any interval, a huge set of letters automatically yields words you recognize.
- The same method finds coded messages in _War and Peace_. It does not matter which translation or language is used. All you need is lots of letters and lots of combinations.
- He compares this directly to A/B tests and combinations of "patterns" in web analytics software.

chunks.heading: The coin-flip math: rare events become common when you look often enough
chunks.text:
Jason uses a fair-coin experiment to show why searching for interesting results is not the same as running an experiment.

- One 10-flip trial: 10 heads in a row is a 1 in 1024 event, so a coin that does it once is suspicious.
- Run 1000 ten-flip trials: a fair coin still lands 3-7 heads per trial, but in 1000 trials there is a 62% chance of seeing 10 heads at least once.
- Key line: "Those events are rare, but I'm flipping so much that rare events will naturally occur."
- In a real experiment, a very unlikely result suggests something systematic. When you are "seeking interesting results" instead, highly unlikely events necessarily happen, yet you still conclude something systematic is at work.
- He ties this to scaling: scale makes rare things common, which is one reason scaling a business is so hard.

chunks.heading: How the fallacy shows up in marketing and sales data
chunks.text:
Jason maps the coin-flip lesson onto Google Analytics and similar tools.

- There are a hundred ways to slice and dice data. Compare enough variables enough ways and some correlation will appear, for example "when we use landing page variation C along with AdWord text F, our conversion rate is really high on Monday mornings."
- He says this makes you:
  - like the baseball announcer, tumbling combinations of factors until something "significant" falls out;
  - like someone running 1000 coin-flip trials and looking only at the all-heads one to declare the coin "biased";
  - someone seeing streaks and hoping an extra-high conversion rate is evidence of a controllable, systematic force.
- Examples he gives: "We tried 10 AdWords variants and combination D is the clear winner," and "We sliced our Google Analytics data every which way, and these 4 patterns emerged."

chunks.heading: The fix: form a theory, then test it
chunks.text:
Jason says apparent patterns are fine for forming a theory. The error is skipping the test, which turns science into baseball announcing.

- Ad copy: do not use a thesaurus to generate 10 ad variants. Decide which pain-points or language you think will grab potential customers and test that theory specifically.
- Analytics: do not root around hoping to find a combination with a good conversion rate. Decide beforehand which conversion rates matter for which cohorts, then measure and track only those.
- Customer research: do not ask customers leading questions or collect scattered thoughts. Form hypotheses and test them intentionally.
- Advice: do not blindly follow the startup founder who dramatically succeeded (the "1-in-1000 coin flip" of survivorship). Gather advice and observations that align with your style and goals.
- Keep testing your theories, because the environment changes, you change, or you may find something better.

chunks.heading: Quotes he uses
chunks.text:
- Asimov: "The most exciting phrase in science isn't 'eureka,' but rather, 'that's funny.'" Jason's use: a surprising pattern is a prompt to form a hypothesis, not a conclusion.
- Fermi: "There are two possible outcomes: if the result confirms the hypothesis, then you've made a measurement. If the result is contrary to the hypothesis, then you've made a discovery." This only works if you had a hypothesis beforehand.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jason Cohen argues founders overfear the 800-lb gorilla. Big companies are slow, only play in big markets, and are boxed in by their brand and existing revenue, so a small company can use their entry to validate its market, pick niches they ignore, and win by doing what they structurally cannot. The more dangerous rival is another scrappy startup.

chunks.heading: Why big-company competition matters less than founders fear
chunks.text: Jason Cohen says every small software company on Earth is under threat from a big competitor, so the threat alone is not fatal and may not even be important. His advice is to redirect that angst toward the real danger, small startups. He says big companies are slow dinosaurs: whatever they do now is probably what they will do in two years, possibly four. The same message, product and pricing, and they still fumble new platforms like Facebook. The scary competitor is "another scrappy, smart startup like yours," the "tree-shrew" that watches from afar, skips your mistakes and copies the good parts.

chunks.heading: Aim to own a piece of the market, not to beat Google
chunks.text:
- Jason argues the goal is a solid company you are proud of that "pays handsomely" without needing to be worth $1B.
- The question is "How can you own your little piece of the world", not "How can you wrest $100m of revenue from a big guy."
- He says "It's not your purpose to 'beat' another company." It is to define yourself on your own terms, not by being like or unlike someone else.
- Setting your sights on a competitor is fine, for example discounting for customers who switch to you.
- The only thing that ultimately matters is that you earn more and more customers, whether or not anyone else does too.

chunks.heading: A big player entering your market can raise your value
chunks.text:
Jason says a gorilla can be an advantage, especially if it enters after you are established. His example is Smart Bear, which makes a peer code review tool (Code Collaborator).

- Any Microsoft code review tool would only work with Microsoft's own version control system and inside Visual Studio. It would not support ClearCase, run in Eclipse, or serve Java well.
- Even if Microsoft owned 100% of the Visual Studio market, that leaves every other market.
- Microsoft's competitors (IBM, CA, Oracle, Serena, CompuWare, HP) would then need a code review tool right away to stay level on competitive-analysis charts. The fastest route is buying the #1 or #2 code review company, which is Smart Bear, and it is profitable.
- So a Microsoft copy would validate the market and raise Smart Bear's value.
- What actually happened: Microsoft added "shelving" and put the least possible effort into code review, essentially a check-box saying a review happened somewhere. Smart Bear sells a lot of Code Collaborator to Visual Studio shops.
- Jason's lesson: they validated the market by entering, but because they are huge they could not make it good enough to stop him.

chunks.heading: Go where big companies can't follow: small-but-real markets
chunks.text:
- Big companies play only in big markets. With expensive machinery and bureaucracy, building something new takes "a dump truck of money and dozens of man-years", so the opportunity must be enormous.
- Even a success in a small market would not move the needle at the top.
- Microsoft can't attack a market unless it can earn at least $1B, yet Jason notes you would be happy in a market where you rake in "only" $100M.
- He is not recommending micro-niches with seven potential customers on Earth.
- Avoid massive general markets like "everyone with a digital camera", "anyone with a smart phone" or "all software developers."

chunks.heading: Do what they structurally cannot do
chunks.text:
Jason says big companies' advantages (money, brand, team, large customer base, many customers who never switch even to a clearly better alternative) come with restrictions. Their brand ("eBay is trustable", "Apple is cool", "IBM is safe") is a force you probably can't overcome. But the same attributes limit them:

- They can't release a completely revamped new version because they can't retrain 200,000 users.
- They can't take risks, because protecting the existing revenue stream beats everything, even at the cost of their ultimate demise.
- They can't turn new ideas into released code quickly, because of requirements, documents, designers, approvals, schedules, testing and vetting.
- They can't change their image. If they have a reputation for bad tech support, most people keep thinking so even after it is fixed.
- They can't react quickly to market shifts, with too many layers of people and process and careers tied to the status quo.

chunks.heading: Examples of what incumbents cannot copy
chunks.text:
- **Intuit and Mint:** Intuit needs to look solid and timeless, its developers know C++ and desktop apps, and it can't retrain computer-phobic Quicken home users, so it could not create Mint.
- **IBM and small consulting:** IBM's expensive infrastructure, dev teams and sales channels exist to command multi-million-dollar consulting deals. That makes small deals unprofitable for it, so small consulting shops never worry about competing with IBM.
- **The takeaway:** They can't change their product, so you can innovate without competition. They can't change their image, so you can fill the gap. They can't listen to a customer and ship an impact a week later; you can. "Do what they can't do, be what they're not," and you won't have to compete on those points.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jason Cohen argues tech support is the face of your company and often the only human contact customers have with you. At Smart Bear, great support closed individual and six-figure enterprise deals without a traditional sales team, and doubled as the closest thing to customer development for a bootstrapper.

chunks.heading: Tech support as the face of the company
chunks.text:
Jason argues tech support is the only human interaction most customers ever have with a company, so it is the brand, the positioning and a sales channel. He rejects the view of support as the bottom of the food chain (angry customers, answering phones, no power to fix things) and says that attitude means missing channels for marketing, product development and sales. His analogy: David Beckham looks like the "quintessential picture of manly sportif" but his voice is a surprise nobody forgets. A home page is the public face only until someone "opens their mouth", and the question is what happens when the company's bullet points collide with its behavior.
- "Are you really going to leave that up to your worst-treated, least-paid, least-qualified employees?"

chunks.heading: Tech support is sales: how Smart Bear sold without "sales"
chunks.text:
At Smart Bear, Jason's company, he says they made millions of dollars in both individual and enterprise sales, including six-figure deals, without "sales" in the usual sense. By that he means the processes, personalities and management single-mindedly focused on hauling in revenue on a quarterly schedule. There was no golf and no Salesforce. Their tech support was the sales function.
- His definition of the purpose of tech support: "to make your customers fantastic at their jobs, which happen to involve your product." He credits the idea to Kathy Sierra.
- Make the customer awesome and she gives you money so she can keep being awesome. "That's sales."

chunks.heading: How to run support so customers become more successful
chunks.text:
Jason's tactics for turning support into customer enablement:
- Don't just locate a menu command. Find out what the customer is trying to accomplish and help with that.
- Don't just explain a feature. Help them use the result to impress their boss.
- Don't just apologize for a missing feature. Help them work around it and succeed anyway.
- Support staff know the product and problem space better than customers, so making customers far more successful than they would be on their own is "not that hard."
- Enabling customers is about the entire company, not only the product.

chunks.heading: Low expectations make support a cheap way to delight customers
chunks.text:
Everyone's stereotype of support is negative: a reboot as the answer to a font question, up-sells during a billing-address change, phone menu mazes that ask for the account number three times. Jason's view is that when customers expect "a turd sandwich" and get "a turkey club with chipotle aioli", they earn the company outsized credit.
- Observed results: users tweeting about the service, people switching to a service because of its support, and customers following a company's tweets and telling their own followers to do the same.
- He calls this a better "social media outreach" program than hiring interns to spray comments on random blogs.
- Support has "under-promise" built in. Even acting like a human being puts a company ahead, and answering email with a non-automated response is "killing it."
- A pleasant surprise is rare in business, so being the company where it happens every day is a cheap opportunity.

chunks.heading: Support as the closest thing to getting "outside the building"
chunks.text:
Steve Blank's advice is that everything you need to know about customers is outside the building: talking face to face and watching them react. Jason agrees, but notes that a bootstrapper or "work-a-preneur" with no travel budget is at the desk most of the time (he says 94%). For them, tech support is the next-best source of customer development, because it is where people complain about what is broken, missing or confusing.
- Cataloging problems is not enough. The insight is in the meta-questions.
- To answer them you have to go back and forth with customers to reach the root cause.
- You need to read hundreds of emails to get a gut feel for what customers experience, which he says you cannot get from an "Incident Summary Report" or similar automation.

chunks.heading: Meta-questions to ask about every support confusion
chunks.text:
When a customer is confused, the immediate job is to set them straight, but Jason lists questions that turn it into product development.
- Tactical:
  - What caused the confusion?
  - Is the customer's world-view different from mine?
  - Is our terminology wrong?
  - Are we using the wrong metaphors?
  - Do I need to optimize the new-user experience instead of the expert-user experience?
- Strategic:
  - Does this hiccup reveal a customer pain point I didn't know existed but can solve?
  - Is there enough evidence of a conceptual mismatch that I should pivot?
  - Is there a new product idea here?
  - If customers are abusing my product to get what they really want, can I provide that from the start?
- Example: the last line of questioning is how Smart Bear came to be a company about peer code review and not "version control data mining." Jason says that without it "you wouldn't be reading this right now."
- His conclusion: tech support is "the closest, most honest chance for product development", more straightforward than going through traditional sales, because it is where real users discover and report on the product.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jason argues founders should build something people want to buy rather than aim to be "disruptive." Disruption is hard to pitch, unwanted by most people, often unprofitable for the disruptor, and usually a hindsight label. He cites Smart Bear, ITWatchDogs and WP Engine as modest, well-executed wins.

chunks.heading: Making something people want beats being "disruptive"
chunks.text:
- Jason is wary of founders who pitch "disruptive" products. Disruption is "occasionally a consequence of innovation," but when it becomes the primary purpose, "you've lost sight of why you should be doing any of this in the first place."
- He says to worry about making something useful and delightful, and less about disrupting everything.
- "Disruptive" is the modern word for what used to be called a "paradigm shift."
- Disruptive products can generate billions, which is why venture capitalists love them, and he says their goals make that rational.
- Disruption is rare and usually expensive. It is hard to name a disruptive technology that didn't need hundreds of millions or billions of dollars of investment ahead of revenue.
- Most founders don't have access to that capital. Many would rather build an idea they understand, one that makes a living and that people want and need.

chunks.heading: Incremental improvement is a legitimate strategy
chunks.text:
- "There's nothing wrong with incremental improvement." He asks what is wrong with doing something interesting, useful and new but not transcendental.
- His preferred approach is to take a known problem in a known market and do it better, or with a fresh, unique perspective.
- You don't have to create a new market or turn everyone's assumptions upside down to succeed, and he questions whether you should try.
- Simple, modest goals are the most likely to succeed and the most likely to make you happy.
- "It's not 'aiming low' to attempt modest success." Making a nice living for yourself is not failure.
- He argues you are more likely to change the world if you don't try to change everything at once.
- Modesty applies both to what you count as success and to what you try to achieve each day.
- He quotes Kathy Sierra: insisting something be "Deeply Meaningful With Purpose can sometimes suck the joy from it."
- He doesn't say disruptive pursuits are wrong. Modest goals are simply much more likely to be achieved.

chunks.heading: Disruptive benefits are hard to explain, which makes them a poor sales pitch
chunks.text:
- Using Twitter circa 2010 as the example, he notes that explaining why it is a fundamental shift in how you meet and interact with people is hard. Listeners typically respond with "I don't need to know what everyone had for lunch."
- Good explanations exist, but they are lengthy and need listeners with patience and open minds, "two attributes in short supply."
- His rule: "'It's hard to explain' means it's a terrible sales pitch." "You just need to try it" and "trust me" don't work.
- Twitter could get away with that, but 100 other social-networking and link-sharing networks that didn't survive couldn't. Ask them, he says, about selling intangible benefits.
- A 2024 editor's note says the point held up: most people who became obsessed with social media didn't become obsessed with Twitter.

chunks.heading: People don't want to be disrupted
chunks.text:
- Founders and readers of startup blogs are more open to new ideas than most people. Most people are creatures of habit.
- They "don't want their lives turned upside down." They complain even when a toolbar is rearranged, and cringe at a new social media craze, hoping it is a passing fad.
- Change is hard, so a person has to be experiencing real pain before they want to change.
- It is easier to sell a point-solution for a point-problem than to get people to change how they live.
- Identifying specific pain points and showing how your software addresses them is easier than tapping into a general malaise and promising a better world.

chunks.heading: Famous disruptors usually started as "just better"
chunks.text:
- Google was roughly the 11th major search engine (he cites a count of 18 in a linked history), not the first. "A better search engine" was hardly a new idea.
- Google is seen in hindsight as transforming how people find information and how internet advertising works, "but the genesis was just 'better'" than the engines before it.
- Citing Scott Berkun, he points to the iPod. It was not the first of its kind. Earlier crappy devices sold well enough to prove a market existed but had no clear winner.
- The iPod won on design alone. It had no new market, no innovative features and no better sound quality or battery life, and it wasn't concerned with "disrupting" everything else.
- His conclusion: setting out to be disruptive isn't how quality, sustainable companies are built. "Disruption, like expertise, is a side-effect of great success, not a goal unto itself."

chunks.heading: Disruptors often don't capture the money
chunks.text:
- Companies that built high-speed internet fiber backbones and large data centers changed how business is done worldwide, but many went bankrupt in the 2000 tech bubble. Survivors still haven't recovered the infrastructure cost.
- Research labs show the same pattern. Xerox PARC invented the mouse, Ethernet, laser printers, windowing user interfaces and the fax machine (as the essay states), and made no money on them. AT&T Bell Labs invented Unix, C, wireless Ethernet and the laser, and also made no money.
- He offers possible reasons without settling on one:
  - Disruptors may be before their time and unable to hold out until others appreciate the innovation.
  - Innovation and business sense may be decoupled.
  - "Version 1" of anything is inferior to "version 3." By version 2 there are new competitors who didn't pay to invent version 1, watched its failures, and can jump straight to version 3.
- His bottom line: "Disruption is often unprofitable."

chunks.heading: His own examples of modest, profitable companies
chunks.text:
- **Smart Bear:** it took an existing practice, peer code review, and solved five specific pain points (annoyances and time-wasters). He made millions of dollars from it.
- It "wasn't worth a hundred million dollars" at the time and didn't turn anyone's world inside-out. He found it fulfilling that people were happier doing their jobs with the product.
- A 2024 note says Smart Bear kept growing for ten years afterward, acquired other profitable bootstrapped software-quality companies, and was sold for nearly $2B. None of its products were "disruptive," but all were well executed.
- He is sure that trying to fundamentally change how everyone writes software would have failed.
- **ITWatchDogs:** the problem was simple, since server-room gear fails when rooms get hot. The solution was a thermometer with a web page that emails or pages you if it's too hot.
- It had many competitors: APC (about a $1.5 billion market cap), NetBotz (millions in revenue and funding) and small operations of about $2M a year like his own.
- Its edge was an inexpensive product with 80% of competitors' features, "but nothing disruptive." The company was profitable and sold for millions of dollars, though he made less money personally than at Smart Bear.
- He is sure that trying to change how IT departments monitor server rooms would have failed.
- **WP Engine (2024 note):** it is still growing and profitable at hundreds of millions of dollars in revenue and powers 2.5% of the largest websites in the world.
- It wasn't built to "fundamentally change how websites are created." The founders saw how to dramatically improve something people already did by the millions, running WordPress sites.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jason Cohen argues that Lean, A/B testing and metrics-only thinking can crowd out creative product decisions that earn customer love. Using the costly, "non-optimal" mini-viewer in his first product, Code Historian, he shows that extra-effort delight can win customers in ways metrics don't capture.

chunks.heading: Creative work earns love that metrics can't measure
chunks.text:
Jason argues that the push toward optimization, A/B tests, metrics and funnels risks killing the fun and value of creative product work. He wants room for "taste" alongside data.

- Demanding overwhelming customer outcry before any product change means you never build the cool, effortful feature people love.
- Doing the minimum is efficient but not thrilling. Being "lean" doesn't stir hearts, and being effective isn't the same as being playful.
- He supports Lean principles and agrees most companies have too little objective feedback, not too much.
- His complaint is that every article turns the creative process of business and product design into "Vulcan objectivity."
- His position: "Sometimes you should do something just because it's cool. There's such a thing as product 'taste.'"

chunks.heading: Love is a stronger signal than utility, and it doesn't come from checklists
chunks.text:
Jason cites a blogger's praise of his iMac as "a beautiful magic floating screen filled with win."

- He calls this a stronger endorsement than "It saved me $725,231." It is "beyond utility" and "this is love."
- He asks whether love comes from feature bullet points, A/B tests, or implementing whatever tops a GetSatisfaction list.
- His answer is that it comes from something "less incremental, less data-driven, more gut feel, more emotional."
- Love can also drive willingness to pay, which he links to elsewhere ("Love wins").

chunks.heading: Case study: the Code Historian "mini-viewer" (2002)
chunks.text:
Code Historian was Jason's first product at Smart Bear, in 2002. It was the first file difference viewer with built-in version control support, showing historical versions of a file side by side with one-click switching between versions.

- Its mini-viewer was a UI element in the bottom-right corner that summarized added, changed and removed lines, so users could see how many changes there were and where.
- It also showed the current scroll position with black brackets, and used color to show kinds of change.
- He calls it "in every measurable sense a terrible business decision."
- Competitors used what he calls "boogers": small marks smeared along the scrollbar showing where differences are. He admits he enjoyed mocking them.

chunks.heading: Why the mini-viewer lost on every "lean" argument
chunks.text:
Jason lists six standard arguments that said he should have used boogers:

1. Boogers were semi-standardized, and the principle of "least surprise" says to honor familiar metaphors. No one else had a mini-viewer.
2. Boogers take minimal screen space, a strip no wider than a scrollbar, sometimes drawn on top of it. The mini-viewer had real width and claimed the right side of the screen.
3. Boogers sit next to the scrollbar, where users already look when navigating.
4. Boogers need less computation than the mini-viewer's color-variation algorithm.
5. Boogers are drawn once and change only on window resize. The mini-viewer had to redraw as the user scrolled, so speed mattered. Drawing directly on screen flickers, so it needed off-screen buffering. He says: "the mini-viewer is a lot more programming effort with a lot more chance for bugs."
6. The mini-viewer didn't convey more information than boogers.

chunks.heading: The result: customers loved it anyway
chunks.text:
- "Everyone loved the mini-viewer."
- Users emailed to say they bought Code Historian just because of it.
- Developers wrote in asking how he rendered it so efficiently.
- It was a consistent high point in product reviews.
- His takeaway: it was wasteful but fun, with no measurable usability benefit, yet "filled with win." It "took extra effort but it was endearing," an attribute "not easily captured with metrics and spreadsheets."

chunks.heading: When to cut corners and when to add delight
chunks.text:
Jason keeps the balance explicit rather than rejecting efficiency.

- In many areas of business and product development, you should stop obsessing and cut corners.
- Often it is right to accept 80% of the benefit for 20% of the effort.
- Customers generally prefer the right features over more features.
- But "sometimes it's your job to fill the screen with joyous win."
- Practical reading: pick a few places where costly, non-optimal delight is worth it, and don't demand data justification for every one.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jason Cohen argues the "butterfly effect" idea in marketing, where tiny design or psychological nudges drive big results, is mostly noise. In a world of competing stimuli, subtle influences cancel out, so effort should go to large, obvious levers like a popular blogger's mention, a spreadable story, or thrilling one customer.

chunks.heading: Big, non-subliminal effects beat subtle nudges
chunks.text:
- Jason is skeptical of "butterfly effect" marketing: the idea that tiny changes (a button color, a logo palette, a background shade) reliably cause big outcomes. He grants it is a seductive story and that psychology studies show subtle environmental effects on behavior.
- His core objection is that real life, and the internet especially, is a "hailstorm of influences." If a person is "constantly influenced in all directions, the forces cancel each other out, and none of them matter."
- The internet is noisier still. Competing with the real world and with "tabbed browsing, Twitter alerts, back buttons, bouncing tray icons, and instant messaging" drowns out most subtle effects.
- His conclusion: "Take care of the big stuff."
- A 2024 editor's note adds that most of the cited psychology studies (priming, marble-moving, old-age words) have since been debunked because they can't be reproduced. That is further reason to doubt applying them in marketing, even for the subset that may be true.

chunks.heading: What counts as "big stuff" in marketing
chunks.text:
Jason contrasts subtle tweaks with "big-ass, in-yo-face, non-subliminal effects." His examples:

- **A popular blogger mentioning you** is more influential than your logo color. His example: "200 words from Seth Godin is good for 10s of 1000s of unique visitors."
- **A compelling story people intrinsically want to spread** beats building a snappy animation for your home page.
- **Thrilling one person in a product demo** is worth more money than 1,000 website visitors being "branded" as trustworthy by a steel-blue palette and stoic font. He says he'd rather have "one Tom" (a delighted customer) than ten thousand StumbleUpon hits.

chunks.heading: How to prioritize effort
chunks.text:
- Spend time on the large levers (distribution, word of mouth, deep customer delight) rather than chasing optimizations that "will be wiped away by the ambient noise of life."
- Treat claims like "a small change to your download page results in 20% more trials" or "a subtle shift in background color increases time-on-site by 27 seconds" with suspicion, since they are exactly the stories that optimization consultants want you to believe.
- He is not saying design and attention to detail are worthless ("although maybe it isn't" valuable, he notes, pointing to a separate essay on design). His point is that most such efforts are overwhelmed by distraction.

chunks.heading: Why the subtle-effects story is appealing but misleading
chunks.text:
- It is believable because the mathematical butterfly effect is real for certain complex systems such as weather, economics and fractals.
- It is comforting because it implies everyone has power to change the world through tiny actions.
- It is attractive to marketers as an "inside scoop about how to manipulate strangers on the sly," like subliminal messaging but more pervasive.
- Jason's counter: even if individual stimuli work in a lab, in the wild they are one of thousands competing, so betting your marketing on them is a poor use of time.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jason Cohen explains how to start a company while employed without legal trouble. He covers choosing a business that fits your constraints, embracing slow growth, being open with your employer, and managing scarce time. Goal: build something solid enough to quit your day job.

chunks.heading: Choosing a side business that fits the constraints of a day job
chunks.text:
Jason says a side venture has constraints a "normal" business doesn't:
- He can't answer the phone or email during business hours.
- He can't afford to hire three developers.
- He has to work in fits and spurts.

His advice is not to fight these constraints but to "turn them into competitive advantages."

- **Don't promise what you can't deliver.** If the website claims "stupendous customer service" but there's no phone number and a 10:00am email isn't answered until that night, that is a "missed expectation." He calls it "pissing in the wind"; it comes right back at you.
- **Use the day-job income to underprice.** If someone complains there's no phone number, point out that at $5/mo you can't afford a phone staff.
- **Pick a product where simplicity is an advantage.** "We do only one thing and we do it better than anyone" is a good marketing slogan. He notes you don't have time to build a Microsoft Excel knock-off, so don't try.

chunks.heading: Embrace slow growth for a bootstrapped side project
chunks.text:
Jason argues that any bootstrapped company should aim for slow, consistent growth rather than explosive growth, and that this matters most for a business run in spare time.

- Hoping a blog post gets 267 votes on Hacker News, or that a v1.1 release sets the blogosphere ablaze, is not a plan.
- Slow growth maximizes the chance of success because success doesn't depend on some unlikely, massive event outside your control.
- Slow growth lets you change drastically in the early days without sinking the company.
- Because you have a job, you don't need explosive growth to be successful.

chunks.heading: The real goal: enough to quit the day job
chunks.text:
Jason says the immediate goal isn't to make millions but to "build a business just solid enough to quit your day job."

- It means enough profit that you can already live (frugally) off the company.
- Or it means enough customers to have "proved" a viable business model, so you can raise money on sensible terms.
- He is explicit that quitting and hoping revenue will show up is not the plan.

chunks.heading: Tell your employer about the side project, in writing
chunks.text:
Jason's core legal advice: the best way to avoid a lawsuit is to prove your employer knows about the side project. He is not a lawyer and says none of this is legal advice.

- He knows founders want to operate in secret because they fear being fired, distrusted, or looked at funny at lunch.
- His reply: what's worse, one of those things or a lawsuit? If you don't think they'd sue, you shouldn't fear telling them. They'll find out anyway, so tell them on your own terms.
- He says he has always told his employer and "it always worked out for the best."
- He has been on both sides: he has done a startup while employed, has employed people capable of running their own side startup, and has known people who were sued over it, "and not all of them won."

**His letter template** is a short note "To Whom it may Concern" that says:
- He has a hobby that does not in any way conflict with work, described in a sentence.
- He works on it only at home on his own time, it is not in conflict with his employee agreement, he owns it, and the company has no ownership or rights to it.
- Like any hobby, it could generate a small amount of income.
- If it ever conflicted with his job, it's his responsibility to notify them immediately.

**Get it signed by someone with authority.** That means someone who can legally represent the company, typically a C-level officer or the company's legal counsel. A supportive boss signing is not good enough because "he can't speak for the company."

chunks.heading: Check your employment agreement before starting
chunks.text:
Jason's template letter says the side business doesn't conflict with the employment agreement, and he says that had better be true.

- Employment agreements are typically biased toward the employer. Some have outrageous clauses claiming anything you do, even at home, on your own time, and unrelated to work, is automatically company property.
- Some also make you responsible for identifying and reporting those things, with "no limit" to the damage you could have caused if you don't.
- Courts have thrown out some egregious contracts, but that's unusual, you can't depend on it, and you don't want to go to court at all. You also signed it.
- Action: read the agreement and confirm the side business is legal under it. If it isn't, write a letter like the template that specifically states this is a valid exception to the employment agreement.

chunks.heading: Never use company property or company internet
chunks.text:
Jason says the typical clause that anything done physically at work, or on company-owned software and equipment (laptop, customer lists, Photoshop), belongs to the company is fair. If the project is really on the side and really yours alone, it can't be assisted by a company laptop, software, or connection.

- Be paranoid: assume every laptop records keystrokes, clicks, screenshots, sites, and emails, and that internet activity is logged.
- Don't try to hide it with tools like an anonymizer plus Gmail over SSL. Covering your tracks looks like a sign you're doing something wrong.
- If the company sues, "discovery" lets them search your email records. If they find 100 emails you sent during work hours, "You lose."
- His summary: "Just don't do it."

chunks.heading: Time management techniques for a side startup
chunks.text:
Jason says a startup generates infinite work and already takes the 40 hours a week you don't have, so you can't afford bad habits or working on the wrong tasks. He admits he is naturally bad at personal time management (procrastinates, disorganized). He says there's no silver bullet and workflow is personal, but lists these techniques:

- Check email infrequently.
- Inbox Zero: process email until nothing remains, for psychological and practical benefits.
- GTD (Getting Things Done): he says it "literally changed my life"; few people implement 100% but everyone can take away a trick or two.
- Work in sprints (Pomodoro-style): short, focused bursts eliminate the waste from context-switching and interrupt-driven behavior.
- Sleep enough: trading an hour of sleep for an hour of coding "is never efficient," because productivity plummets.
- Use RescueTime (free) to see empirically where time goes. Its founder, Tony Wright, started that company while employed and wrote about it.
- Optimize the slowest tasks first: fixing the slowest tasks raises overall productivity more than you'd expect.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jason Cohen proposes an exercise: imagine your company may have only one advantage over competitors, and build the whole sales talk-track around it. Focusing on one owned benefit sharpens the pitch, homepage, ads, demos and product, and he shows how a single advantage can answer a range of skeptical objections.

chunks.heading: Why one advantage beats many
chunks.text:
Jason argues that a company should be able to win a sales conversation with a single advantage it owns completely. He frames this as a forcing exercise: imagine you are allowed only one advantage over the competition, then build the 30-second pitch, the skeptical-question handling, and the close around it.

- He says the skill pays off in every sales call, whether you are defending a few advantages against a specific competitor, arguing the virtues of small businesses over large ones, or answering a perceived lack of functionality.
- "Hanging your hat on just one advantage *that you can own completely* is stronger than diluting your message by making many assertions."
- The same focus carries beyond sales calls. Your homepage, advertisements, 30-second pitch, blog and Twitter topics, and 5-minute product demo all reinforce one singular point.
- Everyone then knows who you are and where you stand, especially your ICP (Ideal Customer Profile).
- On that one point, you are untouchable.
- His closing question: "Why try to defend ten points when you only need one or two to make your case?" He urges focusing message, behavior, UX, product, target customer, and sales pitch, because "It's already hard enough to stake out a niche in this massive world! Don't dilute your message."

chunks.heading: Positioning as "Most Expensive" (the Cadillac)
chunks.text:
Jason's first worked example claims to be the most expensive and the best, and uses that one claim to answer every objection. He admits "most expensive" does not automatically imply "best," so you say that up front and argue that here you get what you pay for.

- **Against open-source ("it's free"):** "Open-source is free like puppies are free." You do not write a check, but you support it for life. Employee time, working around bugs, and relying on the internet for tech support are not free.
- **Reframe the price:** the revenue is not lining pockets, it is spent making the customer maximally effective. Examples: answering the phone on the first ring, connecting customers directly with developers instead of off-shore Level 1 support, staying on the line at 3am, and doing conference calls on best practices for the customer's use case.
- **Against a big competitor's 24/7 support:** argue quality, not quantity. Level 1 support and email are staffed by actual software developers who can read the code, and can change the code to fix a bug or add a feature. Their consultants write blog posts on best practices, live with the team every day, and train with top experts the company can afford because it is the Cadillac.
- **Against a cheaper, simpler competitor:** doing less does not mean easier to use. The company integrates with 20 other packages, which does not add complexity for a customer who ignores an integration. "There's a myth that 'more features are always more complex,' but that's just bad user interface design." High price funds top UI experts to avoid that mistake.
- **Against "I still have to justify the budget":** factor in the cost of failing. That means months of installing, integrating, training and customizing, then ripping the tool out and starting over. Better support and more features make that less likely. Add the personal angle: "besides the catastrophic expense, what's the effect on your personal career? What's best for you *and* your company is to bet on the best."

chunks.heading: Positioning as "Obsessed with Quality"
chunks.text:
The second example builds the whole pitch on quality, and Jason is careful not to over-promise.

- **Opening:** software is so crappy that people expect failure, bugs and helplessness. The pitch is that this is unacceptable.
- **Handle "so you have no bugs?" honestly:** no, but the company is maniacal about finding bugs and incredibly fast at fixing them. It is "not unusual to have a fix in under 24 hours." All software can have bugs, "but no one is more committed to fixing them."
- **Against a competitor with more features:** more bullet points is not always better, and the more features a product has, the worse each feature usually is. Test it, such as uploading a huge file to the competitor's tool and watching it break. Claiming a feature that is "full of holes" is dishonest; the company would rather have fewer features it stands behind.
- **Against free open-source:** free until you hit a bug, a security breach you did not notice for two years, incorrect data, or a need with no one to ask. "You can fix it yourself" is not free, and if the project rejects your patch you must re-patch on every update.
- **The proof point:** the company never charges for bug fixes, even years later, because it is "100% committed to quality code."

chunks.heading: Positioning as "Small Company"
chunks.text:
The third example turns small size into the advantage, and answers the usual fears about small vendors.

- **Opening:** if you haven't worked with a small company, expect smart people you can talk to, who care and go out of their way to make you successful.
- **"Small companies fail":** big companies are not stable either. They are hit by recessions and accounting scandals, and they cut or sell product lines, even profitable ones. You cannot know when a big company will discontinue your product.
- **"They have 1000 developers and support engineers":** "Willing" to help, but able? Developers are shielded by powerless Level 1 support that feels like a shield, not a help. Big companies ship infrequently, so you may wait a year for a fix. A small company lets you complain directly to the engineers and get fixes in weeks, sometimes days.
- **"Do you have 24/7 support?":** no. He contrasts "folks we've never met $1.25/hour to answer the phone at 3am PST so they can tell you to reboot your machine and RTFM" with paying actual software developers $75/hour to talk with the customer about exactly what's wrong. They sometimes write special code just to get the customer running again until a proper fix ships.
- **"They have more features":** the customer really wants their specific needs met, and "more features" only potentially means that. The key question is what happens in six months when the customer finds 10 more things they need. The small company commits to proactive meetings to learn what the customer needs and add those features as soon as it can.
- **A reframing question for buyers:** don't ask "Which tool will satisfy my needs today," ask "One year from now, which tool will be satisfying my needs, including the ones I can't foresee?"

chunks.heading: How to use the exercise
chunks.text:
- Run the one-advantage exercise to get a clear talk-track, even if you never run with a single advantage in practice. Jason admits of each example, "Will this work? I don't know, but at least the talk-track is clear."
- Use the single advantage as a lens to answer any skeptical question: each objection (price, features, support, risk) is answered by rolling it back to the one thing you own.
- Practice the skill because every real sales call involves defending a few advantages against a competitor, a size class, or a perceived functionality gap.
- Apply the same narrowing to the homepage, ads, pitch, content topics and demo so they all say the same thing.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jason Cohen pushes back on the "10,000 hours to expertise before success" idea. He argues successful entrepreneurs don't start as experts; career and expertise develop together, helped by luck, and genuinely new things have no prior experts. The takeaway: stop chasing arbitrary credentials and get back to work.

chunks.heading: You don't need to be an expert first
chunks.text:
- Jason is "sick of being admonished that success is predicated on spending the next 10,000 hours of my life becoming 'an expert.'" He calls the idea bullshit.
- He argues people get so busy trying to turn themselves into outliers that they forget what actually matters.
- The "10,000 hours" and "ten years of very focused, everyday work" rules are, in his view, arbitrary definitions and unnecessary prerequisites to success.
- His conclusion: stop being distracted by them and "just get back to work."

chunks.heading: Expertise is not required for success (Penelope Trunk example)
chunks.text:
- Jason's test case: Penelope Trunk wrote that she is not an expert in anything and is not making headway, and equated being an expert with success.
- Her blog had 48,767 subscribers at the time. She also had a six-figure book deal and had written for the Wall Street Journal and Time.
- He says she is clearly a success, so her problem is not a lack of expertise but the same irrational, commonplace feelings of inadequacy (impostor syndrome) that he shares.
- His logic: if someone who fails her own definition of "expert" is obviously successful, then "being an expert isn't required for being successful."
- Note the scale he points out: millions of people try to become "expert" enough at something to reach that level of success, and almost none of them will.

chunks.heading: Why "10,000 hours" evidence is weak, and talent matters
chunks.text:
- He rejects the claim that today's high school swimmers beating old Olympic records proves expertise is just time spent. In his view that only shows there are more swimmers, more chances to find and train great ones, and better diet, training, technology and facilities.
- Even if it takes that much sheer effort, he says it clearly also takes talent.
- Personal evidence: he practiced piano an hour a day for more than ten years and became good. But others who practiced twice as much were worse, and others who practiced less are much better.
- He says we all know this, and asks why we let people tell us otherwise.

chunks.heading: Successful founders didn't start as experts
chunks.text:
- "Not one of the successful entrepreneurs I know *started* as an expert."
- Career and expertise are developed simultaneously. Success comes when that is coupled with a few key events, "due as much to luck as effort."
- Examples he gives:
  - Sergey and Larry were not advertising experts before they started Google.
  - Joel Spolsky was not a blogging expert before starting Fog Creek.
  - Jason knew nothing about peer code review before starting Smart Bear.
- In each case being an expert up front would have been impossible: Google reinvented advertising, there were no "blogs" when Joel started posting essays, and there was no code review tool until Jason invented one.

chunks.heading: Innovation defies prior expertise
chunks.text:
- His core principle: "Innovation defies prior expertise."
- If you are building something new, there is no established body of expertise to master first, so waiting to become an expert is a trap rather than a plan.
- Practical takeaway: start building the company or product and let your skill grow alongside it, instead of delaying until you feel qualified.
- Related mindset point: feeling like you are not an expert enough is often impostor syndrome, not a real gap, so don't treat it as a reason to hold back.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jason Cohen explains that sunk costs (money, time and effort already spent and unrecoverable) should be ignored when deciding what to do next, yet human loss aversion makes us cling to them. He applies it to startup situations: pet features, marketing slogans, bad hires, endless A/B iteration, and long-shot enterprise deals.

chunks.heading: Sunk costs are gone whatever you do next, so ignore them
chunks.text:
Jason defines a sunk cost as "money you've already spent and cannot get back." He says a rational actor ignores it completely, because the money is gone whichever action comes next. He says many of his own mistakes trace back to failing to recognize sunk cost.

- **Clear case:** a banner ad cost $1000 to design and $2000 to run for three months. Results were horrible: barely any clicks and no purchases. Nobody spends more on that ad. Whether $30 or $30,000 had been spent, continuing is still not worth it.
- **Harder case:** a company burns $20m on a new plant and needs another $10m to finish. A $2m retrofit of a different plant appears. The $20m is unrecoverable, so the real choice is $2m versus $10m, and they should abandon the original project.
- **Why it usually goes wrong:** the person who owns the project would have to stand up and say "I'm responsible for this hugely wasteful endeavor, and now I want you to trust my judgment as I pull the plug and do something completely different."
- He rejects the idea that this is a big-company problem: startups are not too smart or agile to make the same mistakes ("that's crap").

chunks.heading: Why people hold on: loss aversion and the endowment effect
chunks.text:
- Jason says "it's not just politics, it's human nature." The related terms are Loss Aversion and the Endowment Effect, which are subtly different but close enough for his purposes.
- Core idea: "We place excessive value on that which we own, or which we perceive we own."
- **Duke tickets:** students who lost the lottery for scarce game tickets would pay an average of $170 for one. Students who won would sell for an average of $2,400. Both had made the same effort, but owners valued the randomly assigned ticket far higher.
- **Horse bettors:** people who have already placed bets are more optimistic about winning than people still in line.
- **Movies:** most people won't walk out of a movie they hate because that "wastes money," even though the money can't be recovered and they could be doing something more enjoyable.
- **Touching items:** just touching an item in a store makes you more likely to buy it.
- It is so deeply ingrained that gut reactions don't change even when you know about it. That is why he says you must be especially vigilant.

chunks.heading: Killing pet features and recycled ideas
chunks.text:
- **Pet feature:** you built a hard-to-implement feature and you're proud of it. Customers don't care, and it causes confusion and bugs. Even if customer XYZ says it's neat, the effort is sunk whether or not the feature fits. He says to kill the feature.
- **Clever marketing slogan:** it came out of hours of brainstorming and arguing, but it doesn't quite fit the business. Don't try to "waste not" it by forcing it in somewhere. As with all writing, "you have to learn how to throw things out."

chunks.heading: Firing the hire who isn't working out
chunks.text:
- The scenario: the newest hire passed the interview and tests, but isn't a culture fit, isn't learning fast enough, and others are resentfully covering the slack.
- The trap is thinking "it was so much work finding them and we've put all this effort into training them; maybe they'll change?" Jason says they won't, and deep down you know it.
- The time is sunk. He calls this one of the most expensive mistakes you can make, but says prolonging the inevitable is worse.
- It is also bad for the employee, who deserves a chance to find a job where they can succeed.

chunks.heading: Endless marketing iteration and A/B testing
chunks.text:
- A marketing effort doesn't work, so you A/B test a pair. The second is a little better but not much. You iterate again, and again.
- His question: when do you stop and realize that incremental iteration isn't always enough, and that repeated experimentation can produce false positives?
- The sunk-cost pull is continuing to tweak something because you've already invested in it, instead of trying something new.
- He links to his related pieces on creativity over optimization and p-hacking.

chunks.heading: Walking away from the big deal that never closes
chunks.text:
- Example: a 500-seat sale to a big-name company, with a 9-month trial. They keep finding reasons not to buy: "deal-breaker" features, "critical" bugs, budget allocations that never materialize.
- The pull to continue: the sale would mean so much, you've spent hundreds of hours with them, and you've added special features, so surely they'll buy eventually.
- In his experience they often won't, or they buy just 10 seats so you can't claim they're "still trialing."
- His read: this is a sign of poor fit, and the time-suck won't vanish after they buy. "Let it go."
- His rule: you need profitable customers and advocates, not merely customers.

chunks.heading: Sunk costs in personal choices
chunks.text:
- Example: you studied Biology as a teenager, before you knew what makes you happy or where your talents lie. Friends and family expect a lab career. Should you throw away the work and expectations to become a caterer?
- Jason's point is that attachment to sunk costs is natural. It hurts to admit wasted time, money, energy and reputation.
- His conclusion: "it's even worse to irrationally prolong the waste."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jason Cohen borrows Scott Berkun's "Rude Q&A": write down the nastiest, smartest, even unfair questions about your company, then answer them. The exercise tests your ideas and forces sharper messaging, target customer and features. He gives a starter list of startup questions and a worked answer about why his own blog should exist.

chunks.heading: Stress-testing your pitch with a "Rude Q&A" instead of waiting for the market to do it
chunks.text:
Jason's core idea: before you pitch, launch, or raise money, write down the nastiest questions a smart, hostile critic would ask, then answer them in writing. He borrows the concept of Rude Q&A from Scott Berkun and treats it as the startup equivalent of swinging a heavy bat before stepping up to the plate.

- "Nothing clarifies things quite like a hyperactive, all-knowing, all-seeing, real asshole of a devil's advocate beating the living crap out of you."
- The hardest part is generating the questions, because the best ones target exactly the assumptions you least want to examine.
- Questions should include unfair ones and ones built on wrong information, since reporters, clients and the public ask those too.
- Answers to unfair questions take longer to write because they must be more polite and mature than the question, and must refute its assumptions without being dismissive.
- Jason's advice if you're unhappy with some answers: that's a good sign. It means you're being honest, so keep looking for better answers and discuss the hard ones with other people.

chunks.heading: What the exercise forces you to sharpen
chunks.text:
Jason argues the value isn't only testing whether the idea survives. Being grilled removes the room to be vague about the things that matter most:

- Marketing messages: no space for generic claims.
- Target customer profile: you must know exactly who it's for.
- Feature set: you must defend what's in and what's missing.
- How you differ from competitors and where you are strongest.
- Exactly what customer pain you solve and why customers should love you.
- Company values, and which compromises you are or aren't willing to make.

His point is that a hostile question leaves no leniency for "we're better, faster, more customer-focused" answers.

chunks.heading: A starter list of hostile startup questions
chunks.text:
Jason offers these as generic seeds, to be made more specific to your own business:

- Your biggest competitor just dropped their price to $0. How do you justify your price?
- If your idea is good, copycats will come from incumbents and startups, funded and bootstrapped, large and small. How will you persevere?
- If the economy stays bad for two more years, how do you survive?
- "The last thing anyone needs is *another damn tool*." What's the overwhelming reason to look at you?
- Competitor X is doing better than you. What are you going to do about it?
- If you raised prices 50%, would any customers stay? How do you get 10x more of those customers?
- What are the top three features your competitor has that you lack, and what's your plan for the next six months?
- How can you call yourself an expert after only a year?
- There are only two of you. What if someone leaves?
- What's the single most important thing to accomplish in the next 12 months, and how will you do it? (Do you even know what it is?)
- Your growth will top out because of high cancellation. How do you fix so many people disliking you even after buying?
- What are three tangible, undeniable ways your product saves more money than it costs and more time than it consumes?
- Truly great products and companies are rare. What makes you think you have what it takes?
- Thousands of consultants claim high quality, on time, on budget, happy customers. What makes you different?

chunks.heading: Make the questions specific: the "why read this blog" example
chunks.text:
Jason says generic questions are only a start; you need specific attacks. For his own blog he sharpened "why should I read it?" into: there are already too many startup blogs, those are far more popular, their authors more famous with excellent advice, and Smart Bear's success is nothing like Steve Blank's. Why should anyone listen to you?

His answer, in two parts:

1. **Every piece of advice has a counter-argument, so the goal is to find advice that fits your context.** Someone must point out that he made millions with poor graphic design and too many features, against Jason Fried's "simple design is better than complex features." Likewise, against Seth Godin's "1,000 true fans" idea, someone should say it isn't true in practice. Readers need to match advice to their own goals, personality, constraints and strengths, so a blog sourced from his specific experience helps people become a better version of who they already are.
2. **Impact doesn't depend on inventing the idea.** Think of your best teacher or mentor: they didn't invent the subject. What changes lives is the exposition, the turn of phrase, and the accidental time and place where someone hears an idea for the seventh time and is finally ready for it. He says he has received thousands of messages saying his writing changed someone or was "what I really needed to hear today," and suggests that may be the definition of life's purpose.

He notes the answer was written in 2010, just before founding WP Engine (which became a hyper-growth unicorn), and says it's more instructive to see how he answered before earning that credibility.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: A practical checklist from running dozens of tradeshow booths at Smart Bear. Covers setting a goal, presenting, booking meetings with press and customers, using the booth as live market research and pitch testing, and following up afterward.

chunks.heading: Why Jason attends tradeshows: set a goal first
chunks.text:
Jason treats tradeshows as expensive: a booth runs $2k-$20k, travel about $1,000/day, plus a week at the show and weeks of prep. Because of that cost he insists on one primary goal, which drives every other decision and tells you afterward whether the show was worth repeating. Example goals he lists:
- Make a sale on the floor
- Get at least 20 genuine prospects
- Talk with 10 industry leaders
- Find 10 good recruiting prospects
- Find 3 serious investors
- Ask potential customers 3 specific things (market research)

His experience: running booths at dozens of shows. He also says "Quality not quantity": six solid conversations with likely buyers beat giving away 200 pieces of branded swag to people who won't remember you.

chunks.heading: Planning 3-6 months out: presentation, message, booth, print, staffing
chunks.text:
- **Always schedule a vendor presentation.** Even 20 people for 45 minutes is worth far more than 100 people at the booth for 5-60 seconds. He often gets a few sales from the talk alone.
- **Pick one short main message.** You get about 3 seconds to make someone stop, like a home page. The goal is to make people stop, not explain everything. Boil it to one short sentence.
- **Pick the booth early; location matters.** Good spots: next to the bathroom (everyone passes it), near the front doors, nearer the room center than the ends, and aisle corners (more traffic, and your stuff can spill over the edge).
- **Start print work early.** He has "never" gotten what he wanted from a print shop on the first try. Screen colors and Pantone swatches don't match the print. Ask for the techie in the back (who knows InDesign, DPI, CMYK, vector vs. raster), not the counter salesperson.
- **Staff at least 3 people.** Two at the booth (busy times, restocking, breaks) and one roaming and attending meetings.
- **Book all travel early** for cheaper fares and no sold-out surprises.
- **Make the booth different.** Most booths have a logo, banner, a "clever" phrase and adjectives like "fast" and "scalable." Do something different; it needn't be amazing.
- **Order shirts and swag early** since customization takes time. At least have a "tradeshow shirt."

chunks.heading: One month out: postcards, email, meetings, promotion, the box
chunks.text:
- **Postcard mailers work.** Offer something cool or expensive at the booth, redeemable only by bringing the postcard. Attendees keep it handy (seeing your marketing repeatedly), seek you out, and you collect their name, company and address for follow-up. Put the booth number on it.
- **Emails probably work** because you can put the show's name in the subject line.
- **Set meetings proactively.** Aim for at least 5 per day, using clearly non-spam subjects like "At [Tradeshow]: Can we chat for 5 minutes?" Targets:
  - Magazine editors (online and offline). He says he has "been published in every major programming magazine," almost all traced to talking with editors at tradeshows.
  - Bloggers you like
  - Existing customers
  - Prospects trialing your product
  - Vendors
  - Competitors
  - Potential partners
  - Dinner or drinks after the show also works.
- **Promote the show:** add the show info and booth number to everyone's email signature, plus any giveaway.
- **Bring a cheap plastic "box of everything"** (he says you'll use an unpredictable subset every time): multiple pens, Sharpie, Scotch and masking tape, extension cord, plug bar, post-its, rubber bands, tiny stapler, highlighter, paper clips, scissors, all-in-one tool, medicine (Tylenol, Advil, Motrin, DayQuil), zip-ties, generic business cards.
- **Wear comfortable shoes.** You stand far longer than usual. Use floor pads or pay the venue to pad your booth carpet.

chunks.heading: At the booth: how to engage people
chunks.text:
- **Ask questions instead of pitching.** Be genuinely interested in what they do. They'll then ask for your pitch as reciprocation, which gives you permission to sell and a listening audience.
- **Don't open with "how are you doing?"** Open with something specific you offer; even "Are you interested in [thing you do]" is better, though still weak.
- **Use it as market research.** Prepare 3-5 questions to ask passersby. No need to record carefully: "the big trends will be obvious and the rest is noise."
- **A/B test your pick-up line** all show long, like a landing page. After the 100th pitch you'll know what gets people to stop, laugh, or say "tell me more," and he says to put that on your home page.
- **Stand, don't sit.** Sitting looks like you don't want to be there, and the head-height difference is off-putting.
- **Get into the aisle** rather than standing behind the table; one person inside the booth, another in the aisle directing people in. During high traffic, being a barrier forces people to squeeze past, giving a chance to engage. He links the "guy in a bear suit" lesson.
- **Quality of staff:** sales people aren't enough. Attendees want to "geek out" with peers, so bring people who don't normally go on sales calls.
- **Note the jokes.** People will make fun of you; if no one does, they may not understand what you do.

chunks.heading: Booth attractions: demos, video, food, raffles, parties
chunks.text:
- **Moving pictures:** use a big monitor or, better, a bright projector with a demo movie playing, not a static screenshot or a stuck demo. At Smart Bear other vendors said "OMG we have to do that next year."
- **Always be able to demo.** "Nothing is more sticky than a live demo," more than swag, brochures, phrases or raffles. Prefer a projector so passersby get hooked; at least a large monitor, "not your laptop screen."
- **Free food** works better than most freebies; the more "real" the better (cookies over candy). Put it at the center of the booth so people must talk to take it.
- **Raffle something.** Not a sales tool, but it draws a crowd, and crowds make others think the booth is interesting. Some people returned the next day saying they hadn't stopped earlier because the booth was swamped. Require contact info to enter (form, badge scan, business card); the leads are weakly qualified but better than nothing.
- **Host your own happy hour.** Rent a room at or near the venue with wine, beer and basic food; invite people at the show and in pre-show mailers. It is cheaper than you'd think, and people are relaxed and willing to talk about your product to reciprocate.
- **Don't depend on the internet.** Show internet is spotty; demos and note-taking must work offline.

chunks.heading: Capturing leads and networking during the show
chunks.text:
- **Take names, not brochure handouts.** Attendees get stuffed with paper that gets lost. Scan badges or take business cards and mail something afterward so it's waiting on their desk without tradeshow distraction.
- **Write notes on their business card** (you'll talk to hundreds and forget). If the card can't take notes, stick a post-it to it.
- **Add contacts on LinkedIn every night.** Most accept if you add them the same day and mention the conference.
- **Walk the floor and talk to every vendor.** Commiserate about the show, look for ways to work together (usually nothing results, but they remember you), skip their salespeople and meet the founder.

chunks.heading: After the show: follow up and mine what you learned
chunks.text:
- **Follow up.** He estimates a 99% chance attendees have forgotten you, even if they took swag or a brochure. Remind them and take them up on offers of a demo, trial, or reviewing an article draft.
- **Apply what you learned about selling:**
  - Which one-liners got attention, and how to use them on the home page
  - New AdWords text to try
  - How to change the 2-minute demo
  - What people said about competitors and your best retorts
- **Apply what you learned about the product** from demoing it about 50 times:
  - Existing features that weren't obvious
  - Features people kept asking for that you lack
  - Demo parts that dragged or confused viewers
  - Terminology newbies didn't understand
  - What people hated about competitors (keep that advantage) and loved about them (close the gap)

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jason Cohen explains that feeling like a fraud is near-universal among high performers and founders, and that it comes from perfectionism rather than confidence. He separates constructive self-doubt, which drives learning and effort, from harmful doubt, which drives hiding and avoidance. He also gives concrete reframes for answering the inner voice.

chunks.heading: Feeling like a fraud is normal, and Jason says the cause explains the cure
chunks.text:
Jason felt like a fraud every day in Smart Bear's early years. He sold a "wobbly, buggy tool" and called himself an expert in a field that didn't exist, since Smart Bear made the first commercial tool for peer code review. His friend Jason Young, 16 years in, told him: "I've been at this for 16 years and I still feel like a fraud." Jason's takeaways:
- Looking back, the feelings were misplaced. The tool saved customers time and headache, and he had seen more teams in more situations than anyone doing the day job.
- "Emotions don't respond to logic." The feelings don't go away even when they ought to.
- He cites Mike Meyers, Jodie Foster and Fields Medalist June Huh as people with the same doubt.
- Cited figures: "40% of successful people consider themselves frauds", and 84% of surveyed entrepreneurs and small business owners scored as feeling like impostors at moderate, frequent or intense levels.

chunks.heading: The specific doubts a founder carries early on
chunks.text:
Jason lists the doubts he had while building Smart Bear:
- Did the claim that the tool "cuts code review time in half" hold up, or had he just repeated it so often he stopped questioning it?
- Should he handle large purchases with no knowledge of accounting, cash flow, invoicing or purchase orders, while Accounts Payable belittled him?
- Who was he to teach "best practices" for code review, even in a published book?
- Was he too young, the tool too crappy to charge for, or himself too inexperienced without an MBA or sales training?
- Was Smart Bear a "real company"?

Sales, he found, "isn't as mystical and unknowable as I feared."

chunks.heading: Signs you have it
chunks.text:
Jason's checklist:
- You dismiss compliments and awards as "no big deal."
- Mild, constructive criticism crushes you.
- You think you're less capable than others believe, and fear being found out.
- You think peers are more "adult" and "have their shit together."
- You credit successes to luck and failures to ability.
- You struggle to take credit for accomplishments.
- You feel like the embodiment of "fake it until you make it."

chunks.heading: Why founders feel this: perfectionism, not confidence
chunks.text:
Jason argues the entrepreneur-as-confident-genius stereotype is wrong.
- A perfectionist sees flaws in everyone's work, so she wants to do it her way and struggles to delegate.
- She also sees an endless stream of flaws in her own work, and can't accept that others are impressed by what she sees as mediocre works-in-progress.
- "Our entrepreneurial motivation is not confidence, it's an insatiable desire to do it our way."
- Doing it your own way is not the same as being confident it is the correct way. It means never accepting any idea as best, even if you prefer yours to everyone else's.

chunks.heading: Telling constructive doubt from harmful doubt
chunks.text:
Jason says the feeling can be useful if it pushes you to learn. He quotes Andy Wibbels: "If I don't feel like a fraud at least once a day then I'm not reaching far enough."

**Constructive:**
- Doubt your "expert" title, so read, write and immerse yourself in the field daily.
- Doubt your software quality, so fix bugs fast, write unit tests proactively and thank customers for their patience.
- Doubt you deserve your reputation, so work to earn it.
- Notice you're not yet as good as you want to be, and see yourself slowly improving.
- Not a "real company" yet, so focus on making customers successful until they stop caring about company size.

**Harmful:**
- Worrying nightly about being exposed and scanning for trivially easy "escape-hatch" jobs.
- Covering software flaws with graphic design and heavy sales pitches.
- Losing sleep over fear of exposure.
- Avoiding speaking, writing or programming, and feeling like a trapped animal when forced to do them.
- Feeling guilty whenever someone pays you or believes you.

His advice is to recognize which mode you're in and deal with it logically.

chunks.heading: Four questions to answer the impostor voice
chunks.text:
- **Add "yet."** "I can't do this job... yet." "I don't deserve the title I have... yet."
- **"Am I a curious student?"** If you saw a student humbly and energetically pursuing growth, you'd think "good for them, how can I help," not "impostor for not being an expert." Acting as a curious student is being a student, "which is awesome."
- **"Do I deserve to be peers with my peers?"** Yes. Neil Gaiman and Neil Armstrong feel the same way, and you know both are wrong.
- **"Do I deserve the title or responsibility I have?"** Did "some idiot" give you a hand-out for nothing? If not, you earned it.
- **"I feel stretched and don't know what I'm doing."** Jason calls that "the human condition... for humans who strive." Only the ignorant and foolhardy fail to see there's more to learn. Discomfort while striving is normal, not evidence you shouldn't be doing it.

chunks.heading: The last-resort argument when logic fails
chunks.text:
Jason's closing argument:
- You believe Mike Meyers, Jodie Foster and June Huh are talented, and might believe Jason is an expert in peer code review and startups.
- Yet they and he doubt themselves daily, "and we're wrong." So "if we're wrong, you're wrong too."
