- Don't stop striving. Stop holding yourself to an impossible standard and stop worrying what others think: "They're not thinking about you at all."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jason Cohen explains why he sold Smart Bear in 2007 despite 100% annual growth. He argues you can chase "Rich" while behaving like "King" by running a profitable, durable business, and that crossing the "Freedom Line" matters more than squeezing out a bigger exit.

chunks.heading: Why Jason sold Smart Bear: the "Rich and King" hybrid
chunks.text:
- Jason sold Smart Bear in December 2007, after a buyer offered him enough money that he "never [has] to work again."
- He used Noam Wasserman's "Rich or King" framework: "Rich" founders are in it for the money, "King" founders for lifestyle and identity.
- Wasserman says successful founders pick one up front and stay consistent. Jason says he mixed the two and it worked.
- His goal was always "Rich," specifically acquisition. He achieved it by running the company as if the goal were "King."
- He doesn't see a contradiction: a long-term, sustainable business is exactly the kind that gets acquired.
- He tells people the hard part is that "King" companies like 37signals and FogCreek would never sell, which is rational for them. His own choice was rational too.

chunks.heading: Profit as the rule behind every decision
chunks.text:
- Everyone Jason hired was told up front: "we're here to make money, and if someone offers to buy the company someday, I'm going to sell it, and all of us will make money."
- "Profit was the rule behind every choice we made." The end goal was acquisition, but he argues the best way to get acquired is to be profitable.
- Why profit matters to a buyer:
  - It proves the business is operating well.
  - It validates the market.
  - It makes minimum valuation easy.
  - The buyer converts balance-sheet cash into bottom-line P&L, which every large company wants.
- The biggest benefit: profit means you don't need to sell. He argues you have little negotiating power in any deal unless you can happily walk away.
- He notes (editor's note) this applies to small self-funded companies, which are most attractive as cash machines. Other companies sell on growth or daily active users.

chunks.heading: Building a genuine company while aiming to sell
chunks.text:
- Jason says he would only be happy building a great company, which meant:
  - A product that solves a real pain.
  - White-glove customer service, with "tech support" as the only sales force.
  - Leaving the world a little better than he found it.
  - Employees who are smart, get things done, and are trusted with any decision.
- He openly admits he also wanted the ego rewards of running a company:
  - Saying "I run my own company" at parties.
  - A free book that got popular enough that people asked him to sign it (the joke was that signing doubled its value).
  - Walking a tradeshow floor like "Norm on Cheers," knowing everyone.
  - Speaking at venues like the Business of Software Conference.
  - Using Smart Bear's success to give his blog credibility.

chunks.heading: The Freedom Line: why crossing it matters more than how far
chunks.text:
- Jason describes a non-linear relationship between cash in personal savings and financial freedom.
- There is a "Freedom Line" where savings alone fund a reasonably lavish lifestyle, freeing you from restrictions on life, family and career.
- Two observations:
  1. Crossing from left to right of the line changes your life fundamentally, giving freedom to do what makes you happy, forever.
  2. Once you cross it, it matters little how far past it you go. $100m versus $10m is a different lifestyle, but nowhere near as critical as crossing the line.
- Implication: it almost didn't matter what the offer was, so long as it was big enough to cross the line.

chunks.heading: The Box Game: why not wait for a bigger exit
chunks.text:
- The common argument against selling: the company was growing 100% year over year and profitable, so waiting a year would double revenue and make it "six times more valuable" (assuming a 3x revenue valuation, his 2009 ballpark for a growing software company).
- Jason's counter is the Box Game:
  - Box A holds $10. Box B has a 50% chance of $20 and a 50% chance of nothing. Most people pick B, because the stakes are trivial and it's more exciting.
  - Change it: Box A holds $10,000,000. Box B has a 50% chance of $20,000,000 and 50% of nothing. You pick A.
- The two boxes are statistically equal. The choice measures your attitude toward risk, not math or intelligence.
- Rule: a chance of moving further is not worth giving up certainty of a life-altering event, namely crossing the Freedom Line.

chunks.heading: Evidence the risk was real: the 2008 crash
chunks.text:
- Jason says the economic crash in 2008 made the correctness of his choice "painfully clear." Holding out for "another year and far more money" would have meant finding an empty box.
- He cites a case he knows firsthand (company unnamed), offered a deal at the same time as him:
  - The founder wanted to roll the dice and delayed the buyer.
  - Two quarters passed and revenue failed to grow, so the buyer cancelled the deal.
  - Months later, with a recession in sight, the founder went back willing to take a low offer. The buyer refused.
- He points to other founders who passed on a deal in 2007 and sold for a fraction of it in 2012.
- He adds that running a company can get very hard in the later years, and that most founders are in his position rather than a "King" one.

chunks.heading: What the sale bought him
chunks.text:
- Since December 2007 he has the freedom to work on any project he wants for the rest of his life.
- He no longer worries about bills, debt, housing, or paying for any college his daughter chooses.
- He can stay home with his wife and new baby girl as long as he wants.
- His summary on money: they say it can't buy time and memories, but "in the sense of securing that freedom, it can."
- He notes that 100% of the negative reactions to the sale ("sell-out," "how could you sell your baby") came from people who had never started a company.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jason Cohen argues the top way to raise revenue is learning why the 99.9% of prospects who look but don't buy walk away, not talking only to existing customers. He lists eleven low-effort tactics, such as optional download forms, paying for lost-sale interviews, uninstaller surveys, and free licenses in exchange for feedback sessions.

chunks.heading: Get feedback from lost sales, not from the customers who already bought
chunks.text: Jason argues the number one way to raise revenue is learning why people check out the product but don't buy. Adding features, polishing the website and even talking to existing customers are all weaker. Existing customers "bought in spite of your faults"; the 99.9% of potential customers who didn't buy are the ones who can tell you what blocks sales. In his 2009 essay he lists 11 ways to gather this data, most doable in under a day.

chunks.heading: Collect emails before downloads and run an opt-in newsletter
chunks.text:
- Jason adds a short, optional form before a download, eBook or whitepaper so he can follow up. Objection: forms reduce downloads. At Smart Bear, adding the form had "no impact in the number of downloads. None."
- If a hundred people download in silence and don't buy, "it doesn't matter that they downloaded."
- Follow-up matters because, in his experience, about half of trial downloaders never started the trial, about half got stuck and stopped silently, and about half don't realize you're a friendly small company that wants them to succeed.
- Asking non-buyers "why" often gets answers.
- He recommends an honest, opt-in, no-spam newsletter list even if you have no time or content yet, since someone will want it later. Most people on such lists aren't paying customers, so it gives you reasons to ping interested non-buyers.
- Newsletter ideas: praise new release features, a tip about a lesser-known feature, a customer success story, an article about you or why services like yours are valuable, a partnership announcement, a time-limited coupon, or an offer to demo when you're in their city.

chunks.heading: Pay non-buyers for 15 minutes of feedback
chunks.text:
- Find contact info for people who trialed but didn't buy and offer something free if they talk for 15 minutes about why.
- At Smart Bear the company gave $2010 to Wikipedia, $5 at a time, as the incentive. He calls it "amazingly successful."
- Incentive options: cool stuff that does good for the world (e.g. something from Etsy), a charity donation ($25 to Kiva, Wikimedia Foundation or Free Software Foundation), a $25 Amazon coupon, company swag (T-shirt, mug, mousepad), or desirable unrelated items (an XKCD cartoon calendar, Despair posters).
- Worth $25 at least, probably $50. Run it until you hear the same things repeatedly, or budget $1000 and run until it's gone.

chunks.heading: Interview one existing customer about the buying experience
chunks.text:
Existing customers can't explain why others don't buy, but they can describe the trial and purchase process. Carve out at least 15 minutes (a customer discovery call is a good excuse) and ask:

- How did they hear about you? (shows which marketing sources deserve more spend)
- What website information convinced them to download? (shows which messages matter; make buried ones obvious and use them in ads)
- What was the main reason they bought? (their primary pain point, to put on the home page and ads)
- What part of the trial was confusing or difficult? (where others probably drop out)

chunks.heading: Mine testimonials for the real reasons customers buy
chunks.text:
- Testimonials are marketing material and also reveal the real pain you solve and the actual impact on customers' lives.
- Check whether what customers highlight is obvious to new website visitors and trial users. If customers don't mention something you thought was great, reconsider whether it matters. "Listen to your customers' point of view, not yours. Listen to their stories, not your vision."
- Example: a Siemens program manager said Code Collaborator "was like someone broke the ice in our group" and that people "came out of our cubes and actually talked to each other." It says nothing about features or competitors; it's about a social change from isolation to collaboration. That is reflected in the product tagline: "When code review is easy and fun, it actually gets done."

chunks.heading: Add in-product feedback hooks: uninstaller, Help menu link, quit prompt
chunks.text:
- Uninstaller: ask why they didn't buy. People like giving opinions; a WindowTabs founder said it was "eye-opening." Firefox even asks when you cancel an install. Most responses are empty or "You suck," but some are "gold."
- Don't build custom forms. Pop open an email client or a web form. Add an optional field: "If you'd like to be notified when we address the problems you've raised, put your email address here."
- Link or Help menu item: use human wording like "Complain" or "Yell at us"; plain "Feedback" is too corporate. At Smart Bear a sizable share of all feedback email came from this link, and it takes about an hour to add. No proxy servers or complex forms needed; open a Contact Us page or the email client.
- A prompt on exit during a trial is no worse than any other buy-now box but has more upside (suggestion credited to Keith of Redcort).

chunks.heading: Trade free software for reviews or feedback sessions
chunks.text:
- Free copies for reviews give both feedback and publicity. Bad publicity isn't a big risk: if the product is dead on arrival, nobody writes about it, because "I couldn't get it installed" isn't an interesting article. Mixed but detailed reviews can make people more likely to try a product than pure rave reviews. Small bloggers are the most willing to help; even one with 17 RSS subscribers gives useful feedback.
- For trial users who won't buy (the boss won't release money), give them the software free only if they get on the phone for 30 minutes about why. You lose no sale, since they weren't going to buy; the cost is unpaid tech support.
- Limit it (e.g. one free seat per company) and end the program once you've had about 10 meetings and know how to convert their peers. Recipients also tell friends, which is free publicity.

chunks.heading: Pitch locally and use public feedback boards
chunks.text:
- Pitch to a local startup, entrepreneur or user group. Even without great feedback, preparing the pitch forces you to rethink what's interesting about the product, which often reshuffles ideas on the home page and ads. A user group of potential customers is a friendly place to practice a sales pitch.
- UserVoice or GetSatisfaction (free or cheap) collect feedback and let people vote on each other's ideas. Allow anonymous responses so people aren't discouraged by account creation. At Smart Bear, hundreds of entries and comments and thousands of votes never required deleting anything, so moderation is easy.
- His closing advice: if you aren't getting data about lost sales daily, "you're in the dark." Even if you think you already know the answers, try it; being wrong could decide whether you build something people pay for.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Early-stage companies with a shaky v1.0 and downloads but few sales should stop coding and interview the people who left without buying. Cohen dismantles the common excuses (new feature, polish, I'm a user myself, it's marketing's job) and argues feedback from lost sales is the only real fix.

chunks.heading: Why people don't buy: talk to lost sales, not existing customers
chunks.text:
Jason says an early-stage company's core problem is "we don't have enough sales", usually shown as many downloads or signups with few purchases. This is the stage where v1.0 is shaky but should be more viable than it is, and the website copy is good enough to get people to sign up or download. He says the problem has one solution: get feedback from lost sales, which means empirical data rather than the founder's own theories about why people aren't buying.

- The people to talk to are those who found the site, read the copy, downloaded the product, and then "gave up without even an email".
- They are the low-hanging fruit, "in your grasp", and should be buying today.
- They have self-identified as the ideal customer, yet the product didn't deliver on the promises made.
- He cites Steve Johnson: "All the answers are outside the building." He also cites Eric Ries: "Not listening is the cardinal sin."
- He admits he used to hold the "I already know why" attitude himself, and says technical founders fight this advice hardest.

chunks.heading: Existing customers can't explain why others don't buy
chunks.text:
- Jason says to follow customer requests, especially early, but that existing customers only help increase the product's value.
- Customers bought in spite of the barriers to sale, so they can't identify those barriers.
- He calls using them to diagnose sales problems "classic survivor bias".
- The 98% of trial users who didn't buy hold the keys to more sales.

chunks.heading: "We need New Feature X" is almost never the answer
chunks.text:
- He says "this is almost never true" and challenges readers to find a successful v1.0 product that lacked obvious features.
- The world is full of successful v1.0 products without obvious features.
- He points to a post by Ben Yoskovitz on the "one more feature" fallacy.
- He quotes a Nintendo line: "the most important feature is the one no one asks for."
- If a founder has no evidence a new release will lift revenue, he asks why release it. The only draw is that it's different, and "more stuff" may not address why people download and then abandon.
- Until the founder can answer that with empirical data, there is no reason to expect the new features to be more compelling than the last ones.

chunks.heading: Don't wait for polish, and don't trust your own taste as a user
chunks.text:
- On cleaning up before seeking feedback: the first version of Smart Bear's code review product was so hard to decipher that he can't understand how it got customers. People used it "in spite" of the problems, not because of them.
- If you solve a genuine pain, people will try the software, complain, ask for features and engage. If that isn't happening, you're solving the wrong problem or not making it obvious, and that is critical to revenue.
- After a redesign you get used to it and are embarrassed by the old version. He concludes polish isn't important if you don't have enough revenue.
- Being a user yourself usually means you have 100 feature ideas, but "more features" is almost certainly not the problem. The vision is also almost certainly not how the company will unfold.
- Real impediments are often mundane. Examples he gives: new users see a blank screen and don't know what to do, so they abandon the trial; the installer fails under Vista, so people give up.
- Being a user is the worst position for judging the new-user experience, because you can't be objective or think like a user of below-average intelligence. He says "Most of your users are dumb; almost all are dumber than you are. You are not your typical user."

chunks.heading: Founders don't "just know" and can't hide in the code
chunks.text:
- On "Apple just knows what's cool": he calls it completely untrue and notes Steve Jobs specifically talks about getting feedback from customers.
- On "revenue is a marketing/sales function, I need to be heads-down in the code": he says in a startup it is everyone's job to get revenue.
- Day-to-day tasks can be divided between founders, since not everyone needs to write to bloggers or watch Twitter live-search.
- But if you don't know why people aren't buying, that is the number one bug and number one feature to work on.
- He says there are many ways to change the product or website in under a day to start fixing the problem.
- He says "it's marketing's job" really means "I'm not going to help get revenue", and calls that unacceptable.

chunks.heading: Follow-up resources Jason points to
chunks.text:
- He has posted eleven specific ways to get more feedback from lost sales, almost all taking less than a day to implement (longform.asmartbear.com/more-sales-customer-feedback/).
- He has described his system for creating questions and conducting customer interviews, which he says he used to build two unicorns (longform.asmartbear.com/customer-development/).
- His closing line is "So you have no excuse."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: A satirical essay that applies social media marketing rules to kindergarten to expose their absurdity. It implicitly critiques forced authenticity, content-formula thinking, daily posting for top-of-mind, how-to eBooks from the already-popular, transactional compliments, and monetizing attention too early. Mostly humor with little direct actionable advice.

chunks.heading: Social media marketing advice fails when applied literally in kindergarten
chunks.text:
Jason's essay "If Kindergarten were like Social Media Marketing" (2009) satirizes common social media marketing rules by applying them to five-year-olds. Each rule is shown to break once the social context it depends on is removed. The essay ends with the question "OK, class, what have we learned?" and leaves the answer to the reader.

- **The format:** a bulleted list of kindergarten scenarios, each mapping to one piece of conventional social media advice.
- **Implied point:** these rules are repeated as universal truths, but they only work (if at all) in specific contexts, and following them mechanically produces absurd or counterproductive outcomes.

chunks.heading: "Be authentic" does not mean disclose everything
chunks.text:
The essay links to Jason's separate piece "Authentic is Dead". In the satire, a teacher gives a "stern lecture on the value of being authentic." Richard Neuman then admits he pooed his pants at recess and buried the evidence under the blue slide.

- His bravery is "not met with the loving acceptance the teacher had promised."
- The joke: radical transparency has real social costs, and the audience does not owe you the acceptance that the advice promises.
- The lesson for marketers: honesty is not the same as indiscriminate disclosure, and the promise that openness will be rewarded is often false.

chunks.heading: Headline formulas make boring content sound like marketing
chunks.text:
The teachers explain that "What I did on summer vacation" doesn't grab attention. They propose three headline patterns instead:

- **Actionable:** "Five ways to have fun on summer vacation"
- **Provocative:** "Why waterparks are more dangerous than you think"
- **Personally relatable:** "What Dora the Explorer won't tell you about summer vacation"

These are the standard blog-title formulas (list posts, contrarian claims, tie-ins to something the audience already knows). Applying them to a child's honest essay shows how formulaic and hollow they can be when the content has no substance behind them.

chunks.heading: Posting frequency as a rule: "stay top-of-mind"
chunks.text:
In the satire, children are told to make at least one drawing or painting every day. The reasoning: "Refrigerator art goes stale quickly and you want to stay top-of-mind with your parents."

- This mocks the advice to publish constantly to remain visible.
- The implication is that frequency for its own sake has diminishing returns. A daily drawing is less valued by parents than an occasional one.

chunks.heading: Publishing "how to be popular" advice does not make you popular or help others
chunks.text:
Rachel Davis, "the most popular girl in class," writes an eBook explaining how other kids can get popular too.

- It is "well received from pre-K through third grade."
- It contains "clear examples and actionable advice."
- Yet "somehow the unpopular kids still never get invited to the cool kids' slumber parties."

The point: advice from someone who already has an audience is not transferable to people who lack one. Her popularity came from something other than the tactics in the book, so the book teaches readers little about how to replicate it. This parodies authors with large followings who sell guides on building a following.

chunks.heading: Flattery and relationship-building tactics backfire when they are transparent
chunks.text:
Bobby Gray learns that "making nice comments about people helps forge relationships," so he compliments the entire kickball team.

- Result: "He is denied the coveted spot and earns the nickname 'Bobby Bootlicker.'"
- The lesson: mass, indiscriminate compliments read as manipulation. Relationship-building tactics applied as a mechanical routine are recognized as such.

chunks.heading: Follower counts versus real relationships, and monetizing the wrong way
chunks.text:
Two further scenarios cover audience size and revenue.

- **Friends versus followers:** Children are told that having a lot of friends matters less than having a few genuine friends who will play with you "even after you throw up all over the good blocks in front of the whole entire class." They agree in principle, but Patrick "still cries when he gets only three stickers in his Valentine's Day booklet." The satire: people say quality beats quantity, yet still feel and respond to the raw count.
- **Monetization:** Genevieve Morrow puts Google ads on her finger paintings, "but they don't generate enough cash to cover her candy necklace habit." She only makes real money by "converting her afternoon lemonade stand to resell WordPress Themes to second graders looking to enhance their personal brand." The point: ad revenue on content rarely pays, and the money in social media is often made by selling tools and services to other people trying to do social media (a business that sells to people trying to build an audience, rather than the content itself).

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jason argues that early-stage founders hurt themselves by posing as big, "professional" companies. Your next sale is an Early Adopter, not Lockheed Martin, so your public persona should be human, specific, and small-team, which attracts the customers who will actually help you build the right product.

chunks.heading: Early adopters are the only customers a tiny company can win first
chunks.text:
Jason's core claim is that a pre-traction company should not try to look big. His next sale will not be "a 1000-seat order from Lockheed Martin", and he tells founders to repeat that line. He says he has sold software to every size of company, from indie hackers to IBM to Lockheed Martin.

- Today's product is a "shaky version one-dot-oh" with undiscovered bugs.
- It is "missing 90% of the features" big companies require.
- It has no case studies, no proper manual, no ROI model and no large, referenceable customer.
- That makes it a mismatch for big enterprises, but a perfect match for Early Adopters.

chunks.heading: Who Early Adopters are and why they buy from a small company
chunks.text:
Early Adopters want to live on the bleeding edge.

- They like new technology even if it is buggy, and don't mind "a hundred bugs so long as they get fixed fast".
- They like small companies where they have a personal relationship with the founders, get lots of attention, and see their ideas implemented quickly.
- They want to be involved in the process.
- They take the risk because new technology can help them beat competitors, through features only they have, distribution channels they can win in, or another competitive advantage.
- Most companies won't take risks for any reason, so Early Adopters are a winning niche for founders willing to serve them.

Jason's example is Tom, a customer. At Smart Bear he had ten or twenty Early Adopters like him before the product was stable and rich enough to attract bigger companies.

chunks.heading: Why Early Adopters are what a young company needs
chunks.text:
This is the stage when the company needs help building the right product. It doesn't need people who download, get discouraged and never call back. It needs "a chatty Cathy who wants to dive in and help out."

His conclusion is to define the ideal customer persona tightly around the people who love the company as it is today, because that is where it will succeed.

chunks.heading: The mistake: acting like a big company in public
chunks.text:
Jason made this mistake himself before he had a single customer. He believed he had to look like a "real company":

- culture-neutral language
- stock photos of cheerful coworkers around a laptop
- standard marketing-speak

His original About page said Smart Bear was "the leading provider of enterprise version control data-mining tools" whose Code Historian software was used "for risk-analysis, root-cause discovery, and software development decision-support." He admits he wasn't sure what "leading provider" or "data mining" even meant there.

He says the fear that looking small loses sales is backwards: the big-company persona alienates the best customers, the Early Adopters.

chunks.heading: What the small-company persona looks like
chunks.text:
His replacement About copy was: "Hi, I'm Jason and I built an inexpensive tool for visualizing what's in your version control system. It's useful for answering questions like 'When was the last time we changed this file?' Check it out and tell me what sucks!"

The persona should signal to Early Adopters: a cool new company with a fresh product and attitude, a product rough around the edges but ripe for feedback and collaboration, a company that is small today but thinking big. His checklist:

- **Show you understand her pain.** Don't use content-free phrases like "Provide the ability to quickly and easily do XYZ so you can go back to accomplishing high-value tasks."
- **Come across as a passionate small team that wants to make a difference,** not a big, established, safe company.
- **Display your phone number and Twitter account on the home page** instead of hiding behind "Contact Us" forms.
- **Promote real things:** forums, a blog, and a weekly all-customer virtual meeting where everyone gives feedback. Don't promote features and benefits you haven't implemented yet.
- **Be specific and meaningful, be human, be yourself.** His closing line: "Stop hiding."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jason Cohen argues that learning only from successes is a deep statistical trap. Using WWII bomber armor, the file-drawer effect, ESP experiments, and Good to Great, he shows how business advice may be luck dressed up as insight, and says to prefer advice that makes you think.

chunks.heading: Survivor bias makes most business advice unreliable
chunks.text:
- Jason argues that learning only from successful founders is a deeper problem than people realize. Success stories are the "survivors," and the failures that hold equally valid (and perhaps more instructive) lessons go unseen.
- He asks whether "failure could contain more lessons than success."
- His working test for any advice: what would the failures who did the same things look like?

chunks.heading: The bullet-hole planes: the data is in what's missing
chunks.text:
- In WWII, English engineers mapped bullet holes on returning bombers. Hits clustered on the wings, tail and rear gunner's station, with few in the cockpit or fuel tanks.
- The tempting conclusion is to armor where the holes are. Jason says that is wrong: planes hit in the cockpit or fuel tanks never made it home. Holes on returning planes mark spots that are "by definition relatively benign."
- The real data is in the planes that were shot down.
- Definition he gives: survivor bias is "drawing conclusions only from data that is available or convenient and thus systematically biasing your results."
- Business application: you read about successes, but the businesses that "never made it home" are invisible.

chunks.heading: The file-drawer effect: invisible evidence
chunks.text:
- Journals publish extraordinary results, so statistically insignificant studies get abandoned or stowed away. This is called the "file-drawer effect," and it is insidious because it is invisible.
- He quotes Peter Norvig: when a paper says "this could only happen by chance one in twenty times," similar experiments may have been run twenty times without being published.
- Pharma example: more than two-thirds of studies of anti-depressants given to depressed children found no better than sugar pills, but companies published only the positive trials.
- Business application: Harvard Business School case studies include only success stories.
- His Starbucks test: "what if twenty other coffee shops had the same ideas, same product, and same dedication as Starbucks, but failed?" That would change what we can learn from Starbucks.

chunks.heading: The Margaret coin-flip: finding a winner in a crowd proves nothing
chunks.text:
- Rhine's 1930s ESP experiments screened 500 people on a 25-card Zener deck, re-tested the high scorers, and treated the one repeat passer as evidence of genuine ESP.
- Jason's analogy: put 1000 people in a room to flip a coin ten times. One woman, Margaret, gets ten heads, a 1-in-1024 chance for her specifically.
- But the experiment was "let 1000 people flip and find Margaret in the crowd." The chance that somebody flips ten heads is about 62%.
- When many people attempt a feat, normally unlikely events will happen, so Margaret's result says nothing about her abilities.
- Applied to himself: three consecutive successful companies might just mean he is the one in the crowd who guessed right three times, with no reason to believe a fourth would succeed.
- 2023 note: he has since done it a fourth time with WP Engine (200,000 customers, hundreds of millions in ARR, profitable). He says he "still wouldn't change a word" and may still be Margaret. He allows that he may have earned "additional benefit of the doubt," but the warning remains.

chunks.heading: Evidence from business books: Good to Great and In Search of Excellence
chunks.text:
- Steven Levitt (Freakonomics) tested this directly. *Good to Great* analyzed eleven companies that went from mediocre to stock-market stars, concluding the common trait was a "culture of discipline."
- Fannie Mae, one of the eleven, collapsed as Levitt read the book. Circuit City, also extolled, went bankrupt.
- An investment in the eleven companies in 2001, when the book came out, would have underperformed the S&P 500.
- Jason's critique of the method: the author combed 1435 companies and picked eleven, which is "the ESP experiment all over again." The book also never asked whether the other 1424 companies showed a "culture of discipline" too, since that may be common regardless of performance.
- Levitt found the same effect in *In Search of Excellence* (1980s).
- Levitt's point, which Jason endorses: these books are backward-looking but implicitly promise the principles will keep working. To the extent that doesn't hold, it "calls into question the basic premise of these books."
- Jason still loves *Good to Great* because he thinks its ideas are "timeless and excellent."

chunks.heading: How to treat advice, including his own
chunks.text:
- Jason admits his own advice may suffer from this: he did not start Smart Bear with a fixed philosophy, a fixed customer or even fixed products. His philosophy is post-hoc and might be "survivor bias."
- He raises the possibility that he is like Rhine, convinced of "objective measures of success" while living in "an egotistical, possibly even narcissistic dream world."
- Readers cannot fully verify whether any advice suffers from this. Simply being aware of survivor bias makes you less likely to be taken in.
- Practical filter: prefer advice that
  - makes you think rather than giving answers,
  - forces you to answer tough questions,
  - helps you extend your existing strengths,
  - helps you become a better version of the person you already are.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jason Cohen uses a Darwinian analogy (the sterile mule) to argue that virality needs "grandchildren": content your followers want to repeat, not just consume. He recommends making retransmission frictionless by writing the share text for people, but admits the real driver is genuinely remarkable content.

chunks.heading: Virality needs a message that gets repeated, not just read (the "mule" test)
chunks.text:
Jason argues "survival of the fittest" is an incomplete reading of Darwin. His example is the mule: it survives, eats and avoids predators, but it is sterile, so it is a genetic dead end ("Mule == Evolution Fail"). The better definition of fitness is "children who themselves make the fittest children."

- Applied to sharing, a message is not viral because your direct followers (the children) find it interesting.
- It is viral when those followers want to repeat it to their own audience (the grandchildren), so a chain reaction continues.
- He frames the contest as competing for attention instead of food. A link "goes viral" when it is being retransmitted (retweeted) more often than it dies (not retweeted).
- He dislikes the phrase "going viral" itself, comparing it to "a one-night stand without protection" and a self-fulfilling prophecy.

chunks.heading: The chain letter shows the mechanism: the message itself demands retransmission
chunks.text:
Jason points to the chain letter as the original viral message. It spread not because you sent it to ten people, but because it required each recipient to do the same.

- His takeaway: "The message itself needs to suggest retransmission."
- The message must contain the instruction or invitation to pass it on. Hoping people share it is not enough.

chunks.heading: Ask for the retweet explicitly, and write the retweet for them
chunks.text:
The simplest tactic is to ask outright. He contrasts a plain tweet of a link with the same tweet that says "please RT". Because most people retweet with the retweet button, the plea is preserved and carried to the next generation.

- Example tweet text he offers: "[Cool Tool, plz R/T!] Find out who's talking about your blog! http://LinksFor.Us"
- The ask has to be explicit, because without it the message does not suggest its own retransmission.

chunks.heading: Remove every barrier to sharing: do the thinking for your friends
chunks.text:
Jason uses a product launch example (v1.0 of a free blogger service, LinksFor.Us) to show how not to ask for help.

- Bad ask: "tell everyone you know and help me kick-start this. I'll buy you a beer." He says this "gives Francis work to do": what to post, how to say it in 140 characters, how much time to spend, and whether Francis is even sober.
- Better ask: "Tear down every barrier they have for retransmission. Do the thinking for them."
- Steps in the improved email:
  1. Frame the request as small: "just 60 seconds of your time."
  2. Supply a ready-made tweet.
  3. Supply ready-made text for an email or LinkedIn message, written so the recipient can paste it as-is (for example, "Hi! My friend Jason just released a new, free service for bloggers that shows who is talking about or linking to your blog posts.").
  4. Thank them in advance and offer a small thank-you (a beer).

chunks.heading: The real driver: content so good people want to spread it
chunks.text:
Jason admits that when his own posts went viral, it was not because of these techniques. It was because many people found the content "genuinely useful or entertaining or inspiring, or hopefully all of the above."

- His number one rule: "Have overwhelmingly awesome content." It should be so good that people intrinsically want to spread it. Then it is worth being smart about helping them do so.
- Evidence: the most popular YouTube videos (the most viral of all) are not company campaigns pushing a product or service, with music videos the exception. People shared them because they plainly liked them, not because of a crafted campaign.
- He has no formula for it: "What's the mechanistic formula for generating incredible, remarkable content? Ha ha, let me know when you find one."

chunks.heading: Being noticed is not being remarkable
chunks.text:
Jason endorses Seth Godin's distinction: "Being noticed is not the same as being remarkable. Running down the street naked will get you noticed, but it won't accomplish much. ... If you put it on a T-shirt, would people wear it?"

- Stunts that win attention do not necessarily earn the repeat sharing that drives a chain reaction.
- A useful test for virality is whether people would voluntarily attach their name to your message and pass it on.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jason Cohen argues that a bootstrapped company consumes all available time, and that maximizing the chance of success means putting work before health and family for a period. He frames it as a deliberate, time-boxed tradeoff best made when you have few dependents and enough savings, not a lifelong lifestyle.

chunks.heading: Startups consume all available time, so health and family get sacrificed
chunks.text:
- Jason's thesis: "Maximizing your chance for success means sacrificing health and family." He says this applies to small, bootstrapped companies, and he frames it as a trade-off to accept knowingly, not as a lifestyle to recommend.
- He admits that more hours do not automatically mean more output. Studies show an under-slept, foggy brain is not offset by extra hours, and optimizing how you spend time can multiply productivity several times over, which hours alone cannot match.
- He still holds that the path to success in a tiny company runs through sacrifice.
- He cites examples of founders who paid physically and personally: Jeremiah Owyang (out of shape, stressed, bad sleep, high blood pressure), Mark Cuban (slept on a couch or floor, seven years without a vacation, "I was focused") and Penelope Trunk (always sick, "There's no time for family").
- He dismisses the objection "many workaholics succeed, but that's not the only path" by pointing out the structural problem: the work never runs out.

chunks.heading: The "Rule of Time in Startups": a bootstrapped company takes all of it
chunks.text:
- Jason compares it to the "Rule of Closets": the stuff you own expands to fill all available closet space, and adding shelves just reveals you have more stuff.
- His version: "How much time does a bootstrapped company take? All of it."
- Even ten people could hardly keep up with everything in small business. His list: creating, consulting, designing, fixing, self-promotion, blogging, networking, bookkeeping, taxes, customer support and cultivation, and reading startup blogs for ideas.
- He adds the hidden time sinks, such as losing an afternoon troubleshooting an outsourced IP phone system that was supposed to let you "work from anywhere."
- With one, two or three people, "of course it takes all your time." The same holds for someone running a startup on the side of a day job, who has no time to exercise or play with kids before bed.

chunks.heading: Obsession, not passion, is what makes a small company go
chunks.text:
- He says: "It takes obsession to make a little company go. Forget 'passion'... it's 'obsession.'"
- The distinction: passion means you love working; obsession means you cannot stop working.
- You put your entire self on the line: finances, career and ideas.
- The obsession persists away from the office, at lunch with a friend or reading to your kids. His wife pointed out in the early years of Smart Bear that his "mental and emotional bandwidth" was entirely consumed. "You're physically there, but you're not really there."
- He calls the pattern "self-destructive devotion" and says you don't go through "this meat grinder" because you merely "like something a lot." His line: "If you love it so much, why don't you marry it?" "Exactly."

chunks.heading: Accept the penalty deliberately, and time it to your life stage
chunks.text:
- Jason concedes that the work-life-balance advice from life coaches is correct as a way to live your whole life. His point is that you must decide whether it is OK to incur the penalty right now.
- His own timing: he did it in his 20s with no kids, enough savings to risk everything for a while, and a wife who ran her own business and so understood the workload and why he spaced out at dinner.
- Conditions that made it workable for him: no dependents, financial runway, and a spouse who understood.
- His bottom line: "Every successful bootstrapper I know puts work before self." He adds the qualifier "until financial freedom is achieved," meaning the self-sacrifice phase ends once financial freedom is reached.
- He did the same himself.

chunks.heading: Context from the editor's note (written 15+ years later)
chunks.text:
- The essay dates from 2009, before the "Hustle Culture" label and before Lean Startup, and was somewhat controversial even then.
- Jason says he stands by the original claim: startups take all the time and take sacrifice.
- He rejects the way people interpret those ideas today, and does not endorse the modern "toxic hustle culture" reading.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jason argues that "small is risky" is backwards. Using Bingo Card Creator and Balsamiq as examples, he shows a tiny, focused niche with a strong customer need keeps growing in a recession, while a venture-funded company chasing a hot market is more fragile. A goal of $200k-$1M/year removes most failure risks.

chunks.heading: Why small, focused startups survive recessions ("too small to fail")
chunks.text:
Jason argues that a startup aiming at a small, focused niche can keep growing through a recession, because small removes the risks that kill big, funded companies.

Evidence he cites (2009):
- Bingo Card Creator (Patrick McKenzie, one-man company, launched 2006) just had its biggest month ever. February, March and April 2009 were its three biggest months since inception.
- Balsamiq Studios (UI mock-up product) netted $162k in its first year, 2008. It took in $35k in the first week of April 2009 alone.
- His label for both: "too small to fail."

chunks.heading: The condition: small niche, strong need, happy customers
chunks.text:
- Jason's formula: if the niche is small enough, the customer need strong enough, the marketing targeted enough, the product good enough and the customers happy enough, they will buy, recession or not.
- He admits it is a lot of "if"s, but argues it can work.

chunks.heading: Match the goal to the size: $200k to $1M a year, not $100M
chunks.text:
- Aiming to sell $100,000,000 of software a year will almost certainly fail. It takes years, many people you haven't hired, a massive market, beatable competitors, and probably debt or investors. A down economy could be the undoing.
- Aiming to run a smaller successful business, happy at $1,000,000/year or even $200,000/year, makes many problems fall away.
- He says "when you just need to be Ramen-profitable," you can do it even in a recession.
- "Prevailing wisdom is that 'small is risky.' It's just the opposite."

chunks.heading: Marketing is cheap in a small market
chunks.text:
- You don't need a big budget to get noticed. You know where customers gather: forums, blogs, community sites, influencers, local groups.
- You know the AdWords keywords and they're easy to optimize (he points to Patrick's AdWords optimization write-up).
- It takes time, not a lot of money, to participate and get noticed.

chunks.heading: Become the world expert of the niche
chunks.text:
In a small market you can build:
- The most popular blog and most frequented forum.
- The best collection of how-tos and the most comprehensive eBook.
- The simplest yet most complete software.
- Jason's own example: the most popular paperback book on a subject, 50,000 copies and counting.

chunks.heading: Competitors are manageable
chunks.text:
- Competitors are easy to find, track and analyze. They may be weak, or there may be room for several winners.
- You may never meet an 800-lb gorilla, because the addressable market is too small for it to be profitable. His example: "Microsoft isn't going to make a Bingo-card creator."
- A competitor starting now will be far behind; if you keep moving they won't catch up.

chunks.heading: Delight customers one by one
chunks.text:
- You can build fans and cheerleaders who will buy everything you make and spread the word (the "1,000 true fans" idea).
- You can quickly collect testimonials that sell better than any brochure.
- His advice: "just be yourself."

chunks.heading: Why recessions hit small markets less
chunks.text:
- Customers have a strong need, not a passing interest.
- Existing customers have a personal relationship with you and will go out of their way to help you succeed.
- Because you're small, 99.99% of your customers are still in your future, so there are always new customers to find.
- Small also opens options that incumbents can't compete with.
- His closing wager: in a year, who survives, Balsamiq or a company with $30m paid-in capital that "wasn't profitable even before the recession" but has "amazing growth potential in a hot market"? And "whose founders are more likely to put $1m cash in their pocket over the next few years?" His summary question: "what's wrong with small?"

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jason Cohen argues that listing brand adjectives like "fast, easy, scalable, robust" destroys believability. Authentic values are demonstrated through concrete actions (return policies, answering the phone, real testimonials), and only after you walk the walk have you earned the right to call it out.

chunks.heading: Show, don't tell: authentic values come from actions, not adjective lists
chunks.text:
Jason argues that a company's values are communicated through what it does, not through the adjectives it lists in marketing copy.

- "The cardinal rule of authenticity and believability is that actions speak louder than words."
- Corollary: if you have to tell someone something is true, they automatically don't believe you. An honest person doesn't walk around asking "Hey, did you know I'm honest?"
- Values are "the reason for your actions, the theme behind your words, and the underlying consistency in how you do business", not words to be shoe-horned into tag-lines or stapled onto disingenuous mission statements.
- The rule applies to customer service, the website, how you sell, and even how you hire, not just to commercials.

chunks.heading: Why adjective lists and "Mad Libs" copy backfire
chunks.text:
Jason criticizes the common marketing exercise of listing every adjective you want customers to associate with the company or product.

- He cringes at the size and scope of such lists. The bigger problem comes when the marketing department "plays Mad Libs" with them.
- His example is Sun GlassFish Enterprise Server copy: "easy to use, fast, and scalable ... easy to download, develop, and deploy ... robust, highly-available, and cost-effective." He calls it *prima facie* false.
- His test: have you ever used a system that embodied every one of those attributes, with no trade-offs, no compromise, A-plus-plus on every count? No.
- Result: the reader doesn't know which claims are true, so they distrust all of them, and nothing tangible has been communicated.

chunks.heading: The actor's "motivation" analogy
chunks.text:
Jason compares company values to a character's motivation in acting.

- A character's motivation is the secret reason she is angry, depressed or indifferent. Actors often invent a detailed back-story for how the character got to this point.
- You don't publish the back-story. His example: you don't announce "Darth Vader is disillusioned with the notion of a Republic." "Explanation ruins everything!"
- Applied to business: values should drive visible behavior and consistency, not be explained out loud.

chunks.heading: Apple as the model of demonstrating values without words
chunks.text:
Jason says Apple has mastered conveying values without stating them.

- Apple's values include "design is paramount," "form over function," and even "Apple is cool."
- An iPod wouldn't be cool because a corporation claimed it was, and listing features and benefits wouldn't convey it either.
- Apple's iPod commercial instead shows the product and the feeling. He contrasts this with how "standard" marketing machinery would portray the same features and benefits.

chunks.heading: Replace claims with proof: action versus slogan pairs
chunks.text:
Jason gives concrete swaps where a policy or behavior replaces a claim.

- High-quality product: don't say "Your satisfaction is important to us"; have a 90-day no-questions-asked return policy.
- Caring about talking to customers: don't play a recorded message saying their call is important; simply answer the phone.
- Customers love you: don't say "100 companies use our software"; have a web page with 100 stellar testimonials.
- Treating employees as human beings: don't call them "resources" (he links this to his argument that labels matter); mock companies that do, and display testimonials from your own employees.

chunks.heading: Once you walk the walk, you can call it out
chunks.text:
Jason says that after the behavior is real, you have earned the right to mention it, and the words then work because they point at something tangible.

- Quality: "We're so confident in the quality of our hammer, if ever breaks we'll swap it out with a brand-new replacement. For free!"
- Service: "At MyCo, a human being always answers the phone. Why? Because business is personal."
- Social proof: "Don't take our word for it, read for yourself what our customers say. Did we pick the best ones? Well yeah, but we have 100 'best ones!'"
- Culture, from Fog Creek: "What if programmers were treated like rock stars? ... management, not coding, is the support function. ... people love working here."
- The underlying values are still words like quality, service, happy customers and great place to work, but they appear as tangible demonstrations, not trite phrases plastered in all the expected places.

chunks.heading: Takeaway: values are the means, not the end
chunks.text:
- "Let values motivate action. Values are the means to the end. Get to the end."
- "Actions count; words don't."
- Practical test for any claim in copy: can you replace it with a policy, a behavior, or evidence the customer can see?

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jason Cohen tells how an early customer, Tom, put up with a buggy first product and drove a big enterprise order because Jason was honest about being a one-person shop. Early adopters want to take part in building the product, and pretending to be bigger than you are loses the people who would have loved you as you are.

chunks.heading: Honesty about being small wins early customers
chunks.text:
- Jason argues customers forgive honest mistakes from earnest people, not from "stolid, cold, inhuman corporations."
- In Smart Bear's first year his code review software was buggy, yet early customers were fiercely loyal.
- He ties that loyalty to honesty about who he really was: a company of one.
- "Truth is such a rare thing, it is delightful to tell it." (Emily Dickinson, which he quotes approvingly)

chunks.heading: The Tom story: a customer who knew Jason was a one-man shop
chunks.text:
- Tom, a customer at a large company with thousands of employees and billions in revenue, phoned Jason. Jason notes software developers rarely call anyone.
- Tom had spent six weeks sending real bug reports. He debugged a lot of Jason's code himself, with help from his own employees.
- Tom then listed 20 new features he wanted. On timing he said: "Oh, I know you're just a one-man shop, so just do your best. If you get through this half as fast as you get through bugs, we'll be fine."
- Jason always wrote "we" and used support@smartbear.com, never his own name. Tom still figured it out from the writing style and from always reaching only Jason on the main line.
- Jason had been told big companies don't buy from one-man shops. He nearly gave the defensive line that he used consultants when workload rose (which wasn't true) and nearly started pitching service quality.
- He decided that would insult Tom's intelligence and set the relationship back. Tom was effectively saying: "I know who you really are, and I accept it. I still want to do this."
- Jason chose to match that honesty.

chunks.heading: Why Tom put up with so much: customers who become heroes
chunks.text:
- Jason visited Tom in Ottawa to meet two of Tom's bosses about a widespread purchase and roll-out of the peer code review tool.
- Tom introduced Jason as a small Austin company he found half a year earlier and had been guiding so the tool "now works perfectly for our environment." Tom also claimed he did sixty code reviews every day.
- The bosses checked Tom's evidence and approved the roll-out, which became a big order for Jason.
- Jason's conclusion: "Tom was a hero." Tom got fewer bugs in delivered code and trained new hires faster, not by buying from IBM or adopting a process from Dr. Dobbs, but by finding a small company and directing its product.
- Tom put up with screens locking up, reviews disappearing, installers installing the wrong files and occasional out-of-memory crashes.
- Jason says Tom tolerated it because:
  - It was just him and Jason.
  - He knew Jason always kept his word.
  - He could stick his neck out for Smart Bear without being let down.
  - Jason would keep the product solving his problems as it changed.
- Tom pinned his reputation on the product and won, and lived vicariously through Smart Bear as a product designer.
- Jason adds that if he hadn't owned up and behaved honestly, none of this might have happened.

chunks.heading: Who your first hundred customers really are
chunks.text:
- Jason says the first hundred won't be big companies with bureaucratic purchasing that you bluff through, or well-known consumer-advocacy bloggers.
- They will be early adopters: people who like trying new things, like working with new companies that still have spark and something to prove, want to be part of the creative process, and want to say they were there at the beginning.
- If you pretend to be something you're not, they'll see through it.
- The cost: "You've lied to those who would have loved you for who you are," which is not how you build a relationship.
- He links this to targeting your ideal customer persona.

chunks.heading: Honesty is a small-company advantage
chunks.text:
- Jason is clear it doesn't mean never telling a lie. Authenticity doesn't mean abandoning social white lies; there is a business equivalent of "No those pants don't make you look fat."
- He says honesty should in theory be easier, quoting Mark Twain: "if you tell the truth you don't have to remember anything."
- In practice, businesses are accustomed to "fluffing your feathers and putting on a show," so acting like a normal human being takes effort.
- "Be yourself" is as hard in business as in personal life, but worth it.
- He calls this one of the few advantages small companies have over big ones: "Use it."
- Context he gives: this happened before "relationship" became a marketing buzzword, before blogs and Twitter.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jason Cohen gives a simple, statistically sound formula for judging A/B tests: take half the gap between winner and loser (D) and the total trials (N), and the result is significant only if D² > N. Small samples can't detect modest differences, so test radically different variants rather than tweaks.

chunks.heading: A/B tests need a simple significance check, not a tool's say-so
chunks.text:
Jason argues that A/B testing tools often use misleading or incorrect math about whether a result is "statistically significant." He offers a simple, mathematically sound formula you can run yourself. The cost of guessing wrong is real:
- Wait too long between tests and you waste time.
- Don't wait long enough, and you "think" a variant is better. You then build new variants on that false assumption, a wild goose chase.
- The correct move after an inconclusive test is usually to come up with a completely new test.

He says human intuition is bad at this. People misjudge rare events and "can't distinguish between patterns and noise."

chunks.heading: The rule: D squared must exceed N
chunks.text:
For a two-variant test (AdWords clicks, conversions, or a hamster's choices):
1. Let N be the total number of trials (A plus B).
2. Let D be half the difference between the winner and the loser.
3. The result is statistically significant only if D² > N.

Examples he works through:
- **AdWords day one:** 31 clicks vs 19. N = 50, D = 6, D² = 36. Not bigger than 50, so not significant.
- **AdWords day two:** 62 vs 38. N = 100, D = 12, D² = 144. Significant.
- **Hammy the Hamster:** chose organic 8 times and conventional 4 times, "twice as often." N = 12, D = 2, D² = 4. Not significant.
- **6 clicks vs 1:** N = 7, D = 2.5, D² = 6.25. Inconclusive even though A beats B six to one. "With only a few data points, you really don't know anything yet."

chunks.heading: How big a gap you need at a given sample size
chunks.text:
Results are significant only if the ratio of winner to loser exceeds (√N + 2) / (√N − 2). Jason's figures:
- **N = 50:** the winner needs almost double the loser's clicks, e.g. a 10% vs 5% conversion rate. He says this is rare, so you can almost never find a significant test from 50 clicks.
- **N = 100:** the winner must be at least 50% higher than the loser.
- **N = 1800:** needed to detect a winner only 10% larger than the loser.

Small N means only big differences are detectable.

chunks.heading: Test big differences, not tweaks
chunks.text:
Because variants are often less than 10% apart (he cites "2.4% vs 2.2% conversion rate"), he draws these conclusions:
- "You need to be seeking big differences, not subtle ones."
- Test wildly different designs rather than tweaks. Tweaks can only be tested when N is enormous.
- If a test keeps running and still isn't significant, you aren't learning anything. The variants aren't meaningfully different for your readers, so it's time to try something new.
- Check the formula as the test accumulates data. The day-one AdWords result became significant on day two with the same proportions and double the volume.

chunks.heading: Where the formula comes from
chunks.text:
- The right test is Pearson's chi-squared, not the Student t-test. The t-test suits continuous, normally distributed variables; chi-squared suits categorical outcomes from independent trials, which is what an A/B test is.
- The null hypothesis is that results are due to chance alone, so the expected split is N/2 for each variant.
- For two variants the statistic simplifies to χ² = 4D²/N.
- At one degree of freedom, χ² must exceed 3.8 for 95% confidence and 6.6 for 99%.
- Jason picked 4 as a round threshold, giving D² > N.
- If D² is more than double N, you are well past 99% confidence.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jason Cohen argues that success is neither pure luck nor pure merit: good and bad luck swirl constantly, and what is not luck is how you use it. His practical answer is to treat every decision as an empirical test, measuring everything so you can keep what works and eject what doesn't.

chunks.heading: Luck is always present, but how you use it is not luck
chunks.text:
Jason argues that people who call his success "lucky" are being dismissive: the hours, the decisions and the product sense did not happen by accident. He also accepts that luck sits underneath every part of a business. His resolution is a distinction between luck and what you do with it.

- "Good luck and bad luck are constantly swirling around you. How you *use* it, is not luck."
- Success in business doesn't mean you "got lucky." It means you used luck: "taking advantage of the good, identifying and ejecting the bad."
- Jason says "both things can be true": the effort was real and luck buoyed it.
- He answers the "it was luck" line with the work behind Smart Bear:
  - 60-hour weeks with no pay for years, at the cost of his health.
  - Inventing a unique product in a market that didn't exist yet.
  - Cultivating relationships with the best customers and listening to their needs with a specific framework.
  - Negotiating a sale that put more money in his employees' pockets than any other job would have.

chunks.heading: Every decision at Smart Bear had both an intentional part and a lucky part
chunks.text:
Jason says he can pick any decision in Smart Bear's history and the same pattern appears: success tied to something intentional that also leveraged something lucky.

- Customers: he cultivated relationships with them, but it was lucky that customers showed up at all.
- Google Ads: they found him through ads, and he started right when AdWords were new and cheap. Everyone used Google, but AdWords weren't yet "saturated with garbage."
- Marketing: he chose "effective, brief marketing messages" with an "authentic voice," but he was lucky to have a mentor who had already taught him how.
- WP Engine, in a 2024 update (founded a year after this essay):
  - It became a unicorn about fourteen years later and is 100x larger than Smart Bear ever was.
  - It took a great idea, great execution and immense effort from thousands of people.
  - It also took luck: the WordPress market stayed healthy and fast-growing throughout.
  - The WordPress community gave the company the benefit of the doubt at first and supported it later.
  - He was able to hire many talented people.
  - Serious competitors took ten years to understand how big the market was.
- Even intentional choices rarely work first time. You have to "experiment and fail" before finding success. Pushing through is tenacity, but there is luck in how quickly you find success, whether you ever do, and whether you can tell the difference.

chunks.heading: Personal luck and privilege are tailwinds, not a reason to discount effort
chunks.text:
Beyond operational luck, Jason names personal luck, which many call "privilege" and Warren Buffett calls "winning the genetic lottery."

- He lists the components:
  - Being born in this era rather than the Middle Ages.
  - Being born in the US, "easily the most supportive place to start a company."
  - A stable household.
  - Certain talents, such as building software, problem-solving, tenacity and focus.
  - Ethnicity, gender and having all body parts in good working order.
- None of this negates the value or necessity of hard work and good choices. Neither can you ignore these tailwinds in the final equation of "success."

chunks.heading: Failure is mostly bad luck, but the response to it is a choice
chunks.text:
Jason applies the same lens to failures, using Smart Bear's advertising.

- Many marketing and advertising attempts flopped.
- Ads in certain magazines bombed. In some cases he spent many thousands of dollars, then a significant percentage of revenue, on ads that didn't net a single sale.
- An ad that fails utterly in one magazine after working in another is bad luck.
- The choice to cancel some ads and not others is not luck.
- Making sure individual print ads could be measured was also a choice. Without that, he says, "we wouldn't have been able to distinguish success from failure, and then indeed our destiny would be controlled by luck alone."
- 2024 note: every magazine he used to advertise in has gone out of business.

chunks.heading: Treat every decision as an empirical test
chunks.text:
Jason's practical conclusion is a way of operating that lets you capture good luck and shed bad luck.

- "Your best bet for success is to treat all your decisions as empirical tests."
- "Try anything, measure everything, and follow what works, even if that means changing everything."
- He says confidence and experimentation are not contradictory (he links this to "strong opinions, weakly held").
- Measurement is what separates luck from skill. If you can't tell which ad worked, luck controls your outcome. If you can, you keep winners and cut losers.

chunks.heading: Ask "how did you know" questions, not "what inspired it"
chunks.text:
Jason notes that luck rarely comes up when he talks to other entrepreneurs, who want stories, tips and how things work. He says they want to know how to think, not how to copy.

- The wrong question: "What inspired that idea?"
- The right question: "How did you know when an idea was right?"
- An even more specific version: "How does one know whether a print ad is working?"
- The useful lesson from a success story is the method for evaluating ideas, not the origin of the idea.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jason Cohen debunks the "1% better per day = 37x" idea and shows why a one-time 2-3x productivity gain is still achievable. Using an average-speed puzzle, he argues low-velocity activity (email, idle meetings, calendar management) drags down your average, so the lever is eliminating it, measured with a tool like RescueTime, not working harder.

chunks.heading: Why a "1% better per day" goal can't make Jason 37x more productive
chunks.text:
Jason rejects the Zappos COO's claim that improving 1% a day makes you "37x better" in a year. The compounding arithmetic is fine. His objection is that nobody can keep raising daily output by a full percent every day. Things "rarely compound like that, even at slow rates," and other factors overwhelm the simplistic idea.

- His push-up example: if you can do 1 push-up and improve 1% a day, you do 37 a day at the end of year one and 1,369 a day at the end of year two. "Yeah right."
- He calls the 37x claim "poppycock" and impossible.
- He argues that "2x better is possible", but it is a one-time doubling, not a repeating compounding rate.

chunks.heading: The speed puzzle: low-velocity time wipes out high-velocity gains
chunks.text:
Jason uses a drive-to-your-mother's-house puzzle to show why gains in your fast periods barely move your overall average.

- The setup: the house is 60 miles away. You hit traffic and average 30 mph over the first 30 miles, which takes an hour.
- The question: how fast must you drive the second half to average 60 mph for the whole trip? It is impossible. Averaging 60 mph requires covering all 60 miles in one hour, and that hour is already gone. Even at 1000 mph, the trip average stays under 60.
- Doubling your speed in the second half raises the trip average only from 30 to 40 mph.
- Quadrupling it raises the average only to 48 mph.
- His takeaway: "periods of low velocity wash away gains of high velocity."
- He says the same math applies to anything measured per hour: emails processed, code written, prose written, any "gettin' stuff done" per hour.

chunks.heading: Why productivity is stuck: half the day moves at 30 mph
chunks.text:
Jason says most people's day is full of low-velocity activity, and that is what holds the average down.

- Examples he gives: dealing with emails you didn't need to see, dawdling in a meeting that hasn't started, reading blogs, managing the calendar.
- "When half your day moves at 30 mph, it's impossible to make up the time during the other half."
- Even a 37x improvement in some areas might not make you 2x more productive overall, because the slow stuff drags the average down.
- This is also why the 1% idea fails: low-velocity time makes it too hard to improve even 1% overall, every day, for a year.

chunks.heading: The fix: eliminate the low-velocity work
chunks.text:
Jason's conclusion is to cut low-velocity activity instead of speeding up what you already do fast.

- "The thing to do is eliminate the low-velocity stuff."
- Learning to type faster is good, but cutting the time spent processing useless email may help more.
- To get roughly 2x, "identify the biggest perpetrators of low-velocity activity and eliminate them."
- He also says to make sure your "big rock" tasks are the right ones, linking his essay on rocks, pebbles and sand.
- None of this requires working later or harder: "Just stop averaging down!"

chunks.heading: Measuring where time goes with RescueTime
chunks.text:
Jason uses RescueTime, a free tool, to find the low-velocity activity. He shares his own numbers from one week.

- Almost 8 hours of email in the week, which he describes as "a solid, uninterrupted, full day of nothing but email."
- About 45 minutes in "Calendars." A drill-down showed almost an hour in Google Calendar. The week was packed with events, but time in the calendar app means managing meetings, not attending them.
- An average of 5.5 hours of real activity per day, even though he was in the office over 8 hours every day. The rest went to meetings, office chatter and lunch.
- His read on the "mythical eight-hour workday": you are starting from 5-6 productive hours, and even then much of that goes to fielding email.

chunks.heading: What he changed after seeing the numbers
chunks.text:
- He now notices sooner when an office conversation has gone past the point of being productive.
- He points to the many existing tips for processing email more efficiently (he links 43folders' inbox-zero material).
- His stated principle: once you see the numbers, the correction is easy.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jason Cohen argues against the "X is Y for Z" high-concept pitch because it is too brief, ambiguous, and defines you as a copy of something else. He prefers a clear positioning statement and a full product pitch, illustrated with a compact-projector example.

chunks.heading: Why the high-concept pitch fails, and what Jason uses instead
chunks.text:
Jason rejects the "high-concept pitch" (popularised by Venture Hacks): a three-word phrase that borrows a known successful product. Examples he cites: "YouTube is Flickr for video," "LinkedIn is Facebook for business," "Twitter is Blogger for Attention Deficit Disorder." His position: "I like brevity, but I don't like the high-concept pitch." It omits so much that it becomes ambiguous, and it "defines you as a copy of something else."

- He wants a company to define itself on its own terms, with clarity.
- His core objection: "When you use only three words and when you invoke something well-known and complicated, it's not clear what message will be received."
- He calls himself "brevity's biggest fan", but argues "there's such a thing as 'too brief.'"

chunks.heading: The three layers of messaging Jason uses
chunks.text:
He separates three artifacts, each with a different job:

- **Elevator pitch:** critical to the business, not just for pitching but to crystallize the company's goals in the founder's own mind.
- **One-line positioning statement:** a single clear sentence defining the company. It is not used on customers. It is something to "tack on your wall", a target that all marketing and communication should work towards.
- **High-concept pitch:** the even tighter analogy phrase, which he declines to use.

He sticks with Eric Sink's definition of the positioning statement as "the fundamental particle in my marketing universe."

chunks.heading: Worked example: a portable projector
chunks.text:
Jason illustrates with a hypothetical compact projector.

**Product pitch** (all the details and reasons to buy):
- Weighs under a pound, the size of a cell phone.
- Uses bright LEDs, so you never blow out a $100 bulb.
- Salespeople don't have to haul equipment or plug into venue projectors that are missing "yellow" or can't run at the laptop's resolution.
- Works 100% of the time and is small enough to get through airport security in a jacket pocket.

**Positioning statement:** "A compact, portable, rugged projector that eliminates surprises on the road." Short, yet it still carries the primary features and benefits.

**High-concept version:** "iPhone for projectors." It sounds good at first (easy to use, pretty, coveted, commercially successful, and the analogy fits size and portability), but it fails on the details below.

chunks.heading: How an analogy imports unwanted attributes
chunks.text:
Borrowing a famous product imports all of its attributes, including bad ones for your audience. For "iPhone for projectors," Jason lists these risks (as of 2009):

- iPhones had a reputation for not working well with Microsoft Office. That is particularly bad for traveling salespeople, who live on PowerPoint and Outlook, not GMail and Open Office.
- He spoke to a business traveler who avoided the iPhone specifically because it lacked Exchange integration (since fixed).
- iPhones are seen as inflexible and not customizable, and they "bucket you in a culture."
- After the v2.0 software problems, "buggy" could also be implied.

Takeaway: you don't control which of the analogy's attributes the listener picks up.

chunks.heading: On investor advice that "the product is nothing"
chunks.text:
Jason pushes back on the Venture Hacks line that "for investors, the product is nothing."

- He accepts the underlying point: product is not strategy, and product strategy interests investors more than feature bullets.
- But he considers "is nothing" an exaggeration to make a point.
- He has met an investor for whom it was literally true, and advises: "steer clear." His reasoning: "Strategy with zero product understanding isn't strategy."
- Despite the disagreement, he recommends Venture Hacks as a must-read for anyone funding or selling a company.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jason Cohen explains why crowds are brilliant at estimating facts (jelly beans, Millionaire audience polls) because random errors cancel out. The same mechanism ruins creative work, where votes act as vetoes that leave bland, lowest-common-denominator output. Startups need a niche they can own, not a safe middle.

chunks.heading: The wisdom of crowds works only when there is an objectively correct answer
chunks.text:
Jason opens with jelly-bean and game-show evidence, then explains where it breaks.
- Michael Mauboussin (2007): 73 Columbia Business School students guessed the beans in a jar. Guesses ranged from 250 to 4,100; the actual count was 1,116.
- The average individual error was 700, a 62% miss, so the students were "awful estimators". The group average was 1,151, just 3% off, and only 2 of the 73 students guessed better.
- Jack Treynor's 1987 version: 850 beans, 56 students, group average 2.5% off, only one student better. It has been repeated many times with similar results.
- His rule: "There is 'wisdom in the crowd' when there is an objectively-correct answer, and when the errors cancel out."

chunks.heading: Why the crowd beat the "smartest friend" on Who Wants to be a Millionaire
chunks.text:
Jason uses the show's lifelines as a natural experiment.
- The studio audience picked the correct answer 91% of the time, across all domains and difficulty levels. Their only qualification was being in a TV studio that afternoon.
- "Phone a friend" (the smartest person the contestant knows, with Google and Wikipedia) was right only 65% of the time.
- Takeaway: for factual questions, a crowd of average people beats a single expert.

chunks.heading: The mechanism: ignorant votes cancel out and a few informed votes decide
chunks.text:
Jason works the arithmetic to show why crowds are right.
- Take 100 audience members where only 16 know the answer is A and the other 84 vote randomly. The expected result is roughly 37, 21, 21, 21.
- A mere 16% of voters made A the clear winner, nearly double the next closest answer, because "the ignorant people vote randomly and their votes cancel out".
- More complex scenarios give the same distribution. For example, 11 know it's A, 15 each know B, C or D is wrong and vote randomly among the rest, and 44 have no clue.
- The crowd is only wise when ignorance is random noise rather than systematic bias.

chunks.heading: Votes are vetoes, so the crowd kills innovation
chunks.text:
Jason explains why the same process fails for creative work.
- The holiday-meal analogy: some guests can't take spice, Uncle Bill is allergic to garlic, Aunt Sarah skips red meat, Timmy won't eat anything green. The only dish that pleases everyone is bland chicken and rice.
- Chicken and rice doesn't please anyone; it is just what everyone "hated the least".
- His key line: "Votes don't converge on something wonderful. Rather, votes are *vetoes*."
- "In creative work, votes eliminate the interesting edges, because votes result in subtracting rather than adding, leaving only the boring residue that no one hated enough to vote off the island."
- "That's not how great products are made."

chunks.heading: Where consensus is the right goal and where it isn't
chunks.text:
- A wedding caterer serving 300 guests should cook chicken and rice. Nobody goes to a wedding for the food, so the goal is to annoy as few guests as possible.
- Startups are different. Jason says design-by-committee is "the antithesis of innovation", and average products for the average consumer are the opposite of innovation and probably a bad product strategy.
- Small companies need a niche, "a market space they can completely, unquestionably own, not some gray middle-ground where your attempt to offend no one also means exciting no one."
- He is skeptical of messaging, product features and ad layouts honed by focus groups, because these are creative decisions that require innovation.

chunks.heading: Rule of thumb for using crowd input
chunks.text:
