- Use crowds (surveys, polls, averaging many estimates) for questions with a factual, objectively right answer, such as estimates and forecasts, where individual errors are independent.
- Don't use votes, focus groups or committee consensus to decide positioning, features or design, where you need a distinctive point of view.
- Jason's further reading on when crowds are wise: Surowiecki's *The Wisdom of Crowds* (five elements of a wise crowd) and Scott Page's *The Difference* (diversity makes a group smarter), which inspired his Millionaire example.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jason Cohen recounts nearly giving a "sales veteran" partner 50% of Smart Bear and renaming it, and uses dieting as an analogy: no advice is objectively right, only right for you and sustainable. He lists practical filters for judging advice (context match, questions over commands, measurable ideas, gut feel).

chunks.heading: Don't let advice change who you are
chunks.text:
- Jason (founder of Smart Bear, which he later sold; "it's worth over $2,000,000,000" now) argues that advice should help you become a better version of yourself, not change who you are.
- He tells the "Frank vs. Gerry" story as the core lesson. Frank, a silver-haired ex-VP of Sales, joined 18 months after Smart Bear started. Gerry, Jason's co-founder in ITWatchDogs and mentor, sold companies for $100 million without setting foot on a golf course.
- Frank's demands:
  - Rename to "Software Test and Deployment Systems, Inc" (STDS), because "Big companies like acronyms."
  - Get patents "to keep competitors at bay."
  - Hire a sales team, because "software doesn't sell itself."
  - Lighten up and knock off early on Fridays.
  - 50% of the company, a salary, 35 hours a week, and no investment.
- Jason said no. Two weeks later he landed a $50,000 deal with Intuit. A few years later Smart Bear did millions in revenue with big companies, still called Smart Bear, with no patents and no sales guys.
- Gerry's reaction to Frank's pitch was a list of facts about the deal. Jason says Gerry framed his view as "pointed questions."
- Saying no to Frank was hard, because Frank had the expertise and Jason felt he was the one who was wrong. Without Gerry he "would have gone through with it."

chunks.heading: There is no objective "best" advice, only what works for you
chunks.text:
- Jason compares startup advice to dieting. Every approach has been touted as healthy and as poison, so the only question is "What works *for me*?"
- For nearly every "X is right" success story there is an equally compelling "X is wrong" story:
  - Prices low vs. prices high.
  - A big Twitter following with no ads vs. paid ads and no social media.
  - Scratching your own itch vs. researching an underserved niche.
  - A founder who is an expert in the field vs. one who brought a new perspective.
- He says the right answer depends on your market, competitors, customers, price point, business model, team, strengths, goals, financing and culture.
- Stories like Steve Jobs, Bill Gates, Mark Zuckerberg, Jason Fried or Pieter Levels are outliers even among their contemporaries. "No one should attempt to follow their unique paths."
- In diets, half the answer is physiology (how your body reacts) and half is sustainability. In business he maps these to company fit and whether you can keep doing it long-term.
- Sustainability examples:
  - If you find Twitter insipid, Facebook unserious and Instagram fake, forcing yourself to post there won't work. Most companies' marketing isn't primarily powered by social media.
  - Thousands of successful companies have crappy design. If you're not a designer and don't care to invest in one, ask what makes companies succeed despite poor design.
- Things that need fresh willpower every day don't last.

chunks.heading: Test whether it's insight or an excuse
chunks.text:
- Ask whether you like the advice because it justifies behavior you know is wrong, or because it clearly articulates a ground truth.
- Example: if you inherently dislike social media, you can find advice saying it doesn't matter. Did you enjoy it because it feels correct, or because it lets you avoid the truth that social media is critical in your chosen market?
- Asking yourself proactively makes the answer "often" clear, even though these are feelings.
- The reverse also applies: pay attention to advice that triggers an immediate, automatic revulsion. Often the feeling is right because it signals a context mismatch. But if you are wrong about something, "this is what it feels like to discover that. This is an opportunity; don't waste it!"

chunks.heading: Check the advisor's context
chunks.text:
- Rule of thumb: "Advisors give advice to themselves." Within their own goals, world-view, markets, products, customers and competitors they can give great advice. Outside that, "who knows?"
- Ask whether the advisor matches you on all those dimensions. If so, it may be relevant wisdom, even if hard to hear.
- If not, either ignore it completely ("Focus!") or run it through a substantial mental filter.
- The boundary of an advice's context is often unknown to both advisor and advisee.

chunks.heading: Prefer questions to commands, and constructive to merely critical
chunks.text:
- The best advice comes as a series of questions from a devil's advocate, not a barrage of commands. Pointed questions make you defend your choices and challenge assumptions without implying they're false.
- Rarely will an advisor know more than you about your domain, but an outside voice still helps. He compares it to Roger Federer's coach, who is "a mirror and a provocateur," not someone who is "better at tennis."
- Frank stated axioms. Gerry asked questions that required rebuttal or agreement.
- Jason suggests playing devil's advocate periodically: find an intelligent foe, take her to lunch, and follow Scott Berkun's "Rude Q&A."
- "It's easy to cut down ideas; it's hard to create and execute them." He can find someone who thinks any idea is dumb. Constructive means constructing, so look for advice with a clear method for implementation and a clear way to know whether it's working.
- Look for an advisor who volunteers a clear way to measure the idea's success. Then the idea is self-evaluating and you can change course if it doesn't work for you. He says this is the guiding principle behind Smart Bear's marketing.

chunks.heading: Tradition, relationships and gut feel
chunks.text:
- "This is how it's done" is almost never a good reason by itself. It's just momentum.
- Example: Smart Bear posts its prices on the internet rather than negotiating, even though enterprise software is rarely sold that way. It's honest and makes business sense.
- He also warns that many founders treat tradition as something to contradict. Much of tradition is hard-won wisdom, so traditional answers carry neither positive nor negative baggage and should be investigated like any other idea.
- Actively build a network of trusted advisors: local entrepreneurs, online forums, even bloggers you like. "Everyone needs a Gerry or two." Advisors won't always agree, but nothing beats running ideas past people you respect who have your interests at heart, even if their advice turns out wrong.
- Your gut often knows the answer. When both "X" and "Not-X" are convincingly peddled as The One True Way, you may need something outside pure logic. If you find yourself vigorously agreeing with a new idea, "that might be all the evidence you need."
- He adds that "no one knows what's right, not even me."
- Closing logic: being yourself is the only thing you'll be good at, and that gives you the leverage you need to win.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jason Cohen argues that a founder's first idea is probably wrong and rarely matters, because the real business emerges from building and watching what happens. He cites PayPal, Flickr and his own Smart Bear as companies that pivoted away from weak initial ideas. Waiting for a perfect idea is the mistake; a small market is enough to start.

chunks.heading: Jason treats the first idea as disposable
chunks.text:
- Jason argues that a founder's first idea probably sucks, "and it doesn't matter" because the business will probably turn out to be something completely different.
- He pushes back on a friend who waited to start a company until the idea was "completely fleshed out". He says the only way to find the right idea is to try the wrong one and see what happens.
- He says you won't find it "by fiddling around with PowerPoint slides and Photoshop mock-ups". His advice is to get out there and make some mistakes.

chunks.heading: PayPal began as a Palm Pilot money-beaming idea
chunks.text:
- In 1998 a company received $4.8 million in funding to "beam money between Palm Pilots". Jason code-names the product MoneyBeamer.
- The flow was clumsy:
  - Alice and Bob both had MoneyBeamer installed on their Palm Pilots.
  - The app only remembered that Alice wanted to pay Bob.
  - The money moved later, when Alice synced her Palm Pilot to her computer and dialed up to the internet.
- Jason asks whether you'd have invested in an idea like that. His point is that you'd have been wrong, because it was PayPal.
- The company's encryption work, combined with an idea for a consumer-targeted online banking system, made it the easiest way to send money by email.
- PayPal sold to eBay for $1.3 billion. At the time of writing it processed $2,000 of payments every second.

chunks.heading: Flickr grew out of a game that never launched
chunks.text:
- Game Neverending was an in-browser multiplayer online game "with no way to win, nor any definition of success". It never saw the light of day.
- Alpha testers found one feature most interesting: dragging game objects into chat windows to share them. The engineers read that as a useful enhancement to chat in general.
- As the game fizzled, they built a Flash app for real-time chat plus file sharing, with an emphasis on images.
- The app was only real-time, so pictures vanished when you closed it. Jason says this was fatal, because people cared more about the sharing than the real-time part.
- The team rewrote it as a regular website, and that became Flickr, the largest photo-sharing site in the world. It had 3 billion photos, with 5,000 more uploaded every minute.

chunks.heading: Smart Bear's own pivots
chunks.text:
- Jason's first product at Smart Bear was Code Historian. It dug through a file's history to show what changed. He calls the name accurate but the product "almost useless".
- He walks through the company's website over the years, from hideous to presentable. He says the early versions sold several tools, and some looked like a "Suite".
- At one point the company sold six different tools. The only one that mattered in the end was Code Reviewer. His take on the later site is that you "admit 'code review' is all that matters".
- The lesson is that the product you launch with is rarely the one that ends up mattering. The company he ended up with was built around code review, not the original idea.

chunks.heading: Start small, because you'll figure out the rest
chunks.text:
- Jason quotes Neil Davidson, co-founder of Red Gate Software: "You don't need stratospheric growth and a billion-dollar addressable market to bootstrap a software company. A $50,000 market opportunity is enough to get you off the ground--once you get started you'll figure out the rest."
- Jason cites Red Gate as the example. It started as yet another online bug-tracking system that no one cared about.
- It became a popular seller of SQL database tools with 95,000 customers.
- His takeaway is that you need a small foothold to get started, not a huge market.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Using Picasso's classical mastery and Volkswagen's "Lemon" ad, Jason Cohen argues that rules are reasonable defaults, not straightjackets. Breaking them works only when you understand them and do it deliberately. Innovation often comes from breaking a rule no one else will.

chunks.heading: Learn the rules first, then break them with purpose
chunks.text:
Jason argues that rule-breaking only works when the breaker has proven mastery of the rules. The choice to break them is what separates innovation from error.

- Picasso painted "The First Communion" at 15, a fully classical work. Jason's point is that this proves later "crazy" work like "Dora Maar au Chat" (sold for $95 million at auction in 2006) was a choice, not an inability to paint conventionally.
- "The choice is everything." Without proof of competence, Picasso could have been dismissed as a hack.
- Takeaway: "When you know the rules, you're allowed to break the rules."
- Warning: "if you never bothered to learn the rules, you're probably just mistaken."

chunks.heading: Rules are defaults, not straitjackets
chunks.text:
- Jason treats rules as "a reasonable default when we don't have a better idea."
- "There's no rule that can't be broken, so long as it's broken with purpose."
- He says truly innovative ideas are "frequently the result of breaking a rule that no one else is willing to break."

chunks.heading: Case study: Volkswagen's "Lemon" ad breaks the no-negative-words rule
chunks.text:
- The rule: never use negative words in headlines, because you don't want people subconsciously associating negative words with your product. It matters for advertising and branding.
- Volkswagen's 1960s ad called its own car a "Lemon", about the worst thing you can say about a car, and it got attention.
- Jason notes the casual style of the copy is "as effective and relevant today as it was in the 1960s."

chunks.heading: Why the VW ad worked: the copy resolves the negative
chunks.text:
- The body copy reveals the "lemon" is a car rejected for a blemished chrome strip on the glove compartment that "you wouldn't have noticed."
- It uses concrete proof of quality control: 3,389 inspectors at the Wolfsburg factory, 3,000 VWs produced daily (more inspectors than cars), every shock absorber tested, every windshield scanned, 189 check points, and one VW in fifty rejected.
- It ties the process to customer benefit: lasts longer, needs less maintenance, and a used VW depreciates less than any other car.
- The payoff line flips the negative: "We pluck the lemons; you get the plums."
- Jason's read: the authors "played with words exactly enough to get your attention but not so subtly that you missed the point." That balance came from understanding why the rule exists.

chunks.heading: Applying the lesson in marketing and product decisions
chunks.text:
- Before breaking a convention (headline rules, pricing norms, positioning norms), be able to state why the rule exists and what risk it guards against.
- Break it deliberately, and design the rest of the execution (like VW's fine print) to neutralize that risk.
- Treat the rule-break as the attention mechanism, and make sure the payoff makes the point unmistakable.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jason Cohen argues that a pitch must survive real-world distraction, not just ideal full-attention conditions. Like Snoop Dogg testing tracks on a crackly cassette player, test your messaging in noisy conditions, check that fragments still intrigue, and repeat your message so some of it breaks through.

chunks.heading: Pitch must survive noise, not just full attention
chunks.text: Jason argues that a company's pitch is judged under distraction, not in a quiet room. Prospects are like teenagers on a car stereo: they have tiny speakers, background chaos and competing interests. He frames the real competitor as "competition for *attention*," not features or benefits. His standard: "It's not enough to be compelling when you have 60 uninterrupted, full-attention seconds. Your pitch has to work in the noise."

chunks.heading: The Snoop Dogg cassette-player test
chunks.text:
Jason uses Snoop Dogg's track vetting as the model for stress-testing a message.
- On MTV Cribs, Snoop did not use a sound-proof room or $50,000 speakers. He played sample tracks on a cassette player on the floor, turned up so it crackled and distorted.
- The reason: songs must sound good on a cheap car stereo with distractions, tiny speakers and a messy back seat.
- Music producers recommend mixing on crappy speakers. Jason's takeaway: "If it sounds good on crap, it will sound good anywhere."
- He applies the same logic to a pitch: test it in degraded conditions, not ideal ones.

chunks.heading: Every medium has its own distractions
chunks.text:
Jason lists how attention gets competed away in each channel:
- **Web page:** "You've got mail" alerts, instant messages about funny YouTube videos, and the "back" button as the ultimate escape.
- **Magazine ad:** a ringing phone, and a more interesting picture on the next page.
- **10-second pitch at parties and tradeshows:** cocktails, room noise, and a more interesting story in the adjoining conversation.

The point holds regardless of medium: assume partial, interrupted attention.

chunks.heading: Test a spoken pitch in a noisy environment
chunks.text:
- Record the pitch in a noisy place, such as a bar or a playground.
- Play it back and ask whether it still makes sense when you can only make out about 60 percent of the syllables.
- Ask friends to point out what is engaging and what is not.

chunks.heading: Test printed material by covering parts of it
chunks.text:
- Lay the printed piece on a table and cover different parts with a magazine.
- The whole message does not need to shine through.
- The check is whether the visible fragments are eye-catching enough that someone notices them and becomes interested.

chunks.heading: Repeat the message to push some of it through
chunks.text:
- Distractions and other priorities will sit between you and your target most of the time.
- Jason recommends marketing techniques that repeat a message: newsletters, a blog, Twitter, Facebook.
- Repeating often enough can push *some* of your communications through the chaos. He frames this as partial success ("some"), not guaranteed delivery.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jason Cohen argues that "and more" in business names and signage is usually untrue, dilutes passion, and signals an incomplete message. Instead, state specifically what you are, be passionate about it, and make sure your ideal customer understands.

chunks.heading: "And more" is lazy marketing: say what you are
chunks.text:
- Jason argues that the phrase "...and more!" is "ubiquitous and less meaningful" than almost any other. He used to think it was a harmless waste of words, then decided he was wrong.
- His test: swap in absurd nouns ("Bed, Bath, and Robots!", "Bed, Bath, and Velociraptors!"). The suffix is so empty that anything fits.
- His conclusion: "'and more' is a weak declaration that your message is incomplete." A phrase that doesn't commit to anything doesn't get people interested, excited, or through the door.

chunks.heading: Most "and more" claims aren't even true
chunks.text:
- Jason checked real sites using the phrase and found most were about one thing only.
  - "Pumpkins and More" is a site about pumpkins and nothing else.
  - "The German Way and More" covers German life and culture.
  - "Law and More" is a blog by and for lawyers, and "Cooking and More" is only about cooking.
  - "Tourism and More" is actually about Tourism and Security (and its company shield says "Security," not "more").
  - "Rain Barrels and More" is a company that makes only rain barrels.
- His point: the phrase is both useless and inaccurate, so it adds a false claim on top of a vague one.

chunks.heading: Replace "and more" with enthusiasm and commitment
chunks.text:
- If a business does one thing, say so with passion instead of hedging. Jason's rewrites for the pumpkin site: "Everything Pumpkin," "Pumpkins Supreme," "Nothin' but Pumpkin," "Pumpkin Lovers."
- For the German site he suggests "The German Way Explained" or "The German Way in English."
- Specialization is a selling point: "When I need information about pumpkins, I want someone fully committed to pumpkindom!"
- On the rain barrel company: "How much more do they know about rain barrels than anyone else? How many stories could they tell?" He says "and more" dilutes "this otherwise incredible message" and douses a singular passion. He would rather buy from "passionate rain barrel people."

chunks.heading: When "and more" is true, it still doesn't work
chunks.text:
- Jason concedes that Bed Bath & Beyond really does sell more than bed and bath goods, so "and Beyond" is at least informative.
- The case for it: the listed items attract some people, and "and beyond" tells the rest "we have more!"
- His rebuttal: "I don't buy it." Someone uninterested in bed and bath products is unlikely to care about air fresheners and cutlery, and simply saying "and beyond" won't stir them into action.
- He gives the name a pass partly for the alliteration, but says non-committal phrases generally don't get people interested.

chunks.heading: Takeaway: own what you are
chunks.text:
- "Forget about 'more.' Just say what you are. Own it."
- It should be possible to convey the purpose of a business in a phrase without ambiguity.
- He ties this to knowing your ideal customer: make sure "Carol gets it" (his ideal customer persona) and the rest follows.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jason Cohen reconciles two conflicting rules: always search for disproof of your beliefs, yet never change a proven strategy flippantly. His answer is that how weakly you hold an opinion should depend on how much work went into forming it. Illustrated with an AdWords specialist asking to change battle-tested landing page copy.

chunks.heading: Reconciling conviction with openness: weight your opinions by how they were formed
chunks.text:
- Jason's operating attitude, "strong opinions, weakly held" (a phrase he credits to Paul Saffo), is that conviction is necessary for action but must be tempered by a constant search for disproof.
- He says being wishy-washy gets in the way of inspiring people, working toward a goal and getting things done. Ignoring contrary evidence is "irresponsible and even dishonest."
- His summary of the tension: "A strategy that changes all the time cannot be executed, but a strategy that never changes is definitely incorrect."

chunks.heading: "Weakly" is a dial set by where the opinion came from
chunks.text:
- Jason argues the two forces reconcile once you see that how weakly you hold an opinion should depend on how it was originally formed.
- Low-consideration opinions: made without real thought, so easy to change. His example is Smart Bear's website having a "Resources" page separate from an "External Articles" page for no reason. If someone offers a different idea with a rationale, make the change.
- High-consideration opinions: forged with a great deal of work, so they need proportionally strong evidence to overturn.
- His rule: "If it deserved this much consideration before, it deserves the same consideration now. Perhaps more."
- His one-line summary: "Be ready to change with reason, but don't change for no reason."

chunks.heading: What a hard-won marketing message looks like
chunks.text:
- Jason describes Smart Bear's marketing message as the product of many years of work. Everyone in the office, and people beyond it, brainstormed ideas, vetoed concepts, defended theories and crafted phrases.
- It went through iterations, with success measured objectively (e.g. AdWords conversion rates) and subjectively (e.g. reactions when giving talks at conferences).
- The message had worked on the web, in print, at trade shows and in demos.
- Because of that history, he treats it as something that shouldn't be changed flippantly.

chunks.heading: Handling an outsider who wants to change your messaging
chunks.text:
- The case: Smart Bear hired a dedicated in-house AdWords pro, a full-time job because the algorithms, monitoring and tools change regularly.
- Part of the job is perfecting landing pages. The page should be tuned to match the ad text, both to entice customers and because AdWords placement depends on the relevance of the page's content.
- The AdWords pro began asking them to change the proven marketing message on those landing pages.
- Jason has no problem with criticism, noting that the purpose of Smart Bear's software is to generate criticism. The question was whether to let an "outsider" with no context change proven text.
- The case for listening: a stranger unencumbered by history and biases may supply the insight needed to disprove assumptions. New perspectives add depth, and old ideas shouldn't be kept just because they're venerable.
- The case against: Jason cites Ted Matthews's argument that branding doesn't work unless you stick to your guns, and that new hires quickly suggest change without understanding the battle behind a decision. He compares this to wanting to rewrite an application because of a little ugly code.
- His resolution: he disagrees with Ted that "branding" can be a shield against good ideas, however entrenched the old ones are. But where existing ideas are proven and great work has molded them, new ideas should be held to proportionally high standards.

chunks.heading: Practical test for whether to change something
chunks.text:
- Ask how much consideration and testing produced the current choice. Little or none: change it readily when given a reason.
- A lot, backed by measured results: demand evidence at the same level before overturning it.
- Neither "never change" nor "always change" is acceptable. Both are failures to weigh the evidence.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jason Cohen attacks generic marketing language ("a leading provider of...", "solutions") using real company descriptions as examples. He argues the causes are fear, laziness, and incompetence, and that if you can't say what you do in a few specific words, customers won't get it either.

chunks.heading: Meaningless marketing language costs you customers
chunks.text:
Jason argues that vague corporate marketing language (buzzwords, "solutions," "a leading provider of") signals nothing and pushes readers away.

- His test: does "a leading provider of" make you think "Awesome, I found the leader!"? It doesn't. At best you skim past an "overused phrase, devoid of meaning." At worst you lose interest and click "Back."
- His example is Omniture's description: "a leading provider of online business optimization software, enabling customers to manage and enhance online, offline and multi-channel business initiatives." It turns out they do web analytics.
- His fix: just say "web analytics," then spend the remaining words on how you differ from other web analytics companies.

chunks.heading: The word "solution" is a red flag
chunks.text:
Jason singles out "Solution" as perhaps the worst offender.

- Many sites make visitors choose between "Products" and "Solutions" in the main menu, and a visitor can't tell which to pick. He asks what a "solution" is and how it differs from a product.
- His favorite example is AT Systems, whose motto, "The system is the solution," is printed on the side of an armored truck. The company moves money around, and the motto says nothing about that.
- The company name plus a motto still leaves the question "What do they do?" unanswered. That is the failure.

chunks.heading: Why marketing teams write meaningless phrases
chunks.text:
He offers three reasons and rejects all of them as valid.

- **Fear.** Generic, widely-used phrases don't offend and don't invite lawsuits, since "it's hard to sue over meaningless words." That may work at a big company, but "in a startup you can't afford to be bland and wishy-washy."
- **Laziness.** "A leading provider of business solutions" is easier than nailing your message. Doing it right means knowing your customer, boiling the company down to its essentials, and being succinct, evocative and specific. "It's hard! ... It's easier not to."
- **Incompetence.** If you don't know what sets your product apart, can't articulate the niche you own, or can't describe your perfect customer, you fall back on generic phrases.

chunks.heading: The test: say it in a few specific words
chunks.text:
- His rule: "If you can't articulate your product in a few, choice, specific, words, your potential customers won't get it either."
- A company description should say what the product is, for whom, and how it differs, in concrete terms.
- A weak description leaves a reader unable to guess what the company does. He uses the webMethods boilerplate as the "tragic example": "business integration software to integrate, assemble and optimize available IT assets to drive business process productivity," plus "innovative, enterprise-class" and "tangible business value."
- His closing instruction: "Take a scalpel to your marketing content. Make every word count."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jason Cohen uses a Korean restaurant waiter's broken-English answer ("Dolsot bibimbap better!") to argue that the messenger matters more than the message once a human relationship begins. Websites need specificity, but in sales, support and tradeshow conversations, genuine passion, knowledge and a desire to make the customer successful is what sells.

chunks.heading: Genuine enthusiasm from the messenger beats polished marketing copy in a live relationship
chunks.text:
- Jason's story: at a Korean restaurant, he asked the waiter the difference between bibimbap and dolsot bibimbap. The answer was only "Dolsot bibimbap better!" He ordered the dolsot, a dish served in a hot stone pot, which was $1 more and, in his words, "2x better."
- The rice gets crispy, the egg cooks, and the veggies and meat stay extra hot.
- Jason says the vague answer was "perfect," and that his own usual advice (be specific, differentiate, make every phrase meaningful) did not apply here.
- The reason: the answer was not in an ad, a datasheet or a "30-second elevator pitch mechanically regurgitated on a tradeshow floor." It came from a hard-working person who barely spoke the language but did his best to steer Jason to the right choice.
- His conclusion: "It's the messenger, not the message, that made the experience wonderful."

chunks.heading: Obsessive excitement is contagious and sells
chunks.text:
- Jason states the principle: "Being obsessively and genuinely excited about something is contagious. And good sales. In any industry, with any product."
- A salesperson's real belief in the product persuades more than the exact words used.
- The waiter had skin in the game: he worked at the restaurant constantly, was probably related to the owner, and wanted the customer to pick the better, pricier option.
- The upsell worked because it was sincere: a customer who trusts that the person wants them to enjoy the meal will pay the extra $1 for a dish that is twice as good.

chunks.heading: Where specificity matters and where passion matters more
chunks.text:
- Jason distinguishes channels. Websites are not relationships; they are "attention-getters and information-distributers." There, marketing copy must be specific and differentiated, as he argues in his other writing on specificity and differentiation.
- Once a human relationship begins, he says the most important thing is to be genuine in passion, knowledge and desire to make customers successful.
- He lists the situations where this applies: sales pitches, tech support and tradeshow booths.
- Practical takeaway: write precise, differentiated copy for the web, but staff live conversations with people who truly care about the product and the customer's success, rather than scripted pitch-reciters.

chunks.heading: Hire and prepare customer-facing people for authenticity, not scripts
chunks.text:
- Implied tactic from Jason's example: scripts and memorized elevator pitches are weaker than a person who knows the product well and believes in it.
- The three traits he names for the human side of selling are passion, knowledge, and a desire to make customers successful.
- Even imperfect language skills did not matter, because the waiter's care came through and pushed the customer to the right choice.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jason argues that in an overwhelmed small company, gut-feel procrastination can beat formal prioritization. Many problems resolve themselves, many tasks matter less than they seem, and batching low-value chores frees time for the one or two things that win. He also says to allow some fun to avoid burnout.

chunks.heading: Procrastination as a prioritization tool for a swamped small company
chunks.text:
Jason argues that procrastination is a legitimate, even necessary, tool for running a small business, and he calls himself a habitual procrastinator. His reasoning: you are overwhelmed with work, so you cannot do everything, and trying to will hurt you.

- Backlog at Smart Bear after five years and fifteen employees: a dense whiteboard of marketing ideas, dozens of index cards of feature ideas, and 7,000 open issues and minor feature requests in FogBugz that nobody has time to glance at.
- He says it was "a hundred times worse" at the start, when one person did all the work.
- The ideal founder is tireless, willing to do every job, hyper-organized, and only works on the highest-value tasks. Jason admits he is not that last part.
- He cites Mark Twain: "Don't put off 'till tomorrow what you can put off 'till the day after tomorrow."
- His conclusion: formal prioritization may be best in theory, but plain gut-feel procrastination can be the right way to go. "You can't do everything, so don't."

chunks.heading: Many things resolve themselves if you ignore them
chunks.text:
Jason's main practical argument is that waiting filters out false urgency. Examples he gives:

- The big feature you got worked up about yesterday seems unimportant the next day.
- A feature a customer calls vital turns out to be an intern's suggestion and not actually blocking the sale.
- An apparent fundamental bug turns out to be a misconfiguration.
- An "important" meeting turns out to be unimportant.
- The email you didn't answer resolved itself.

Delay costs little for these items, and it saves you from doing work that never mattered.

chunks.heading: Even critical-seeming tasks like accounting can be deferred
chunks.text:
Jason says many tasks matter less than you think, including accounting.

- Costs of neglect: late fees, lost receipts, penalties from the IRS.
- His claim: those financial burdens are "more than compensated" by the extra revenue from signing up one more customer with the time saved.
- Batching helps: it is faster to enter 100 receipts into QuickBooks once a month than three a day. Small tasks carry context-switch overhead, and you get faster at typing and keyboard shortcuts when you repeat the same action hundreds of times in a row.
- This applies to financial tasks in particular, which are faster done in one big sweep than as they trickle in.

chunks.heading: Win by getting a few things right, not everything
chunks.text:
Jason's strategic point: companies succeed because they got just a few things really right, not because they had no problems, bugs, design flaws, or perfect books.

- Spending less time on time-sucking details frees time for the "1-2 most important things."
- Focusing on those few things is "how you win."
- Tactic: let low-value details slide on purpose so the important work gets your best hours.

chunks.heading: Allow yourself fun to avoid burnout
chunks.text:
Jason says you sometimes need to do fun work at the expense of stated priorities.

- Most of what you do in a small company isn't work you enjoy, so frustration and burnout are easy to slide into.
- Recovering with "plain fun" is part of the job.
- His rule: "Whatever the cost of putting off duties, burn-out is even more costly."

chunks.heading: Mindset: rationalize if you must, but don't beat yourself up
chunks.text: Jason admits he is rationalizing ("Yeah I know I'm rationalizing") but stands by the conclusion that you cannot do everything, so you shouldn't try. He closes with: "And don't beat yourself up over it." The takeaway is to treat a long undone list as normal for a founder, not as a personal failing.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jason Cohen argues that shipping fast with messy code is the right early choice, but it creates tech debt that behaves like a mortgage: you pay interest in bugs and only slowly reduce principal. He explains when to shift from time-to-market to quality and how to win the argument for refactoring with non-technical stakeholders.

chunks.heading: The "quality mortgage" analogy for tech debt
chunks.text:
Jason frames software quality as a mortgage. Shippable, salable software is the house you want today, and the debt is the quality and maintainability of the code. You can't build a near-bug-free application outright (he says that would take ten years), so you take out a mortgage to build v1.0 in six months.

- Early on, taking on this debt is the right move. When a company is new and still seeking its niche, "the most important thing is to get the software out the door fast, bugs and all."
- The emphasis eventually shifts from time-to-market to reducing tech support calls and not upsetting tens of thousands of existing users with a dud release.
- He calls the debt a "necessary evil in early software development," and says "just plan on paying it back."
- He notes a "fine line" separates debt as a lever for acceleration from debt as an insurmountable drag.

chunks.heading: How the debt accrues and what it costs
chunks.text:
Jason says you eventually pay the debt back "with interest," and the interest is paid in bugs.

- Many of those bugs were preventable had there been time for unit tests, good design, manual tests and use-cases.
- Fixing surface bugs doesn't fix the underlying problems in the code. He compares this to the first years of a mortgage, where you pay interest without reducing principal.
- Fixing the most heinous bugs and moving on is still the right choice at first.
- Symptoms of a company deep in quality debt: years of squeezing in "must-have" features for big customers stretch code beyond its original design, core modules are "riddled with landmines," engineers are afraid to change anything even with unit tests, and the tacit assumptions of the two founders aren't obvious to the next ten hires.

chunks.heading: Why slow, incremental paydown often isn't enough
chunks.text:
Jason describes the "pay principal slowly" approach and its limits.

- Examples of incremental paydown: refactor one file while adding a feature, add full unit test coverage for a handful of core methods, write a manual test plan for one complex dialog box. He calls this "all good."
- At that rate, though, it can still take ten years to pay back.
- Unlike a house, software keeps expanding with new features and gets reused beyond its original conception. Without fixing the underlying mess, and the process that produced it, you may never catch up. He likens this to an interest-only mortgage.
- At some point it becomes intolerable, and "it's time to pay down the principal in earnest," which requires allocating time for major rework.

chunks.heading: Winning the political fight to refactor
chunks.text:
Jason says getting the right to refactor can be politically tough, especially with non-technical stakeholders. He gives rebuttals to three common objections.

- **"Clean-up is invisible to users; we need new features."** The bugs messy code produces are visible to users. Time spent fixing those bugs could have gone to features, and the longer you stay in quality debt, the longer each new feature takes.
- **"We don't have time for clean-up."** Fixing bugs generated by the problem instead of the problem itself is like "whacking weeds every weekend instead of pulling them up by the roots." He cites Ben Franklin's "an ounce of prevention is worth a pound of cure," which he renders as prevention being sixteen times more valuable than cure.
- **"Developers made this mess; they should fix it on their own time."** He argues that shipping fast and responding quickly to early-adopter feedback, even as the product morphed from its original conception, is what produced the current customers and revenue.

chunks.heading: Advice to CEOs on handling tech debt
chunks.text:
- Don't finger-point; he says it "impedes resolution."
- Instead, challenge developers to reduce bug reports. This is easily measured, so you can track time versus results.
- He observes that developers prefer building new features to fixing bugs, so "if they're begging for time to fix bugs, it's serious."
- He adds that Martin Fowler made the same point in his "TechnicalDebt" piece.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jason Cohen takes the winning Othello AI strategy (minimize the opponent's legal moves) and applies it to competitive strategy. Rather than only maximizing your own position, force competitors into low-percentage, expensive paths via exclusive deals, overpaying for top ad slots, and owning the "expert" position in your market.

chunks.heading: Competitive strategy as limiting the competitor's options
chunks.text: Jason Cohen takes a lesson from computer Othello. In the 1990s the winning AI strategy did not maximize its own tile count or board position. It scored each position by how many valid moves the opponent had, where fewer was better. Jason's summary: "Limiting choice is more important than what the choices are." He argues the same principle applies to business competition.

chunks.heading: The Othello lesson: minimize the opponent's moves
chunks.text:
- Typical board-game AI looks many moves ahead and rates each resulting position. The hard part is the "goodness" metric.
- Conventional Othello metrics counted your own tiles and valued edge tiles above middle ones.
- The winning metric was different: how many valid moves does my opponent have?
- The insight is that the contest is less about your own pieces and more about shrinking what the other side can do.

chunks.heading: Defensive sports as the same pattern
chunks.text:
- A defense can never cover every contingency, so it forces the offense into higher-risk, lower-percentage plays.
- Basketball: you can't cover the long shot and the charge at once, so you elect to give up the low-percentage three-point shot.
- Football: you can't cover both in-routes and out-routes, so you force a throw into as much traffic as possible.

chunks.heading: The business question to ask
chunks.text: Competitors always have options. Jason's question is: "How can you limit their choices to things that are low-percentage or expensive?" The goal is to make them spend more money, get more lucky, or be more creative to compete.

chunks.heading: Tactics that limit competitors' choices
chunks.text:
- **Honor the competitor's coupons.** This removes the coupon as a way for the competitor to "beat" you, so it is no longer a choice for building a competitive edge.
- **Overpay for the best advertising slots.** You are paying too much if you measure direct ROI alone. The extra value is forcing competitors into a low-converting ad position, which means many fewer customers at any price.
- **Pay for exclusive deals with the largest affiliates.** Again you overpay on direct ROI, but competitors are forced onto affiliates who can generate only about 1/10th the leads.
- **Exclusive deals with brand-name suppliers.** Suppliers are often invisible to customers, but sometimes their identity is known or integration with a well-known brand is part of your value proposition. If customers value that integration and you make it exclusive, competitors must find other, less-desirable ways to deliver it, or cede the capability to you.
- **Patents, with a caveat.** Patents limit how a competitor can compete, since others must think of another way. Jason says this is useless in software, where it is always easy to do it another way. Software companies don't protect themselves with patents; other moats are available instead (he links his essay on moats).

chunks.heading: How Smart Bear applied it
chunks.text:
- Smart Bear positioned itself as "the experts in code review." Evidence Jason lists: they literally wrote the book, ran the largest-ever study on code review, have years of history, and have the most popular tool.
- This makes it expensive and slow for a competitor to claim parity, let alone surpass them. It is possible but very hard to compete on that basis.
- Why it matters: in Jason's opinion, being "the expert" is the best qualifier for their market, the Enterprise. Customers include Microsoft, Qualcomm, Intuit, IBM and Adobe.
- Those customers care less about "lowest cost" or "simplest installation" (though Jason notes their installation is simple).
- If his opinion is right, he has removed the single best product-positioning choice from competitors, who must take a less desirable, lower-percentage path.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jason Cohen explains the Opposite Test for product marketing: negate each feature or benefit bullet, and if the negative is ridiculous, the original is meaningless and undifferentiating. Real positioning comes from claims whose opposite is a valid strategy, ideally with acknowledged trade-offs. The one exception is a generic claim you can truly own, like "fastest."

chunks.heading: The Opposite Test for positioning and feature bullets
chunks.text:
Jason is tired of generic feature/benefit bullet points ("Easy to use," "Robust features," "Innovative systems," "Customer-first"). He argues they're easy to mock and they don't differentiate, because every competitor claims the same things.

He runs the test on each bullet:

1. Construct the negative of the statement.
2. Ask whether the negative is ridiculous.
3. Ask whether anyone could build a rational strategy around the negative, or whether a competitor already has.
4. If the negative is ridiculous, the bullet is "trivial, obvious, mandatory, or at least undifferentiating from the competition."

He calls such a bullet "weak, it's boring, and most importantly, it's meaningless." It takes up space on the page, and in your head, that should go to the differentiating things your product strategy is built on.

He notes the idea is well-worn and independently arrived at. Roger L. Martin asks "Is the opposite stupid on its face?" Al Ries and Jack Trout, in *Positioning*, ask whether it would make sense if a competitor did the exact opposite. It's also called the Reversibility Test.

chunks.heading: Worked examples: what passes and what fails
chunks.text:
**Fails (throw it out):**
- "Easy to use" → "Difficult to use." Funny; no one would claim it.
- "Enables communication" → "Blocks communication." No one would admit that.

**Passes:**
- "Stores files as big as 100 terabytes" → "Cannot handle huge files." Not ridiculous, and sadly true of many systems.
- "Fully open source" → "Closed source." Most companies do exactly that, so it's a real choice.
- "Fully backward-compatible, even after twenty years." Most software eventually ships breaking changes to enable new architecture or features. Compatibility matters when millions of users run on-premise software with old components (e.g. WordPress plugins). The cost is that it hamstrings UX innovation, workflow and feature innovation, and architecture and performance work. Sometimes a breaking change is needed to stay modern.
- From his own product (Smart Bear's Code Collaborator): "Integrates with seven version control tools." The negatives ("not integrated with version control" or "integrated with [one tool]") are true of competitors. Going deep on a single API instead of wide across many is a valid, practiced strategy, so the statement differentiates.

chunks.heading: Second check: does the claim carry an acknowledged downside?
chunks.text:
Jason adds another way to tell whether you pass: **whether there are negative consequences from your statement, which you acknowledge.**

- Supporting multiple version control systems buys compatibility.
- Supporting only one buys a deeper, more sophisticated workflow integration.
- A single team probably uses only one system, so it might prefer the "one" product. Choosing "multi" therefore has a direct cost, which makes it a real decision.

A claim with no cost and no tradeoff is usually a generic one.

chunks.heading: Replacing generic bullets is hard, and that's the point
chunks.text:
If you're using generic bullets now, replacing them isn't easy. You have to work out:
- What is strongest about your product.
- How specifically it beats the alternatives.
- How to say that pithily.

He calls this a useful exercise in itself.

chunks.heading: The one exception: a generic you truly own
chunks.text:
A generic claim is fine if it's your single biggest differentiator, where you're truly 10x better than the competition on that dimension and so "own" the concept as your identity.

His example is "Fastest." The negative is funny (slow operation means "lots of time staring into frozen progress bars"), but it works if it's your top priority. His tactics:
- Make it the bi-line: "The fastest ____."
- Prove it with benchmarks.
- Explain that speed isn't only about saving operator time. It enables entirely new features. If operation X is normally too slow for anyone to use, and your system completes it in two milliseconds, it becomes a feature. Even if a competitor technically has it, you make it practical.

chunks.heading: How it fits his broader positioning principles
chunks.text:
Jason says the Opposite Test is another way of saying:
- Be specific.
- Avoid buzzwords.
- Commit fully to your ideal customer and what they value.
- Tell the truth.

He calls it a critical component of having a great strategy and great positioning.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jason Cohen argues that "act now" discounts breed mistrust, invite endless haggling, attract the worst customers and signal a weak brand. Instead, announce a coming price increase and offer to lock in the current rate, which protects customers, implies growth and builds loyalty.

chunks.heading: Why Jason refuses to discount, and what he does instead
chunks.text:
Jason argues that the typical software sales move, "buy now and I'll give you a discount," is worse than a price lock. He compares two approaches:

1. "If you buy now, I'll give you a discount."
2. "The price is going up, but if you buy now I will lock in your rate."

He says "the evidence is overwhelmingly in favor of #2," even though #1 gives the customer a lower price. Most software companies use #1, often to force a close before month-end or quarter-end. He asks why 90% of them still pick it.

chunks.heading: Why discounting breeds mistrust
chunks.text:
From the customer's point of view, a discount for acting now means the original price was never the real price.

- The "price" must have included a slice of pure profit the seller is willing to give up.
- The customer concludes they were being gouged, and only learned it because it was the end of the quarter.
- Jason says "#1 breeds mistrust," the opposite of what a seller wants to build.
- A price lock works the other way: "In #2 you're looking out for my interests." The seller warns of a possible rate increase and protects the customer from it.
- The customer knows an increase may not come soon, or at all. It still reads as protection, not a gouge that was graciously revealed.
- He ties this to the "Love" type of willingness-to-pay.

chunks.heading: The Parasoft `.TEST` story: discounting turns a customer into a hostage
chunks.text:
About four years before writing (circa 2004), Jason trialed Parasoft's `.TEST`.

- The software was buggy. Even after hours of remote-desktop sessions with tech support, it would not stay up long enough to scan his code.
- The salesman quoted $20,000. Jason had expected $2,000 and said free tools (FxCop, NUnit) could do the same thing.
- Jason said it was "an order of magnitude problem." The next day the salesman called back with $1,500.
- Jason did not buy. A reference customer told him he had paid $20,000 and had not even installed it yet, because "the demo looked great."

Jason's lessons:

- If the price can drop from $20,000 to $1,500, it might drop to $1,000. The customer now "doesn't know where the floor is" and has every incentive to haggle.
- The process drags out, "ending at gunpoint." In his words: "Meanwhile your 'customer relationship' is now more of a 'hostage situation.'"
- The seller gains maybe 10% on each order but creates an adversarial relationship.
- That is a bad trade in enterprise sales, where a pilot might be 30 seats and the roll-out 2,000. Souring the customer over 10% on the 30-seat part risks the 2,000-seat order.
- Word also gets around. If the reference customer learned the product was available for $1,500, inconsistent pricing would look unfair and dishonest. "Goodbye 2,000-seat order."

chunks.heading: Discounting damages your brand image
chunks.text:
Jason separates this from the honesty argument.

- Companies known for discounting include Wal-Mart, Target and Walgreens.
- Quotes for 1,000 desktops from Microsoft, Oracle or IBM are "negotiable, everything's discountable." That conjures haggling and struggle, or at worst low quality and a desperate need to "meet numbers" at the expense of everything else.
- Companies that never discount include Apple, Google (AdWords prices are not haggled) and Constant Contact. There are no discounts on iPhones.
- Their image is "Desirable. The best. Worth paying for."
- His rule: "The leader doesn't have to compromise. The leader isn't desperate for orders."

chunks.heading: Discounts attract the wrong customers
chunks.text:
Jason asks what kind of customer responds to discounts, coupons and "act now" language.

- Not the customers who find the most value in the product.
- Not the ones whose opinions you want when planning the next round of features.
- Not the ones who will love the brand and spend more with you over time.
- His conclusion: "Strategy #1 attracts the least-valuable customers and repels the best ones, while establishing a weak brand."

chunks.heading: Why a price lock signals growth and community
chunks.text:
Jason says a price-increase message does two things that a discount cannot.

**It implies growth.**
- It plants the idea of higher prices in the customer's head.
- Software "supply" is unlimited, so a rising price must mean rising demand.
- Customers will not do this reasoning consciously, but the product feels more valuable.
- His framing: "Discounts feel like unloading unwanted product; price increases feel like success."

**It makes the customer part of a club.**
- The customer got in early, on the ground floor, before the product takes off and prices rise.
- They are rewarded for loyalty and for taking a risk with you, with price protection.
- He calls it a "thank-you" and says this is "actually a good reason to give some a discount," and you are giving it proactively.

chunks.heading: Summary: discount versus price lock
chunks.text:
Jason's side-by-side comparison:

- **Discount (#1):** less money now, an adversarial relationship, a never-ending struggle over money, and a message that the product may need a discount to be desirable.
- **Price lock (#2):** more money now, a consistent and fair pricing policy, an inclusive and special customer relationship, and a message of market leadership and growth.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jason Cohen uses Malcolm Gladwell's success despite debunked theories to argue that stories persuade more than correct logic does. His takeaway is Seth Godin's: marketing is telling a good story, and most other factors are second-order effects.

chunks.heading: Why Gladwell's flawed theories still win: the story is what sells
chunks.text:
- Jason notes Malcolm Gladwell is about as successful as a non-fiction writer can be. *The Tipping Point* was a surprise #1 best-seller for months in 2000, and several of its stories became part of American vernacular.
- Jason says "it all appears to be wrong. And no one seems to care."
- He still likes Gladwell, whose books "are entertaining and they make you think."
- His explanation: Gladwell is "a master storyteller." Readers who have been "beguiled with interesting, provocative stories" happily accept his "unproven, non-sequitur conclusions."

chunks.heading: Broken Windows: the claim that fell apart
chunks.text:
- Gladwell defines the Tipping Point as the critical point where a system can go either way. A trend can take off or fizzle, and a few small changes can snowball into big effects.
- His example was Broken Windows, credited (in Jason's telling) with fixing New York City's crime problem in the early 1990s. The city fixed small, easy things such as squeegee guys, Times Square, and pictures of real windows over broken ones in burnt-out crack houses, and crime fell fast.
- Jason's counterpoint is that correlation does not imply causation. Doing X and then seeing Y does not mean X caused Y.
- Steven Levitt's chapter in *Freakonomics* points out that crime fell everywhere in America, at the same time, whatever each city or state was trying (more police, curfews, after-school programs, Broken Windows). That implies none of those was the primary factor.
- Levitt's common factor is Roe v. Wade in 1973, which meant millions fewer unwanted births and fewer people at highest risk for crime turning 18 in 1991. Jason adds that states that legalized abortion earlier saw crime drop 18 years after their own legalization.

chunks.heading: Critics, and Gladwell's non-defense
chunks.text:
- Duncan Watts built a career in network theory partly by debunking the "Tipping Point of trends" idea. Jason quotes him: "It sort of sounds cool... But it's wonderfully persuasive only for as long as you don't think about it."
- Watts takes Gladwell's studies one by one and shows how each was misunderstood or misapplied.
- Gladwell does not defend himself. He says books and articles can only "uncover a little piece of the bigger picture."
- Jason calls this a cop-out. The book reads as if it is convincing you of a theory, and he thinks Gladwell was too embarrassed to say, "Yeah, it's wrong, but at least it had a lot of great stories."
- Jason points out the irony that Gladwell blurbed *Freakonomics* ("Prepare to be dazzled") even though its main argument disproves the central theory of *The Tipping Point*.

chunks.heading: Marketing lesson: tell a good story
chunks.text:
- Jason read Gladwell's *Blink* cover to cover. He shouted at its "illogical conclusions and meandering, self-inconsistent theories" yet loved every page and did not want it to end.
- He ties this to Seth Godin's argument that marketing should be defined as telling a good story.
- His closing line: "Sometimes everything else is a second-order effect."
- The takeaway is that a compelling story can carry a product or an idea further than its underlying rigor, and audiences may not care that the logic is weak.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jason argues that claims like "unmatched customer service" are meaningless noise ("if it's on the outside, it's not on the inside"). Instead, invite prospects to test your support during the trial and let them draw their own conclusions. This builds trust during the initial demo.

chunks.heading: Say it on the outside only if you can prove it on the inside: let prospects test your support themselves
chunks.text:
Jason cites "Brandon's Rule": "If it's on the outside, it's not on the inside." Examples are the People's Republic of China (not a Republic), Smucker's "100% Simply Fruit" spreads (30% juice), and "Scrubs will be right back after these messages" (no more Scrubs after the final break).

- When something is true, you don't need to announce it, convince people of it, or draw attention to it.
- Claims like "We put customers first," "We treat customers as partners," and "We have unmatched customer support" are the kind of thing that signals the opposite.

chunks.heading: Why great support can't be sold with words
chunks.text:
Jason says support quality is something a customer notices right away: whether the phone gets answered quickly, whether the person on the other end genuinely helps, and whether the account manager keeps providing service after the sale.

- He has heard a C_O say countless times that "What distinguishes us from our competitors is better customer service."
- In theory good service is a competitive advantage, the primary way to build solid relationships, a driver of word-of-mouth advertising ("the best kind"), and can win a sale even after an unfavorable first impression.
- But "you can't convince people you have good support by telling them so. In fact, telling them so might turn them off."

chunks.heading: Demo tactic: invite prospects to trial your tech support
chunks.text:
In demos, Jason tells prospects: "While you're trialing our software, also trial our tech support. Give 'em a call and test it out. Make sure we're responsive and helpful."

- Steps: (1) make the invitation during the demo; (2) point them at the real support line; (3) let them judge responsiveness and helpfulness themselves.
- It works because the claim is verified by the prospect's own experience rather than asserted by the seller.

chunks.heading: Honest, verifiable claims leave a mark
chunks.text:
Jason's line: "When you hit someone over the head with honesty, it leaves a mark."

- People are used to hearing "We have unbeatable customer service" and "Customer service is priority number one," so the words are "water off a duck's back." Even when true, they're meaningless.
- Inviting a trial gets amazing reactions. One prospect told him: "I've never had a vendor actually encourage me to call them for support."
- Jason replied: "Well, I could tell you we have great customer service, but you wouldn't believe me." The prospect answered: "I don't have to call. I already know you guys are going to rock."

chunks.heading: Build the relationship during the initial demo
chunks.text:
Jason asks when you last built that kind of relationship with a potential customer during the initial demo, and answers that it comes "just by being honest."

- Principle: don't say it, do it. Encourage potential customers to notice, and let them come to their own conclusions.
- Applies beyond support to any quality claim (service, quality, responsiveness): demonstrate it rather than announce it.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jason Cohen lists the small, tangible milestones that made Smart Bear feel like a real company, from POs and a first employee to a sign on the building. He adds that the pitch even a receptionist can give matters more than polish, and closes with a 2023 story of seeing the WP Engine sign go up.

chunks.heading: What "real company" milestones Jason uses (and why the sign mattered most)
chunks.text:
Jason (founder of Smart Bear, started 2002) kept asking: "When do you know you're a real company?" He answers with a checklist of milestones, and he treats them as real signals of maturity rather than vanity.

His list of "you're a real company when...":
- You have a domain name that isn't weird.
- Your business cards don't say "VistaPrint" on the back.
- You take purchase orders in addition to credit cards, and you accept that you must ship the product before they pay you.
- You switch from Quicken to QuickBooks.
- You hire the first real, full-time employee.
- You pay someone else to print pay stubs and handle monthly employment taxes because you're tired of doing it yourself.
- You have a sign on the building.
- A real artist does your website and handouts.

chunks.heading: The sign on the building as the milestone that stuck
chunks.text:
Jason bolded one item: "You have a sign on the building." It is the one that "always stuck with me."

- Smart Bear got its sign roughly a year before the 2007 post, and he calls it "a proud moment."
- Years later (the 2023 addendum), he stood in a public park with WP Engine CEO Heather Brunner and a few dozen of the hundreds of WP Engine employees, watching the company sign go up on the building in Austin, Texas.
- He treats a physical, public sign as the moment a company becomes undeniably real, more than any internal operational change.

chunks.heading: Operational maturity signals: payments, payroll, accounting
chunks.text:
Several of his markers are about stopping the scrappy, do-it-yourself way of running the business:
- **Payments:** moving from credit-card-only to taking POs, and being fine with shipping before getting paid (invoicing terms rather than prepayment).
- **Accounting:** upgrading from Quicken to QuickBooks.
- **Payroll:** outsourcing pay stubs and employment tax filings once doing it yourself is just a chore.
- **Hiring:** the first real, full-time employee.
- **Brand polish:** a domain name that isn't weird, business cards that don't say "VistaPrint" on the back, and a professional artist designing the website and handouts.

chunks.heading: Usage numbers as a "real company" feeling
chunks.text:
Jason also tied the feeling to customer scale:
- In 2007, the 8000th user of Smart Bear's software products came online, which "makes me feel like a real company."
- Smart Bear had a book with a glossy cover (his peer code review book) with over 7,000 copies in circulation.
- 2009 update: 45,000 books and 30,000 paying users.
- He joked that the only thing missing was a 256-page hard-backed glossy book chronicling the company's ascent, like one he saw in Adobe's lobby.

chunks.heading: Lesson from the Adobe lobby: the receptionist's pitch
chunks.text:
Visiting Adobe's Ottawa office, Jason saw a 256-page color hardcover book about the company in the lobby.
- He asked everyone he met about it; no one but the receptionist had ever seen it.
- The receptionist knew exactly what their branch did and could explain why people bought their products in about 15 seconds.
- Her elevator pitch was better than the 10-minute diatribe he got from a senior manager later that day.
- Takeaway implied: a clear, short explanation of what the company does and why customers buy matters more than polished corporate artifacts.

chunks.heading: The 2023 story: the sign on the childhood bagel-run building
chunks.text:
Sixteen years later, Jason retired the dated items (paying employees is no longer hard; VistaPrint and Quicken feel like relics) and told a new story.
- As a boy in Austin, "Downtown" felt like a frightening place the family never went (government buildings, law firms, perceived crime).
- The family drove to the edge of Downtown for "real" bagels, because his parents, who grew up in and around New York City, insisted there was only one place for them.
- He remembers a long, sloping ramp leading to a parking garage and waiting in the car, staring at the scary office building across the street.
- Forty years later, that same building is where WP Engine's sign went up. The company's logo was checked against a phone photo to make sure each piece was oriented correctly ("We couldn't remember ourselves!").
- The punchline is the building itself: "You're a real company when..." the sign goes up on a building that has been imprinted on your memory since childhood.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jason Cohen describes using a developer in a panda suit as the Smart Bear tradeshow mascot. The bear drew crowds, created a physical traffic funnel past the booth, and started real conversations because people assumed it was a hired student. A lesson in unconventional, memorable booth tactics, with the bear's calm presence at an awards show getting repeated mentions.

chunks.heading: Booth positioning: a mascot as a traffic funnel, not a gimmick
chunks.text:
Jason Cohen ran Smart Bear Software, which sold peer code review tools and an Eclipse/Subversion integration. His company mascot was a bear, played by developer Roy, and he treated the bear as a real tradeshow tactic at SD West. He explains why it worked, with specific mechanics.

- Tradeshow booths "need something to help them stand out", and a person in a bear suit is one way to do it.
- Everyone notices the bear. Most people drift toward it and are usually smiling. A few go out of their way to avoid getting close or making "eye contact".
- Roy, who writes Eclipse plug-ins, really wanted to be the bear and was good at it. He spent a lot of time in the bear head at the office to learn where the ears, head, eyes and chin were. Jason once saw him fixing an obscure bug in the Subversion/Eclipse integration while wearing the full outfit.

chunks.heading: Physical placement: why the bear in the aisle funnels people to the booth
chunks.text:
Jason calls the bear's position in the aisle in front of the booth "unintentionally brilliant". His chain of reasoning:

1. You have to walk around the bear, because the suit plus personal space creates a significant no-fly zone.
2. There was always a crowd around the bear checking it out and seeing if it could talk, which enlarges that zone.
3. To get past, you must swing all the way to one side of the aisle (where the booth was) or the other.
4. So you end up getting the pitch and seeing the product even if you avoid the bear.
5. The leftover space between bear and booth was so small it created a logjam. Stuck in front of the booth, you might as well watch the movie and take a free book.

The takeaway is that booth layout can force exposure. The attention-getter and the pitch material (a movie, a free book) should be arranged so avoiding one means meeting the other.

chunks.heading: Using the mascot to start real conversations
chunks.text:
- People assume a poor high school student was hired to stand around in the suit. So when the bear engages someone in a discussion of peer code review, they are surprised enough to actually talk about it.
- Cupping the vestigial ears and bending them forward while saying "come again" makes people crane their necks toward the fluffy blobs. Jason notes no one considers that this doesn't actually help a human hear better.
- At least 10 other vendors at the show commented "That guy must have lost a bet", so the bear drew attention from peers as well as prospects.
- The bear also drew unsolicited jokes (Stephen Colbert bear references) and even a proposition: a woman said it would be great to have a bear mow the lawn. Roy said the bear was not for sale. Jason thought he should have heard her out, since "everything can be had for a price, even a mowing bear".

chunks.heading: Awards shows: standing out by staying calm
chunks.text:
- The bear also attended the Jolt Award ceremony and stood out there. The presenter (Craig) mentioned the bear three times during the ceremony.
- Eric's explanation, which Jason relays: it worked because Roy was not jumping around or calling attention to himself. He sat calmly, as if it's normal that a bear would attend the Jolt Award.
- Lesson: a memorable gimmick lands better when played deadpan than when it tries hard for attention.

chunks.heading: Limits of the stunt
chunks.text:
- Jason's P.S.: the bear was not a juggling bear. Roy couldn't see well enough out of the neck area to juggle. He got three balls going by throwing them off his furry belly to reduce error, but it looked weird, so the idea was dropped.
- Jason also notes Roy does juggle flaming clubs outside the suit, which is why a juggling bear seemed plausible.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jason Cohen explains how Code Collaborator was sold bottom-up by genuinely removing pain for developers, long before "product-led growth" had a name. When pitching a CTO top-down, he refuses ROI-chart selling and gives the same honest pitch: this saves developers time and increases happiness.

chunks.heading: Bottom-up selling: solve the pain for the people in the trenches
chunks.text:
- Jason sold Code Collaborator, peer code review software, to Fortune 500 companies from the bottom up, more than a decade before "Product-Led Growth" became a term. It was one-time-license software, not recurring revenue.
- The pitch is that the tool "removes pain." Developers carry the burden of review: gathering files and diffs, packaging and sending them, tracking comments across email and continents, chasing fixes, and timing reviews with stop-watches and line-counters for metrics.
- His sales model: "Genuinely solve a genuine problem for the folks in the trenches, then they beg their bosses to buy the tool to alleviate pain."
- Managers like peer code review because it finds bugs, especially documentation, maintainability and mentoring issues that no automated tool or unit test catches. They also like the reports that "prove" productivity.
- He says removing pain is "really the only reason anyone buys our tool."

chunks.heading: Why a metrics-and-reports-only tool fails
chunks.text:
- If the product only generated metrics and reports, managers would like it but developers would "(rightly!) revolt and circumvent the system."
- Circumvention makes the reports meaningless anyway, so the manager's value depends on the user's value.
- He distrusts top-down mandates ("Hey we just bought a new tool! Time to do code reviews!") because they land on users as an imposition.

chunks.heading: Selling top-down to a CTO without changing the pitch
chunks.text:
- When he did pitch a public company's CTO (not his usual route), he used the same message he gives developers: "This will save your developers time and increase happiness."
- He contrasts this with tools sold only top-down, built on ROI charts promising something like "$142,245 saved in the first 9 months," metrics reports without interpretation, and a $75k entry price.
- He doesn't think an ROI formula is the point: "If you don't believe that proof-reading code will uncover defects, an ROI formula isn't going to convince you otherwise."
- If the buyer already believes review finds defects, the cost of the tool is trivial next to an undiscovered defect, especially one shipped to a customer.

chunks.heading: Principle: tell the same truth to every level of the org
chunks.text:
- "The sales books say otherwise, but I think you have to stick to the truth and stick by your mates in the trenches."
- His test: "If we're not truly making software better and people's lives better, screw it!"
- He argues executives "aren't as insensitive as the sales books would have you believe," so an honest, user-centered pitch can work on the brass too.
- In a 2024 editor's note he observes that this bottom-up approach predated Product-Led Growth, "So, maybe it always was!"

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jason Cohen explains how he skipped registering smartbear.com when it cost almost nothing, a squatter grabbed it, and he ended up paying $2000 after failed offers and a legal letter. The lesson: cheap protective purchases like a domain should be made immediately, because squatters watch business records and excuses don't help.

chunks.heading: Why Jason didn't register smartbear.com at launch
chunks.text:
- Smart Bear began as a sole proprietorship. In Feb 2003 Jason converted it to a single-member LLC, "mostly just to see what it was like" (single-member LLCs and sole proprietorships have identical tax consequences: none).
- Code Historian and Code Reviewer were shareware at the time, and the company name didn't seem to matter. He owned `codehistorian.com` and thought that was better, so he never registered `smartbear.com`.
- He rejects every excuse he could offer: no money (but the domain was cheap), didn't expect things to go well (but it was cheap insurance), didn't think anyone was watching (but domain squatters monitor chamber of commerce records and grab whatever they find). His verdict: "There's no excuse."
- The lesson he draws is to act fast: hesitating on a cheap, obvious purchase cost him $2000.

chunks.heading: How the squatter ended up with the domain
chunks.text:
- By the time Jason came to his senses, a squatter had taken `smartbear.com`. First the page was just broken, then it said the domain was for sale at $2000.
- Jason settled for `smartbearsoftware.com`.
- The cost of the workaround was practical: the name is awkward to say over the phone. He would have to explain "Smart Bear Software. One word. That's 'bear' as in the animal... You have to have the software."

chunks.heading: Negotiating and legal options against the squatter
chunks.text:
- Jason offered the squatter $1000. It was rejected.
- He sent a lawyer letter, which was ignored.
- He asked the lawyer what actually pursuing the squatter would cost: a minimum of $2500. His takeaway: "(Oh. That's how the price is set.)" Squatters price just below the cost of legal action.
- He pointed out the Smart Bear trademark. The squatter replied that it wasn't a registered trademark.
- Jason started registering all the company's trademarks, but years later the process was still in its last stage and not finished.

chunks.heading: What finally made him pay
chunks.text:
- The other Bears pushed him: "Just get the domain. We know it sucks. We know it's unfair. But stop making us type 'software' all the time like chumps."
- The final straw was a conversation with Chris Boyd, co-founder of Midas Networks, who told him, "you just have to pay those guys." Jason says Chris "always tells it straight," and that was when he knew he was sunk.
- On 2007-01-23 he bought `smartbear.com` for the $2000 asking price. He notes this was a matter of principle as much as money ("It's the principle of the thing though").

chunks.heading: Takeaways on domains and early decisions
chunks.text:
- Register the company-name domain on day one, even when the product has its own domain and the company is tiny.
- The cost of registering early is trivial next to the later cost: the $2000 purchase price, plus the extra friction of a longer domain and the time spent negotiating.
- Don't count on trademarks or lawyers to recover a squatted domain: an unregistered trademark gives little leverage, and legal action costs more than the squatter's asking price.
- When a squatter holds a name you need and legal options cost more than the price, paying the asking price can be the rational choice.

44 years ago, Michael Porter told us (in 𝘊𝘰𝘮𝘱𝘦𝘵𝘪𝘵𝘪𝘷𝘦 𝘚𝘵𝘳𝘢𝘵𝘦𝘨𝘺) there are only three main strategies:

1. Differentiated-best
2. Lowest cost
3. Niche

Many strategic thinkers since have suggested that only the first two exist, and the third is a question of market scope/segmentation, or that “niche” is an enabling constraint to be “differentiated,” ie by restricting “for whom.”

Perhaps even “lowest cost” could be seen as “best, along the dimension of price.”

Which brings us to the crux of strategy: in what way are you differentiated-and-best, for whom?

Because of course just being different for the sake of difference, doesn’t result in sales and love. It has to be “best” too.

I’m not sure I like this as a final definition. For example, “best” doesn’t quite capture the products that people truly love, that build a community around, that associate that brand with themselves.

I still like my “love, utility, coercion” framework rather than “best.”

Still, “different, generating love and utility mostly, for a well-defined segment,” while a few extra words, feels great as our strategic goal, aka our “vision.”

Then the actual strategy is the set of self-consistent (at least), self-reinforcing (at best) decisions about what we are and ARE NOT going to do, to achieve that goal.
